Surah An-Nisa (The Women)
One hundred and seventy-six verses, Medinan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾.

Know that this surah contains many kinds of obligations (al-taklif al-shar'i). God, may He be exalted, commanded people at the beginning of this surah to show compassion toward children, women and orphans, to be merciful to them, to deliver their rights to them, and to safeguard their property for them. With this meaning the surah concludes, namely His saying: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalala﴾ [An-Nisa: 176]. In the course of this surah He also mentions other kinds of obligations, namely the command to purity, the prayer, and fighting the polytheists. Since these obligations are burdensome to the souls because of their weight on natural dispositions, He therefore opened the surah with the cause for which these burdensome obligations must be borne, namely fear of the Lord who created us and the God who brought us into existence. Hence He said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you﴾. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Al-Wahidi transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿O mankind﴾, that this address was to the people of Mecca. But the usulis (scholars of legal theory, usul al-fiqh) among the exegetes have agreed that the address is general to all those who are legally responsible (mukallafun), and this is the more correct view, for several reasons:

The first: the word "people" (al-nas) is a plural to which the definite article has been prefixed, so it conveys comprehensiveness (al-istighraq).

The second: He made the command to fear God dependent upon the cause that He is the Creator of them from a single soul. This cause is general with respect to all those who are legally responsible, in that they were all created from Adam, peace be upon him. When the cause is general, the ruling is general.

The third: The obligation of piety is not restricted to the people of Mecca; rather it is general for all the worlds. When the word "people" is general to all, and the command to piety is general to all, and the cause of this obligation, which is that they were created from a single soul, is general with respect to all, then to say it is restricted is extremely far-fetched. Ibn Abbas's argument is His saying: ﴿Fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ [An-Nisa: 1]. This is specific to the Arabs, because appealing by God and by kinship is a custom peculiar to them. They say: "I ask you by God and by kinship," and "I implore you by God and by kinship." Since this is so, His saying ﴿Fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ is restricted to the Arabs, so the beginning of the verse, which is His saying ﴿O mankind﴾, would be restricted to them too, because His saying at the beginning of the verse ﴿fear your Lord﴾ and His saying after that ﴿fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ are both directed to one addressee. It may be answered that it has been established in usul al-fiqh that the specificity of the end of a verse does not prevent the generality of its beginning. So His saying ﴿O mankind﴾ is general to all, and His saying ﴿Fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ is specific to the Arabs.

The second issue: He, may He be exalted, made this opening the opening of two surahs in the Qur'an. The first is this surah, which is the fourth surah of the first half of the Qur'an. The second is Surah al-Hajj, which is also the fourth surah of the second half of the Qur'an. Then, in this surah, He gave the cause for the command to piety by something that indicates knowledge of the origin (al-mabda'), namely that He created the creation from a single soul. This indicates the perfection of the Creator's power, the perfection of His knowledge, the perfection of His wisdom and His majesty. In Surah al-Hajj He gave the cause for the command to piety by something that indicates perfect knowledge of the return (al-ma'ad), namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, the quaking of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [Al-Hajj: 1]. Thus He made the beginning of these two surahs an indication of knowledge of the origin and knowledge of the return. Then He placed the surah that indicates the origin before the surah that indicates the return. Under this inquiry there are many secrets.

* * *

The third issue: Know that He, may He be exalted, commanded us to piety and mentioned right after it that He created us from a single soul. This suggests that the command to piety is grounded in His having created us from a single soul, and it is necessary to explain the connection between this ruling and that attribute. We say: our statement "He created us from a single soul" includes two qualifiers. One is that He created us. The second is the manner of that creation, namely that He created us only from a single soul. Each of these two qualifiers has an effect on the obligation of piety.

As for the first qualifier, namely that He created us, there is no doubt that this meaning is a cause for our obligation to submit to the obligations of God, may He be exalted, and to submit to His commands and prohibitions. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: since He is the Creator of us and the one who brought our essences and attributes into being, we are His servants and He is our master (mawla). Lordship (al-rububiyya) requires that His commands be carried out over His servants, and servanthood (al-ubudiyya) requires submission to the Lord, the Originator and the Creator.

The second: bringing into existence is the ultimate of bounty and the final point of benevolence. For you were non-existent and He brought you into being; dead and He gave you life; powerless and He empowered you; ignorant and He taught you. As Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Who created me, and He guides me﴾ ﴿and who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 78-79]. Since all blessings are entirely from God, may He be glorified, it is obligatory upon the servant to repay those blessings by showing submission and obedience, and by abandoning rebellion and obstinacy. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿How do you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life again﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 28].

The third: since it has been established that He is the Originator, the Creator, the God and the Lord of us, it is obligatory upon us to occupy ourselves with His servanthood, and to guard against everything He forbade and warned against. It is also necessary that none of these acts should bring about any reward at all. For since these acts of obedience became obligatory in return for the earlier blessings, it is impossible that they should become a cause for reward, because the discharge of a right to the one who deserves it does not entail anything else. This holds if we grant that the servant performed those acts of obedience on his own initiative from the outset. How much more so, when this is impossible: for performing acts of obedience occurs only if God creates the capacity for obedience and creates the motive for obedience. And when the capacity and the motive are present, their combination necessitates the servant's performance of the obedience. Since this is so, that obedience is a bounty from God upon His servant, and a master who grants his servant a favor does not make that favor a cause for another favor owed by the servant. This, then, is the indication that His being our Creator obligates us to His servanthood and to avoiding His prohibitions.

As for the second qualifier, namely that the specific fact that He created us from a single soul obligates us to obedience and to avoiding disobedience, its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: the creation of all human individuals from a single human being is a stronger proof of the perfection of power, in that if the matter were by nature and inherent property, what was produced from a single human would have been nothing but things similar in attribute and alike in form and nature. But since we see among human individuals the white, the black, the red, the brown, the handsome and the ugly, the tall and the short, this indicates that their Administrator and Creator is a free chooser, not a natural force that acts by itself, nor a necessitating cause. Since this subtle point indicates that the Administrator of the world is a free chooser, powerful over all possibilities, knowing all knowables, then the obligation to submit to His commands, orders and prohibitions follows. Thus the connection of His saying ﴿fear your Lord﴾ with His saying ﴿who created you from a single soul﴾ is most fitting and coherent.

The second aspect: when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the command to piety, He mentioned right after it the command to goodness toward orphans, women and the weak. That all creation is created from a single soul has an effect on this meaning. This is because close relatives must have some kind of connection and intimacy that produces greater love. For this reason a person rejoices in the praise of his relatives and ancestors, and grieves at their blame and their being disparaged. The Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: "Fatimah is a part of me; whatever hurts her hurts me." Since the matter is so, the benefit in mentioning this meaning is that it becomes a cause for increasing the compassion of creatures toward one another.

The third aspect: when people know that all are from a single person, they abandon boasting and arrogance, and show humility and good character.

The fourth aspect: this indicates the return, for since He, may He be exalted, is able to bring forth from the loins of a single person individuals who differ, and to create from a drop of semen a person of wondrous composition and delicate form, how then could the revival of the dead, their resurrection and their gathering be deemed unlikely? Thus the verse indicates the return from this aspect: ﴿so that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did, and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [An-Najm: 31].

The fifth aspect: al-Asamm said: the benefit in it is that reason has no proof that creatures must be created from a single soul; rather, that is known only through revealed evidence (al-dala'il al-sam'iyya). The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was unlettered; he did not read a book nor study under a teacher. So when he reported this meaning, it was a report of the unseen, and therefore a miracle. The summary is that His saying ﴿created you﴾ is a proof for knowledge of divine unity (al-tawhid), and His saying ﴿from a single soul﴾ is a proof for knowledge of prophethood.

If it is said: how can it be correct that all of mankind be created from a single soul, given their multitude and the smallness of that soul?

We say: God has explained the intended meaning, for when Adam's spouse was created from part of him, and then the creation of their offspring came about from their drop, and so on forever, it became permissible to attribute the creation of all of them to Adam.

The fourth issue: The Muslims are unanimous that the intended meaning of "single soul" here is Adam, peace be upon him, except that the attribute was made feminine according to the wording of "soul" (nafs). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you slain a pure soul, not in retribution for another soul?﴾ [Al-Kahf: 74]. And a poet said:

Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore; so you too are a caliph, that is perfection.

They said: this feminine form follows the wording of "caliph" (khalifa).

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and created from it its spouse﴾ contains issues:

The first issue: The intended meaning of this "spouse" is Eve. Regarding whether Eve was created from Adam there are two opinions. The first, which is held by most, is that when God created Adam, He cast sleep upon him, then created Eve from one of his left ribs. When he awoke he saw her, inclined toward her and became attached to her, because she was created from a part of his parts. They argued for this with the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Indeed, woman was created from a crooked rib. If you try to straighten her you will break her, and if you leave her, there will remain crookedness in her; so enjoy her with that crookedness."

The second opinion, which is the choice of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, is that what is meant by His saying ﴿and created from it its spouse﴾ is: from its kind (min jinsiha). This is like His saying: ﴿And God made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾ [An-Nahl: 72], and like His saying: ﴿when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164], and His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves﴾ [At-Tawbah: 128]. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the first opinion is stronger, so that His saying ﴿created you from a single soul﴾ is correct; for if Eve had been created from the beginning, mankind would have been created from two souls, not from a single soul.

It may be answered that the particle "min" (from) indicates the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghaya). Since the beginning of creation and origination occurred with Adam, peace be upon him, it is correct to say: "He created you from a single soul." Also, since it has been established that He, may He be exalted, is able to create Adam from dust, He is also able to create Eve from dust. Since this is so, what is the benefit in creating her from a rib of Adam?

**Second issue:** Ibn ʿAbbas said: Adam was named so because God created him from the surface (adim) of the whole earth, its red and its black, its good and its bad. Therefore his offspring include the red and the black, the good and the bad. As for the woman, she was named Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) because she was created from a rib of Adam's ribs, so she was created from a living thing, and for this reason she was named Ḥawwāʾ.

**Third issue:** A group of the naturalists (al-Ṭabāʾiʿiyyūn) used this verse as evidence. They said: God's words ﴿Who created you from a single soul﴾ indicate that all of mankind was created from the single soul. His words ﴿and from it He created its mate﴾ indicate that its mate was created from it. Then He said, describing Adam: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:59), which indicates that Adam was created from dust. Then He said concerning all creatures: ﴿From it We created you﴾ (Ṭā-Hā 20:55). All these verses indicate that what comes into being only comes into being from a prior material, and that the creation of a thing out of pure non-existence and absolute nothingness is impossible.

The theologians (al-Mutakallimūn) answered: The creation of a thing from a thing is impossible according to reason. For if this created thing is the very same thing that existed before, then it was not created at all. And if it was not created, it is impossible for it to be created from something else. And if we say that this created thing is different from what existed before, then this created thing, this newly originated thing, came into being and existed out of pure non-existence. Thus it is established that for a thing to be created from something other than itself is impossible according to reason. As for the particle "min" (from) in this verse, it indicates the beginning of the end point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), in the sense that the beginning of the coming into being of these things is from those things, not in the sense of need or dependence, but merely in the sense of occurrence.

**Fourth issue:** The author of al-Kashshāf said: It was read as ﴿wa-khāliqun minhā zawjahā wa-bāththun minhumā﴾ with the active participle form, as the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied meaning is "He is the Creator."

* * *

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And from the two of them He spread forth many men and women﴾.

On this there are issues:

**First issue:** Al-Wāḥidī said: "Baththa minhumā" means He dispersed and scattered. Ibn al-Muẓaffar said: al-baththu is your scattering of things. It is said: he dispersed the horses in the raid (baththa al-khayla fī al-ghāra), and the hunter dispersed his dogs. God created the creation and dispersed them upon the earth. And I spread out the rugs (baththtu al-busuṭ) when I unfolded them. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and scattered carpets﴾ (al-Ghāshiyah 88:16). Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: Some of the Arabs say abathha Allāhu al-khalq (God scattered the creation).

**Second issue:** He did not say "and He spread forth men and women from them," because that would necessitate that they were spread forth from themselves, and that is impossible. Therefore He turned away from this wording to His words: ﴿And from the two of them He spread forth many men and women﴾.

If it is asked: Why did He not say "many men and many women"? And why did He specify the attribute of multitude for men and not for women?

We say: The reason, and God knows best, is that the fame of men is more complete, so their multitude is more apparent. Therefore they were singled out for the attribute of multitude. This is like an indication that what is fitting for men is prominence, going out and appearing, while what is fitting for women is concealment and obscurity.

**Third issue:** Those who say that all human individuals were like atoms (al-dharr) and were gathered in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, take His words ﴿And from the two of them He spread forth many men and women﴾ literally. Those who deny this say: The intended meaning is that He spread forth from the two of them their offspring, and from their offspring other groups, so the whole is attributed to them both by way of majāz (metaphorical usage).

* * *

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed God is ever Watchful over you﴾.

On this there are issues.

**First issue:** ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿tasāʾalūna﴾ with light stress (takhfīf), and the rest read it with heavy stress (tashdīd). Whoever read it with heavy stress intended "tatasāʾalūna" and assimilated the tāʾ into the sīn, because they share being among the tongue letters and the roots of the front teeth, and because they share being voiceless (al-hams). Whoever read it lightly deleted the tāʾ of "tatafāʿalūna" because of the convergence of similar letters, so he treated it with deletion just as the first treated it with assimilation. This is because when similar letters converge they are lightened sometimes by deletion and sometimes by assimilation.

**Second issue:** Ḥamzah alone read ﴿wal-arḥāmi﴾ with the mīm in the genitive (jarr). Al-Qaffāl, may God have mercy on him, said: This reading has also been transmitted from outside the Seven, from Mujāhid and others. As for the rest of the readers, all of them read the mīm in the accusative (naṣb). The author of al-Kashshāf said: It was read ﴿wal-arḥāma﴾ in all three vowel forms. As for Ḥamzah's reading, most of the grammarians held that it is faulty. They said: This entails coordinating a noun with an attached pronoun in the genitive, and that is not permissible. They argued for its impermissibility with several points:

The first: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The attached pronoun in the genitive has the status of a particle, so it is not permissible to coordinate an explicit noun with it. We say that the attached pronoun in the genitive has the status of a particle for several reasons:

The first: It is never separated at all, just as tanwīn (nunation) is never separated. The hāʾ and kāf in His words "bihi" and "bika" are never found separated from the preposition, so it is like tanwīn.

The second: In the preferred usage, they delete the yāʾ from the vocative construct (al-munādā al-muḍāf), just as they delete tanwīn from the singular noun, as in their saying "yā ghulāmi" (O boy). So the attached pronoun in the genitive resembles tanwīn in this respect. It is established, then, that the attached pronoun in the genitive has the status of the particle of tanwīn, so it is not permissible to coordinate an explicit noun with it. For a condition of coordination is that there be resemblance between the coordinated and that which it is coordinated with, and where that resemblance is absent here, coordination is not permissible.

The second: ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā said: They did not find it good to coordinate an explicit noun with a pronoun in the nominative. So one may not say "idhhab wa-Zayd" (go, and Zayd) or "dhahabtu wa-Zayd" (I went, and Zayd). Rather they say "idhhab anta wa-Zayd" (go you and Zayd) and "dhahabtu anā wa-Zayd" (I went, I and Zayd). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ (al-Māʾidah 5:24). Although the attached pronoun in the nominative may be separated, and so it is stronger than the attached pronoun in the genitive, it is still impermissible to coordinate an explicit noun with it. Therefore, with the attached pronoun in the genitive, which absolutely cannot be separated, it is more fitting that coordination be impermissible.

The third: Abū ʿUthmān al-Māzinī said: The coordinated and that which it is coordinated with share a relation. The first may be coordinated with the second only if the second may be coordinated with the first, and this meaning is not present here. For you do not say "marartu bi-Zayd wa-bika" (I passed by Zayd and you), so likewise you do not say "marartu bika wa-Zayd" (I passed by you and Zayd).

Know that these arguments are not strong in dismissing the reports transmitted about the dialects. For Ḥamzah is one of the Seven readers, and it is evident that he did not come up with this reading on his own, but transmitted it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). That necessitates certainty about the soundness of this dialect, and analogy diminishes in the face of transmission, especially with analogies of this kind, which are weaker than a spider's web. Furthermore, this reading has two explanations:

One: It is on the basis of repeating the preposition, as if it were said: "tasāʾalūna bihi wa-bil-arḥām" (you ask one another by Him and by the wombs).

Two: This occurs in poetry. Sībawayh cited on this:

*Today you have indeed begun to satirize us and to insult us,*
*so go away, for what is with you and with the days is strange.*

And he also cited:

*We hang our swords on pillars like these,*
*and between them and the heel is a stretch of the nafānif valley.*

It is strange that these grammarians find it good to establish this dialect by these two anonymous verses, yet do not find it good to establish it by the reading of Ḥamzah and Mujāhid, even though both were among the great scholars of the early generations in the science of the Qurʾān. Al-Zajjāj argued against the soundness of this reading on the level of meaning, with the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not swear by your fathers." For if you coordinate "al-arḥām" with the pronoun referring to the Name of God, this would imply permission to swear by the wombs. This can be answered: this is a report of an action they used to perform in the pre-Islamic period, since they used to say: "I ask you by God and by the womb (al-raḥim)." Reporting this action of theirs in the past does not contradict the prohibition of it in the future. Also, the hadith prohibits swearing only by fathers, whereas here it is not so, but rather it is an oath by God first, followed by mention of the womb linked to it. This does not contradict the meaning of that hadith. This is the sum of the discussion concerning the reading ﴿wal-arḥāmi﴾ in the genitive.

As for its reading in the accusative, there are two explanations:

The first, which is the choice of Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā: It is a coordination with the place (maḥall) of the preposition and its object, as in the verse:

*So we are not with the mountains, nor with the iron.*

The second, which is the view of most of the commentators: The implied meaning is "And fear the wombs, lest you sever them." This is the view of Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd, al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. On this explanation, the accusative of "al-arḥām" is by coordination with His words ﴿God﴾, meaning: fear God, and fear the wombs, i.e., fear the due rights of the wombs, so maintain them and do not sever them. Al-Wāḥidī, may God have mercy on him, said: It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by way of incitement (al-ighrāʾ), meaning: "and the wombs, guard them and maintain them," like your saying "the lion, the lion!" This interpretation indicates the prohibition of severing kinship and indicates the obligation of maintaining it.

As for the reading in the nominative, the author of al-Kashshāf said: It is nominative as a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is omitted, as if it were said: "And the wombs are likewise," meaning: "and the wombs are among what is to be feared," or "and the wombs are among what one asks by."

* * *

**Third issue:** He, exalted is He, first said: ﴿Fear your Lord﴾, then after it said: ﴿And fear God﴾. In this repetition there are several explanations:

The first: It is the emphasis of the command and urging toward it, like your saying to a man: "Hurry, hurry!", which is more emphatic than your saying "Hurry!"

The second: The first is a command to fear God because of the blessing of creation and other favors, and the second is a command to fear God because of the occurrence of mutual asking (tasāʾul) concerning what one party seeks from another.

The third: He first said ﴿Fear your Lord﴾, and secondly said ﴿And fear God﴾. The word "Rabb" (Lord) indicates nurture and benevolence, while "Ilāh" (God) indicates dominance and awe. So He commanded them to fear Him on the basis of encouragement, then repeated the command to fear Him on the basis of warning, as He said: ﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and in hope﴾ (al-Sajdah 32:16), and He said: ﴿And they call upon Us in hope and in fear﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:90). It is as if it were said: He has nurtured you and been good to you, so fear opposing Him, for He is severe in punishment and mighty in power.

**Fourth issue:** Know that asking by God and by the wombs is said to be like saying: "By God I ask you," "By God I intercede with you," "By God I swear to you," and other such expressions by which a person emphasizes his request from another, and seeks the other's compassion in seeking his right from him, or his bounty, his help, or his support. As for Ḥamzah's reading, its meaning is evident: "And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs," because it has become customary among the Arabs that one of them may seek another's compassion by the womb, saying: "I ask you by God and the womb." Sometimes he mentions only the womb, saying: "I ask you by the womb." The polytheists used to write to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We beseech you by God and the womb not to send to us so-and-so and so-and-so." As for the reading in the accusative, its meaning returns to this, and the implied meaning is: "Fear God, and fear the wombs." Al-Qāḍī said: This is one of the things that indicate that a single word may be intended to convey different meanings, because the meaning of fearing God differs from the meaning of fearing the wombs. Fearing God is by committing oneself to obeying Him and avoiding His disobedience, while fearing the wombs is by maintaining them and not severing them, in matters pertaining to righteousness, bounty, and kindness. It may be answered that He, exalted is He, perhaps spoke this word twice, and on this assumption the difficulty disappears.

Fifth issue: Some have said that the word "rahim" (womb/kinship) is derived from "rahmah" (mercy), which is blessing (ni'mah). They cited what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Allah the Exalted says: I am the Merciful (al-Rahman), and this is the womb (al-rahim); I derived its name from My name." The point of comparison is that by virtue of this state, mercy occurs from some people toward others. Others said: rather, the word "rahim" is derived from the womb (rahim) in which bestowal takes place, and that is the original. Some said: rather, each of the two is an original in itself, and dispute over such matters is minor.

Sixth issue: The verse indicates the permissibility of asking by Allah, the Exalted. Mujahid reported from Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever asks you by Allah, give to him." And from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us with seven things, among them: fulfilling the oath (ibrar al-qasam)."

Seventh issue: The words of the Exalted, ﴿and the wombs﴾, indicate the magnification of the right of kinship and the emphasis of the prohibition against severing it. The Exalted said: ﴿Would you, if you turned away, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad: 22], and He said: ﴿They observe neither kinship nor covenant regarding a believer﴾ [al-Tawbah: 10]. It was said regarding the first that it refers to blood relationship. He said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to parents﴾ [al-Isra: 23], and He said: ﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy﴾ [al-Nisa: 36]. And from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah the Exalted says: I am the Merciful, and this is the womb; I derived its name from My name. Whoever maintains it, I maintain him, and whoever severs it, I sever him." And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is nothing in which Allah is obeyed that brings a quicker reward than maintaining kinship, and there is no deed through which Allah is disobeyed that brings a quicker punishment than rebellion (al-baghy) and a false oath (al-yamin al-fajirah)." And from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Charity and maintaining kinship: through them Allah increases one's lifespan, averts an evil death, and through them Allah averts what is feared and what is disliked." He, peace be upon him, also said: "The best charity is that given to a relative who is hostile (al-kashih dhu al-rahim)." It was said: al-kashih is the enemy. Thus, by the indication of the Book and the Sunnah, the obligation of maintaining kinship and the deserving of reward through it is established. Then the followers of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, built two issues upon this principle:

The first: that if a man owns a relative within the prohibited degrees (dhu rahim mahram), he is freed by him, such as a brother, sister, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle. He said: Because if ownership remained, the use of him as a servant would be permissible by consensus, but such use is a source of estrangement which causes the severing of kinship, and that is prohibited according to this principle; therefore ownership must not remain.

The second: that the gift to a relative within the prohibited degrees may not be revoked, because such revocation is an estrangement which causes the severing of kinship, so it must not be permitted. The discussion of these two issues is mentioned in the works of disputed matters (al-khilafiyyat).

Then, the Exalted concluded this verse with what serves as promise, warning, encouragement and admonition, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you﴾ [al-Nisa: 1]. The Raqib (watchful) is the observer who guards over all your actions. One whose description is such must be feared and hoped in. Thus He made clear that He knows the secret and what is more hidden, and that when this is so, a person must be cautious and fearful regarding what he does and what he abandons.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verse 2:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.﴾

Know that when He opened the surah with what indicates that the servant must submit to the obligations of God, may He be glorified, and guard against what displeases Him, He then began to explain the categories of obligations.

The first category concerns the property of orphans, and this is the verse. Also, in the previous verse He enjoined kinship ties, and so in this verse He enjoined care for orphans, because they have come to a state where they have no guardian and no one who is deeply compassionate toward them. Their condition differs from that of one who has a близ kinship tie that is affectionate toward him because of birth or kinship. So He said: ﴿And give the orphans their property.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse:

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The orphans (*yatama*) are those whose fathers have died and who have been left alone without them. *Al-yutm* means solitude, and from it comes *al-ramla al-yatima* (the lone sand dune) and *al-durra al-yatima* (the unique pearl). It has been said that orphanhood among humans is from the father's side, and among animals from the mother's side. He said: The proper meaning of this term is that it should apply to both the young and the old, since the solitude from parents remains. However, by customary usage this term has come to be restricted to one who has not reached the level of men. When he becomes such that he is self-sufficient in securing his own interests, without a guardian who looks after him and a trustee who manages his affairs, the term ceases to apply to him. The Quraysh used to say to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "The orphan of Abu Talib," either by analogy or by describing the condition he was in when he was a young child raised in the care of his uncle, as a way of belittling him. As for his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "There is no orphanhood after puberty," this is a teaching of the Law, not a teaching of the language; meaning, once he has reached puberty (*ihtilam*), the rules of children no longer apply to him. Abu Bakr al-Razi narrated in *Ahkam al-Qur'an* that his grandfather wrote to Ibn Abbas asking him about the orphan: when does his orphanhood end? Ibn Abbas wrote back: When maturity of judgment (*rushd*) is perceived in him, his orphanhood ends. In some narrations: "A man may be grasping his beard and his orphanhood has still not ended." Thus Ibn Abbas informed that the name "orphan" may still apply after puberty if maturity of judgment is not perceived in him. Then Abu Bakr said: The name "orphan" may also be applied to a woman who is separated from her husband. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The orphan woman is to be consulted," and she is not consulted except when she is of age. A poet said:

*"Indeed, the graves marry the widowed women and the orphaned widows."*

The conclusion from all that we have mentioned is that the name "orphan," according to the original meaning of the language, includes both the young and the old, but according to customary usage it is restricted to the young.

**The second issue:** Here there is a question: How did he make the plural of *yatim* into *yatama*? *Yatim* is on the pattern *fa'il*, and the pattern *fa'il* is pluralized as *fa'la*, like *marid* / *mardha*, *qatil* / *qatla*, and *jarih* / *jarha*.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: There are two explanations:

The first: It is said that the plural of *yatim* is *yatma*, and then the pattern *fa'la* is pluralized as *fa'ali*, like *asir* / *asra* / *usara*.

The second: It is said that the plural of *yatim* is *yata'im*, because *yatim* functions as a noun, like *sahib* and *faris*, and then *yata'im* is changed to *yatama*. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: It is permissible to say *yatim* / *yatama*, like *nadim* / *nadama*, and it is also permissible to say *yatim* / *aytam*, like *sharif* / *ashraf*.

**The third issue:** Here is a second question: We have mentioned that the name "orphan" is restricted to the young. So as long as he is an orphan, it is not permissible to hand over his property to him. And when he becomes an adult such that it is permissible to hand over his property to him, he no longer remains an orphan. So how did He say: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾?

The answer to this is in two ways:

The first: We say that what is meant by "orphans" are those who have reached maturity and grown up. Then there are two explanations here:

One: He called them "orphans" according to the original meaning of the language.

Two: He called them "orphans" because their time of orphanhood is recent, even though it has now ended, as in His saying: ﴿Then the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ (al-Shu'ara: 46), meaning those who had been magicians before prostrating. Also, God called approaching the end of the waiting period "reaching the term," in His saying: ﴿So when they have reached their term, retain them﴾ (al-Talaq: 2), meaning approaching the term. And what indicates that what is meant by "orphans" in this verse is those who have reached maturity is His saying: ﴿And when you hand over their property to them, have witnesses over them﴾ (al-Nisa: 6). Taking witnesses is not valid before puberty, but is valid only after puberty.

The second way: We say that what is meant by "orphans" is the young, and according to this way there are two explanations in the verse:

One: His saying "give" (*wa'tu*) is an imperative, and an imperative only applies to the future. So the meaning is: those who are now orphans, give them their property after the attribute of orphanhood has ceased from them. According to this explanation, the contradiction is removed.

Two: The meaning is: give the orphans, while they are still orphans, what they need for their maintenance and clothing. The benefit of this is that one might think it is not permissible to spend their property on them while they are young, so God permitted that. There is a difficulty in this: if this were what was meant, He would have said: "Give them from their property," but since He made the giving of all their property obligatory, that interpretation falls away.

**The fourth issue:** Abu Bakr al-Razi narrated in *Ahkam al-Qur'an* from al-Hasan that he said: When this verse was revealed concerning the property of orphans, they disliked mixing with them and separated the orphans' property from their own. They complained of this to the Prophet ﷺ, and God revealed: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 220). Abu Bakr al-Razi said: I think this is a mistake by the narrator, because what is meant by this verse is giving them their property after puberty. The narrator confused it with another verse. This is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, who said: "When God revealed: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ (al-An'am: 152) and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ (al-Nisa: 10), those who had orphans in their care went and separated their food from his food and their drink from his drink. This was hard on the orphans, so they mentioned it to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and God revealed: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Reforming them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 220). So at that point they mixed their food with theirs and their drink with theirs."

The commentators said: The correct view is that it was revealed concerning a man from Ghatafan who had much wealth belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the boy reached maturity, he asked for his property, but his uncle refused him. They both came to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. When the uncle heard it, he said: "We obey God and we obey the Messenger. We seek refuge in God from the great sin," and he handed his property over to him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul and obeys his Lord in this way, He will make his abode..." meaning, his Paradise. When the boy took his property, he spent it in the way of God. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The reward is secured and the burden remains." They said: "O Messenger of God, we understand that the reward is secured, but how does the burden remain when he is spending it in the way of God?" He said: "The reward of the boy is secured, and the burden remains upon his father."

**The fifth issue:** Abu Bakr al-Razi used this verse as evidence that the foolish person (*safih*) is not placed under restriction (*hajr*) after the age of twenty-five. He said: Because His saying ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ is unrestricted and includes the foolish person, whether maturity of judgment has been perceived in him or not. The action according to it was abandoned before the age of twenty-five by the scholars' consensus that perceiving maturity of judgment before reaching this age is a condition for the obligation to hand over property to him. This consensus does not exist after this age, so it is obligatory to apply the command after this age according to the apparent ruling of this verse.

Our companions answered him: This verse is general, because He mentioned the orphans in it collectively. Then they were distinguished afterward by His saying: ﴿And test the orphans﴾ (al-Nisa: 6), and by His saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ (al-Nisa: 5). By these two verses He prohibited giving them their property when they are foolish. And there is no doubt that the specific takes precedence over the general.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good.﴾ There are several issues concerning this:

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Do not substitute" means "do not take in exchange" (*la tastabdilu*). The *tafa'ul* form used with the meaning of *istif'al* is not rare, as in *ta'ajjal* meaning *isti'jal* (hastening), and *ta'akhkhur* meaning *isti'khar* (delaying). Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: It is said: "He substituted one thing for another" when he took it in its place.

**The second issue:** There are several interpretations of this substitution:

**The first interpretation:** Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: Do not take the forbidden, which is the property of orphans, in exchange for the lawful, which is your own property that has been permitted to you from earnings and from God's provision spread throughout the earth, so that you consume it in its place.

**The second:** Do not take the bad matter, which is the misappropriation of orphans' property, in exchange for the good matter, which is preserving it and abstaining from it. This is the view of most scholars: that the guardian of the orphan would take the good from his property and put in its place the inferior, substituting counterfeit for genuine and emaciated for fat.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* criticized this interpretation, saying: This is not substitution (*tabaddul*) but exchange (*tabdil*), unless he were to honor a friend of his and take from him a lean animal in place of a fat one from the orphan's property.

**The fourth:** This substitution means that they consume the orphan's property as a loan with an obligation to replace it afterward, and in this case they would be substituting the bad for the good.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property.﴾ There are two interpretations here:

**The first:** It means: Do not add their property to your property in spending, until you separate your property from theirs in the matter of benefiting from them.

**The second:** "To" (*ila*) has the meaning of "with" (*ma'a*), as He said: ﴿Who are my helpers in the cause of God?﴾ (Al 'Imran: 52), meaning "with God." The first is more correct.

Know that although He mentioned eating, what is meant by it is disposal (*tasarruf*). This is because just as eating the property of an orphan is forbidden, so too are all other dispositions that destroy those properties forbidden. The evidence for this is that there is property that cannot be eaten, so it is established that what is meant is disposal. He mentioned eating only because it is the most common purpose for which disposal occurs.

If it is said: Since He forbade them from consuming the property of orphans unjustly in the first verse, that prohibition included eating it alone and eating it together with other things. So what is the benefit of repeating the prohibition against eating it together with their own property?

We say: Because when they are independent of the orphans' property through what God has provided them of lawful means, yet they still covet the orphans' property, the ugliness is greater and the blame more deserved.

* * *

[Page 139]

Know that after this He informed creation that consuming an orphan's property through any forbidden means is a great sin. So He said: ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin (*huban kabiran*).﴾ Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The pronoun refers to the eating, because His saying ﴿And do not consume﴾ indicates eating. And *al-huwb* means a great sin. The Prophet ﷺ, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, the divorce of Umm Ayyub is a sin (*lahuwb*)." Similarly, *al-hawb*, *al-hab*, and *al-hub* are three dialectal forms in the noun and the verbal noun. Al-Farra' said: *Al-hawb* is used by the people of the Hijaz, and *al-hab* by Tamim, and it means sin. The Prophet ﷺ, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "My Lord, accept my repentance and wash away my sin (*hawbati*)." The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *Al-hawb* and *al-hab* are like *al-qawl* and *al-qal* (speech). Al-Qaffal said: It seems the origin of the word is from *al-tahawwub*, which means feeling pain, so *al-huwb* is committing that from which the one who commits it feels pain. The Basran grammarians said: *Al-hawb* with a fatha on the *ha'* is a verbal noun, *al-huwb* with a damma is the noun, and *al-hawba* is a single occurrence, and then parts of it enter into one another, just as *al-kalam* is a noun, then one says "I have spoken to him a speech (*kalaman*)," and it becomes a verbal noun. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: al-Hasan recited *hawban*, and it has been read as *haban*.

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾.

Know that this is from the second type of rulings that he mentions in this surah, which is the ruling on marriages. There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: *al-ikhsat* (إقساط) means *al-adl* (justice). It is said: *aqsata al-rajul* (أقسط الرجل) when he acted justly. God the Exalted said: ﴿And act justly; indeed, God loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. *Al-qist* means justice and fairness. God the Exalted said: ﴿Be steadfast in upholding justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. Al-Zajjaj said: The root of *qasata* and *aqsata* is the same, from *al-qist*, which means a share. When they say *qasata* meaning "he oppressed," they mean that he wronged his companion in his share that belonged to him. Do you not see that they say *qasatahu* when you overcome him in his share? So *qasata* was formed on the pattern of *zalama* (he wronged), *jara* (he transgressed) and *ghalaba* (he overcame). When they say *aqsata*, the meaning is that he became one who possesses a just share, so it was formed on the pattern of *ansafa*, when one brings fairness and justice in his speech, his action and his distribution.

**The second issue:** Know that His saying ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾ is the condition (*shart*), and His saying ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3] is the consequent (*jaza'*). It is necessary to explain how this consequent is connected to this condition. The exegetes have several views on this:

The first: It was narrated from Urwah that he said: "I said to Aisha: What is the meaning of God's saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾? She said: O son of my sister, it refers to the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, and he desires her wealth and her beauty, but he wants to marry her for less than her dowry. Then, when he marries her, he treats her badly, knowing that she has no one to defend her or to repel the evil of that husband from her. So God the Exalted said: ﴿And if you fear that you will wrong the orphans when marrying them, then marry from other than them what seems good to you of women.﴾" Aisha, may God be pleased with her, said: "Then the people asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about them after this verse, so God the Exalted revealed: ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127]." She said: "His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127], what is meant by it is this verse, which is His saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly.﴾"

[Page 140]

The second view regarding the interpretation of the verse: When the previous verse was revealed concerning orphans and the great sin (*hawb*) of consuming their property, the guardians feared that the sin would befall them by neglecting justice in the rights of the orphans, so they became reluctant to be their guardians. A man among them might have ten wives or more under him, and he would not fulfil their rights nor treat them justly. So it was said to them: If you fear neglecting justice in the rights of the orphans and become reluctant about it, then be fearful of neglecting justice with women, so limit the number of those you marry. For whoever becomes reluctant about a sin, or repents of it while committing its like, is as if he were not reluctant.

The third view of the interpretation: They were reluctant about the guardianship of orphans, so it was said: If you fear regarding the rights of orphans, then be fearful of adultery, so marry what is lawful for you of women, and do not hover around what is forbidden.

The fourth view of the interpretation: What was narrated from Ikrimah, who said: A man would have several women, and he would have orphans under his care. When he spent his own wealth on the women, and no wealth remained for him and he became needy, he would begin spending the wealth of the orphans on them. So God the Exalted said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾, meaning with the multiplicity of wives. Therefore, He prohibited you from marrying more than four, so that this fear would disappear. If you fear regarding the four as well, then (marry) one. He mentioned the excessive extreme, which is four, and the deficient extreme, which is one, and by this He alerted to what lies between them. As if God, the Exalted, had said: If you fear (injustice) with four, then three; if you fear, then two; if you fear, then one. This view is closer (to the truth). For God, the Exalted, warned against excessive marrying because of what may occur from the guardian in transgressing the property of the orphan, due to the need for large expenditure when marrying many wives.

* *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three or four; but if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable so that you do not deviate﴾.

Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The people of the apparent meaning (*Ahl al-Zahir*) said: Marriage is obligatory. They held to this verse, because His saying ﴿marry﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. Al-Shafi'i, in demonstrating that it is not obligatory, relied on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free, believing women, then (marry) from what your right hands possess of believing maidservants…﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], up to His saying: ﴿That is for whoever fears sin among you; but to be patient is better for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. So God judged that abstaining from marriage in this situation is better than doing it, and this indicates that it is not even recommended (*mandub*), let alone obligatory.

**The second issue:** He said *ma tāba* (what seems good) and did not say *man tāba* (whoever seems good), for several reasons:

The first: He intended by it the category, as you say: "What do you have?" and a man or a woman answers. The meaning is: what is that thing you have, and what is that reality you have?

The second: *Ma* together with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun (*masdar*), and its estimation is: "marry the good of women."

The third: *Ma* and *man* may interchange. God said: ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5], and He said: ﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 3]. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' related: "Glory to what the thunder glorifies Him with." And He said: ﴿And among them is he who walks on his belly﴾ [al-Nur: 45].

The fourth: He used *ma* to treat females as non-rational beings. From this is His saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6].

**The third issue:** Al-Wahidi and the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: His saying ﴿what seems good to you﴾ means what is lawful for you of women, because among them are those whose marriage is forbidden, which are the categories mentioned in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. But in my view this is open to scrutiny. This is because we have shown that His saying ﴿marry﴾ is a command of permission. So if what is meant by His saying ﴿what seems good to you﴾ is "what is lawful for you," the verse would be like saying: "We have permitted you to marry those whose marriage is permitted for you." That would strip the verse of its benefit. Furthermore, even if the verse is interpreted according to what they mentioned, the verse becomes ambiguous (*mujmal*) without doubt, since the causes of lawfulness and permissibility are not mentioned in this verse. Whereas if we interpret *tayyib* as the soul's approval and the inclination of the heart, the verse is general (*'amm*) and is subject to specification (*takhsis*). It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) that whenever there is a conflict between ambiguity and specification, removing the ambiguity takes priority, because a general text that has been specified remains a proof in what is not the object of specification, whereas an ambiguous text is not a proof at all.

**The fourth issue:** *Mathna wa-thulatha wa-ruba'a* means: two by two, three by three, and four by four. It is not declined (*ghayr munsarif*), and in this there are two views:

The first: Two features are combined in them: *al-'adl* (deviation from the original form) and *al-wasf* (being a descriptive form). As for *al-'adl*, it is that you mention a word and intend by it another word, as you say: "Umar" and "Zufar" and you intend by them "Amir" and "Zafir." Likewise here, by your saying *mathna* you intend "two by two," so it is deviated (*ma'dul*).

As for it being a descriptive form, its evidence is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Possessors of wings, two, three and four﴾ [Fatir: 1], and there is no doubt that it is a descriptive form.

The second view explaining why these forms are not declined: In them there are two instances of deviation, because they are deviated from their original forms as we have explained, and also they are deviated from their repetition. For when you say *mathna* you do not mean only "two," but "two by two." So when you say, "Two men came to me or three," your purpose is only to report the arrival of this number. But when you say, "The people came *mathna*," it indicates that their arrival in order was two by two. Thus it is established that two kinds of number occur in these words, and therefore they must be prevented from taking the nunation (*sarf*). This is because when two causes combine in a noun, this necessitates its being prevented from declension, since for this reason it becomes a substitute from two directions, and so it resembles the verb, and therefore its declension is prohibited. Likewise, when deviation occurs in it from two directions, it must be prevented from declension. And God knows best.

**The fifth issue:** The people of verification (*Ahl al-Tahqiq*) said: His saying ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ does not include slaves. This is because the address only includes a person for whom a woman is lawful and who is able to marry her, whereas a slave is not like that, as evidenced by the fact that he cannot marry except with his master's permission. This is shown by the Qur'an and the report (*khabar*). As for the Qur'an, it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿God presents an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ [al-Nahl: 75]. His saying ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ negates that he is independent in marriage. As for the report, it is his saying, peace be upon him: "Any slave who marries without his master's permission is an adulterer (*ʿāhir*)." Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that this verse does not include the slave.

Having understood this introduction, we say: Most jurists hold that the marriage of up to four is legislated for free men, not for

[Page 142]

slaves. Malik said: It is lawful for a slave to marry up to four, and he held to the apparent meaning of this verse.

The answer on which reliance is placed is that al-Shafi'i argued that this verse is restricted to free men by two other proofs besides what we have mentioned:

The first: He, the Exalted, said after this verse: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess﴾, and this applies only to free men.

The second: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if they give you willingly a part of it, then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾ [al-Nisa': 4], and a slave does not consume what his wife willingly gives up of the dowry; rather, it belongs to his master. Malik said: When two independent general statements occur, the addition of a restriction to the latter does not necessitate its inclusion in the former.

Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, answered that these addresses in these verses came in succession in one sequence. When their restriction to free men was known in some of them, it became known that all of them are like that. Some jurists knew that the apparent meaning of this verse includes slaves, but they specified this generality by analogy. They said: We agree that slavery has an effect on reducing the rights of marriage, such as divorce and the waiting period (*'idda*). Since the number is among the rights of marriage, it must be that a slave receives half of what a free man receives. But the first answer is better, stronger, and God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** A group, among them al-Suddi, held that it is permissible to marry any number one wishes, and they relied on the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, they held to this verse in three respects:

The first: His saying ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ is an unrestricted statement covering all numbers, as evidenced by the fact that there is no number except that it is valid to make an exception from it, and the function of an exception is to remove what would otherwise have been included.

The second: His saying ﴿two, three and four﴾ is not suitable as a specification of that generality, because specifying some numbers by mention does not negate the establishment of the ruling for the rest. Rather, we say: the mention of these numbers indicates the removal of hardship and restriction absolutely. For when a man says to his son, "Do what you wish; go to the market, to the city, and to the orchard," it is an explicit delegation to him of the reins of choice absolutely, and the removal of restriction and hardship from him absolutely. It is not a specification of permission to those mentioned things; rather, it is permission for what is mentioned and what is other than it. So likewise here. Furthermore, mentioning all numbers is impossible, so when some numbers are mentioned after His saying ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾, that is an indication that permission for all numbers has been granted.

Third: the particle "wa" (and) denotes general conjunction, so His words ﴿two, three, and four﴾ permit this combined number, which comes to nine. The truth, however, is that it permits eighteen, because His words "two" do not mean only two but "two and two," and the same applies to the rest. As for the report, there are two ways to argue from it:

First: It is established by mass transmission (tawatur) that the Prophet (ﷺ) died leaving nine wives. Then Allah the Exalted commanded us to follow him, saying: ﴿So follow him﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. The least degree of a command is permissibility.

Second: A man's sunnah is his way or practice. Marrying more than four was the practice of the Messenger, peace be upon him, so it became a sunnah for him. Moreover, he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me." The apparent meaning of this hadith requires that blame fall upon whoever abandons marrying more than four, so at the very least it establishes the basic permissibility.

Know that the jurists' reliance in establishing a limit (of four) rests on two things:

First: the report, which is that Ghaylan embraced Islam while having ten wives, and the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Keep four and separate from the rest." It is also reported that Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah embraced Islam while having five wives, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Keep four and separate from one."

Know that this route is weak for two reasons:

First: since the Qur'an indicates that there is no limit, then restricting it by this report would be abrogating the Qur'an with a solitary report (khabar al-wahid), and that is not permissible.

Second: the report is an incident of a specific situation. Perhaps the Prophet, peace be upon him, only commanded him to keep four and separate from the rest because combining the four with the others was impermissible, either because of kinship or because of fosterage. In sum, this possibility remains in this report, so the Qur'an cannot be abrogated by something like it.

The second route: the consensus (ijma') of the jurists of the major cities that it is not permitted to exceed four. This is the reliance, and it faces two questions. First: consensus neither abrogates nor is abrogated, so how can it be said that consensus abrogated this verse? Second: among the community there are some eccentric groups who do not hold that exceeding four is prohibited, and consensus is not established when one or two dissent.

The answer to the first: consensus reveals that an abrogating ruling existed in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). The answer to the second: the one who opposes this consensus is from the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah), so his opposition carries no weight.

If it is said: if the matter is as you have stated, then in this case it would have been more fitting to say "two or three or four," so why did He use the conjunction "wa" instead of "aw" (or)?

We say: had He used the word "aw," that would imply that it is permitted only in one of these categories, and that it is not permitted for them to combine these categories, meaning that some would marry two, others three, and a third group four. But when He expressed it with the particle "wa," this indicates that each group is permitted to choose one of these categories. A parallel example is when a man says to a group: "Divide this money, which is a thousand, two by two, three by three, and four by four." What is meant is that some of them may take two and two, others may take three and three, and a third group may take four and four. Thus the benefit here of omitting "aw" and using "wa" is what we have mentioned, and Allah knows best.

Seventh issue: His words ﴿two, three, and four﴾ are in the accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) relating to "what is good (tayyib)." Its implied sense is: "Marry the good women for yourselves, counted in this number: two each, three each, and four each."

* * *

His the Exalted's words: ﴿But if you fear that you will not deal justly, then one or what your right hands possess﴾.

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: The meaning is: if you fear that you will not be just among these numbers, just as you feared failing to be just with more than them, then be content with one wife or with a slave woman. He made equal in ease and facility between a single free wife and slave women without limit. By my life, they carry less responsibility and are lighter in burden than the (demanding) camels; it does not matter to you whether you have more or fewer of them, whether you divide among them equally or not, whether you practice withdrawal (ʿazl) or not.

The second issue: "fa-wahidah" was recited with the final letter in the accusative (fa-wahidatan), and the meaning is: "then commit to" or "then choose one," and leave plurality altogether, for the whole matter revolves around justice, so wherever you find justice, you must adhere to it. It was also recited in the nominative (fa-wahidatun), and the implied sense is: "then one suffices," or "then one is enough for you, or what your right hands possess."

The third issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, may argue from this verse to show that occupying oneself with voluntary acts of worship is better than marriage. This is because Allah the Exalted, in this verse, gave the choice between marrying one woman and taking a slave concubine, and a choice between two things indicates equality between them regarding the intended wisdom, just as when a physician says: "Eat an apple or a pomegranate," which indicates that each of them stands in place of the other in fulfilling the purpose. Just as the verse indicates this equality, so reason also indicates it, because the aim is tranquility, mutual companionship, protection of religion, and the affairs of the household, and all of these are attained by both means. Moreover, if we assume the discussion concerns a woman who was a slave, whom he then freed and married, then here the equality between marriage and taking a concubine clearly appears. Since it has been established by this verse that marriage and taking a concubine are equal, we say: we agree that occupying oneself with voluntary acts is better than taking a concubine, so it must be better than marriage, because what exceeds one of two equals necessarily exceeds the second equal.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾, and on this there are two issues.

The first issue: "adna" (nearer) here means "closer," and the sense is: "That is closer to your not being unjust." The omission of "min" (from) is acceptable because the context indicates it.

The second issue: there are several interpretations of ﴿not being unjust (ta'ūlū)﴾:

The first: its meaning is: do not act tyrannically and do not incline (away from justice). This is the view preferred by most exegetes (mufassirun), and it has been transmitted as a statement traced to the Prophet: "'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His words ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾ that he said: 'Do not act tyrannically.'" In another narration: "that you do not incline." Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: both wordings are transmitted. The root meaning of 'awl is inclination. It is said: "al-mizan 'āla 'awlan" (the scale tilted) when it inclined, and "al-hakim 'āla fi hukmihi" (the judge deviated in his ruling) when he acted unjustly, because when he acts unjustly he has inclined. They recited to Abu Talib:

"With a scale of justice that does not cheat by a single grain, and a true weigher whose weight does not deviate."

It is also reported that a Bedouin was judged against by a judge, and he said to him: "Are you inclining against me (ta'ūlu 'alayya)?" It is also said: "'alat al-fariḍah" (the estate's shares increased) when its shares grew, and "a'altuhā" (I increased it) when you add to its shares. It is known that when its shares increase, it has deviated from balance. These derivations show that the original root of this word is inclination, and then by custom it became specific to inclining toward oppression and injustice. This is the discussion establishing this view, which most scholars hold.

The second view: some said: the meaning is "that you do not become poor." It is said: "rajul 'a'il" meaning a poor man, because when his dependents are few, his expenses are few, and when his expenses are few, he does not become poor.

The third view: it has been reported from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾ means: that is nearer to your dependents not being numerous. Abu Bakr al-Razi said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: People have criticized him on this in three respects:

One: there is no disagreement between the early generations and everyone who has transmitted the exegesis of this verse that its meaning is: do not incline and do not act unjustly.

Two: it is an error in language, because if it were said: "That is nearer to your not having dependents (tu'ilu)," that would be correct, but interpreting (ta'ūlū) as (tu'ilū) is an error in language.

Three: He the Exalted mentioned one wife or what the right hands possess, and slave women, as dependents in the same position as women, and there is no disagreement that a man may take as many as he wishes through ownership of slave women, so we know that the intended meaning is not the multiplicity of dependents.

The author of al-Nazm added a fourth objection: He the Exalted said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿But if you fear that you will not deal justly, then one﴾ and did not say "that you will not be poor," so the answer must be connected to this condition, and its answer can only be the opposite of justice, which is injustice, not the multiplicity of dependents.

I say:

As for the first objection, it is extremely weak, because it has not been transmitted from al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, that he criticized the statement of the exegetes that the meaning of the verse is: do not act unjustly and do not incline. Rather, he mentioned another interpretation. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that when earlier scholars mention an interpretation of a verse, that does not prevent later scholars from deriving another interpretation of it. Were it not permissible, the subtleties that later scholars derived in explaining the words of Allah would be rejected as false. It is known that only a blind follower of an earlier authority (muqallid khalaf) would say this. Furthermore: who informed al-Razi that this interpretation which al-Shafi'i mentioned was not mentioned by any one of the Companions and the Successors? And how could we not say so, when it is well known that Tawus used to recite: "That is nearer to your not being overburdened (tu'ilū)." And if it is established that the earlier scholars treated this reading as a recitation, then treating it as an interpretation is more fitting. Through these points, the extreme ignorance of al-Razi in this objection is established.

As for the second objection, we say: you have transmitted this word's lexical meaning from al-Mubarrad, but through your ignorance and your eagerness to criticize the leading mujtahids and the great scholars, and your extreme dullness, you did not realize that this criticism which al-Mubarrad mentioned is false. Its falsehood is shown in several respects:

The first: it is said: "'alat al-mas'alah" (the issue increased) when its shares grew and multiplied, and this meaning is close to inclination, because when a thing inclines, the directions of desire and the motives of will multiply. If that is so, the meaning of the verse becomes: "That is nearer to your not multiplying." And when you do not multiply, a person does not fall into injustice and oppression, because the vehicle of injustice and oppression is multiplicity and frequent association. By this route, this interpretation returns to something close to the first interpretation which the majority chose.

The second: when a person says: "So-and-so has a long sword-belt and much ash," and when he is asked what this means, it is good to say: "It means he is tall and very hospitable." It is not meant that the explanation of "long sword-belt" is "tall," but rather that the intended purpose of the statement is this meaning. Scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-bayan) call this expression of a thing by way of metonymy (kinayah) and allusion (ta'ridh), and its essence returns to one principle, namely indicating a thing by mentioning its necessary consequences. Here, multiplicity of dependents necessarily entails inclination and injustice, and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, made the multiplicity of dependents a metonymy for inclination and injustice, since multiplicity of dependents is never free of inclination and injustice. So he made this an interpretation of it, not by direct equivalence, but by metonymy and implication. This method is well known in the Book of Allah. Since al-Shafi'i was fully aware of the various modes of Arabic speech, he found it fitting to mention this expression. As for Abu Bakr al-Razi, since he was dull of disposition and far from the modes of Arabic speech, he, of course, did not recognize the fine point in it.

The third aspect: what the author of al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari) mentioned, namely that this interpretation is derived from your saying: "'āla al-rajulu 'iyālahu, ya'ūluhum" (a man supported his dependents), like their saying: "mānahum, yamūnuhum" when he spent on them, because whoever has many dependents is bound to support them, and in that there is what makes it difficult for him to maintain the limits of scrupulousness (wara', piety in avoiding doubtful matters) and to earn what is lawful and good provision. Thus it is established by these aspects that what was mentioned by the Imam of the Muslims, al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is of the utmost excellence, and that criticism only arises from great stupidity and little knowledge.

As for the third objection, which is his statement that the multiplicity of dependents does not differ whether the woman is a wife or a slave, its answer has two aspects:

The first: what al-Qaffal, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned, namely that if the female slaves are many, he may require them to earn, and when they earn, they spend on themselves and on their master as well, and in that case the dependents become few. But if the woman is free, the matter is not like this, so the difference is clear.

The second: that when a woman is a slave, if the master becomes unable to support her, he sells her and rids himself of her. But if she is free, he has no choice but to support her, and custom indicates that as long as the husband keeps the wife, she does not demand from him the dower (mahr, the marriage payment), but if he attempts to divorce her, she demands the dower from him, and so the husband falls into a predicament (mihna, trial).

As for the fourth objection, which is what al-Jurjani, the author of al-Nazm (Sahib al-Nazm), mentioned, the answer to it has two aspects:

The first: what al-Qadi (the judge) mentioned, namely that the aspect mentioned by al-Shafi'i is preferable, because if it were understood as injustice, it would be a repetition, since that is already understood from his saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly." But when we interpret it according to what al-Shafi'i mentioned, no repetition arises, so it is better.

The second: we say, grant that the matter is as you have stated, yet we have shown that the interpretation mentioned by al-Shafi'i, upon careful examination, returns to the mention of the first interpretation, but by way of allusion and indirect reference. And if this is the case, then this objection has been removed. This is the completion of the discussion on this point, and success is from Allah.

[p. 146]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 4:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾.

On the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿And give the women﴾ is addressed to whom? There are two opinions. The first is that this is addressed to the guardians of the women. This is because the Arabs in the Jahiliyya would not give the women any of their dowries. For this reason, they would say to a man who had a daughter born to him: "Congratulations on the *nafijah*!" Its meaning is that you will take her dowry in camels and add it to your camels, so your wealth swells (*tanfuju malaka*), that is, you magnify it. Ibn al-A'rabi said: the *nafijah* is what a man takes from the *hulwan* (the gift given to the father) when he marries off his daughter. So God, may He be exalted, forbade this and commanded that the right be handed over to its people. This is the view of al-Kalbi, Abu Salih, and the choice of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba.

The second opinion is that the address is to the husbands. They were commanded to give the women their dowries. This is the view of 'Alqama, al-Nakha'i, and Qatada, and the choice of al-Zajjaj, who said: "Because there is no mention of the guardians here, and what comes before this is addressed to those who marry, namely the husbands."

**The second issue:** Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: It is possible that what is meant by *iytaa'* (giving) is handing over (*munawalah*), and it is possible that what is meant is commitment (*iltizam*). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿until they give the jizya willingly while humbled﴾ [al-Tawba: 29], and the meaning is until they undertake it and commit to it. On the first view, it is as if what is meant is that they were commanded to pay the dowries that they had specified for the women. On the second view, what is meant is that intimacy is not made lawful except in exchange for a consideration that is binding, whether or not it has been specified, except what was particular to the Messenger ﷺ regarding the woman who gives herself in marriage (*al-mawhuba*). Then he, may God have mercy on him, said: It is permissible that the speech comprises both meanings together. And God knows best.

**The third issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: (*sadaqatihinna*) means their dowries. In the hadith of Shurayh: "Ibn 'Abbas judged for her the *sadaqa* (dowry)." He read (*sadqatihinna*) with a fatha on the *sad* and sukun on the *dal*, as a lightened form of *sudqatihinna*. (*sudqatihinna*) with a damma on the *sad* and sukun on the *dal* is the plural of *sudqa*. It was also read (*sudqatahunna*) with a damma on both the *sad* and the *dal*, in the singular, and it is the heavier form of *sudqa*, like his saying, in *zulma* (darkness): *zulumah*. Al-Wahidi said: the root (*s-d-q*) on this arrangement is for completeness and soundness. So the dowry was called *sadaq* and *sadaqa*, because the marriage contract is completed and perfected by it.

**The fourth issue:** Regarding the explanation of *nihla* (gift), there are several views.

*The first:* Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd said: it means an obligation (*fari'a*).
