They explained *nihla* as an obligation because *nihla* in language means religious conviction, creed, law, and school of thought. It is said: "So-and-so *yantahilu* such-and-such," if he adheres to it as his religion, and "his *nihla* is such-and-such," that is, his religion and doctrine. So His saying: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾ means: give them their dowries, for this is a *nihla*, that is, a law, a religion, and a doctrine; and whatever is a religion and doctrine is an obligation.

*The second:* al-Kalbi said: *nihla* means a gift and a present. It is said: "I *nahaltu* so-and-so something, *anhalhu nihlatan wa nuhlan*." Al-Qaffal said: its original sense is attributing a thing to other than its owner. It is said: "This is a *mankul* poem," that is, attributed to other than its composer, and "I *intahaltu* such-and-such," if you claim it and attribute it to yourself. On this view, the dowry is a gift from whom? There are two possibilities. The first: it is a gift from the husband, because the husband does not own anything in exchange for it, since the womb (*al-bud'*) is in the woman's ownership after marriage just as it was before. So the husband gave her the dowry and did not take from her a consideration that he owns. Thus it has the sense of a *nihla* for which there is no equivalent in return. What the husband deserves from her by the marriage contract is only the permission (*al-istibaha*), not ownership. Others said: God, may He be exalted, made the benefits of marriage, namely the satisfaction of desire and procreation, shared between the two spouses; then He commanded the husband to give the wife the dowry, so this was a gift from God from the outset.

*The third view on the meaning of nihla:* Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of His saying (*nihla*) is "from good will," because *nihla* in language is a gift without taking a consideration, as a man gives his child something of his wealth. What is given without seeking a consideration is only given from good will. So God commanded giving the women their dowries without their demand or dispute, because what is taken through litigation is not called *nihla*.

**The fifth issue:** If we take *nihla* to mean religious obligation, then regarding its grammatical state (*nasb*) there are two possibilities:

The first: it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), and the meaning is: give them their dowries out of religious duty.

The second: it is a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the dowries, that is, a religion from God that He legislated and imposed.

As for if we take *nihla* to mean a gift, its grammatical state is again two possibilities:

The first: it is in the accusative as an infinitive (*masdar*). This is because *nihla* and *iytaa'* (giving) mean the same as *i'ta'* (giving). So it is as if it were said: "Bestow upon the women their dowries as a gift," that is, give them their dowries from the goodwill of your souls.

The second: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). Then there are two possibilities:

The first: it is a state of those addressed, that is, give them their dowries while you are giving them with pleasant souls.

The second: it is a state of the dowries, that is, given and bestowed from the goodwill of souls.

**The sixth issue:** Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, said: a valid seclusion (*al-khalwa al-sahiha*) establishes the dowry in full. Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: it does not establish it in full. Abu Hanifa argued for the soundness of his view with this verse, because this text requires the obligation of giving the dowry absolutely and without restriction. It was abandoned in cases where there was neither consummation (*al-masis*) nor seclusion, so when these two occur, it remains necessary to follow what the verse requires.

Our companions answered: this [verse] is general, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them and you have already specified for them an obligation, then half of what you specified﴾ [al-Baqara: 237] indicates that in such a case only half the dowry is obligatory. This verse is specific, and there is no doubt that the specific takes precedence over the general.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they give you willingly a portion of it, then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, commanded them to give the women their dowries, He followed it with mention of the permissibility of accepting their remission and gift to him, lest one think that he is obligated to give her her dowry even if her soul is content with leaving it. On the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *nafsan* (in souls) is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*). The meaning is: their souls were pleased for you regarding a portion of the dowry, by transferring the action from the souls to them. So the soul came as a specification, as they say: "You are good in face (*husnun wajhan*)." The action originally belonged to the face, but when it was transferred to the owner of the face, the face came as a specification of the place of the action. Similar to it: "I cooled my eye (*qarrat bihi 'aynan*)" and "I was constricted in regard to him (*dayiqtu bihi dharan*)."

**The second issue:** He only made the soul singular because the purpose of it is to clarify the place of the action, and this is achieved by the singular, and similar is "twenty dirhams." Al-Farra' said: if it were made plural it would be correct, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in works?﴾ [al-Kahf: 103].

**The third issue:** The *min* (from) in His saying (*minhu*) is not partitive (*lil-tab'idh*) but explanatory (*lil-tabyin*). The meaning is: regarding a thing of this kind, which is a dowry, like His saying: ﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. This is because if the woman's soul were content regarding the entire dowry, it would be lawful for the husband to take all of it.

**The fourth issue:** *minhu* means: from the dowries, or from that. It is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 15], after mention of the desires. It is narrated that when Ru'ba said:

*fihā khuṭūṭun min sawādin wa balaq*
*ka'annahu fī l-jildi tawlī'u l-bahaq*

("In it are lines of blackness and whiteness, as if on the skin is the pattern of leprosy (*al-bahaq*)")

it was said to him: The pronoun in his saying *ka'annahu* (as if it), if it refers to the lines (*khutut*), then you should have said *ka'annaha*; and if it refers to the blackness and whiteness, then you should have said *ka'annahuma*. He said: I meant "as if that." There is another aspect, which is that *sadaqat* here has the sense of *sadaq* (dowry), because if you said: "Give the women their dowry (*sadaqahunna*)," the intended meaning would be achieved. There is a third aspect: the benefit of making the pronoun masculine is that it refers to part of the dowry, and the purpose of it is to encourage her not to give away except part of the dowry.

**The fifth issue:** The meaning of the verse is: if they give you something of the dowry from good will, not because of the badness of your character with them or your poor treatment of them, then consume it and spend it. The verse contains evidence of the narrowness of the path in this matter and the obligation of caution, since He made the condition depend on the goodwill of the soul, saying: ﴿if they are pleased (*tibna*)﴾ and did not say "if they give or are generous," indicating that what is taken into account is her soul's withdrawal from the thing given while being content.

**The sixth issue:** *al-hanii'* and *al-mari'* are two adjectives derived from *hanu'a al-ta'am* and *maru'a*, when food is palatable without any disturbance in it. It was said: *al-hanii'* is what the eater enjoys, and *al-mari'* is what has a praiseworthy outcome. It was also said: what goes down smoothly in its passage. It was said that the passage of food from the throat to the stomach's mouth is called *al-mari'* because the food goes down smoothly in it, which is its *inisa'*. Al-Wahidi related from some of them that the origin of *hanii'* is from *al-hana'*, which is the treatment of mange with tar, so *hanii'* is a cure from mange. The commentators said: the meaning is that when wives give their dowries to their husbands from good will, there is no blame upon the husbands in that, neither in this world nor in the next. In sum, it is an expression of making lawful, of emphasis on permissibility, and of removing blame.

**The seventh issue:** His saying: ﴿hanii'an mari'an﴾ is a descriptor of the verbal noun, that is, an eating that is *hanii'* and *mari'*; or it is a circumstantial state of the pronoun, that is, eat it while it is *hanii'* and *mari'*. It may be paused upon at His saying (*fakuluhu*), then one begins with His saying ﴿hanii'an mari'an﴾ as a supplication, and also on the basis that they are two descriptors placed in the position of two verbal nouns, as if it were said: "*hana'a*, *mara'a*" (may it be pleasant and wholesome).

**The eighth issue:** This verse indicates several matters. Among them: the dowry belongs to her, and the guardian has no right in it. Among them: the permissibility of her giving the dowry to the husband, and the permissibility of the husband taking it, since His saying ﴿then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾ indicates both meanings. Among them: the permissibility of her giving the dowry before receiving it, since God, may He be exalted, did not distinguish between the two situations.

Here there is a point of inquiry: His saying ﴿then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾ covers the case where the dowry is a specific thing (*'ayn*). As for when it is a debt (*dayn*), the verse does not cover it, for one does not say to what is in the liability: "Consume it with satisfaction and ease."

We say: what is meant by His saying ﴿then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾ is not the act of eating itself, but rather it means the permissibility of dispositions (*tasarrufat*). He only mentioned eating specifically because most of the purpose of wealth is eating. A parallel to it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], and He said: ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾.

**The ninth issue:** Some scholars said: if she gives and then after the gift she demands it back, it is known that her soul was not content with it. It is related from al-Sha'bi that a woman came with her husband to Shurayh regarding a gift she had given him, and she was seeking its return. Shurayh said: "Return it to her." The man said: "Did not God say: ﴿if they give you willingly a portion of it﴾?" He said: "If her soul had been content with it, she would not have taken it back." It is also related from him: "I rule for them regarding what they gave, and I do not rule for him, because they are deceived." And it is related that a man from the family of Abu Mu'ayt was given by his wife a thousand dinars as a dowry that she had owed him. He stayed a month, then divorced her. She brought a case against him before 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. The man said: "She gave it to me with her soul content." 'Abd al-Malik said: "Indeed, the verse that follows it: ﴿then do not take from it anything﴾ [al-Nisa': 20] — return it to her." And from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he wrote to his judges: "Women give out of desire or out of fear, so whichever woman gave something and then wished to take it back, that is hers." And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of support; but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them a kindly word.﴾

Know that this is the third type of the rulings mentioned in this surah.

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is as if He, exalted is He, were saying: Although I commanded you to give orphans their property and to hand over the bridal gifts of women to them, I only said that when they are intelligent, adult, and capable of preserving their property. But if they are not adults, or not intelligent, or if they are adults and intelligent yet foolish and wasteful, then do not hand their property over to them, and hold it on their behalf until the foolishness leaves them. The purpose of all of this is caution in preserving the property of the weak and the incapable.

On the verse there are several issues:

First issue: There are two opinions regarding the verse. The first: it is addressed to the guardians (awliya'), as if He, exalted is He, said: O guardians, do not give those under your guardianship who are foolish their property. The evidence that it is addressed to the guardians is His saying: ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾. Also, according to this opinion, the connection of the verse with what precedes it is good, as we have established.

If it is said: According to this interpretation, it should have been said: "And do not give the foolish their property," so why did He say "your property"?

We say: In answer there are two points:

The first: He attributed the property to them not because they own it, but because they hold the right of disposal over it, and minimal grounds suffice for a good attribution.

The second: This attribution is good by treating the unity of kind as the unity of the individual. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], and His saying: ﴿what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and His saying: ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], and His saying: ﴿then you are these who kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]. It is known that a man among them did not kill himself, but some of them killed others, and all were of one kind. Likewise here, property is something by which the human kind benefits and which it needs. Because of this kind-unity, the attribution of the property of the foolish to their guardians is good.

The second opinion: this verse is addressed to fathers. God forbade them, when their children are foolish and cannot independently preserve and manage property, to hand over their property or part of it to them, because of the corruption that would result. On this view the attribution of the property to them is literal. On this opinion the purpose of the verse is to urge the preservation of property and the striving that it not be lost or destroyed. That indicates that he does not have the right to consume all his property and destroy it, and when his end approaches, it is obligatory upon him to bequeath his property to a trustworthy person who will preserve that property for his heirs. We have said that the first opinion is preferable for two reasons. Among what indicates this preference is that the apparent sense of the prohibition is prohibition (tahrim), and the community (ummah) has agreed that it is not forbidden for him to give his young children and women whatever he wishes of his property, and they agreed that it is forbidden for the guardian to hand the property over to the foolish. Since that is so, the verse must be understood according to the first opinion, not this second opinion. And God knows best.

The second: He said at the end of the verse: ﴿and speak to them a kindly word﴾. There is no doubt that this exhortation is more fitting for orphans, because a person is by nature compassionate toward his child, so he says to him only what is good; this exhortation is needed mainly with orphans who are strangers. It is also not impossible to understand the verse as applying to both interpretations. The judge (al-Qadi) said: This is remote, because it requires understanding His saying "your property" both literally and figuratively together. It can be answered that His saying "your property" indicates that those properties are specifically theirs in a way that allows them to dispose of them. Then the specificity is present in property that is owned by him and in property that is owned by a child, except that its disposal is restricted. This difference lies in a concept outside the concept derived from His saying "your property." Since that is so, it is not far-fetched to take the expression in both senses, insofar as the expression conveys one meaning shared by both.

Second issue: They mentioned several interpretations of what is meant by "the foolish" (al-sufaha'):

The first: Mujahid and Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, said: the foolish here are women, whether they are wives, mothers, or daughters. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, and what supports this is what Abu Umamah narrated: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the Fire was created only for the foolish," saying it three times, "Indeed the foolish are women, except a woman who obeys her guardian."

If it is said: If the intended meaning of "the foolish" were women, he would have said "al-safa'ih" or "al-safihat" as the plural of "safihah," like ghara'ib and gharibat as the plural of gharibah.

Al-Zajjaj answered: "al-Sufaha'" as the plural of "safihah" is permissible, just as "al-Fuqara'" as the plural of "faqirah" is permissible.

The second opinion: al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd said: by "the foolish" here is meant the foolish among the children. It means: do not give your property, which is your means of support, to your foolish son, lest he corrupt it.

The third opinion: The intended meaning of "the foolish" is women and children, according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. They said: if a man knows that his wife is a foolish, corrupting woman, and that his son is a foolish, corrupting boy, then it is not appropriate for him to give either of them power over his property so that they corrupt it.

The fourth opinion: The intended meaning of "the foolish" is everyone who lacks intellect sufficient to preserve property. This includes women, children, orphans, and everyone described by this attribute. This opinion is preferable, because specification without evidence is not permissible. We have mentioned in the surah al-Baqarah that safah is lightness of intellect; for this reason the sinner is called a foolish (safih), because he has no weight with the people of religion and knowledge, and one who is deficient in intellect is called foolish because of the lightness of his intellect.

Third issue: Foolishness in these people is not a description of blame, nor does it convey the meaning of disobedience to God, exalted is He. They were called foolish only because of the lightness of their intellects and their deficiency of discernment for taking charge of preserving property.

Fourth issue: Know that God, exalted is He, commanded the responsible persons in several places in His Book to preserve property. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾ [and] ﴿indeed the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra': 26–27], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute﴾ [al-Isra': 29], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. God has also encouraged the preservation of property in the verse on debt, where He commanded writing, witnessing, and pledging. Reason also supports this, because a person who is not at ease of mind cannot undertake the pursuit of the interests of this world and the Hereafter, and one is not at ease of mind except through property, for by it one is enabled to bring benefits and repel harms. Whoever seeks this world for this purpose, the world is for him one of the greatest means helping him to attain the happiness of the Hereafter; but whoever seeks it for its own sake and for its very self, it is one of the greatest obstacles to gaining the happiness of the Hereafter.

Fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support (qiyaman)﴾ means that your standing and your livelihood are not achieved except through this property. Since property is a cause of standing and self-sufficiency, He named it "qiyam" by way of calling the effect by the name of the cause, as an intensification; that is, this property is itself your standing and the pursuit of your livelihood. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿qiyaman﴾ as "qiyaman" (qiyam). It is said: "hadha qayyim" and "qiyam," as He said: ﴿a upright religion, the creed of Abraham﴾ [al-An'am: 161]. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read "qiwaman" with a waw. The qiwam of a thing is that by which it is maintained, like your saying: "the mulak (sovereignty) of the matter is that by which it is possessed."

Sixth issue: Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: an adult who squanders property and corrupts it is placed under interdiction (yuhjar 'alayhi). Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, said: he is not placed under interdiction. The argument of al-Shafi'i: he is foolish, so he must be placed under interdiction. We say he is foolish because safih in the language means one whose weight is light. There is no doubt that one who squanders property and corrupts it without benefit has no weight in the hearts of intelligent people, so he is light in their estimation, and it is therefore necessary to call him a safih. Once this is established, it follows that he falls under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them a kindly word﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, forbade giving property to the foolish, He then commanded three things: the first of them is His saying: "and provide for them," meaning: spend upon them. The meaning of provision (rizq) from servants is an allowance assigned for a known time; it is said: "so-and-so provided for his dependents," i.e., he allotted to them. He said "from it (fiha)" and did not say "from them (minha)," lest that be a command to make part of their property their provision; rather He commanded them to make their property the place of their provision, by trading with it and making it grow, so that they take their provision from the profits and not from the principal sums. The second is His saying: "and clothe them," and its meaning is clear. The third is His saying: ﴿and speak to them a kindly word﴾.

Know that He, exalted is He, commanded this only because a good word affects the heart and removes foolishness, whereas the opposite of a kindly word increases the foolish one in foolishness and deficiency.

The exegetes mentioned several interpretations of "a kindly word":

One: Ibn Jurayj and Mujahid said: it is a good promise of righteousness and kindness. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is like saying, "If I profit on this journey of mine, I will do for you what you deserve, and if I gain in my campaign, I will give you."

Two: Ibn Zayd said: it is supplication, such as saying, "May God grant us and you well-being, may God bless you." In sum, whatever souls are at ease with and love, of speech and deed, is kindly, and whatever they reject, dislike, and recoil from is reprehensible.

Three: Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: teach them, along with feeding and clothing them, the matters of their religion relating to knowledge and action. Four: al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: the kindly word is that if the one under guardianship is a child, the guardian informs him that the property is his property and that he is its keeper, and that when his childhood ends he will return the property to him. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿As for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾ [al-Duha: 9], meaning: do not deal with him by dominating him as you deal with slaves; and similarly His saying: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word﴾ [al-Isra': 28]. If the one under guardianship is foolish, he admonishes him, advises him, urges him to prayer, encourages him to abandon squandering and extravagance, and informs him that the end of squandering is poverty and need of people, and similar words of this kind. This interpretation is the best of all the interpretations we have related.

[Page 153]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then, if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property. Do not consume it extravagantly or hastily before they grow up. Whoever is rich should abstain, and whoever is poor may eat with reasonable provision. When you hand over their property to them, call witnesses against them, and Allah suffices as Reckoner.﴾

Know that when Allah, Exalted is He, had previously commanded the giving of the orphan's property to him, saying, ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, He explained in this verse when He gives them their property. He mentioned this verse and made two conditions for handing their property over to them. The first is reaching marriageable age (bulugh al-nikah), and the second is perceiving sound judgment (iynas al-rushd). Both must be established before their property may be handed over to them. There are several issues in the verse:

[Page 153 continues]

**First issue:** Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the dispositions (tasarrufat) of a discerning, intelligent minor are valid with the permission of the guardian (wali). Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are not valid. Abu Hanifa argued for his view from this verse, because His saying, ﴿Test the orphans until they reach marriageable age﴾, indicates that this testing occurs before puberty. The purpose of this testing is to examine his condition, namely whether he has a disposition suitable for buying and selling. This examination only takes place if he is permitted to buy and sell. Even if this meaning is not the examination itself, it is included in the examination, as evidenced by the fact that an exception may be made: one says, "Test the orphans, except in buying and selling." The function of an exception is to exclude what would otherwise be included. Thus it is established that His saying, ﴿Test the orphans﴾, is a command to the guardians to permit them to buy and sell before puberty, and this requires the validity of their dispositions.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, answered by saying: the meaning of His saying, ﴿Test the orphans﴾, is not permission for them to dispose of property during childhood. This is shown by His saying after it, ﴿Then, if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property﴾. He only commanded handing over property to them after puberty and the perception of sound judgment. Since it is established by the implication of this verse that property may not be handed over to him during childhood, it follows that his dispositions during childhood may not be valid, because there is no one who distinguishes between the two cases. Thus, by what we have mentioned, the indication of this verse supports the view of al-Shafi'i. As for the argument they used, its answer is: the purpose of "testing" is to examine his intellect and investigate his condition, whether he has understanding, reason, and the ability to know benefit and harm. This is done when the guardian buys and sells in the presence of the child, and then the child is questioned about the circumstances of that buying and selling and the benefits and harms in them. Without doubt, testing and trial are achieved by this degree. Furthermore: suppose we grant that he hands him something to buy or sell. Why do you say that this degree indicates the validity of that buying and selling? Rather, if he buys and sells and his intellect is tested by it, then the guardian afterwards completes that sale and that purchase. This is a possibility, and Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** The meaning of "reaching marriageable age" is the wet dream (ihtilam) mentioned in His saying, ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty﴾. According to the consensus of most jurists, it refers to reaching the level of men, at which point the pen (of accountability) is recorded against a person and he becomes liable to the hudud (prescribed punishments) and the rulings. The wet dream was called "reaching marriageable age" because it is the emission of the gushing fluid that occurs in intercourse.

Know that there are five signs of puberty. Three of them are shared between males and females: the wet dream, a specific age, and the growth of coarse hair on the pubic area. Two are specific to women: menstruation and pregnancy.

**Third issue:** As for the perception of sound judgment, there must be an explanation of "perception" and an explanation of "rushd" (sound judgment). As for perception, His saying "you perceive" (aanastum) means "you know," and it is also said "you see." The root meaning of iynas in the language is sight, and from it is His saying: ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the mount; he said…﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]. As for rushd, it is known that it does not mean the rushd that has no connection to the good management of his property. Rather, it must be intended that he knows how to manage his property well, so that no extravagance comes from him and he is not in a position where others can deceive him. Then the scholars differed on whether righteousness in religion must also be included. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, it is necessary. According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, it is not considered. The first view is preferable, and it is supported by several arguments:

First: the people of the language said that rushd is attaining what is good, and one who corrupts his religion does not attain what is good.

Second: rushd is the opposite of ghayy (error). Allah says: ﴿The right course has become distinct from error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. Ghayy is misguidance and corruption. Allah says: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. Thus He made the one who disobeys a ghawiy (one who has gone astray). This indicates that rushd is not realized except together with righteousness in religion.

Third: Allah says: [Page 154] ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud: 97]. This negates rushd from him, because he did not observe the interests of religion. And Allah knows best.

Having understood this, we say: the benefit of this disagreement is that al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that a person of immoral conduct (fasiq) is to be placed under interdiction (hajr), while Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, does not hold this view.

**Fourth issue:** They agreed that if he reaches puberty without rushd, his property is not handed over to him. Then, according to Abu Hanifa, his property is not handed over to him until he reaches twenty-five years of age. When he reaches that, his property is handed over to him in every case. He considered this age because the period of male puberty by age is, in his view, eighteen years. When seven years are added to it, which is a period regarded as significant for changes in human conditions, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Command them to pray at seven," then the period in which changes in conditions can occur is complete. At that point his property is handed over to him, whether sound judgment has been perceived in him or not. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is never handed over to him except upon perceiving sound judgment. This is also the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both.

Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for Abu Hanifa from this verse, saying: there is no doubt that the term rushd applies to intellect in general, and Allah stipulated rushd in an indefinite form and did not stipulate every kind of rushd. So the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that once intellect is attained, what the verse stipulates has been attained. Therefore, it would necessitate the permissibility of handing over property to him, and abandoning this ruling for the period under twenty-five years, so it is obligatory to act according to the verse for the period beyond twenty-five years. It may be answered that He said: ﴿Test the orphans﴾, and there is no doubt that the intended testing is in matters related to the interests of preserving property. Then He said: ﴿Then, if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over﴾, and it must be that what is meant is: if you perceive in them sound judgment in preserving property and managing its interests. For if this is not the meaning, the structure of the text falls apart and the parts would have no connection to one another. Once this is established, we know that the condition required in the verse is the attainment of rushd in safeguarding the property. At this point, Abu Bakr al-Razi's argument collapses, and indeed this verse becomes evidence against him, because He made the safeguarding of property's interests a condition for handing it over to him. If this condition is missing after twenty-five years, then it is necessary that property not be handed over to him. Also, a clear analogy (qiyas jali) strengthens the argument from this text, because a child is denied his property only due to the absence of intellect that guides how to preserve property and how to benefit from it. If this meaning is present in a young man or an old man, he has the same ruling as a child. Thus it is established that there is no basis for the view of those who say that when he reaches twenty-five years, his property is handed over to him even if sound judgment has not been perceived in him.

**Fifth issue:** If he reaches puberty with rushd and then changes and becomes foolish (safih), he is placed under interdiction according to al-Shafi'i, and he is not placed under interdiction according to Abu Hanifa. This issue has already been discussed under His saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾. A clear analogy also indicates this, because this verse indicates that if he reaches puberty without rushd, his property is not handed over to him. The reason his property is not handed over to him is so that the property does not become wasted, and so that it remains reserved for the day of his need. This meaning exists in foolishness that arises later, so it is necessary to take it into account. And Allah knows best.

**Sixth issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf said: the benefit of indefinitely stating rushd is to draw attention to the fact that what is considered is rushd in disposing of property and in trade. Or it indicates that what is considered is the attainment of some degree of rushd and the appearance of some trace of it, so that the complete attainment of rushd is not awaited.

**Seventh issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf said: Ibn Mas'ud recited "fa-in ahastum" (if you sense), with the meaning of "ahasstum" (you sensed), and he said:

*"He sensed it, so they were fierce toward him."*

It is also recited as rashadan (with two fathas) and rushudan (with two dammas).

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then hand over to them their property﴾. The meaning is that when the two conditions are fulfilled, namely reaching puberty and the perception of sound judgment, it becomes obligatory to hand over their property to them. Allah did not mention full intellect along with these two conditions, because the perception of sound judgment is not achieved except with intellect, since it is an added matter beyond intellect.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not consume it extravagantly or hastily before they grow up﴾. That is, extravagant and hasty in reaching their maturity. Or it means: due to your extravagance and haste in their maturity, you are careless in spending it, saying, "We will spend as we wish before the orphans grow up, and then they will take it from our hands." Then He divided the matter according to whether the guardian is rich or poor, saying: ﴿Whoever is rich should abstain﴾. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: one who abstains from something (ista'affa 'an al-shay') and one who refrains (affa) is one who refrains from it and leaves it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: istaʿaffa is more emphatic than ʿaffa, as if one seeks an increase in chastity. And He said: ﴿Whoever is poor may eat with reasonable provision﴾.

Scholars differed over whether the guardian may benefit from the orphan's property. There are several opinions on this issue. One of them is that he may take from the orphan's property an amount he needs and an amount equal to the wage for his work. Those who held this view argued with several arguments:

First: His saying, ﴿And do not consume it extravagantly﴾, implies that he may consume it to the extent of need.

Second: He said: ﴿Whoever is rich should abstain, and whoever is poor may eat with reasonable provision﴾. His saying, ﴿Whoever is rich should abstain﴾, does not mean prohibiting the rich guardian from benefiting from his own property. Rather, it means prohibiting him from benefiting from the orphan's property. Since that is the case, it follows that His saying, ﴿Whoever is poor may eat with reasonable provision﴾, is permission for the guardian to benefit from the orphan's property to the extent of need.

Third: His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ [al-Nisa: 10]. This is evidence that the property of an orphan may be consumed both unjustly and justly. Were it not so, His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾, would have no purpose. This indicates that a needy guardian may eat from his property with reasonable provision.

Fourth: what has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a man said to him: "I have an orphan under my guardianship. May I eat from his property?" He said: "With reasonable provision, without accumulating wealth and without protecting your property with his property." He said: "May I strike him?" He said: "As you would strike your own child."

Fifthly: it is reported that Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to Ammar, Ibn Mas'ud and Uthman ibn Hunayf: "Peace be upon you. To proceed: I have assigned to you a sheep every day, half of it for Ammar, a quarter for Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and a quarter for Uthman. Indeed, I have placed myself and you in relation to Allah's property in the position of the guardian of an orphan's property: whoever is wealthy should abstain, and whoever is poor should eat in a reasonable manner." And it is related from Ibn Abbas that a guardian of an orphan said to him: "May I drink from the milk of his camels?" He said: "If you tend their strayed animals, repair their watering trough, apply tar to their mangy camels, and water them on the day they come to water, then drink, without harming the offspring and without excessive milking." And also from him: "He may strike with his hand along with their hands, and eat in a reasonable manner, and let him not wear a turban or anything above it."

Sixthly: since the guardian has undertaken to manage the child's affairs, it is necessary that he be able to eat from his property in proportion to his labour, by analogy with the collector who takes and gathers the zakat, for he is allotted a share of those alms. So it is here too. This is the explanation of this position.

The second position: he may take from the orphan's property, to the extent he needs, as a loan (qard), and then when he becomes well-off he repays it; if he dies without being able to repay, there is nothing upon him. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliyah, and it is the majority of reports from Ibn Abbas. Some scholars restricted this lending to the principal capital of wealth, such as gold, silver and others. As for consuming the milk of livestock, using slaves and riding animals, it is permissible for him provided it does not harm the property. This is the view of Abu al-Aliyah and others, and they argued that Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you hand over to them their property﴾, so He made the handing over of property to them the ruling concerning property.

The third position: Abu Bakr al-Razi said: "What we know from the school of our companions is that he does not take either as a loan or as a beginning (of ownership), whether he is wealthy or poor." He argued for this with verses. Among them is His saying: ﴿Give orphans their property﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin﴾. Among them is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blaze﴾ [an-Nisa: 10]. Among them is His saying: ﴿And that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ [an-Nisa: 127]. Among them is His saying: ﴿And do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188]. He said: "This verse is definitive (muhkam), restricting an orphan's property for his guardian in both wealth and poverty." His saying: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ is ambiguous (mutashabih) and open to more than one meaning, so it must be referred back, because of its ambiguity, to those definitive verses.

But in my view, this verse does not indicate what al-Razi claimed. As for His saying: ﴿And give orphans their property﴾ [an-Nisa: 2], it is general, whereas the verse we are discussing is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾, it applies to this case only if it is established that the guardian's eating from the child's property in a reasonable manner is injustice, and the dispute is precisely about that. This is the same answer regarding His saying: ﴿And do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188]. As for His saying: ﴿And that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ [an-Nisa: 127], it applies to the point of dispute only if it is established that this eating is not justice, and the dispute concerns only that. Thus it is established that his argument at this point is invalid and weak. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿So when you hand over to them their property, then call witnesses against them﴾.

Know that the community (ummah) agrees that when a guardian hands over the property to the orphan after he has reached maturity, it is preferable and more cautious for him to call witnesses against him, for several reasons:

The first: if the orphan has evidence of receiving the property, he is further from claiming what is not his.

The second: if the orphan makes a false claim, the guardian can produce the testimony that he handed over his property to him.

The third: that the guardian's trustworthiness and innocence be made manifest. A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever finds a lost item (luqatah), let him call upon two just witnesses, and let him neither conceal it nor hide it." So he commanded him to call witnesses so that his trustworthiness would be shown and suspicion removed from him. Thus it is established, by the consensus and reason we have mentioned, that the more cautious course is to call witnesses.

They differed over whether, if the guardian claims after the orphan's maturity that he has handed the property over to him, he is to be believed. Likewise, if he says: "I spent on him during his childhood," is he to be believed? Malik and al-Shafi'i said: he is not believed. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: he is believed. Al-Shafi'i argued from this verse, for His saying: ﴿then call witnesses against them﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. Al-Shafi'i also said: the guardian (qayyim) is not trusted by the orphan; he is trusted only by the authority of the Law. Abu Bakr al-Razi criticised this statement, with great foolishness, and said: "If what he mentioned were a reason for denying belief, then a judge would have to be disbelieved when he tells the orphan: 'I have handed it over to you,' because he has not entrusted him. Likewise he would have to say of a father who, after the child's maturity, says: 'I have handed your property over to you,' that he is not believed, because he has not entrusted him. He would also be obliged to impose liability on them if, after maturity, they both agree that the property has perished, because he kept his property without being entrusted with it." It is said to him: "Your statement is far removed from the meanings of jurisprudence. As for the comparison with the judge, it is far-fetched, for the judge is an arbiter, so suspicion must be removed from him so that his judgment may be binding; otherwise, anyone against whom the judge rules could attribute to him lying, bias and flattery, and then the judge would need another judge, leading to an infinite regress (tasalsul). It is known that this meaning does not exist in the case of an orphan's guardian. As for the father, the difference is clear for two reasons:

The first: his compassion is more complete than that of a stranger, and the lack of suspicion regarding the father does not entail the lack of suspicion regarding a stranger. As for when they agree after maturity that the property has perished, we say: if he admits that it perished through his negligence, then liability is imposed on him here; but if he admits that it perished not through his negligence, then here his word must be accepted, otherwise that would become an obstacle preventing people from accepting guardianship, and this serious matter would suffer disorder. As for calling witnesses when returning the property after maturity, it does not lead to this harm, so the difference is evident. What confirms this difference is that before this verse He mentioned something indicating that a circumstance arose that gives rise to suspicion, namely His saying: ﴿And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, before they grow up﴾. This indicates that it is customary for guardians to frequently commit injustice against orphans and children. Thus this verse indicates that the causes of suspicion regarding an orphan's guardian are strongly established."

* * *

Then He said after it: ﴿So when you hand over to them their property, then call witnesses﴾, which indicates that the purpose of it is the protection of the child's interest, for if he cannot claim to have handed over the property except in the presence of a witness, that prevents him from wrongdoing, cheating and diminishing it. And since this is the case, we know that His saying "then call witnesses" is obligatory by the apparent force of the command, and likewise the circumstances and interests require it. Then al-Razi said: "What indicates that he is believed without witnesses is the agreement of all that he is commanded to keep and preserve it as a trust, until he delivers it to the orphan at the time of its entitlement. So he is in the position of deposits and profit-sharing (mudarabat), and therefore he must be believed on the return just as the depositary is believed on the return of a deposit." It is said to him: As for the difference between this case and the case of a deposit, al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, has already stated it, and your objection to that difference has already been refuted. Moreover, your habit is to disregard the Book of Allah in favour of a weak analogy that you imagine, and such jurisprudence is conceded to you, and sharing it with you is not required. And success is from Allah.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is sufficient as Reckoner (hasib)﴾. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Azhari said: hasib may mean "one who reckons" (muhasib), or it may mean "sufficient" (kafi). From the first is the expression people use to a man as a threat: "Allah is his hasib," meaning Allah will call him to account for the wrongdoing he commits. Similar to our saying hasib in the sense of muhasib is our saying shareeb in the sense of mushārib (one who drinks with another). From the second is their saying: "Allah is your hasib," meaning "Allah is sufficient for you."

Know that this is a warning to the guardian of the orphan and an informing of him that He the Exalted knows his inner state just as He knows his outward state, so that he does not intend or do with his property anything unlawful, and that he maintains complete trustworthiness in this until his property reaches its owner. This purpose is achieved whether we interpret hasib as "reckoner" or as "sufficient."

Know also that the bā' in His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah﴾ and ﴿Sufficient is your Lord﴾ [al-Isra: 65] is, throughout the Qur'an, superfluous (za'idah). This is how al-Wahidi reported it from al-Zajjaj. And "hasiban" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: Allah suffices, in the state of being a reckoner, and in the state of being sufficient.

**[p. 158]**

The Almighty said: ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much, an obligatory share.﴾

Know that this is the fourth category of rulings mentioned in this surah, and it concerns inheritance (mawarith) and the fixed shares (fara'id). The verse contains several issues.

**The first issue:** the occasion of revelation of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari died leaving three daughters and a wife. Two men from his paternal cousins, who were his executors (wasiyyan), came; they were called Suwayd and 'Arfajah, and they took his property. Aws's wife came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and related the matter, and she mentioned that the two executors had given her nothing, and had given his daughters nothing of the wealth. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Return to your house until I see what Allah brings about regarding your matter." Then this verse was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it indicated that men have a share and women have a share, but Allah, exalted is He, did not specify the amount in this verse. So the Messenger ﷺ sent to the two executors and said: "Do not touch any of Aws's property." Then afterward this was revealed: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ (al-Nisa: 11), and the obligatory share of the husband and the share of the woman were revealed. The Messenger ﷺ, upon him be prayers and peace, then ordered the two executors to give the wife an eighth and to keep the share of the daughters. After that, he ﷺ sent to them both, saying: "Give the daughters' share to them," and they gave it to them. This is what is said regarding the occasion of revelation.

**The second issue:** The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) did not give inheritance to women or children. They would say: "None inherits except one who thrusts with spears, defends the territory, and seizes the spoils." Allah, exalted is He, clarified that inheritance is not restricted to men; rather, it is a matter shared between men and women. So He mentioned this general principle in this verse, and then mentioned the detail afterward. And there is no impediment: when a people have a custom of giving inheritance only to the adults and not to the young, nor to women, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, may transfer them from that custom little by little, gradually. This is because departing from a custom is difficult and heavy on the soul; when it is done all at once, its impact on the heart is great, but when it is gradual, it becomes easy. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, first mentioned this general principle, and then followed it with the detail.

* * *

**The third issue:** Abu Bakr al-Razi (al-Jassas) used this verse as evidence for the inheritance of dhawu al-arham (distant blood relatives, such as those not among the fixed-share heirs). He said: Because paternal aunts, maternal aunts, and the children of daughters are among the close relatives, it is obligatory that they enter under His words: ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave.﴾ At most, the amount of that share is not mentioned in this verse; but we establish that they deserve the basic share by this verse, and as for the amount, we derive it from other proofs.

Our companions (the Hanafi scholars) answered him in two ways:

The first: He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿an obligatory share﴾, meaning a determined share. By consensus (ijma'), dhawu al-arham do not have a determined share. Therefore it is established that they are not included in this verse.

The second: This verse is restricted to the close relatives. So why do you say that dhawu al-arham are among the close relatives? The clarification of this is that either "the close relatives" means those who are closer than something else, or it means those who are closest of all things. The first is invalid, because it would imply that most of creation enters under it; for every person has a kinship with others, either by a near connection or a distant one, namely the connection to Adam, peace be upon him, and necessarily he is closer to him than his descendants. Thus it would follow that all creation enters under this text, which is invalid. Since this possibility is invalid, the text must be taken to mean the second possibility: that "the close relatives" are those who are closest of all people to the deceased, and that is none other than the parents and the children. Therefore it is established that dhawu al-arham do not enter into this text.

It may be said: If we take "the close relatives" to mean the parents, it would entail repetition. We reply: "The close" (al-aqrab) is a genus under which two species fall: the parent and the child. So it is established that He mentioned the parent, then mentioned "the close relatives," and so the meaning is that He mentioned the species, then mentioned the genus, and no repetition follows.

**[p. 159]**

**The fourth issue:** Regarding His words "nasiban" (a share) in its case-ending, there are several possibilities:

The first: It is in the accusative of specification (al-nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas), meaning: "I mean a fixed, determined, obligatory share."

The second: It may be in the accusative of the verbal noun (masdar), since nasib is a noun with the sense of a verbal noun, as if it was said: "an obligatory apportioning," like His words: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾ (al-Nisa: 11), meaning "a fixed apportionment."

**The fifth issue:** The root meaning of fard (obligation/fixed share) is notching or cutting (al-hazz). For this reason, the notch in the bow's string-notch (siyah al-qaws) is called fard, and the notch in arrows (al-qidah) is also called fard; it is a mark that distinguishes it from others. And the fursah (fursa) is the mark at the water-dividing point, by which every person with a right knows his right of drinking. This is the root meaning of fard in the lexicon. Then, the companions of Abu Hanifa restricted the term fard to what is known to be obligatory by a definitive proof, and the term wajib (obligatory) to what is known to be obligatory by a presumptive proof. They said: Because fard is an expression for notching and cutting, while wujub is an expression for falling; it is said: "wajabat al-shams" when the sun set, and "wajaba al-ha'it" when the wall fell, and "sami'tu wajbatan," meaning a fall. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when their sides fall (wajabat junubuha)﴾ (al-Hajj: 36), meaning they fell. Thus it is established that fard is an expression for notching and cutting, and that wujub is an expression for falling. And there is no doubt that the effect of notching and cutting is stronger and more complete than the effect of falling. For this reason, the companions of Abu Hanifa restricted the term fard to what is known to be obligatory by a definitive proof, and the term wujub to what is known to be obligatory by a presumptive proof.

Having understood this, we say: What they have established decides against them, that this verse does not encompass dhawu al-arham. This is because the inheritance of dhawu al-arham is not among what is known by a definitive proof through the consensus of the Ummah; therefore their inheritance is not a fard. The verse only encompasses the prescribed inheritance (al-tawrith al-mafrud), so it necessarily follows that with certainty this verse does not encompass dhawu al-arham. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, Verse 8**

[Page 160]

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word.﴾

There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue:** Know that His statement, ﴿when the division is attended﴾, does not specify which division is meant. For this reason, the exegetes have several opinions about it.

The first opinion: when God, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse that women share with men the right to an inheritance, and He knew that among the relatives some inherit and some do not, and that those who do not inherit may attend the time of the division, then if they were left completely deprived, this would weigh heavily on them. Therefore God commanded that something be given to them at the division, so that good manners and good companionship would be achieved. Then those who hold this view differ. Some say that this is obligatory, and some say that it is recommended (mandub). As for those who hold that it is obligatory, they differ on several matters.

One of them: some say that if the heir is an adult, he is obliged to give those who attend the division a portion of the property, in an amount that his soul is content to give. If the heir is a minor, the guardian is obliged to give them from that property. Others say that if the heir is an adult, he is obliged to give from that property, and if he is a minor, the guardian is obliged to apologize to them and say: "I do not own this property; it belongs to these weak ones who do not understand what rights they have. When they grow up, they will recognize your right." This is the "kind word".

[Page 161]

The second: al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said that this giving (al-radkh) applies only to the division of physical objects. When the matter reaches the division of lands, slaves and similar things, he says to them a kind word, such as saying to them: "Go, may God bless you."

The third: they said that the amount which must be given (al-radkh) is a small thing, and there is no specified measure for it by consensus (ijma').

The fourth: that on the assumption that this ruling is obligatory, this verse is abrogated (mansukhah). Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Ata, said: "This verse is abrogated by the verse of inheritance." This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Dahhak. In the narration of Ikrimah, he said: "The verse is muhkamah (not abrogated)." This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. These scholars used to give those who attended some of the estate.

It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq divided his father's inheritance while Aisha was alive, and he did not leave anyone in the house without giving him something, and he recited this verse. All of this is the detail of the view of those who said that this ruling was established as obligatory.

Others said that it was established as recommended and desirable, not as an obligation or a requirement. This recommendation applies only when the heirs are adults. If they are minors, there is nothing but the kind word. This is the position on which the jurists of the cities (fuqaha' al-amsar) rely. They argued that if these people had a specified right, God, exalted is He, would have explained the amount of that right, as He did with the other rights. Since He did not explain it, we know that it is not obligatory. Also, if it were obligatory, the motivation to transmit it would have been strong, because of the intense eagerness of the poor and needy to know its measure. If it were so, it would have been transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur). Since this is not the case, we know that it is not obligatory.

**The second opinion** concerning the interpretation of the verse: that the intended meaning of "the division" is the bequest (wasiyyah). When those who do not inherit, from among the relatives, orphans and needy, attend it, God, exalted is He, commands that a share of that bequest be given to them, and He says to them along with that a kind word at the time, so that this will be a cause for joy reaching them in the present and in the future. The first opinion is more preferable, because the inheritance was mentioned earlier and the bequest was not mentioned earlier. It may be said that this opinion is preferable, because the verse preceding it concerned the bequest.

**The third opinion** concerning the interpretation of the verse: His statement, ﴿when the division is attended by relatives﴾, means by "relatives" those who inherit, and by ﴿orphans and the needy﴾ those who do not inherit.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word﴾. His statement "provide for them" refers to the relatives who inherit, and His statement ﴿speak to them a kind word﴾ refers to the orphans and the needy who do not inherit. This view is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

**The second issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in His statement ﴿provide for them from it﴾ refers to what the parents and the close relatives left. Al-Wahidi said: the pronoun refers to the inheritance. In this case, the reference is to the meaning of the division, not to its wording, as in His statement: ﴿Then he brought it out from his brother's bag﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. The "sa'" (drinking vessel) is masculine and is not referred to by a feminine pronoun, but it was intended as "mashrabah" (a drinking bowl), so the pronoun referred to the meaning and not to the wording. According to this reading, the intended meaning of "the division" is "the thing divided", because provision comes from what is divided, not from the act of division itself.

**The third issue:** He mentioned the orphans before the needy because the weakness of the orphans is greater and their need is more pressing. Therefore, giving charity to them is more excellent and greater in reward.

[Page 161 continued]

**The fourth issue:** The most likely view is that the intended meaning of "the kind word" is that one should not follow the gift with reminders of favor (mann) or harm (adha) in speech. Or it may mean a promise of more in the future and an apology to the one to whom nothing was given.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 9:

God's words: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them. So let them fear God and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first issue:** The conditional clause, which is his words ﴿if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them﴾, is a relative clause (ṣilah) modifying "those who" (alladhīna). The meaning is: "Let those fear whose characteristic is that, if they left behind offspring who were weak, they would fear for them." As for the one over whom they would fear, it is not specified, and we will mention the views of the exegetes (mufassirūn) on it.

**The second issue:** There is no doubt that his words ﴿let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them﴾ require caution on behalf of weak offspring. The exegetes have several views on this:

The first view: This is addressed to those who sit beside a sick person and say, "Your offspring will not avail you anything against God, so bequeath your wealth to so-and-so and so-and-so." They keep urging him to bequeath to outsiders until nothing at all of his wealth remains for the heirs. So it is said to them: Just as you dislike your children remaining in weakness and hunger without wealth, fear God and do not compel the sick person to deprive his weak children of his wealth. The sum of the matter is that you would not accept such an act for yourself, so do not accept it for your Muslim brother. On the authority of Anas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself."

The second view: Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit said: I asked Miqsam about this verse, and he said: It concerns the man whom death is approaching and who wishes to bequeath to outsiders. Whoever is with him says to him, "Fear God and keep your wealth for your child," even though that person himself would like to be bequeathed to. According to the first view, the verse is taken as forbidding those present from encouraging the bequest; according to the second view, it is taken as forbidding those present from forbidding the bequest. The first is preferable, because his words ﴿if they left behind them weak offspring﴾ resemble the first view and are closer to it.

The third view: It is possible that the verse is addressed to one whose end is near, and the intended meaning is to forbid him from excessive bequests, so that his heirs are not left lost and hungry after his death. Then, if this verse was revealed before the bequest was limited to one third, the meaning is that he should not make the estate wholly consumed by the bequest. If it was revealed after the bequest was limited to one third, the meaning is that he should also bequeath one third, but even reduce it if he fears for his offspring. It is related from many of the Companions that they bequeathed small amounts for this reason, and they used to say: "A fifth is better than a quarter, and a quarter is better than a third." The report about Sa'd supports this, namely the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "A third, and a third is a lot. It is better for you to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them destitute, begging from people."

[Page 162]

The fourth view: This is a command to the guardians of an orphan. It is as if God the Exalted said: Let those who fear for their children after their death, lest the wealth of the weak orphan, who is the offspring of another, be lost while he is in their care, fear. The purpose of the verse according to this view is that God, glory be to Him, moves them to preserve his wealth, and that they place themselves in its custody, and the caution in this matter is in the position of what a person loves for his own offspring, had he left them behind with wealth. The Qadi said: This is more fitting with what precedes and follows of the verses concerning orphans, for God made the last of what He called them to, regarding the preservation of the orphan's wealth, to remind them of the state of themselves and their offspring if they imagine it. There is no doubt that this is among the strongest incentives and motivations for this purpose.

**The third issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari) said: It has been read as ḍu'afā', ḍu'afá, and ḍa'afá, like sukārā and sakārá. Al-Wāḥidī said: Ḥamzah read ﴿ḍi'āfan khāfū 'alayhim﴾ with imālah (the inclination of the vowel toward i) in both words. Then he said: The reason for inclining ḍi'āf is that any form on the pattern fi'āl whose first letter is an elevated consonant with a kasrah, such as ḍi'āf, ghilāb, and khibāb, is good to incline. That is because the voice ascends with the elevated consonant and then descends with the kasrah, so it is preferable not to ascend with emphasis after the kasrah until the sound is produced in one manner. As for the inclination in (khāfū), it is good because it demands the kasrah that is in (khiftu). Then he said: ﴿So let them fear God and speak words of appropriate justice﴾, which is like a restatement of what preceded, as if he said: So let them fear God regarding the matter previously mentioned and its caution, and let them speak words of appropriate justice when they wish to move others to an action or deed. The appropriate speech (al-qawl al-sadīd) is justice and correctness in speech.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: The appropriate speech from guardians (awṣiyā') is that they should not harm orphans, and should address them as they address their own children with kindness, and when they speak to them they should say, "O my son, O my child." The appropriate speech from those seated beside the sick person is that they should say: If you wish to bequeath, do not be extravagant in your bequest, and do not harm your children, like the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to Sa'd. The appropriate speech from heirs at the division of the inheritance, to those present who do not inherit, is that they should speak to them gently and single them out for honor.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verse 10:**

The Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans wrongfully, they only fill their bellies with fire, and they will burn in a blaze.﴾

Know that the Exalted emphasized the threat concerning consuming an orphan's property unjustly. The threat recurs many times in these verses, again and again, against whoever does this, as in His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.﴾ And His saying: ﴿Let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them.﴾ Then He mentioned after them this verse on its own, as a threat against whoever consumes their property. All of this is a mercy from God the Exalted toward orphans, because on account of their complete weakness and helplessness they deserve from God additional care and honor. How strongly this threat indicates the vastness of His mercy, the abundance of His pardon and His bounty! For when orphans reach the utmost point of weakness, God's care for them reaches the utmost point.

There are several issues in this verse:

**The first issue:** This verse indicates that the property of an orphan may be consumed without wrongdoing, for otherwise this specification would serve no purpose. This is what we mentioned earlier: a guardian in need may eat from his property in a reasonable manner.

**The second issue:** As for His saying: ﴿they only fill their bellies with fire﴾, there are two views. The first is that it is to be taken literally. Al-Suddi said: when a man consumes an orphan's property unjustly, he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with flames coming out of his mouth, his ears, and his eyes, and everyone who sees him will recognize that he consumed an orphan's property. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw a people who had lips like the lips of camels, and an angel had been assigned to them who takes hold of their lips and then places in their mouths a stone of fire that comes out from their lower parts. I said, 'O Jibril, who are these?' He said, 'These are the ones who consume the property of orphans unjustly.'"

The second view is that this is a figurative extension, and the meaning is that consuming an orphan's property is like consuming fire, in that it leads to fire and necessitates it. The name of one of two mutually implying things may be applied to the other, as in His saying: ﴿and the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. The Qadi said: this view is better than the first, because His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only fill their bellies with fire﴾ refers to each individual, so interpreting it in the figurative sense we mentioned is preferable.

**The third issue:** One may say: eating occurs only in the belly, so what is the benefit of His saying: ﴿they only fill their bellies with fire﴾?

Its answer: it is like His saying: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167]. Speech occurs only with the mouth. And He said: ﴿but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46]. The heart is only within the breast. And He said: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. Flying occurs only with wings. The purpose of all of this is emphasis and intensification.

**The fourth issue:** Although He mentioned eating, what is intended by it is every kind of destruction, for the harm to the orphan does not differ whether his property is destroyed by eating or by another means. He mentioned eating and intended by it all destructive dispositions for several reasons:

First: most of an orphan's property at that time consisted of livestock, whose meat one eats and whose milk one drinks. So the speech came in accordance with their customs.

Second: it is customary that one who spends his wealth on whatever he wishes, whether for good or for evil, is said to have "eaten" his wealth.

Third: eating is the most important of the dispositions sought from property.

**The fifth issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) said: the verse indicates the threat against everyone who does this act, whether he is a Muslim or not, because His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ is general and includes everyone. Thus it indicates certainty regarding the threat. And His saying: ﴿and they will burn in a blaze﴾ necessitates the certainty that if they die without repentance, they will definitely burn in this blaze.

As for the answer to this, we have mentioned it in full in Surah al-Baqarah. Then we say: why is it not possible that this threat is specific to disbelievers, based on His saying: ﴿and the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254]?

Then the Mu'tazilah said: it is also not permissible that the consumption of a small amount of his property falls under this threat, because the threat is conditional upon there being no repentance and no obedience greater than that disobedience. Since this is the case, what is certain is that one who is among the people of the threat is one whose disobedience is a major sin and is not accompanied by repentance. Therefore it is necessary to seek the amount that counts as large from the property consumed. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: its amount is five dirhams, because that is the amount for which the threat was stated in the verse about hoarding (kanz) in withholding zakat (obligatory alms).

This is the gist of what the Qadi mentioned. It is said to him: you have contradicted the apparent meaning of this generality in two respects.

One: you added to it the condition of the absence of repentance.

Two: you added to it the condition that it not be minor. And if that is permissible for you, why is it not permissible for us to add to it the condition of the absence of pardon? At most one would say: we have not found evidence indicating that pardon occurs. But we answer this in two ways:

One: we do not concede that there is no evidence for pardon; rather, the evidence is abundant, as we established in Surah al-Baqarah.

Two: suppose you did not find it. Still, not finding something does not establish the certainty of its non-existence; rather, the possibility remains. In that case, the use of this verse for certainty and definiteness is removed.

*[Page 163]*

**The sixth issue:** The Exalted mentioned the threat against those who withhold zakat in terms of branding: ﴿On the day it is heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads, their sides, and their backs are branded with it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. He mentioned the threat against the consumer of an orphan's property as the filling of the belly with fire. There is no doubt that this threat is more severe. The reason is that in the matter of zakat, the poor person does not own any portion of the nisab (the minimum threshold of wealth); rather, the owner is obligated to transfer to him a portion of his property. Here, however, the orphan is the owner of that property, so withholding it from the orphan is more vile, and therefore the threat is more severe. Also, the poor person may be an adult who is able to earn, whereas the orphan, because of his youth and weakness, is incapable. Therefore the threat concerning the destruction of his property is more severe.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and they will burn in a blaze﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, read (وسَيُصْلَوْنَ) with a dammah on the yaa', meaning they will be made to enter the fire, in the passive voice whose agent is not named. The rest read it with a fatha on the yaa'. Abu Zayd said: it is said that "al-rajul sala al-nar, yaslaha, salan and sila'an," and he is "sali al-nar" (one who burns in the fire), and they are "salun" and "salaa'." The Exalted said: ﴿except for one who is destined to burn in the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 163]. And He said: ﴿more deserving of it for burning﴾ [Maryam: 70]. And He said: ﴿They will burn in it, Hell﴾ [Ibrahim: 29]. Al-Farra' said: al-Sila is the name of fuel, and it is al-Sila'; if you kasra the ص it is extended, and if you fatha it, it is shortened. And whoever puts a dammah on the yaa' is from their saying "asla-hu Allah harr al-nar, is'a'an" (God made him endure the heat of the fire). He said: ﴿So We will make him burn in fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 30]. And the Exalted said: ﴿I will make him burn in Saqar﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26]. The author of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary) said: it was read as (سَيُصْلَوْنَ) with a dammah on the yaa' and with the lam lightened and with it doubled.

**The second issue:** Al-Sa'ir is the blazing fire. It is said: "sa'artu al-nar, as'aruha, sa'ran," so it is maskura and sa'ir. Al-sa'ir is derived from maskura in the way that "kaff khadib" is derived from "makhdubah" (a hand dyed). He said "sa'iran" because what is meant is a fire among fires, unspecified, whose ultimate intensity no one knows except God the Exalted.

**The third issue:** It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on people, and they became wary of mixing with orphans entirely, so the matter became difficult for the orphans. Then the Exalted revealed His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. Some ignorant people said that this verse was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) by that verse, but this is far-fetched, because this verse concerns the prohibition of wrongdoing, and this does not become abrogated. Rather, the intent is that mixing with orphans' property, if it is done in a wrongful manner, is among the greatest gates of sin, as in this verse, and if it is done in the manner of nurturing and kindness, it is among the greatest gates of righteousness, as in His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. And God knows best.

*[Page 164]*

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females. And if there are [only] daughters, two or more, for them is two thirds of what he left; and if there is only one, for her is half.﴾

Concerning this verse there are several issues.
