The First Issue: Know that the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to inherit by two things: one of them is lineage (nasab), and the other is covenant (ʿahd). As for lineage, they did not give inheritance to young children or to females. Rather, they only gave inheritance to those male relatives who fought on horses and took the spoils. As for covenant, it is of two kinds:

The first: alliance (ḥilf). A man in the Jahiliyyah would say to another: "My blood is your blood, my destruction is your destruction; you inherit from me and I inherit from you; you seek vengeance for me and I seek vengeance for you." When they made a pact in this manner, whichever of them died before the other, the living one would have what he had stipulated from the property of the deceased.

The second: adoption (tabanni). A man among them would adopt the son of another, and he would be attributed to him instead of his biological father, and would inherit from him. This adoption is a type of contractual agreement. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), He left them, at the beginning of the matter, in what they had been upon in the Jahiliyyah. Some scholars said: rather, Allah confirmed them in that, saying: ﴿And for each We have made heirs of what is left by parents and close relatives﴾ [al-Nisa': 33], and the meaning is inheritance by lineage. Then He said: ﴿And those whom your oaths have bound, give them their share﴾ [al-Nisa': 33], and the meaning of this is inheritance by covenant. But the earlier scholars said: the meaning of His saying ﴿and those whom your oaths have bound, give them their share﴾ is not a share of property; rather, the meaning is: give them their share of support, sincere counsel, and good companionship. This is the explanation of the causes of inheritance in the Jahiliyyah.

As for the causes of inheritance in Islam: we have mentioned that at the beginning it confirmed alliance and adoption, and added two other matters. The first: emigration (hijrah), so the muhajir would inherit from the muhajir, even if he was a stranger to him, when each of the two was especially close to the other through great association and sincere friendship; and a non-muhajir would not inherit from him, even if he was one of his relatives. The second: brotherhood (muʾākhāh), the Messenger (ﷺ) would establish brotherhood between every two of them, and this was a cause of inheritance. Then Allah, the Exalted, abrogated all these causes by His saying: ﴿And blood relatives are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. And what has been settled upon by the religion of Islam is that the causes of inheritance are three: lineage, marriage, and patronage (walāʾ).

The Second Issue: Narrated by ʿAṭāʾ, who said: "Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ was martyred and left two daughters, a wife, and a brother. The brother took all the property. The woman came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, these are the two daughters of Saʿd, and Saʿd was killed, and their paternal uncle has taken their property.' The Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'Return, for perhaps Allah will decide concerning it.' Then she came back after some time and wept, and this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned their uncle and said: 'Give the two daughters of Saʿd two-thirds, and their mother one-eighth, and what remains is for you.' This was the first inheritance distributed in Islam."

The Third Issue: Regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are two views:

The first: when Allah, the Exalted, explained the ruling concerning the property of orphans and what guardians owe regarding it, He explained how this orphan comes to own property through inheritance, and this could not be done without explaining the general rulings of inheritance.

The second: Allah, the Exalted, established the ruling of inheritance in general terms in His saying: ﴿For men is a share of what is left by parents and close relatives﴾ [al-Nisa': 7]. So after that general statement, He mentioned this detailed explanation, saying: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children.﴾

* * *

The Fourth Issue: Al-Qaffal said: His saying ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ means: Allah says to you a word that brings you to fulfill the rights of your children after your death. The root of iṣāʾ (enjoining) is ittiṣāl (connection): one says waṣā yaṣī when he connected, and awṣā yūṣī when he caused to connect. So when one says awṣānī (he enjoined me), its meaning is that he caused me to reach knowledge of what I need to know. Likewise waṣṣā, which is intensive. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of His saying here, "yūṣīkum" (enjoins you), is "yafriḍu ʿalaykum" (imposes upon you), because the enjoining from Allah is a binding command. The evidence for this is His saying:

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right. This He has enjoined upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and there is no doubt that this is obligatory upon us.

If it is said: In the language one does not say uṣīka li-kadhā (I enjoin you for such-and-such), so how does He say here: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾?

We say: Since enjoining is a speech, for this reason, after His saying ﴿Allah enjoins you﴾, He mentioned a new statement and said ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 29], meaning Allah said to them "forgiveness," because promising is a speech.

The Fifth Issue: Know that He, may He be exalted, began with mentioning the inheritance of children, and He did so because a person's attachment to his child is the strongest of attachments. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fatimah is a part of me." Therefore, for this reason Allah placed their inheritance first.

Know that children have two states: a state of being alone, and a state of being together with the parents. As for the state of being alone, there are three cases, because the deceased either leaves behind males and females together, or leaves only females, or only males.

The First Case: when he leaves behind males and females together. Allah has explained the ruling for this in His saying: ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾.

Know that this implies several rulings: First, if the deceased leaves one son and one daughter, the son has two shares and the daughter has one share. Second, if the heirs are a group of males and a group of females, each male has two shares and each female has one share. Third, if there are other heirs alongside the children, such as the parents and the spouses, they take their shares, and what remains after those shares is divided among the children, so that for the male is what is equal to the share of two females. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ implies these many rulings.

The Second Case: when he dies and leaves only females. He, may He be exalted, explained that if they are more than two, they have two-thirds, and if there is only one, she has half. However, He did not explicitly state the ruling for two daughters. Scholars differed on this. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported that he said: two-thirds is the obligatory share of three or more daughters; as for the obligatory share of two daughters, it is one-half. He argued for this by saying that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if they are women more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, and the word "in" (if) in the language is for conditionality, and this indicates that taking two-thirds is conditional upon their being three or more, and this negates the two daughters receiving two-thirds.

The answer is in several ways:

First: this argument is binding upon Ibn ʿAbbas himself, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if there is only one, for her is half﴾, so He made the attainment of half conditional upon her being one, and this negates the attainment of half as a share for two daughters. Thus it is established that if this argument were sound, it would overturn his own view.

Second: we do not accept that the word "in" indicates the negation of the ruling when the attribute is absent. This is shown by the fact that if the matter were so, a contradiction would arise between these two verses, because consensus has established that the share of two females is either one-half or two-thirds; and if the word "in" were conditional, one would have to say that one of the two is invalid. Thus it is established that holding the conditional sense leads to falsehood, so it is false. Also, He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and if you do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], and said: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer if you fear﴾, and it is not possible for these verses to convey the meaning of conditionality.

Third in the answer: in the verse there is a transposition (taqdim wa-taʾkhir), and the intended sense is: "If they are two or more, then for them is two-thirds." This is the answer to Ibn ʿAbbas's argument. As for the rest of the community, they agreed that the share of two daughters is two-thirds. They said: we know this through several ways:

First: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: we know it from His saying: ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾, because whoever dies and leaves a son and a daughter, the son's share must be two-thirds according to His saying ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾. When the male's share is equal to the share of two females, and the male's share here is two-thirds, it must necessarily follow that the share of the two daughters is two-thirds.

Second: Abu Bakr al-Razi said: if someone dies and leaves a son and a daughter, the daughter's share here is one-third, by the evidence of His saying ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾. When the daughter's share alongside a male son is one-third, then it is more fitting that their share alongside another female child should be one-third, because the male is stronger than the female.

Third: His saying ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ implies that the share of two females is greater than the share of one female; otherwise it would follow that the share of the male is equal to the share of one female, and this is contrary to the text. When it is established that the share of two females is greater than the share of one, we say it must be two-thirds, because there is no one who makes a distinction.

Fourth: We have mentioned in the occasion of revelation of this verse that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave the two daughters of Saʿd ibn al-Rabiʿ two-thirds, and this indicates what we have said.

Fifth: He, may He be exalted, mentioned in this verse the ruling for one daughter and the ruling for three or more, and did not mention the ruling for two. And in explaining the inheritance of sisters He said: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, for her is half of what he left﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], ﴿and if there are two sisters, for them are two-thirds of what he left﴾ [al-Nisa': 176]. Here He mentioned the inheritance of one sister and of two sisters, and did not mention the inheritance of many sisters. So each of these two verses became general in one respect and specific in another. We say: since the share of two sisters is two-thirds, the two daughters are more entitled to that, because they are closer to the deceased than sisters are. And since the share of many daughters does not exceed two-thirds, the share of many sisters should not exceed that either, because the daughter, being more closely connected to the deceased, makes it impossible for the weaker to be greater than the stronger.

This is the entire collection of the arguments mentioned in this chapter. The first three of these arguments are derived from the verse, the fourth is taken from the Sunnah, and the fifth is from clear analogy (qiyas jali).

As for the Third Case: when he dies and leaves only male children. We say: as for a single son, when he is alone he takes the whole property. This is explained in several ways:

The first is from the implication of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾, for this indicates that the male's share equals the share of two females.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said regarding daughters: ﴿And if there is only one, for her is half﴾, so it follows from these two verses together that the share of a lone son is the entire property.

The second: we derive this from the Sunnah, namely His saying, upon him blessings and peace: "Whatever the shares leave, it goes to the nearest male agnate." There is no dispute that a son is a male agnate, and since the son takes everything that remains after the shares, it follows that when there are no shares he takes the whole.

The third: the nearest of the agnates to the deceased is the son, and by consensus he has no fixed portion of the inheritance. So when there is no sharer with a fixed share, he cannot take a particular portion in a way that would take a greater amount than the rest; therefore he must take the whole.

If it is said: the share of two females is two-thirds, so His saying ﴿for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ requires that the share of the male, in absolute terms, be one-third, and this negates that he takes the whole property.

We say: what is meant by it is the state of being together, not the state of being alone, and two proofs indicate this:

*[p. 168 continues]*

The first point: the verse's words "Allah enjoins you concerning your children" require that children exist, and His words "For the male, the like of the portion of two females" require that there be both a male and a female there. The second point: He, exalted is He, mentioned right after it the case of a single heir. All of this applies when a person dies leaving only one son. But if he dies leaving several sons who share the same basis of entitlement with no preference among them, then the property must be divided among them equally. And Allah knows best.

Two questions remain concerning the verse.

**The first question:** There is no doubt that a woman is weaker than a man, for several reasons.

First, her weakness in going out and appearing in public, since her husband and relatives prevent her from doing so.

Second, the deficiency of her intellect and her greater susceptibility to deception and being deceived.

Third, that once she mixes with men she becomes open to suspicion. Since her weakness is established as greater, it is necessary that her share of the inheritance be larger. If it is not larger, then it should be at least equal. So what is the wisdom in Allah making her share half of the man's share?

The answer to this has several aspects.

The first: a woman's expenditure is smaller, because her husband spends on her, whereas a man's expenditure is greater, because he is the one who spends on his wife. Whoever has greater expenditure is more in need of wealth.

The second: a man is superior to a woman in his creation, in his intellect, and in religious offices, such as eligibility for judgeship and leadership of prayer. Also, a woman's testimony is half the testimony of a man. Whoever is like this should receive a greater favour.

The third: a woman has little intellect and great desire, so when abundant wealth is added to her, corruption becomes great. The poet said:

*Leisure, youth and wealth*
*Are a corruption for a man, of what a corruption!*

And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6–7]. The condition of a man is different from this.

The fourth: because of the perfection of his intellect, a man spends wealth on what brings him a good reputation in this world and a great reward in the Hereafter, such as building hospices (*ribat*), aiding the distressed, and supporting orphans and widows. A man is able to do this because he mixes with people a great deal, whereas a woman's mixing with people is little, so she is not able to do that.

The fifth: it is narrated that Ja'far al-Sadiq was asked about this matter, and he said: Hawwa' (Eve) took a handful of wheat and ate it, and took another handful and hid it, then took another handful and gave it to Adam. When she made her own share twice the share of the man, Allah reversed the matter upon her, and made the woman's share half the man's share.

**The second question:** Why did He not say, "For the two females, the like of the portion of the male," or, for example, "For the female, half the portion of the male"?

The answer has several aspects.

The first: since the male is superior to the female, He mentioned him before mentioning the female, just as He made his share twice the share of the female.

The second: His words "For the male, the like of the portion of two females" indicate the superiority of the male by direct implication (*mutabaqah*) and the deficiency of the female by necessary implication (*iltizam*). Had He said, "As you have mentioned," it would have indicated the deficiency of the female by direct implication and the superiority of the male by necessary implication. So the first way was preferred, as an indication that striving to publicize virtues must take precedence over striving to publicize vices. For this reason He said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against them﴾ [al-Isra': 7]. He mentioned "good" twice and "evil" only once.

The third: they used to give inheritance to males only, not to females, and this was the reason for the revelation of this verse. So it was said: It is sufficient for the male that He made his share twice the share of the female; it is not fitting for him to aspire to make the female entirely deprived of inheritance. And Allah knows best.

* * *

*[p. 169]*

**The sixth issue:** There is no doubt that the term "child" (*walad*) applies to a son in the literal sense (*haqiqah*). There is also no doubt that it is used for a grandson through a son, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O children of Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 26], and He said to those who lived in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿O children of Israel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. However, the question is whether the word "walad" applies to a son's son as a metaphor (*majaz*) or as a literal meaning.

If we say it is a metaphor, then we say: It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) that a single word cannot be used at one time in both its literal and its metaphorical sense together. In that case it is impossible for Allah, by His words "Allah enjoins you concerning your children," to intend both the child of the loins (son) and the child of a son (grandson) together.

Know that the way to resolve this difficulty is to say: We do not derive the ruling on a son's child from this verse, but from the Sunnah and from analogy (*qiyas*). But if we wished to derive it from this verse, we would say: The "child" and the "child's child" have not been intended together by this verse. This is because the children of a son do not inherit except in one of two situations: either when the child of the loins is entirely absent, or when the child of the loins does not take the whole inheritance; in that case they divide what remains. But that a son's child should be entitled to inherit together with the child of the loins, in a share-partnership among them as the children of the loins are entitled among themselves, is not the case. On this basis, the indication of this verse concerning "child" and concerning "child's child" does not entail that a single word was intended in both its literal and metaphorical senses together. This is because when it is intended to mean the child of the loins, it is not intended to mean the child's child, and when it is intended to mean the child's child, it is not intended to mean the child of the loins. The conclusion is that this verse is sometimes addressed to the child of the loins and sometimes to the child's child, and in each of these two situations the word means one thing.

As for if we say that the application of the term "child" to the child of the loins and to the child's child is literal, then if we make the word *mushtarak* (homonymous, having two meanings) between them, the difficulty returns. This is because it has been established that it is not permissible to use a homonymous word to express its two meanings together. Rather, it is necessary to make it *mutawati'* (univocal, applying equally) between them, like the word "animal" in relation to man and horse. What shows the correctness of this is His words: ﴿And the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], and there is consensus that this includes the son of the loins and the children of a son. On this assumption, the difficulty disappears.

Know that this discussion we have mentioned, as to whether "son" includes a son's children, applies equally to whether the word "father" and "mother" include grandfathers and grandmothers. There is no doubt that this does occur, on the evidence of His words: ﴿We worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. But the more evident view is that it is not in the literal sense, for the Companions agreed that there is no ruling for the grandfather mentioned in the Qur'an, and if the name "father" included the grandfather in the literal sense, this agreement would not be valid. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** Know that the generality of His words, "Allah enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the portion of two females," has been claimed to be restricted in four cases.

One: a free person and a slave do not inherit from each other.

Two: a killer by deliberate intent does not inherit.

Three: people of two different religions (*millah*) do not inherit from each other. This is a report that the community received with acceptance, and it reached the level of what is widely transmitted (*mustafid*). Two branches follow from it.

*The first branch:* They agreed that a disbeliever does not inherit from a Muslim. As for whether a Muslim inherits from a disbeliever, most scholars said that he also does not inherit. Some said that he does inherit. Al-Sha'bi said: Mu'awiyah judged by this and wrote to Ziyad about it, and Ziyad sent that to Shurayh the judge and ordered him to follow it. Shurayh had previously judged that there was no inheritance, but when Ziyad ordered him, he judged accordingly and would say: "Thus did the Commander of the Faithful judge."

The argument of the first group is the generality of his words, peace be upon him: "People of two religions do not inherit from each other."

The argument of the second group is what is narrated: that Mu'adh was in Yemen, and they mentioned to him that a Jew had died and left a Muslim brother. He said: "I heard the Prophet, peace be upon him, say: 'Islam adds and does not subtract.'" Then they reinforced this by saying: The apparent meaning of His words, "Allah enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the portion of two females," requires that a disbeliever inherit from a Muslim and a Muslim from a disbeliever. However, we restricted it by his words, peace be upon him: "People of two religions do not inherit from each other," because this report is more specific than that verse, and the specific takes precedence over the general. Likewise here, his words "Islam adds and does not subtract" are more specific than his words "People of two religions do not inherit from each other," so it is necessary to give it precedence over it. Indeed, this restriction is more appropriate, because the apparent meaning of this report is reinforced by the generality of the verse, whereas the first report is not so. The most that has been said in reply is that his words "Islam adds and does not subtract" are not explicit in the matter of inheritance, so it is necessary to apply them to all other circumstances.

*The second branch:* If a Muslim apostatizes and then dies or is killed, they agreed that the wealth he acquired during the time of apostasy is not inherited, but goes to the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*). As for the wealth he acquired while he was a Muslim, there are two opinions. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not inherited but goes to the public treasury. Abu Hanifah said: his Muslim heirs inherit it.

The argument of al-Shafi'i is that we have agreed to give preference to his words, peace be upon him, "People of two religions do not inherit from each other," over the generality of His words, "For the male, the like of the portion of two females." The apostate and his Muslim heirs are people of two religions, so inheritance must not take place.

If it is said: It is not permissible to say that the apostate's ownership ceased at the end of his Islam and passed to the heir; on this assumption, the Muslim inherits only from a Muslim, not from a disbeliever.

We reply: If a Muslim were to inherit from an apostate, it would have to be either that he inherits him while the apostate is alive, or after his death. The first is invalid, and it is not lawful for him to dispose of those properties, on the basis of His words: ﴿Except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6], and this is invalid by consensus. The second is invalid, because the apostate at his death is a disbeliever, so it would lead to inheritance taking place between people of two religions, which contradicts the report. Nothing remains here except to say that he inherits from him after his death, by reference back (*istinad*) to the last moment of his Islam. However, the claim of reference back is invalid, because since ownership was not established during the apostate's life, if it were to be established after his death in such a way that it is considered established during his lifetime, it would entail carrying out a disposition in a past time, and that is invalid by the basic dictates of reason. If reference back is interpreted as clarification (*tabyin*), the discussion returns to the claim that the heir inherited from the apostate while the apostate was alive, and we have already refuted that. And Allah knows best.

*The fourth restriction:* Among the restrictions of this verse, and the view of most mujtahids (qualified jurists), is that prophets, peace be upon them, are not inherited from. The Shi'a (partisans of 'Ali) disagreed with this. It is narrated that when Fatimah, peace be upon her, demanded the inheritance and they prevented her from it, they argued with his words, peace be upon him: "We, the company of the prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity." At this point Fatimah, peace be upon her, argued with the generality of His words: "For the male, the like of the portion of two females." It seems she was pointing out that the generality of the Qur'an may not be restricted by a report of a single narrator (*khabar al-wahid*). Then the Shi'a said: Even granting that the generality of the Qur'an may be restricted by a report of a single narrator, it is not permissible here, and its explanation is in three aspects.

The first: that it contradicts His words, exalted is He, reporting about Zechariah, peace be upon him: ﴿He shall inherit me and inherit from the family of Jacob﴾ [Maryam: 6], and His words: ﴿And Solomon inherited David﴾ [al-Naml: 16]. They said: It is not possible to interpret that as the inheritance of knowledge and religion, because that would not be inheritance in the true sense, but rather a new, original acquisition. Inheritance is realized only in wealth, in the literal sense.

Second thing: the passage's main content. Let me produce the translation.

And secondly: the one who needed to know this question were only Fatimah, ʿAli, and al-ʿAbbas, and these were among the great ascetics, scholars, and people of religion. As for Abu Bakr, he had no need at all to know this question, because he was not one who would imagine that he would inherit from the Messenger, peace be upon him. So how would it befit the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to convey this matter to one who has no need for it, and not convey it to one who has the greatest need to know it?

Thirdly: it is possible that his saying, "What we leave behind is charity" (ṣadaqah), is a relative clause (ṣilah) for his saying, "We are not inherited from" (lā nūrath), and the meaning is: the thing that we leave behind is charity, so that thing is not inherited.

If it is said: on this reading, there remains no special privilege for the Messenger in this.

We say: rather, the privilege remains, given the possibility that when prophets resolve to give something in charity, the thing leaves their ownership by the mere resolve, and no heir inherits it from them; and this meaning is absent with respect to others.

The answer: Fatimah, peace be upon her, was content with Abu Bakr's statement after this debate, and consensus was established upon the correctness of what Abu Bakr held, so this objection falls. And God knows best.

* * *

The eighth issue concerning this verse: His saying, "For the male is the like of the portion of two females" (lil-dhakari mithlu ḥaẓẓi l-unthayayn), means "for the male among them," and the returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, as in your saying: "Ghee is two mann for a dirham." And God knows best.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "But if they are women more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he left" (fa-in kunna nisā'an fawqa ithnatayni fa-lahunna thuluthā mā taraka), the meaning is: if the daughters, or the females born, are pure women with no male among them. His saying "more than two" (fawqa ithnatayn) may be a second predicate for "kunna," or it may be an attribute of "nisā'an," meaning women exceeding two. Here there are questions.

First question: His saying, "For the male is the like of the portion of two females," is a statement made to explain the male's share among the children, not to explain the share of the two females; so how is it appropriate to intend it with His saying, "But if they are women," when that is to explain the share of females?

The answer has two aspects:
First: We have shown that His saying, "For the male is the like of the portion of two females," indicates that the portion of two females is two-thirds. So when He mentioned what indicates the ruling for two females, He said after it, "But if they are women more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he left," meaning: if they are a group of mature women, however many they number, then for them is what is for two, namely two-thirds, so it is known that the ruling for a group is the ruling for two without any difference. Thus it is established that this conjunction is appropriate.
Second: The mention of the two females has already preceded, so this statement suffices to make this conjunction fitting.

Second question: Is it valid that the pronouns in "kunna" and "kānat" be undetermined (mubham), with "nisā'an" and "wāḥidatan" serving as their explanation, on the basis that "kāna" is complete (tāmmah)?

Answer: The author of al-Kashshaf mentioned that this is not far-fetched.

Third question: "Nisā'" is a plural, and the minimum of plural is three, so "nisā'" must necessarily be more than two; what is the benefit of the restriction by His saying "more than two"?

Answer: Whoever holds that the minimum plural is two, this verse is his proof. Whoever holds that it is three says: this is for emphasis, as in His saying, "They only eat fire into their bellies," and His saying, "Do not take two gods; He is only one God" [al-Naḥl: 51].

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "But if she is one, for her is the half" (wa-in kānat wāḥidatan fa-lahā al-niṣf), we say: Nāfi' read "wāḥidatun" with a nominative (rafʿ), and the rest read it with an accusative (naṣb). As for the nominative, it is based on "kāna" being complete; the preferred reading is the accusative, because the one preceding it has a predicate in the accusative, namely His saying, "But if they are women," and the estimate is: "if the ones left behind or the ones inheriting are women, then likewise here." The estimate is: "and if the one left behind is one female." Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "al-nuṣf" with a damma on the nūn.

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: "And for his two parents, to each one of them is a sixth of what he left, if he has a child" (wa-li-abawayhi li-kulli wāḥidin minhumā al-sudusu mimmā taraka in kāna lahu walad).

Know that when He, Exalted, mentioned the manner of inheritance of children, He mentioned after it the inheritance of the two parents. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Ḥasan and Nuʿaym ibn Abī Maysarah read "al-sudus" with lightening (takhfīf), and likewise "al-rubuʿ" and "al-thumun."

The second issue: Know that the parents have three states.

The first state: that a child exists with them, and this is what is meant by this verse. Know that there is no dispute that the term "walad" applies to male and female. This state can occur in three ways:
One: that with the two parents there is one male child, or more than one male child; here, the two parents each receive a sixth.
Second: that with the two parents there are two daughters or more; here too the ruling is what we have mentioned.
Third: that with the two parents there is one daughter; here, the daughter has a half, the mother has a sixth, and the father has a sixth by the ruling of this verse. The remaining sixth is also for the father by the ruling of agnatic residue (taʿṣīb). Here there are questions.

First question: There is no doubt that the right of the parents upon a person is greater than the right of his child upon him, and the right of the parents has reached the point that God linked obedience to Him with obedience to them, saying: "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents" [al-Isrāʾ: 23]. If that is so, what is the reason that He made the children's share greater and the parents' share smaller?

The answer to this is in the utmost beauty and wisdom: because the parents have little of their life remaining, so their need for wealth is small; as for the children, they are in the time of youth, so their need for wealth is great, and the difference is evident.

Second question: To what does the pronoun in His saying "wa-li-abawayhi" refer?

Answer: It is a pronoun referring to something not mentioned, and the intended meaning is: "and for the two parents of the deceased."

Third question: What is meant by "the two parents"?

Answer: They are the father and the mother. The original form for the mother is to be called "abah," so "abawān" is the dual of "ab" and "abah."

Fourth question: How is the construction of this verse?

Answer: His saying, "li-kulli wāḥidin minhumā," is a substitute (badal) for His saying "li-abawayhi," by repetition of the governing element. The benefit of this substitution is that if it were said, "and for his two parents is the sixth," its apparent meaning would be that they share in it.

If it is said: why was it not said, "for each one of his two parents is a sixth"?

Page 173

We say: because in substitution and detailing after generalization there is emphasis and reinforcement, and "al-sudus" is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is "li-abawayhi," and the substitution lies between them for clarification.

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: "But if he has no child, and his two parents inherit from him, then for his mother is one-third" (fa-in lam yakun lahu walad wa-warithahu abawāhu fa-li-ummihi al-thuluth).

In the verse there are two issues:

The first issue: Know that this is the second state of the parents' conditions, which is that no child exists with them, and there is no other heir besides them; and this is what is meant by His saying, "and his two parents inherit from him." Here, for the mother is one-third, and that is a fixed share (farḍ) for her, and the remainder is for the father. That is because His saying "and his two parents inherit from him" apparently indicates that he has no heir besides them; and if that is so, the total of the estate belongs to them both. So if the mother's share is one-third, the remainder, which is two-thirds, must be for the father. Here the property between them is "for the male is the like of the portion of two females," as in the case of the children. Two branches follow from what we have mentioned:

The first: The previous verse indicated that the father's fixed share is one-sixth, and in this case he takes two-thirds, but he takes the sixth by fixed share and the half by agnatic residue.
The second: Since it has been established that he takes a half by agnatic residue in this case, it must be that the father, when alone, takes the whole estate, because the characteristic of the agnate (ʿaṣabah) is to take all when alone. All of this is when the deceased has no heir except the two parents. As for when his parents inherit with one of the spouses, most of the Companions held that the husband takes his share, then one-third of what remains is given to the mother, and the remainder is given to the father. Ibn ʿAbbas said: his share is given to the husband, one-third to the mother, and the remainder is given to the father; and he said: "I do not find in the Book of God one-third of what remains." It is reported from Ibn Sirin that he agreed with Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the wife and the parents, but disagreed regarding the husband and the parents, because it leads to the female having the like of the portion of two males. As for the wife, it does not lead to that. The majority's arguments are several:

First: The basic principle of inheritance is that whenever a man and a woman of one kind gather, the male has the like of the portion of two females. Do you not see that the son with the daughter is so? God said: "God enjoins you concerning your children: for the male is the like of the portion of two females" [al-Nisāʾ: 11]. Also the brother with the sister is so; God said: "And if they are brothers and sisters, men and women, then for the male is the like of the portion of two females" [al-Nisāʾ: 176]. Also the mother with the father is so, because we have shown that if there is no heir other than them, then for the mother is one-third, and for the father two-thirds. Having established this, we say: when the husband takes his share, the remainder must remain between the two parents in thirds, with the male having the like of the portion of two females.

Second: The two parents resemble two partners between whom there is property; when some portion of it becomes due to be taken, the remainder remains between them according to the first entitlement.

Third: The husband took his portion by the ruling of the marriage contract, not by the ruling of kinship, so it resembles a bequest (waṣiyyah) in the division of the remainder.

Fourth: If a woman leaves a husband and two parents, then the husband has a half; so if we give the one-third to the mother and the sixth to the father, it would follow that the female has the like of the portion of two males, and this is contrary to His saying: "For the male is the like of the portion of two females."

Know that the first three arguments come back, in their totality, to specifying the generality of the Qur'an by analogy (qiyās). As for the fourth argument, it is a specification of one of the two generalities by the second generality.

Page 174

The second issue: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "fa-li-ummihi" with a kasra on the hamza and the mim, and they stipulated for the permissibility of this kasra that what precedes it be a kasrah letter or a yā'.

As for the first: like His saying, "in the bellies of your mothers" (fī buṭūni ummahātikum).
As for the second: like His saying, "in its mother a messenger" (fī ummihā rasūlan).
When this condition is not present, there is nothing but the damma, like His saying: "And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign" [al-Muʾminūn: 50]. As for the rest, they read the hamza with a damma. As for the reasoning of those who read with a kasra, al-Zajjaj said: they found the damma after the kasra in His saying "fa-li-ummihi" burdensome, because the lām, due to its close connection with "umm," the combined whole became like a single word; and there is no pattern "fiʿul" with a kasra on the fāʾ and a damma on the ʿayn in the speech of the Arabs; so the damma was made a kasra. As for the reasoning of those who read the hamza with a damma, they kept it according to the original form, and it does not necessitate the use of "fiʿul," because the lām is in the status of the separate. And God knows best.

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: "But if he has brothers, then for his mother is one-sixth" (fa-in kāna lahu ikhwatun fa-li-ummihi al-sudus).

Know that this is the third state of the parents' conditions, which is that brothers and sisters exist with them. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: They agreed that one sister does not reduce the mother from one-third to one-sixth, and they agreed that three reduce, and they differed regarding two sisters. Most of the Companions held the view of establishing the reduction (ḥajb) as with three. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they do not reduce, as in the case of one. Ibn ʿAbbas's argument is that the verse indicates that this reduction is conditioned on the existence of brothers, and the word "ikhwah" is a plural, and the minimum plural is three, as established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh); so when three do not exist, the condition of reduction is not met, so the reduction must not occur. It is reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said to ʿUthmān: "By what did the two brothers come to reduce the mother from one-third to one-sixth? God only said, 'But if he has brothers,' and 'the two brothers' in the language of your people are not 'brothers'?" ʿUthmān said: "I cannot reject a judgment that was rendered by those before me and that has proceeded through the regions."

Know that in this narration there is evidence that the minimum plural is three, because Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that together with 'Uthman, and 'Uthman did not deny it. Both of them were of pure Arab lineage and among the scholars of the language, so their agreement is a proof in this matter.

Know also that the scholars have two opinions on the minimum plural. The first is that the minimum plural is two. This is the view of Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, may Allah have mercy on him, and they argued for it with several points:

The first is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Your two hearts have certainly inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], and a single person cannot have more than one heart.

The second is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if they are women above two﴾. The qualification "above two" is only fitting if the word "women" is applicable to two.

The third is the saying: "Two and what is above them is a jama'ah (group)." The proponents of this view claim that the apparent meaning of the Book requires the exclusion (hajb) of the mother by two brothers. However, what we have upheld in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) is that the minimum plural is three. On this basis, the apparent meaning of the Book does not require the exclusion by two brothers; what requires it is analogy (qiyas). Its formulation is that we say: two sisters exclude, and if that is so, two brothers must also exclude. We say that two sisters exclude because we see that Allah the Exalted placed two females in the same position as three in the matter of inheritance. Do you not see that the share of two daughters and the share of three daughters is two-thirds? Likewise, the share of two sisters from the mother and the share of three is one-third. This inductive survey requires that exclusion be achieved by two sisters, just as it is achieved by three sisters. Thus it is established that two sisters exclude, and when this is established for two sisters, it necessarily follows for two brothers, since no one makes a distinction. This is the best that can be said on this point, and it has a difficulty: applying analogy to fixed shares is hard, because their rationale is not understood, so it becomes mere comparison without a common ground. It may be said that it is not relied upon by way of analogy, but by way of induction, because multiplicity is an indicator of generality. However, this method is extremely weak. And Allah knows best.

Know that this was strengthened by the consensus of the Successors (tabi'un) on the rejection of Ibn 'Abbas's view. In usul al-fiqh, the more correct position is that a consensus that arises after a disagreement is authoritative. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: If the brothers exclude the mother from one-third to one-sixth, they do not inherit anything at all. Rather, the father takes all the remainder, which is five-sixths: a sixth by fixed share (fard) and the rest by agnatic residue (ta'sib). Ibn 'Abbas said: The brothers take the sixth from which they excluded the mother, and what remains goes to the father. His argument is that induction shows that whoever does not inherit does not exclude. These brothers, since they excluded, must inherit. The argument of the majority is that when there were no brothers, the property belonged to the two parents, and when the brothers exist, Allah the Exalted mentions them only as those who exclude the mother from one-third to one-sixth. Being an excluder does not necessarily mean being an heir. Therefore, after this exclusion, the property must remain in the ownership of the two parents as it was before. And Allah knows best.

* *

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿after a bequest he bequeaths or a debt﴾.

Know that the matters of bequests are mentioned at the end of this verse, and here there are several issues.

The first issue: When Allah the Exalted mentioned the shares of the children and the parents, He said: ﴿after a bequest he bequeaths or a debt﴾. That is, these shares are only given to these persons after the bequest and the debt are set aside. This is because the first thing removed from the estate is the debt, so that if the debt consumes the entire property of the deceased, the heirs have no right in it. But if there is no debt, or if there is a debt that has been paid and something remains after it, then if the deceased made a bequest, the bequest is taken out of one-third of what remains, and then the remainder is divided as inheritance according to the obligatory shares of Allah.

The second issue: It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "You recite the bequest before the debt, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided the debt before the bequest." Know that his intention, may Allah be pleased with him, was precedence in mention and wording, and his intention was not that the verse requires the bequest to precede the debt in ruling, because the word "aw" (or) does not indicate sequence at all.

Know that the wisdom in placing the bequest before the debt in wording is in two respects:

The first: The bequest is property taken without compensation, so its delivery is difficult for the heirs, and therefore its fulfilment is liable to neglect, unlike the debt, since the hearts of the heirs are at ease about paying it. For this reason, Allah mentioned the bequest before the debt in wording, to urge its fulfilment and encourage its payment. Then He emphasized this encouragement by putting "aw" between the bequest and the debt, to alert that both are equal in the obligation of payment.

The second: Just as the shares of inheritance are postponed after the debt, so they are postponed after the bequest. Do you not see that if he bequeaths one-third of his property, the shares of the heirs are considered only after the one-third is handed over to the beneficiary? So Allah joined the mention of the debt and the bequest to let us know that the shares of inheritance are considered after the bequest just as they are considered after the debt. Rather, He distinguished between the debt and the bequest in another respect: if some of the property is lost, the loss enters into the shares of the beneficiaries and the shares of the heirs, but this is not so with the debt, for if some of the property is lost, the whole debt is settled from what remains, and if the debt consumes it all, the right of the beneficiary and the rights of the heirs are all void. Thus the bequest resembles inheritance in one respect and the debt in another. As for its resemblance to inheritance, it is what we mentioned: whenever some property is lost, the loss enters the shares of the bequest-holders and the heirs. As for its resemblance to the debt, it is because the shares of the heirs are considered after the bequest just as they are considered after the debt. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Someone may say: What is the meaning of "aw" here? Why was it not said: "after a bequest he bequeaths and a debt"? The answer is in two respects:

The first: "Aw" means permissiveness, as when someone says: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin." The meaning is that each of them is fit to be sat with. If you sit with al-Hasan, you are correct; or with Ibn Sirin, you are correct; and if you sit with both, you are correct. But if he said: "Sit with the two men," and you sat with one of them and left the other, you would not be complying with the command. Likewise here, if he had said "after a bequest and a debt," it would have required that in every property both matters must occur, and it is known that this is not so. But when it is expressed with "aw," the meaning is that if one of them exists, the inheritance comes after it, and likewise if both exist.

The second: When the word "aw" is placed after a negation, it takes the meaning of "wa" (and), as in His saying: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or an ingrate﴾ [al-Insan: 24], and His saying: ﴿We forbade them their fats, except what their backs or the entrails carry, or what is mixed with bone﴾ [al-An'am: 146]. Here "aw" carries the meaning of "wa." Likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿after a bequest he bequeaths or a debt﴾: since it carries the meaning of an exception, it is as if He said: "Except that there is a bequest or a debt," so that what is meant is after both of them together.

The fourth issue: Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (yuwsa) with a fatha on the sad, in the passive form whose subject is not named. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sad, attributed to the one who bequeaths, and this is the preferred reading, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿from what he left, if he has a child﴾.

* *

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit. An obligation from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾.

Know that this is a parenthetical statement between the mention of the heirs and their shares, and His saying: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾. It is required of a parenthetical statement that what is inserted should confirm and suit what it is inserted between. So we say: When the Exalted mentioned the shares of the children
[Page 177]
and the shares of the parents, and these shares were different, and the intellects are not guided to the quantity of these determinations, a person may think that if the division had been made in another way, it would have been more beneficial and more suitable for him, especially since the division of inheritance among the Arabs was in this manner, and they used to bequeath to strong men and did not bequeath to children, women, and the weak. So Allah the Exalted removed this doubt by saying: "You know that your intellects do not encompass your interests. You may believe something to be good for you when it is pure harm, and you may believe something to be pure harm when it is pure benefit. As for the Wise, Merciful God, He is the One who knows unseen matters and their outcomes." It is as if it were said: "O people, leave the determination of inheritances by the measures that your intellects find pleasing, and obey Allah's command in these determinations which He has set for you." So His saying: ﴿Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾ is an indication of abandoning what the inclination of the nature leans toward in dividing inheritance among the heirs. And His saying: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾ is an indication of the obligation to submit to this division which the Law has determined and decreed.

The commentators mentioned several meanings of His saying: ﴿nearer to you in benefit﴾:

The first: The meaning is nearer to you in benefit in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah intercedes for some of them on behalf of others. The most obedient of you to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, among the children and the parents, is the highest in rank in Paradise. If the father is higher in rank in Paradise than his child, Allah raises his child to him by his request, so that his eye may be comforted by this. If the child is higher in rank than his parents, Allah raises his parents to him. So He said: ﴿you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾, because neither of them knows whether his benefit in Paradise from this is greater or from that.

The second: The meaning is the manner in which some of them benefit others in this world, through what He has made obligatory of spending on them, rearing them, and defending them.

The third: The meaning is the possibility that this one may die before that, and thus inherit from him, or vice versa.

His saying: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive, meaning: He made this obligatory as an obligation. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾. The meaning is that Allah's division of these inheritances is better than the division toward which your natures incline, because He, the Exalted, knows all knowable things, so He knows what benefits and harms are in the division of inheritances. He is also Wise, who commands only what is most beneficial and best. When the matter is so, His division of these inheritances is better than the division you desire. This is similar to His saying to the angels: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

If it is said: Why did He say ﴿was Knowing and Wise﴾ when He is so now?

We say: Khalil said: Reporting about Allah with these words is like reporting in the present and future tenses, because He, the Exalted, is exalted above being subject to time. Sibawayh said: When the people witnessed knowledge, wisdom, grace, and beneficence, they were amazed, so it was said to them: "Indeed, Allah was like that," and He has never ceased to be described by these attributes.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):

[Page 178]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is one-fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for them is one-fourth of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, then for them is one-eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, presented the categories of heirs in these verses in the best of arrangements. This is because the heir is either connected to the deceased without an intermediary or with an intermediary. If he is connected to him without an intermediary, then the cause of the connection is either lineage (nasab) or marriage (zawjiyyah). Thus three categories arise here. The most noble and highest of them is the connection that arises directly through lineage, and that is the kinship of birth (qarabat al-wilada), which includes children and parents. So God, exalted is He, put the ruling of this category first.

Second: the connection that arises directly through marriage. This category is lower in nobility than the first, because the first is essential (dhati) and this second is incidental (arodi), and the essential is more noble than the incidental. This category is what is intended by this verse which we are now explaining.

Third: the connection that arises through an intermediary, and this is what is called kalala. This category is posterior to the first two for several reasons:

The first: children, parents, husbands and wives are not subject to total exclusion from inheritance, whereas the kalala may be totally excluded.

The second: each of the first two categories is attributed to the deceased without an intermediary, whereas the kalala is attributed to the deceased through an intermediary, and what is established directly is more noble than what is established through an intermediary.

The third: a person's association with parents, children, husband and wife is greater and more complete than his association with the kalala. Great association is a cause of affection and compassion, and that necessitates intense concern for their conditions. So for these three reasons and similar ones, God, exalted is He, delayed the mention of the inheritance of the kalala until after the first two categories. How excellent this arrangement is, and how well it accords with the rules of rational principles.

There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Since He made the share of the male equal to the share of two females in the category of lineage, likewise He made the share of the male equal to the share of two females in the category of cause (i.e., marriage). Know that one and many are equal in the one-fourth and one-eighth, and a child from that spouse and from another are equal in the reduction from a half to a quarter or from a quarter to an eighth. Know also that there is no distinction regarding the child between male and female, nor between son and son's son, nor between daughter and son's daughter. And God knows best.

The second issue: Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: it is permissible for a husband to wash his wife (after death). Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, said: it is not permissible. The argument of al-Shafi'i is that after death she is still his wife, and so it is lawful for him to wash her. The proof that she is his wife is the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾. He called her a wife at the very moment He established for the husband half of her property at her death. If it is established that the husband has half of her property at her death, then it is necessary that she be his wife after her death. If this is established, then it is necessary that it be lawful for him to wash her, because before the marriage it was not lawful for him to wash her, and when the marriage was established it became lawful for him to wash her, and the recurrence (of the ruling with the cause) is an apparent indication of causation. The argument of Abu Hanifa is that she is not his wife and it is not lawful for him to wash her. The proof that the marriage does not continue: if she were his wife, it would be lawful for him after death to have intercourse with her, by His saying: ﴿except from their wives﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6]. If this is established, then it is necessary that the lawfulness of washing not be established, because if it were established, it would be established either together with the lawfulness of looking, which is invalid by His saying, peace be upon him: "Lower your gaze except toward your wife," or without the lawfulness of looking, which is invalid by consensus.

The answer: When the two verses conflict regarding the establishment and non-establishment of marriage, preference must be given. We say: if she were not a wife, the saying ﴿half of what your wives leave﴾ would be metaphorical; and if she were a wife while intercourse with her is not lawful, it would entail specification (takhsis). We have mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence that specification is preferable, so the preference lies on our side. How is this, when we know that in many cases the marriage exists while lawfulness of intercourse does not, such as during menstruation and post-natal bleeding, and during the day of Ramadan, and while she is occupied with performing the obligatory prayer and the obligatory pilgrimage, and while she is in the waiting period (iddah) from intercourse by doubt. Also, we have explained in the disputed matters that the lawfulness of intercourse was established contrary to the (general) proof because of its many benefits. After death, none of those benefits remain, so it returns to the original prohibition. As for the lawfulness of washing, its establishment after death is a source of many benefits, so it is necessary to affirm its continuation. And God knows best.

The third issue: In the verse there is an indication of the superiority of men over women, because when He mentioned men in this verse He addressed them directly, and when He mentioned women He mentioned them in the third person. Also, God addressed men in this verse seven times, and mentioned women in it in the third person fewer times than that. This indicates the preference of men over women. How excellent is His attention to this subtlety, for He preferred men over women in the share, and by this subtlety He drew attention to their greater superiority over them.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if a man leaves an inheritance as kalala, or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they are partners in the third, after any bequest that is made or debt, without harm. An injunction from God. And God is Knowing, Forbearing.﴾

Know that this verse explains the inheritance of the third category of heirs, namely the kalala, who are those connected to the deceased through an intermediary. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: The statements of the Companions regarding the interpretation of kalala are numerous. The preference of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, is that it is a term for anyone other than parents and child. This is the chosen view and the correct opinion. As for Umar, may God be pleased with him, he used to say: kalala is anyone other than a child. It is narrated that when he was stabbed he said: "I used to think that kalala is one who has no child, but I am ashamed to oppose Abu Bakr. Kalala is whoever is other than father and child." There is another narration from Umar on this: suspension (of judgment). He used to say: "Three things, that the Messenger of God ﷺ had clarified them for us would be dearer to me than the world and all that is in it: kalala, caliphate, and usury."

The evidence that indicates the correctness of the view of al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, consists of several points:

The first: Adhering to the derivation of the word kalala, and in this there are several aspects:

The first: It is said: "The kinship (rahim) between so-and-so and so-and-so became kallat" when the relationship became distant, and "so-and-so carried so-and-so, then became kalla from him" when he became distant. Thus the distant relationship was called kalala from this aspect.

The second: It is said: "The man kalla yakullu kallan and kalalah" when he became exhausted and his strength went away. Then they used this word metaphorically for the kinship that arises not from birth, because we have explained that this kinship arises through an intermediary, so there is weakness in it. And by this it becomes clear that it is far-fetched to include parents in kalala, because their affiliation to the deceased is without an intermediary.

The third: Kalala in the basic language is an expression for encompassing. From it comes al-iklil (the crown), because it encompasses the head; and from it al-kull (the whole), because it encompasses what enters it; and it is said "the cloud was crowned (takallala al-sahab)" when it became encompassing on all sides. Knowing this, we say: those other than father and child were only called kalala because they are like a circle encompassing the person and like a crown encircling his head. As for the kinship of birth, it is not like that, for in it some branch off from others and some are generated from others, like a single thing that grows in one continuous line. For this reason the poet said:

A lineage that follows, elder after elder, like a spear, joint upon joint.

As for kinship other than birth-kinship, such as brothers, sisters, paternal uncles and paternal aunts, their lineage has connection and encompassing of the one to whom they are attributed. Thus it is established by these derivational aspects that kalala is an expression for anyone other than parents and child.

The second proof: God, exalted is He, mentioned the word kalala in His Book only twice, in this surah: one in this verse, and the second at the end of the surah, which is His saying: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning kalala. If a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, she has half of what he left﴾ [al-Nisa': 176]. Umar ibn al-Khattab used this verse as evidence that kalala is only one who has no child, saying: "Because what is mentioned here in explaining kalala is that he has no child." However, we say: this verse indicates that kalala is one who has neither child nor parent. That is because God, exalted is He, ruled for the inheritance of siblings while the deceased is kalala, and there is no doubt that siblings do not inherit while the two parents are alive, so it is necessary that the deceased not be kalala while the two parents are alive.

The third proof: God, exalted is He, mentioned the ruling of child and parents in the preceding verses, then followed it with the mention of kalala, and this arrangement requires that kalala be anyone other than parents and child.

The fourth proof: the saying of al-Farazdaq:

You inherited the spear of kingship, not from kalala, from the two sons of Manaf, Abd Shams and Hashim.

This verse indicates that they did not inherit kingship from kalala, and indicates that they inherited it from their fathers, and this requires that the father not be included in kalala. And God knows best.

The second issue: Kalala may be made a descriptive term for the heir and for the deceased. If we make it a description of the heir, the intended meaning is anyone other than children and parents; and if we make it a description of the deceased, the intended meaning is the one whose estate is inherited, other than parents and children. As for the proof that this term is used of the heir: what Jabir narrated, who said: "I fell ill with an illness from which I was healed, near death. The Prophet ﷺ came to me and I said: O Messenger of God, I am a man whom none inherits from except a kalala." He meant by this that he had neither parent nor child. As for its being used of the deceased: the verse we have narrated from al-Farazdaq, for its meaning is that you did not inherit kingship from paternal uncles but from fathers, so he called the paternal uncle kalala, and here he is a testator, not an heir. Knowing this, we say: what is intended by kalala in this verse is the deceased who leaves neither parents nor child, because this description was considered in the deceased who is the testator, not in the heir whose condition does not differ by reason of whether he has a child or a parent or not.

The third issue: It is said "rajul kalala," "imra'ah kalala," and "qawm kalala," and it is not made dual or plural, because it is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-dalala and al-wakala.

Knowing this, if we make it an attribute of the heir or of the deceased, it has the meaning of "one possessing kalala," as one says: "so-and-so is of my kinship (qaraba)," meaning "of those who are my relatives." The author of al-Kashshaf said: it may also be an attribute in the manner of hajaja and faqaqa for the fool.

The fourth issue: His saying, "yuwarathu" (is inherited) has two possibilities:

The first: that it is taken from warithahu al-rajul (a man inherits him), and in this case the man is the one from whom inheritance is taken. Regarding the parsing of "kalala" there are several aspects:

The first: the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the meaning is: "is inherited while being kalala," and kalala is a verbal noun that took the place of a state; its estimate being: "is inherited, being one whose kinship is encompassing (mutakallil al-nasab)."

The second: that His saying "yuwarathu" is a descriptive term for "rajul," and "kalala" is the predicate of "kana," and the estimate is: "if there is a man from whom kalala is inherited."

The third: that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: "is inherited on account of its being kalala."

**The second possibility:** Regarding His words ﴿yuwarathu﴾ (is inherited), it may be derived from *awratha, yuwrithu* (to cause to inherit). On this reading, the man is the heir, and the accusative of *kalalah* (a person who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants) is also parsed in the ways already mentioned.

**The fifth issue:** Al-Hasan and Abu Raja al-Utaridi read *yuwrathu* and *yuwarrathu*, with the light and the intensive forms, both with the active sense.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And if a man or a woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants, and he has a brother or a sister, then each of the two shall have a sixth﴾, there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Here there is a question. He, Exalted is He, said ﴿if a man is inherited from in kalalah, or a woman﴾, and then said ﴿and he has a brother﴾. So He referred to the man with a pronoun, but He did not refer to the woman with one. What is the reason for this?

The answer: al-Farra' said, "This is permissible. When two terms with the same meaning are joined by *aw* (or), it is permissible to attribute the predicate to whichever of them is intended, and it is also permissible to attribute it to both of them. You say, 'Whoever has a brother or a sister, let him maintain ties with him,' meaning the brother, or 'let him maintain ties with her,' meaning the sister. If you say, 'let him maintain ties with both of them,' that is also permissible."

**The second issue:** The commentators here are unanimous that by "brother and sister" is meant the brother and sister from the mother's side. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite: "and he has a brother or a sister from the mother." They judged this way because He, Exalted is He, said at the end of the surah: ﴿Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalalah﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], and there He assigned two-thirds to two sisters and the whole estate to brothers. Here He assigned a third to brothers and sisters. Therefore the brothers and sisters meant here must be other than the brothers and sisters in that verse. So what is meant here is the brothers and sisters from the mother only, while there it refers to the brothers and sisters from both parents, or from the father.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿But if they are more than that, they shall share in the third﴾. Thus He made clear that their share, however many they are, does not exceed one-third.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿after any bequest that is made or debt﴾. On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that the apparent meaning of this verse entails the permissibility of bequeathing the whole estate, or any portion of it. Among the hadiths that agree with this verse is what Nafi' narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not right for a Muslim who has property to bequeath, that two nights should pass while his bequest is not written down with him." This hadith also indicates an unrestricted permission for bequests, however they are intended. However, we say: these general terms are restricted in two respects:

*The first:* the amount of the bequest. It is not permissible to bequeath the whole estate, by the evidence of the Qur'an and the Sunnah. As for the Qur'an: the verses that establish inheritance, in general and in detail. As for the general: His words ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾. It is known that bequeathing the whole estate would entail abrogating (*naskh*, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) this text. As for the detailed: these are the verses of inheritance, such as His words ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾. It is also indicated by His words ﴿Let those fear who, if they left behind weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾. As for the Sunnah: it is the well-known hadith on this subject, namely his words, peace and blessings be upon him: "A third, and a third is much. Indeed, if you leave your heirs wealthy, it is better than leaving them dependent, begging from people."

Know that this hadith indicates several rulings:

First: a bequest is not permissible beyond one-third.

Second: the preferable course is to bequeath less than one-third, because of his saying: "and a third is much."

Third: if a person leaves a small amount of property and his heirs are poor, then the best for him is not to bequeath anything, because of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "If you leave your heirs wealthy, it is better than leaving them dependent, begging from people."

Fourth: it indicates the permissibility of bequeathing all the property if he has no heir, since the prohibition is for the sake of the heirs; when they do not exist, permissibility is required.

*The second:* the restriction of the general scope of this verse concerning the beneficiary. It is not permissible to make a bequest to an heir, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Certainly, there is no bequest to an heir."

**The second issue:** Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: If a person delays zakat and the pilgrimage until he dies, both must be paid from his estate. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: they are not obligatory. The proof of al-Shafi'i: obligatory zakat and obligatory pilgrimage are a debt, so they must be paid by this verse. We say they are a debt because both language and the Shari'ah indicate this. As for language: debt (*dayn*) is an expression for a matter that compels submission. It was said in the well-known supplications: "O You before whom the necks submit," meaning they yielded. As for the Shari'ah: it is related that the woman of Khath'am asked the Messenger (ﷺ) about the pilgrimage that was owed by her father. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "What do you think? If your father had a debt and you paid it, would it have been accepted?" She said: "Yes." He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Then the debt of Allah is more deserving to be paid." If it is established that it is a debt, it must be given precedence over inheritance, because of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿after any bequest that is made or debt﴾. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: what is mentioned in the verse is an absolute debt, and the Prophet (ﷺ) called the pilgrimage a debt to Allah, and an absolute term does not include a restricted one.

We say: this is extremely weak, because once it is established that this is a debt, and it is established by the ruling of the verse that debt takes precedence over inheritance, the intended conclusion necessarily follows. The discussion of the absolute and the restricted is an irrelevant matter that does not undermine this claim. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** Know that His words, Exalted is He, ﴿without causing harm﴾ are in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: he bequeaths them while not causing harm to his heirs.

Know that harm in bequests occurs in several ways:

First: bequeathing more than one-third.

Second: acknowledging, for a stranger, the whole of his property or part of it.

Third: acknowledging a debt against himself that has no reality, in order to block the inheritance from the heirs.

Fourth: acknowledging that a debt he was owed by another has been fully collected and reached him.

Fifth: selling something for a low price, or buying something for a high price, all for the purpose that the property not reach the heirs.

Sixth: bequeathing a third not for the sake of Allah, but for the purpose of reducing the rights of the heirs. This is the form of harm in bequests.

Know that the scholars said: the preferable course is to bequeath less than one-third. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Bequeathing a fifth is dearer to me than bequeathing a quarter, and bequeathing a quarter is dearer to me than bequeathing a third." Al-Nakha'i said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away without making a bequest, and Abu Bakr passed away after making one. If a person makes a bequest, it is good; and if he does not, it is also good."

[Page 183]

Know that it is better for a person to consider the amount he will leave behind and who will inherit from him, and then make his bequest in accordance with that. If his property is small and the heirs are many, he should not bequeath. If the property is large, he should bequeath according to the property and according to their need after him, whether it is little or much. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Causing harm in a bequest is among the major sins." This is indicated by the Qur'an, the Sunnah and reason. As for the Qur'an: His words ﴿These are the limits of Allah, and whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾. Ibn Abbas said regarding bequests: ﴿and whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ refers to what was said about bequests. As for the Sunnah: Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Causing harm in a bequest is among the major sins." And from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a man may do the deeds of the people of Paradise for seventy years, but if he deviates in his bequest, his life is sealed with the evil of his deeds, and he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may do the deeds of the people of the Fire for seventy years, but then he acts justly in his bequest, and his life is sealed with the good of his deeds, and he enters Paradise." He, peace and blessings be upon him, also said: "Whoever cuts off an inheritance that Allah has prescribed, Allah will cut off his share of Paradise." It is known that adding to a bequest is a cutting off from the inheritance. As for reason: opposing the command of Allah at the nearness of death indicates a severe audacity toward Allah, and a great rebellion against submitting to His obligations, and that is among the greatest of major sins.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿as an injunction from Allah﴾, and on this there are two questions:

**The first question:** How is His word ﴿waṣiyyatan﴾ (as an injunction) in the accusative?

The answer has several aspects:

First: it is an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: Allah enjoins you with this as an injunction, like His words ﴿as an obligation from Allah﴾.

Second: it may be in the accusative governed by His words ﴿without causing harm﴾, meaning: the injunction of Allah must not be harmed in that a bequest must not exceed one-third.
