Third: the intended meaning may be: an injunction from Allah concerning the children, and that one should not leave them dependent, begging from the people's faces because of extravagance in bequests. This aspect is supported by the reading of al-Hasan: "without causing harm to an injunction" in the construct form.

**The second question:** Why did He end the first verse with ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾, and end this verse with ﴿an injunction from Allah﴾?

The answer: the word *farḍ* (obligation) is stronger and more emphatic than the word *waṣiyyah* (injunction). So He concluded the explanation of the inheritance of the children with the mention of an obligation, and concluded the explanation of the inheritance of the kalalah with an injunction, to indicate that although all of it must be observed, the first category, which is attending to the condition of the children, takes precedence. Then He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, Forbearing﴾, meaning: He is All-Knowing of whoever acted unjustly or justly in his bequest, ﴿Forbearing﴾ toward the unjust, not hastening to punish him. This is a warning. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 13–14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits (hudud) of Allah. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally; and that is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment.﴾

Page 184

There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: after explaining the shares of inheritance, He, exalted is He, mentioned the promise and the threat, encouraging obedience and warning against disobedience, so He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾. On this there are two points.

The first point: what does "these" (tilka) refer to? There are two opinions. The first is that it refers to the rules of inheritance.

The second opinion is that it refers to everything He mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to this point: the explanation of the wealth of orphans, the rulings on marriage, and the rules of inheritance. This is the view of al-Asamm. The argument for the first view is that the pronoun returns to the nearest thing mentioned. The argument for the second view is that its return to the nearest thing does not preclude its return to the more distant things, and when there is no barrier to its return to the more distant, there is a reason to make it return to all of them.

The second point: the intended meaning of "the limits of Allah" is the prescribed portions that He mentioned and explained. The limit (hadd) of a thing is its boundary by which it is distinguished from other things, as in "the boundaries (hudud) of a house." A statement that indicates the reality of a thing is called its definition (hadd), because that statement prevents anything other than it from entering into it, and "other" means everything besides it.

The second issue: some said that His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ and His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ are specific to those who obey or disobey in the obligations mentioned in this surah. But the scholars (al-Muhaqqiqun) said: rather, it is general, including this and other things, because the expression is general, so it must encompass all. At most, this general statement was mentioned after specific obligations, but this alone does not require restricting the generality. Do you not see that a father may turn to his son and rebuke him over a specific matter, then say: "Beware of opposing me and disobeying me," and his intention is to prevent him from disobeying him in all matters? So it is here. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (nudkhiluhu jannatin, nudkhiluhu naran) with the nun (we) in both places, while the rest read with the ya' (he).

As for the first: it is in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), as in His saying ﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector﴾, then He said ﴿We shall cast﴾ with the nun.

As for the second: its reasoning is evident.

The fourth issue: here there is a question, namely that His saying ﴿He will admit him to gardens﴾ is suitable for the singular, and then His saying after it ﴿abiding therein﴾ is suitable for the plural, so how is the reconciliation between them?

The answer: the word "man" (whoever) in His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾ is singular in form but plural in meaning, so both readings are valid.

The fifth issue: "khalidin" and "khalidan" are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "nudkhiluhu." The sense is: We will admit him, abiding, into the Fire.

* * *

The sixth issue: the Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that the sinful among the people of prayer will remain eternally in the Fire. This is because His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits﴾ is either specific to those who transgressed the limits previously mentioned, which are the limits of inheritance, or it includes that and other things. On either assumption, it necessarily follows that whoever transgresses in inheritance enters this threat, and this is general regarding whoever transgresses, whether he is of the people of prayer or not. So this verse indicates the certainty of the threat and that the threat is eternal. It cannot be said that this threat is specific to those who transgress the limits of Allah, and that this is only realized in the case of the disbeliever, since he is the one who transgresses all the limits of Allah. We say: this is refuted in two ways:

The first: if we took this verse to refer to transgressing all the limits of Allah, the verse would be devoid of benefit, because Allah, exalted is He, forbade Judaism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism, so transgressing all His limits would be to abandon all these prohibitions, and abandoning them would be by practicing Judaism, Zoroastrianism, and Christianity together, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that transgressing all the limits of Allah is impossible. So if the meaning of the verse were that, the verse would cease to be meaningful. Therefore we know that its meaning is any limit whatsoever of the limits of Allah.

The second: this verse is mentioned directly after the verses on the division of inheritance, so the meaning of His saying ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ is transgressing the limits of Allah in the matters mentioned in these verses. On this assumption, this question falls away.

This is the conclusion of the Mu'tazilah's argument. We have discussed this issue at length in Surat al-Baqarah. There is no harm in repeating a portion of it here, so we say:

We agree that this threat is specific to the absence of repentance, because the evidence shows that if repentance occurs, this threat no longer applies. Likewise, it is permissible that it be conditioned upon the absence of pardon, for if there is evidence that pardon occurs, then the continuation of this threat becomes impossible when pardon occurs. We have mentioned the many proofs for the occurrence of pardon. Then we say: this generality is restricted to the disbeliever, and two things indicate this:

The first: when we say to you: what is the proof that the word "man" (whoever) in a conditional context indicates generality? You say: the proof is that an exception may be made from it, and an exception removes from the statement what would have been included had it not been there. So we say: if this proof is valid, it indicates that His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ is specific to the disbeliever, because all sins may validly be excepted from this expression. One says: "Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, except in disbelief, and except in wickedness." The function of an exception is to remove what would have been included without it. This implies that His saying ﴿whoever disobeys Allah﴾ refers to all kinds of sins and vices, and that is realized only in the case of the disbeliever. As for the claim that performing all sins is impossible, since practicing Judaism and Christianity together is impossible, we say: the apparent meaning of the expression requires generality unless there is a rational or legal specifier. On this assumption, their objection falls away and what we have mentioned is strengthened.

The second proof that this verse is specific to the disbeliever: His saying ﴿whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ indicates that he is one who commits disobedience and sin, and His saying ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾, if it meant the same thing, would entail repetition, which contradicts the original principle. So it must be taken to mean disbelief. As for the claim that we take this verse to refer to transgressing the limits mentioned in inheritance:

We say: granted that this is so, the question we raised still falls away by this statement, because transgression in the limits of inheritance is sometimes by believing that those obligations and rulings are true and binding to accept, yet one abandons them, and sometimes by believing that they were enacted without wisdom or correctness. This latter is the extreme of transgressing the limits. As for the first, it is hardly said of such a person that he transgressed the limits of Allah, for otherwise repetition would occur, as we have mentioned. So we know that this threat is specific to the disbeliever who does not accept what Allah mentioned in this verse concerning the division of inheritance. This is what is specific to this verse among the topics of discussion. As for the remaining questions, they were already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 13–14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits (hudud) of Allah. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally; and that is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment.﴾

Page 184

There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: after explaining the shares of inheritance, He, exalted is He, mentioned the promise and the threat, encouraging obedience and warning against disobedience, so He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾. On this there are two points.

The first point: what does "these" (tilka) refer to? There are two opinions. The first is that it refers to the rules of inheritance.

The second opinion is that it refers to everything He mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to this point: the explanation of the wealth of orphans, the rulings on marriage, and the rules of inheritance. This is the view of al-Asamm. The argument for the first view is that the pronoun returns to the nearest thing mentioned. The argument for the second view is that its return to the nearest thing does not preclude its return to the more distant things, and when there is no barrier to its return to the more distant, there is a reason to make it return to all of them.

The second point: the intended meaning of "the limits of Allah" is the prescribed portions that He mentioned and explained. The limit (hadd) of a thing is its boundary by which it is distinguished from other things, as in "the boundaries (hudud) of a house." A statement that indicates the reality of a thing is called its definition (hadd), because that statement prevents anything other than it from entering into it, and "other" means everything besides it.

The second issue: some said that His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ and His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ are specific to those who obey or disobey in the obligations mentioned in this surah. But the scholars (al-Muhaqqiqun) said: rather, it is general, including this and other things, because the expression is general, so it must encompass all. At most, this general statement was mentioned after specific obligations, but this alone does not require restricting the generality. Do you not see that a father may turn to his son and rebuke him over a specific matter, then say: "Beware of opposing me and disobeying me," and his intention is to prevent him from disobeying him in all matters? So it is here. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (nudkhiluhu jannatin, nudkhiluhu naran) with the nun (we) in both places, while the rest read with the ya' (he).

As for the first: it is in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), as in His saying ﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector﴾, then He said ﴿We shall cast﴾ with the nun.

As for the second: its reasoning is evident.

The fourth issue: here there is a question, namely that His saying ﴿He will admit him to gardens﴾ is suitable for the singular, and then His saying after it ﴿abiding therein﴾ is suitable for the plural, so how is the reconciliation between them?

The answer: the word "man" (whoever) in His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾ is singular in form but plural in meaning, so both readings are valid.

The fifth issue: "khalidin" and "khalidan" are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "nudkhiluhu." The sense is: We will admit him, abiding, into the Fire.

* * *

The sixth issue: the Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that the sinful among the people of prayer will remain eternally in the Fire. This is because His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits﴾ is either specific to those who transgressed the limits previously mentioned, which are the limits of inheritance, or it includes that and other things. On either assumption, it necessarily follows that whoever transgresses in inheritance enters this threat, and this is general regarding whoever transgresses, whether he is of the people of prayer or not. So this verse indicates the certainty of the threat and that the threat is eternal. It cannot be said that this threat is specific to those who transgress the limits of Allah, and that this is only realized in the case of the disbeliever, since he is the one who transgresses all the limits of Allah. We say: this is refuted in two ways:

The first: if we took this verse to refer to transgressing all the limits of Allah, the verse would be devoid of benefit, because Allah, exalted is He, forbade Judaism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism, so transgressing all His limits would be to abandon all these prohibitions, and abandoning them would be by practicing Judaism, Zoroastrianism, and Christianity together, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that transgressing all the limits of Allah is impossible. So if the meaning of the verse were that, the verse would cease to be meaningful. Therefore we know that its meaning is any limit whatsoever of the limits of Allah.

The second: this verse is mentioned directly after the verses on the division of inheritance, so the meaning of His saying ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ is transgressing the limits of Allah in the matters mentioned in these verses. On this assumption, this question falls away.

This is the conclusion of the Mu'tazilah's argument. We have discussed this issue at length in Surat al-Baqarah. There is no harm in repeating a portion of it here, so we say:

We agree that this threat is specific to the absence of repentance, because the evidence shows that if repentance occurs, this threat no longer applies. Likewise, it is permissible that it be conditioned upon the absence of pardon, for if there is evidence that pardon occurs, then the continuation of this threat becomes impossible when pardon occurs. We have mentioned the many proofs for the occurrence of pardon. Then we say: this generality is restricted to the disbeliever, and two things indicate this:

The first: when we say to you: what is the proof that the word "man" (whoever) in a conditional context indicates generality? You say: the proof is that an exception may be made from it, and an exception removes from the statement what would have been included had it not been there. So we say: if this proof is valid, it indicates that His saying ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ is specific to the disbeliever, because all sins may validly be excepted from this expression. One says: "Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, except in disbelief, and except in wickedness." The function of an exception is to remove what would have been included without it. This implies that His saying ﴿whoever disobeys Allah﴾ refers to all kinds of sins and vices, and that is realized only in the case of the disbeliever. As for the claim that performing all sins is impossible, since practicing Judaism and Christianity together is impossible, we say: the apparent meaning of the expression requires generality unless there is a rational or legal specifier. On this assumption, their objection falls away and what we have mentioned is strengthened.

The second proof that this verse is specific to the disbeliever: His saying ﴿whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ indicates that he is one who commits disobedience and sin, and His saying ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾, if it meant the same thing, would entail repetition, which contradicts the original principle. So it must be taken to mean disbelief. As for the claim that we take this verse to refer to transgressing the limits mentioned in inheritance:

We say: granted that this is so, the question we raised still falls away by this statement, because transgression in the limits of inheritance is sometimes by believing that those obligations and rulings are true and binding to accept, yet one abandons them, and sometimes by believing that they were enacted without wisdom or correctness. This latter is the extreme of transgressing the limits. As for the first, it is hardly said of such a person that he transgressed the limits of Allah, for otherwise repetition would occur, as we have mentioned. So we know that this threat is specific to the disbeliever who does not accept what Allah mentioned in this verse concerning the division of inheritance. This is what is specific to this verse among the topics of discussion. As for the remaining questions, they were already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 15 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you. If they testify, then confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in the preceding verses the command to treat women well and to live with them kindly, and what relates to this topic, He added to that a severity toward them regarding the lewdness they commit. In reality, this is a kindness to them and a concern for their affairs in the Hereafter. There is also another benefit: that the command of Allah to men to treat women well should not become a cause for abandoning the establishment of the prescribed penalties (hudud) against them, which would lead to their falling into various kinds of corruption and ruin. There is also a third benefit, which is to show that Allah, just as He exacts His dues from His creation, likewise exacts His dues from them, that there is no favoritism in His rulings, that He has no kinship with anyone, and that the foundation of this Law is fairness and guarding in every matter against both extremes of excess and negligence. So He said: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾. There are several issues in this verse:

**The first issue:** *al-latī* (اللَّاتِي) is the plural of *al-latī* (اللَّتِي). The Arabs have several forms for the plural of *al-latī*: *al-lātī*, *al-lāt*, *al-lawātī*, and *al-lawāt*. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: The Arabs say in the plural for non-animate things *al-latī* (الَّتِي), and for animate beings *al-lātī* (اللَّاتِي), as in His saying: ﴿your wealth which Allah has made for you a means of support﴾ [an-Nisa: 5], and in this verse He said *al-lātī* and *al-lā'ī* (اللَّائِي). The distinction is that the plural of non-animate things follows the pattern of a single thing, whereas the plural of animate beings is not like that; rather, each one of them is not distinguished from the others by specific qualities and attributes. This is the distinction. Among the Arabs, however, are some who equate the two categories, saying: *mā fa'alat al-hindāt allatī min amrihā kadhā* (what did the female-names do, which concerning their matter was thus), and *mā fa'alat al-athwāb allatī min qiṣṣatihinna kadhā* (what did the garments do, which concerning their story was thus). The first usage is the preferred one.

**The second issue:** His saying *yaʾtīna al-fāḥisha* (يَأْتِينَ الفاحِشَةَ) means *yafʿalnahā* (they do it). It is said: *ataytu amran qabīḥan*, i.e., I did an ugly thing (*faʿaltuhu*). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You have certainly done a thing terrible﴾ [Maryam: 27], and He said: ﴿You have certainly done a thing monstrous﴾ [Maryam: 89]. In expressing the undertaking of lewd acts by this phrase there is a subtle point: when Allah forbade the responsible person from doing these sins, He does not help the responsible person to commit them. Rather, the responsible person seems to have gone to them of his own accord and chosen them merely by his natural disposition. For this reason, it is said that he "came to that lewdness and went to it." However, this subtle point is only complete according to the view of the Mu'tazila. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it is *yaʾtīna bil-fāḥisha* (يَأْتِينَ بِالفاحِشَةِ). As for *al-fāḥisha* (الفاحِشَةُ), it is the ugly deed. According to the lexicographers, it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), like *al-ʿāqiba*. It is said: *faḥuṣa al-rajulu yafḥush fuḥshan wa fāḥisha*, and *afḥasha* when he brings forth ugly speech or deed. They agreed that *al-fāḥisha* here means fornication (zina), and the term *al-fāḥisha* was applied to fornication because of its excess of ugliness over many other ugly acts.

It may be objected: Disbelief is uglier than it, and killing a soul is uglier than it, yet these are not called *fāḥisha*.

We reply: The reason for this is that the powers that govern the human body are three: the rational power (*al-nāṭiqa*), the irascible power (*al-ghaḍabiyya*), and the appetitive power (*al-shahwāniyya*). The corruption of the rational power is disbelief, innovation, and what resembles them. The corruption of the irascible power is killing, rage, and what resembles them. The corruption of the appetitive power is fornication, sodomy, lesbianism, and what resembles them. The lowest of these three powers is the appetitive power, so its corruption is the lowest kind of corruption. For this reason, this act was specifically designated as *fāḥisha*. And Allah knows best His intent.

* * *

**The third issue:** Concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾, there are two views.

The first: What is meant is fornication. This is because when a woman is accused of fornication, no one has a way against her except that four male Muslim witnesses testify that she committed fornication. If they testify against her, she is confined in a house, imprisoned until she dies or Allah ordains for them a way. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

The second view, which is the choice of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani: What is meant by His saying: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾ is lesbians (sahhaqat), and their penalty is confinement until death. And by His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾ [an-Nisa: 16] are the people of sodomy (liwat), and their penalty is harm by word and deed. What is meant by the verse mentioned in Surat an-Nur is fornication between a man and a woman, and its penalty for a virgin is flogging, and for a married person (muhsan) is stoning. Abu Muslim argued for this with several points:

*First:* His saying: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾ is specific to women, and His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾ is specific to men, because His saying *al-ladhāni* (اللَّذانِ) is the dual form of the masculine.

It may be objected: Why could it not be that what is meant by *al-ladhāni* is a male and a female, but the masculine form was given precedence?

We reply: If that were the case, He would not have singled out the mention of women beforehand. Since He singled out their mention, and then after it mentioned His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾, this possibility is dismissed.

*Second:* According to this interpretation, there is no need to assert abrogation (naskh) in any of the verses; rather, the ruling of each of them remains valid and established. According to the interpretation you have mentioned, it is necessary to assert abrogation. Therefore, this view is preferable.

*Third:* According to the way you have mentioned, His saying: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾ would be about fornication, and His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾ would also be about fornication, so the same thing would be repeated twice in the same place, and that is ugly. According to the way we have stated, this does not occur, so it is preferable.

*Fourth:* Those who say that this verse was revealed about fornication interpreted His saying: ﴿or Allah ordains for them a way﴾ as stoning, flogging, and banishment. This is not valid, because these things are upon them (ʿalayhinna), not for them (lahunna). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has acquired﴾ [al-Baqara: 286]. As for us, we interpret that as Allah facilitating for her the fulfillment of desire through the means of marriage.

Then Abu Muslim said: What indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When a man mounts a man, they are both fornicators, and when a woman mounts a woman, they are both fornicators."

The opponents argued against Abu Muslim's view with several points:

*First:* This is a view that none of the earlier exegetes held, so it is false.

*Second:* It has been narrated in a hadith that he, peace be upon him, said: "Allah has made a way for them: the married (thayyib) is stoned, and the virgin (bikr) is flogged." This indicates that this verse was revealed concerning fornicators.

*Third:* The Companions differed regarding the rulings on sodomy, and none of them relied on this verse. Their not relying on it, despite their great need for a text indicating this ruling, is one of the strongest proofs that this verse does not concern sodomy.

As for the answer to the first: this claim of consensus is disputed, since Mujahid, one of the great exegetes, said this view. Furthermore, we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that deriving a new interpretation of a verse that the earlier scholars did not mention is permissible.

As for the answer to the second: this requires abrogating the Qur'an by a solitary report (khabar al-wahid), which is not permissible.

As for the answer to the third: the Companions' question was whether the prescribed penalty (hadd) is to be applied to the male sodomite. This verse offers no indication either by negation or affirmation of that, so they did not refer to it.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The majority of the exegetes claim that this verse is abrogated (mansukha). Abu Muslim said it is not abrogated. As for the exegetes, they built this on their principle, which is that this verse explains the ruling for fornication, and it is known that this ruling has not remained, so the verse is abrogated. Then, those who hold this view differed again into two positions:

The first: this verse became abrogated by the hadith narrated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take from me, take from me! Allah has made a way for them: the virgin with the virgin, and the married with the married. The virgin is flogged and exiled, and the married is flogged and stoned." Then this hadith became abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [an-Nur: 2]. By this method it is established that the Qur'an may be abrogated by the Sunnah, and the Sunnah may be abrogated by the Qur'an, contrary to the view of al-Shafi'i, who said that neither of them is abrogated by the other.

The second position: this verse became abrogated by the verse of flogging.

Know that Abu Bakr al-Razi, out of his intense eagerness to criticize al-Shafi'i, said: The first position is preferable, because if the verse of flogging had come before His saying "Take from me," then His saying "Take from me" would have no benefit. Therefore, it must be that His saying "Take from me" came before the verse of flogging. In this case, the verse of confinement is abrogated by the hadith, and the hadith is abrogated by the verse of flogging. Thus it is established that the Qur'an and the Sunnah may each abrogate the other.

Know that al-Razi's statement is weak in two respects:

*The first:* what Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi mentioned in *Ma'alim al-Sunan*. He said: Abrogation did not occur in this verse or in this hadith at all. This is because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way﴾ indicates that their confinement in the houses is extended until the point at which Allah ordains for them a way. That way was unspecified. When he, peace be upon him, said: "Take from me! The married is stoned, and the virgin is flogged and exiled," this hadith became an explanation of that verse, not an abrogation of it. It also became a specification (takhsis) of the general wording of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [an-Nur: 2]. It is well known that treating this hadith as an explanation of one of the two verses and a specifier of the other is preferable to ruling that abrogation occurred repeatedly. Moreover, the verse of confinement is definitely unspecified (mujmal), since there is nothing in the verse indicating what that way is like. So it needs a clarifier. The verse of flogging is specified, and it needs a specifier. So we have made this hadith a clarifier of the verse of confinement and a specifier of the verse of flogging. As for the view of the companions of Abu Hanifa, abrogation occurred in three ways:

*The first:* the verse of confinement became abrogated by the evidences for stoning. Thus it is clear that what we have said is the truth, about which there is no doubt.

*The second:* in refuting al-Razi's statement: You establish that it is impossible for the verse of flogging to come before His saying "Take from me." Why then did you say that this verse must come after it? Why is it not permissible to say that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger (ﷺ) mentioned that? Its supposition is that His saying: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [an-Nur: 2] is specified by consensus with respect to the free Muslim married person, and delaying the explanation of the specifier from the general wording that has been specified is not permissible according to you and according to most of the Mu'tazila, because it causes confusion. Since that is so, it is established that the Messenger (ﷺ) only said that concurrently with the revelation of His saying: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾. In this case, your claim that the hadith came before the verse of flogging falls away.

All of this is a derivation from the view of those who say: this verse, namely the verse of confinement, was revealed concerning fornicators. Thus it is established that according to this view, the evidence did not establish that it is abrogated. As for the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, it is clear that it is not abrogated. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Those who hold that this verse was revealed concerning fornication face the following objections:

**The first question: what is meant by His saying ﴿from your women﴾?**
The answer has several aspects.
First, it means "from your wives," as in His saying ﴿And those who divorce by zihar from their women﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3], and His saying ﴿from your women with whom you have consummated the marriage﴾ [al-Nisa: 23].
Second, it means "from your women," that is, from the free women (al-hara'ir, free women as opposed to slave women), as in His saying ﴿and call upon two witnesses from your men﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. The purpose is to show that there is no prescribed punishment (hadd) for slave women.
Third, it means "from your women," that is, from the believing women.
Fourth, it means "from your women," that is, from the previously married women (al-thayyibat), not the virgins (al-abkar).

**The second question: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿keep them confined in the houses﴾?**
The answer: keep them confined in your houses permanently, imprisoned. The wisdom behind this is that a woman only falls into fornication (zina) when she goes out and appears in public. So if she is confined in the house, she cannot commit fornication. And if she remains in this state, she becomes accustomed to chastity and to fleeing from fornication.

**The third question: what is the meaning of ﴿until death takes them﴾ (yatawaffahunna al-mawt), when death and taking-to-death (tawaffi) have the same meaning, so that in the reckoning it becomes: "or death makes them die"?**
The answer: it is permissible that it means "until the angels of death take them," as in His saying ﴿those whom the angels take in death﴾ [al-Nahl: 28] and ﴿Say: the angel of death who has been charged with you will take you in death﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. Or it means "until death seizes them and completes their souls."

**The fourth question: you explain His saying ﴿or God makes for them a way﴾ by the hadith in which he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "God has made for them a way: the virgin is flogged and the previously married is stoned." This is far-fetched, because this "way" is against them, not for them, since stoning is undoubtedly more severe than confinement.**

The answer: the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) himself explained the "way" in this manner when he said: "Take from me, God has made for them a way: the previously married with the previously married is a hundred lashes and stoning with stones, and the virgin with the virgin is a hundred lashes and exile for a year." Since the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) explained the "way" in this manner, it is necessary to be certain of its authenticity. Also, the word has a basis in the Arabic language, for whatever delivers one from something is a "way" for him, whether it is lighter or heavier.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 16:

The Exalted said: ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you, harm them. But if they repent and amend, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir read (wallatani and hadhani) with a doubled nun (wallaththani, hadhanni), while the rest read with a single nun. Abu Amr agreed with Ibn Kathir in His words (fa-dhannika). As for the reason for doubling, Ibn Miqsam said: Ibn Kathir doubled these nuns for two reasons. The first: to distinguish between the dual of declinable nouns (asma' mutamakkina) and that of indeclinable ones. The second: that "alladhi" and "hadha" are built upon a single letter, the dhal, so they wished to strengthen each of them by adding to its nun another nun of the same kind. Others said: the reason for doubling in them is that the nun in them is not the nun of the dual, so he wished to distinguish between them and the dual nun. It was also said: they added the nun for emphasis, just as they added the lam. As for Abu Amr's specifying the compensatory doubling in the indefinite (demonstrative) forms and not in the relative (mawsula) forms, it is likely that this was because he saw that deletion is more constant in the demonstrative, so its entitlement to compensation was stronger.

The second issue: Those who said the first verse concerns adulterers said this verse also concerns adulterers. At this point they differed about what the cause of this repetition is and what its benefit is, and they mentioned several views:

The first: that what is meant by His words ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾ is the female fornicators, and what is meant by ﴿And the two of you who commit it among you﴾ is the male fornicators. Then He, the Exalted, assigned confinement in the house to the woman and assigned harm to the man. The reason is that a woman only falls into fornication when she goes out and appears in public; so when she is confined to the house, the source of this disobedience is cut off. As for the man, he cannot be confined to the house, because he needs to go out to maintain his livelihood, arrange his affairs, and earn the sustenance of his dependants. Therefore the punishment of the adulterous woman was made confinement in the house, and the punishment of the adulterous man was made that he be harmed; so if he repents, his harming is abandoned.

It is also possible to say that harm was common to both the man and the woman, while confinement was specific to the woman; so if they both repent, the harm is removed from them and confinement remains upon the woman. This is the best of the views mentioned.

The second: al-Suddi said: what is meant by this verse is the virgin men and women, and by the first verse the married (thayyib), and in that case the difference between the two verses becomes evident. They said: several things indicate this interpretation.

The first: that He, the Exalted, said ﴿those of your women who commit lewdness﴾, attributing them to their husbands.

The second: that He named them "women" (nisa'), and this name is more suited to the married.

The third: that harm is lighter than confinement in the house, and the lighter punishment is for the virgin rather than the married.

The fourth: al-Hasan said: this verse was revealed before the preceding verse, and the meaning is: "And the two who commit lewdness among women and men, harm them; but if they repent and amend, leave them alone." Then His words were revealed: ﴿Confine them to the houses﴾, meaning: if they do not repent and persist in this ugly act, then confine them to the houses until their condition becomes clear to you. This view, in my opinion, is very remote, because it entails disorder in the arrangement of these verses.

The fifth: what we related from Abu Muslim, that the first verse concerns female homosexuals (sihaqat) and this verse concerns male homosexuals (liwat), and its explanation has already preceded.

The sixth: that the meaning is that He, the Exalted, explained in the first verse that witnesses to fornication must be four; so He explained in this verse that if they are witnesses, they should harm them and frighten them with referral to the imam and the prescribed punishment, but if they repent before referral to the imam, then leave them.

The third issue: They agreed that the realization of this harm requires harm by the tongue, which is rebuke and reproach, such as saying: "Evil is what you have done, you have exposed yourselves to Allah's punishment and wrath, you have removed yourselves from the name of uprightness, and you have nullified your eligibility to testify."

They differed about whether beating is included in it. From Ibn Abbas it is reported that they are beaten with sandals. The first view is preferable, because the apparent meaning of the text is only harm, and that is achieved by mere verbal harm, and there is no indication in the text of beating, so it is not permissible to resort to it.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But if they repent and amend, then leave them alone﴾, meaning: cease harming them.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾. The meaning of "Tawwab" is that He returns to His servant with His grace and forgiveness when he repents to Him from his sin. As for His words ﴿ever Accepting﴾, its explanation has already preceded.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse that those who commit immorality, if they repent and reform, the harm is removed from them, and He also stated in general terms that He is Oft-Returning and Most Merciful, He then mentioned the time of repentance and its condition, and encouraged them to hasten it, lest death come upon them while they are persisting, and then repentance would not benefit them. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: As for the reality of repentance, we have mentioned it in Surah al-Baqarah in the commentary on His saying: ﴿So He turned to you in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. The judge (al-Qadi ['Abd al-Jabbar]) argued, by this verse, that it is rationally obligatory upon Allah to accept repentance, from two aspects:

The first: the word "ʿalā" (upon) denotes obligation, so His saying: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who﴾ indicates that it is rationally obligatory upon Allah to accept it.

The second: If we take His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ to mean mere acceptance, there would be no difference between it and His saying ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾, since this too is a report of an occurrence. But if we take the former to mean the obligation of acceptance and the latter to mean the occurrence, the difference between the two verses becomes clear and there is no repetition.

Know that the claim of an obligation upon Allah is false, and several points indicate this:

The first: The necessary consequence of obligation is deserving blame upon omission. This necessary consequence either is impossible to be established with regard to Allah, exalted is He, or it is not impossible with regard to Him. The first is false, because the omission of that obligatory act, since it entails this blame, and this blame is impossible to be established with regard to Allah, exalted is He, it must be that this omission is impossible to be established with regard to Allah. And if the omission is rationally impossible to be established, the act becomes necessary to be established; then Allah, exalted is He, would be one who acts by essence and not an agent by choice, and that is false. As for if deserving blame is not impossible to occur with regard to Allah, exalted is He, then whatever is possible does not necessarily entail an impossibility upon supposing its occurrence; so it would follow that the God, while being God, could be described as deserving blame, and that is an impossibility that no rational person would say. Since these two divisions are invalid, it is established that the claim of an obligation upon Allah, exalted is He, is false.

The second argument: The capability of the servant with respect to the act of repentance and its omission is either equal, or not equal. If it is equal, then the performance of repentance is not preferred over its omission except by a determinant. Then that determinant, if it arose from no originator, would entail the negation of the Creator; and if it arose from the servant, the division returns. And if it arose from Allah, then the servant only undertook repentance through Allah's aid and strengthening; so that repentance is a favour from Allah, exalted is He, upon His servant, and a master's favour upon his servant does not oblige him to favour him again. Thus it is established that the proceeding of repentance from the servant does not oblige Allah to accept it. And if the servant's capability is not suited to both omission and performance, then compulsion is more binding, and when that is so, the claim of an obligation is more evidently false and corrupt.

The third argument: Repentance is an expression for regret over what has passed and resolve to abandon it in the future. Regret and resolve belong to the category of aversions and volitions, and aversion and volition do not arise by the choice of the servant; otherwise, to bring them about he would require another volition, and an infinite regress would follow. And when that is so, the occurrence of this regret and this resolve is purely by Allah's creating, and the act of Allah does not oblige Allah to another act. Thus it is established that the claim of an obligation is false.

The fourth argument: Repentance is, according to their view, an act that occurs by the choice of the servant; so if that became a cause for an obligation upon Allah, the act of the servant would be effective upon the essence of Allah and His attributes, and no rational person would say that.

As for the answer to what they argued with: He, exalted is He, promised the acceptance of repentance from the believers; and when Allah promises something, and the breaking of His promise is impossible, that is like an obligation. By this interpretation, the use of the word "ʿalā" is correct, and by this path the difference between His saying ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾ and His saying ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾ became evident.

If it is said: When He reports the acceptance of repentance, and whatever Allah reports as occurring must necessarily occur, then it follows for you that He is not a free chooser.

We say: The report of an occurrence follows the occurrence, and the occurrence follows the bringing-about, and the follower does not change the principle. So He is a free chooser in that bringing-about. As for you, you say that the occurrence of repentance, insofar as it itself is effective, makes acceptance obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, and no rational person would say that; thus the difference is evident.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, conditioned the acceptance of this repentance with two conditions. One of them is His saying: ﴿for those who do evil in ignorance﴾. Regarding this there are two questions. The first: whoever commits a sin without knowing it is a sin does not deserve punishment, because error is lifted from this community; so according to this, those who do evil in ignorance have no need of repentance. The second question: the word "innamā" (only) denotes restriction, so the apparent meaning of this verse requires that whoever proceeds to evil while knowing it to be evil, his repentance is not accepted; and that is false by consensus.

The answer to the first question: the Jew chose Judaism while not knowing it to be a sin, although he deserves punishment for it.

The answer to the second question: whoever commits disobedience in ignorance of its being disobedience is in a lighter state than one who commits it knowing it to be disobedience. And since that is so, indeed He specified the first category with the obligation of accepting repentance, an obligation by way of promise and generosity; as for the second category, since their sin is graver, He did not mention for them this emphasis regarding the acceptance of

صفحة ٥

repentance; so this verse indicates from this aspect that the acceptance of repentance is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He.

When you have understood the answer to these two questions, let us mention the aspects that the commentators mentioned in explaining ignorance (jahala).

The first: The commentators said: Everyone who disobeys Allah is called ignorant, and his act is called ignorance. Allah, exalted is He, said, reporting about Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿I would incline towards them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. And He said, relating that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to his brothers: ﴿Do you know what you did with Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾ [Yusuf: 89]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "O Nuh, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work is not righteous. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ [Hud: 46]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow. They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67]. A master may say to his servant, while blaming him for an act: "O ignorant one, why did you do such and such?" The reason for applying the name ignorant to one who disobeys his Lord is that if he had employed the knowledge he possessed of reward and punishment, he would not have proceeded to disobedience; so when he did not employ that knowledge, it became as though he had no knowledge. On this path the disobedient one to his Lord is called ignorant; and on this aspect the disobedience includes whether the person committed it knowing it to be disobedience or in ignorance of that.

The second aspect in explaining ignorance: that a person commits disobedience while knowing it to be disobedience, except that he is ignorant of the measure of its punishment. We know that when a person proceeds to what is not fitting while knowing it is not fitting, but he does not know the measure of the harms that will result from its consequence, it is valid to say, by way of metaphor, that he is ignorant of his act.

The third aspect: that it means a person commits disobedience while not knowing it is disobedience, but on condition that he is able to know that it is disobedience; for on this assessment he deserves punishment. And for this meaning we are agreed that the Jew deserves punishment for his Judaism, even though he does not know that Judaism is disobedience; since he was able to acquire knowledge that Judaism is a sin and disobedience, that suffices for establishing the deserving of punishment. What is excluded from what we have mentioned is the sleeper and the forgetful, for he committed the ugly act but was not able to know it was ugly. This view is preferable to others because the word "ignorance" in the first two aspects is taken as metaphor, while in this aspect it is taken literally; however, on this aspect, only one who does ugly deeds without knowing their ugliness falls under the verse, whereas the deliberate one does not fall under the verse, and his state is known only by way of analogy: since repentance is obligatory for this ignorant one, it is all the more obligatory upon the intentional one; this is the discussion of the first condition of repentance. As for the second condition, it is His saying: ﴿then they repent soon after﴾. They have agreed that the intended meaning of this "soon" is the arrival of the time of death and the witnessing of its terrors. He, exalted is He, called this period "soon" for several reasons:

The first: the term is coming, and everything that is coming is near.

The second: to alert that the span of a human's life, however long it may be, is brief and near, for it is enclosed by the two ends of eternity without beginning and without end; when you divide the span of your life against what lies on its two ends, it becomes like nothing.

The third: that a person expects at every moment the descent of death upon him, and one in such a state is described as near.

If it is said: What is the meaning of "min" (from) in His saying: ﴿soon﴾?

The answer: It is for the starting point, meaning that he makes the beginning of his repentance a time near to the disobedience, so that he does not fall into the group of the persistent. As for one who repents after the disobedience by a long time, and before death by a long time, he is outside those specified with the honour of the binding acceptance of repentance upon Allah by His saying: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾ and by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾. And whoever's repentance does not fall within this aspect, it suffices him to be among those promised with the word "perhaps" in His saying: ﴿Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 102]. There is no doubt that between the two ranks there is a difference that is not hidden. It was said: its meaning is partitive, meaning they repent within part of a near time, as though He, exalted is He, named the period between the occurrence of disobedience and the presence of death a near time; so in whatever part of this time he repents, he is one who repents "from soon"; otherwise, he is one who repents "from far."

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned these two conditions, He said: ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness.﴾

If it is said: What is the benefit of His saying: ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾ after His saying: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾?

We say: there are two aspects to it:

The first: His saying: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾ is an informing that it is obligatory upon Allah to accept it, obligatory by way of generosity, grace and benevolence, not the obligation of entitlement; and His saying: ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾ is a report that He will do that.

Secondly: the words of Him, ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah﴾, mean: the only guidance to repentance, the direction towards it, and the assistance in it, are incumbent upon Allah, the Exalted, with regard to the one who commits a sin out of ignorance, then repents of it soon after, abandons persistence in it, and seeks forgiveness for it. Then He said: ﴿So those - Allah will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, meaning: the servant whose condition is this, when he repents, Allah accepts his repentance. Thus, what is intended by the first is granting success in repentance, and by the second, the acceptance of repentance.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, that is, Allah was ever Knowing that he committed that disobedience only because desire, anger and ignorance had overpowered him, and Wise in that, since the servant has this attribute, and then he repented of it soon after, it is necessary, in generosity, to accept his repentance.

He, Exalted is He, said: "And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now,' nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment." [Qur'an 4:18]

Know that when Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the conditions of acceptable repentance, He followed it with an explanation of the repentance that is not accepted. The verse contains several issues.

**The first issue:** The verse indicates that whoever is present at death and witnesses its terrors, his repentance is not accepted. This issue contains two discussions.

**The first discussion:** There are several proofs that the repentance of one whose condition we have described is not accepted:

The first is this verse itself, which is explicit regarding the matter sought.

The second is His saying: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ (Ghafir: 85).

The third is His statement describing Pharaoh: ﴿When drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims." "Now?" ﴾ ﴿And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ (Yunus: 90–91). So Allah did not accept his repentance at the moment of witnessing the punishment. Had he brought that faith a moment before that hour, it would have been accepted.

The fourth is His saying: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 99–100).

The fifth is His saying: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you, and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous." But Allah will never delay a soul when its time has come﴾ (al-Munafiqun: 10–11). In these verses Allah informs us that repentance is not accepted at the presence of death.

The sixth is what Abu Ayyub narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not yet gharghara" – that is, as long as the soul has not yet rattled in his throat. It is narrated from 'Ata': "Even if it is just before his death by the time of a she-camel's milking interval (fuwaq al-naqah)." It is narrated from al-Hasan that when Iblis was sent down to the earth he said: "By Your might, I will not leave the son of Adam as long as his soul is in his body." He (Allah) said: "By My might, I will not close the door of repentance to him as long as he has not yet gharghara."

Know that His saying: ﴿When death comes to one of them﴾ means the signs of the descent of death and its nearness. It is like His saying: ﴿It is prescribed for you that when death approaches one of you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 180).

**The second discussion:** The scholars (al-Muhaqqiqun) said: The nearness of death does not prevent the acceptance of repentance. Rather, what prevents the acceptance of repentance is witnessing the states through which knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, is obtained necessarily. We say that mere nearness to death does not prevent the acceptance of repentance, for several reasons:

The first: Allah caused a group of people to die and then revived them, such as a group from the Children of Israel and the children of Ayyub (peace be upon him). Then He obligated them after that revival. This shows that witnessing death does not nullify obligation (taklif).

The second: The hardships that one who is near death endures are like the hardships of severe colic (qawlanj) or like those a woman endures in labor, or greater. If these hardships do not prevent the continuation of obligation, then the same applies to those hardships.

The third: When one is near death and his pains become severe, his dependence on Allah becomes stronger, and He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ (al-Naml: 62). So the increase of pains at that time being a cause for the acceptance of repentance is more fitting than being a cause for its non-acceptance. Thus it is established by these considerations that the mere nearness to death and the mere increase of pains and hardships cannot be what prevents the acceptance of repentance. Rather, we say: What prevents the acceptance of repentance is that when a person near death witnesses states and terrors, his knowledge of Allah becomes necessary (darurIyyah) at the moment he witnesses those terrors. And whenever his knowledge of Allah becomes necessary, the obligation falls from him. Do you not see that the people of the Hereafter, when their knowledge becomes necessary, the obligation falls from them, even though there is no death or punishment there? For their repentance at the Gathering and the Reckoning, and before entering the Fire, is not accepted.

Know that there is a deep, fundamental (usuli) inquiry here. The people of the Resurrection witness only that they have become living after they were dead, and they also witness the great Fire and all kinds of terrors. None of that necessitates that knowledge of Allah becomes necessary. This is because knowing that the occurrence of life after it was non-existent requires an agent is, according to most of the Mu'tazilah shaykhs, a speculative (nazari) knowledge. Even if it is said that this knowledge is necessary, the knowledge that reviving cannot be valid from other than Allah is undoubtedly speculative. As for knowing that the creator of those great fires is none other than Allah, this too is inferential (istidlali). So how can it be claimed that the people of the Hereafter, due to witnessing its terrors, know Allah by necessity? Then suppose the matter is as they say: why did you claim that when knowledge of Allah becomes necessary, it prevents the validity of obligation? For the servant, even with his necessary knowledge of the existence of the God who rewards and punishes, may still commit disobedience, because he knows that He is Generous, that the servant's obedience does not benefit Him and his sin does not harm Him. If that is the case, why did they say that this necessitates the removal of obligation? Furthermore: what these Mu'tazilah say, that knowledge of Allah in the abode of obligation must be speculative, and when it becomes necessary the obligation falls, is a weak statement. This is because whoever has knowledge of Allah in his heart: if the possibility of its opposite is still present in his heart, then this is supposition (zann), not knowledge; and if the possibility of its opposite is not present, it is impossible that there be another knowledge stronger and more certain than it. In that case, no difference at all remains between necessary knowledge and speculative knowledge. Thus it is established that these things the Mu'tazilah mention are weak and feeble words, and that He, Exalted is He, does what He wills and decrees what He intends. He, by His grace, has promised the acceptance of repentance at certain times, and by His justice He has informed us of the non-acceptance of repentance at another time. He may reverse the matter, making the accepted rejected and the rejected accepted: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ (al-Anbiya': 23).

**The second issue:** He, Exalted is He, mentioned two categories. In the first category He said: ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah for those who do evil out of ignorance﴾, and this indicates that accepting their repentance is obligatory.

In the second category He said: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾. This is a definitive statement that He does not accept the repentance of these. So, by the rule of rational division (al-taqsim al-'aqli), between these two categories there remains a third category: those for whom Allah, Exalted is He, has not definitively stated the acceptance of their repentance, nor definitively stated its rejection. Since the first category is those who do evil out of ignorance, and the second category is those who do not repent except at the sight of the punishment, it must follow that the intermediate category between these two is those who do evil deliberately and then repent. Allah has not informed us that He accepts their repentance, nor that He rejects it. Rather He has left them under His will, just as He left their forgiveness under His will, when He said: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa': 48).

**The third issue:** When He explained that whoever repents upon the arrival of the signs of death and its precursors, his repentance is not accepted, He said: ﴿Nor those who die﴾. In this there are two possible meanings:

The first: It means those whose death has drawn near. The meaning is that just as repentance from sins is not accepted near death, likewise faith is not accepted near death.

The second: It means that if disbelievers die in disbelief, then even if they repent in the Hereafter, their repentance will not be accepted.

**The fourth issue:** The Wa'idiyyah (those who hold to the doctrine of the threat) cling to this verse to support their school of thought in two ways:

The first: They said that He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers.﴾ So He conjoined "those who do evil deeds" with "those who die while they are disbelievers," and the conjoined is different from that to which it is conjoined. Therefore it is established that the first group are not disbelievers. Then He said concerning all of them: ﴿Those, We have prepared for them a painful punishment,﴾ and this requires that this threat applies to both disbelievers and sinners.

The second: He informed us that there is no repentance for them at the moment of direct witnessing (mu'ayanah). If He were to forgive them despite their not repenting, this announcement would have no meaning.

The answer: We have already gathered the whole body of threat-related general statements in the commentary on His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ (al-Baqarah: 81). We answered their reliance on these, and mentioned many answers. There is no need to repeat them for each of these general statements. Then we say: The pronoun must return to the nearest mentioned item. The nearest mentioned item to His saying ﴿Those, We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ is His saying ﴿nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. So why is it not permissible that His saying ﴿We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ refers to disbelievers only? The detailed explanation of this is that He, Exalted is He, informed us about those who do not repent except at death, that their repentance is not accepted. Then He mentioned the disbelievers after that, and explained that their faith at death is not accepted. There is no doubt that the disbeliever is worse in act and lower in rank before Allah than the sinner, so He must single him out with additional humiliation and degradation. Thus it is permissible that His saying ﴿Those, We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ is specific to disbelievers, clarifying that they are singled out, because of their disbelief, for additional punishment and humiliation.

As for the second point they relied upon: He informed us that there is no repentance at direct witnessing, and if there is no repentance, then there arises the possibility of punishment and the possibility of forgiveness. This involves some kind of intimidation. It is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (al-Nisa': 48). Moreover, this is an argument from implication (dalil al-khitab), which the Mu'tazilah do not hold. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** He, Exalted is He, conjoined the disbelievers to those who repent at the sight of death. The conjoined is different from that to which it is conjoined. This requires that the sinner among the people of prayer is not a disbeliever. This nullifies the statement of the Khawarij that the sinner is a disbeliever. It cannot be said that what is meant here is the hypocrite (munafiq), because the sound position is that the hypocrite is a disbeliever. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars﴾ (al-Munafiqun: 1). And Allah knows best.

**The sixth issue:** *A'tadna* means "We have prepared and made ready." Its parallel is His saying concerning the Fire of Hell: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24). Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that the Fire is created, because the painful punishment is nothing other than the Fire of Hell and its cold, and His saying ﴿We have prepared (a'tadna)﴾ is a report about the past. This indicates that the Fire is created from this aspect. And Allah knows best.

[p. 10]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force. And do not confine them that you may take away part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. And if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes in it much good.﴾

Know that after describing repentance, He, may He be exalted, returned to the rulings concerning women. Know that the people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) used to harm women in many kinds of harm and wronged them in various ways, so Allah, may He be exalted, forbade them from these in these verses.

The first type is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women by force﴾. Concerning it there are two issues.

The first issue: There are two opinions regarding the verse. The first: In the Jahiliyyah, when a man died and had a wife, his son from another wife or some of his relatives would come and throw his garment over the woman and say, "I have inherited his wife just as I have inherited his property." Thus he had more right to her than other people and than she herself. If he wished, he would marry her without a dowry, except the first dowry which the deceased had given her. And if he wished, he would marry her to someone else and take her dowry, giving her nothing of it. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse, and made clear that this is forbidden, and that a man does not inherit the wife of the deceased. According to this opinion, what is meant by His saying, ﴿that you inherit women﴾ is the women themselves, and that they are not inherited from the deceased.

The second opinion: The inheritance refers to property. The heir of the deceased had the right to prevent her from marrying until she died, so that he could inherit her property. Thus He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit their property while they are unwilling.﴾

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read كُرْهًا (*kurhan*) with a *ḍamma* on the *kaf*. In al-Tawbah (﴿Spend willingly or unwillingly﴾ [al-Tawbah: 53]) and in al-Ahqaf (﴿His mother carried him unwillingly and bore him unwillingly﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]), all of these are with *ḍamma*. ʿĀsim and Ibn ʿĀmir read with *ḍamma* in al-Ahqaf, and the rest with *fatḥa*. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read with *fatḥa* in all of these. Al-Kisa'i said: "They are two dialects with one meaning." Al-Farra' said: "*Kark* with *fatḥa* means compulsion, and with *ḍamma* means hardship. Whatever one is compelled to is *kark* with *fatḥa*, and whatever comes from one's own self is *kurh* with *ḍamma*."

The second type of the matters which Allah forbade concerning women is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not confine them that you may take away part of what you have given them﴾. Concerning it there are several issues.

The first issue: Regarding the position of ﴿And do not confine them﴾ there are two opinions. The first: It is in the accusative by coordination with the particle *an* (that), its estimate being: "It is not lawful for you to inherit women by force, nor that you confine them," according to the reading of ʿAbd Allah. The second: It is in the jussive by the prohibition, coordinated with what preceded, its estimate being: "And do not inherit, and do not confine."

The second issue: *al-ʿaḍl* means prevention, and from it comes *al-dāʾ al-ʿuḍāl* (an incurable disease). Its full discussion has already preceded in His saying: ﴿So do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232].

The third issue: Who is addressed in His saying ﴿And do not confine them﴾? Concerning it there are opinions. The first: Some men among them disliked their wives and wanted to separate from them, so they would treat them badly and constrict them until they ransomed themselves from him with their dower. This opinion is the choice of most of the exegetes. It is as if He said: "It is not lawful for you to marry them by compulsion, and likewise it is not lawful for you, after marrying them, to confine them and detain them that you may take away part of what you have given them." The second: It is an address to the heir, that he should abandon preventing her from marrying whomever she wishes and wants, as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do. His saying ﴿that you may take away part of what you have given them﴾ means that they would detain the widow, their aim being that the woman would surrender what she had taken from the inheritance of the deceased.

The third: It is an address to the guardians, and a prohibition to them from preventing the woman.

The fourth: It is an address to the husbands. In the Jahiliyyah they would divorce the woman and would prevent her from remarrying and would constrict the matter for her, with the aim that they would take something from her.

The fifth: It is general to all of them.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾, concerning it there are several issues.

The first issue: Regarding the clear immorality there are two opinions. The first: It is *nushūz* (disobedience), ill temper and harming the husband and his family. The meaning is: unless the bad companionship comes from their side, in which case you are excused for seeking *khul*' (divorce by ransom). This is indicated by the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: ﴿unless it is excessively foul upon you﴾.

The second opinion: It is adultery. This is the view of al-Hasan, Abu Qilabah and al-Suddi.

The second issue: His saying ﴿unless they come﴾ is an exception from what? There are several aspects.

The first: It is an exception from taking the properties, meaning it is not lawful for him to detain her out of harm until she ransoms herself from him, except if she has committed adultery. Those who hold this view differ: some say this ruling remains and was not abrogated; others say it was abrogated by the verse of flogging.

The second: It is an exception from the detention and confinement mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿then confine them in the houses﴾. This is the view of Abu Muslim, who claimed that it is not abrogated.

The third: It is possible that this is an exception from His saying: ﴿And do not confine them﴾, because *al-ʿaḍl* is detention, so confinement in the house is included in it. Thus the guardians and the husbands were forbidden from confining them in houses, except if they commit a clear immorality; at that point it becomes lawful for the guardians and husbands to confine them in houses.

The third issue: Nafi' and Abu ʿAmr read *mubayyinatin* (with a kasra on the *yāʾ*) and *āyātin mubayyanāt* (with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ*) wherever it occurs. He said: In His saying ﴿mubayyinat﴾ [al-Nur: 34] he intended to make them manifest, while in His saying ﴿with a clear immorality﴾ he did not intend to make it manifest. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿĀsim read both with fatḥa, and the rest read both with kasra. As for the one who reads with fatḥa, he has two aspects:

The first: The immorality and the signs have no actual agency; rather, it is Allah, may He be exalted, who has made them clear.

The second: The immorality becomes clear, so if four witnesses testify against it, it becomes manifest. As for the signs, Allah, may He be exalted, has made them clear. As for the one who reads with kasra, his reasoning is that when the signs become clear and manifest, they become causes of clarity, and when they become causes of clarity, it is permissible to attribute the clarifying to them, just as idols, since they were causes of misguidance, it is apt to attribute the misguiding to them, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, they have led many of the people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 36].

The third type of obligations related to the circumstances of women is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾. The people used to treat women badly in companionship, so it was said to them: ﴿And live with them in kindness.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: It is fairness in the night and in maintenance, and gentleness in speech.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if you dislike them﴾, that is, you dislike their company in kindness and their companionship, and prefer to separate from them, ﴿then perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes in it much good.﴾ Regarding the pronoun in His saying ﴿in it﴾, to what does it refer? There are two aspects:

The first: The meaning is that if you dislike their companionship, then keep them in kindness, for perhaps there is much good in their companionship. Those who held this view sometimes interpreted the much good as a child who is born, so that dislike turns into love and aversion into desire. And sometimes as: when he disliked her company yet bore that disliked situation, seeking the reward of Allah, and spent on her and was good to her against his natural inclination, he deserved a great reward in the Hereafter and a fine commendation in this world.

The second: That the meaning is: if you dislike them and desire to separate from them, perhaps Allah will make in that separation for them much good, by which that woman is freed from this husband and finds a better husband than him. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa': 130]. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Asamm. The Qadi said: "This is far-fetched, because He, may He be exalted, urged, by what He mentioned, a course of continuing in companionship. So how would He intend separation by it?"

**The fourth type of rulings concerning women.**

﴿And if you desire to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take anything back from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin? And how could you take it when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾
