His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you desire to replace one wife with another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take anything back from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin? And how could you take it when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ There are several issues:

**The first issue:** In the first verse, when He, exalted is He, permitted harming wives if they commit an obscenity, He clarified in this verse the prohibition of harm outside the case of obscenity, saying: ﴿And if you desire to replace one wife with another﴾. It is reported that a man among them, when he inclined toward marrying another woman, would accuse his own wife of obscenity, until he forced her to ransom herself from him with what he had given her, so that he could redirect it toward marrying the woman he wanted. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you desire to replace one wife with another﴾, to the end of the verse. The *qinṭār* (a great amount of wealth) is the great wealth, and its explanation has already passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And heaped-up quantities of gold and silver﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 14].

**The sixth issue:** They said: The verse indicates the permissibility of excess in the bridal gift (*mahr*). It is reported that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said from the pulpit: "Beware, do not exaggerate in the bridal gifts of your women." A woman stood up and said: "O son of al-Khaṭṭāb, Allah gives us, and you forbid?" and she recited this verse. So ʿUmar said: "Every person is more learned in jurisprudence than ʿUmar," and he retracted his disapproval of excess.

In my view, the verse contains no indication of the permissibility of excess, because His saying: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ does not indicate the permissibility of giving a heap of gold, just as His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 22] does not indicate the existence of gods. The conclusion is that making one thing a condition for another does not require that the condition itself be possible to occur. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever has a man slain for him, his family has a choice between two options," and this does not require the permissibility of killing. A man may say: "If God were a body, He would be created," and this is true, yet it does not follow from it that our saying "God is a body" is true.

**The third issue:** This verse includes both the case where he has given her her bridal gift and the case where he has not given it, because he concluded the contract upon that bridal gift according to the ruling of Allah, so there is no difference between the case where he has actually given her the bridal gift and the case where he has not given it.

**The fourth issue:** Abū Bakr al-Rāzī argued by this verse that a valid seclusion (*khalwa ṣaḥīḥa*) confirms the bridal gift. He said: Because Allah, exalted is He, forbade the husband from taking anything of it from her, and this prohibition is absolute; the ruling is not implemented before seclusion, so it must remain in effect after seclusion. He said: It is not permissible to say that it is restricted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified for them an obligation, then half of what you specified﴾ [al-Baqara: 237]. This is because the Companions differed over the interpretation of *masīs* (touching). ʿAlī and ʿUmar said: The meaning of *masīs* is seclusion. ʿAbd Allāh said: It is intercourse. When it has become a matter of disagreement, it is impermissible to make it a restrictor of the general wording of this verse.

The response: The verse mentioned here is specific to what occurs after intercourse, based on His saying: ﴿And how could you take it when you have gone in unto one another﴾, and the "going in unto one another" is intercourse according to the view of most exegetes. We will establish the evidence for the soundness of this.

**The fifth issue:** Know that ill treatment (*sūʾ al-ʿishra*) is either from the side of the husband or from the side of the wife. If it is from the side of the husband, it is disliked for him to take anything of her bridal gift, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you desire to replace one wife with another﴾

﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take anything back from it﴾ is explicit that if the discord (*nushūz*) is from his side, he is forbidden from taking anything of her bridal gift. Then, if a khul‘ (divorce by ransom) takes place, the husband owns the compensation of the khul‘, just as a sale at the time of the call to prayer is forbidden, yet it still transfers ownership. If the discord is from the side of the woman, then taking the compensation of the khul‘ is lawful here, because of His saying: ﴿And do not restrain them in order to take back part of what you have given them, unless they commit a flagrant obscenity﴾.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** *Buhtān* (slander) linguistically means a lie that a person confronts his companion with, by way of obstinate denial. Its root is from *buhita al-rajul*, when a man becomes bewildered. So *buhtān* is a lie that bewilders a person because of its enormity. Then every falsehood at which one is bewildered by its falseness was called *buhtān*. From this is the hadith: "If you confront your brother with what is not in him, you have indeed slandered him."

**The second issue:** Why is His saying ﴿buhtānan﴾ in the accusative case? There are several views:

**The first:** Al-Zajjāj said: *Buhtān* here is a verbal noun placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), and the meaning is: Would you take it while being slanderers and sinners?

**The second:** The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: It is possible that it is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), even though it is not in reality the goal, like your saying: "He sat back from the fighting out of cowardice."

**The third:** It is in the accusative by removing the preposition, meaning: by slander.

**The fourth:** There is an ellipsis in it, its estimate being: You would incur by it slander and sin.

**The third issue:** Concerning the naming of this taking as "slander," there are several aspects:

**The first:** He, exalted is He, prescribed for her that bridal gift, so whoever reclaims it is as though he were saying: "That was not an obligation," and so it becomes slander.

**The second:** At the time of the contract, he undertook to deliver that bridal gift to her and not to take it from her, so when he takes it, that first statement becomes slander.

**The third:** We have mentioned that it was among their custom that when they wished to divorce a wife, they would accuse her of obscenity until she feared and bought her own freedom from him with that bridal gift. Since this matter occurred in this manner in most cases, it was treated as though each of the two was the other.

**The fourth:** He, exalted is He, mentioned in the preceding verse: ﴿And do not restrain them in order to take back part of what you have given them, unless they commit a flagrant obscenity﴾, and the apparent state of a Muslim is that he does not oppose the command of Allah. So if he takes something from her, that indicates she has committed a flagrant obscenity. If the matter is not so in reality, then describing that taking as slander is correct, in that it indicates her committing obscenity while the matter is not so. There is another explanation: taking the wealth is both an attack on her person and a taking of her property, so it is slander from one aspect and injustice from another aspect, and therefore it is a great sin among the major sins.

**The fifth:** The punishment for slander and manifest sin was known to them, so His saying: ﴿Would you take it by slander﴾ means: Would you take the punishment for slander? It is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who devour the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 10].

**The fourth issue:** His saying: "(Would you take it)" is an interrogative in the sense of denial and magnification, and the meaning is that the apparent situation is that you do not do such an act, given the clear ugliness of it in the sacred law and in reason.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 21:**

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how could you take it back when you have gone in to one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned several reasons for this prohibition. The first: this taking back implies attributing to them a clear immorality, and that is slander (buhtan), and slander is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir). The second: it is a manifest sin, because this wealth is her right. Whoever restricts the matter for her so that he may use that constriction and restriction as a means to take the wealth, which is itself an injustice, then there is no doubt that using one injustice as a means to another injustice is a manifest sin. The third is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how could you take it back when you have gone in to one another﴾, and in it are two issues.

**The first issue:** The root of *afda* (أفضى) is from *al-fada'*, which means spaciousness. It is said: *fada yafdu fudu'an wa fada'an* when it became spacious. Al-Layth said: *afda fulan ila fulan*, meaning he reached him, and its origin is that he came into his space and expanse. The commentators have two views on *al-ifda'* in this verse:

The first: *al-ifda'* here is a metaphor (kinaya) for sexual intercourse (al-jima'). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi, and the preference of al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah, and the position of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him), because according to him, if the husband divorces before consummation (al-masis), he may reclaim half of the dower (mahr), even if he was alone with her.

The second view on *al-ifda'*: that he is alone with her even if he has not had intercourse with her. Al-Kalbi said: *al-ifda'* is that he is with her under one blanket, whether he has had intercourse with her or not. This view is the preference of al-Farra' and the position of Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him), because valid seclusion (al-khalwa al-sahiha) establishes the dower.

Know that the first view is more correct, and several points support it:

The first: al-Layth said: *afda fulan ila fulana*, meaning he came into her space and expanse. It is known that this meaning truly occurs at the time of intercourse. As for other than the time of intercourse, this is not realized.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned this in the context of wonder, saying: ﴿And how could you take it back when you have gone in to one another﴾. The wonder is complete only if this *ifda'* is a strong cause for the arising of intimacy and affection, and that is intercourse, not mere seclusion. Therefore it is necessary to interpret *al-ifda'* as that.

The third: *al-ifda'* to her must be explained by an action from him that reaches her, because the word *ila* (إلى) indicates the end of the goal. Mere seclusion is not like that, because in pure seclusion no action of either of them reaches the other. So it is impossible to explain His saying ﴿when you have gone in to one another﴾ by mere seclusion.

If it is said: When they lie under one blanket and touch, then *al-ifda'* has occurred from one of them to the other, so that should be sufficient, and you do not hold this.

We say: There are two positions. One says the dower is not established except by intercourse. The other says it is established by mere seclusion. No one in the community (al-umma) says it is established by touching and lying together. So this view is void by consensus (ijma'). Thus there remains, in explaining the *ifda'* of one of them to the other, only one of two things: either intercourse, or seclusion. The view of seclusion is void for what we have explained. So what remains is that the intended meaning of *al-ifda'* is intercourse.

The fourth: Before seclusion, the dower was not established, and the Law linked its establishment to the *ifda'* of one party to the other. The matter is ambiguous as to whether the intended *ifda'* is seclusion or intercourse. When doubt arises, what was the case before must remain as it was, which is non-establishment. By these points the preference of al-Shafi'i's position became clear, and Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** His saying: ﴿And how could you take it back when you have gone in to one another﴾ is an expression of wonder (kalimat ta'ajjub), meaning: For what reason and for what purpose do you do this? She has given herself to you and made her very self your pleasure and enjoyment, and complete intimacy and full affection have arisen between you. How is it fitting for a sensible person to reclaim from her something he gave her willingly? This is not fitting at all for one who has a sound nature and an upright disposition.

The fourth of the aspects by which Allah made it a barrier to reclaiming the dower: His saying: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾. Regarding this solemn covenant (mithaqan ghalidhan) there are several views:

The first: al-Suddi, Ikrimah and al-Farra' said: it is your saying, "I have married you this woman on the basis of what Allah has taken for women over men, of keeping in good manner or releasing with kindness." It is known that if he forces her into giving the dower, then he has not released her with kindness, but rather released her with harm.

The second: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: the solemn covenant is the word of marriage (kalimat al-nikah) contracted upon the bridal gift (sadaq), and that word is a word by which the private parts of women become lawful. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fear Allah regarding women, for you have taken them under the trust of Allah, and you have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah."

The third: His saying: ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾, meaning: they have taken from you, because of the *ifda'* of one of you to the other, a solemn covenant. He described it as solemn because of its strength and greatness. And they said: companionship of twenty days is a kinship; how much more so what occurs between the spouses of union and mingling?

PART 1 OF 3 — Al-Razi's Mafatih al-Ghayb, commentary on Surah 4, verse 22

The fifth type of matters which God, exalted is He, has imposed in this verse, from among the matters relating to women:

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an indecency and hateful and an evil way.﴾

The Exalted's statement: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an indecency and hateful and an evil way.﴾ On this there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of the exegetes said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance) used to marry the wives of their fathers, so God forbade them from that act through this verse.

The second issue: Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: It is forbidden for a man to marry the woman who was fornicated with by his father. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is not forbidden. Abu Hanifa argued with this verse, saying: God, exalted is He, forbade a man to marry a woman who was married (nakaha) by his father, and nikah is an expression for wata' (sexual intercourse), so it is a prohibition against marrying a woman whom his father had intercourse with. We only say that nikah is an expression for wata' for several reasons:

The first: The Exalted's statement: ﴿So she is not lawful to him after [that] until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. He attributed this marriage (nikah) to the husband, and the nikah attributed to the husband is wata', not 'aqd (contract), because a person cannot marry his own wife, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible. Also, if the intended meaning of nikah in this verse were 'aqd, then lawfulness (tahlil) would be achieved by the mere contract; and since it is not achieved thereby, we know that the intended meaning of nikah in this verse is not 'aqd, so it is necessarily wata', since there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The second: The Exalted's statement: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age (nikah)﴾ [al-Nisa': 6]. The meaning of nikah here is wata', not 'aqd, because the capacity for 'aqd was always present.

The third: The Exalted's statement: ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. If the meaning here were 'aqd, it would entail falsehood.

The fourth: The statement of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "The one who marries by hand is cursed" (nakih al-yad mal'un). It is known that the intended meaning is not 'aqd but wata'. Thus it is established by these points that nikah is an expression for wata', and so the Exalted's statement ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾ means: and do not have intercourse with those whom your fathers had intercourse with, and this includes both the one who was married and the one who was fornicated with. It may be said: Just as the word nikah is used with the meaning of wata', it is also used with the meaning of 'aqd. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32]; ﴿so marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]; ﴿when you marry believing women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]; and the statement of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "I was born of nikah and not born of sifah (illicit intercourse)." So why is it more appropriate to take the word to mean wata' rather than 'aqd?

Page 16

They answered this in three ways:

The first: That which al-Karkhi held, namely that the word nikah is a literal (haqiqah) meaning for wata' and a figurative (majaz) meaning for 'aqd, based on the evidence that the word nikah in its original linguistic sense is an expression for ḍamm (joining together), and the meaning of joining is present in wata' not in 'aqd, so the word nikah is literal for wata'. Then 'aqd was named by this name because 'aqd, being the cause of it, the name of the effect was applied to the cause, just as 'aqiqah is the name for the hair on a child's head at birth, and then the sheep slaughtered at the shaving of that hair is called 'aqiqah; so likewise here.

Know that it was al-Karkhi's view that it is not permissible to use a single word in its literal and figurative senses together, in the same respect. Therefore he would say: what is derived from this verse is the ruling of wata'; as for the ruling of 'aqd, it is not derived from this verse, but from another path and another proof.

The second way: Some people held that a homonymous (mushtarak) word may be used in both of its meanings together. This speaker said: The aforementioned verses indicate that the word nikah is literal for both wata' and 'aqd together, so the statement ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾ is a prohibition against both wata' and 'aqd together, taking the word in both of its senses.

The third way in argument: This is the view of one who says: a homonymous word may not be used in both its meanings together. They said: It has been established by the aforementioned proofs that the word nikah has been used in the Qur'an for wata' at times and for 'aqd at other times, and to say it is homonymous or figurative is contrary to the original principle; it is necessary to make it literal for the common element between them, which is the meaning of ḍamm, so that both homonymy and figurative usage are avoided. If that is so, then the statement ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾ is a prohibition against the common element between these two categories, and a prohibition against the common element between two categories necessarily entails a prohibition against each of the two categories, for prohibiting marriage (tazwij) is a prohibition against both 'aqd and wata' together. This is the most that can be said in setting out this argument.

The answer to it is from several aspects:

The first: We do not concede that the name nikah applies to wata'. The arguments they cited for this are countered by the following:

One of them: the statement of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "Nikah is my sunnah." There is no doubt that wata', insofar as it is wata', is not a sunnah of his; otherwise it would follow that illicit intercourse would be a sunnah of his. Since it is established that nikah is a sunnah, and it is established that wata' is not a sunnah, it is established that nikah is not an expression for wata'. Likewise the reliance on his statement: "Marry, so that you may multiply," for if wata' were named nikah, this would be permission for wata' in general. Likewise the reliance on the Exalted's statement: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32], and His statement: ﴿so marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3].

It may not be said: Since a conflict has arisen between these proofs, preference lies with us, for if we say that wata' is named nikah in the literal sense, it would entail the introduction of figurative usage into our proofs, and when there is a conflict between figurative usage and specification (takhsis), upholding specification is preferable.

For we say: You concede that the word nikah is used for 'aqd. So if we say that nikah is literal for wata', it would entail specification in the verses we mentioned, and it would entail figurative usage in the verses in which nikah is mentioned in the sense of 'aqd. But if we say that nikah in those verses means wata', then we are not obliged to specification. Thus your view entails both figurative usage and specification, while our view entails figurative usage only, so our view is preferable.

Page 17

The second of the aspects indicating that nikah is not literal for wata': the statement of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "I was born of nikah and I was not born of sifah." He established himself as born of nikah and not born of sifah, and this requires that sifah not be nikah; sifah is wata', so this requires that wata' not be nikah.

The third: whoever swears concerning children of fornication that they are not children of nikah does not break his oath; if wata' were nikah, he would have to break it. This is clear evidence that wata' is not named nikah in the literal sense.

Second: Even if we concede that wata' is named nikah, 'aqd is also named by it, so why is it more appropriate to interpret the verse according to what you mentioned than according to what we mentioned?

As for the first way, which al-Karkhi mentioned, it is extremely feeble, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: wata' is the effect (musabbab) of 'aqd. Just as it is good to apply the name of the effect to the cause figuratively, so likewise it is good to apply the name of the cause to the effect figuratively. Just as it may be said: nikah is a name for wata', then this name was applied to 'aqd because it is the cause of wata', so likewise it may be said: nikah is a name for 'aqd, then this name was applied to wata' because wata' is its effect. So why should one of them be more appropriate than the other? Rather, the possibility we mentioned is more appropriate, since the cause entailing the effect is more complete than the effect entailing a specific cause, for it is not impossible that one real outcome has many causes, such as ownership, which is acquired through sale, gift, bequest and inheritance. There is no doubt that mutual implication is a condition for the permissibility of figurative usage. Thus it is established that the claim that the name nikah is literal for 'aqd and figurative for wata' is preferable to the reverse.

The second: If nikah were literal for wata' and figurative for 'aqd, and it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that a single word may not be used in its literal and figurative senses together, then it would follow that the verse does not indicate the ruling of 'aqd. Although al-Karkhi accepted this, it is refuted by decisive proof, for the exegetes agreed that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that they used to marry the wives of their fathers, and the Muslims agreed that the occasion of revelation must necessarily fall within the verse, though they differed on whether anything other than it falls within the verse.

As for the occasion of revelation falling within it, that is agreed upon by the community. So when it is established by the consensus of the exegetes that the occasion of revelation of this verse is 'aqd, not wata', and it is established by the consensus of the Muslims that the occasion of revelation must be intended, it is established by consensus that the prohibition of 'aqd is intended by this verse. Thus al-Karkhi's view stands in opposition to this decisive proof, and it is therefore corrupt and definitively rejected.

As for the second of what they mentioned, namely that we carry the word nikah on both of its meanings, we say: this too is false, and we have explained the reason for its falsehood in the principles of jurisprudence.

As for the third way, it is the best of the ways mentioned in this section, but it is also weak, because the joining (ḍamm) present in wata' is an expression for the contiguity and adhesion of bodies, whereas the joining present in 'aqd is not like that, for offer and acceptance are non-persisting sounds, so the meaning of joining, meeting and contiguity in them is impossible. If that is so, it is established that there is no common concept between wata' and 'aqd such that it may be said that the word nikah is literal for it. When this is discarded, nothing remains but to say that the word nikah is homonymous between wata' and 'aqd, and that it is literal for one of them and figurative for the other, and at that point the discussion returns to

Page 18

the first two ways. This is the summarized discussion on this.

The second way in answering this argument: we say: Suppose we concede that nikah means wata'. But why do you say that the Exalted's statement ﴿what your fathers married﴾ means the women who were married? The evidence against this is their consensus that the particle "mā" is literal for non-rational beings. So if its intended meaning here were the women who were married, this would entail a figurative usage, which is contrary to the original principle. Rather, the grammarians agreed that "mā" together with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar). So the sense of the verse is: "And do not marry the marriage of your fathers." On this basis, the intended meaning is a prohibition against your marrying a marriage like the marriage of your fathers, for their marriages were without a guardian (walī) and without witnesses, were temporary, and were by way of coercion and compulsion. So God, exalted is He, forbade them by this verse from such marriages. This view is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari in his commentary on this verse.

**[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verse 22 (part 2 of 3)]**

The third answer to this argument: We grant that what is meant by His words ﴿what your fathers married﴾ is the women they married, and the implied sense is: "Do not marry those whom your fathers married." But His words "those whom your fathers married" are not explicit in generality, as shown by the fact that it is valid to prefix the words "all" and "some" to them. One may say: "Do not marry all that your fathers married," and "Do not marry some of those whom your fathers married." If this were explicit in generality, prefixing "all" would be redundant, and prefixing "some" would be deficient. It is known that this is not the case. Therefore it is established that His words ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾ do not signify generality, and if they do not signify generality, they do not encompass the place of dispute.

It may be objected: If it does not signify generality, then directing it to some of its categories would not be preferable to directing it to the rest, so it would become ambiguous (mujmal) and not informative, and the default is that it should not be so.

We reply: We do not grant that, on the supposition that it does not signify generality, directing it to some of its categories is not preferable to directing it to others. This is because the exegetes have unanimously agreed that the occasion of its revelation was nothing other than marrying the wives of fathers. Therefore directing it to this category is preferable. On this supposition, it does not follow that the verse is ambiguous, nor that it encompasses the place of dispute.

The fourth answer: We grant that this prohibition encompasses the place of dispute, but why do you say that it signifies prohibition (tahrim)? Are not many categories of prohibition not signifying prohibition, but signifying reprehension (tanzih)? So why do you say that the matter is not as such? At most, one can say: "This is contrary to the default (asl), but it must be resorted to when evidence indicates it." We shall mention the proofs of the validity of this marriage, God willing.

The fifth answer: Even granting that what you have mentioned indicates the invalidity of this marriage, there is here what indicates the validity of this marriage, and it is from several aspects:

The first argument: This marriage is concluded (muntaqid), so it must be valid. The demonstration that it is concluded: according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, it is forbidden by this verse, and among his school's principles is that the prohibition of a thing indicates that the thing itself is concluded. This is the root of his position in the question of the invalid sale and the fasting of the day of sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). It follows from the combination of these two premises that this marriage is concluded according to Abu Hanifa's principle. When the position that it is concluded in this instance is established, the position that it is valid must be established, because there is no one who distinguishes between them. This is a good argument by way of imposition (ilzam) against them regarding the validity of this marriage.

[p. 19]

The second argument: The generality of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. This is a prohibition against marrying polytheistic women, and it extends the prohibition to a limit, which is their belief. A ruling that extends to a limit ends upon the attainment of that limit. Therefore the prohibition on marrying them must end upon their belief, and when the prohibition ends, permissibility is attained. This implies the permissibility of marrying them absolutely, and there is no doubt that the woman who was the father's concubine (mazniyya) and others are included in this generality. At most, one can say that this generality has been subject to specification (takhsis) in some places, but it remains a proof in the place other than the place of specification. Likewise, we cite all the general texts found in the domain of marriage, such as His words: ﴿And marry the single among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32], and His words: ﴿So marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. Also, we rely on His words: ﴿And there is made lawful for you what is beyond that﴾. No one may say that His words ﴿beyond that﴾ is a pronoun referring to what was mentioned previously, and among what was mentioned previously is His words: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾. This is because the pronoun must refer to the nearest of the things mentioned, and the nearest of what was mentioned to it is from His words: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾. Therefore His words ﴿And there is made lawful for you what is beyond that﴾ refer to it, and His words ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾ are not included in it. Also, we rely on the general wording of the hadiths, such as the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "If there comes to you one whose religion you are pleased with, then marry him," and his words: "Marry your daughters to equals (akfa')." All these general texts encompass the place of dispute.

Know that we have shown in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that preponderance by the multiplicity of evidences (kathrat al-adilla) is permissible. Given this, we say: On the supposition that it is established for them that marriage is literally sexual intercourse (wat') and metaphorically a contract ('aqd), then if we interpret the verse as referring to the contract, we incur only one metaphor. But if we interpret that verse as referring to the prohibition of marriage, we incur these numerous specifications. Thus the preponderance lies on our side due to the multiplicity of evidences.

The third argument: The well-known hadith on this question, the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The unlawful does not make the lawful unlawful." At most, it may be said: If a drop of wine falls into a jug of water, then here the unlawful has made the lawful unlawful. And if the woman who is lawfully married becomes mixed with foreign women and becomes indistinguishable from them, then here too the unlawful has made the lawful unlawful. However, we say: the entry of specification into it in some cases does not prevent using it as evidence.

The fourth argument: By way of analogy (qiyas). We say: the factor that makes marriage permissible is present, and the distinction between the place of consensus (mahall al-ijma') and the place of dispute is clear, so the position of permissibility must be affirmed. As for the factor that makes it permissible, it is that we analogize the marriage of this woman to the marriage of all other women when the agreed-upon conditions are present, with the common element being the benefits (masalih) inherent in marriage. As for the distinguishing factor, it is that this prohibition of marriage (mahramiyya) was established by the Law only in an effort to preserve the connection (wusla) produced by the marriage contract, and it is known that this does not befit fornication (zina).

The explanation of the first point: Whoever marries a woman—if the man's father and son were not to enter upon the woman, and the woman's mother and daughter were not to enter upon the man, then the woman would remain like one confined in a house, and most of the benefits for the husband and wife would be lost. And if we permitted this entry without ruling it a prohibition of marriage (mahramiyya), then perhaps the gaze of one would extend to the other, and inclination and desire would arise. And upon marrying her mother or her daughter, an intense enmity would arise between them, because harm coming from relatives has a stronger impact, is more painful and more influential. And upon the arising of intense enmity, divorce and separation occur. But when the prohibition of marriage is established, desires are cut off and lust is restrained, so that harm does not occur, and the marriage between the spouses remains free from this corruption.

[p. 20]

Thus it is established that the purpose of the Law's ruling on this prohibition of marriage is to strive for the perpetuation of the connection between the spouses. And since the purpose of legislating the prohibition of marriage is to preserve that connection, it is known that the connection arising through marriage is desired to endure. Therefore the Law's ruling establishing this prohibition of marriage is congruent with it. As for the connection arising through fornication, it is not desired to endure, so the Law's ruling establishing this prohibition of marriage is not congruent with it. This is an acceptable and fitting argument in distinguishing the two cases. This is also the statement of Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, when he debated this question with Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, saying: "An intercourse for which you are praised, and an intercourse for which you are stoned—how can they be alike?" Let us suffice with this amount of discussion on this question.

Know that the reason for mentioning this extensive treatment here is that Abu Bakr al-Razi (al-Jassas) was lengthy on this question in his book. That lengthiness was nothing but prolixity in confused words and corrupt, feeble arguments. Then, when the matter reached a debate with Imam al-Shafi'i, he was discourteous and exceeded his bounds, plunged into foolishness, neglected to establish the proofs, and overlooked the presentation of his arguments. Then, after writing many pages of trifles from which neither his school gained benefit nor his opponents were harmed, he displayed severe disparagement and great arrogance regarding the abundance of knowledge of his companions and the scarcity of knowledge of those who differ from them. Had he been a man of learning, he would have wept over himself for those words with which he tried to support his position, and would have learned the proofs from those who were qualified to know them. Whoever looks at our book and at his book, and is fair, will know that we took from him a pebble (kharaza) and then made it a pearl (lu'lu'a) through the intensity of refinement and establishment. Then we answered him with sound answers in accordance with the principles of jurisprudence and conforming to the rules of fiqh. We ask Allah for a good end, continued success, and support.

* * *

The third question: The exegetes have mentioned several views regarding His words ﴿except what has already passed﴾:

The first, which is the best of them: what al-Sayyid, author of Hall al-Muqil, mentioned, saying: "This is an exception in meaning, because His words ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ refer to what occurred before the revelation of the verse of prohibition, for that is pardoned."

The second: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "This is like the exception of 'except that their swords' from His words ‘and there is no fault in them’." It means: If it is possible for you to marry what has already passed, then marry it, for nothing else is lawful to you. That is not possible, and the aim is hyperbole in its prohibition and blocking the way to its permissibility, as one says: "until the crow turns white" and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle."

The third: This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), because it is not permissible to make an exception of the past from the future. The meaning is: "But what has already passed, indeed Allah has overlooked it."

The fourth: "Illa" here means "after," as in His words: ﴿They will not taste death therein except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], meaning after the first death.

The fifth: Some said its meaning is: "except what has already passed, for you are upheld in it." They said: He, peace be upon him, allowed them to remain with them for a period, then ordered them to separate from them. He did this so that their abandonment of this evil custom would occur gradually. It has also been said that this is an error, because he, peace be upon him, did not allow anyone to marry his father's wife, even during the Jahiliyya. Al-Bara' narrated: "That the Prophet, peace be upon him, sent Abu Burda to a man who had married his father's wife, to kill him and take his property."

The fourth question: To what does the pronoun in His words "innahu" refer? There are two views:

The first: It refers to this marriage before the prohibition. Allah, may He be exalted, informed that what He forbade them had always been detested in their hearts and abhorred by them. The Arabs used to call a man's child by his father's wife "maqti" (a hated one). This is because a father's wife resembles the mother, and marrying mothers was among the most hideous things to the Arabs. Since this marriage resembled that, it was necessarily considered reprehensible by them. So Allah made clear

[p. 21]

that this marriage had always been detestable and abhorrent.

The second: The pronoun refers to this marriage after the prohibition. Allah, may He be exalted, made clear that it was an abomination (fahisha) in Islam and hateful in the sight of Allah. He said "kana" (it was) to show that it was, in the ruling of Allah and in His knowledge, described by this attribute.

The fifth question: He, may He be exalted, described it with three attributes:

The first of them: that it is an abomination (fahisha). He described this marriage as an abomination because, as we have explained, a father's wife resembles the mother, so intimacy with her is among the most abominable of abominations.

The second: hatred (maqt). It is an expression for a hatred combined with contempt, arising from an ugly act committed by its doer. When it comes from Allah toward a servant, it indicates the utmost disgrace and loss.

Third, His saying: ﴿And it is evil as a way﴾. Al-Layth said: "Sa'a" (ساءَ) is an intransitive verb whose subject is an implied pronoun, and "sabilan" (سَبِيلًا) is in the accusative as an explanation (tamyiz) of that subject, just as He said: ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾ [al-Nisa': 69]. Know that the degrees of ugliness are three: ugliness in the intellects (al-'uqul), in the sacred law (al-shara'i'), and in customs (al-'adat). So His saying: ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination﴾ points to intellectual ugliness (al-qubh al-'aqli), His saying: ﴿and hateful﴾ points to legal ugliness (al-qubh al-shar'i), and His saying: ﴿and evil as a way﴾ points to ugliness in convention and custom (al-'urf wal-'adah). When these aspects are combined in it, it has reached the utmost in ugliness. And God knows best.

**[Page 22]**

**The sixth category of rulings concerning women mentioned in these verses:**
﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters.﴾

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, explicitly stated the prohibition of fourteen categories of women. Seven of them are prohibited by lineage: mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brothers' daughters, and sisters' daughters. Seven others are not prohibited by lineage: milk mothers, milk sisters, the mothers of wives, the daughters of wives (on condition that the husband has consummated the marriage with the wives), wives of sons, and wives of fathers. However, the wives of sons are mentioned here, and the wives of fathers are mentioned in the preceding verse. There is also the prohibition of combining two sisters. In the verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** Al-Karkhi (*al-Karkhi*) held that this verse is *mujmal* (ambiguous, requiring clarification). He said: "Because the prohibition in it is attributed to mothers and daughters, and prohibition cannot be attributed to physical entities but only to actions, and the action is not mentioned in the verse, it is not preferable to attribute this prohibition to some actions that cannot be performed upon the persons of mothers and daughters over others. Thus the verse became ambiguous from this aspect."

The answer to this is from two aspects:

**The first:** The placing of His statement, ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾, indicates that what is meant by His statement ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ is the prohibition of marrying them.

**The second:** It is known necessarily from the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) that what is meant by it is the prohibition of marrying them. The principle in this is that when prohibition and permissibility are attributed to physical entities, what is meant is the prohibition of the action that is customarily sought from them. So when it is said, "Forbidden to you are carrion and blood," everyone understands that what is meant is the prohibition of eating them. When it is said, "Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, and your sisters," everyone understands that what is meant is the prohibition of marrying them. When the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases," everyone understood that what is meant is that it is not lawful to shed his blood. Since these matters are known necessarily, raising doubts about them is tantamount to undermining self-evident truths and resembles sophistry (*sufsata'iyya*, the method of fallacious argument), and so it is extremely feeble. And God knows best.

Yet I have a discussion on this from other aspects:

**The first:** His statement, ﴿Forbidden to you﴾, is in the form of the passive voice (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu*, the verb whose agent is not named). So there is no explicit statement that the agent of the prohibition is God, exalted is He. Unless that is established, the verse does not convey anything else, and the only way to establish it is by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus). So this verse alone conveys nothing; rather, consensus on this premise is required along with it.

**The second:** His statement, ﴿Forbidden to you﴾, is not an explicit text establishing the prohibition as permanent. The quantity mentioned in the verse can be divided into the perpetual and the temporary. It is as if He, exalted is He, said at one time: "Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters until such-and-such a time only," and at another time: "Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters permanently and eternally." Since what is mentioned in the verse is fit to be the subject of division into these two types, it is not an explicit text on permanence. Therefore, this permanence is not derived from the apparent meaning of the verse, but from a separate indication.

**The third:** His statement, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, is a direct address (*khitab mushafaha*), so it is restricted to those present. Establishing this prohibition for everyone is derived from a separate proof.

**The fourth:** His statement, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, is a report of the establishment of this prohibition in the past. The apparent meaning of the wording does not encompass the present or the future, so that is not known except by a separate proof.

**The fifth:** The apparent meaning of His statement, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, requires that He has prohibited for each person all of their mothers and all of their daughters. It is known that this is not the case. Rather, what is intended is that He, exalted is He, matched plural with plural, which requires matching the individual with the individual. This requires that God, exalted is He, has prohibited for each person his own mother specifically and his own daughter specifically. This involves a kind of deviation from the apparent meaning.

**The sixth:** His statement, "Forbidden (*hurrimat*)," its apparent meaning implies a prior state of permissibility. For if it were always characterized by prohibition, then His statement "Forbidden" would be a prohibition of what is already prohibited in itself, and that would be the creation of the existent, which is impossible. Thus it is established that what is meant by His statement ﴿Forbidden﴾ is not the renewal of the prohibition, such that the aforementioned problem would arise. Rather, what is meant is the report of the occurrence of the prohibition. Thus it is established by these aspects that the apparent meaning of the verse alone is not sufficient to establish the intended ruling. And God knows best.

* * *

**Second issue:** Know that the prohibition of mothers and daughters has been established from the time of Adam (peace be upon him) until now. No permissibility of marrying them has been established in any of the divine religions. Rather, Zoroaster, the prophet of the Magians, did say it was permissible. However, most Muslims agree that he was a liar. As for marrying sisters, it has been reported that this was permissible in the time of Adam (peace be upon him), and God only permitted it out of necessity. I have seen some scholars deny this and say: "God used to send a *hawari* (a woman of paradise) from the Garden for the sons of Adam (peace be upon him) to marry." This is far-fetched, because if the wives of his sons and the husbands of his daughters were from the people of paradise, then this progeny would not be from the children of Adam alone, and that is false by consensus.

The scholars mentioned that the reason for this prohibition is that intercourse is humiliation and degradation. A person is ashamed to mention it and does not undertake it except in a private place, and most kinds of insults are only done by mentioning it. If this is so, it is obligatory to protect mothers from it, because a mother's favor upon her child is the greatest form of favor, so it is obligatory to protect her from this degradation. A daughter is like a part of a person and a portion of him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fatimah is a part of me," so it is obligatory to protect her from this degradation, because intimacy with her is akin to degradation. The same applies to the rest. And God knows best.

Now let us begin with the details. We say:

* * *

**The first category of prohibited women: mothers.** In this there are issues:

**First issue:** Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: *ummahat* is the plural of *umm* (mother). The original form of *umm* is *ummahah*, and the *ha'* was dropped in the singular. The poet said:

*"My mothers are Khindif, and Elias is my father."*

*Umm* may also be pluralized as *ummat* without a *ha'*, and it is mostly used for non-human animals. The poet al-Ra'i said:

*"The swift camels of Mundhir and Muhariq, their mothers and their stock were tamed."*

**Second issue:** Every woman through whom your lineage traces back to you by birth, through your father or through your mother, by one degree or several degrees, whether through females or males, she is your mother. Here there is a discussion: there is no doubt that the word *umm* is literally (*haqiqa*) applied to the biological mother. As for grandmothers, it is either literal or metaphorical (*majaz*). If the word *umm* is literal for both the biological mother and grandmothers, then it is either *mutawati'* (a word applying to a shared meaning among its referents) or *mushtarak* (a homonym, a word with several distinct meanings). If it is *mutawati'*, meaning that the word *umm* is assigned to a common quality between the biological mother and all grandmothers, then according to this assumption His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ is an explicit text on the prohibition of the biological mother and the prohibition of all grandmothers.

If the word *umm* is *mushtarak* between the biological mother and grandmothers, then this branches out from the question of whether a homonymous word may be used for both of its meanings simultaneously. Whoever permits this applies the word here to all of them, and then the prohibition of grandmothers is explicitly stated. Whoever says it is not permitted, those who hold this view have two approaches in this matter:

One: there is no doubt that the word *umm* here is intended to mean the biological mother, so the prohibition of marrying her is derived from this aspect. As for the prohibition of marrying grandmothers, it is not derived from this text, but from consensus.

Two: He, exalted is He, spoke with this verse twice, intending a different meaning each time. As for when we say the word *umm* is literal for the biological mother and metaphorical for grandmothers, it has been established that it is not permissible to use a single word at one time both literally and metaphorically. In that case, the two approaches we mentioned return to the case where the word *umm* is literal for both the biological mother and grandmothers.

* * *

**Third issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: If a man marries his mother and consummates the marriage with her, he incurs the *hadd* (the prescribed legal punishment). Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: He does not incur it. The argument of al-Shafi'i is that the existence of this marriage and its non-existence are equivalent, so this intercourse is pure fornication (*zina mahd*), and therefore he incurs the *hadd* according to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them with a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. We say that the existence of this marriage and its non-existence are equivalent because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, and it is known necessarily from the religion of Muhammad (peace be upon him) that God's intention from this verse is the prohibition of marrying them. Once this is established, we say: what exists is nothing but the form of offer and acceptance. If this contract were to take place, then either it is said that it occurred in reality or in the legal ruling. The first is false, because the form of offer and acceptance is speech, which is an accident that does not endure, and acceptance does not exist except after the offer, and the occurrence of a contract between what exists and what does not exist is impossible. The second is false, because the Law has clearly explained in this verse the invalidity of this contract, and with this contract being definitively invalid in the legal ruling, how can it be said that it is legally concluded? Thus it is established that the existence of this contract and its non-existence are equivalent. And once that is established, the remainder of the branching and the argument is as preceded.

* * *

**The second category of prohibited women: daughters.** In this there are two issues:

**First issue:** Every female whose lineage traces back to you by birth, by one degree or several degrees, through females or males, she is your daughter. As for the son's daughter and the daughter's daughter, are they called daughter literally or metaphorically? The discussion on this is exactly what we mentioned concerning mothers.

**Second issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: A girl created from the water of fornication is not prohibited to the fornicator. Abu Hanifa said: She is prohibited. The argument of al-Shafi'i is that she is not his daughter, so she must not be prohibited. We say she is not his daughter for the following reasons:

**[Commentary of al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on Surah 4, verse 23, part 2 of 4]**

The first point: Abu Hanifah must either establish that she is his daughter on the basis of reality, which is that she was created from his water (*ma'*), or on the basis of the ruling of the Shari'ah (*hukm al-shar'*) that this lineage is established. The first is invalid according to his own school, both *tard* (the inclusive test, where the cause is present and so is the ruling) and *'aks* (the reverse test, where the ruling is absent and so is the cause). As for *tard*: if he buys a virgin slave-girl, deflowers her, and keeps her in his house, and she bears a child, it is known that this child was created from his water. Yet Abu Hanifah said: "The lineage is not established except by acknowledgment (*istilhaq*)." If the cause were the child being formed from his water, he would not have hesitated over establishing this lineage without acknowledgment. As for the reverse test: if an easterner marries a woman from the west and a child is born there, Abu Hanifah established the lineage here even though it is certain that the child was not created from his water. Thus it is established that making formation from his water a cause of lineage is invalid, by *tard* and by *'aks*, according to Abu Hanifah's view. And if we say that lineage is established only by the ruling of the Shari'ah, then here the Muslims are agreed that the child of fornication has no lineage with the fornicator. If he were ascribed to the fornicator, the judge would be obliged to prevent that ascription. Thus it is established that her ascription to him is impossible, neither on the basis of reality nor on the basis of the ruling of the Shari'ah.

The second point: the use of his (ﷺ) saying: "The child belongs to the bed, and the adulterer gets the stone." His saying "the child belongs to the bed" implies that lineage is restricted to the marriage bed.

The third point: if she were his daughter, she would receive inheritance, because of the words of Allah ﴿The male's share is equal to the share of two females﴾ [4:11]. She would also have the right of compulsion (*wilayat al-ijbar*) in marriage, because of his (ﷺ) saying: "Marry your daughters to suitable husbands." He would also be obliged to maintain her and to provide her custody, and seclusion with her would be permitted. Since none of this is established, we know that daughterhood is negated. And when it is established that she is not his daughter, it must be permissible for him to marry her. This is because the prohibition on marrying her is either due to daughterhood, or due to the fact that fornication creates the prohibition of in-law relationship (*musahara*). This restriction is established by consensus (*ijma'*). Daughterhood is invalid, as we have mentioned, and the prohibition of in-law relationship through fornication is also invalid, as the explanation of this issue has already passed. Thus it is established that she is not forbidden to the fornicator. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

The third category of the prohibited: sisters. This includes full sisters (from both father and mother), half-sisters from the father only, and half-sisters from the mother only.

The fourth and fifth categories: paternal and maternal aunts. Al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Every male to whom your lineage traces back, his sister is your aunt (*'ammah*). The aunt may be from the mother's side, being the sister of your mother's father. And every female to whom your lineage traces back by birth, her sister is your maternal aunt (*khalah*). The maternal aunt may be from the father's side, being the sister of your father's mother.

The sixth and seventh categories: daughters of a brother and daughters of a sister. The discussion of daughters of a brother and daughters of a sister is like the discussion of daughters of the loins (*banat al-sulb*).

[page 25]

These seven categories are prohibited by the explicit text of the Book, by lineage and by kinship (*arham*).

The exegetes said: Every woman whom Allah has forbidden to marry by lineage and kinship, her prohibition is permanent and never lifted in any way. As for those women who are lawful to marry but then become prohibited due to a subsequent cause, they are the ones mentioned in the rest of the verse.

\* \* \*

The eighth and ninth categories: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through fosterage﴾.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through fosterage﴾.

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: He called the nursing women "mothers" because of the prohibition, just as Allah called the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) "mothers of the believers" in His words: ﴿His wives are their mothers﴾ [33:6], because of the prohibition.

The second issue: In this verse Allah explicitly stated the prohibition of mothers and sisters through fosterage. However, the prohibition is not confined to them, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by fosterage." We know that the matter is so by the indication of these verses. This is because when Allah called the nursing woman "mother" and the nursed one's sister "sister," He thereby indicated that He has made fosterage follow the pattern of lineage. For Allah prohibited seven through lineage: two of them are those connected by birth, namely mothers and daughters, and five of them are through the relationship of siblingship, namely sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, daughters of a brother, and daughters of a sister. Then, when Allah began to address the rulings of fosterage, He mentioned one example from each of these two categories as an alert to the rest. From the category of birth relations He mentioned mothers, and from the category of sibling relations He mentioned sisters. By mentioning these two examples from these two categories, He indicated that the situation in the matter of fosterage is like the situation in lineage. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) confirmed this explanation with his explicit words: "What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by fosterage," so the explicit hadith matches the implied meaning of the verse. This is a subtle explanation.

\* \* \*

The third issue: The fostering mother of a person is the woman who nursed him. Likewise, every woman who is connected to that nursing woman by motherhood, whether through lineage or through fosterage, is also a mother. The situation of the father is like that of the mother. When you know the mother and the father, you also know the daughter by that same path. As for sisters, there are three types. The first is your sister by your father and mother, who is a young unrelated girl whom your mother nursed with your father's milk, whether she nursed her together with you or with a child before you or after you. The second is your sister by your father only, not by your mother, whom your father's wife nursed with your father's milk. The third is your sister by your mother only, not by your father, whom your mother nursed with other milk. When you know this, it becomes easy for you to know the paternal aunts, maternal aunts, daughters of a brother, and daughters of a sister.

The fourth issue: Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Fosterage establishes prohibition on condition that there are five sucklings. Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: A single suckling is sufficient. This issue has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. Abu Bakr al-Razi argued from this verse, saying: Allah linked this designation, meaning motherhood and siblingship, to the act of nursing. Therefore, wherever this act occurs, the ruling must follow from it. Then he questioned himself, saying: The words of Allah ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾ are like the words of someone who says: "And your mothers who gave you," and "your mothers who clothed you." This implies that the attribute of motherhood and sisterhood precedes the act of nursing. Indeed, if Allah had said, "Those who nursed you are your mothers," your purpose would still be achieved.

He answered this by saying: Nursing is what gives her the mark of motherhood. Since the designation is deserved by the existence of nursing, the ruling is attached to it. This is unlike the words "and your mothers who clothed you," because the designation of motherhood is not derived from clothing.

He said: What indicates that this is understood from this verse is what is narrated: a man came to Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) and said: Ibn al-Zubayr said: There is no harm in one suckling or two sucklings. Ibn Umar said: The decree of Allah is better than the decree of Ibn al-Zubayr. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and your sisters through fosterage﴾. He said: So Ibn Umar understood from the apparent wording the prohibition by a small amount of fosterage.

Know that this answer is extremely weak. As for his saying that the designation of motherhood comes only from the act of nursing, we say: Is the dispute about anything other than this? In my view, the designation of motherhood comes from fosterage only after five times, whereas in your view it comes from the mere basic act of nursing. You only relied on this verse to establish that basic principle. So when you establish the argument from this verse on this principle, you have proved the proof by what is to be proved, which is circular and invalid. As for relying on Ibn Umar's understanding that the verse indicates the prohibition by the mere act of nursing, it is opposed by the fact that Ibn al-Zubayr did not understand it that way. Each of them was among the jurists of the Companions and among the scholars of the Arabic language. How then can one's understanding be taken as proof while the other's understanding is not taken as proof against the view of his opponent? Were it not for the severe bias that blinds the heart, the weakness of these words would not be hidden.

Then Abu Bakr al-Razi began to rely, in establishing his school, on hadiths and analogies. Whoever speaks about the rulings of the Qur'an must mention only what he derives from the verse itself. As for anything beyond that, it belongs properly to the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*).

\* \* \*

The tenth category of the prohibited: the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾. On this there are two issues:

The first issue: This verse includes the original mothers and all their grandmothers on both the father's and mother's side, just as we explained the same in the case of lineage.

The second issue: The view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*) is that whoever marries a woman, her mother becomes forbidden to him, whether he has consummated the marriage with her or not. But a group of the Companions claimed that the woman's mother becomes forbidden only by consummating the marriage with the daughter, just as the stepdaughter (*rabibah*) becomes forbidden only by consummating the marriage with her mother. This is the view of Ali, Zayd, Ibn Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Jabir, and it is the most apparent of the reports from Ibn Abbas. Their proof is that Allah mentioned two rulings, namely His words: ﴿And the mothers of your wives and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾ [4:23], then He mentioned a condition, namely His words: ﴿of your wives with whom you have consummated [the marriage]﴾ [4:23]. Therefore that condition must apply to both sentences together.

The argument of the first view is that His words: ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾ form a complete sentence in itself, and no indication has shown that this condition returns to it. Therefore it must be held to remain on its general meaning. We say that this condition does not return to it, for several reasons:

The first: A condition must be attached to something mentioned earlier. If we attach it to one of the two sentences, there is no need to attach it to the second sentence. So attaching it to the second sentence is abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence, and that is not permissible.

The second: The generality of this sentence is known, while the return of the condition to it is only possible. It is not permissible for the condition to be specific to the last sentence alone, but it is permissible for it to return to both sentences together. Yet holding that this condition returns to both sentences is abandoning the apparent generality by a doubtful specifier, and that is not permissible.

The third: If this condition returned to the first sentence, then either it would be restricted to it, or it would be connected to it and to the second sentence as well. The first is invalid, because on this assumption it would necessitate the prohibition of stepdaughters absolutely, and that is invalid by consensus. The second is also invalid, because on this assumption the structure of the verse would become: "And the mothers of your wives from among your wives with whom you have consummated [the marriage]." Then the word *min* (from) here would mean distinction (*tamyiz*). Then it says: "And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, from your wives with whom you have consummated [the marriage]," and the word *min* here would mean the starting point of the extent, as one says: "The daughters of the Messenger from Khadijah." This would require using a single word, which is shared (*mushtarak*), in both of its meanings at once, and that is not permissible. It can be answered by saying: the word *min* here expresses connection, as in His words: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [9:67], and as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am not of *dadd* (idle play), nor is *dadd* of me." The general meaning of mere connection is present in both the wives and the stepdaughters together.

The fourth point regarding the evidence for what we have said: what ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If a man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her mother, whether or not he has consummated the marriage with the daughter. And if he marries the mother and does not consummate the marriage with her, then divorces her, he may marry the daughter if he wishes." Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari criticized the soundness of this hadith. ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud used to give the ruling that one may marry the mother of a woman if he divorced the daughter before touching her, and he was at that time in Kufa. It so happened that he went to Medina and found the people unanimously opposed to his ruling. When he returned to Kufa, he did not enter his house until he had gone to that man, knocked on his door, and ordered him to dismount from that woman.

Qatadah narrated from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab that Zayd ibn Thabit said: "If a man divorces his wife before consummation and wishes to marry her mother, then if he divorces her before consummation he may marry her mother; but if she dies, he may not marry her mother." Know that he distinguished between death and divorce regarding the prohibition only because divorce before consummation does not carry with it any of the rulings of consummation. Do you not see that no ʿiddah is obligatory upon her? As for death, since it has the status of consummation in regard to the obligation of ʿiddah, God therefore made it a cause of this prohibition.

* * *

The eleventh category of prohibited women:

﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage; but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, there is no blame upon you﴾.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage; but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, there is no blame upon you﴾.

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: *al-rabāʾib* (stepdaughters) is the plural of *rabība*, which is the daughter of a man's wife from another man. Its meaning is "one who is raised" (*marbūbah*), because the man raises her (*yarubbuhā*). It is said: "I raised so-and-so" (*rababtu fulānan arubbuhu*) and "I raised him" (*rabbabtuhu urabbīhi*), with the same meaning. *Al-ḥujūr* is the plural of *ḥijr*, and it has two forms. Ibn al-Sikkit said: the *ḥajr* of a person and his *ḥijr* (with fatḥ and kasr) are both used. The meaning of His words ﴿in your guardianship﴾ is in your upbringing; it is said: "So-and-so is in the *ḥijr* of so-and-so" when he is in his upbringing. The reason for this metaphor is that everyone who raises a child seats him in his lap (*ḥijr*), so the *ḥijr* came to be an expression for upbringing, just as it is said: "So-and-so is in the custody (*ḥaḍānah*) of so-and-so," and its origin is from the *ḥiḍn*, which is the armpit. Abu ʿUbayda said: "in your *ḥujūr*" means "in your houses."

The second issue: Mālik ibn Aws ibn al-Ḥadathān narrated from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The stepdaughter, if she was not in the husband's *ḥijr* and was in another city, then he divorced the mother after consummation, it is permissible for him to marry the stepdaughter." It is also reported that he (may Allah be pleased with him) argued for this by saying that God said: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾, making her being in his *ḥijr* a condition for her being his stepdaughter; so if she is not in his upbringing nor in his *ḥijr*, the condition has failed, and therefore the prohibition should not be established. This is a good argument. As for the rest of the scholars, they said: if a man consummates the marriage with a woman, her daughter becomes forbidden to him, whether or not she was in his upbringing. The evidence for this is the words of the Most High: ﴿but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, there is no blame upon you﴾; He tied the lifting of blame to the mere absence of consummation, and this requires that what necessitates the blame is merely consummation. As for the answer to the argument of the first view, it is that the general and most common case is that the daughter of a man's wife is in his upbringing; so this statement is about the general case, not that this qualifier is a condition for the establishment of this prohibition.

The third issue: Abu Bakr al-Razi relied, to establish that fornication (*zina*) entails the prohibition of affinity (*muṣāharah*), on the words of the Most High: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage﴾. He said: because "consummation" (*al-dukhūl*) is a term for sexual intercourse in general, whether the intercourse was by marriage or by illicit union; so this indicates that fornication with the mother makes the daughter forbidden. This argument is extremely weak, for this verse is restricted to a woman who was lawfully married, for two reasons. The first: this verse refers to a woman who was among his wives before he consummated the marriage with her, and the one fornicated with is not like that, so she cannot be included in the verse. The proof of the first is in two respects:
The first: His words ﴿from your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage﴾ indicate that her being among his wives precedes his consummation with her.
The second: He the Most High divided their wives into those who have been consummated with and those who have not, by His words ﴿but if you have not consummated the marriage with them﴾. Since their wives are divided into these two categories, we know that a woman's being among his wives is something distinct from consummation with her. As for the proof that the fornicated woman is not like that: in marriage, the woman becomes one of his wives by the force of the contract, whether or not he consummated with her; but in fornication, no other state arises before the consummation that makes her one of his wives. Thus it is established that the fornicated woman is not included in this verse. The second reason: if one bequeaths to "the wives of so-and-so," this adulteress is not included among them; and likewise if one swears an oath concerning "the wives of the sons of so-and-so," the oath is neither broken nor fulfilled by this adulteress. Thus the weakness of this argument is established. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The twelfth category of prohibited women:

﴿And the wives of your sons who are of your loins﴾. The words of the Most High: ﴿And the wives of your sons who are of your loins﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is not permissible for a father to marry his son's slave-girl. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is permissible. Al-Shafiʿi argued: "The son's slave-girl is a *ḥalīlah* (spouse), and the son's *ḥalīlah* is forbidden to the father." As for the first premise, its demonstration comes through an inquiry into the word *ḥalīlah*. We say: *ḥalīlah* is of the form *faʿīlah*, which may carry the sense of the active or the passive participle, so there are two possibilities:
One: that it is derived from *ḥill*, which is permissibility, so *ḥalīlah* would mean *muḥallah*, i.e., made lawful. There is no doubt that the slave-girl is like this, so she must be a *ḥalīlah* for him.
The second: that it is derived from *ḥulūl* (indwelling), so *ḥalīlah* is an expression for something that is a place of indwelling, and there is no doubt that the slave-girl is the place where the master dwells, so she is a *ḥalīlah* for him. As for when we take *ḥalīlah* in the sense of the active participle, there are also two possibilities:
The first: that because each of the two is so closely joined to the other, it is as if they both dwell in one garment, in one covering, and in one house; and there is no doubt that the slave-girl is like this.
The second: that each of them is, as it were, indwelling in the heart and soul of the other, because of the intensity of love and intimacy between them; so by the combination of what we have mentioned, it is established that the son's slave-girl is a *ḥalīlah*. As for the second premise, namely that the son's *ḥalīlah* is forbidden to the father, it is by His words ﴿and the wives of your sons who …﴾. It may not be said: the people of the language say "the *ḥalīlah* of a man is his wife." For we say: we have already shown, through these four kinds of derivation that are evident, that the word *ḥalīlah* includes the slave-girl; so the transmitted statement you cite is not to be relied upon, and how could it be, since it is testimony to a negation? For we do not deny that the word *ḥalīlah* includes the wife; but we interpret it with a meaning that includes both the wife and the slave-girl; so the saying of one who claims it is not so is testimony to a negation and is not to be heeded.

* * *

The second issue: His words ﴿who are of your loins﴾ are a precaution against the adopted son (*al-mutabannā*). In early Islam the adopted son had the status of a son, and a man's *ḥalīlah* is not forbidden to him if the one he adopted as a son is not of his loins. "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyyah, who was the daughter of Umayma bint ʿAbd al-Muttalib, and Zaynab was the daughter of the paternal aunt of the Prophet (ﷺ), after she had been the wife of Zayd ibn Ḥārithah. The polytheists said: 'He has married the wife of his son.' So God revealed: ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 4], and He said: ﴿so that there may be no restriction upon the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 37]."

* * *

The third issue: the apparent sense of His words ﴿And the wives of your sons who are of your loins﴾ does not include the wives of sons by nursing (*raḍāʿah*). When He said at the end of the verse ﴿and lawful for you is what lies beyond that﴾, it follows from the apparent sense of the two verses that marrying the wives of sons by nursing is permitted. However, he (peace be upon him) said: "What is forbidden by blood (*nasab*) is forbidden by nursing." This indicates the prohibition of marrying the *ḥalīlah* of a son by nursing, because His words ﴿and lawful for you is what lies beyond that﴾ encompass both nursing and non-nursing relations, so His words "What is forbidden by nursing is what is forbidden by blood" are more specific than it; thus they made the general wording of the Qur'an specific by a report of a single transmitter (*khabar al-wāḥid*). And Allah knows best.

* * *
