The fourth issue: they agreed that the prohibition of marrying a son's *ḥalīlah* takes effect by the contract itself, just as the prohibition of marrying a father's *ḥalīlah* takes effect by the contract itself, because the general wording of the verse includes the son's *ḥalīlah*, whether or not she has been consummated with. As for what is reported, that Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about His words ﴿And the wives of your sons who are of your loins﴾, that He did not make clear whether this ruling is restricted to the case where the son has consummated with her or is not restricted thus, Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Leave ambiguous what Allah left ambiguous." His purpose in this ambiguity is not that the ruling is unclear or doubtful; rather the purpose of this ambiguity is permanence. Do you not see that he said of the seven women prohibited by blood that they are among the "ambiguous ones," meaning those whose prohibition is established permanently? So here too, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The fifth issue: they agreed that this verse requires the prohibition of a grandson's *ḥalīlah* upon the grandfather, and this indicates that a son's son is applied to as being "of the loins" of the grandfather, and this indicates that a son's son is related to the grandfather by birth.

* * *

The thirteenth category of prohibited women:

﴿And that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed; indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed; indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His words ﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾ are in the nominative position, because the implied sense is: "Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters and the combining of two sisters."

The second issue: combining two sisters occurs in three ways: either he marries both together, or he owns both together, or he marries one and owns the other. As for combining two sisters in marriage, that occurs in two ways:
One: that he contracts marriage with both of them at once. The ruling here is then either combination, or specification, or choice, or nullification. As for combination, it is invalid by the ruling of this verse—so they said—except that this is problematic according to the principle of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him; for prohibition does not entail nullity according to Abu Hanifa. Do you not see that combining divorces is forbidden in his view, yet it takes effect? Likewise the prohibition of selling one dirham for two dirhams did not prevent the contract from being concluded; and likewise the case with all invalid transactions. Thus it is established that arguing from a prohibition to invalidity does not hold up according to his view.
If they say: "This also applies to you, for divorce during menstruation, or in a purity period in which one has had intercourse with her, is forbidden, yet it takes effect."

We say: there is a subtle and fine distinction between the two cases, which we have mentioned in *al-Khilafiyyat*. Whoever wants it should seek that book. Thus it is established that combining (the two sisters) is invalid. As for designating one of them (as the valid marriage) being invalid too, that is because preferring one without a preponderant reason is invalid. As for giving the choice (takhyir) being invalid, that is because saying "choice" requires that the contract come into existence and remain in force until the time of designation, and we have already shown that this is invalid. Nothing remains except the view that both contracts are invalid.

The second form of combining: that he marries one of them and then marries the other after her. Here it is ruled that the second marriage is void, because prevention (daf') is easier than removal (raf').

As for combining two sisters through ownership of slave-women (milk al-yamin), or by marrying one and acquiring the other as a slave-woman, the Companions disagreed about it. 'Ali, 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn 'Umar said: combining them is not permitted. The rest permitted it. As for the first group, they argued for their view that the apparent meaning of the verse requires the prohibition of combining two sisters absolutely, so combining them should be forbidden in all circumstances. It is also reported from 'Uthman that he said: "One verse made them lawful and another verse made them unlawful, and making lawful is preferable." The verse that requires the permission is His words: ﴿And the married women among women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾ [an-Nisa': 24], and His words: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6].

The answer to this is in two parts:

The first: these verses also indicate the prohibition of combining, because the Muslims have agreed that it is not permitted to combine two sisters in lawful sexual intercourse. So we say: if combining them in ownership were permitted, combining them in intercourse would be permitted, because of His words: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–6]. But combining them in ownership is not permitted. Thus it is established that this verse, by indicating the prohibition of combining them in ownership, is more appropriate than indicating permission.

The second: even if we grant that it indicates the permission of combining, we say that the preponderance lies with the side of prohibition. Several arguments show this:

The first: his words, peace be upon him: "Haram and halal never come together without haram overcoming halal."

The second: there is no doubt that caution lies in abstaining, so it is obligatory, because of his words, peace be upon him: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

The third: the basis of intimate relations (al-abda') originally rests on prohibition. This is evidenced by the fact that when the indications for the existence of a contract with its conditions and for its absence are equal, it is obligatory to say that it is prohibited. Moreover, marriage involves great benefits; if it were free of humiliation and harm, it would have to be legislated for mothers, because bestowing benefit upon them is recommended, because of His words: ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. Since that is forbidden, we know that it includes a mode of humiliation and harm. When this is so, the original state of it is prohibition, and permissibility is established only through an external factor. When this is established, it becomes clear that the preponderance lies with the side of prohibition. This is the explanation of the position of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, on this matter. As for the widely known view among the jurists, which is that it is permitted to combine two sister slave-women in ownership, then if he has intercourse with one of them, the second becomes unlawful for him, and this prohibition does not cease until his ownership of the first is removed by sale, gift, manumission, kitabah, or marriage.

* * *

The third issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: marrying the sister of a woman during the 'iddah of her sister after a final divorce (bain) is permitted. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is not permitted. The argument of al-Shafi'i: the combining has not occurred, so the prohibition should not arise. We say the combining has not occurred because the marriage of the divorced woman has ended, as evidenced by the fact that he may not have intercourse with her, and if he did, he would be liable for the hadd (prescribed punishment). We say that since combining has not occurred, the prohibition should not arise, because of His words after enumerating the prohibited women: ﴿And lawful for you is what lies beyond those﴾ [an-Nisa': 24]. There is no doubt that all those impediments are absent except the fact of combining two sisters. So when it is established by evidence that combining is absent, it is obligatory to say that it is permitted.

If it is said: the marriage still continues in some respects, as evidenced by the obligation of 'iddah and the obligation of maintenance for her.

We say: marriage has one reality, and one reality cannot be simultaneously existing and non-existing. Indeed, if this reality could be divided into two halves, so that one of them existed and the other did not, that would be valid. But if the single reality is not capable of being halved, this view is false. As for the obligation of 'iddah and the obligation of maintenance: know that if marriage has taken place, the power to restrain her has been established, and this does not produce the conclusion that the power to restrain her was established by the marriage, because denying the consequent (istithna' 'ayn al-tali) does not produce a conclusion. In sum, establishing a right of restraint after the marriage has ended by another means is intelligible in general. But to hold that the marriage continues while it is being said to be absent is something reason does not accept. And deriving the rulings of the Shari'ah in accordance with reason is more appropriate than interpreting them in a way whose falsity is known by immediate reason. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: if a disbeliever embraces Islam while having two sisters as wives, he may choose whichever of them he wishes and separate from the other. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if he married both of them at one time, he is separated from both of them; and if he married one first and the other second, he chooses the first and separates from the second. Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for Abu Hanifa with His words: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾. He said: this is a general address, so it includes both believer and disbeliever. When it is established that it includes the disbeliever, the marriage must be invalid, because a prohibition indicates invalidity.

It is said to him: you built this argument on the premises that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Shari'ah and that a prohibition indicates invalidity, yet Abu Hanifa holds neither of these two principles. If he says: they are sound according to your view, then this argument is binding upon you. We say: our statement that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Shari'ah does not mean in worldly rulings. For as long as he is a disbeliever, it is not possible to impose upon him the branches of Islam. When he embraces Islam, everything that passed falls from him by consensus. Rather, what is meant is the rulings of the Hereafter: that the disbeliever is punished for abandoning the branches of Islam just as he is punished for abandoning Islam itself. Once you know this, we say: we agree that if a disbeliever married without a guardian (wali) or witnesses, or married by force, then after embracing Islam that marriage is upheld in his case. Thus it is established that the address with the branches of the Shari'ah has no effect on worldly rulings regarding the disbeliever. The argument of al-Shafi'i: "Fayruz al-Daylami embraced Islam while having eight women as wives, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'Choose four and separate from the rest.'" He gave him the choice among them, and this contradicts what you have mentioned regarding the order. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: His words, ﴿except what has already passed﴾. There is the well-known difficulty here: the sense of the verse is "Your mothers are forbidden to you, and so-and-so, except what has already passed," and this implies an exception of the past from the future, which is not permitted. Its answer is given by the explanations mentioned in His words: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [an-Nisa': 22]. The meaning is that what has passed is forgiven, as evidenced by His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The fourteenth category of forbidden women:

﴿And all married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful for you are all others beyond these.﴾

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And all married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful for you are all others beyond these.﴾

In this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Ihsan (chastity, or being protected) linguistically means prevention, and likewise al-Hasanah (protection). It is said: a city is ḥaṣīnah and a coat of mail is ḥaṣīnah, meaning it prevents its owner from being wounded. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80], meaning, to prevent you and guard you. Al-Ḥiṣn is a fortified place, because it prevents whoever intends it harm. Al-Ḥiṣān with a kasra is a stallion horse, because it prevents its owner from destruction. Al-Ḥaṣān with a fatḥa is a chaste woman, because she prevents her private part from corruption. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12].

Know that the word iḥṣān comes in the Qur'an in several meanings:

The first: freedom, as in His statement: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning free women. Do you not see that if he slanders one who is not free, he is not flogged eighty lashes? Likewise His statement: ﴿Upon them is half the punishment of what is upon the chaste women﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], meaning free women. Likewise His statement: ﴿And whoever among you is not able to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], meaning free women.

The second: chastity, as in His statement: ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], and His statement: ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], and His statement: ﴿and she who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Anbiya: 91], meaning she kept her chaste.

The third: Islam. Of this is His statement: ﴿And when they are protected [by marriage]﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], which was explained as: when they have embraced Islam.

The fourth: a woman being married. It is said: a muḥṣanah woman is one who has a husband. His statement: ﴿And the married women among women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾ means those who have husbands. The evidence that this is the meaning is that He, exalted is He, conjoined the muḥṣanāt with the forbidden categories, so iḥṣān must be a cause of prohibition. It is known that freedom, chastity and Islam have no effect on that, so the meaning must be the married woman, because a woman's having a husband has an effect on her being forbidden to others.

Know that the four meanings share the original linguistic meaning, which is prevention. That is because we have mentioned that iḥṣān is an expression for prevention. Freedom is a cause of protecting a person from the execution of another's command over him; chastity also prevents a person from embarking on what is not fitting; likewise Islam prevents from much of what the soul and desire call to; the husband also prevents the wife from many matters, and the wife prevents the husband from falling into fornication. For this reason the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "Whoever marries has protected half of his religion." Thus it is established that all these meanings return to that linguistic meaning. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: al-Wahidi said: The reciters differed regarding "al-muḥṣanāt." They read with a kasra and a fatḥa on the ṣād throughout the Qur'an, except in this verse, where they all agreed on the fatḥa. Whoever read with the kasra made the verb belong to them, meaning: they embraced Islam, chose chastity, married, and protected themselves by these matters. Whoever read with the fatḥa made the verb belong to others, meaning their husbands protected them. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: a married dhimmi who commits adultery is stoned. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he is not stoned. The proof of al-Shafi'i is that adultery occurred together with iḥṣān, and that is a cause for the permissibility of blood. So it must be established that blood is permissible, and when that is established, it must be by way of stoning. As for our saying that adultery occurred together with iḥṣān: this depends on establishing two conditions. One: the occurrence of adultery, which is beyond doubt. Two: the occurrence of iḥṣān, which is present, because His statement: ﴿And the married women among women﴾ shows that the intended meaning of the muḥṣanah is the married woman, and this woman is married, so she is muḥṣanah. Thus it is established that adultery occurred with iḥṣān. We say that adultery with iḥṣān is a cause for the permissibility of blood because of his statement, prayer and peace be upon him: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except for one of three things," and among them his statement: "adultery after iḥṣān." He made adultery after iḥṣān a cause for the permissibility of blood with regard to a Muslim, and the Muslim is the locus of this ruling. As for the cause, it is simply adultery after iḥṣān, as shown by the fact that the particle of causation entered upon it. At most, the ruling in the case of a Muslim is that adultery after iḥṣān is a cause for the permissibility of blood; but the fact that he is a Muslim is the locus of the ruling, and the specificity of the locus of the ruling does not prevent extension to another locus, otherwise analogy would be entirely invalid. As for the cause, it is what the particle of causation entered upon, namely the quiddity of adultery after iḥṣān. When this quiddity occurs in the case of the married dhimmi, it must be that the permissibility of blood occurs in his case too. Thus it is established that his blood is permissible. Then there are two methods here: if we wish, we may suffice with this much, since we claim he is of permissible blood and the opponent does not hold this, so the opponent is silenced; or we say: since it is established that his blood is permissible, it must be by way of stoning, because no one distinguishes between them.

If it is said: what you have mentioned, if it indicates that the dhimmi is muḥṣan, there is here something that indicates he is not muḥṣan, namely His statement, prayer and peace be upon him: "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not muḥṣan." We say: it is established by the evidence we mentioned that the dhimmi is muḥṣan, and it is established by this report you mentioned that he is not muḥṣan. So we say: he is muḥṣan in the sense that he has a spouse, and not muḥṣan in the sense that his slanderer is not flogged. The statement "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not muḥṣan" must be understood as meaning that his slanderer is not flogged, not that he is not flogged for adultery, because it described him with the attribute of shirk, which is a crime, and what is mentioned after a crime must be something suitable to be a punishment. Our saying that his slanderer is not flogged is suitable to be a punishment; but our saying that he is not flogged for adultery is not suitable to be a punishment for him. So the meaning of his statement "Whoever associates partners with Allah is not muḥṣan" is what we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: regarding His statement: ﴿And the married women among women﴾ there are two views. One: what is meant by them is those who have husbands. On this reading, regarding His statement ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾ there are two aspects.

The first: that a woman who has a husband is forbidden to anyone other than her husband, except when she becomes the property of a person, in which case she becomes lawful to the owner.

The second: that what is meant here by ownership of the right hand is ownership by marriage, and the meaning is that women who have husbands are forbidden to you, except when you possess them by a new marriage after separation has taken place between them and their husbands. The purpose of this statement is to deter from fornication and to prohibit intercourse with them except by a new marriage, or by ownership of the right hand if the woman is a slave. He expressed that by ownership of the right hand because ownership of the right hand is present both in marriage and in ownership.

The second view: that what is meant here by the muḥṣanāt is free women. The evidence for this is His statement, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿And whoever among you is not able to marry free believing women, then from what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa: 25]. Here He mentioned the muḥṣanāt, then after that said: ﴿And whoever among you is not able to marry the muḥṣanāt﴾ [al-Nisa: 25], so the meaning of muḥṣanāt there is what is meant here; and there the muḥṣanāt means free women, so it is likewise here. On this view, regarding His statement ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: what is meant by it is: except the number that Allah made your possession, which is four. So the sense becomes: free women are forbidden to you, except the number Allah made your possession, which is four.

The second: free women are forbidden to you, except what Allah established as ownership over them for you, and that is when the guardian and witnesses are present and the other conditions recognized in the Sharia are met. The first interpretation of His statement ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾ is the preferred one, and His statement supports it: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5-6]. He made ownership of the right hand an expression for the establishment of ownership over them, so it must be explained here by that; because explaining the speech of Allah by the speech of Allah is the closest of ways to truth and correctness. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fifth issue: they agreed that if one of the spouses is taken captive before the other and brought to the abode of Islam, separation occurs. As for when both are taken captive together: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: here the marriage is dissolved, and it becomes lawful for the owner to make her clean (istibra') by delivering the child if she is pregnant by her husband, or by menstruation. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is not dissolved. The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that His statement ﴿And the married women among women﴾ requires the prohibition of women who have husbands; then His statement ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾ requires that when ownership arises the prohibition is lifted and lawfulness occurs. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: if separation occurred merely by the arising of ownership, then separation would have to occur through buying a slave-woman, receiving her as a gift, or inheriting her, and it is known that this is not so. It is said to him: it is as if you have not heard that the general after specification is a proof for what remains. Also: what occurs at captivity is the creation of ownership over her, whereas at sale ownership is transferred from one person to another; so the first is stronger, and the difference is clear.

* * *

The sixth issue: the position of ʿAli, ʿUmar and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf is that when a slave-woman who has been married is sold, divorce does not fall upon her, and the jurists of today are in consensus on this. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Jabir and Anas said: when she is sold, she is divorced. The proof of the majority: "When ʿAʾishah bought Barirah and freed her, the Prophet ﷺ gave her the choice, and she was married." If divorce occurred by the sale, that choice would have no purpose. Some narrated in the story of Barirah that he, peace be upon him, said: "The sale of a slave-woman is her divorce." The proof of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Masʿud is the generality of the exception in His statement: ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾. The essence of the answer to this returns to specifying the generality of the Qur'an by a single report (khabar al-wahid). And Allah knows best. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the mention of the forbidden categories with His statement: ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar) not from the same root as the verb, since His statement ﴿You are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa: 23] indicates the sense of writing. So the sense is: the prohibition of what has been mentioned of the forbidden categories has been decreed upon you as a writing from Allah. The coming of a masdar not from the verb's root is common; its parallel is ﴿and you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass as the passing of clouds — the handiwork of Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 88].

The second: al-Zajjaj said: it may also be in the accusative by way of command, with "upon you" explaining it, so the meaning is: adhere to the decree of Allah.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And lawful for you are all others beyond these﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿wa-uḥilla lakum﴾ in the passive voice, coordinated with His statement ﴿You are forbidden﴾; the rest read with a fatḥa on the alif and the ḥa, coordinated with "the decree of Allah," meaning Allah has decreed upon you the prohibition of these things and made lawful for you what lies beyond them.

**The second issue:** Know that the apparent meaning of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, requires the permissibility of everyone other than the categories mentioned. However, evidence has indicated the prohibition of other categories besides those mentioned, and we will mention them.

**The first category:** A woman may not be combined with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt. The Prophet ﷺ said: "A woman shall not be married while she is with her paternal aunt, nor while she is with her maternal aunt." This is a well-known, widely circulated report (*mashhur mustafid*). It has perhaps been said that it reached the level of *tawatur* (mass-transmitted, *mutawatir*). The Khawarij claimed that this is a single report (*khabar wahid*), and that specifying the general (*'umum*) of the Qur'an by a single report is not permissible. They argued for this with several points:

The first: The general wording of the Book is definitive in its text (*maqtu' al-matn*) and apparent in its indication, whereas a single report is probable in its text (*maznun al-matn*) and apparent in its indication. So the single report is weaker than the general wording of the Qur'an. Preferring it over the Qur'an, based on giving precedence to the weaker over the stronger, is therefore impermissible.

The second: Among the well-known reports is the report of Mu'adh, which prevents giving precedence to a single report over the general wording of the Qur'an in two respects. He said: "By what will you judge?" He said: "By the Book of God." He said: "And if you do not find it?" He said: "By the Sunnah of the Messenger of God" (ﷺ). So he gave precedence to adhering to the Book of God over adhering to the Sunnah, and this prevents giving precedence to the Sunnah over the Book. Also, he said: "And if you do not find it?" He said: "By the Sunnah of the Messenger of God" (ﷺ). He made the permissibility of adhering to the Sunnah conditional upon the absence of the Book by the word *in* ("if"), which is for conditionality, and what is conditional upon a condition is absent when the condition is absent.

The third: Among the well-known reports is his saying, peace be upon him: "When a report from me is transmitted to you, present it to the Book of God. If it agrees with it, accept it; otherwise, reject it." This report requires that a single report not be accepted except when it agrees with the Book. So when the report about the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt contradicts the apparent meaning of the Book, it must be rejected.

[Page 36]

The fourth: The words of His, Exalted is He, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, together with His, peace be upon him, saying: "A woman shall not be married while she is with her paternal aunt," the situation regarding these two cannot escape three possibilities. Either it is said: the verse was revealed after the report, in which case the verse abrogates the report (*nasikh lil-khabar*), because it is established that when a general (*'amm*) text comes after a specific (*khass*) one, the general abrogates the specific. Or it is said: the report came after the Book, and this requires the abrogation of the Qur'an by a single report, which is impermissible. Or it is said: they came together, and this is also invalid, because under this assumption the verse alone would be ambiguous, and the point of proof would be the combination of the verse with the report. It is not permissible for the infallible Messenger to spread the ambiguity while not spreading the proof. So the Messenger ﷺ would have been obliged not to let anyone hear this verse except together with this report, and to make a clear obligation upon the whole community that they should not convey this verse to anyone except together with this report. If that were so, the dissemination of this report would have to be equal to the dissemination of this verse. Since that is not the case, we know the falsity of this division.

The fifth point: Even if the soundness of this report were established with certainty, adhering to the verse would still be preferable to adhering to the report. Its explanation is in two respects:

The first: His words, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, are an explicit text in permission, just as His words, ﴿Forbidden to you are﴾ [al-Nisa: 23], are an explicit text in prohibition. As for the words of the Prophet ﷺ, "A woman shall not be married while she is with her paternal aunt," this is not an explicit text, because its apparent form is informative (*ikhbar*), and taking an informative form to mean a prohibition is a metaphor (*majaz*). Furthermore, given this assumption, the indication of the wording of prohibition upon prohibition is weaker than the indication of the wording of permission upon the meaning of permissibility.

The second: His words, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, are explicit in permitting everything other than what is mentioned. His words, "A woman shall not be married while she is with her paternal aunt," are not explicit in generality. Rather, its possibility of referring to a previously known particular (*al-ma'hud al-sabiq*) is more apparent.

The sixth point: He, Exalted is He, thoroughly enumerated in this verse the explanation of the categories of prohibited women, counting fifteen categories. Then, after this complete detailing and this extreme thoroughness, He said: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾. So if permissibility did not hold for everyone other than these mentioned categories, this thoroughness would become pointless and vain, and that is not fitting for the speech of the Most Wise of the wise. This is the statement of the aspects of the objection in this matter.

The answer has several aspects:

The first: what al-Hasan and Abu Bakr al-Asamm mentioned, namely that His words, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, do not require establishing permissibility in a perpetual manner. This aspect, in my view, is the most correct in this matter. The proof of this is that His words, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, are information about the permitting of everything other than what is mentioned. It does not clarify whether the permitting of everything other than what is mentioned occurred in a perpetual manner or not. The proof that it does not indicate perpetuity is that this concept can be divided into the perpetual and the non-perpetual. It is said at one time: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ forever; and at another time: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ until such-and-such a time. If His words ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ were explicit in perpetuity, this division would not be possible. Also, His words ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ convey only the permitting of those other than those mentioned, and sound reason testifies that permission is more general than perpetual permission and temporary permission. Once this is established, we say: His words ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ convey only the permissibility of those other than those mentioned at that time. As for the permissibility of them at other times, the wording is silent about it, neither affirming nor denying it. The permissibility of those other than those mentioned was established at that time, and the later emergence of the prohibition of some of them does not constitute a specification (*takhsis*) of that text, nor an abrogation (*naskh*) of it. This is a sound, rational, established aspect. By this same method we also say: His words ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa: 23] are not an explicit text on the perpetuity of this prohibition, and that perpetuity we know only through mass transmission (*tawatur*) from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ, not from this wording. This is the relied-upon answer on this point.

The second aspect: We do not concede that the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt is not mentioned in the verse. Its explanation is in two respects:

The first: He, Exalted is He, prohibited combining two sisters, and their being two sisters is appropriate to this prohibition, because sisterhood is a close kinship, and close kinship is appropriate to greater connection, compassion and honor. The fact that one of them is a co-wife of the other causes great estrangement and intense aversion, and between these two states there is a great incompatibility. Thus it is established that their being sisters is appropriate to the prohibition of combining them in marriage. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) that mentioning a ruling together with a descriptive attribute appropriate to it indicates, by the wording, that the ruling is caused (*mu'allal*) by that attribute. So it is established that His words ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ indicate that close kinship is a barrier to combining in marriage. This meaning is present between a woman and her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, so the ruling mentioned for the two sisters is also mentioned for the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt by way of implication, and indeed here it is more fitting. That is because the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt resemble the mother with respect to the daughter of a brother and the daughter of a sister, and they resemble the child with respect to the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt. The requirement of such a kinship for avoiding harm is stronger than the requirement of the kinship of sisterhood for preventing harm. So His words ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ are a barrier against the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt by way of greater priority (*bi-tariq al-awla*).

The second: He explicitly prohibited marriage to the mothers of wives, saying: ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾. The word "mother" may apply to the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt. As for applying it to the paternal aunt, this is because He, Exalted is He, said, reporting about the sons of Ya'qub, peace be upon him: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. So He applied the word "father" to Isma'il, although he was an uncle (*'amm*). If the uncle is a father, then the paternal aunt must be a mother. As for applying the word "mother" to the maternal aunt, this is indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ [Yusuf: 100], where what is meant is his father and his maternal aunt, for his mother had died at that time. So it is established by what we have mentioned that the word "mother" may apply to the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt, and therefore His words ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾ include the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt in some respects.

Having known this, we say: His words ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ mean what is beyond these mentioned women, whether they are mentioned by explicit statement, or by clear indication, or by subtle indication. Since this is so, the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt are not outside the mentioned women.

The third aspect: In answer to the doubt of the Khawarij, we say: His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, are general (*'amm*), and His words, "A woman shall not be married while she is with her paternal aunt, nor while she is with her maternal aunt," are specific (*khass*), and the specific takes precedence over the general. Then there are two ways here. One way is to say: this report reached the level of mass transmission in fame, and specifying the general of the Qur'an by a mass-transmitted report is permissible. In my view, this aspect is like obstinate denial (*mukabara*), because although this report is at the height of fame in our time, when it ultimately traces back to single-narrator transmission, it does not cease to belong to the category of single reports. The other way is to say: specifying the general of the Book by a single report is permissible, and its justification is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence. This is the summary of the discussion on this subject, and the relied-upon answer for us is the first aspect.

**The third category of specifications included in this generality:** A woman divorced three times is not lawful, but this specification was established by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful for him after that until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230].

**The fourth category:** The prohibition of marrying a woman in her waiting period ('*iddah*). Its evidence is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228].

[Page 38]

**The fifth category:** Whoever has a free woman in his marriage is not permitted to marry a slave woman. This is by consensus. According to al-Shafi'i, one who is able to afford a free woman (*qadir 'ala tawl al-hurra*) may not marry a slave woman. The evidence for this specification is His words: ﴿And whoever among you is not able to afford to marry believing free women, then from what your right hands possess [of believing slave women]﴾ [al-Nisa: 25]. The explanation of the indication of this verse for this claim will come later.

**The sixth category:** It is forbidden for him to marry a fifth wife. Its evidence is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Two, three, or four﴾ [al-Nisa: 3].

**The seventh category:** Mutual cursing (*al-mula'anah*). Its evidence is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Those who have engaged in mutual cursing shall never be together again."

* *

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿that you seek with your wealth, chaste, not fornicating﴾.

In this there are issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding the grammatical position of His words ﴿that you seek [an tabtaghu]﴾, there are two opinions. The first: it is in the nominative case as an apposition (*badal*) of *ma* ("what"), and the meaning is: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, and lawful for you is that you seek," according to the reading of the one who reads *wa-uhilla* with a *damma* on the alif. As for the one who reads it with a *fatha*, the position of *an tabtaghu* is in the accusative. The second: its position, according to both readings, is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, as if it were said: *li-an tabtaghu* ("for the sake of seeking"), and the meaning: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, for the purpose of your seeking with your wealth." His words ﴿chaste [muhsinin]﴾ mean: in a state of your being chaste, not fornicating. His words ﴿chaste [muhsinin]﴾ mean: those who abstain from adultery. His words ﴿not fornicating [ghayr musafihin]﴾ mean: not committing adultery. This is a repetition for emphasis. Al-Layth said: *al-sifah* and *al-musafahah* are debauchery, and its root in the language is from *al-safh*, which is pouring, as one says: "tears are flowing (*sawafih*) and poured (*masfuhah*)." God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿or blood poured forth [damam masfuhan]﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. And "so-and-so is a *saffah* of blood," meaning one who sheds it. Adultery is called *sifah* because the adulterer has no aim except pouring out the drop of semen.

**If it is said:** Where is the object (*maf'ul*) of *tabtaghu*?

**[Page 38 continues]**

We say: the implied meaning is: "And lawful to you is what lies beyond that, for the purpose of seeking them (in marriage)," meaning: "that you seek what lies beyond that." The mention of it has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it. And God knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "There is no bridal gift (*mahr*) less than ten dirhams." Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It is permissible with a little or a lot, and there is no fixed minimum for it." Abu Hanifa argued from this verse, because God restricted the permission with a condition, namely seeking (them) with their wealth (﴿with your wealth﴾), and one or two dirhams are not called wealth, so it is necessary that they cannot be made a bridal gift.

If it is said: "One who has ten dirhams is not described as having wealth, yet you permit them to be a bridal gift."

We reply: The apparent meaning of this verse requires that ten (dirhams) not be sufficient. However, we set aside the apparent meaning of the verse in this case because of the proof of *ijma'* (consensus) that it is permissible. So we adhere to the apparent meaning of the verse regarding less than ten.

Know that this argument is weak, because the verse indicates that seeking (them) with wealth is permissible, and it contains no indication that seeking (them) without wealth is not permissible, except by way of *mafhum* (implication), and you do not hold that view. Then we say: What indicates that there is no minimum for the bridal gift consists of several points:

**The first proof:** Relying on this verse. Because His saying ﴿with your wealth﴾ places plural against plural, it requires the distribution of the individual over individuals. This requires that each one be able to seek marriage with whatever is called wealth. Little and much are equal in this reality and in this name. Therefore it follows from this verse that marriage may be sought with anything that is called wealth, without any fixed amount.

**The second proof:** Relying on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified for them a bridal gift, then half of what you have specified﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:237]. The verse indicates that half falls away from the one mentioned. This requires that if the contract was made at the outset for one dirham, only half a dirham would be obligatory upon him. You do not hold this view.

**The third proof:** The traditions. Among them is what has been related: "A woman was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), and a man had married her for a pair of sandals." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Are you content to give yourself for a pair of sandals?" She said: "Yes." So the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it. The apparent meaning is that the value of a pair of sandals is less than ten dirhams, for such a man and woman, whose marriage is only possible for a pair of sandals, would be in extreme poverty, and the sandals of such a person are of very little value. Among them is what has been related from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever gives a woman in marriage a handful of flour, or barley-meal, or food, has made her lawful (to himself)." Among them is what has been related in the story of the woman who gave herself (in marriage), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the man who wished to marry her: "Seek (something), even if it be an iron ring." And that is not worth ten dirhams.

* * *

**The third issue:** Abu Hanifa said: If he marries her on condition of teaching her a surah of the Qur'an, that does not constitute a bridal gift, and she is owed the bridal gift of her equivalent (*mahr al-mithl*). Then he said: If he marries a woman on condition of his service for one year, then if he is free she is owed the bridal gift of her equivalent, and if he is a slave she is owed one year of service. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is permissible to make that a bridal gift. Abu Hanifa argued for his position with several points:

**The first:** This verse, because He, may He be exalted, made the condition for the lawfulness (of marriage) that seeking (it) be with wealth, and wealth is a name for material things, not for benefits.

**The second:** He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if they give you willingly some of it, then consume it with enjoyment and satisfaction﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:4]. That is a description of material things.

Al-Shafi'i answered the first point by saying that the verse indicates that seeking (marriage) with wealth is permissible, and it does not state whether seeking (marriage) without wealth is permissible or not. As to the second point: the word *ita'* (giving) includes benefits that are stipulated just as it includes material things. As to the third point: the address came in the general and the most common manner.

Then al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) argued for the permissibility of making a benefit a bridal gift with several points:

**The first proof:** His saying, may He be exalted, in the story of Shu'ayb: ﴿I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾ [al-Qasas 28:27]. He made those benefits the bridal gift. The default in the law of those before us is that it continues until a *nasikh* (abrogating ruling) comes.

**The second proof:** When the woman who gave herself (in marriage) found that the man who wished to marry her had nothing, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you have anything of the Qur'an with you?" He said: "Yes, the surah of such-and-such." He said: "I have married her to you for what you have of the Qur'an." And God knows best.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Abu Bakr al-Razi said: The verse indicates that the manumission of a slave-woman cannot be her bridal gift, because the verse requires that the *bud'* (intimacy, i.e., the marital union) be a form of wealth. As for what has been related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "freed Safiyyah and made her manumission her bridal gift," that is among the special privileges of the Messenger (ﷺ).

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿muhsinin﴾ (﴿chaste, not debauched﴾). There are two views on it:

One of them: that what is meant is that they become *muhsinin* (chaste) by means of the marriage contract.

The second: that *ihsan* (chastity or protected status) is a condition for the permission mentioned in His saying ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾. The first is preferable, because under this interpretation the verse remains general and its meaning is known. Under the second interpretation, the verse becomes *mujmal* (ambiguous), because the *ihsan* mentioned in it is not specified, and what is conditioned upon an ambiguous matter is itself ambiguous. Taking the verse in a way that gives it a known meaning is preferable to taking it in a way that leaves it ambiguous.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them, give them their ujur (compensation), as an obligation﴾.

Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *Istimta'* (enjoyment) in language means benefiting, and everything that is benefited from is *mata'* (provision/enjoyment). One says: "A man enjoyed his child (*istamta'a bi-waladihi*)." And one says of someone who died in the prime of his youth: "He did not enjoy his youth (*lam yatamatta' bi-shababihi*)." He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, some of us have enjoyed others﴾ [al-An'am 6:128]. And He said: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:20], meaning: you hastened to benefit from them. And He said: ﴿So you enjoyed your share (*bi-khalaqikum*)﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:69], meaning: your portion and share of the world. In His saying ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them﴾ there are two views:

The first: "So for whatever of the married women you have enjoyed, whether by intercourse or by the contract with them, give them their ujur in return for it." Then the pronoun returning to *ma* (what) was dropped because there is no ambiguity, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve﴾ [al-Shura 42:43], where the pronoun has been omitted from it.

The second: that *ma* in His saying ﴿what lies beyond that﴾ means "women," and *min* in His saying ﴿of them﴾ is partitive. The pronoun in His saying ﴿bihi﴾ (﴿of it﴾) returns to the wording of *ma*, because it is singular in wording, while in His saying ﴿give them their ujur﴾ it returns to the meaning of *ma*, because it is plural in meaning. And His saying ﴿ujurahunna﴾ means their *muhur* (bridal gifts). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford (*tawlan*) to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:25], up to His saying: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their families and give them their ujur﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:25], meaning the bridal gifts. Likewise His saying here: ﴿give them their ujur﴾. And He said in another verse: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you marry them when you have given them their ujur﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10]. The bridal gift was called *ajr* (wage/compensation) only because it is the substitute for benefits, not a substitute for material things, just as the substitute for the benefits of a house or a riding animal is called *ajr*. And God knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** Al-Shafi'i said: Valid seclusion (*khalwa sahihah*) does not make the bridal gift fixed. Abu Hanifa said it does make it fixed. Al-Shafi'i argued for his view from this verse, because His saying ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them, give them their ujur﴾ indicates that the obligation to give them their bridal gifts was on account of enjoying them. If valid seclusion were to fix the bridal gift, the apparent meaning would be that valid seclusion precedes enjoying them, so the bridal gift would be fixed before enjoyment. Its being fixed before enjoyment would prevent that fixing from being connected to enjoyment, whereas the verse indicates that the fixing of the bridal gift is connected to enjoyment. Thus it is established that valid seclusion does not fix the bridal gift.

[Page 41]

* * *

**The third issue:** Concerning this verse there are two views. The first, which is the view of the majority of the scholars of the Ummah, is that His saying ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ means seeking women with wealth by way of marriage, and His saying ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them, give them their ujur﴾ means: if he enjoys her by consummation, he gives her the full bridal gift, and if he enjoys her by the marriage contract, he gives her half the bridal gift.

The second view is that the intended meaning of this verse is the ruling on *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), which is a term for a man hiring a woman for a known wealth for a specified term, and then having intercourse with her. They agreed that it was permissible at the beginning of Islam. It has been related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Makkah for his *'umrah*, the women of Makkah adorned themselves, and the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) complained of the length of celibacy. He said: "Enjoy (*istamti'u*) these women." They differed as to whether it was abrogated or not. The majority of the Ummah held that it became abrogated. Some held that it remained permissible as it was. This view is related from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Imran ibn Husayn.

As for Ibn 'Abbas, there are three reports from him:

The first: the view of unrestricted permissibility. 'Umarah said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about *mut'ah*: "Is it fornication (*sifah*) or marriage?" He said: "Neither fornication nor marriage." I said: "Then what is it?" He said: "It is *mut'ah*, as God said." I said: "Does it have a waiting period ('iddah)?" He said: "Yes, its waiting period is one menstrual cycle." I said: "Do the two inherit from each other?" He said: "No."

The second report from him: when people quoted poetry against Ibn 'Abbas's fatwa on *mut'ah*, Ibn 'Abbas said: "May God fight them! I did not issue a fatwa permitting it absolutely. But I said that it is lawful for one in necessity, just as carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine are lawful for him."

The third report: that he acknowledged that it had become abrogated. 'Ata' al-Khurasani related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So for those whom you have enjoyed of them﴾ that he said: "This verse became abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq 65:1]." It is also related that at his death he said: "O God, I repent to You of my statement about *mut'ah* and *sarf* (exchange of currency)."

As for 'Imran ibn Husayn, he said: "The verse of *mut'ah* was revealed in the Book of God, may He be exalted, and no verse came after it abrogating it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded us with it, and we enjoyed it. He died and did not forbid us from it. Then a man said by his own opinion whatever he wished." As for the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), the Shi'ah relate from him the permissibility of *mut'ah*. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari related in his *Tafsir* from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Had 'Umar not forbidden people from *mut'ah*, none would have committed fornication except a wretch." Muhammad ibn 'Ali, known as Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, related: "'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by Ibn 'Abbas while he was issuing a fatwa permitting *mut'ah*, and the Commander of the Faithful said: 'He (ﷺ) forbade it, and the flesh of domestic donkeys.'" This is what pertains to the reports.

The majority argued for the prohibition of *mut'ah* with several points:

**The first:** Intercourse is lawful only with a wife or a slave-woman, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:5-6]. And this woman is undoubtedly not a slave-woman, nor is she a wife. What indicates this consists of several points:

**One:** If she were a wife, inheritance would take place between them, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:12]. By agreement, there is no inheritance between them.

**Two:** Lineage would also be established, based on his saying (ﷺ): "The child belongs to the bed (*al-walad lil-firash*)." By agreement, lineage is not established.

**The third argument:** If the waiting period (*'iddah*) were obligatory for her, that would follow from His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. Know that this argument is a sound and well-established statement.

**The second argument:** What is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said in his sermon: "There were two forms of *mut'ah* (temporary enjoyment) in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I forbid them and I punish for them." This statement was mentioned in the gathering of the Companions, and no one denied it. So the situation here is one of only three possibilities:

Either it is said that they knew the prohibition of *mut'ah* and remained silent. Or they knew that it was permissible but remained silent out of flattery (*mudahanah*). Or they did not know whether it was permissible or prohibited, and so they remained silent because they were undecided about it. The first is what is sought. The second would entail declaring 'Umar and the Companions to be disbelievers, because whoever knows that the Prophet ﷺ ruled that *mut'ah* was permissible, and then says that it is prohibited and forbidden without any abrogation of it, is a disbeliever in Allah. Whoever affirms him in this, knowing that he is wrong, is also a disbeliever. This entails declaring the whole Community to be disbelievers, and that is the opposite of His words: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

The third possibility is that they did not know whether *mut'ah* was permissible or forbidden, and that is why they remained silent. This also is false, because *mut'ah*, if it were permissible, would be like marriage, and people's need to know the status of each of the two is general for everyone. Such a matter is not allowed to remain hidden; rather, knowledge of it must become widely known. Just as all of them knew that marriage is permissible and that its permissibility has not been abrogated, the situation regarding *mut'ah* must be the same. Since these two possibilities are invalid, it is established that the Companions remained silent about denouncing 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, only because they knew that *mut'ah* had been abrogated in Islam.

If it is said: What you have mentioned is refuted by the report that 'Umar said: "I will not be brought a man who has married a woman for a fixed term except that I will stone him." There is no doubt that stoning is not permissible, yet the Companions did not denounce him when he said this. This shows that they used to remain silent about denouncing falsehood.

We say: Perhaps he was mentioning that as a form of threat, deterrence and political measure (*siyasah*), and such political measures are permissible for the ruler when there is a benefit. Do you not see that the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Whoever withholds the *zakah* from us, we will take it from him and half of his wealth"? Taking half of a person's wealth from one who withholds *zakah* is not permissible, but the Prophet ﷺ said that for the sake of intensifying deterrence. So it is the same here, and Allah knows best.

**The third argument that *mut'ah* is prohibited:** What Malik related from al-Zuhri, from 'Abd Allah and al-Hasan, the two sons of Muhammad ibn 'Ali, from their father, from 'Ali: "That the Messenger ﷺ forbade *mut'ah* with women and forbade eating the flesh of domestic donkeys." And al-Rabi' ibn Sabrah al-Juhani related from his father, who said: "I went early to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found him standing between the Corner and the Station, leaning his back against the Ka'bah, saying: 'O people, I had commanded you to enjoy these women. Indeed, Allah has prohibited them to you until the Day of Resurrection. So whoever has any of them, let him release her, and do not take back anything of what you have given them.'" And it is related from him ﷺ that he said: "The *mut'ah* of women is forbidden." These three reports were mentioned by al-Wahidi in *al-Basit*. It is evident that marriage is not called *istimta'* (enjoyment), because we have explained that *istimta'* is pleasure, and mere marriage is not like that.

**As for those who hold that *mut'ah* is permissible,** they have argued with several proofs:

**The first proof:** Relying on this verse, meaning His words, exalted is He: ﴿that you seek [them] with your wealth, chaste, not fornicating. So for what you have enjoyed from them, give them their wages﴾. In using this verse there are two methods:

**The first method:** We say that *nikah al-mut'ah* (temporary marriage) is included in this verse, because His words ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ encompass the one who seeks enjoyment of a woman with his wealth on a permanent basis and the one who seeks it with his wealth on a time-limited basis. Since each of the two types is included in it, His words ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth﴾ require the permissibility of both types, and that requires the permissibility of *mut'ah*.

**The second method:** We say that this verse is specifically about the explanation of *nikah al-mut'ah*, and its explanation is from several aspects:

**First:** It is related that Ubayy ibn Ka'b used to recite (*fa-ma istamta'tum bihi minhunna ila ajalin musamman fa-atuhunna ujurahunna*, "for what you have enjoyed from them until a specified term, give them their wages"). This is also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, and the Community did not denounce them for this reading. So that was a consensus of the Community on the soundness of this reading. Its demonstration is what you have mentioned regarding 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he forbade *mut'ah* and the Companions did not denounce him: that was a consensus on the soundness of what we have mentioned, and likewise here. Since the soundness of this reading is established by consensus, the claim is established.

**Second:** The thing mentioned in the verse is merely seeking with wealth. Then He commanded giving them their wages after enjoying them. That indicates that mere seeking with wealth makes intercourse permissible, and mere seeking with wealth occurs only in *nikah al-mut'ah*. As for unrestricted marriage, lawfulness there is achieved only by the contract, with a guardian and witnesses, and mere seeking with wealth does not confer lawfulness. So this indicates that this verse is specific to *mut'ah*.

**Third:** In this verse the giving of wages is made obligatory by mere enjoyment, and enjoyment is an expression of pleasure and benefit. But in marriage, giving of wages is not obligatory upon enjoyment at all, but upon the marriage. Do you not see that by mere marriage half the dowry becomes due? It is evident that marriage is not called enjoyment, because we have explained that enjoyment is pleasure, and mere marriage is not like that.

**Fourth:** If we interpreted this verse as the ruling of marriage, it would require repeating the explanation of the ruling of marriage within one surah, because He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of this surah: ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four﴾ [al-Nisa: 3], then He said: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a free gift﴾ [al-Nisa: 4]. But if we interpret this verse as explaining *nikah al-mut'ah*, that would be a new ruling, so interpreting the verse this way is preferable, and Allah knows best.

**The second proof for the permissibility of *nikah al-mut'ah*:** The Community agrees that *nikah al-mut'ah* was permissible in Islam, and there is no disagreement among anyone of the Community about it. The disagreement is only about whether an abrogating text has come. So we say: If an abrogating text existed, that abrogation would either be known by mass transmission (*tawatur*) or by solitary reports (*ahad*). If it were known by mass transmission, then 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas and 'Imran ibn Husayn would have been denying what is known to be established by mass transmission from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ, and that would entail declaring them disbelievers, which is definitely false. And if it were established by solitary reports, this too is false, because since the permissibility of *mut'ah* is known by consensus and mass transmission, its establishment is known with certainty. So if we abrogated it by a solitary report, it would entail making the speculative override the certain, and that is false.

They said: What also shows the invalidity of the claim of this abrogation is that most reports say: "The Prophet ﷺ forbade *mut'ah* and the flesh of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar," while most reports say that he, upon him be blessings and peace, permitted *mut'ah* during the Farewell Pilgrimage and on the day of the Conquest. These two days are later than the day of Khaybar, and that indicates the falsehood of what is related, that he, peace be upon him, abrogated *mut'ah* on the day of Khaybar, because an abrogating text cannot precede the text it abrogates. As for the statement of one who says that permission and prohibition occurred repeatedly, and abrogation repeatedly, it is weak, and none of the reliable scholars has said it, except those who wanted to remove the contradiction from these reports.

**The third proof:** What is related: "That 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said from the pulpit: 'There were two forms of *mut'ah* that were legislated in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and I forbid them: the *mut'ah* of Hajj and the *mut'ah* of marriage.'" This is from him an explicit statement that the *mut'ah* of marriage existed in the time of the Messenger ﷺ. His saying "and I forbid them" indicates that the Messenger ﷺ did not abrogate it, and it was only 'Umar who abrogated it. Once this is established, we say: this statement indicates that the lawfulness of *mut'ah* was established in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, that he, peace be upon him, did not abrogate it, and that there is no abrogation except 'Umar's abrogation. Once this is established, it must not become abrogated, because what was established in the time of the Messenger ﷺ and was not abrogated by the Messenger cannot become abrogated by the abrogation of 'Umar. This is the argument which 'Imran ibn Husayn used when he said: "Allah sent down a verse about *mut'ah* and did not abrogate it with another verse, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to do *mut'ah* and did not forbid us from it. Then a man said by his opinion whatever he wished," meaning that 'Umar forbade it. This is the sum of the arguments of those who hold that *mut'ah* is permissible.

**The answer to the first argument** is that we say: this verse includes the meaning that its intended sense is *nikah al-mut'ah*, and its explanation is from three aspects. First: He, exalted is He, mentioned the prohibited persons for marriage first, in His words: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾. So the meaning of this permission is the same as the meaning of that prohibition there. But the meaning of the prohibition there is marriage, so the meaning of the permission here must also be marriage. Second: He said ﴿chaste﴾, and chastity (*ihsan*) occurs only in a valid marriage. Third: His words ﴿not fornicating﴾: He named adultery *sifah* (fornication), because there is no purpose in it except pouring out water, and no offspring or other benefits of marriage are sought in it. *Mut'ah* is intended for nothing but pouring out water, so it is fornication. This is what Abu Bakr al-Razi said.

As for what he mentioned in the first aspect: it seems that He, exalted is He, mentioned the categories of those whose intercourse is forbidden to a person, then said ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾, meaning: lawful to you is intercourse with what is beyond these categories. So what corruption is there in this statement? As for his second statement, that chastity occurs only in a valid marriage, he gave no evidence for it. As for his third statement, that adultery is called fornication only because there is no purpose in it except pouring out water, and *mut'ah* is not like that, since its purpose is pouring out water by a lawful, permitted means from God, then if you say: *mut'ah* is forbidden, we say: this is the very point of the debate, so why do you say that the matter is so? It becomes evident that the argument is weak. What must be relied upon in this matter is that we do not deny that *mut'ah* was permissible. What we say is that it was abrogated. On this assumption, even if this verse indicated that it was legislated, that would not harm our position. This is also the answer to their reliance on the reading of Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas, since that reading, even if established, indicates only that *mut'ah* was legislated, and we do not dispute that. What we say is that abrogation came upon it, and the proofs you have mentioned do not refute our claim.

As for their statement: "The abrogating text is either mass-transmitted or solitary":

We say: Perhaps some of them heard it and then forgot it. Furthermore, when 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned that in the great gathering, they remembered it and recognized his truthfulness in it, so they accepted the matter from him.

As for his saying: "'Umar attributed the prohibition of *mut'ah* to himself":

قُلْنا: قَدْ بَيَّنّا أنَّهُ لَوْ كانَ مُرادُهُ أنَّ المُتْعَةَ كانَتْ مُباحَةً في شَرْعِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ) وأنا أنْهى عَنْهُ لَزِمَ تَكْفِيرُهُ وتَكْفِيرُ كُلِّ مَن لَمْ يُحارِبْهُ ويُنازِعْهُ، ويُفْضِي ذَلِكَ إلى تَكْفِيرِ أمِيرِ المُؤْمِنِينَ حَيْثُ لَمْ يُحارِبْهُ ولَمْ يَرُدَّ ذَلِكَ القَوْلَ عَلَيْهِ، وكُلُّ ذَلِكَ باطِلٌ، فَلَمْ يَبْقَ إلّا أنْ يُقالَ: كانَ مُرادُهُ أنَّ المُتْعَةَ (temporary marriage) كانَتْ مُباحَةً في زَمَنِ الرَّسُولِ (ﷺ)، وأنا أنْهى عَنْها لِما ثَبَتَ عِنْدِي أنَّهُ (ﷺ) نَسَخَها (abrogated it, naskh)، وعَلى هَذا التَّقْدِيرِ يَصِيرُ هَذا الكَلامُ حُجَّةً لَنا في مَطْلُوبِنا، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿فَآتُوهُنَّ أُجُورَهُنَّ فَرِيضَةً﴾ والمَعْنى أنَّ إيتاءَهُنَّ أُجُورَهُنَّ ومُهُورَهُنَّ (bridal gifts, mahr) فَرِيضَةٌ لازِمَةٌ وواجِبَةٌ، وذَكَرَ صاحِبُ ”الكَشّافِ“ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَرِيضَةً﴾ ثَلاثَةَ أوْجُهٍ: أحَدُها: أنَّهُ حالٌ مِنَ الأُجُورِ بِمَعْنى مَفْرُوضَةٍ. وثانِيها: أنَّها وُضِعَتْ مَوْضِعَ إيتاءٍ، لِأنَّ الإيتاءَ مَفْرُوضٌ. وثالِثُها: أنَّهُ مَصْدَرٌ مُؤَكَّدٌ، أيْ: فَرَضَ ذَلِكَ فَرِيضَةً.

[صفحة ٤٥ / Page 45]
﴿ولا جُناحَ عَلَيْكم فِيما تَراضَيْتُمْ بِهِ مِن بَعْدِ الفَرِيضَةِ إنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا﴾ .
* * *
ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿ولا جُناحَ عَلَيْكم فِيما تَراضَيْتُمْ بِهِ مِن بَعْدِ الفَرِيضَةِ إنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا﴾ .
وفِيهِ مَسائِلُ:
المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: الَّذِينَ حَمَلُوا الآيَةَ المُتَقَدِّمَةَ عَلى بَيانِ حُكْمِ النِّكاحِ قالُوا: المُرادُ أنَّهُ إذا كانَ المَهْرُ مُقَدَّرًا بِمِقْدارٍ مُعَيَّنٍ، فَلا حَرَجَ في أنْ تَحُطَّ عَنْهُ شَيْئًا مِنَ المَهْرِ أوْ تُبَرِّئَهُ عَنْهُ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ، فَعَلى هَذا: المُرادُ مِنَ التَّراضِي الحَطُّ مِنَ المَهْرِ أوِ الإبْراءُ عَنْهُ، وهو كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ لَكم عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنهُ نَفْسًا فَكُلُوهُ هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾ [النساء: ٤] وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿إلّا أنْ يَعْفُونَ أوْ يَعْفُوَ الَّذِي بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ النِّكاحِ﴾ [البقرة: ٢٣٧] وقالَ الزَّجّاجُ: مَعْناهُ لا إثْمَ عَلَيْكم في أنْ تَهَبَ المَرْأةُ لِلزَّوْجِ مَهْرَها، أوْ يَهَبَ الزَّوْجُ لِلْمَرْأةِ تَمامَ المَهْرِ إذا طَلَّقَها قَبْلَ الدُّخُولِ، وأمّا الَّذِينَ حَمَلُوا الآيَةَ المُتَقَدِّمَةَ عَلى بَيانِ المُتْعَةِ قالُوا: المُرادُ مِن هَذِهِ الآيَةِ أنَّهُ إذا انْقَضى أجَلُ المُتْعَةِ لَمْ يَبْقَ لِلرَّجُلِ عَلى المَرْأةِ سَبِيلٌ البَتَّةَ، فَإنْ قالَ لَها: زِيدِينِي في الأيّامِ وأزِيدُكِ في الأُجْرَةِ كانَتِ المَرْأةُ بِالخِيارِ، إنْ شاءَتْ فَعَلَتْ، وإنْ شاءَتْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ، فَهَذا هو المُرادُ مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿ولا جُناحَ عَلَيْكم فِيما تَراضَيْتُمْ بِهِ مِن بَعْدِ الفَرِيضَةِ﴾ أيْ مِن بَعْدِ المِقْدارِ المَذْكُورِ أوَّلًا مِنَ الأجْرِ والأجَلِ.
* * *
المَسْألَةُ الثّانِيَةُ: قالَ أبُو حَنِيفَةَ (may Allah be pleased with him): إلْحاقُ الزِّيادَةِ في الصَّداقِ جائِزٌ، وهي ثابِتَةٌ إنْ دَخَلَ بِها أوْ ماتَ عَنْها، أمّا إذا طَلَّقَها قَبْلَ الدُّخُولِ بَطَلَتِ الزِّيادَةُ، وكانَ لَها نِصْفُ المُسَمّى في العَقْدِ، وقالَ الشّافِعِيُّ (may Allah have mercy on him): الزِّيادَةُ بِمَنزِلَةِ الهِبَةِ، فَإنْ أقْبَضَها مَلَكَتْهُ بِالقَبْضِ، وإنْ لَمْ يُقْبِضْها بَطَلَتْ. احْتَجَّ أبُو بَكْرٍ الرّازِيُّ لِأبِي حَنِيفَةَ بِهَذِهِ الآيَةِ فَقَوْلُهُ: ﴿ولا جُناحَ عَلَيْكم فِيما تَراضَيْتُمْ بِهِ مِن بَعْدِ الفَرِيضَةِ﴾ يَتَناوَلُ ما وقَعَ التَّراضِي بِهِ في طَرَفَيِ الزِّيادَةِ والنُّقْصانِ، فَكانَ هَذا بِعُمُومِهِ يَدُلُّ عَلى جَوازِ إلْحاقِ الزِّيادَةِ بِالصَّداقِ، قالَ: بَلْ هَذِهِ الآيَةُ بِالزِّيادَةِ أخَصُّ مِنها بِالنُّقْصانِ؛ لِأنَّهُ تَعالى عَلَّقَهُ بِتَراضِيهِما، والبَراءَةُ والحَطُّ لا يَحْتاجُ إلى رِضا الزَّوْجِ، والزِّيادَةُ لا تَصِحُّ إلّا بِقَبُولِهِ، فَإذا عُلِّقَ ذَلِكَ بِتَراضِيهِما جَمِيعًا دَلَّ عَلى أنَّ المُرادَ هو الزِّيادَةُ.
والجَوابُ: لِمَ لا يَجُوزُ أنْ تَكُونَ الزِّيادَةُ عِبارَةً عَمّا ذَكَرَهُ الزَّجّاجُ ؟ وهو أنَّهُ إذا طَلَّقَها قَبْلَ الدُّخُولِ، فَإنْ شاءَتِ المَرْأةُ أبْرَأتْهُ عَنِ النِّصْفِ، وإنْ شاءَ الزَّوْجُ سَلَّمَ إلَيْها كُلَّ المَهْرِ، وبِهَذا التَّقْدِيرِ يَكُونُ قَدْ زادَها عَمّا وجَبَ عَلَيْهِ تَسْلِيمُهُ إلَيْها، وأيْضًا عِنْدَنا أنَّهُ لا جُناحَ في تِلْكَ الزِّيادَةِ إلّا أنَّها تَكُونُ هِبَةً، والدَّلِيلُ القاطِعُ عَلى بُطْلانِ هَذِهِ الزِّيادَةِ أنَّ هَذِهِ الزِّيادَةَ لَوِ التَحَقَتْ بِالأصْلِ لَكانَ إمّا مَعَ بَقاءِ العَقْدِ الأوَّلِ، أوْ بَعْدَ زَوالِ العَقْدِ، والأوَّلُ باطِلٌ؛ لِأنَّ العَقْدَ لَمّا انْعَقَدَ عَلى القَدْرِ الأوَّلِ، فَلَوِ انْعَقَدَ مَرَّةً أُخْرى عَلى القَدْرِ الثّانِي، لَكانَ ذَلِكَ تَكْوِينًا لِذَلِكَ العَقْدِ بَعْدَ ثُبُوتِهِ، وذَلِكَ يَقْتَضِي تَحْصِيلَ الحاصِلِ وهو مُحالٌ. والثّانِي باطِلٌ لِانْعِقادِ الإجْماعِ (consensus, ijma') عَلى أنَّ عِنْدَ إلْحاقِ الزِّيادَةِ لا يَرْتَفِعُ العَقْدُ الأوَّلُ، فَثَبَتَ فَسادُ ما قالُوهُ، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.
ثُمَّ إنَّهُ تَعالى لَمّا ذَكَرَ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ أنْواعًا كَثِيرَةً مِنَ التَّكالِيفِ والتَّحْرِيمِ والإحْلالِ، بَيَّنَ أنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِجَمِيعِ المَعْلُوماتِ لا يَخْفى عَلَيْهِ مِنها خافِيَةٌ أصْلًا، وحَكِيمٌ لا يُشَرِّعُ الأحْكامَ إلّا عَلى وفْقِ الحِكْمَةِ، وذَلِكَ يُوجِبُ التَّسْلِيمَ لِأوامِرِهِ والِانْقِيادَ لِأحْكامِهِ، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

[Page 46]

**The seventh category of the obligations mentioned in this surah:**

﴿And whoever among you is not able to marry free, believing women, let him marry from what your right hands possess of your believing young women. And Allah knows best your faith; you are of one another. So marry them with the permission of their families and give them their dowries in a fair manner, as chaste women, not fornicating nor taking secret lovers. And when they are married, if they commit immorality, for them is half the punishment of free women. That is for whoever among you fears hardship, but to be patient is better for you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever among you is not able to marry free, believing women...﴾ (the verse as above). It contains several issues:

**The first issue:** Al-Kisa'i read *al-muhsināt* with a kasra on the ṣād, and likewise *muḥṣanātin ghayra musāfiḥāt* and *fa-'alayhinna niṣfu mā 'alā al-muḥṣanāt*, all with a kasra on the ṣād. The rest read them with a fatḥa. The reading with a fatḥa (*al-muḥṣanāt*) means "those who are married," and the reading with a kasra (*al-muḥṣināt*) means "the chaste and the free." And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** *Al-ṭawl* (abundance, means): it means excess, and from it comes *al-taṭawwul*, which is bestowing favour. Allah says: ﴿the Owner of bounty﴾. It is said: *taṭāwala li-hādhā al-shay'* meaning he reached for this thing, just as one says "so-and-so's hand is outstretched." The root of this word is from *al-ṭūl* (length), which is the opposite of shortness, because when something is long it has completeness and addition, just as when it is short it has deficiency and lack. Wealth is also called *ṭawl*, because by it one attains desired things that cannot be attained in poverty, just as by length one reaches what cannot be reached by shortness.

Having understood this, we say: *al-ṭawl* is ability, and it is in the accusative as the object of *yastaṭi'* (is able), and *an yankiha* (to marry) is in the accusative position as the object of the ability.

If it is said: *al-istiṭā'ah* is ability, and *al-ṭawl* is also ability, so the meaning of the verse becomes: "whoever among you is not able to have the ability to marry the chaste women," so what is the benefit of this repetition in mentioning ability?

We answer: The matter is as you have said, and the better formulation is: the meaning is "whoever among you does not have the capacity (*istiṭā'ah*) for marriage with the chaste women." On this understanding the difficulty disappears. This is what relates to the language.

As for what the exegetes have said, there are several views:

The first: "Whoever is not able, through wealth and ample means, to reach marriage with a free woman, let him marry a slave woman."

The second: that *nikāḥ* (marriage) be interpreted as *waṭ'* (intercourse). The meaning would be: "whoever among you is not able, by means, to have intercourse with free women, let him marry a slave woman." On this interpretation, whoever does not have a free woman under him may marry a slave woman. This interpretation suits the school of Abu Hanifa, for his position is that if one has a free woman under him, it is not permissible for him to marry a slave woman, whether or not he is able to marry a free woman.

The third: that one be content with a free woman, so that he may marry a slave woman whether or not he has a free woman under him. All these views arose because the word *istiṭā'ah* is open to all these interpretations.

**The third issue:** The meaning of *al-muḥṣanāt* in His words ﴿whoever among you is not able to marry the chaste women﴾ is the free women. This is shown by the fact that Allah, when marrying free women is impossible, permitted marrying slave women, so *al-muḥṣanāt* must mean those who are the opposite of slave women. The reason free women are called *al-muḥṣanāt* according to the reading of whoever reads with a fatḥa on the ṣād is that they are protected by their freedom from the conditions into which slave women fall, for it is apparent that a slave woman is often going out, coming in, humiliated and degraded, whereas the free woman is protected and guarded from these deficiencies. As for the reading with a kasra on the ṣād, the meaning is that they have protected themselves by their freedom.

\* \* \*

**The fourth issue:** The position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that Allah, Exalted is He, stipulated three conditions for marrying slave women. Two of them concern the one marrying, and the third concerns the woman married. As for the two concerning the one marrying: the first is that he is not able to afford the dowry required for marrying a believing free woman. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿whoever among you is not able to marry free, believing women﴾. So the lack of ability (*ṭawl*) is an expression for lacking what one would marry a free woman with.

If it is said: a man who is able to marry a slave woman is able to marry a poor free woman, so where does this difference come from?

We answer: It was customary for slave women to have lower dowries and maintenance, because they were occupied with serving their masters, and on this basis the difference appears.

As for the second condition, it is the one mentioned at the end of the verse, namely His words: ﴿That is for whoever among you fears hardship﴾, meaning one who reaches severe distress in being without a spouse.

As for the third condition required concerning the woman married: that the slave woman be a believer, not an unbeliever. For if the slave woman is an unbeliever she is deficient in two respects: slavery and disbelief. There is no doubt that the child follows the mother in freedom and slavery, and in that case the child would be born a slave under the ownership of an unbeliever, so the child would suffer the deficiency of slavery and the deficiency of being owned by an unbeliever.
