These three conditions are therefore binding according to al-Shafi'i for the permissibility of marrying a slave woman.

As for Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, he says: if one has a free woman under him, it is not permissible for him to marry a slave woman; but if he does not have a free woman under him, it is permissible for him, whether or not he is able to marry a free woman. Al-Shafi'i argued for his position with this verse, and his argument is in two ways:

The first: Allah mentioned the lack of ability to afford a free woman, then mentioned right after it marrying a slave woman. This attribute suits this ruling, because a person may need intercourse, and if he is unable to have intercourse with a free woman because of the burden of her maintenance and dowry, he should be permitted to marry a slave woman. Given this, we say: when a ruling is mentioned immediately after an attribute suited to it, this juxtaposition in mention indicates that the ruling is conditioned by that attribute. Given this, we say: if marrying a slave woman were permissible regardless of the ability to afford a free woman, and also when one has that ability, then the lack of this ability would have no effect on this ruling at all. But we have shown that the verse indicates that this lack has an effect on this ruling. Thus it is established that it is not permissible to marry a slave woman while one is able to afford a free woman.

The second: we rely on the verse by way of implication (*mafhūm*), namely that specifying a thing by mention indicates the negation of the ruling for what is other than it. The evidence for this is that if a speaker says, "The dead Jew does not see anything," everyone laughs at this statement and says: if the non-Jew also does not see, what is the benefit of restricting it to being a Jew? When we observed that people of common usage find this statement objectionable, and they explain this objection by this reason, we knew that the people of language agree that restriction by attribute implies the negation of the ruling outside the place of the restriction.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: specifying this state by mentioning permissibility within it does not indicate the prohibition of what is other than it, like His words: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31], and there is no indication in it that killing is permitted when this state ceases; and His words: ﴿Do not consume usury, doubled and multiplied﴾ [Al 'Imran: 130], and there is no indication in it that consuming it is permitted when this state ceases.

It is said to him: the apparent wording requires that, but he (Abu Bakr) abandoned acting upon it because of a separate (*munfaṣil*) proof, just as for you the apparent form of a command is obligation, yet it is abandoned in many cases because of a separate proof. The sound objection to the argument from the verse is what we mentioned, when we said: why could it not be that the intended meaning of marriage is intercourse? The meaning would then be: "whoever among you is not able to have intercourse with a free woman," and this is the case for one who does not have a free woman under him, so it is permissible for him to marry a slave woman. On this interpretation the verse becomes a proof for Abu Hanifa.

Its answer: most of the exegetes interpreted *ṭawl* as wealth, and the effect of lacking wealth is on the inability to conclude the contract, not on the inability to have intercourse. Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for the soundness of his view by general expressions, such as His words: ﴿So marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]; His words: ﴿And marry those among you who are single﴾; His words: ﴿And lawful for you is what lies beyond that﴾; and His words: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾, which includes slave women of the People of the Book. And the meaning of *iḥṣān* here is chastity.

The answer: our verse is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general. Furthermore, it has been particularized in the case where one has a free woman under him, and it was specified only in order to protect the child from being born enslaved, and this reason is present in the point of dispute.

\* \* \*

**The fifth issue:** The apparent meaning of His words: ﴿whoever among you is not able to marry free, believing women﴾ requires that faith be a condition for the free woman. Based on this: if one is able to marry a free Kitabiyyah (woman of the People of the Book) but is not able to afford a free Muslim woman, it is permissible for him to marry a slave woman. Most scholars hold that mentioning faith in relation to free women is recommended and desirable, because there is no difference between a free Kitabiyyah and a believing woman in the abundance or scarcity of maintenance costs.

\* \* \*

**The sixth issue:** Some people said: it is not permissible at all to marry Kitabiyyah women, and they argued with these verses. They said: Allah has shown that when one is unable to marry a free Muslim woman, it becomes binding for him to marry a Muslim slave woman. If marrying a Kitabiyyah free woman were permissible, then when one is unable to marry a free Muslim woman, a Muslim slave woman would not be specifically required, and that negates the indication of the verse. Then they reinforced this indication with His words: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. We have shown with many proofs, in our commentary on this verse, that the Kitabiyyah is a polytheist.

\* \* \*

**The seventh issue:** The verse indicates a warning against marrying slave women, and that it is not permissible to undertake it except in cases of necessity. The reasons for this are several:

The first: the child follows the mother in slavery and freedom, so if the mother is a slave, the child is born a slave, and this entails deficiency with respect to that person and to his child.

The second: a slave woman may have become accustomed to going out, appearing, and mixing with men, and become extremely shameless, and perhaps may have become accustomed to immorality, and all of this is harmful to husbands.

The third: the right of her master over her is greater than the right of her husband, so such a wife is not wholly devoted to her husband as a free woman would be. Therefore the husband may greatly need her and yet find no way to her, because the master prevents and holds her back.

The fourth: the master may sell her to another person. According to the view of those who say that selling a slave woman is divorcing her, she becomes divorced whether the husband wills it or not. According to the view of those who do not hold this, the second master may travel with her and her child, and that is among the greatest harms.

The fifth: her dowry belongs to her master, so she cannot give her dowry to her husband as a gift nor release him from it, unlike a free woman.

For these reasons, Allah has permitted marrying slave women only as a concession. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**His words, Exalted is He:** ﴿So from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾. It contains several issues:

The First Issue: His saying, ﴿So from what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: let him marry from what your right hands possess. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this means the slave-girl of your sister, for a man may not marry his own slave-girl.

The Second Issue: "al-Fatayat" (the female slaves) is the plural of fatat, and a male slave is fata. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you say 'my slave' (ʿabdi), but let him say 'my young man' (fatayya) and 'my young woman' (fatati)." A recent young female is called fatat, and a young male is called fata. A female slave is called fatat whether she is old or young, because she is like the young woman in that she is not treated with the honour due to an elder.

The Third Issue: His saying, ﴿from your believing young women﴾ indicates the restriction of marrying a slave-girl to the case where she is a believer. Therefore it is not permissible to marry a female slave who is a People of the Book. This applies whether the husband is free or a slave. This is the view of Mujahid, Saʿid and al-Hasan, and the view of Malik and al-Shafiʿi. Abu Hanifa said: it is permissible to marry a female slave who is a People of the Book.

The argument of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him: His saying, ﴿from your believing young women﴾ is a restriction of the permissibility of marrying a slave-girl to her being a believer, and this negates the permissibility of marrying a non-believer by the two considerations we mentioned in the issue of the lack of means to marry a free woman. Also, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221].

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is on several grounds: the textual and the analogical. As for the textual, it is the general statements we mentioned when he relied on them in the issue of the lack of means to marry a free woman, the strongest of which is His saying: ﴿And chaste women from those who were given the Book before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. As for the analogical, it is that we agree that a free woman of the People of the Book is permissible, and a slave woman of the People of the Book is also permissible; so likewise, if one marries a slave woman of the People of the Book, it must be permissible.

The answer to the general statements: our proofs are specific, so they take precedence over the general statements. The answer to the analogy: al-Shafiʿi said that if one marries a free woman of the People of the Book, there is one deficiency, but if one marries a slave woman of the People of the Book, there are two kinds of deficiency: slavery and disbelief, so the difference is evident.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your faith﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: act according to the outward appearance of faith, for you are charged according to outward matters, and Allah takes charge of the inner secrets and realities.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿some of you are from others﴾, and in it are two views:

The first: all of you are the children of Adam, so let no pride prevent you from marrying slave-women in cases of necessity.

The second: the meaning is that all of you share in faith, and faith is the greatest of virtues. When sharing in the greatest of virtues is achieved, the disparity in what lies beyond it is not to be regarded. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. Al-Zajjaj said: this second view is more appropriate, because the mention of believing women came first, or because nobility through the nobility of Islam is more fitting than through all other attributes. This strengthens the view of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that faith is a condition for the permissibility of marrying a slave-woman.

Know that the wisdom in mentioning this phrase is that the Arabs used to boast about lineages, so in mentioning this phrase He informs that Allah does not regard or pay attention to it. It is related from the Messenger (ﷺ) that he said: "Three things from the affairs of the Jahiliyya will remain among the people in Islam: slandering lineages, boasting of ancestry, and seeking rain through the stars." And the people of the Jahiliyya used to belittle the son of a non-Arab mother (ibn al-hajin), so He mentioned this phrase as a rebuke to them for the morals of the people of the Jahiliyya.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, explained the manner of this marriage, saying: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾. In it are two issues:

The first issue: They agreed that the marriage of a slave-woman without the permission of her master is invalid, and the Qur'an and analogy indicate this. As for the Qur'an, it is this verse, for His saying: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾ requires that permission be a condition for the validity of the marriage, even though marriage is not obligatory. It is like His (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever enters into a salam (advance sale), let him do so by a known measure, a known weight, and a known term." Salam is not obligatory, but when one chooses to enter into it, he must fulfil these conditions. Likewise marriage, though not obligatory, when one wishes to marry a slave-woman, he must not marry her except with the permission of her master. As for analogy: the slave-woman is the property of her master, and after the marriage most of her benefits are rendered void for him, so it is not permissible except with his permission. Know that the wording of the Qur'an is restricted to the slave-woman, but as for the male slave, this has been established regarding him by the hadith from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a slave marries without the permission of his master, he is an adulterer."

* * *

The second issue: al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: A sane adult woman's marriage is not valid except with the permission of a guardian (wali). Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is valid. Al-Shafiʿi argued from this verse, and his reasoning is that the pronoun in His saying: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾ refers to the slave-women, and a slave-woman is a person described by the attribute of slavery, and the attribute of slavery is a passing attribute. The indication of a person described by a passing attribute does not extend to that attribute. Do you not see that if someone swears not to speak with this young man, and then he becomes an old man and he speaks with him, he breaks his oath? Thus it is established that the indication of a person described by an accidental, passing attribute remains after that attribute has ceased. Given this, we say: His saying ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾ is an indication of the slave-women, and this indication must remain when slavery is removed from them and they acquire the attribute of freedom. If that is so, then a free, adult, sane woman in this case cannot have her marriage validated without the permission of her guardian, and if this is established in this case, this ruling must be established in all cases, since no one distinguishes between them.

Abu Bakr al-Razi argued from this verse against al-Shafiʿi's position in this issue, saying: His school holds that a woman has no legal expression in the contract of marriage, so according to this it is not permissible for a woman to give her slave-girl in marriage; rather, his school holds that she may appoint another to marry off her slave-girl. He said: this verse refutes that, because the apparent meaning of this verse indicates sufficiency with the permission of her people, so whoever says that this is not sufficient has abandoned the apparent meaning of the verse.

The answer, from several angles:

First: the meaning of permission is consent, and according to us the consent of the master is indispensable; as for whether it is sufficient, there is no proof in the verse for it.

Second: "their people" is an expression for whoever has the power to marry them, and that is either the master if he is a man, or the guardian of her master if her master is a woman.

Third: suppose that "the people" is an expression for the master, it is still general, encompassing males and females, and the evidences indicating that a woman may not marry herself on her own are specific. The Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "The adulteress is she who marries herself off." By this hadith it is established that she has no legal expression in marrying herself, so it must be that she has no legal expression in marrying off her slave-girl, since no one distinguishes between them. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And give them their bridal payments according to what is reasonable﴾. In it are two issues:

The first issue: In interpreting the verse there are two views:

The first: the meaning of "ujur" (payments) is the dowries (mahr), and on this reading the verse indicates that the dowry is obligatory upon the one who marries her, whether or not a dowry was specified, because He, the Exalted, did not distinguish between one for whom a dowry was specified and one for whom it was not in imposing the dowry. That He intended the customary dowry (mahr al-mithl) is indicated by His saying ﴿according to what is reasonable﴾, and this phrase is used only in matters based on reasoning and strong presumption regarding what is customary and well known, like His saying: ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233].

The second: al-Qadi said: the meaning of "ujur" is the maintenance (nafaqa) owed to them. The one who said this argued: this view is preferable to the first, because the dowry is fixed, and there is no sense in stipulating "reasonable" for it. So it is as if He, the Exalted, made clear that her being a slave does not affect the obligation of her maintenance and sustenance, just as with a free woman, once the master has given her and her husband access to one another in the customary way. Then al-Qadi said: Although the wording may bear what we have mentioned, most exegetes take it to mean the dowry, and they understood His saying "according to what is reasonable" as paying the dowry to her in the good customary manner, upon demand, without delay or postponement.

The second issue: Abu Bakr al-Razi, in Ahkam al-Qur'an, reported from some of the companions of Malik that the slave-woman is the one entitled to receive her dowry, and that if her master hires her out for service, the master is the one entitled to the wage, not she. These people argued regarding the dowry from this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And give them their payments﴾. As for the majority, they argued that her dowry belongs to her master by text and analogy. As for the text, it is His saying: ﴿Allah presents an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ [al-Nahl: 75], which negates that the owned slave possesses anything at all. As for analogy: the dowry is due as compensation for the benefits of intimacy, and those benefits belong to the master, who is the one who permitted them to the husband under the condition of marriage, so he must be the one entitled to their exchange.

The answer to their reliance on the verse, from several angles:

First: if we take "ujur" in the verse to mean maintenance, the question disappears entirely.

Second: He attributed the giving of the dowries to them because it is the price of their intimacy, and in His saying "give them" there is nothing that necessitates that the dowry becomes their property. Rather, he (ﷺ) said: "The slave and what is in his hand belong to his master," so the dowry becomes the master's property by this route. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Chaste, not fornicating, nor taking secret lovers﴾. In it are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "muhsanat" means chaste (ʿafaʾif), and it is a circumstantial state (hal) of His saying ﴿so marry them with the permission of their people﴾. The apparent meaning of this requires the prohibition of marrying adulteresses among the slave-women. People differed on whether marrying adulteresses is permissible; we will mention this in His saying ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. Most scholars hold that it is permissible, so this verse is taken to indicate recommendation and preference. His saying ﴿not fornicating﴾ means not adulteresses (zawan), ﴿nor taking secret lovers﴾, the plural of khidn, like atrab the plural of tirb. The khidn is the one who takes you as a lover, who is with you in every matter, outward and inward. Most exegetes said: the fornicator (musafiha) is she who hires herself out to any man who wants her, and the one who takes a khidn is she who takes a particular lover. The people of the Jahiliyya distinguished between these two categories, and they did not judge the one with a lover to be an adulteress. Since this distinction was regarded by them, Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned each of these two categories separately and explicitly forbade both together. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾ [al-A'raf: 33].

The second issue: al-Qadi said: this verse is one of the things relied on by those who do not make faith a condition for marrying slave-girls, because if that were a condition, then their being chaste would also be a condition, and this is not a condition.

The answer: this clause is conjoined not to the mention of the believing slave-girls, but to His saying: ﴿so marry them with the permission of their people and give them their payments﴾, and there is no doubt that all of this is obligatory, so we know that the lack of obligation in this does not entail the lack of obligation in what precedes it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when they are married, if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free women﴾. In it are several issues:

First issue: Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr (on the authority of ʿĀṣim) read (uḥṣinna) with a fatḥah on the alif, while the rest read it with a ḍammah on the alif. Whoever reads it with a fatḥah means: they embraced Islam. This is what ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi and al-Suddi said. Whoever reads it with a ḍammah means: they became chaste (muḥṣanāt) through marriage. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Mujahid said. Some scholars criticised the first reading, saying: God described the slave-women as believers in His words, ﴿from your believing slave-girls﴾, and it would be far-fetched to say "your believing slave-girls" and then say "if they embrace faith, then their status is such-and-such." It may be answered that God mentioned two rulings. The first concerns the marriage of slave-women, and He made faith a condition in it by His words, ﴿from your believing slave-girls﴾. The second concerns the ruling on what is required of them when they commit an immoral act, and He mentioned their state of faith in this ruling too, which is His words, ﴿and when they are chaste﴾.

Second issue: There is a strong difficulty in the verse. The chaste women in His words, ﴿then upon them is half of what is upon the chaste women﴾, either mean married free women, or they mean free virgins. The reason the term "chaste" is applied to them is their freedom. The first possibility is problematic, because the punishment for married free women for adultery is stoning. This would require that half of the stoning be due for the adultery of slave-women, and it is known that this is invalid. The second possibility is that the intended meaning is free virgins. Then half of what is due for them is fifty lashes, and this amount is due for the adultery of a slave-woman whether she is chaste or not. In that case this ruling would be attached merely to the occurrence of adultery from them, whereas the apparent meaning of the verse requires that it be attached to the combination of the two matters: chastity and adultery. This is because His words, ﴿and when they are chaste, then if they commit an immoral act﴾, form a condition following a condition, which by explicit text requires that the ruling be conditioned on both. So this is a strong difficulty in the verse.

The answer: We choose the second possibility. His words, ﴿and when they are chaste﴾, do not mean that this chastity is a condition for fifty lashes to be due for her adultery. Rather, the meaning is that the punishment for adultery is made more severe upon marriage. So if such a woman commits adultery after being married, her punishment is fifty lashes and no more. Therefore, before marriage this same amount is even more appropriate. This falls under what operates as an implication from the text, because when there is a factor that makes the punishment more severe, and the punishment is lessened due to slavery, then this amount being due when that aggravating factor is absent is even more fitting. God knows best.

* * *
Page 53

Third issue: The Khawarij agreed in denying stoning, and they argued with this verse: God required of the slave-woman half of what is required of the free chaste woman. So if stoning were due upon the free chaste woman, it would follow that the requirement for the slave-woman would be half a stoning, and that is invalid. Therefore it is established that what is due upon the married free woman is only flogging. The answer to this is what we mentioned in the previous issue. The full discussion of it is mentioned in Surat al-Nur, in the commentary on His words, ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer—flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2].

Fourth issue: Know that the jurists have made this verse a principle for the reduction of the ruling of the slave compared with that of the free person in matters other than the hadd (prescribed punishment), although there are matters in which this reduction is not required. God knows best.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿That is for one of you who fears hardship (ʿanat)﴾. They did not disagree that this refers to marrying slave-women. It is as if He said: "So from what your right hands possess, from your believing slave-girls, for one of you who fears hardship." The ʿanat is severe, harsh harm. God said regarding what He permitted concerning mixing with orphans: ﴿And God knows the corrupter from the reformer. And if God willed, He would have put you in difficulty﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220], meaning He would have made the matter severe for you, obliging you to separate your food from theirs, so severe harm would befall you. And He said: ﴿They wish you would suffer; hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ [Al ʿImran: 118], meaning: they love that you fall into severe harm. The commentators have two opinions on it. The first: intense sexual desire and great arousal may sometimes lead to fornication, so one falls into the prescribed punishment in this world and into great punishment in the Hereafter. This is the ʿanat. The second: intense sexual desire and great arousal may lead a person to severe illnesses. For women it may lead to constriction of the womb, and for men it may lead to pains in the hips and back. Most scholars hold the first view, because it is the one that suits the explanation in the Qur'an.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾. There are two issues in this:

First issue: The meaning is that marrying slave-women, after observing its three conditions—namely, inability to marry a free woman, the presence of ʿanat, and the slave-woman being a believer—is better left aside, because of the harms that arise from this marriage that we have explained.

Second issue: The school of Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, holds that occupying oneself with marriage is superior to occupying oneself with voluntary acts of worship. If their position is that occupying oneself with marriage is superior to occupying oneself with voluntary acts absolutely, whether the marriage is to a free woman or to a slave-woman, then this verse is a clear text against their view. If they say: "We do not prefer marrying a slave-woman over voluntary acts," then this argument falls. However, I have not seen this distinction in any of their books. God knows best.

Then God the Exalted concluded the verse with His words: ﴿And God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This is as a confirmation of what He mentioned, that leaving this marriage is better. That is, although what requires prohibition from this statement has occurred, God has permitted it to you because of your need for it, so this is from the category of forgiveness and mercy. God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

Page 54

In this passage there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning the lam in His saying ﴿li-yubayyina lakum﴾ (in order that He may make clear to you), there are two views:

The first: They said that the lam may stand in place of "an" (that) after verbs such as aradta (I wanted) and amarta (I commanded). It is said: aradta an tadhhaba and aradta li-tadhhaba (I wanted you to go), and amartuka an taqum and amartuka li-taqum (I commanded you to stand). The Exalted said: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 8], meaning they wish to extinguish. And He said: ﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 71].

The second view: We say that there is an implied element (idmar) in the verse, and the sense is: Allah desires the sending down of these verses in order to make clear to you your religion and your law. The same applies to the rest of the verses they mentioned. Thus His saying ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ means they wish their scheming and obstinacy in order to extinguish, and "we have been commanded with what we have been commanded" in order that we submit.

The second issue: Some exegetes said that His saying ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾ has one meaning, and the repetition is for emphasis. This is weak. The truth is that what is meant by His saying ﴿li-yubayyina lakum﴾ is that the Exalted has made these obligations clear to us, and distinguished within them the lawful from the unlawful and the good from the ugly.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾, and on this there are two views:
One: that this is evidence that everything He made clear to us as forbidden or permitted regarding women in the preceding verses was likewise the ruling in all the sacred laws and religions.

The second: that this is not what is meant; rather what is meant is that the Exalted guides you to the ways of those before you in showing what benefit (maslahah) you have in it, as He made it clear to them. For although the laws and obligations differ in themselves, they agree in the matter of benefits.

There is also a third view: that the meaning is that He guides you to the ways of those before you, of the people of truth, so that you avoid falsehood and follow truth.

* * *
Then the Exalted said: ﴿and to turn to you in forgiveness﴾. Al-Qadi said: its meaning is that just as the Exalted desired from us the act of obedience itself, He therefore made it clear and removed doubt about it; likewise, negligence and neglect have occurred from us, so He desires to turn to us in forgiveness, because the responsible person may obey and thereby deserve reward, or may disobey and then need to make amends through repentance.

Know that there is a difficulty in the verse: the truth is either what the People of the Sunnah say, that the act of the servant is created by Allah the Exalted, or the truth is what the Mu'tazilah say, that the act of the servant is not created by Allah the Exalted. The verse is problematic according to both views. As for the first view: on this view, whatever Allah the Exalted desires certainly comes about; so if He desires to turn to us, repentance must come about for all of us, and it is known that this is not the case. As for the second view: He the Exalted desires from us that we repent by our own choice and action, yet His saying ﴿and to turn to you﴾ apparently indicates that He is the one who creates repentance in us and that this repentance comes to us. So this verse is problematic according to both views.

The answer: We say that His saying ﴿and to turn to you﴾ is explicit that He is the one who performs repentance in us, and reason also confirms it, because repentance is an expression for regret regarding the past and resolve not to return in the future; regret and resolve belong to the category of volitions (iradat), and a volition cannot itself be willed, otherwise infinite regress would follow. Therefore volition cannot be the act of a human being. We thus know that this regret and this resolve do not arise except by the creation of Allah the Exalted. So this rational proof becomes evidence for the soundness of

Page 55
what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates, namely that He the Exalted is the one who turns to us. As for his saying: "If He turned to us, this repentance would have come about," we say: His saying ﴿and to turn to you﴾ is addressed to the community, and He did turn to them regarding marrying mothers and daughters and the other prohibited things mentioned in these verses, and that repentance came about for them. Thus the difficulty is removed. And Allah knows best.

* * *
Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾, meaning: All-Knowing of your conditions, All-Wise in everything He does to you and decrees over you.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance, but those who follow their appetites desire that you should deviate with a tremendous deviation.﴾

On this verse there are two issues:

The first issue: It has been said that the Magians (al-Majus, Zoroastrians) used to permit marriage with sisters and with the daughters of brothers and sisters. When God Most High forbade these, they said: "You permit marrying the daughter of your maternal aunt (khala) and paternal aunt (amma), yet your maternal and paternal aunts are forbidden to you. So marry also the daughters of the brother and the sister." Then this verse was revealed.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilites said: God's saying ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾ indicates that God Most High desires repentance from all, and obedience from all. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: This is impossible. For God Most High knows of the sinner that he will not repent, and His knowledge that he will not repent, together with his repentance, are two contraries; and that knowledge cannot cease to be. And given the necessity of one of the two contraries, desiring the other contrary would be desiring what He knows to be impossible, and that is impossible. Furthermore, if He Most High desires repentance from all, while Satan desires that you deviate with a tremendous deviation, and then what Satan desires occurs and not what the Merciful desires, then the penetration of Satan into the dominion of the Merciful would be more complete than the penetration of the Merciful into His own dominion, and that is impossible. Therefore it is established that God's saying ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾ is an address to specific people for whom this repentance occurs.

Then He said: ﴿Allah desires to lighten (the burden) for you, and man was created weak﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding "lightening" (al-takhfif) there are two opinions.

The first: What is meant by it is the permission to marry a slave woman (amah) in cases of necessity. This is the view of Mujahid and Muqatil. The others said: this is general in all the rulings of the Sharia, and in everything He made easy for us and facilitated for us, as a kindness from Him toward us, and He did not make the obligation heavy upon us as He made it heavy upon the Children of Israel. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I have come to you with the easy, tolerant monotheism (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah)."

The second issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: This indicates that the act of the servant is not created by Allah, the Exalted. For if it were so, then the disbeliever would have disbelief created in him and then be told: "Do not disbelieve." This is the greatest form of burdening. And [He] does not create faith in him, nor (does He give) the servant the power to create faith, and then tell him: "Believe." This is the greatest form of burdening. He said: It also indicates that the obligation of what is not within one's capacity does not occur, because it is the greatest form of burdening.

The answer: It is countered by knowledge and motive, and by most of what we have mentioned.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And man was created weak﴾. The meaning is that, because of human weakness, He lightened his obligation and did not burden it. The closer view is that weakness in this place is not to be understood as weakness of constitution, but rather as the great number of motives toward following desire and pleasure, so that this becomes like a reason why he is too weak to bear opposing it. We said that this aspect is preferable because weakness in constitution and strength, if Allah strengthens his motive toward obedience, would be in the category of strength, and one who is strong in constitution and instrument, if his motives toward obedience are weak, becomes in the category of the weak. Thus the effect in this domain is due to the weakness and strength of the motive, not to the weakness and strength of the body. All of this is the judge's speech, and it is a good speech, but it demolishes its own foundation. For when he conceded that what affects the existence and non-existence of the act is the strength and weakness of the motive, then had he reflected, he would have known that the strength and weakness of the motive must have a cause. If that is due to another motive from the servant, it leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul). If all of it is from Allah, then that is the truth from which there is no escape, and the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah is entirely void. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Eight verses in Surat al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than what the sun rises upon and sets: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾, ﴿Allah desires to lighten for you﴾, ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147].

Muhammad al-Razi, the author of this book, may Allah conclude his life with goodness, says: O Allah, make us, by Your grace and mercy, worthy of it, O Most Generous of the generous and O Most Merciful of the merciful.

**The eighth type of the obligations mentioned in this surah.**

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except in the case of trade by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you. And whoever does that in aggression and wrongfulness, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾

**The Exalted's statement:** ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except in the case of trade by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you. And whoever does that in aggression and wrongfulness, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾

Know that there are two views on the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses:

The first: When He, the Exalted, explained how one may dispose of persons through marriage, He mentioned after it how one may dispose of wealth.

The second: al-Qadi said: When He mentioned seeking marriage with wealth, and commanded the giving of dowries and maintenance, He then explained how wealth is to be disposed of, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾.

[p. 57]

In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** He, the Exalted, specified eating here by mention, although all other dispositions carried out in an unlawful manner are forbidden, because the greatest purpose of wealth is consumption. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ [an-Nisa': 10].

**The second issue:** They mentioned two interpretations of *al-batil* (the unlawful, the baseless):

The first: It is a term for everything that is not permitted in the Sharia, such as usury (riba), usurpation (ghasb), theft (sariqa), embezzlement (khiyana), false testimony, taking property by a false oath, and denying a right. In my view, taking the verse in this sense implies that it is general (mujmal), because the sense of the verse becomes: "Do not consume your wealth that you have placed among yourselves by an unlawful means." Since the lawful means are not mentioned here in detail, the verse is necessarily general.

The second: What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, may God be pleased with them both: that *al-batil* is everything that is taken from a person without any exchange (iwad). On this interpretation the verse is not general. However, some said that it is abrogated (mansukh). They said: When this verse was revealed, people became scrupulous about eating anything at someone else's house, and this was hard on people, so God abrogated it by His saying in Surat an-Nur: ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾ [an-Nur: 61]. Also, the apparent meaning of the verse, if we interpret *al-batil* as we have mentioned, forbids gifts and donations. It may be said that this is not abrogation (naskh) but specification (takhsis). For this reason, ash-Sha'bi narrated from 'Alqama, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: This verse is muhkam (firm, not abrogated); it has not been abrogated and will not be abrogated until the Day of Resurrection.

**The third issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾ includes consuming the property of another unjustly and consuming one's own property unjustly, because His saying: ﴿your wealth﴾ includes both categories together, just as His saying: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ indicates the prohibition against killing others and against killing oneself unjustly. As for consuming one's own property unjustly, it is spending it in acts of disobedience to God. As for consuming another's property unjustly, we have already enumerated it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿except in the case of trade by mutual consent from you﴾, and in this there are issues:

**The first issue:** 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (تِجارَةً) [*tijaratan*, in the accusative], and the rest read it in the nominative (*tijaratun*). As for the one who reads it in the accusative, it is on the reading of *kana* as the incomplete (*naqisa*) verb, and the sense is: "except that the trade be a trade." As for the one who reads it in the nominative, it is on *kana* as the complete (*tamma*) verb, and the sense is: "except that a trade come into existence and occur." al-Wahidi said: The preferred reading is the nominative, because whoever reads it in the accusative must supply a pronoun referring to the trade, saying: its sense is "except that the trade be a trade," and a pronoun referring to something before it is mentioned is not strong, although it is permissible.

**The second issue:** His saying: (إلّا) [*illa*, "except"] has two possibilities:

The first: It is a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati'), because trade by mutual consent is not of the same kind as consuming wealth unjustly. So *illa* here has the meaning of *bal* ("but rather"), and the sense is: "but rather, it is permissible to consume it by trade by mutual consent."

The second: Some people said that the exception is continuous (muttasil), and they supplied something, saying: the sense is: "Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, even if you are mutually agreed, such as usury and other things, except that it be a trade by mutual consent."

Know that just as what is gained through trade is permissible, so too is wealth gained through gift, bequest, inheritance, receiving charity, dower (mahr), and compensation for injuries (arsh al-jinayat), for the causes of ownership are many apart from trade.

[p. 58]

If we say that the exception is discontinuous, there is no difficulty, for He, the Exalted, mentioned here one cause of ownership and did not mention the rest, neither by negation nor by affirmation.

And if we say that the exception is continuous, that would be a ruling that what is other than trade does not confer permissibility, and in this case there must be either abrogation or specification.

**The third issue:** ash-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: The prohibition in transactions (mu'amalat) indicates invalidity. Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, said: It does not indicate that. ash-Shafi'i argued for the soundness of his position with several points:

The first: All property belongs to God, the Exalted. So when He permits some of His servants certain dispositions, this is like when a person appoints an agent (wakil) for certain dispositions. Then, if the agent acts contrary to the wish of the principal, that is not valid by consensus. So if a disposition carried out contrary to the wish of the permitting owner is not valid, then a disposition carried out contrary to the wish of the real owner is more fitting not to be valid.

Second: These invalid dispositions either necessarily bring about the existence of the forbidden thing that is prohibited, or they do not. If the first is the case, it is necessary to say that they are void, by analogy with invalid dispositions, the common factor being the effort to prevent the source of the prohibition from coming into existence. If the second is the case, it is necessary to say that they are valid, by analogy with valid dispositions, the common factor being that they are dispositions free of any corrupting element. Thus it is established that a disposition must occur in one of these two ways. As for the claim of a disposition that is neither valid nor void, that is impossible.

Third: His saying, "Do not sell a dirham for two dirhams," is like His saying, "Do not sell a free person for a slave." Just as this prohibition, by its wording, is an abrogation of the law, so too is the first. And since that is an abrogation of the law, it is invalid for it to be a ruling-conferring statement. And God knows best.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: The option of the meeting (khiyar al-majlis) is not established in pure exchange contracts (uqud al-mu'awadat al-mahda), and ash-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: It is established.

Abu Hanifa argued from texts:

The first of them: this verse, for His saying: ﴿except in the case of trade by mutual consent from you﴾ apparently requires permissibility when mutual consent is present, whether or not separation has taken place.

The second: His saying: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], which obliges every contracting party to fulfil what he has contracted for himself.

The third: His saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with the goodwill of his soul." Goodwill has been obtained here by the contract of sale, so permissibility must be obtained.

The fourth: His saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Whoever buys food, let him not sell it until he takes possession of it." He permitted its sale after taking possession.

The fifth: What is narrated, that he, upon him be peace, "forbade the sale of food until it is measured with the sa' (sa'), and permitted its sale once it has been measured, and did not stipulate separation in it."

The sixth: His saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "A child cannot repay his father, unless he finds him enslaved and buys him and frees him." They agreed that as soon as he buys him, manumission takes place, and this indicates that ownership is obtained by the mere contract.

Know that ash-Shafi'i accepts the generality of these texts, but he says: You established the option of sight (khiyar al-ru'yah) in buying what the buyer has not seen, based on a hadith on which the transmitters agreed was weak. So we too establish the option of the meeting based on a hadith on which the scholars of hadith agreed to accept, and that is his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted." The interpretations of Abu Hanifa's companions of this report and their answers are mentioned in the books of disputed questions (al-Khilafiyyat). And God knows best.

* * *

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.﴾ They agreed that this is a prohibition against some of them killing others, [p. 59] and He said "yourselves" (*anfusakum*) because of his saying, upon him be peace: "The believers are like a single soul." Also, the Arabs say: "We have been killed, by the Lord of the Ka'bah," when one of them is killed, because the killing of one of them is treated as the killing of all of them.

They differed as to whether this address is a prohibition to them against killing themselves. Some of them denied it and said: A believer, with his faith, is not permitted to be forbidden from killing himself, because he is compelled not to kill himself. This is because the deterrent from it in this world is present, namely severe pain and great blame, and the deterrent from it in the Hereafter is also present, namely deserving a great punishment. And when the deterrent is pure, he refrains from doing it, and when that is so, there is no benefit in forbidding it. This prohibition could only be mentioned regarding one who believes about killing himself what the people of India believe, and that cannot apply to a believer. It may be answered that a believer, despite being a believer in God and the Last Day, may suffer such grief and harm that killing himself would seem easier than that, and for this reason we see many Muslims kill themselves for the same reason we have mentioned. If that is so, there is benefit in forbidding it. Also, there is another possibility, as if it were said: Do not do what makes you deserving of being killed: killing, apostasy, and adultery after being married. Then He, the Exalted, showed that He is Merciful to His servants, and for the sake of His mercy He forbade them from everything that would entail hardship or trial for them. It was also said: He, the Exalted, commanded the Children of Israel to kill themselves so that it would be a repentance for them and an expiation of their sins. And He has been Merciful to you, O community of Muhammad, in that He did not impose upon you those difficult obligations.

Then He said: ﴿And whoever does that out of transgression and wrongdoing, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is always easy for Allah.﴾

Know that there are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: The scholars differed over what the phrase ﴿whoever does that﴾ refers back to, and they gave several opinions:

First: ʿAṭāʾ said: it is specific to the unlawful killing of a soul, because the pronoun must refer back to the nearest thing previously mentioned.

Second: al-Zajjāj said: it refers back to killing a soul and consuming wealth falsely, because both are mentioned in one verse.

Third: Ibn ʿAbbās said: it refers back to everything that Allah has forbidden from the beginning of the sūrah up to this place.

The second issue: He said ﴿out of transgression﴾ only because among what preceded is one party killing another, and that may be lawful, as in retaliation (qawad); and among what preceded is taking wealth, and that may be lawful, as in blood-money (diyah) and other cases. For this reason, the Exalted made transgression a condition for this threat.

The third issue: The Muʿtazilah said: this verse indicates the certainty of the threat against the people of the prayer (ahl al-ṣalāh). They said: although His saying ﴿We will drive him into a Fire﴾ does not by itself indicate eternal abiding (takhlid), whoever holds with certainty to the threat against sinners also holds to their eternal abiding, so the establishment of one entails the establishment of the other, since there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The answer to this has been given in full in several places earlier, but what we say here is: this is specific to the disbelievers, because He said: ﴿whoever does that out of transgression and wrongdoing﴾, and there must be a distinction between transgression (ʿudwān) and wrongdoing (ẓulm) to avoid repetition. So wrongdoing is understood as the case where his intention is to overstep the commands of Allah, and there is no doubt that whoever is like this is a disbeliever. It cannot be said: Did He not describe them as believers when He said ﴿O you who believe﴾? How then can it be said that the intended people are the disbelievers? We say: your position is that whoever enters under this threat is not a believer at all. So on this position you must say that they were believers, and then when they committed these acts they no longer remained in the state of faith. If you must say this statement, then why would this statement not be valid from us too, in establishing what we have said? And Allah knows best.

Page 60

Then the Exalted concluded the verse by saying: ﴿and that is always easy for Allah.﴾

Know that all possibilities are equal in relation to the power of Allah, and at that point it is impossible to say that some acts are easier for Him than others. Rather, this address was revealed in the manner of speech customary among us, as in His saying: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Or its meaning is emphasis in threatening, namely that no one can escape from Him or prevail against Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to a noble entrance﴾.

Know that when Exalted God had mentioned the threat (wa'id), He followed it with a detailed explanation of what is connected to it, so He mentioned this verse. In it there are several issues.

The first issue: Some people have said that all sins and disobediences are major sins (kaba'ir). Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Everything in which God is disobeyed is a major sin. Whoever commits any of them should seek God's forgiveness, for God Exalted does not keep in the Fire forever anyone of this community except one who apostatizes from Islam, or one who denies an obligation, or one who denies predestination (qadar)." Know that this view is weak, for several reasons:

The first argument: this verse itself. If all sins were major sins, it would not be valid to distinguish between what is expiated by avoiding the major sins and the major sins themselves.

The second argument: the saying of Exalted God: ﴿And every small and great thing is written down﴾ [al-Qamar: 53], and His saying: ﴿It leaves out nothing small or great but has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49].

The third argument: the Messenger (ﷺ) explicitly stated that certain sins by name are major sins, as in his saying: "The major sins are: associating partners with God, the perjury that cuts off (al-yamin al-ghamus), disobedience to one's parents, and killing a soul." This indicates that among sins there are some that are not major sins.

The fourth argument: the saying of Exalted God: ﴿But He made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. This is clear that the forbidden things are of three categories:
The first of them: disbelief (kufr).
The second: wickedness (fusuq).
The third: disobedience (‘isyan).
There must be a difference between wickedness and disobedience for the conjunction to be valid, and that is nothing other than the difference we have mentioned between minor sins and major sins: major sins are wickedness, and minor sins are disobedience. Ibn 'Abbas argued with two points:
One of them: the abundance of the blessings of the one who is disobeyed.
The second: the greatness of the one who is disobeyed. If we consider the first, then God's blessings are unlimited, as He said: ﴿If you should count God's blessing, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. If we consider the second, then He is the most majestic and greatest of existing things. In either case, disobedience to Him must be of the utmost gravity. Thus it is established that every sin is a major sin.

The answer is in two parts:
The first: just as He, Exalted, is the most majestic and noblest of existing things, so He is the most merciful of the merciful and the most generous of the generous, and the most free of need of the obedience of the obedient and of the sins of the sinners, and all of this necessitates the lightness of the sin.
The second: Suppose that all sins are major from the standpoint that they are sins, yet some of them are greater than others, and that necessitates variation.

Page 61

When it is established that sins are of two kinds, some minor and some major, then those who hold this are of two groups. Some of them say: the major sin is distinguished from the minor sin in its own essence and reality. Others say: this distinction arises not in their essences but according to the state of their doers. We will explain each of these two views.

As for the first view: its proponents disagree greatly, and we will point to some of it:
The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Everything that comes in the Qur'an joined with a mention of threat is a major sin, such as killing a sacred soul, slandering chaste women, fornication, usury, consuming the property of orphans, and fleeing from battle."
The second: Ibn Mas'ud said: "Begin Surat al-Nisa'. Everything God has forbidden up to the thirty-third verse is a major sin," then he said: "Its confirmation is: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾."
The third: some people said: "Every deliberate act is a major sin." Know that these sayings are weak.

As for the first: every sin must be deserving of blame in this world and punishment in the next, so the claim that everything that comes in the Qur'an joined with threat is a major sin implies that every sin is a major sin, and we have refuted this.

As for the second: it is also weak, because God Exalted mentioned many major sins in the other surahs, and there is no sense in restricting them to this surah.

As for the third: it is also weak, because if by "deliberate" one means that the doer is not forgetful of his act, then whatever is of this state is what God forbade, and so according to this every sin must be a major sin, which we have refuted. And if by "deliberate" one means committing the disobedience while knowing that it is disobedience, then it is known that the Jews and Christians disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ) while not knowing that it is disobedience, and yet it is a great disbelief. Thus these three views are refuted.

Al-Shaykh al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, in the selections from his book Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din, gave a long section on the distinction between major and minor sins, and he said: "All of this is the view of those who say that major sins are distinguished from minor sins by their own essences and selves."

As for the second view, which is the view of those who say that major sins are distinguished from minor sins by considering the states of their doers: these are the ones who say that every act of obedience has a measure of reward, and every act of disobedience has a measure of punishment. When a person performs an act of obedience and merits a reward by it, then commits an act of disobedience and merits a punishment by it, the relation between the reward of the obedience and the punishment of the disobedience, by rational division, falls into three ways:
One: that they balance and equal each other. This, though possible by rational division, the textual evidence indicates does not occur, for He said: ﴿A party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]; had such a responsible person existed, he would be neither in the Garden nor in the Blaze.
The second: that the reward of his obedience exceeds the punishment of his disobedience. Then that punishment is cancelled (yanhabitu) by an equal amount of reward, and some reward remains over. Such a disobedience is the minor sin, and this cancellation is called expiation (takfir).
The third: that the punishment of his disobedience exceeds the reward of his obedience. Then that reward is cancelled by an equal amount of punishment, and some punishment remains over. Such a disobedience is the major sin, and this cancellation is called nullification (ihbat). By this discourse the difference between the major sin and the minor sin becomes clear. This is the view of the majority of the Mu'tazilah.

Page 62

Know that this discourse is built upon principles, all of which are false in our view.

The first of them: that this rests on the premise that obedience necessitates reward and disobedience necessitates punishment. This is false, because we have shown in many places of this book that an act's issuing from the servant is not possible unless God creates in him a motive that necessitates that act; and when this is so, it is impossible that obedience should necessitate reward or disobedience necessitate punishment.

The second: even granting that the matter is as they say, we know by the immediate intellect (badihat al-'aql) that the one who occupies himself with the Oneness of God, His sanctification, service and obedience for seventy years, the reward of the totality of these many acts of obedience during this long period is far greater than the punishment for drinking a single drop of wine, even though the community is agreed that drinking this drop is a major sin. If they persist and say: "Rather, the punishment for drinking this drop exceeds the reward of monotheism and all acts of obedience for seventy years only," they have nullified their own foundation, for they build these questions upon the principle of the rational goodness and ugliness of acts. And among matters firmly established in minds is that whoever makes the punishment for this measure of offence exceed the reward of those great acts of obedience is an oppressor. If they reject the judgment of reason in this place, they have nullified for themselves the doctrine of rational good and evil, and then all these principles are nullified against them.

The third: God's blessings are numerous and precede the obedience of His servants, and those preceding blessings necessitate these acts of obedience. Thus performing acts of obedience is the discharge of what was owed because of the preceding blessings, and such a thing does not necessitate anything else in the future. And if that is so, then none of the acts of obedience necessitates reward at all. And if that is so, then every act of disobedience committed has a punishment exceeding the reward of its doer, so all acts of disobedience would have to be major sins. This too is false.

The fourth: this discourse is built upon the doctrine of nullification (ihbat), and we have mentioned the many arguments against the doctrine of nullification in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah. Thus it is established that what the Mu'tazilah have held concerning the distinction between the minor and the major sin is a false view. And success is from God.

* * *

The second issue: People have disagreed over whether God has distinguished the totality of major sins from the totality of minor sins or not. Most of them said: God has not distinguished the totality of major sins from the totality of minor sins. For when He made clear in this verse that avoiding the major sins causes the minor sins to be expiated, then when the servant knows that the major sins are nothing but these specific categories, he knows that whenever he refrains from them his minor sins become expiating. That would be an incitement (igra') for him to commit those minor sins, and incitement to what is ugly does not befit the whole. But if God does not distinguish all major sins from all minor sins, and it is not known of any sin that it is minor, and there is no sin one may undertake without its being possible that it is major, then that will be a deterrent for him from committing it. They said: an analogue of this in the Law is the concealing of the Middle Prayer (al-salat al-wusta) among the prayers, the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) among the nights of Ramadan, the hour of response (sa'at al-ijabah) among the hours of Friday, and the time of death at all times. The upshot is that this principle requires that God not specify in any sin that it is minor, and not specify that the major sins are only such-and-such, for if He specified that, then everything else would be minor, and the minor would then be known. However, it is permissible that He specify in some sins that they are major. It is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "What do you count as the major sins?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Associating partners with God, killing a sacred soul, disobedience to one's parents, fleeing from the battle, sorcery, consuming the property of orphans, false testimony, consuming usury, and slandering chaste, unwary women." It is narrated from Abdullah ibn 'Umar that he mentioned them and added to them: taking lawfully the sacred House's visitors (istihlal amin al-bayt al-haram), and drinking wine. And from Ibn Mas'ud that he added to them: despair of God's mercy (al-qunut min rahmat Allah), despair of God's mercy (al-yas min rahmat Allah), and feeling secure from God's plan (al-amn min makr Allah). And it is mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that they are seven, then he said: "They are nearer to seventy." In another narration: "nearer to seven hundred." And God knows best.

Page 63

* * *

The third issue: Abu al-Qasim al-Ka'bi argued from this verse for the certainty of the threat against the perpetrators of major sins. He said: "By this verse God has removed the doubt concerning the threat, for after mentioning the major sins, He made clear that whoever avoids them, He will expiate his bad deeds from him. This indicates that if they do not avoid them, they are not expiated. And if God could forgive them the major and minor sins without repentance, this discourse would not be valid."

Our companions answered him in several ways:
The first: you either derive your proof from this verse by saying that when He mentioned that avoiding major sins expiates bad deeds, it follows that when major sins are not avoided, they are not expiated, because specifying a thing by mention indicates the negation of the ruling for what is other than it. But this is invalid, since for the Mu'tazilah this principle is false, and for us it is a weak, speculative indication. Or you derive your proof from the fact that what is made dependent by the word "in" (in) upon a thing is absent when that thing is absent, and this too is weak, and verses indicate it...

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 31 (part 2 of 2):

First: His saying, ﴿And give thanks to Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. Thanks is obligatory whether Allah is worshipped or not.

Second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. Fulfilling a trust is obligatory whether or not the one entrusted was actually entrusted.

Third: ﴿But if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. Taking testimony from a man and two women is permissible whether or not the two men are present.

Fourth: ﴿And if you find no scribe, then a pledge taken in hand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. Pledging is legislated whether or not a scribe is found.

Fifth: ﴿And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. Compelling someone to prostitution is forbidden, whether or not they desire chastity.

Sixth: ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Marriage is permissible whether or not that fear arises.

Seventh: ﴿There is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 101]. Shortening the prayer is permissible whether or not fear arises.

Eighth: ﴿But if there are women more than two, then for them is two-thirds of what he leaves﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. The two-thirds is the right of three or more, and it is likewise the right of two.

Ninth: His saying, ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two, then send an arbiter from his people﴾ [al-Nisa': 35]. That is permissible whether or not fear arises.

Tenth: His saying, ﴿If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾ [al-Nisa': 35]. Harmony may come about without their desiring it.

Eleventh: His saying, ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa': 130]. Wealth may be attained without that separation. There are many verses of this kind. It is therefore established that what is made conditional by the particle "in" (inna) on a thing does not necessarily become non-existent when that thing does not exist. It is strange that the position of al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) is that what is made conditional by "in" on a thing does not become non-existent when that thing does not exist. Yet in tafsir he approved the argument of al-Ka'bi from this verse, and this shows that a person's love for his school may lead him into what he should not do.

The second answer: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said that this verse came directly after the verse in which Allah forbade marrying the prohibited women, withholding women (from marriage), taking the wealth of orphans, and other things. So Allah said: If you avoid these major sins which We have forbidden you, We will expiate from you what you committed of them in the past. And if this interpretation is possible, it is not required to read the verse as the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) do. Al-Qadi criticised this interpretation in two ways. The first: His saying, ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾, is general, so restricting it to what was previously mentioned is not permissible. The second: His saying that by their avoiding these prohibited acts in the future Allah expiates what occurred of them in the past is a distant statement, because their situation is one of two conditions. Either they repented of everything previously committed, so repentance has already removed the punishment for those things, and avoiding these major sins is not needed; or they did not repent of everything previously committed, so from where does it follow that avoiding these major sins necessitates the expiation of those misdeeds?

The answer to the first: We do not claim with certainty that His saying, ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾, refers to what was previously mentioned. Rather, we say that it is possible, and with this possibility the verse cannot be specifically read as they claim.

The answer to the second: Your statement, "From where does it follow that avoiding these major sins necessitates the expiation of those misdeeds?", is a question, not a proof of the invalidity of this division. By this measure the possibility is not nullified, and once this possibility is present, the argument you cited is refuted. And Allah knows best.

The third answer to this argument: If we grant them all that they intend, the verse contains nothing beyond saying that whoever does not avoid major sins will not have his misdeeds expiated. In that case this verse becomes general in threat, and the general threats in the Qur'an are not few. Therefore, what we have said as an answer to all the other general statements is an answer to their reliance on this verse. So I do not know of any special distinction of this verse in this matter. Since this is so, al-Ka'bi's claim that Allah has, through this verse, removed the doubt on this question has no basis.

The fourth answer: Among these major sins there may be something that is major in relation to one thing and minor in relation to another. The same applies to minor sins. However, what is judged as major in an absolute sense is disbelief (kufr). Once this is established, why should it not be possible that what is meant by His saying, ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾, is disbelief? This is because disbelief has many kinds: among them, disbelief in Allah, in His prophets, in the Last Day, and in His laws. So the meaning is that whoever avoids disbelief, whatever lies beyond it is forgiven. This possibility fits and agrees with the explicit statement of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. And if this is possible, indeed apparent, their reliance on the universal (in this matter) collapses. And success is from Allah.

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah said that upon avoiding major sins, the forgiveness of minor sins is obligatory. According to us, nothing is obligatory upon Allah; rather, everything He does is grace and kindness. The proofs for this issue have already been mentioned.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will admit you to a noble entrance﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first issue: Al-Mufaddal reported from 'Asim the recitation "yukaffar" and "yudkhilkum" with the letter ya' in both places, referring to the third person (absent) pronoun. The rest read with the letter nun, as a resumption of the promise. Nafi' read "mudkhalan" with a fatha on the mim, and so did (he) in al-Hajj. The rest read it with a damma. They did not differ regarding "mudkhala sidq" (a true entrance), which is with a damma. With a fatha, the intended meaning is the place of entering; with a damma, the intended meaning is the verbal noun, which is the act of admitting. That is: and He will admit you into an admission that is noble. He described the admission as noble, meaning that this admission will be accompanied by nobility, in contrast to those of whom Allah said: ﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell﴾ [al-Furqan: 34].

The second issue: Mere avoidance of major sins does not necessitate entry into Paradise. Rather, obedience must accompany it. The sense is: if you perform all the obligatory duties and avoid all major sins, We will expiate for you the remainder of your misdeeds and admit you into Paradise. This is one of the things that necessitates entry into Paradise. It is known that the absence of one cause does not necessitate the absence of the effect. Rather, here there is another cause, the original and strong cause, which is Allah's grace, His generosity, and His mercy, as He said: ﴿Say: By the grace of Allah and by His mercy, let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus: 58]. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 32:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of His bounty. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that there are two aspects to the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses.

The first: al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: When Allah, in the preceding verse, forbade them from consuming wealth by falsehood and from killing one another, He commanded them in this verse with what makes it easy for them to abandon these prohibited acts, namely that each person be content with what Allah has apportioned to him. For if he is not content with that, he falls into envy (ḥasad, resentment at another's blessing). And if he falls into envy, he inevitably falls into taking wealth by falsehood and into killing souls. But if he is content with what Allah has decreed, he is able to guard against wronging both lives and wealth.

The second aspect concerns the manner of the arrangement: taking wealth by falsehood and killing a soul are acts of the limbs. So He first commanded their abandonment, so that the outward would be purified of ugly deeds, and that is the sharia (the revealed law). Then He commanded, after that, the abandonment of encroaching upon people's lives and wealth in the heart through envy, so that the inward would be purified of blameworthy character traits, and that is the ṭarīqa (the spiritual path). Then there are issues in the verse:

**First issue:** Tamannī (wishing) according to us is an expression for willing what is known or thought not to occur. For this reason we say: if Allah willed from the disbeliever that he believe while knowing that he will not believe, then He would be one who wishes. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds human justice and free will as central principles) said: The prohibition concerns a speaker's saying "I wish it had happened" or "I wish it had not happened." This is far-fetched, because a mere word, if it has no meaning, is not a wish. Rather, one must inquire into the meaning of this word, and it has no meaning except what we have mentioned: willing what is known or thought not to occur.

**Second issue:** Know that the levels of felicities (saʿādāt) are either psychological (nafsāniyya), physical (badaniyya), or external (khārijiyya).

As for the psychological felicities, they are of two kinds:

One: what relates to the theoretical faculty, namely perfect intelligence, complete intuition, and knowledge that exceeds the knowledge of others in quantity and quality.

The second: what relates to the practical faculty, namely chastity (ʿiffa), which is a mean between insensibility and debauchery; courage (shajāʿa), which is a mean between recklessness and cowardice; and the practical use of wisdom, which is a mean between foolishness and cunning. The totality of these states is justice (ʿadāla).

As for the physical felicities: health, beauty, and long life, together with pleasure and delight therein.

As for the external felicities: they are the abundance of righteous children, the abundance of kinsfolk, the abundance of friends and helpers, complete leadership, the effectiveness of speech, and being beloved to people, well remembered among them, and obeyed in command among them. This is the indication to the totality of felicities. Some of them are innate, with no way to acquire them, and some are acquired. And what is acquired, when the rational person reflects on it, he finds it also to be pure bounty from Allah, for there is no preponderance of motives, removal of obstacles, and attainment of causes except by Him. Otherwise the cause of striving and effort would be shared, and the attainment of felicity and reaching the sought goal would not be shared. These are the divisions of the felicities in which Allah favors some of them over others.

* * *

**Second issue (continued):** When a person witnesses various kinds of virtues present in another person, and finds himself empty of all of them or of most of them, then his heart is pained and his thoughts are troubled. Then two states arise here:
