The first: that he wishes for the removal of those felicities from that person.

The second: that he does not wish that, but rather wishes for the attainment of the like of them for himself.

As for the first, it is blameworthy envy, because the primary intent of the Governor of the universe and its Creator is benevolence toward His servants, generosity to them, and the outpouring of all kinds of bounty upon them. So whoever wishes for the removal of that, it is as if he objected to Allah in what is the primary intent of creating the world and bringing the responsible beings into existence. Also, he may perhaps believe in himself that he is more deserving of those blessings than that person, and this would be an objection against Allah and a disparagement of His wisdom. All of this casts a person into disbelief and the darkness of innovation, and removes from his heart the light of faith. Just as envy is a cause of corruption in religion, so it is also a cause of corruption in this world, for it severs affection, love, and friendship, and turns all of these into their opposites. For this reason Allah forbade His servants from it, saying: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others.﴾

Know that the reason for the prohibition of this envy differs according to the roots of the religions. As for the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿa (the people of the Sunna and the community, the mainstream Sunni school), it is that He, the Exalted, is the Doer of what He wills: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:23]. So there is no objection to Him in His action, and there is no room for anyone to dispute with Him. Everything He does, He does without any cause for His doing. Given this, the doors of talk and counter-talk are closed, and the paths of objections are rejected. As for the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, this path is also closed, because He, glorified is He, is the Knower of the unseen, so He is more knowing than His creation of the aspects of benefit and the subtleties of wisdom. For this very meaning He said: ﴿And if Allah had expanded provision for His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾ [al-Shūrā 42:27]. On either reckoning, every rational person must be content with the decree of Allah, glorified is He. For this same meaning, the Messenger (ﷺ) related from the Lord of Might that He said: "Whoever submits to My decree, endures My trial, and gives thanks for My blessings, I will record him as a ṣiddīq (a man of great truthfulness) and resurrect him on the Day of Resurrection with the ṣiddīqīn. And whoever is not content with My decree, does not endure My trial, and does not give thanks for My blessings, let him seek a lord other than Me."

This is the discussion concerning the case where a person wishes for the removal of that blessing from that person. And among the things that confirm this is what Ibn Sīrīn related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man should not make a proposal upon the proposal of his brother, nor bid upon the bid of his brother, nor should a woman ask for the divorce of her sister so that she may take her place, for Allah is the one who provides for her."

The purpose of all of this is to emphasize the prohibition of envy.

As for when a person does not wish for that removal, but rather wishes for the attainment of the like of it for himself, some people permitted this. However, the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn, the careful scholars) said: This too is not permissible, because that blessing may be a corruption for him in religion and a harm to him in this world. For this reason the verifiers said: It is not permissible for a person to say, "O Allah, give me a house like the house of so-and-so, and a wife like the wife of so-and-so." Rather he should say: "O Allah, give me what is good for my religion, my world, my hereafter, and my livelihood." And if a person reflects much, he will not find a supplication better than what Allah mentioned in the Qur'an as a teaching for His servants, and it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ [al-Baqara 2:201]. Qatadah related from al-Hasan that he said: Let no one wish for wealth, for perhaps his ruin will be in that wealth, as in the case of Thaʿlaba. And this is what is meant by His saying in this verse: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾

* * *

**Third issue:** They mentioned several aspects regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl):

The first: Mujahid said: "Umm Salamah said: O Messenger of Allah, the men go out to fight and we do not fight, and they have double what we have in inheritance. Would that we were men! So the verse was revealed."

The second: al-Suddi said: When the verses of inheritance were revealed, the men said: "We hope to be favored over women in the Hereafter just as we have been favored in inheritance." And the women said: "We hope that the burden upon us will be half of what is upon the men, just as in inheritance." So the verse was revealed.

The third: When Allah made the inheritance of the male equal to the share of two females, the women said: "We are more in need, because we are weak, and they are more capable of seeking livelihood." So the verse was revealed.

The fourth: "A woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: The Lord of men and women is one, and you are the Messenger to us and to them. Our father is Adam and our mother is Eve. So what is the reason that Allah mentions men and does not mention us?" So the verse was revealed. She said: "The men have preceded us in jihad, so what is ours?" He (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, for the pregnant woman among you is the reward of one who fasts and stands in prayer. When the pains of labor seize her, no one knows what reward she has. When she nurses, for every suck she has the reward of giving life to a soul."

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾

Know that it is possible that the intent of this verse is what relates to the conditions of this world, and that it is what relates to the conditions of the Hereafter, and that it is what relates to both.

As for the first possibility, there are aspects to it:

The first: that the intent is that each group has a share of what it has earned of the blessings of this world, so it is incumbent upon it to be content with what Allah has apportioned to it.

The second: each share is a determined portion of inheritance according to what Allah has ruled, so it is obligatory to be content with it and to leave off objection. And "earning" (iktisāb), according to this view, means attaining and securing.

The third: The people of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) did not give inheritance to women and children, so Allah nullified that by this verse, and made clear that each of them has a share, whether male or female, young or old.

As for the second possibility, namely that the intent of this verse is what relates to the conditions of the Hereafter, there are aspects to it:

The first: the intent is that for each person there is a measure of reward that he deserves by the generosity and kindness of Allah, so do not wish for the opposite of that.

The second: For each person there is a recompense for what he has earned of acts of obedience, so he should not waste it through blameworthy envy. Its implication is: Do not waste your own and wish for what belongs to another.

The third: For men there is a share of what they have earned by reason of their maintaining the women with support, and for women there is a share of what they have earned, meaning guarding their chastity, obeying their husbands, and tending to the affairs of the house, such as cooking, baking, keeping clothes, and the needs of livelihood. So the share, according to this assessment, is the reward.

As for the third possibility, it is that the intent of the verse is all of these aspects together, because this expression admits of them, and there is no contradiction.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ Concerning this there are issues:

**First issue:** Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-saluu Allāha min faḍlihi﴾ without hamza (the glottal stop), on condition that it is an imperative from the verb "to ask," and on condition that it is preceded by a waw or a fa'. The rest read it with hamza throughout the Qur'an.

As for the first: he moved the vowel of the hamza onto the sīn and dispensed with the alif of connection (hamzat al-waṣl, the initial vowel-bearing alif used at the start of speech), so he deleted it.

As for the second: it follows the original form. And they all agreed on His saying ﴿wa-l-yasʾalū﴾ [al-Mumtaḥana 60:10] that it is with the hamza, because it is an imperative for a third-person absent party.

**Second issue:** Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: His saying ﴿min faḍlihi﴾ is in the position of the second object according to the view of Abu al-Hasan, and the second object is omitted according to the analogy of Sibawayh's view, and the qualifier stands in its place, as if it were said: "And ask Allah His blessing from His bounty."

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ is an indication that a person is not permitted to specify something in seeking and supplication, but rather he should seek from the bounty of Allah what would be a cause of his righteousness in his religion and his world, in an unrestricted manner.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of all things.﴾ The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is the One who knows what will be good for those who ask. So the one asking should confine himself to the general, and in his supplication he should guard against specifying, for perhaps that would be pure harm and detriment. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 33 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) to what the parents and close relatives leave, and to those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share. Indeed, Allah is ever a Witness over all things.﴾

There are several issues concerning the verse.

The first issue: Know that the verse can be interpreted so that the parents and close relatives are the inheritors, and it can also be interpreted so that they are the ones from whom inheritance is taken.

As for the first: His saying ﴿And for each We have appointed heirs (mawali) to what he left﴾ means: for each person We have appointed heirs to his estate. Then it is as if it was said: And who are these heirs? So it is said: They are the parents and the close relatives. In this interpretation, there must be a pause at His saying ﴿to what he left﴾.

As for the second, there are two aspects:

The first: the speech is in inverted order, and the implied meaning is: For each thing that the parents and close relatives leave, We have appointed mawali, that is, heirs. The verb (ja'alna, "We appointed") in these two aspects does not take two objects, because the meaning of (ja'alna) here is (khalaqna, "We created").

The second: the implied meaning is: For each people whom We have made mawali, there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave. So His saying (mawali) in this view is an adjective, the modified noun is omitted, the pronoun referring back to His saying (for each) is omitted, and the predicate, which is His saying (a share), is also omitted. According to this estimation, (ja'alna) takes two objects. The first two aspects are preferable, because this aspect involves many omitted elements.

The second issue: (mawla) is a word shared among several meanings:

The first: the freed person (al-mu'tiq), because he is the patron (wali ni'matihi) in his manumission, and for this reason he is called "mawla al-ni'ma" (the patron of the favour).

The second: the freed slave (al-'abd al-mu'taq), because the patronage of his master is connected to his bestowal upon him. This is like how the claimant is called a (gharim, "creditor") because he has the right to insist and demand his right, and the one who is demanded is called a (gharim, "debtor") because the debt is binding upon him.

The third: the ally (al-halif), because the one who makes a pact takes charge of his affair through the oath of alliance.

The fourth: the cousin (ibn al-'amm), because he takes charge of him through support due to the kinship between them.

The fifth: the (mawla wali, "protecting patron"), because he takes charge of him through support. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector (mawla) for them﴾ [Muhammad: 11].

Page 69

The sixth: the (asabah, "agnatic relatives"), and this is what is meant in this verse, because nothing but this meaning suits this verse. It is reinforced by what Abu Salih narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am closer to the believers. Whoever dies and leaves wealth, his wealth goes to his mawali, the 'asabah. And whoever leaves a burden (kall), then I am his guardian." He (ﷺ), upon whom be prayers and peace, also said: "Divide this wealth. Whatever the shares leave, it goes to the closest male 'asabah."

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share﴾. And concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (`aqadat) without an alif and with a light (takhfif) pronunciation, while the rest recited it with an alif and with a light pronunciation. (`Aqadat) means: it attributed the binding to one person. The preferred reading is (`aqadat) with the alif, because the form of mufa'alah indicates the binding of the oath from both parties.

The second issue: (al-aymān) is the plural of (yamin). (Yamin) may mean the hand, and it may mean the oath. If the intended meaning is the hand, then there is a figurative usage (majaz) in three aspects:

The first: the binding is, in the apparent wording, attributed to the hands, while in reality it is attributed to the swearing parties. The reason for this figurative usage is that they used to strike the bargain with their right hands, and one of them would take the hand of the other as a pledge of fulfilment and adherence to the covenant.

The second figurative aspect: the implied meaning is: "And those whom your oaths have bound by their alliance," so the governing noun is omitted and the governed noun is put in its place. This omission is good because the context indicates it.

The third: the implied meaning is: "And those whom they have bound," but the returning pronoun in the relative clause to the relative pronoun is omitted. All of this applies when we interpret (yamin) as the hand. As for when we interpret it as the oath and the swearing, the binding in the apparent wording is attributed to the oath, and this attribution is good because the cause of the binding is the oath. The discussion of the remaining figurative usages is as previously mentioned.

The third issue: Among people, some have said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh), and some have said: it is not abrogated. As for those who say it is abrogated, they are the ones who interpreted the verse according to one of these aspects that we mention:

The first: the meaning of "those with whom your oaths have bound you" is the allies in the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyyah). This is because a man would bind himself to another and say: "My blood is your blood, my peace is your peace, my war is your war. You inherit from me and I inherit from you, you pay blood-money on my behalf and I pay on yours." So this ally would have a sixth of the inheritance. This was abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those related by blood are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], and by His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you﴾ [an-Nisa: 11].

The second: one of them would adopt a stranger as his son, and they are called (ad'iya, "adopted sons"), and they used to inherit through this cause, and then this was abrogated.

The third: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to establish brotherhood (mu'akhah) between every two men of his Companions, and that brotherhood was a cause of inheritance. Know that on all these three aspects, the binding was a cause of inheritance by His saying: ﴿give them their share﴾. Then Allah, may He be exalted, abrogated that by the verses we have recited.

The second view: the view of those who say the verse is not abrogated. Those who hold this view have mentioned several interpretations of the verse:

The first: the implied meaning of the verse is: "And for each thing that the parents and close relatives and those with whom your oaths have bound you leave, We have appointed mawali (heirs). So give them their share," that is, give the mawali and heirs their share. So His saying "and those with whom your oaths have bound you" is conjoined to His saying "the parents and close relatives." The meaning is: for what those with whom your oaths have bound you leave, there is an heir who has more right to it, and Allah, may He be exalted, called the heir a mawla. The meaning is: do not give the wealth to the ally, but to the mawla and the heir. According to this estimation, there is no abrogation in the verse, and this is the interpretation of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i.

Page 70

The second: the intended meaning of "those with whom your oaths have bound you" is the spouses, because marriage is called a binding ('aqd). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not determine the bond of marriage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235]. So He mentioned the parents and close relatives, and with them He mentioned the husband and wife. Its parallel is the verse of inheritance, in that when He explained the inheritance of the child and the parents, He mentioned along with them the inheritance of the husband and wife. According to this, there is also no abrogation in the verse, and this is the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani.

The third: the intended meaning of His saying "those with whom your oaths have bound you" is the inheritance resulting from the cause of walaʾ (patronage). According to this estimation, there is also no abrogation.

The fourth: the intended meaning of "those with whom your oaths have bound you" is the allies, and the intended meaning of His saying "give them their share" is support, sincere advice, friendship in companionship, and sincerity in association. So the intended meaning is not inheritance. According to this estimation, there is also no abrogation.

The fifth: it is reported that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) and his son 'Abd al-Rahman. He (may Allah be pleased with him) had sworn that he would not spend on him nor bequeath anything of his wealth to him. When 'Abd al-Rahman embraced Islam, Allah commanded him to give him his share. According to this estimation, there is also no abrogation.

The sixth: al-Asamm said: it is a share by way of a gift and a present of a small amount, just as Allah, may He be exalted, commanded that for whoever attends the division of the estate, a share be set aside for him, as mentioned earlier. All these aspects are good and possible, and Allah knows best His intended meaning.

The fourth issue: Those who say that His saying "and those with whom your oaths have bound you" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His saying "give them their share," said: The predicate came with the (fa, "then") because the relative pronoun (alladhi) implies the meaning of a conditional, so the predicate necessarily came with the fa, which is His saying "give them their share." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative, in the construction: "Zayd, then strike him."

* * *

The fifth issue: The majority of jurists said: the lower mawla does not inherit from the higher. Al-Tahawi related from al-Hasan ibn Ziyad that he said: he inherits, because of what Ibn 'Abbas narrated, that a man freed a slave of his, then the manumitter died and left nothing but the freed slave, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made his inheritance go to the freed boy. Also, because he is included in the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿And those with whom your oaths have bound you, give them their share﴾.

The answer to the argument from the hadith: perhaps when that wealth went to the public treasury (bayt al-mal), the Prophet (ﷺ) gave it to that boy because of his need and poverty, since it was wealth with no heir, so its proper course is to be spent on the poor.

* * *

The sixth issue: al-Shafi'i and Malik (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: whoever embraces Islam at the hand of a man, and takes him as a protector and binds himself to him by covenant, then dies with no heir other than him, he does not inherit from him, but his inheritance goes to the Muslims. Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: he inherits from him.

The argument of al-Shafi'i: We have explained that the meaning of this verse is: "And for each thing that the parents and close relatives leave, and those with whom your oaths have bound you, We have appointed for him mawali, and they are the 'asabah." Then these 'asabah are either the particular ones, who are the heirs, or the general ones, who are the community of the Muslims. So it is necessary to give this wealth to the general 'asabah, as long as no particular 'asabah are found.

Abu Bakr al-Razi argued for his view that the verse makes inheritance obligatory for the one who took him as protector and bound himself to him. Then Allah, may He be exalted, abrogated it by His saying: ﴿And those related by blood are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. This abrogation only takes place if the blood relatives are found. If they are not found, the ruling must remain as it was.

The answer: We have explained that there is no indication in the verse that the ally inherits, rather we have explained that the verse indicates that he does not inherit, and we have explained that the claim of this abrogation is invalid.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever a Witness over all things﴾. It is a word of promise to the obedient and a word of warning to the disobedient,

Page 71

and (al-shahid, "the Witness") means the one who witnesses and the one who is present. What is meant by it is either His knowledge of all particulars and universals, or His testimony over the creation on the Day of Resurrection concerning everything they did. According to the first estimation, the Witness is the Knowing, and according to the second, He is the one who informs.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend [for maintenance] from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [husbands'] absence what Allah would have them guard. And those [wives] from whom you fear arrogance, admonish them and forsake them in bed and strike them. But if they obey you, seek no means against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Grand﴾.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others﴾, and we have mentioned that the cause of the revelation of this verse was that women spoke about Allah's preference of men over them in inheritance, He, may He be exalted, mentioned in this verse that He only preferred men over women in inheritance because men are in charge of women. Although the two share in each one's enjoyment of the other, Allah commanded men to give women the dower (mahr) and to provide them with maintenance (nafaqah). So the surplus from one side became a counterpart to the surplus from the other side, and it is as though there is no preference at all. This is the explanation of the manner of the arrangement (nazm) of the verse. In the verse there are issues:

The first matter: "al-qiwām" is a noun for one who is thorough in carrying out a matter; it is said: "This is the qayyim (guardian) and qiwām of the woman," meaning the one who takes charge of her affairs and concerns himself with her protection.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: This verse was revealed concerning the daughter of Muhammad ibn Maslamah and her husband Saʿd ibn al-Rabiʿ, one of the chiefs (nuqabāʾ) of the Ansar. He struck her a slap, so she rebelled against his bed and went to the Messenger (ﷺ) and made this complaint, that he had struck her and that the mark of the slap remained on her face. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Take retribution from him." Then he said to her: "Wait until I consider the matter." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Men are the protectors and maintainers of women﴾, that is, they have authority over their discipline and may take hold above their hands. It is as if God, exalted is He, made him a commander over her and an executor of judgment concerning her right. When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We wanted one thing and God wanted another, and what God wants is better." And he abolished retaliation (qiṣāṣ).

Then, when God, exalted is He, established for men a dominion over women and the executing of command over them, He made clear that this is grounded in two matters:

The first of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because God has made some of them to excel over others﴾.

Know that the superiority of men over women is attained in many respects, some of which are real attributes and some of which are legal rulings. As for the real attributes: know that real excellences return in their essence to two things: knowledge and capability. There is no doubt that men's intellects and sciences are greater, and there is no doubt that their capacity for arduous works is more complete. For these two reasons, men have been given preference over women in intellect, resolve, strength, writing in most cases, horsemanship, and archery; and among them are the prophets and the scholars; and among them are the greater and lesser imamate, jihad, the call to prayer (adhān), the khutbah, i'tikāf, and testimony in the hudud and retaliation by consensus. And in marriage contracts according to al-Shafiʿi, may God be pleased with him: an increased share in inheritance, agnatic inheritance (taʿsīb), bearing the diya in killing by error, oaths in the qasāmah, guardianship in marriage, divorce, return (rajʿah), and the number of wives; and lineage is attributed to them. All of this indicates the superiority of men over women.

The second cause for the attainment of this excellence: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and because they spend of their wealth﴾, meaning the man is superior to the woman because he gives her the dower and spends on her. Then God, exalted is He, divided women into two categories, describing the righteous among them as ﴿qānitāt ḥāfiẓāt lil-ghayb bimā ḥafiẓa Allāh﴾ (obedient, guarding in the husband's absence what God has ordained them to guard). There are several issues in this:

The first issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: Ibn Masʿud read: "fa-al-ṣawāliḥ qawānit ḥawāfiẓ lil-ghayb."

The second issue: His saying: ﴿qānitāt ḥāfiẓāt lil-ghayb﴾ has two aspects:

The first: qānitāt means obedient to God; ﴿ḥāfiẓāt lil-ghayb﴾ means maintaining the rights of the husband. He mentioned the fulfilment of God's right first, then followed it with the fulfilment of the husband's right.

The second: the woman's condition is either considered in the presence of the husband or in his absence. As for her condition in the presence of the husband, God has described her as qānitah, and the root of qunūt is continuous obedience. The meaning is that they are upright in the rights of their husbands. The apparent form of this is an informative statement, but what is intended is a command to obedience.

Know that a woman is not righteous unless she is obedient to her husband, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿fa-al-ṣāliḥāt qānitāt﴾, and the alif and lam in the plural indicate comprehensiveness (istighrāq). This requires that every woman who is righteous must be qānitah, obedient. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The word qunūt indicates obedience, and it is general to obedience to God and obedience to husbands. As for the woman's condition in the husband's absence, God, exalted is He, described her by His saying: ﴿ḥāfiẓāt lil-ghayb﴾. Know that al-ghayb is the opposite of al-shahādah (presence), and the meaning is that they guard the obligations of the absent (husband), and that is in several respects:

One: she guards herself against fornication, so that shame does not befall the husband because of her adultery, and so that a child formed from another's sperm is not attributed to him.

Second: guarding his property from loss.

Third: guarding his home from what is not fitting. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of women is one who, when you look at her, pleases you; when you command her, she obeys you; and when you are absent from her, she guards you in your property and her own self." And he recited this verse.

The third issue: "mā" in His saying: ﴿bimā ḥafiẓa Allāh﴾ has two aspects:

The first: it means "that which" (alladhī), and the returning pronoun is omitted, and the estimate is: "by that which God has guarded for them." The meaning is that it is incumbent upon them to guard the rights of the husband in return for what God has guarded their rights over their husbands, since He commanded them to deal justly with them, to keep them with kindness, and to give them their wages. So His saying ﴿bimā ḥafiẓa Allāh﴾ runs in the manner of saying: "this for that," meaning "this in exchange for that."

The second aspect: that "mā" be verbal-masdariyyah (infinitive), and the estimate is "by God's guarding." On this estimate there are two aspects:

The first: that they guard the unseen by means of God's guarding them, meaning that guarding is not made easy for them except by God's grace, so this is of the type of the idāfah of the verbal noun to the agent.

The second: the meaning is that the woman only guards the unseen by means of their guarding God's limits and His commands, for if the woman did not strive to observe God's obligations and endeavour to guard His commands, she would not obey her husband; and this aspect is of the type of the idāfah of the verbal noun to the object.

Know that when He mentioned the righteous women, He mentioned after them those who are not righteous, saying: ﴿wa-allātī takhāfūna nushūzahunna﴾ (And those from whom you fear rebellion).

Know that fear (khawf) is an expression for a state that arises in the heart when there is a presumption that a disliked matter will occur in the future. Al-Shafiʿi, may God be pleased with him, said: ﴿nushūzahunna﴾: rebellion may be by word and may be by deed. The verbal form is like her responding to him when he calls her, and speaking humbly to him when he addresses her, then she changes; the act form is like her standing up for him when he enters upon her, or hastening to his command and hurrying to his bed joyfully when he seeks her, then she changes from all of that. These are signs indicating her rebellion and disobedience; at that point, the presumption of her rebellion and the precursors of these states necessitate the fear of rebellion. As for nushūz, it is disobedience to the husband and rising above him through opposition, and its root is from their saying: "nasaza al-shay'" when it became elevated; from it is said of elevated land: nashz and nashr.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 34:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Admonish them, forsake them in the beds, and strike them﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: As for admonition (al-wa'z), the husband says to her: "Fear Allah, for I have a right over you, return from what you are doing, and know that obeying me is obligatory upon you," and similar words. He does not strike her in this state, because it is possible that her words will suffice for her. If she persists in that disobedience (nushuz), then at that point he forsakes her in the bed, and within this is his refraining from speaking to her. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) also said: He should not extend his forsaking of her in speech beyond three days. Furthermore, when he forsakes her in the bed, if she loves the husband, it is hard for her, so she abandons disobedience; and if she hates him, that forsaking agrees with her, and that is then evidence of the completeness of her disobedience. Among them are those who understood that forsaking to refer to abstention from intimate contact, since the attribution of it to the beds indicates that. Then, at this forsaking, if she remains in disobedience, he strikes her. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Striking is permissible, and leaving it is better.

It was narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "We, the community of Quraysh, used to have our men govern their women. When we came to Madinah, we found that their women governed their men, so our women began to mix with them and they became defiant (dha'ira) toward their husbands, meaning they became disobedient (nashaza) and emboldened. So I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: 'The women have become defiant toward their husbands.' So he permitted striking them. Then a group of women gathered around the chambers of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), all of them complaining about their husbands. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Seventy women have gone around the household of Muhammad tonight, all of them complaining about their husbands. Those are not your best.'"

Its meaning is that those who struck their husbands are not better than those who did not strike. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: This hadith indicates that the preferable course is to leave striking. As for when a man does strike her, the striking must be such that it does not lead to death at all, by being spread over her body and not concentrated in one place, avoiding the face because it is the gathering place of beauty, and it should be less than forty. Some of our companions said: it should not reach twenty, because twenty is a complete legal penalty (hadd) with respect to a slave. Others among them said: the striking should be with a folded handkerchief or with the hand, and he should not strike her with whips or a stick. In summary, leniency is observed in this matter in the most emphatic manner.

I say: What indicates this is that He, exalted is He, began with admonition, then ascended from it to forsaking in the beds, then ascended from it to striking. This is an indication that functions in the manner of an explicit statement that whenever the purpose is achieved by the gentler means, it is obligatory to suffice with it, and it is not permissible to resort to the harsher means. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** Our companions differed. Some said: the ruling of this verse is to be applied in sequence, for although the apparent wording indicates combination, the implication of the verse indicates sequence. The Commander of the Faithful Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: He admonishes her with his tongue; if she desists, then he has no way over her. If she refuses, he forsakes her bed. If she refuses, he strikes her. If she is not admonished by striking, he sends the two arbiters (al-hakamayn). Others said: this sequence is observed when disobedience is feared, but when disobedience is established, there is no harm in combining all of them.

Some of our companions said: the clarification of the school's position is that when he fears disobedience he may admonish her, and as to whether he may forsake her, there is a possibility. When disobedience has appeared, he may admonish her, or forsake her, or strike her.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they obey you﴾, meaning: if they return from disobedience to obedience at this discipline, ﴿then do not seek a way against them﴾, meaning: do not seek against them striking or forsaking as a path of harshness and harm. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Most High, Most Great﴾. His highness is not by elevation of direction, and His greatness is not by greatness of bulk, but rather He is Most High, Most Great, by the completeness of His power and the effectiveness of His will over all possible things. The mention of these two attributes in this place is most fitting, and its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: the intended purpose is to threaten husbands against wronging women. The meaning is that they are weak in repelling your injustice and unable to get redress from you. So Allah, glorified is He, is Most High, Dominant, Great, Able, and will exact redress for them from you and will take their rights from you. Therefore you should not be deceived by your being higher in hand than them and greater in rank than them.

The second: do not seek against them, when they obey you, out of the height of your hands. Indeed Allah is higher than you and greater than everything, and He is exalted above being charged except with truth.

The third: He, exalted is He, despite His loftiness and majesty, does not charge you except with what you can bear. Likewise, do not charge them with your love, for they have no power over that.

The fourth: despite His loftiness and majesty, He does not take the disobedient servant to account when he repents, but forgives him. So when a woman repents from her disobedience, you are more deserving to accept her repentance and abandon punishing her.

The fifth: despite His loftiness and majesty, He has been content from the servant with outward appearances and has not exposed inner secrets. So you are more deserving to be content with the outward state of the woman, and not to fall into searching what is in her heart and conscience of love and hatred.

[Page 74]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two of them, then send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family. If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned, concerning the disobedience (nushuz) of the wife, that the husband should admonish her, then forsake her in bed, then strike her, He made clear that after striking nothing remains except a judicial hearing before one who will grant justice to the wronged party against the wrongdoer. So He said: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two of them﴾ to the end of the verse. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: "*Khiftum* (you fear) means *'alimtum* (you know)." He said: "This is different from His saying, ﴿and those from whom you fear disobedience﴾, for that is to be understood as suspicion (zann). The difference between the two passages is that at the beginning the signs of disobedience appear to him, and at that point fear arises. But after admonition, forsaking and striking, when she persists in disobedience, knowledge has been attained that she is disobedient, so it is necessary to understand fear here as knowledge." Al-Zajjaj criticized this, saying: "*Khiftum* here meaning *ayqantum* (you are certain) is an error, for if we knew the breach in reality we would not need the two arbiters."

The other exegetes answered that although the existence of the breach is known, we do not know whether that breach originated from this one or that one, so the need for the two arbiters is to know this matter. It may also be said: the existence of the breach at present is known, and such a thing does not produce fear; the fear lies in whether that breach will remain or not. So the benefit of sending the two arbiters is not the removal of the breach that is established at present, for that is impossible, but rather the removal of that breach in the future.

**The second issue:** The breach (*shiqaq*) has two interpretations:

First: that each of them does what is hard for the other.

Second: that each of them has come to be on one side (*shiqq*) through enmity and estrangement.

**The third issue:** His saying, ﴿breach between the two of them﴾, means *shiqaqan baynahuma* (a breach between them), except that the verbal noun has been put in construct with the adverbial noun of place/time (*zarf*). Attributing verbal nouns to adverbs of time or place is permissible, since the action occurs within them. It is said: "The fasting of the Day of 'Arafah pleases me," and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33].

**The fourth issue:** Who is the addressee of His saying, ﴿then send an arbiter from his family﴾? There is disagreement. Some said it is the imam (ruler) or whoever is appointed by him, because the execution of the legal rulings belongs to him. Others said that what is meant is each one of the righteous among the community, because His saying, *khiftum* (you fear), is addressed to the plural, and it is no more appropriate to understand it as referring to some than to the rest; so it is necessary to understand it as referring to all. On this basis, His saying, ﴿And if you fear﴾, must be addressed to all the believers. Then He said, *fa-b'athu* (then send), so this must be a command to individuals of the community in this sense. Thus it is established that it applies whether or not an imam exists, so the righteous may send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family for reconciliation. Moreover, this falls under the category of averting harm, and it is permissible for anyone to undertake it.

**The fifth issue:** When a breach occurs between them, that breach is either from both of them, or from him, or from her, or it is unclear. If it is from her, it is disobedience, and we have already mentioned its ruling. If it is from him, then if he has done a permissible act, such as marrying another woman or taking a concubine, the woman should know that this is permitted, and she is to be forbidden from the breach; if she accepts, well and good, otherwise it becomes disobedience on her part. If it is due to injustice from his side, the judge orders him to do what is obligatory. If it is from both of them, or the matter is ambiguous, then the ruling is likewise what we have stated.

**The sixth issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: It is recommended that the judge send two just persons and appoint them as arbiters, and it is preferable that one be from his family and one from her family, because their relatives know their circumstances better than strangers do, and are more eager for what is right. If the two are strangers, it is permissible. The benefit of the two arbiters is that each of them should meet privately with the other spouse and investigate the true state of affairs, so as to know whether the desire of each is to remain in the marriage or to separate. Then the two arbiters meet and do what is right, whether that is pronouncing a divorce or a khul' (divorce by compensation).

***

**The seventh issue:** Is it permissible for the two arbiters to implement a decision binding on the spouses without their consent, such as the husband's arbiter pronouncing a divorce, or the wife's arbiter agreeing to ransom her with some of her property? Al-Shafi'i has two opinions on this:

One: it is permissible. This is the view of Malik and Ishaq.

The other: it is not permissible. This is the view of Abu Hanifa. On this basis, the arbitration is an agency (*wakalah*) like other agencies.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, cited the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, which is what Ibn Sirin narrated from 'Ubaidah, who said: A man and a woman came to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and each of them was accompanied by a group of people. 'Ali commanded them to send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family. Then he said to the two arbiters: "Do you know what is incumbent upon you? If you see fit to reunite them, then reunite them; and if you see fit to separate them, then separate them." The woman said: "I am content with the Book of Allah, the Exalted, regarding what is due from me and what is due to me in it." The man said: "As for separation, no." 'Ali said: "You lie, by Allah, until you acknowledge the same as what she has acknowledged." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: In this hadith there is evidence for each of the two opinions.

As for the evidence for the first opinion: they were sent without the consent of the spouses, and he said, "It is incumbent upon you (*'alaykuma*): if you see fit to reunite them, then reunite them." At the least, his saying "incumbent upon you" means that it is permissible for them to do so.

As for the evidence for the second opinion: since the husband did not consent, 'Ali held back. The meaning of his saying "You lie" is that you are not just in your claim, since you did not do what she did. Some people argued for the first opinion by saying that Allah, exalted is He, called them two arbiters (*hakamayn*), and a *hakam* is a judge (*hakim*), and if He made them judges, then He has empowered them to judge. Others argued for the second opinion by saying that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the two arbiters, He attributed to them nothing except reconciliation, and this implies that what lies beyond reconciliation is not delegated to them.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, ﴿a breach between the two of them﴾, means a breach between the spouses. Although neither of them has been mentioned explicitly, something that indicates them has been mentioned, namely men and women.

***

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them.﴾ In this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** In His saying, ﴿If they both desire﴾, there are several possibilities:

First: If the two arbiters desire good and reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between the two arbiters until they agree on what is good.

Second: If the two arbiters desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between the spouses.

Third: If the spouses desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between the spouses.

Fourth: If the spouses desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between the two arbiters until they act with righteousness. There is no doubt that the wording admits all these possibilities.

**The second issue:** The root of *tawfiq* (harmony/divine enabling) is *muwafaqah* (agreement), which is equality in some matter. So *tawfiq* is the divine grace by which the performance of obedience is brought about. The verse indicates that no aim or purpose is accomplished except by the *tawfiq* of Allah, exalted is He. The meaning is that if the intention of the two arbiters is to reconcile the spouses, Allah will bring about harmony between the spouses.

***

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted.﴾ What is meant by this is a warning to the spouses and to the two arbiters against pursuing what contradicts the path of truth.

[p. 77]

**The Ninth Type: from the duties mentioned in this surah:**

﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the neighbor who is a stranger, the companion at your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not love whoever is self-deluded and boastful.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the neighbor who is a stranger, the companion at your side, the wayfarer, and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allah does not love whoever is self-deluded and boastful.﴾

Know that when Almighty God guided each of the spouses to treat the other well and to remove enmity and harshness, He guided in this verse to the rest of the good characteristics, and He mentioned from them ten types.

**The First Type:** His saying: ﴿Worship Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is "affirm His oneness." Know that worship ('ibadah, meaning devotional service to God) is a term for every act and abstention performed solely because God Almighty commanded it. This includes all acts of the heart and all acts of the limbs, so there is no sense in restricting it to tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). The detailed discussion of worship has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21].

**The Second Type:** His saying: ﴿and associate nothing with Him﴾. This is because, when He commanded worship with His saying ﴿Worship Allah﴾, He commanded sincerity in worship with His saying ﴿and associate nothing with Him﴾, since whoever worships another alongside God is a polytheist and cannot be sincere. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They were commanded only to worship Allah, making their religion sincerely His﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:5].

**The Third Type:** His saying: ﴿and be good to parents﴾. The scholars agreed that there is an elided word here, and the sense is: "and be good to parents with goodness," like His saying: ﴿so strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad 47:4], meaning "so strike them." It is said: "ahsantu bi-fulan" and "ahsantu ila fulan" (I dealt kindly with so-and-so). Kuthayyir said:

*"Treat us harshly or treat us kindly; we shall have no blame from you, nor any rejection, if you have turned away."*

Know that He, exalted is He, linked the obligation of kindness to parents with His worship and His oneness in several places:

First: in this verse.

Second: His saying: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents﴾ [al-Isra 17:23].

Third: His saying: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination﴾ [Luqman 31:14]. This suffices as evidence of the greatness of their right and the obligation of kindness and goodness toward them. Among what indicates the obligation of kindness toward them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them "uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a noble word﴾ [al-Isra 17:23]. He also said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man goodness toward his parents﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:8]. And concerning disbelieving parents He said: ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but keep them company in this world with kindness﴾ [Luqman 31:15].

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The greatest of the major sins are associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, and the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus, an oath sworn to deceive that dooms the swearer to Hell)." And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) from Yemen and asked his permission to go to jihad. He, peace be upon him, said: 'Do you have anyone in Yemen?' He said: 'My two parents.' He said: 'Have your parents given you permission?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Return and ask their permission. If they grant it, then strive; otherwise, be good to them.'"

Know that kindness to parents means that one serves them, does not raise his voice over them, does not speak harshly to them, strives to fulfill their needs, and spends on them according to his ability in righteousness. He should not brandish a weapon against them, nor kill them. Abu Bakr al-Razi (al-Jassas) said: except when one is compelled to do so, that is, if he fears that he will be killed if he does not kill him; then it is permissible for him to kill him, because if he does not do so, he has killed himself by enabling another to do so, and that is forbidden. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade Hanzalah ibn Abi 'Amir the monk from killing his father, who was a polytheist."

**The Fourth Type:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to the near of kin﴾. This is a command to maintain ties of kinship (silat al-rahm), as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah in His saying: ﴿and the wombs﴾.

Know that parents are also among the relatives, but since blood kinship is distinguished by being the closest of kinships and is distinguished by special qualities that are not found in others, Allah the Exalted singled it out in mention from the rest of the categories. So He mentioned in this verse the kinship of blood, and then followed it with the kinship of the womb.

**The Fifth Type:** His saying: ﴿and orphans﴾. Know that the orphan is characterized by two kinds of helplessness:

One: youth.

The second: lack of a provider.

There is no doubt that whoever is in this condition is in utmost helplessness and deserves compassion. Ibn 'Abbas said: [he] should be gentle with them, nurture them, and stroke their heads; and if he is their guardian, let him take great care in protecting their property.

**The Sixth Type:** His saying: ﴿and the needy﴾. Know that although the needy has no wealth, because of his age he can present his own situation to others, and thereby bring benefit or ward off harm. But the orphan has no capacity for this. For this reason Allah mentioned the orphan before the needy. Kindness to the needy is either by giving to him generously, or by a gracious response, as He said: ﴿As for the beggar, do not repel him﴾ [al-Duha 93:10].

**The Seventh Type:** His saying: ﴿and the neighbor who is a relative﴾. It was said: he is the one whose neighborhood is near. And the neighbor who is a stranger (al-jar al-junub) is the one whose neighborhood is distant. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "One who does not let his neighbor feel safe from his harm will not enter Paradise. Indeed, the rights of the neighbor extend forty houses." Al-Zuhri used to say: forty to the right, forty to the left, forty in front, and forty behind.

It is related from Abu Hurayra that it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, so-and-so fasts by day and prays by night, but there is something in her tongue that harms her neighbors; that is, she is abusive." He, peace be upon him, said: "There is no good in her; she is in the Fire." It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, none fulfills the right of the neighbor except one whom Allah has mercy upon, and they are few. Do you know what the right of the neighbor is? If he becomes poor, you enrich him; if he asks you for a loan, you lend to him; if good befalls him, you congratulate him; if harm befalls him, you console him; if he falls ill, you visit him; and if he dies, you accompany his funeral."

Others said: by "the neighbor who is a relative" is meant the near kinsman, and by "the neighbor who is a stranger" is meant the foreign neighbor. It was also read as "wa-l-jara dha al-qurba" in the accusative, in the sense of specification, just as it was read: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:238], as an alert to the greatness of his right, because two grounds of obligation are combined in him: neighborhood and kinship.

**The Eighth Type:** His saying: ﴿and the neighbor who is a stranger﴾. We have already mentioned its explanation. Al-Wahidi said: al-junub is an adjective on the pattern fu'ul, and its root is from al-janabah, the opposite of kinship, meaning the distant. One says: "rajul junub" when he is a stranger, far from his people; and "rajul ajnabi" is one who is distant from you in kinship. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And keep me and my sons away﴾ [Ibrahim 14:35], meaning "distance me." Al-janibani are the two sides, because each of them is distant from the other. From the same root is al-janabah (ritual impurity) from intercourse, because it keeps one far from purity and from attending the mosques for prayer until one performs ghusl. Also from the same root is al-janbān (the two flanks), because each of them is distant from the other. Al-Mufaddal related from 'Asim: "wa-l-jari al-janbi" with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the nun. This can carry two meanings:

One: that by al-janb he means the side, and the sense is "and the neighbor of the side," so the genitive term is elided, because the meaning is understood.

The other: that it is a description in the form of hyperbole, as one says: "fulan karam wa-judu" (so-and-so is generosity and munificence).

**The Ninth Type:** His saying: ﴿and the companion at your side﴾. This is one who accompanies you by being at your side: either a traveling companion, or an adjacent neighbor, or a partner in learning or in a trade, or one sitting beside you in a gathering, a mosque, or elsewhere, by any close companionship that brought you together. You must observe this right, not forget it, and make it a means to kindness. It was said: the "companion at the side" is the wife, for she is with you and lies down at your side.

**The Tenth Type:** His saying: ﴿and the wayfarer﴾. This is the traveler who has been cut off from his homeland. It was also said: the guest.

**The Eleventh Type:** His saying: ﴿and those whom your right hands possess﴾.

Know that kindness to slaves is a great act of obedience. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever buys a servant and his character does not agree with his own, let him sell him and buy another, until his character agrees with his. For people have dispositions, and do not punish the servants of Allah." It is also related that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said at the end of his words: "The prayer, and those whom your right hands possess." It is related that there was a man in Medina who was beating his slave; the slave would say: "I seek refuge in Allah," and the Messenger heard him, while the master kept increasing his beating. Then the Messenger (ﷺ) came and said: "I seek refuge in the Messenger of Allah." So he left him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has more right to be sought for refuge." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, he is free for the sake of Allah." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, had you not said it, the scorch of the Fire would have struck your face."

Know that kindness to them is of several kinds:

First: that one does not burden them with what they cannot bear.

Second: that one does not harm them with harsh speech, but rather treats them with good companionship.

Third: that one gives them of the food and clothing they need. In the pre-Islamic era they used to mistreat the slave; they would compel slave women to prostitution (al-bigha', earning by the use of their bodies). Some said: every living creature is a slave, and kindness to all according to what befits it is a great act of obedience.

Know that the mention of "right hands" is for emphasis, as one says: "your foot walked, and your hand was taken," and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "On the hand is what it has taken." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿of what Our hands have made, livestock﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:71].

When He mentioned these categories, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love whoever is self-deluded and boastful﴾. The mukhtal (self-deluded) is one possessed of conceit and arrogance. Ibn 'Abbas said: by the mukhtal he means the one who is great in his own estimation, who does not fulfill the rights of anyone. Al-Zajjaj said: he mentioned ikhtiyal (self-delusion) here, and we mentioned the derivation of this word in His saying: ﴿and the branded horses﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:14]. The meaning of fakhr (boasting) is self-exaltation, and the fakhur (boastful) is one who recounts his virtues out of pride and self-exaltation. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is one who boasts over the servants of Allah with what Allah has given him of the various kinds of His blessings. Allah, exalted is He, specifically singled out these two attributes for condemnation in this place, because the mukhtal is the arrogant, and whoever is arrogant rarely attends to the observance of rights. Then He added to it the condemnation of the boastful, lest one undertake the observance of these rights for the sake of show and reputation, rather than purely for the command of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people, and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bil-bakhali" (بِالبَخَلِ) with a fatha on the ba' and the kha', and the same in al-Hadid. This is the dialect of the Ansar. The rest read "bil-bukhli" (بِالبُخْلِ) with a damma on the ba' and the kha', and this is the higher (more eloquent) dialect.

The second issue: "Those who are stingy" (الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ) is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿whoever is arrogant and boastful﴾. The meaning is: indeed Allah does not love whoever is arrogant and boastful, nor those who are stingy. Or it is in the accusative as a form of censure (nasb 'ala al-dhamm). It may also be in the nominative as a form of censure (raf' 'ala al-dhamm), and it may be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, as if it were said: "Those who are stingy, and who act and make [such things], deserve every reproach."

Page 80

The third issue: Al-Wahidi said: The word al-bukhl (البُخْل) has four dialectal forms: al-bukhl, like al-qufl; al-bakhal, like al-karam; al-bakhl, like al-faqr; and al-bukhul, with two dammas. This was mentioned by al-Mubarrad. In the language of the Arabs it denotes withholding benevolence, and in the Shari'ah it denotes withholding what is obligatory.

The fourth issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the Jews. They were stingy about acknowledging what they knew of the description of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his attributes in the Torah, and they also commanded their people to conceal it. ﴿And conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ means the knowledge of what is in their Book concerning the attributes of Muhammad ﷺ. (And We have prepared) in the Hereafter for the Jews ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾. Those who supported this view argued that the mention of "disbeliever" at the end of the verse indicates that what is meant at its beginning is the disbeliever. Others said: What is meant by it is stinginess with wealth, because He, exalted is He, mentioned it right after the verse in which He obligated the preservation of people's rights with wealth. He said: ﴿And be good to parents, and to near relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is near, the neighbor who is far, the companion by your side, the wayfarer﴾. It is known that goodness to these people is only by means of wealth. Then He censured those who turn away from this goodness, saying: ﴿Indeed Allah does not love whoever is arrogant and boastful.﴾ Then He joined to it: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾. Therefore this stinginess must be stinginess connected to what precedes it, and that is nothing but stinginess with wealth.

The third view: It is general, covering stinginess with knowledge and religion as well as stinginess with wealth, because the wording is general and all of it is blameworthy, so the wording must be understood as encompassing all of it.

The fifth issue: In this verse He, exalted is He, mentioned three blameworthy states:

The first: that a person is stingy, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Those who are stingy﴾.

The second: that they command others to be stingy. This is the extreme of loving stinginess, and it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾.

The third: His saying: ﴿and conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, for they give the impression of poverty while being rich, of hardship while being well-off, and of incapacity while being able. Moreover, this concealment may take a form that leads to disbelief, such as expressing complaint against Allah, exalted is He, and not being content with the decree and predestination. This reaches the limit of disbelief; therefore He said: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ As for the one who said the verse is specific to the Jews, his statement here is clear, because whoever conceals the religion and prophethood is a disbeliever. It is also possible that what is meant by "disbeliever" here is one who is ungrateful for the blessing, not one who disbelieves in the religion and the Shari'ah.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, and do not believe in God or the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is the companion he has.﴾

There are several issues here.

The first issue: if you wish, you may join "those who" (alladhina) in this verse to "those who" in the verse before it, and if you wish, you may make it in the genitive position, conjoined to His saying: ﴿for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾.

Page 81

The second issue: al-Wahidi said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and this is the view supported by the mention of showing off (riya'), which is a kind of hypocrisy.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah who spent out of enmity toward the Messenger (ﷺ). The better view is to say: when God, exalted is He, commanded good treatment toward those in need, He made clear that those who do not do so are of two kinds.

The first is the miser who never at all comes forward to spend wealth, and they are the ones blamed in His saying: ﴿those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾.

The second is those who spend their wealth, but not for the sake of obedience; rather for the sake of showing off and seeking reputation. This group is also blameworthy. And once the view regarding these two kinds is refuted, there remains only the first kind, namely spending wealth for the purpose of doing good.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is the companion he has.﴾ The meaning is that Satan is a companion to the doers of these deeds, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. God, exalted is He, made clear that he is an evil companion, since he misguides him away from the abode of bliss and brings him to the blazing Fire. This is like His saying: ﴿And among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil. It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Hajj: 3].

Then God exposed them and made clear the evil of their choice in abandoning faith.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 39:**

There are several issues here:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And what would it be upon them﴾, is an interrogative used in the sense of rebuke (inkar). It is permissible for "مَاذَا" (*mādhā*) to be a single unit, so the meaning would be: "And what thing is upon them?" It is also permissible for "ذَا" (*dhā*) to mean "alladhī" (which), with "مَا" (*mā*) standing alone as an interrogative noun, so the meaning would be: "And what is it that is upon them if they had believed?"

**The second issue:** Those who hold that faith is valid by way of taqlid (imitation, unquestioning acceptance) have argued from this verse. They said: His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And what would it be upon them if they had believed?﴾ implies that bringing about faith is extremely easy. If reasoning (istidlal) were required, it would be extremely difficult, for we see that those who reason spend their lifetimes and their reasoning is never completed. This shows that taqlid is sufficient.

The theologians (al-mutakallimun) replied that the difficulty lies in the details, whereas the proofs in their general form (ʿalā sabīl al-jumla) are easy. Know that this topic has deep subtleties (ghawr).

**The third issue:** The majority of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school of theology) have argued from this verse and cited examples for it. Al-Jubba'i said: "If they were unable, it would not be permissible for God to say this, just as one does not say to someone who is being tormented in the Fire, 'What would it be upon you if you were to come out of it and reach Paradise?' and just as one does not say to a hungry person who is unable to obtain food, 'What would it be upon him if he ate?'"

Al-Ka'bi said: "It is not permissible for Him to create disbelief in a person and then say, 'What would it be upon him if he believed?' Just as one does not say to someone whom he has made sick, 'What would it be upon him if he were healthy?' Nor does one say to a woman, 'What would it be upon her if she were a man?' or to an ugly person, 'What would it be upon him if he were handsome?' And just as this statement is not becoming from a sensible person, so it is not becoming from God, exalted is He. Thus refuted is what is said: that although it is ugly from others, it is not ugly from Him, because the dominion is His dominion."

Qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar said: "It is not permissible for a sensible person to order his agent (wakil) to manage an estate while confining him in a way that he cannot leave the confinement, and then say to him, 'What would it be upon you if you managed the estate?' And since whoever mentions such a statement is foolish, this shows that it is not permissible for God, exalted is He. This is the sum of what they mentioned of examples."

Know that the Mu'tazila have greatly relied on the method of praise and blame, reward and punishment, and their opponents have greatly countered them with the two issues of knowledge and the motivating cause (dāʿī). So there is no need to repeat them.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of them﴾. The meaning is that the intention toward showing off (riyāʾ) is only inward and not apparent. So He made clear, exalted is He, that He is knowing of the inner matters just as He is knowing of the outward ones. When a person believes this, it acts as a deterrent for him against the ugly deeds of the heart, such as the motive of hypocrisy, showing off, and seeking reputation.

[Page 82]

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) by an atom's weight; and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾

Know that the connection of this verse is with His saying: ﴿And what would it be upon them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and spent from what Allah has provided them?﴾ (4:39). It is as if He said: indeed Allah does not wrong one whose state is this by an atom's weight, and if it is a good deed He multiplies it, so that this encourages faith and obedience.

Know that this verse includes a promise of three matters.

The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong by an atom's weight﴾, and in it are several issues.

The first issue: *dharra* (an atom, a tiny speck) is, according to the lexicographers, the small red ant. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he put his hand in the dust, then raised it, then blew on it, and then said: each one of these things is a *dharra*. *Mithqal* is a *mif'al* form from *thiql* (weight); one says "this is on the *mithqal* of this," meaning its weight. The meaning of "*mithqal dharra*" is: that whose weight is the weight of an atom.

Know that the purpose of the verse is that He, exalted is He, does not wrong (anyone) in little or in much; but the speech came in terms of the smallest thing people commonly reckon, as His saying indicates: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in anything﴾ (10:44).

The second issue: The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) said: this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is not the creator of the actions of His servants, because among those actions is the wronging of some of them by others. So if the one who brings about that wrong were Allah, then Allah would be the wrongdoer. Also, if He created wrongdoing in the wrongdoer, while that wrongdoer has no power to acquire that wrong when it is absent nor to repel it after it exists, and then He says to one of such a state and description, "Why did you wrong?" and then punishes him for it, this would be pure injustice; and the verse indicates that He is exalted above injustice.

The answer: the counter-argument by knowledge and motive, as has been mentioned many times before, is endless. We have mentioned that the arguments of these Mu'tazila, however numerous and weighty they are, return to a single point, namely their reliance on praise and blame, reward and punishment; and the objection to this point is specific, namely the counter-argument by knowledge and motive. So whenever they repeat that argument, we repeat this objection against them.

[Page 83]

* * *

The third issue: The Mu'tazila said: the verse indicates that He is capable of injustice, because He praised Himself by abandoning it, and one who praises himself for abandoning a foul act is only correct in that praise if he is capable of it. Do you not see that a paralytic cannot correctly praise himself for not going out to steal at night?

The answer: He, exalted is He, praised Himself by saying that slumber and sleep do not overtake Him (2:255), and that did not require that this be possible for Him. He also praised Himself by saying that sight does not perceive Him (6:103), and that did not indicate, according to the Mu'tazila, that sight can perceive Him.

* * *

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazila said: the verse indicates that the servant deserves reward for his obedience, and that if He did not reward him, He would be a wrongdoer; because He, exalted is He, has explained in this verse that if He did not reward them for their deeds, He would have wronged them, and this is not correct unless they deserve reward for their deeds.

The answer: He, exalted is He, promised them reward for those acts; so if He did not reward them for them, that would be in the form of injustice. Therefore the name of injustice was applied to it. What indicates that injustice is impossible for Allah is that injustice, according to you, entails ignorance and need, and both are impossible for Allah; and what entails the impossible is impossible, and the impossible is not within the scope of power. Also, injustice is the disposing of another's property, while the Truth, glorified is He, disposes only of His own property, so it is impossible for Him to be a wrongdoer. Also: a wrongdoer cannot be a god, and a thing cannot be valid unless its implications are valid; so if injustice were valid from Him, the loss of His divinity would be valid, and if that were so, His divinity would be liable to cease, and then He would need, for the attainment of the attribute of divinity for Him, a specifier and an agent, and that is impossible for Allah.

* * *

The fifth issue: The Mu'tazila said: the punishment for one drop of wine nullifies the reward for faith and obedience for a period of one hundred years. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: this is false, because we know by necessity that the reward for all those great acts of obedience over those long years is greater than the punishment for drinking this drop; so cancelling that great reward by punishing this amount of disobedience is injustice, and it is negated by this verse.

The sixth issue: al-Jubba'i said: the punishment for a major sin nullifies the reward of all acts of obedience, and nothing of that punishment is nullified. His son Abu Hashim said: rather, it is nullified (i.e., the punishment is cancelled out by the reward). Know that this principle has become a strong argument for our companions in refuting the doctrine of *ihbat* (the nullification of good deeds by sins). We say: if that reward were nullified, then either its equivalent of punishment would be nullified, or it would not be; and both alternatives are false, so the doctrine of nullification is false. We said that it is not permissible for each of the two to nullify the other, because if the cause of the non-existence of each of them is the existence of the other, then if the two non-existences occurred together, the two existences would occur together, since the cause must necessarily be present with the effect, and that is impossible. And we said that it is not permissible for obedience to be nullified by disobedience, while disobedience is not nullified by obedience, because the servant has gained no benefit at all from those acts of obedience, neither in attracting reward nor in repelling punishment; and that is injustice, and it contradicts His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong by an atom's weight﴾. And since both alternatives are void, the doctrine of the corruption of nullification, as the Mu'tazila hold it, is established.

* * *

The seventh issue: Our companions used this verse to argue that believers will come out of the Fire into Paradise. They said: there is no doubt that the reward of faith, persistence in monotheism, the affirmation that He is the One characterized by the attributes of majesty and honour, and perseverance in placing the forehead on the dust of servitude for a hundred years, is greater in reward than the punishment for a sip of wine. So when this drinker comes on the Day of Resurrection and the amount of the punishment for this disobedience is subtracted from that great reward, a great amount of reward remains for him. If he is then sent into the Fire because of that amount of punishment, and if he remained there, that would be injustice, which is false; so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that he will come out into Paradise.

* * *

The second type of the matters included in this verse: His saying: ﴿and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾, and in it are issues.

The first issue: Naafi' and Ibn Kathir read *hasanatun* with the *damma* (nominative), taking *kana* as the complete verb, and the meaning is: "if a good deed occurs, or happens." The rest read it with the *fatha* (accusative), taking *kana* as the incomplete verb, and the sense is: "if the weight of an atom is a good deed." Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *yudda'ifha* with the doubling (*tashdid*) and without an *alif*, from *tad'if* (multiplication); the rest read *yudā'ifha* with the *alif* and without doubling, from *mudā'afa* (multiplication).

The second issue: *takun* is originally from *kāna yakūnu*. Its original form was *takūnu*; the *damma* was dropped for the jussive, and the *waw* was dropped because it was quiescent and the *nun* was quiescent too, so it became *takun*; then they also dropped the *nun* because it was quiescent. It resembles the letters of softness (long vowels), and the letters of softness when they fall at the end are dropped for the jussive, as in your saying *lam adri* (I did not know), meaning *lā adrī*. The Qur'an came with both deletion and retention. As for deletion, it is here; as for retention, it is like His saying: ﴿If he be rich or poor﴾ (4:135).

The third issue: Through His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong by an atom's weight﴾, He has shown that He does not withhold from them their due at all; and through this verse He has shown that Allah, exalted is He, increases for them beyond what they merit.
