Know that the intended meaning of this multiplication is not multiplication in duration, because the duration of reward is endless, and multiplying the endless is impossible. Rather, the intended meaning is that He multiplies it according to quantity: for example, he deserves for his obedience ten units of reward, and He makes it twenty units, or thirty units, or more. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: a servant will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and a herald will call out over the heads of the first and the last: "This is so-and-so, son of so-and-so; whoever has a right against him, let him come for his right." Then it will be said to him: "Give these people their rights." He will say: "My Lord, from where, when the world has gone?" Then Allah will say to His angels: "Look at his good deeds and give them from them." If an atom's weight of a good deed remains, Allah, exalted is He, will multiply it for His servant and admit him into Paradise by His grace and mercy. The confirmation of this in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, is: ﴿and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾.

And al-Hasan said: His saying: ﴿and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾ is more beloved to the scholars than if He had said: "For one good deed there are a hundred thousand good deeds," because that statement would have a known measure, whereas in this expression no one knows the quantity of that multiplication except Allah, exalted is He. It is like His saying about the Night of Power that it is better than a thousand months.

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: It reached me from Abu Hurayra that he said: Allah gives His believing servant, for a single good deed, a thousand thousand good deeds. Then it so happened that I went to Mecca for pilgrimage or for 'umra, and I met him, and I said: It has reached me from you that you say: "Allah gives His believing servant, for a single good deed, a thousand thousand good deeds." Abu Hurayra said: I did not say that; rather I said: "A good deed is multiplied by two thousand thousand times." Then he recited this verse and said: When Allah says ﴿a great reward﴾, who can estimate its measure?

* * *

The third type of the matters included in this verse: His saying: ﴿and gives from Himself a great reward﴾, and in it are two issues.

[Page 85]

The first issue: *ladun* means the same as *'inda* (at, with), except that *ladun* is more firmly established. A man says "I have wealth with me (*'indī*)" if his wealth is in another land; one does not say *ladayya māl* or *ladunnī*, except for what is present.

The second issue: Know that there must be a distinction between this and His saying: ﴿and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾. What comes to my mind, and knowledge is with Allah, is that this multiplication is of the same kind as that reward, whereas this great reward is not of the same kind as that reward. And it is apparent that this multiplication is of the kind of the pleasures promised in Paradise, whereas this great reward which He gives from Himself is the delight attained at the vision (of Allah) and at total absorption in love and knowledge. He singled out this type with His saying ﴿from Himself﴾ because this kind of joy, happiness, gladness and perfection is not attained by bodily acts; rather it is attained only by what Allah places in the essence of the holy soul of radiance, purity and light. In sum, that multiplication is an indication of bodily felicity, and this great reward is an indication of spiritual felicity.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 41–42:

The arrangement (wajh al-nazm, the coherence of the verses) is that God, exalted is He, explained that in the Hereafter no one is wronged, and that He rewards the doer of good for his good and increases it beyond what is due to him. In this verse He explains that this takes place by the testimony of the Messengers, whom God made the proof against creation. This makes the proof against the evildoer more conclusive, his rebuke greater and his regret more intense, and makes the joy of those who accepted the Messenger and openly obeyed him greater. It is also a threat to the disbelievers, concerning whom God said: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾, and a promise to the obedient, concerning whom God said: ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn Mas'ud: "Recite the Qur'an to me." He said: I said, "O Messenger of God, it is you to whom it was revealed?" He said: "I love to hear it from someone other than myself." Ibn Mas'ud said: So I began Surat al-Nisa', and when I reached this verse, the Messenger (ﷺ) wept. Ibn Mas'ud said: So I stopped reading. Al-Suddi mentioned that the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) testifies for the Messengers that they delivered the message, and the Messenger (ﷺ) testifies for his community that they affirmed it. For this reason He said: ﴿Thus We have made you a median community, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. It is also reported of Jesus, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117].

The second issue: It is a habit of the Arabs that they say, about a thing they expect, "How will you be when such-and-such happens," or "When so-and-so does such-and-such," or "When such-and-such time comes." So the meaning of this statement is: How will you see the Day of Resurrection when God calls upon every community to testify through its Messenger, and calls you to testify against these? That is, against his people addressed by the Qur'an, whom he saw and whose conditions he knew. Then the people of every age testify concerning others whose conditions they witnessed. In this sense Jesus, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117].

[p. 86]
Then He described that Day, saying: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: His saying ﴿those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger﴾ requires that disobedience to the Messenger be distinct from disbelief, because it is not permissible to conjoin a thing with itself. Therefore, the disobedience to the Messenger must be understood as sins other than disbelief. Given this, we say: the verse indicates that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of Islam (furu' al-Islam), and that just as they are punished on the Day of Resurrection for disbelief, they are also punished for those sins. For if that sin had no effect in this matter, mentioning their disobedience in this context would have no purpose.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read ﴿tusawwa﴾ with a dammah on the ta' and a light sin, in the passive form (mā lam yusammā fā'iluhu). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿tusawwā﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a shaddah on the sin, meaning "tatasawwā," so the ta' was assimilated into the sin because they are close in articulation. Doubling the two shaddahs in this recitation is not disliked, because there are parallels in the revealed text, such as His saying ﴿We have taken an omen from you﴾ [al-Naml: 47], ﴿and she adorned herself﴾ [Yunus: 24], and ﴿they remember﴾. In this recitation there is an extension of meaning, namely the attribution of the verb to the earth. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tusawwā﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a light sin, deleting the ta' which Nafi' assimilated, because just as it is altered by assimilation, it is also altered by deletion.

The third issue: They have mentioned several interpretations of His saying ﴿if the earth were leveled over them﴾:

The first: If they were buried, the earth would be leveled over them as it is leveled over the dead.

The second: They would wish that they had not been resurrected, and that they had been as the earth is, equal to it.

The third: The beasts will turn to dust, so they will wish for their state, as in His saying ﴿Would that I had been dust﴾ [al-Naba': 40].

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾. Concerning this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have two approaches:

The first: That this is connected to what precedes it.

The second: That it is a independent statement. If we take it as connected, it allows two aspects:

One of them is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: They will wish that the earth would close over them, and that they had not concealed the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ), nor disbelieved in him, nor been hypocrites. According to this view, the concealment refers to what they concealed of the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: When the polytheists see on the Day of Resurrection that God forgives the people of Islam but does not forgive associating partners with Him, they will say: "Come, let us deny." So they will say: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists," hoping that God will forgive them. Then God will seal their mouths, their hands will speak, and their feet will testify to what they used to do. At that point they will wish that they had been dust, and they will not have concealed from God any statement.

The second approach to interpretation: This statement is a new beginning, since what they did is manifest before God, so how could they be able to conceal it?

The fifth issue: If it is asked, how can this verse be reconciled with His saying ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾?

The answer comes in several aspects:

The first: The stations of the Resurrection are many. In one station they will not speak, which is His saying ﴿You will hear only whispering﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108]. In another station they will speak, as in His saying ﴿We were not doing any evil﴾ [al-Nahl: 28] and their saying ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. So they lie in some stations, and in other stations they confess against themselves to disbelief and ask to be returned, which is their saying ﴿Would that we could be returned and not deny the signs of our Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 27]. The last of these stations is when their mouths will be sealed, their hands, feet and skins will speak. So we seek refuge in God from the disgrace of that Day.

The second: This concealment does not actually occur, but is included in the wishing, as we have explained.

The third: They did not intend to conceal, but reported according to what they imagined, and the meaning is: "By God, we were not polytheists in our own estimation, but we were correct in our assumptions, until we now realize otherwise." The discussion of this issue will come in Surat al-An'am, God willing.

**The tenth type of obligation mentioned in this surah:**

﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying, nor while you are in a state of janabah (ritual impurity), except while passing through, until you have washed yourselves.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying, nor while you are in a state of janabah, except while passing through, until you have washed yourselves.﴾

There are several issues concerning the verse:

**The first issue: concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), they mention two views:**

The first: A group of distinguished Companions were served food and drink by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf at a time when wine was still permitted. They ate and drank, and when they became intoxicated, the time for the Maghrib prayer came. They put one of them forward to lead them in prayer, and he recited: ﴿I worship what you worship, and you are not worshippers of what I worship.﴾ Then this verse was revealed, and they would not drink during the times of the prayers. When they had prayed ʿIshāʾ, they would drink, and they would not wake up except that the intoxication had left them and they knew what they were saying. Then the prohibition of it was revealed absolutely in Surat al-Māʾida. It is related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that when this reached him he said: "O Allah, wine harms the intellects and the wealth, so reveal Your command concerning it." Then the revelation came to them in the verse of al-Māʾida.

The second: Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was revealed concerning a group of senior Companions before the prohibition of wine. They used to drink it, then come to the mosque for the prayer with the Messenger (ﷺ), so Allah forbade them from it.

**The second issue: concerning the word "prayer" (ṣalāh), there are two opinions:**

The first: What is meant by it is the mosque. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḥasan, and al-Shāfiʿī adopted it.

Know that using the word "prayer" to mean the mosque is permissible, and two things indicate this:

The first: It is an instance of the omission of a modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), meaning: do not approach the place of prayer. The omission of a modifier is a common figurative usage (majāz).

The second: His saying: ﴿Had it not been that Allah repels some people by others, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques would have been demolished.﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 40] Here "prayers" (ṣalawāt) means the places of prayer. So it is established that using the word "prayer" to mean the mosque is permissible.

The second opinion, which most scholars hold, is that what is meant by "prayer" in this verse is the prayer itself, i.e., do not pray when you are intoxicated.

Know that the benefit of this disagreement appears in a legal ruling. On the first interpretation the meaning is: do not approach the mosque while you are intoxicated, nor while you are janub, except while passing through. On this view the exception indicates that it is permissible for a janub to cross through the mosque, and this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī. As for the second opinion, the meaning is: do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated, and do not approach it [p. 88] while you are in a state of janabah, except while passing through. What is meant by "one passing through" (ʿābir al-sabīl) is the traveller. This exception then indicates that a janub may proceed to prayer when unable to find water.

The followers of al-Shāfiʿī said: This first opinion is more preponderant, and several points indicate it:

The first: He said: ﴿do not approach prayer,﴾ and nearness and distance cannot be applied to the prayer itself in the literal sense; they apply only to the mosque.

The second: If we interpret it as we have said, the exception is sound. But if we interpret it as you say, the exception is not sound, because someone who is not a traveller but is unable to use water due to severe illness is permitted to pray with tayammum (dry ablution with earth). Given this, interpreting the verse in our way is more appropriate.

The third: If we take "one passing through" to mean a traveling janub, then if he has water, he may not approach prayer at all, and so the exception would need an implied qualification in the verse. And if he does not have water, he may not pray except with tayammum, so this condition would need to be implied in the verse too. But on our reading, we need not imply anything in the verse, so our view is preferable.

The fourth: God, exalted is He, mentions the ruling on travel, the absence of water and the permissibility of tayammum after this, so it is not permissible to read this as referring to a ruling stated in a verse after this one. What confirms this is that all the reciters recommended pausing at His saying: ﴿until you have washed yourselves,﴾ and then beginning again with His saying: ﴿And if you are ill...﴾ because it is a separate ruling. But if we interpret the verse as we have mentioned, we do not need these additions, so what we have said is preferable.

Those who support the second opinion may say: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾ indicates that what is meant by His saying: ﴿do not approach prayer﴾ is the prayer itself, because the mosque contains no lawful speech that prevents intoxication, whereas in the prayer there are specific utterances which prevent it. So interpreting the verse this way is more appropriate. The proponent of the first view may answer that a person goes to the mosque only for the sake of prayer, so anything that disrupts the prayer acts as a barrier to going to the mosque; for this reason this meaning was mentioned.

**The third issue:** Al-Wāḥidī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *sukārā* is the plural of *sakrān* (intoxicated), and every adjective of the pattern *faʿlān* is pluralized as *faʿālā* and *fuʿālā*, like *kasālā* and *kusālā* (lazy). The root meaning of *sakar* in the lexicon is blocking a path. From this comes *sakr al-baththq*, which is blocking it. And his eye became *sukr* (dazed) when it was bewildered. From this is His saying: ﴿Our eyes have only been dazzled,﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 15] meaning they were covered, so their light does not penetrate and they do not perceive things as they really are. From this also comes *sakr al-māʾ*, which is turning water back from its course. And *sukr* from drink is when a person is cut off from the penetration that is normal in the state of sobriety, so his judgment does not penetrate in the way it does when he is sober.

Having understood this, we say: concerning the word *sukārā* in this verse there are two opinions:

The first: What is meant is intoxication from wine, which is the opposite of sobriety. This is the view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors.

The second view, which is that of al-Ḍaḥḥāk, is that what is meant is not intoxication from wine but sleep-intoxication. He said: The word *sukr* is used for sleep, so this word can bear that meaning, and evidence points to it, so it is necessary to adopt it. As for showing that the word can bear this meaning, there are two arguments:

The first: What we mentioned, that the word *sukr* in its original linguistic sense refers to blocking a path. There is no doubt that during sleep the channels of the spirit fill with thick vapours, so those channels become blocked, and the seeing and hearing spirit does not reach the outer body.

The second: The words of al-Farazdaq:

*From travelling and night-marching, one would think that sleep had given him wine to drink at every halting-place.*

Since it has been established that the word can bear this meaning, we say: the evidence points to it, and its explanation has several aspects:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying﴾ apparently means that He forbade them to approach prayer when they reach a state in which they do not know what they are saying. Imposing obligation on such a person is impossible by reason and by transmitted text. By reason, because imposing obligation on such a person would require imposing what cannot be borne. By transmitted text, His (ﷺ) saying: "The pen is lifted from three: from the child until he reaches puberty, from the insane until he recovers, and from the sleeper until he awakens." There is no doubt that this intoxicated person is like the insane, so it is necessary that the obligation be lifted from him.

The second proof: His (ﷺ) saying: "If one of you feels drowsy while in prayer, let him sleep until the drowsiness leaves him, for if he prays while drowsy, he may intend to seek forgiveness but end up cursing himself." This is the substance of al-Ḍaḥḥāk's view.

Know that the sound view is the first opinion, and two things indicate it:

The first: The word *sukr* is literally used for intoxication from drinking wine, and the basic principle in speech is the literal meaning. As for taking it to mean intoxication from love, anger, fear or sleep, all of this is figurative (majāz), and it is only used with a qualifier. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the agony of death has come.﴾ [Qāf: 19] And He said: ﴿You see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated.﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 2]

The second: All the commentators agreed that this verse was revealed concerning the drinking of wine. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that when a verse is revealed concerning a specific event and for a specific cause, it is impossible that this cause is not intended by that verse. As for al-Ḍaḥḥāk's view, how can the prohibition apply to someone who is asleep and understands nothing? We reply: this objection also applies to you, because one can say: how can the prohibition apply to someone who is asleep and understands nothing? Then the answer to it is that what is meant by the verse is the prohibition of drinking that leads to intoxication which disrupts understanding at the time when the prayer is obligatory for them. So the wording departs from prohibiting prayer in a state of intoxication, while what is meant is prohibiting drinking that causes intoxication at the time of prayer. As for the hadith he relied upon, it does not indicate that the intoxication mentioned in the verse is sleep.

**The fourth issue:** Some said: This verse is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of al-Māʾida. I say: The point where one can claim abrogation (naskh, meaning the repeal of an earlier ruling by a later one) is that it may be said: He forbade approaching prayer while intoxicated, extended until the point where a person becomes able to know what he is saying. A ruling extended to a limit requires that the ruling ends at that limit. So this implies the permissibility of approaching prayer when intoxicated, once a person reaches the state of knowing what he says. It is known that when God, exalted is He, prohibited wine through the verse of al-Māʾida, He removed this permissibility. Thus it is established that the verse of al-Māʾida abrogates some of the implications of this verse. This is what came to my mind in explaining this abrogation.

The answer to this: We have shown that the essence of this prohibition returns to a prohibition of drinking which causes intoxication when one is close to prayer. Singling out one thing by mention does not indicate the negation of the ruling for other things, except by way of weak conjecture, and such a thing does not count as abrogation.

**The fifth issue:** The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *sakārā* was read with a fatḥa on the sīn, and *sakrā* (as a plural form) as in *halkā* and *jawʿā*.

\* \* \*

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿nor while you are in a state of janabah, except while passing through.﴾ His saying "nor in a state of janabah" is conjoined to His saying: ﴿while you are intoxicated,﴾ and the *wāw* here is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The sense is: do not approach prayer in the state in which you are intoxicated, and in the state in which you are janub. *Janub* is used for one and many, masculine and feminine alike, because it is a noun that functions like the verbal noun *ijnāb* (the state of being in janabah). We have mentioned that the root meaning of *janābah* is distance, and the one who must perform ghusl is called *junub* because he keeps away from prayer, the mosque and the recitation of the Qur'an until he purifies himself [p. 90]. Then He said: ﴿except while passing through,﴾ and we have mentioned that there are two opinions concerning it:

One: that this passing through refers to crossing through the mosque.

Two: that what is meant by His saying: ﴿except while passing through﴾ is travellers. We have explained how to prefer one of these over the other.

\* \*

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then perform tayammum with clean earth and wipe your faces and hands. Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, mentions here four categories: the ill, the travellers, those who have come from relieving themselves, and those who have touched women.

The first two categories require resorting to tayammum, namely illness and travel.

The last two categories require purification with water when water is available, and with tayammum when water is unavailable. We will mention the ruling for each of these categories.

As for the first cause, which is illness, know that it falls into three types:

The first: that it is such that if he used water he would die, as with severe smallpox and great sores.

The second: that he would not die by using water, but he would experience great pain.

Third, that he not fear death or severe pain, but he fears the persistence of a blemish or defect on the body. The jurists permitted tayammum in the first two cases, and they did not permit it in the third case. al-Hasan al-Basri, however, claimed that tayammum is not permitted in any case except when water is absent, on the evidence that He made the permissibility of tayammum for the sick conditional on not finding water, as shown by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿and you find no water﴾. If this condition is considered in the permissibility of tayammum, then when this condition is absent, tayammum must not be permitted. This is also the view of Ibn Abbas, who used to say: "If Allah willed, He would have afflicted him with something worse than that."

The evidence of the jurists is that He, exalted is He, permitted tayammum for the sick when he does not find water, and there is nothing in it indicating its prohibition when water is found. Then the Sunnah has indicated its permissibility, and what supports it is what is narrated from some of the Companions: that a man was struck by janabah while he had a severe wound. He asked some of his companions, and they ordered him to perform ghusl. When he bathed, he died. The Prophet ﷺ heard of this and said: "They killed him; may Allah kill them." This indicates the permissibility of what we have mentioned.

The second cause: travel. The verse indicates that a traveler who does not find water performs tayammum, whether his journey is long or short, because of this verse.

The third cause: His saying: ﴿or one of you comes from the toilet (al-ghaʼit)﴾. Al-ghaʼit is a low-lying place of the earth, and its plural is al-ghiyatan. When a man wished to relieve himself, he sought a low place of the earth that would screen him from people's eyes. Then the minor impurity itself was named by this term, calling the thing by the name of its place.

The fourth cause: His saying: ﴿or you have touched women﴾. On this there are issues:

Issue one: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "lamastum" without an alif, from al-lams (touching), while the others read "lamastum" with an alif, from al-mulamasah.

Issue two: The exegetes differed concerning the touching mentioned here, on two views:

One: that what is meant by it is intercourse. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah, and the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, because touching with the hand does not nullify purity.

The second: that what is meant by touching here is the meeting of two skins, whether by intercourse or otherwise. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i, and the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him.

Know that this second view is more preferable than the first, because one of the two readings is His saying, exalted is He: "or you have touched women," and touching (al-lams) in its literal sense is touching with the hand. As for restricting it to intercourse, that is a metaphor, and the principle is to carry speech on its literal meaning.

As for the second reading, which is His saying: "or you have touched (lamastum)", it is a form of mufa'alah from al-lams, and that is not literally used for intercourse either, rather it must be carried on its literal meaning as well, so that no contradiction arises between the meanings of the two mutawatir readings. Those who said that the meaning of touching is intercourse argued that the words lams and mass occur in the Qur'an with the meaning of intercourse. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], and in the verse of zihar He said: ﴿before they touch one another﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3]. And it is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Indeed Allah is Modest and Generous; He shies away and uses euphemism, so He expressed intercourse by mulamasah." Also, impurity is of two kinds: the minor, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or one of you comes from the toilet﴾, so if we carry His saying: ﴿or you have touched women﴾ on the minor impurity, nothing would remain for the major impurity to be mentioned in the verse, so it is necessary to carry it on the major impurity.

Know that all that they mentioned is a deviation from the apparent wording without evidence, so it is not permissible. Also, the ruling of janabah has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿nor [come near prayer] while you are junub﴾, so if we carry this verse on janabah it would entail repetition.

Issue three: The people of the apparent (ahl al-zahir) said: the nullification of the ablution applies only to the one who touches, on the apparent wording of His saying: ﴿or you have touched.﴾ As for the one touched, no. al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: rather, the ablution of both is nullified together.

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned these four causes, He said: ﴿and you find no water﴾. On this there are issues:

Issue one: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if the time of prayer enters, and he seeks water and does not find it, performs tayammum and prays, then when the time of the second prayer enters, it becomes obligatory on him to seek again. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is not obligatory.

The proof of al-Shafi'i is His saying: ﴿and you find no water﴾, and the absence of finding indicates that a search preceded it, so a prior search is necessary each time.

If it is said: our saying "he found" does not indicate that a search preceded it, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and He found you lost and guided you﴾, ﴿and He found you in need and made you self-sufficient﴾ [al-Duha: 7], and His saying: ﴿and We found most of them not to be keeping covenant﴾ [al-A'raf: 102], and His saying: ﴿and We found in him no constancy of resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], for searching is impossible for Allah.

We say: searching, although it is impossible with respect to Him, exalted is He, yet when He expelled Muhammad ﷺ from among his people by what was not befitting to his people, that became as if He had sought him; and when He commanded the mukallafun with acts of obedience, then they fell short in them, it became as if He sought something and did not find it. Thus this word in these verses came by way of figurative interpretation from the aspect we have mentioned.

Issue two: They agreed that if he finds water but needs it for his thirst or the thirst of an honored animal, tayammum is permissible for him. As for if he finds only an amount of water that does not suffice for wudu, must he combine the use of that amount of water with tayammum? al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, made it obligatory, holding to the apparent wording of the verse.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then perform tayammum with clean earth (sa'idan tayyiban)﴾. On this there are issues:

Issue one: Tayammum in language is an expression for intention. It is said: amamtuhu, tayammamtuhu, and ta'ammamtuhu, meaning I intended him. As for "ala al-sa'id," it is fa'il in the sense of sa'id (ascending), and al-Zajjaj said: al-sa'id is the surface of the earth, whether it is dust or otherwise.

Issue two: Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if we suppose a rock with no dust on it, and the one performing tayammum strikes his hand on it and wipes, that would be sufficient. al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: rather there must be dust that clings to his hand.

Abu Hanifah argued from the apparent wording of this verse, saying: tayammum is intention, and al-sa'id is what ascends from the earth, so His saying: ﴿then perform tayammum with clean earth﴾ means intend land, and so this amount must be sufficient.

As for al-Shafi'i, he argued with two points:

The first: that this verse here is absolute, but in Surat al-Ma'idah it is restricted, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿then wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. The particle "min" is for partitive meaning, and this cannot apply to a rock with no dust on it. If it is said: the particle "min" is for the beginning of the limit, the author of al-Kashshaf said: no one among the Arabs understands from the saying of a speaker "I wiped his head with oil, with water, with dust" except the meaning of partitive, then he said: and submitting to the truth is more deserving than disputation.

The second: what al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned, namely that He, exalted is He, required in this verse that the sa'id be clean, and clean land is that which produces vegetation, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. So it is necessary that the land which does not produce vegetation is not clean, and His saying: ﴿then perform tayammum with clean sa'id﴾ is a command to perform tayammum with dust only, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation.

The third: that His saying: ﴿clean sa'id﴾ is a command to perform tayammum with clean sa'id, and clean sa'id is the land that has no salt (sabakhah). There is no doubt that tayammum with this dust is permissible by consensus, so it is necessary to carry clean sa'id on it, out of regard for the principle of caution, especially since the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, specified dust with this attribute, saying: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration, and its dust a purifier," and he said: "Dust is the purifier of the Muslim when he does not find water."

Issue three: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and wipe your faces and your hands﴾ is, according to many exegetes, understood as the face and the two hands up to the wrists. According to most jurists, it is obligatory to wipe the two hands up to the elbows, and their argument is that the name "hand" covers the whole of this limb up to the armpits, except that we excluded the elbows from it by the evidence of consensus, so the wording remains covering what is left. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, which is a metaphor for leniency and facilitation, for whoever is customarily forgiving of sinners, it is more fitting that he grant concession to the incapable.

[Page 93]

The Exalted said: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Book, how they buy error and wish that you would stray from the [right] way? And Allah is most knowing of your enemies, and sufficient is Allah as a Protector, and sufficient is Allah as a Helper.﴾

Know that when the Exalted had mentioned, from the beginning of this surah up to this point, many kinds of obligations and legal rulings, He here broke off to explain the legal rulings and to mention the conditions of the enemies of the religion and the stories of earlier peoples. This is because remaining on one type of knowledge wearies the nature and clouds the mind, whereas moving from one type of knowledge to another refreshes the mind and strengthens the faculty of understanding. There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ means: has your knowledge not reached these people? We have already discussed what is involved in it at His saying ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. The summary of the matter is that certain knowledge resembles sight, so it is permissible to make "seeing" a metaphor (isti'arah) for this kind of knowledge.

The second issue: ﴿those who were given a portion of the Book﴾ are the Jews, and this is indicated by several considerations:

The first: His saying after this verse, ﴿of those who are Jews﴾ [al-Nisa': 46], is connected to this verse.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas narrated that this verse was revealed concerning two rabbis of the Jews who used to visit the head of the hypocrites, 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, and his group, and discouraged them from Islam.

The third: The enmity of the Jews was greater than the enmity of the Christians, according to the explicit text of the Qur'an, so it was more appropriate to attribute this meaning to the Jews.

The third issue: The Exalted did not say that they were given the knowledge of the Book; rather He said ﴿were given a portion of the Book﴾, because they recognized from the Torah the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), but they did not recognize from it the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). As for those who embraced Islam, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and recognized both matters, Allah described them as having the knowledge of the Book, saying: ﴿Say: Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you, and whoever has the knowledge of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Know that the Exalted described them with two matters: going astray and leading astray. As for going astray, it is His saying ﴿they buy error﴾, and in it there are several views:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: they prefer denying the Messenger (peace be upon him) so that they may take bribes for that and attain leadership. He expressed this with the word "buying" because whoever buys something prefers it.

The second: In the verse there is an ellipsis (idmar), and its interpretation is: they buy error in exchange for guidance, like His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16], meaning they substitute error for guidance. There is no ellipsis according to al-Zajjaj's view.

The third: The intended meaning of this verse is the common Jews, for they used to give their rabbis some of their wealth, and the rabbis would ask them to support Judaism and to be zealous for it. So they were like one who buys with his wealth doubt and error. There is also no ellipsis according to this interpretation. However, the more appropriate view is that the verse was revealed concerning their scholars. Then, when the Exalted described them with going astray, He afterwards described them with leading astray, saying: ﴿and they wish that you would stray from the [right] way﴾, meaning that they seek to lead the believers astray and to confuse them, so that they would leave Islam.

Know that you will not see a condition worse or more ugly than that of one who combines these two matters, I mean going astray and leading astray. Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾, meaning He, glorified is He, knows the reality of what is in their hearts and breasts of enmity and hatred.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a Protector, and sufficient is Allah as a Helper﴾. The meaning is that when He made clear the severity of their enmity toward the Muslims, He made clear that Allah, the Exalted, is the Protector and Helper of the Muslims, and whoever Allah takes as his protector and helper, the enmity of creation will not harm him. In the verse there are questions:

The first question: The protection of Allah toward His servant is an expression of His support for him, so mentioning the Helper after mentioning the Protector is repetition.

Answer: The protector (al-wali) is the one who disposes of a thing, and one who disposes of a thing is not necessarily its helper, so the repetition is removed.

The second question: Why did He not say: "sufficient is Allah as a Protector and Helper"? And what is the benefit of repeating His saying "sufficient is Allah"?

Answer: Repetition in such a context has a stronger effect on the heart and is more emphatic.

The third question: What is the benefit of the bāʾ (the preposition "bi-") in His saying ﴿sufficient is Allah as a Protector﴾?

Answer: They have mentioned several views:

The first: If it had been said "kafa Allah" (Allah suffices), the verb would be directly connected to the agent. Here the bāʾ has been added to indicate that sufficiency from Allah is not like sufficiency from anyone else in rank and in the greatness of station.

The second: Ibn al-Sarraj said: the implied sense of the sentence is "your reliance upon Allah as a protector suffices," and since "kafa" is mentioned, it indicates reliance, because it derives from its root; just as you say: "whoever lies, it is evil for him," meaning lying is evil for him, and you have omitted it because the verb indicates it.

The third: It occurs to my mind that the bāʾ originally indicates attachment (ilsāq), and that is appropriate only with an agent that has no intermediary between it and the effect. If it had been said "kafa Allah," that would indicate that the Exalted is the doer of this sufficiency, but it would not indicate whether He acts through an intermediary or without one. When you mention the particle bāʾ, it indicates that He acts without an intermediary; rather He, the Exalted, undertakes the achievement of this desired matter directly, without the intermediary of anyone, as He said: ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places and say, "We hear and we disobey," and, "Hear, [but] unheard," and, "Ra'ina," twisting their tongues and slandering the religion. And if they had said, "We hear and we obey, and hear, and look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright. But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a little.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, related about them that they buy error, He explained the manner of that error, which consists of several matters:

The first of them: they used to distort words from their places. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the reference of His saying ﴿Among those who﴾ there are several views:

The first: that it is an explanation of "those who were given a portion of the Book," the meaning being: "Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, among those who are Jews?"

The second: that it relates to His saying ﴿a helper﴾, the meaning being: "And Allah suffices as a helper from those who are Jews." It is like His saying: ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs﴾ [al-Anbiya: 77].

The third: that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "they distort" is its attribute, its meaning being: "Among those who are Jews are a people who distort the words," so the qualified noun is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place.

The fourth: that when He said: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, buying error﴾ [an-Nisa: 44], this remained general in two respects, so it was as if it were said: "And of those are those who were given a portion of the Book?" It was answered and it was said: "Among those who are Jews." Then it was said: "And how do they buy error?" It was answered and it was said: "They distort the words."

Page 95
The second issue: One may say: the noun (al-kalim) is feminine in plural, so it should have been said: "they distort the words from their places" (ʿan mawāḍiʿihā).
The answer: al-Wahidi said: this is a plural whose letters are fewer than those of its singular, and every plural of this kind may be made masculine. It is also possible to say: the femininity of the plural is not a real matter but a verbal one, so both masculine and feminine are permissible in it. It has also been read: yuḥarrifūna al-kalima.

* * *
The third issue: concerning the manner of distortion there are several views:

The first: that they would replace a word with another word, such as their distorting the name "ruba'" (of medium height) from its place in the Torah by placing "Adam is tall" in its stead, and like their distorting "stoning" (al-rajm) by placing "the prescribed punishment" (al-hadd) in its place. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah"﴾ [al-Baqara: 79].

If it is said: How is this possible in a Book whose individual letters and words have reached the level of well-known mass transmission (tawatur) in East and West?

We say: perhaps it may be said: the people were few, and the scholars of the Book were extremely few, so they were able to effect this distortion.

The second: that what is meant by distortion is the casting of false doubts and corrupt interpretations, and turning the wording away from its true meaning to a false meaning by means of verbal tricks, as the people of innovation do in our time with the verses that oppose their doctrines. This is the most sound view.

The third: that they would come into the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and ask him about a matter, and he would inform them so that they might act upon it; then when they left his presence they would distort his speech.

The fourth issue: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned here: ﴿from their places﴾, and in al-Ma'ida: ﴿after their places﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 41]. The difference is that when we interpret distortion as false interpretations, then here His saying ﴿they distort the words from their places﴾ means that they mention corrupt interpretations of those texts, and it does not indicate that they remove that wording from the Book.

As for the verse mentioned in Surah al-Ma'ida, it indicates that they combined the two matters: they would mention corrupt interpretations, and they would also remove the wording from the Book. So His saying ﴿they distort the words﴾ points to false interpretation, and His saying ﴿after their places﴾ points to their removing it from the Book.

* * *
The second kind of their errors: what Allah mentioned by His saying: ﴿and they say, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: that when the Prophet — peace be upon him — commanded them to something, they would say outwardly, "We hear," and say to themselves, "We disobey."

The second: that they would openly say, "We hear and we disobey," to display opposition and to belittle the command.

The third kind of their errors is His saying: ﴿and, "Hear, [but] unheard"﴾.

Know that this expression has two possible senses: it may carry praise and honour, and it may carry insult and abuse. As for its carrying praise, the meaning would be: "Hear, [and may you] hear nothing disagreeable." As for its carrying insult and blame, that is in several respects:

The first: they would say to the Prophet ﷺ, "Hear," and say to themselves, "May you not hear." So His saying ﴿unheard﴾ means: "not hearing," for a hearer is one who is heard, and one who is heard is a hearer.

The second: "unheard" means "not accepted from you, and you are not answered in what you call to," and its meaning is "unheard with a reply that agrees with you," so it is as if you had made nothing heard.

The third: "Hear, [but] unheard" means: "a speech you are pleased with, which one does not hear, since his ears are deaf to it." From what we have mentioned it is established that this expression is capable of both blame and praise, and they would say it for the purpose of insult.

Page 96

The fourth kind of their errors is their saying: ﴿and, "Ra'ina," twisting their tongues and slandering the religion﴾. As for the explanation of "ra'ina," we have mentioned it in Surah al-Baqara, and there are several views:

The first: that this was a word that passed among them in a manner of mockery and derision; therefore the Muslims were forbidden to utter it in the presence of the Messenger ﷺ.

The second: His saying "ra'ina" means "ur'ina sam'aka" (incline your hearing to us), that is, turn your hearing toward our speech, listen to our talk and understand it. This is something that prophets, peace be upon them, should not be addressed with; rather they are to be addressed with reverence and honour.

The third: they would say "ra'ina," and in outward appearance make it seem that they meant "ur'ina sam'aka," while they intended to revile him with "ru'una" (foolishness/rudeness) in their language.

The fourth: they would twist their tongues until their saying "ra'ina" became "ra'ayna" (we pastured), and they meant that you used to pasture sheep for us. As for His saying ﴿twisting with their tongues﴾, al-Wahidi said: the root of "layyan" is "lawyan," because it comes from "lawaytu" (I twisted), but the waw was assimilated into the ya' because it was preceded by a sukun; similarly "al-tayy." Concerning its explanation there are several views:

The first: al-Farra' said: they would say "ra'ina" and intend by it insult, and that is the "layy"; likewise their saying ﴿unheard﴾, by which they meant "may you not hear," and that is the "layy."

The second: that they would join with their tongues what they concealed of insult to what they openly displayed of honour, by way of hypocrisy.

The third: perhaps they would twist their cheeks and tongues when mentioning this speech by way of mockery, as is the custom of one who mocks a person with such gestures. Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that they only did these things to slander the religion, for they used to say to their companions: "We only revile him and he does not know it; had he been a prophet he would have known it." So Allah, exalted is He, made that manifest and revealed to him the wickedness of their hearts, and what they did turned into a proof against their slander of his prophethood, a conclusive proof of his prophethood, because informing of the unseen is a miracle.

If it is said: how did they utter the expression that bears two meanings after they had distorted and said, "We hear and we disobey"?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: we have related from some exegetes that he said: they did not openly say "and we disobey," but said it to themselves.

The second: grant that they did openly express it, yet all the disbelievers would confront him with disbelief and disobedience, and not confront him with reviling and abuse.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they had said, "We hear and we obey, and hear, and look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright.﴾ The meaning is that if they had said, instead of their saying "We hear and we disobey," "We hear and we obey," because of their knowledge of your truthfulness and your showing of the proofs and clear signs time after time; and instead of their saying ﴿hear, [but] unheard﴾ they had said "hear"; and instead of their saying "ra'ina" they had said ﴿look at us﴾, meaning: listen to what we say from us, and look at us until we understand from you, it would have been better for them with Allah and more upright, that is, more just and more correct. From this it is said: "a qawim spear," meaning straight; and "I straightened the thing from crookedness, so it became straight."

* * *
Then He said: ﴿But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾, and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, cursed them only because of their disbelief.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿So they do not believe except a little﴾, and concerning this there are two statements:

One of them: that "little" is an attribute of the people, and the meaning is: "So none of them believe except a few small groups." Then some of them said: that little group was ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions; and it was said: they are those whom Allah knew would believe after that.

The second statement: that "little" is an attribute of the faith, and the sense is: "So they do not believe except with a little faith," for they believed in Allah, the Torah and Moses, but they disbelieved in the rest of the prophets. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi preferred this second view over the first, saying: because "qalilan" is a singular word, and if people were intended by it, it would have been pluralized, like His saying: ﴿Indeed these are a small band (shirdhima qalilun)﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 54]. It may be answered that the form fa'il has come singular while meaning plural, He says: ﴿And excellent are those as companions (rafiqan)﴾ [an-Nisa: 69], and He says: ﴿No intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend, though they will be shown to them (yubassarunahum)﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 10–11]. The return of the reference in plural to the two groups indicates that by them is meant multitude.

**The Words of God Most High: "O you who have been given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what you already have, before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their backs, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath. And the command of God is always carried out."**

Concerning this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** After God mentioned the various kinds of deceit and harm the Jews had committed, He commanded them to believe and attached a severe threat to their refusal. Someone might ask: it would have been more fitting for Him to command them to reflect and contemplate the proofs that establish the truth of His Prophet's mission, so that their faith would be based on reasoning. Instead, He commanded them to believe outright, which seems to be a command to follow blind imitation (taqlid).

The answer: this address is specifically directed at those who were given the Scripture, and this description applies to someone who knows the whole of the Torah. Consider that in the earlier verse He said, ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ [al-Nisa': 44], and He did not say, "Have you not seen those who were given the Scripture," because they did not know everything in the Torah. When He says in this verse, ﴿O you who have been given the Scripture﴾, we know that this obligation applies only to one who knows the entire Torah. Whoever knows all of it also knows the proofs that point to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Torah contained those proofs. This is why He said, ﴿confirming what you already have﴾, that is, confirming the signs present in the Torah that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). When knowledge is established, their disbelief is pure obstinacy. Therefore it is right for God to command them to believe in Muhammad (peace be upon him) with certainty, and to attach a severe threat to that command.

**The second issue:** *Al-tams* (obliteration) means erasure. The Arabs describe a desert as "its landmarks obliterated" (*tamisat al-a'lam*). A road is said to have been *tamasa* or *tumisa* when it became worn away. *Tamasa Allah 'ala basarihi* means God removed and nullified his sight. The wind *tamasat* the traces when it erased them, and *tamastu al-kitab* means I erased the writing. Regarding the obliteration mentioned in this verse, scholars have offered two interpretations:

First, that the word is taken in its literal sense, namely the obliteration of faces.

Second, that the word is taken in its figurative sense.

As for the first view: the meaning of obliterating faces is erasing the outlines of their forms. The face is distinguished from the other limbs by the senses it contains. When these are removed and effaced, that is obliteration. The phrase ﴿and turn them back upon their backs﴾ means turning the faces toward the back of the neck. God made this a punishment because of the disfigurement, mutilation and humiliation it involves, for at that time grief and regret become great. This threat is specific to the Day of Resurrection, as we will establish. What supports this is God's statement, ﴿But as for him who is given his record behind his back﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 10]. When faces are turned to the back of the neck, they are given the book from behind their backs, because in that direction are the eyes and mouths by which the book is perceived and read with the tongue.

As for the second view: the obliteration is meant figuratively. Scholars have mentioned several interpretations:

The first: al-Hasan said that the meaning is "We will obliterate them from guidance and turn them back upon their backs," that is, upon their misguidance. The purpose is to show that they will be cast into kinds of abandonment and darkness of error. A parallel is God's statement, ﴿O you who believe, respond to God and to the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life. And know that God comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. The fuller explanation is that a person, at the beginning of his creation, is accustomed to this sensible world. Then, through reflection and worship, it is as if he travels from the world of sensible things to the world of intelligible things. The world of intelligibles lies ahead of him, and the world of sensibles lies behind him. The one who is forsaken is the one who is turned back from what is ahead of him to what is behind him, as God said describing them: ﴿They will hang their heads﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].

The second: it is possible that the meaning of obliteration is transformation and alteration, and that "faces" means their leaders and dignitaries. The meaning would be: before We change the condition of their dignitaries, stripping them of honor and standing, and clothing them in humiliation, abasement and disgrace.

The third: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said that this threat has already fallen upon the Jews and passed. He interpreted it as referring to the exile of Qurayzah and al-Nadir to Syria. God turned their faces back upon their backs when they returned to Adhri'at and Ariha in the land of Syria, just as they had come from there at first. On this interpretation, the obliteration of faces may have two meanings:

One: the disfigurement of their appearance, as one says, "God obliterated his form," like the saying, "God made his face ugly."

The other: the removal of their traces from the lands of the Arabs and the erasure of their conditions there.

If it is said: God threatened them with the obliteration of faces on the second interpretation, so there is no difficulty at all. But if we explain it according to the first interpretation, taking it in its outward sense, then the answer comes in several ways:

First: God did not make the threatened punishment the obliteration itself. Rather, He made the threatened punishment either obliteration or cursing, for He said, ﴿or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾. He has carried out one of the two, namely cursing, which is His statement, ﴿or curse them﴾, and its outward meaning is not transformation.

Second: God's statement, ﴿Believe﴾, is an obligation directed at them throughout the whole period of their lives. Therefore His statement, ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾, must refer to the Hereafter. The sense becomes: "Believe before there comes a time when We obliterate your faces," and that time is after death.

Third: We have already shown that His statement, ﴿O you who have been given the Scripture﴾, is addressed to all their scholars. The threat of this obliteration was therefore conditional on none of them coming to faith, and this condition was not fulfilled, because 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and a large group of his companions believed. So the conditioned threat lapsed when its condition lapsed. It is said that when this verse was revealed, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before going to his family, and he embraced Islam, saying: "O Messenger of God, I used to think that I would not reach you until my face was turned around on the back of my neck."

Fourth: God did not say, "before We obliterate your faces," but said, ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾. In our view there must be an obliteration or transformation among the Jews before the Hour comes. What indicates that the intended meaning is not the obliteration of the faces of these very people, but rather the obliteration of the faces of others of their kind, is God's statement, ﴿or curse them﴾. Here He mentioned them in the third person, whereas if those addressed were meant, He would have mentioned them in the second person. Taking the verse as a shift of address (iltifat, a change from direct address to third person) is permissible, but the view we have mentioned is more apparent.

\* \* \*

Then God said, ﴿or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾. Muqatil and others said: "We will transform them into apes, as We did to their predecessors." Most of the careful scholars said: "The more apparent reading is to take the verse as referring to cursing in its common sense. Do you not see God's statement, ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from God? Those whom God cursed and with whom He was angry, and whom He transformed into apes and swine﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]." 

[p. 99]

Here God distinguished between cursing and transforming them into apes and swine. There are several questions here.

**The first question:** To whom does the pronoun in ﴿or curse them﴾ refer?

The answer: it refers to the faces, if what is meant is the dignitaries or the owners of the faces, because the meaning is "before We obliterate the faces of a people." Or it refers to those who were given the Scripture, by way of iltifat (shift of address).

**The second question:** The cursing and the obliteration both happened before the threat was pronounced for the act, so they must be the same thing.

The answer: God's cursing them after this threat has a greater effect in disgrace, so the threat is valid in this respect.

**The third question:** God's statement, ﴿O you who have been given the Scripture﴾, is direct address, while His statement, ﴿or curse them﴾, is third-person reference. How can one fit with the other?

The answer: Some have taken this as a shift of address (iltifat), as in God's statement, ﴿Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾ [Yunus: 22]. Others said: this is an indication that the threat applies to others, among those of their kind who deny. I have another possibility: cursing is expulsion and removal, and mentioning someone distant is only done in the third person. So when He cursed them, He referred to them with the third-person form.

\* \* \*

Then God said, ﴿And the command of God is always carried out﴾. There are two issues concerning this:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means that no one can reverse His judgment or annul His command, in the sense that nothing is out of reach for Him that He wishes to do. It is like saying of a thing that is certain to happen: 'This matter is done,' even if it has not yet been done." He said ﴿was﴾ to report the continuing practice of God regarding the earlier prophets: whenever He informed them that He would send down punishment upon them, He would certainly do it. It is as if it were said to them: "You know that God's threat against the earlier nations was certainly fulfilled. So be cautious now, and be on guard against this threat." And God knows best.

**The second issue:** Al-Jubba'i used this verse to argue that God's speech is created (muhdath). He said: God's statement, ﴿And the command of God is always carried out﴾, implies that His command is something done, and the created, the made, and the done are one and the same. This shows that God's command is created and made. This is utterly baseless, because in the language *amr* comes to mean matter, manner and act. God said, ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud: 97], and the meaning here is the same.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a tremendous sin.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, threatened the Jews for their disbelief, and showed that this threat must inevitably come to pass, He then showed that such a threat is specific to disbelief (kufr). As for the rest of the sins, which differ from disbelief, their status is not like that; rather, He, glorified is He, may pardon them. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills.﴾ In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: This verse indicates that the Jew is called a mushrik (one who associates partners with Allah) in the terminology of the Law (shar'). Two arguments show this:

The first: The verse indicates that everything other than shirk is forgiven. So if Judaism were distinct from shirk, it would have to be forgiven by the ruling of this verse; but by consensus it is not forgiven. This shows that it falls under the name of shirk.

The second: The connection of this verse with what precedes it is only because it contains a threat to the Jews. Had Judaism not fallen under the name of shirk, the matter would not be so.

If it is said: The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾ [al-Hajj: 17] up to His saying: ﴿and those who associate partners﴾ [al-Hajj: 17] conjoins the mushrik to the Jew, and this requires distinction.

We say: The distinction arises from the linguistic concept, while the unity arises from the legal (shar'i) concept, and it is necessary to resort to what we have mentioned in order to avoid contradiction. Once this premise is established, we say: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: a Muslim is not executed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection). Abu Hanifa said: he is executed. The proof of al-Shafi'i is that the dhimmi is a mushrik for the reason we mentioned, and the mushrik is one whose blood is permissible to shed, by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: (Kill the mushrikun). So the dhimmi is one whose blood is permissible to shed in the manner we mentioned, and the one whose blood is permissible to shed is the one for whose killer retaliation (qisas) is not obligatory, and the prohibition against killing him does not apply; leaving this evidence in regard to the prohibition, it is necessary that it remain in force regarding the removal of qisas from his killer.

* * *

The second issue: This verse is among the strongest proofs for us regarding the pardoning of the people of major sins (kaba'ir).

Know that the argument from it is in several ways:

The first way: His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ means He does not forgive shirk by way of grace (tafaddul), since by consensus He is not obligated to forgive it, and that is when the mushrik repents of his shirk. If the meaning of His saying "Indeed, Allah does not forgive shirk" is that He does not forgive it by way of grace, then it must be that His saying "and He forgives what is less than that" means that He forgives it by way of grace, so that the negation and the affirmation apply to one meaning. Do you not see that if one says: "So-and-so does not give anyone by way of grace, and gives more by way of obligation," it is understood from him that he gives by way of grace; and even if he states explicitly, "He does not give anyone anything by way of grace, and gives more by way of obligation," every intelligent person judges this speech to be incoherent. Thus it is established that His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ is by way of grace. Once this is established, we say: its intended meaning must be the people of major sins before repentance, because according to the Mu'tazila, the forgiveness of minor sins and the forgiveness of major sins after repentance is obligatory by reason ('aqlan), so the verse cannot be applied to it. When this is settled, nothing remains but to apply the verse to the forgiveness of a major sin before repentance, which is what was to be proven.

The second: He, exalted is He, divided the prohibited matters into two categories: shirk and what is other than shirk. Then what is other than shirk includes major sins before repentance, major sins after repentance, and minor sins. Then He ruled regarding shirk that it is definitively not forgiven, and regarding what is other than it that it is definitively forgiven, but for whomever He wills. So the implied sense of the verse is that He, exalted is He, forgives everything other than shirk, but for whomever He wills. Since the verse indicates that everything other than shirk is forgiven, it must be that major sins before repentance are also forgiven.

The third: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿for whom He wills﴾, thereby attaching this forgiveness to His will, whereas forgiveness of a major sin after repentance and forgiveness of a minor sin is certain and not conditioned upon will, so it must be that the forgiveness mentioned in this verse is the forgiveness of a major sin before repentance, which is what was to be proven. The objectors raised against this last argument that attaching a matter to will does not negate its being obligatory. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿but Allah purifies whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 49]; then we know that He does not purify except one who is worthy of purification, otherwise it would be a lie, and lying about Allah is impossible; so likewise here.

Know that the Mu'tazila have no argument worth considering against these arguments except opposing them with the general wording of the threats (wa'id), and we oppose them with the general wording of the promises (wa'd). The full discussion of this is mentioned in surah al-Baqarah in the commentary on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil and his sin surrounds him—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], so there is no benefit in repeating it. Al-Wahidi related in al-Basit with his chain from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "In the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when a man among us died upon a major sin, we would testify that he was among the people of the Fire, until this verse was revealed, and we refrained from such testimonies." Ibn 'Abbas said: "I hope that just as no deed benefits alongside shirk, so no sin harms alongside tawhid." This was mentioned in the presence of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and 'Umar remained silent. It is also narrated as a marfu' report that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Mark yourselves with faith and affirm it, for just as the good deeds of a mushrik do not remove the mushrik from his shirk, so the sins of a believer do not remove the believer from his faith."

The second issue: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "When Wahshi killed Hamza on the day of Uhud, and they had promised him manumission if he did so, but then they did not fulfill it for him, he and his companions regretted this, and they wrote to the Prophet ﷺ about their sin, and that what prevented them from entering Islam was only the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. They said: 'We have committed everything that is in the verse.' So there was revealed: ﴿except one who repents, believes and does righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 70]. They said: 'This is a severe condition; we fear we will not be able to fulfill it.' So there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. They said: 'We fear we are not among those whom He wills.' So there was revealed: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and at that they entered Islam." Al-Qadi criticized this narration, saying: one who desires faith does not permissibly return to it on this basis; and because His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], if it were on its absolute footing, would be an incitement for them to persist in what they were upon.

The answer to this: It is not far-fetched to say that they regarded the killing of Hamza and the harming of the Messenger as so grave that doubt entered their hearts as to whether this would be forgiven for them or not; for this reason the consultation occurred. As for his saying that this is an incitement to evil: that holds only according to his own school; as for us, who say that He, exalted is He, does whatever He wills, the objection falls away. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a tremendous sin﴾, i.e., he invented a sin that is not forgiven. It is said: "So-and-so fabricated a lie" (iftara) when he fashioned it and invented it, and its root is from al-fary, meaning cutting.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 49–50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who attribute purity to themselves? Rather, God purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged even by the thread of a date-stone.﴾ ﴿Look how they invent lies against God; and sufficient is that as a manifest sin.﴾

Page 102
Know that when Exalted God threatened the Jews with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with others.﴾ At this, they said: "We are not among the polytheists; rather, we are the elect of God, Exalted," as Exalted God related of them that they said: ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and He related of them that they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and He related also that they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. Some of them used to say: "Our forefathers were prophets, so they will intercede for us." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a group of Jews brought their children to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, do these have any sin?' He said: 'No.' They said: 'By Allah, we are no different from these; what we do by night is expiated for us by day, and what we do by day is expiated for us by night.'" In sum, the people had gone to excess in attributing purity to themselves, so Exalted God mentioned in this verse that there is no consideration in a person's attributing purity to himself, and that the only consideration is God's attributing purity to him. There are issues in the verse:

The first issue: "Attributing purity" (al-tazkiyah) in this context means a person praising himself, and from it is the tazkiyah of the one who vouches for a witness (al-mu'addil). Exalted God said: ﴿So do not attribute purity to yourselves; He knows best who is righteous.﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. This is because tazkiyah is connected with piety (taqwa), and piety is a quality within, whose reality none knows except God; therefore tazkiyah is by no means fitting except from God. For this reason Exalted God said: ﴿Rather, God purifies whom He wills.﴾

If it is said: Did not the Prophet ﷺ say: "By Allah, I am trustworthy in the heavens and trustworthy on the earth"?

We say: He said that when the hypocrites said to him: "Be just in the distribution." Also, since God Exalted had already attested to his purity first through the evidence of the miracle, it was permissible for him, unlike others.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Rather, God purifies whom He wills﴾ indicates that faith comes about by the creation of God Exalted, because the most excellent and noblest kinds of purification and cleanliness is faith. So when He mentioned that He is the One who purifies whom He wills, it indicates that the faith of believers came about only by the creation of God Exalted.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged even by the thread of a date-stone﴾ is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong by the weight of an atom﴾ [al-Nisa': 40]. The meaning is that those who attribute purity to themselves will be punished for that attribution to the full extent of their due, without injustice; or the meaning is that those whom God has purified, He will reward for their obedience and will not diminish any of their reward. The fatil (thread) is what you twist between your two fingers of dirt, an form (fa'il) in the sense of maf'ul. From Ibn al-Sikkit: the fatil is what is in the cleft of a date-stone, the naqir is the small point on the back of the date-stone, and the qitmir is the thin skin over the date-stone. All these things are used as examples for something trivial and insignificant, i.e., they will not be wronged, neither a little nor a lot.

* * *
Then Exalted God said: ﴿Look how they invent lies against God﴾, and in it there are two issues:

The first issue: This is an expression of wonder to the Prophet ﷺ at their slander against God, which is their attributing purity to themselves and their fabrication against God, namely their saying: ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and their saying: what we do by day is expiated for us by night.

The second issue: Our position is that a report about a thing which is contrary to what it reports is a lie, whether its speaker knows that it is so or not. al-Jahiz said: the condition of its being a lie is that its contrariness to the fact be known. This verse is evidence for us;

From Ibn al-Sikkit: the fatil is what is in the cleft of a date-stone, the naqir is the small point on the back of the date-stone, and the qitmir is the thin skin over the date-stone. All these things are used as examples for something trivial and insignificant, i.e., they will not be wronged, neither a little nor a lot.

* * *
Then Exalted God said: ﴿Look how they invent lies against God﴾, and in it there are two issues:

The first issue: This is an expression of wonder to the Prophet ﷺ at their slander against God, which is their attributing purity to themselves and their fabrication against God, namely their saying: ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and their saying: what we do by day is expiated for us by night.

The second issue: Our position is that a report about a thing which is contrary to what it reports is a lie, whether its speaker knows that it is so or not. al-Jahiz said: the condition of its being a lie is that its contrariness to the fact be known. This verse is evidence for us;
