because they used to believe in themselves purity and cleanliness, then when they reported purity and cleanliness, God declared them liars concerning it, and this indicates what we have said.
* * *
Then Exalted God said: ﴿and sufficient is that as a manifest sin﴾. It is said "sufficient is He" as an expression of magnification, either in praise or in blame. In praise, as in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is God as a protector, and sufficient is God as a helper﴾ [al-Nisa': 45]; and in blame, as in this place. His saying: ﴿a manifest sin﴾ is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 51–52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book? They believe in jibt and taghut, and they say to those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who believe."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, and whoever Allah curses – you will not find for him a helper.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related about the Jews another kind of deceit, namely that they used to prefer the idol-worshippers over the believers. There is no doubt that they knew this was false, so their insistence upon this statement was purely out of obstinacy and bigotry. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: It is narrated that Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, two Jews, went out to Mecca with a group of Jews to form an alliance with the Quraysh against the Messenger (ﷺ). They said: "You are the People of the Book, and you are closer to Muhammad than we are, so we do not trust your scheming. Prostrate to our gods until our hearts are reassured." So they did that. This is what is meant by their belief in jibt and taghut, for they prostrated to the idols. Then Abu Sufyan said: "Are we better guided in the way, or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "What does Muhammad say?" They said: "He commands the worship of Allah alone, forbids the worship of idols, has abandoned the religion of his forefathers, and has caused division." He said: "And what is your religion?" They said: "We are the custodians of the House, we give water to the pilgrims, we host the guest, and we free the captive." And they mentioned their deeds. He said: "You are better guided in the way." This is what is meant by their saying: ﴿These are better guided in the way than those who believe﴾ [an-Nisa: 51].

The second issue: People have differed concerning jibt and taghut, and they have mentioned several interpretations:

First: The people of language said: every object worshipped besides Allah is jibt and taghut. Then most of them claimed that jibt has no derivation in the language. Al-Qaffal related from some of them that jibt originally is jibs, and the sin was changed into a ta'. Jibs is the wicked and base. As for taghut, it is derived from tughyan, which is excess in disobedience. So whoever calls to major sins is called by this name. Then they extended this name until they applied it to inanimate things, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], attributing misguidance to idols even though they are inanimate.

Second: The author of al-Kashshaf said: jibt is the idols and everything worshipped besides Allah, and taghut is the Satan.

Third: Jibt is the idols, and taghut is the interpreters of the idols, who translate for people falsehoods from them and thereby mislead them. This is related from Ibn Abbas.

Fourth: Ali ibn Abi Talhah related from Ibn Abbas that he said: jibt is the soothsayer, and taghut is the sorcerer.

Fifth: al-Kalbi said: the jibt in this verse is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and the taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and the Jews used to refer to them both. They were named by these two names because of their striving to seduce people and mislead them.

Sixth: Jibt and taghut are two idols of the Quraysh, and they are the two idols to which the Jews prostrated seeking the pleasure of the Quraysh. In sum, the sayings are many, and they are two words that were established as proper names for whoever is extreme in evil and corruption.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, and whoever Allah curses – you will not find for him a helper.﴾ He clarified that upon them is the curse from Allah, which is abandonment and distance, the opposite of what the believers have of nearness and closeness. He then informed that whomever Allah curses, there is no helper for him, as He said: ﴿Cursed wherever they are found; they will be seized and killed with a [terrible] killing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61]. This curse is present in this world, and what is in the Hereafter is greater, a day when no soul will possess anything for another soul, and the command that day belongs to Allah. In it is a promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) of victory and to the believers of strengthening, by way of opposites against opposites, as He said in the preceding verses: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a protector, and sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾ [an-Nisa: 45].

Know that these people only deserved this severe curse because what they mentioned of preferring the worshippers of idols over those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) amounts to sheer obstinacy. How can one who worships other than Allah be in a better state than one who is not content with any object of worship besides Allah? And how can one whose religion is wholly turning toward serving the Creator, turning away from this world and turning toward the Hereafter, be in a lesser state than one who is opposite to him in all these conditions? And Allah knows best.

**Al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, on Surah 4, verse 53:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or do they have a share of the dominion? Then they would not give the people so much as a speck (naqir).﴾

Know that in the preceding verse Allah described the Jews with extreme ignorance, namely their belief that the worship of idols is superior to the worship of Allah the Exalted. In this verse He described them with stinginess (bukhl) and envy (hasad). Stinginess is refusing to give anyone any of the blessing that Allah has granted you. Envy is wishing that Allah would not give anyone else any of the blessings. Stinginess and envy share the fact that the person who has them wants to withhold blessing from others. The miser withholds the blessing of his own self from others, while the envious person wants to withhold Allah's blessing from His servants. He placed that verse before this one because the human soul has two faculties: the cognitive faculty (al-quwwa al-'alima, the faculty of knowing) and the active faculty (al-quwwa al-'amila, the faculty of acting). The perfection of the cognitive faculty is knowledge, and its deficiency is ignorance. The perfection of the active faculty is praiseworthy character, and its deficiency is blameworthy character. The most deficient of blameworthy characters are stinginess and envy, because they are the two sources from which harms return to the servants of Allah.

Having understood this, we say: He placed the description of them with ignorance before their description with stinginess and envy for two reasons.

The first: the theoretical faculty takes precedence over the practical faculty in nobility and rank, and it is its root. Therefore, explaining its condition must come before explaining the condition of the practical faculty.

The second: the cause of stinginess and envy is ignorance, and the cause takes precedence over what it causes. Indeed, Allah mentioned ignorance before stinginess and envy. We have said that ignorance is the cause of stinginess and envy. As for stinginess, giving wealth is a cause of the purification of the soul and of attaining happiness in the Hereafter, while withholding wealth is a cause of holding worldly wealth in one's hand. Thus stinginess calls you to this world and prevents you from the Hereafter, while generosity calls you to the Hereafter and prevents you from this world. There is no doubt that preferring this world over the Hereafter arises only from pure ignorance. As for envy, divinity (al-ilahiyya) is the bestowal of blessings and benevolence upon servants. Whoever dislikes that is, in effect, wishing to remove God from His divinity, and that is pure ignorance. Thus it is established that the original cause of stinginess and envy is ignorance. When Allah mentioned ignorance, He followed it with the mention of stinginess and envy, so that the caused thing would be mentioned right after its cause. This is the indication of the arrangement (nazm) of this verse.

Here there are several issues.

**First issue:** Regarding *am* ("or") here, there are several views.

The first: some said the *mim* is an extra particle (silah), and the intended meaning is *a-lahum* ("do they have?"), because when *am* is not preceded by a question particle, the *mim* in it is a particle of augmentation.

The second: *am* here is connective (muttasilah), and an interrogative meaning has preceded it in sense. This is because when Allah related the words of these accursed ones to the polytheists, that they are better guided in the way than the believers, He followed it with His words ﴿or do they have a share?﴾ It is as if He said: Is it at this that one should be amazed, or at their saying that they have a share of the dominion, even though, if they had a dominion, they would be stingy with the least of the least?

The third: *am* here is disjunctive (munqati'a) and not connected at all to what came before. It is as if, when the first statement was complete, He said: "Rather, do they have a share of the dominion?" This interrogation is in the sense of denial, meaning that they have absolutely no share of the dominion. This view is the most sound of the views.

**Second issue:** They mentioned several interpretations of "dominion" here.

The first: the Jews used to say, "We are more entitled to dominion and prophethood, so how can we follow the Arabs?" So Allah refuted their statement in this verse.

The second: the Jews used to claim that dominion would return to them at the end of time, because a man from the Jews would emerge who would renew their kingdom and state and call to their religion. So Allah refuted them in this verse.

The third: the intended meaning of "dominion" here is *tamlik* (the granting of ownership or power). That is, they could only prevent your prophethood if the granting of power were in their hands, and if the granting of power were in their hands, they would be stingy with the *naqir* and the *qitmir* (the thin membrane on a date stone). So how could they have the ability to affirm or deny? Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: They were owners of gardens and wealth, and they were in power and protection, yet they were stingy toward the poor with the least of the least, so this verse was revealed.

**Third issue:** Allah made their stinginess like an obstacle preventing them from attaining dominion. This indicates that dominion and stinginess cannot coexist. The detailed account of this from the standpoint of reason is that submission to another is in itself something disliked, and a person does not bear what is disliked unless he finds in exchange something desired and sought after. The needs of people surround them from every direction. When a person bestows a benefit upon another, the eagerness of the benefactor for that person's wealth becomes a cause for that person to become submissive and obedient to him. For this reason it is said: "By kindness, the free man is enslaved." If this is absent, the natural aversion to submitting to another remains free of any opposing factor, and so submission never arises at all. Thus it is established that dominion and stinginess cannot coexist.

Furthermore, dominion is of three kinds: dominion over outward matters only, and this is the dominion of kings; dominion over inward matters only, and this is the dominion of scholars; and dominion over both outward and inward matters together, and this is the dominion of the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them. If generosity is among the necessary qualities of dominion, then it is obligatory for the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, to be at the utmost degree of generosity, magnanimity, mercy and compassion, so that each of these characters becomes a cause for the creation's submission to them and their compliance with their commands. The perfection of these qualities is found in Muhammad (peace be upon him).

**Fourth issue:** Sibawayh said: *idhan* ("then/in that case") among the operators of verbs is in the position of *azunnu* ("I think") among the operators of nouns. Its explanation is that when *zanna* (to think) occurs at the beginning of a sentence, it governs the accusative and nothing else, as in your saying: *azunnu Zaydan qa'iman* ("I think Zayd is standing"). If it occurs in the middle, it is permissible to cancel it or to make it operate, as in his saying: *Zaydun azunnu qa'imun* ("Zayd, I think, is standing"), and if you wish you may say: *Zaydan azunnu qa'iman*. If it is placed later, the better option is to cancel it, as you say: *Zaydun muntaliqun zanantu* ("Zayd is departing, I thought"). The reason for what we have mentioned is that *zanna* and similar verbs such as *'alima* ("to know") and *hasiba* ("to reckon") are weak in governing, because they do not really affect their objects. When they come first, their placement at the beginning indicates strong attention, so they become strong enough to exert influence. When they come later, that indicates lack of attention, so they become inoperative. If they occur in the middle, then they are not in the place of full attention from every standpoint, nor in the place of complete neglect from every standpoint, but are intermediate between these two states. Therefore, both operating and cancelling are permissible.

Know that making it operate in the middle position is better, and cancelling it in the later position is better.

Having understood this, we say: the word *idhan* follows this same order. If it comes first, it governs the verb, as in: *idhan ukrimaka* ("then I will honour you"). If it occurs in the middle or at the end, cancelling it is permissible, as in: *ana idhan ukrimuka* ("I, then, will honour you"), and *ana ukrimuka idhan* ("I will honour you then"), where you cancel it in these two positions.

Having understood this introduction, Allah's words ﴿then they would not give the people so much as a speck﴾ contain *idhan* placed first and yet not governing. The commentators gave several explanations for this:

The first: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the sentence, and the intended order is: "they would not give the people so much as a speck, then."

The second: since *idhan* came between the *fa* and the verb, it may be taken as if it were in the middle, and so it is cancelled, just as it is cancelled when it occurs in the middle or at the end. The same applies with the *wa* (and), as in Allah's words: ﴿And then they would not remain after you except a little﴾ [al-Isra: 76].

The third: Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿fa-idhan la yu'tu﴾ (with the verb in the subjunctive), making *idhan* operate in its governing function, which is the accusative.

**Fifth issue:** The lexicographers said: *al-naqir* is a small hollow in the back of a date stone, from which the palm tree grows. Its root is that it is a *fa'il* form from *al-naqr* (striking or hollowing out). It is also said of a piece of wood that is hollowed out: *naqir*, because it is hollowed out. *Al-naqr* means striking a stone or other object with a *minqar*, and the *minqar* is an iron tool like an axe with which stones are cut. The point is that they are stingy even with the least of the least.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 54–55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? Indeed, We gave the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ ﴿Among them were those who believed in it, and among them were those who turned away from it. And sufficient is Hell as a blazing fire.﴾

Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: "am" (or) is munqati'ah (disjunctive), and the implied meaning is: "Rather, they envy the people."

The second issue: Regarding the intended meaning of the word "al-nas" (the people), there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars, is that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). It is permissible for the plural word to be applied to him although he is one person, because there were gathered in him the qualities of goodness that would not be found except scattered among a great multitude. From this one says: "So-and-so is an ummah by himself," meaning he stands in the place of a community. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was an ummah, devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 120].

Page 107

The second opinion: The intended meaning here is the Messenger and those believers who were with him. Those who held this view said: the word "al-nas" is plural, so interpreting it as a plural is preferable to interpreting it as singular.

Know that the mention of "al-nas" is fitting for the intention of a specific group of people, because the purpose of creation is only the performance of worship, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. Since those who fulfil this purpose are none other than Muhammad (ﷺ) and whoever follows his religion, he and his companions are as if they were all of mankind; therefore it is fitting to use the word "al-nas" and intend them specifically.

The third issue: They differed in interpreting the bounty (fadl) for which they became objects of envy, in two opinions:

The first opinion: It is prophethood and the honour that results from it in religion and in this world.

The second opinion: They envied him because he had nine wives.

Know that envy arises only in the presence of excellence; the more complete and perfect a person's excellence, the greater the envy of the envious toward him. It is known that prophethood is the greatest of ranks in religion. Then Allah, exalted is He, granted it to Muhammad (ﷺ) and added to it that He made him, every day, stronger in dominion, greater in power, and more numerous in supporters and helpers, and all of this necessarily brings great envy. As for the multiplicity of wives, it is like a trivial matter compared to what we have mentioned, so it is not possible to interpret this bounty by it. Rather, if "fadl" is taken as a name for everything Allah has bestowed upon him, this too enters under it; but restricting it to that alone is far-fetched.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, clarified that the abundance of Allah's blessings upon him became the cause of the envy of these Jews, He then explained what removes that, saying: ﴿Indeed, We gave the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ The meaning is that among the descendants of Abraham there arose many people who combined prophethood and kingship, and you do not marvel at that nor envy it; so why do you marvel at the condition of Muhammad, and why do you envy him?

Know that "al-Kitab" (the Scripture) refers to the outward aspects of the Sharia, and "al-Hikmah" (wisdom) refers to the inner secrets of reality, and that is the perfection of knowledge. As for the great kingdom, it is the perfection of power. It has been established that true perfections are nothing other than knowledge and power. Thus this statement is an indication that He, glorified is He, gave them the utmost of what befits a human being of perfections; and since that was not deemed improbable concerning them, it is not improbable concerning the right of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also said: when they exaggerated about his wives, it was said to them: How do you consider nine too many for him, when David had a hundred, and Solomon had three hundred free wives and seven hundred concubines?

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Among them were those who believed in it, and among them were those who turned away from it.﴾ They differed about the meaning of "bihi" (in it). Some said: "in him" refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that among these people who were given a portion of the Scripture, some believed and some remained in disbelief and denial. Others said: the intended meaning is those prophets who preceded, peace be upon them. The meaning is that those prophets, despite what I particularized them with of prophethood and kingship, their peoples' customary condition regarding them was that some of them believed in them and some remained in disbelief. So you, O Muhammad, should not marvel at what these people are upon, for the conditions of all nations with all prophets were thus; and this is consolation from Allah, so that you would be more steadfast in patience against what you suffer from them.

Then He said: ﴿And sufficient is Hell as a blazing fire﴾, i.e., Hell is sufficient as a punishment for these disbelievers, both those who came before and those who came after, as a blaze. "Sa'ir" means fuel; it is said: "awqadtu al-nar" and "as'artuha" with one meaning.

Rather, if "fadl" is taken as a name for everything Allah has bestowed upon him, this too enters under it; but restricting it to that alone is far-fetched.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, clarified that the abundance of Allah's blessings upon him became the cause of the envy of these Jews, He then explained what removes that, saying: ﴿Indeed, We gave the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ The meaning is that among the descendants of Abraham there arose many people who combined prophethood and kingship, and you do not marvel at that nor envy it; so why do you marvel at the condition of Muhammad, and why do you envy him?

Know that "al-Kitab" (the Scripture) refers to the outward aspects of the Sharia, and "al-Hikmah" (wisdom) refers to the inner secrets of reality, and that is the perfection of knowledge. As for the great kingdom, it is the perfection of power. It has been established that true perfections are nothing other than knowledge and power. Thus this statement is an indication that He, glorified is He, gave them the utmost of what befits a human being of perfections; and since that was not deemed improbable concerning them, it is not improbable concerning the right of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also said: when they exaggerated about his wives, it was said to them: How do you consider nine too many for him, when David had a hundred, and Solomon had three hundred free wives and seven hundred concubines?

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Among them were those who believed in it, and among them were those who turned away from it.﴾ They differed about the meaning of "bihi" (in it). Some said: "in him" refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that among these people who were given a portion of the Scripture, some believed and some remained in disbelief and denial. Others said: the intended meaning is those prophets who preceded, peace be upon them. The meaning is that those prophets, despite what I particularized them with of prophethood and kingship, their peoples' customary condition regarding them was that some of them believed in them and some remained in disbelief. So you, O Muhammad, should not marvel at what these people are upon, for the conditions of all nations with all prophets were thus; and this is consolation from Allah, so that you would be more steadfast in patience against what you suffer from them.

Then He said: ﴿And sufficient is Hell as a blazing fire﴾, i.e., Hell is sufficient as a punishment for these disbelievers, both those who came before and those who came after, as a blaze. "Sa'ir" means fuel; it is said: "awqadtu al-nar" and "as'artuha" with one meaning.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs – We will surely drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might, Wise.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, after mentioning the threat directed at the particular group among the People of the Book, clarified what encompasses the threat for all disbelievers, so He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The signs (ayat) include everything that points to the Essence of Allah, His acts, His attributes and His names, as well as the angels, the books and the messengers. Their disbelief in the signs does not occur only through outright denial, but in several ways: among them, that they deny that they are signs; among them, that they are heedless of them and do not reflect upon them; among them, that they cast doubts and dubious claims upon them; and among them, that they deny them while knowing them, out of obstinacy and envy. As for the definition and reality of kufr (disbelief), we have mentioned it in Surat al-Baqarah in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6].

The second issue: Sibawayh said: "Sawfa" (سوف, "will surely") is a word used for threat and warning; one says "sawfa af'alu" (I will surely do). The letter sin (س) may take its place, as in His saying: ﴿I will drive him into Saqar﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26]. The word "sawfa" also occurs in promise, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5], and He said: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ [Yusuf: 98]. It has been said: he deferred it to the time of dawn in order to make the supplication certain. In sum, the letter sin (س) and "sawfa" are both specific to the future.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿nusliihim﴾ (We will drive them) means: We will make them enter the Fire. However, His saying ﴿nusliihim﴾ contains an addition beyond that, for it is like: "I roasted it with fire" (shawaytuhu bil-nar). One says: a roasted sheep (shatun maslliyyah), i.e., a roasted (mashwiyyah) one.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment﴾. In this there are two questions:

The first question: Since He, exalted is He, is able to keep them alive in the Fire forever and ever, why did He not keep their bodies in the Fire protected from roasting and burning, even though He delivers to them severe pains, so that there would be no need to replace their skins with other skins?

The answer: He, exalted is He, is not questioned about what He does. Rather, we say: He, exalted is He, is able to deliver to their bodies great pains without putting them in the Fire, even though He, exalted is He, has put them in the Fire.

The second question: If the disobedient skins are burnt, and then Allah creates other skins in their place and punishes them, this would be punishing one who did not disobey, and this is not permissible.

The answer to this is given in several ways:

The first: The roasted is taken to be other than the roasted (al-nadij ghayr al-naḍīj), so the essence is one and what changes is the attribute. When the essence is one, the punishment reaches only the disobedient one. On this reckoning, the intended "otherness" is difference in attribute.

The second: The one punished is the human being, and that skin was not part of the quiddity of the human being, but was like a thing attached to him, extra to his essence. So when Allah renews the skin, and that new skin becomes the means by which the punishment reaches him, this is not a punishment except for the disobedient one.

The third: The intended "skins" are the sarabil (garments), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their garments are of pitch﴾ [Ibrahim: 50]. Thus the renewal of skins is in fact the renewal of garments. Al-Qadi criticized this, saying: it is abandoning the apparent meaning; and also, garments of pitch are not described as "roasted" (nuḍj) but as "burnt" (iḥtiraq).

The fourth: It may be said that this is a metaphor for permanence and non-cessation, as one says of someone whose continuity is intended: "Whenever he ends, he has begun, and whenever he reaches his end, he has begun from his beginning." Likewise His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ means: whenever they think they have been roasted, burnt, and reached destruction, We give them a new strength of life, such that they think they have now come into being and been created. So the purpose is to show the permanence of the punishment and its non-cessation.

The fifth: Al-Suddi said: He, exalted is He, replaces the skins from the flesh of the disbeliever, bringing forth from his flesh another skin. This is far-fetched, because his flesh is finite, so it must be exhausted; and when his flesh is exhausted there must be another way of replacing the skin, and that way was not mentioned earlier. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿so they may taste the punishment﴾. In this there are two questions:

The first question: His saying ﴿so they may taste the punishment﴾ means: that its tasting may continue for them and not cease, like your saying to one who is honoured: "May Allah make you honoured", i.e., may He keep you upon honour and increase you in it. Also, the intended meaning is: that they may taste the punishment in this new state; otherwise they are already tasting it and continuously undergoing it.

The second question: It is only said "so-and-so tasted the punishment" when he has perceived a small amount of it, and Allah has described that they were in the most severe punishment, so how is it fitting that after that He mentions that they tasted the punishment?

The answer: The purpose of mentioning tasting is to inform that their perception of that punishment in every state is like the perception of one who tastes what is tasted, in that no diminishment or cessation enters into it because of that burning.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might, Wise﴾. By "al-'Aziz" is meant: the Able, the Overpowering; and by "al-Hakim" is meant: the One who does only what is right. The mention of these two in this place is most fitting, because there arises in the heart a wonder: how is it possible for a human being to remain in the intense Fire forever and ever? It is said: this is not strange for Allah, for He is the Mighty, the Overpowering over all possibilities; He is able to remove the nature of fire. And there arises in the heart the thought that He is Generous and Merciful; how then does it befit His mercy to punish this weak person to such a great extent? It is said: just as He is Merciful, He is also Wise, and wisdom requires this. For the order of the world cannot remain except by threatening the disobedient, and the threat issued by Him must necessarily be accompanied by fulfilment, to safeguard His speech from falsehood. Thus it is established that the mention of these two words here is in the utmost fitness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 57:

Page 110

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to a shade, deep and extending.﴾

Know that it has been the custom of Allah, exalted is He, in this Noble Book that promise and threat are commonly mentioned together. In this verse there are two issues:

The first issue: This verse indicates that faith (iman) is other than action ('amal), because He, exalted is He, joined action to faith by conjunction ('atf), and the conjoined is different from that to which it is conjoined. The judge (al-Qadi) said: Whenever the word faith is mentioned alone, action enters into it; and whenever action is mentioned along with it, faith means assent (tasdiq). This is far-fetched, because the original state is the absence of homonymy (ishtirak) and the absence of change (taghyir). Were it not so, the Qur'an would cease to be informative. Thus it may be that these words that we hear in the Qur'an each have a meaning beyond what we know, and that the intended meaning of Allah, exalted is He, is that meaning, not this one that our understandings have immediately grasped. This is on the view that the likelihood of homonymy and of univocity is equal. But on the view that the likelihood of remaining on the original and the likelihood of change are equal, this does not follow; for on this assumption it may be said: these words were, in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), set for a meaning other than what we understand now, and then changed to what we understand now. Thus it is established that on these two assumptions the Qur'an ceases to be a proof (hujjah). And when it is established that homonymy and change are contrary to the original state, the judge's argument is refuted.

The second issue: Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned several matters in describing the reward of the obedient:

One of them: that He, exalted is He, will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that the waters of the rivers flow beneath them. Know that if "river" is taken as a name for the place of the water, the matter is as al-Zajjaj said; but if we take it in common usage as a name for that water, there is no need for this implied elision (idmar).

The second: that He, exalted is He, described them as eternal and everlasting. This contains a refutation of Jahm ibn Safwan, who says that the bliss of Paradise and the punishment of Hell come to an end. Also, He, exalted is He, mentioned "everlasting" together with "forever" (abadan); and if khulud were an expression for ta'bid, it would entail repetition, which is not permissible. This shows that khulud is not an expression for ta'bid, but rather for a long stay without indicating whether it is cut off or not cut off. Once this principle is established, the Mu'tazilah's argument by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally – his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa: 93], that the person committing a grave sin remains in the Fire eternally, is refuted; for we have shown, by the indication of this verse, that khulud is for a long stay, not for perpetuity.

The third: His saying: ﴿For them therein are purified spouses﴾, and what is meant is their purity from menstruation, postpartum bleeding, and all the filths of this world. A similar statement is His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses, and they therein abide forever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. The subtle points suitable to this place have already been mentioned under that verse.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿And We will admit them to a shade, deep and extending.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: "al-zalil" does not indicate an action so as to be said to be in the sense of an active or passive participle; rather it is an intensive description of the shade, like the Arabs' saying: "a night that is pitch-dark" (layl alyal).

Know that the lands of the Arabs were extremely hot, so shade was among them the greatest means of comfort; for this reason they used it as a metaphor for comfort. He, upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "The sultan is the shadow of Allah on earth." When shade is an expression for comfort, then "zalil" is a metaphor for great intensity of comfort. This is what my mind inclines to. By this path is repelled the objection of one who says: if there is no sun in Paradise harming with its heat, what is the benefit of describing it as deep shade? And also we see in this world that places where shade persists and the light of the sun does not reach become stagnant and foul air, harmful; so what is the meaning of describing the air of Paradise thus? For in this manner which we have summarized, these doubts are removed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 58 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their rightful owners﴾.

Know that when He, glorified is He, explained some of the states of the disbelievers and explained His threat against them, He returned to mentioning the obligations a second time. Also, when He related about the People of the Book that they concealed the truth, when they said to those who disbelieved, "These are better guided in the way than those who believe," He commanded the believers in this verse to discharge trusts in all matters, whether those matters concern the domain of creeds and religions or the domain of worldly affairs and dealings. Also, when He mentioned in the previous verse the great reward for those who believed and did righteous deeds, and trustworthiness is among the most excellent righteous deeds, He therefore commanded it in this verse. There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: It is reported that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah on the day of the Conquest, Uthman ibn Talhah ibn Abd al-Dar, who was the custodian (sadin) of the Ka'bah, closed the door of the Ka'bah, climbed onto the roof, and refused to hand over the key to him, and said, "If I had known that he was the Messenger of Allah, I would not have prevented him." Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) twisted his hand, took the key from him, and opened the door. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered and prayed two rak'ahs. When he came out, al-Abbas asked him to give him the key and to combine for him the watering duty (al-siqayah) and the custodianship (al-sidanah). Then this verse was revealed, so he commanded Ali to return it to Uthman and to apologise to him. Uthman said to Ali, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and informed the Messenger (ﷺ) that the custodianship would remain among the descendants of Uthman forever. This is the statement of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

Abu Rawq said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Uthman, 'Give me the key.' He said, 'Here it is, by the trust of Allah.' When he (ﷺ) wanted to take it, Uthman closed his hand. The Messenger (ﷺ) said that a second time: 'If you believe in Allah and the Last Day, give me the key.' He said, 'Here it is, by the trust of Allah.' When he wanted to take it, he closed his hand. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said that a third time. Uthman said the third time, 'Here it is, by the trust of Allah,' and handed it to the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) got up to circumambulate with the key in his hand, and he wanted to hand it to al-Abbas. Then he said, 'O Uthman, take the key, on condition that al-Abbas has a share with you.' So Allah revealed this verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said to Uthman, 'Take it, an everlasting and inherited possession, which none will take from you except a wrongdoer.'" Then Uthman emigrated and handed the key to his brother Shaybah, and so it is in his descendants today.

The second issue: Know that the revelation of this verse on account of this incident does not necessitate that it is restricted to this case; rather, all kinds of trusts are included in it. Know that a person's dealing is either with his Lord, or with the rest of the servants, or with himself, and it is necessary to observe trust in all these three categories.

As for observing trust with the Lord, it consists in performing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden, and this is a sea without shore. Ibn Mas'ud said: "Trust is obligatory in everything: in ablution, in ritual impurity, in prayer, in zakat, and in fasting." Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: "Allah, the Exalted, created the private part of a human being and said: 'This is a trust I have deposited with you, so guard it except in its right.'" Know that this is a wide domain. The trust of the tongue is that one does not use it in lying, backbiting, slander, disbelief, innovation, obscenity and the like. The trust of the eye is that one does not use it to look at what is unlawful. The trust of the hearing is that one does not use it to listen to frivolous and forbidden things, to obscenity and falsehoods and the like. The same applies to all the limbs.

As for the second category, which is observing trust with the rest of creation, it includes returning deposits. It includes avoiding fraud in measuring and weighing. It includes not exposing people's faults. It includes the justice of rulers toward their subjects, and the justice of scholars toward the common people, by not compelling them into false partisanship, but rather guiding them to beliefs and actions that benefit them in their worldly life and their hereafter. It includes the prohibition on the Jews from concealing the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and their prohibition from saying to the disbelievers that what you are upon is better than the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). It includes the Messenger's (peace be upon him) command to return the key to Uthman ibn Talhah. It includes the wife's trust toward her husband in guarding her private part, and in not attributing to her husband a child born from another, and in her reporting the end of her waiting period ('iddah).

As for the third category, which is a person's trust with himself, it is that he does not choose for himself except what is most beneficial and most suitable for him in religion and worldly life, and that he does not, out of desire or anger, undertake what harms him in the hereafter. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock." So His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts﴾, includes all of this. Allah has magnified the matter of trust in many places in His Book. He said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and man bore it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. He said: ﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant, shepherds﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 8]. He said: ﴿And do not betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal: 27]. He, peace be upon him, said: "There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness." Maymun ibn Mihran said: "Three things must be rendered to the righteous and the wicked: trust, covenant, and the maintaining of kinship ties." Al-Qadi said: Although the word "trust" (amanah) encompasses all of these, He, the Exalted, said in this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their rightful owners﴾, so it is necessary that the intended meaning of this trust be that which is in the category of property, because it is that which can be rendered to another.

The third issue: "Trust" (amanah) is a verbal noun used to designate the thing entrusted (maf'ul), and that is why it is made plural, for it has been made a pure noun. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been read as "al-amanah" in the singular.

The fourth issue: Abu Bakr al-Razi said: Among trusts are deposits, and it is obligatory to return them upon demand, and most scholars hold that they are not guaranteed (by the depositary). It is reported from some of the early generations (salaf) that they are guaranteed. Al-Sha'bi reported from Anas, who said: A man entrusted me with merchandise, and it was lost from among my garments, and Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) held me liable for it. And from Anas, who said: A man had a deposit with me of six thousand dirhams, and it was lost. Umar said: "Did anything else go with it for you?" I said: "No." So he obliged me to bear the liability. The argument of the well-known view is what Amr ibn Shu'ayb reported from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no liability on a shepherd, nor on one entrusted." As for the action of Umar, it is interpreted to mean that the depositary had confessed to an act that makes him liable.

* * *

The fifth issue: Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: a loan (al-'ariyyah) is guaranteed after its destruction, and Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is not guaranteed. The proof of al-Shafi'i is His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their rightful owners﴾, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. After its destruction, returning it in its form is impossible, and returning its value is returning it in meaning, so the verse indicates the obligation of compensation. A parallel to this verse is the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "The hand is responsible for what it has taken until it returns it." The most that can be said regarding this chapter is that the verse is specified in the case of a deposit, but the general (ruling), after specification, remains a valid proof. Also, we agree that the one who is hired for a price (al-musta'jir / the one who takes in exchange) is liable, and that the depositary is not liable, and the loan falls between them. So we say: the resemblance between the loan and the one who takes in exchange is greater, because each of them took the item for his own purpose, unlike the depositary, who took the deposit for the owner's purpose. Therefore the resemblance between the borrowed item and the item taken in exchange is more complete, and the difference between the borrowed item and the deposit becomes evident. The proof of Abu Hanifah is the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "There is no liability on one who is trusted." We say: it is specified in the case of one who takes in exchange, so likewise in the case of the loan. Also, our proof is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and it is stronger.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Indeed, how excellent is what Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾.

Regarding this there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that trust is an expression for when a right is due to another from you and you render that right to him. This is trust. Judging with right is an expression for when a right is due to a person from another and you order the one upon whom that right is due to deliver it to the one who has that right. Since the correct order is that a person begins with himself in securing benefits and warding off harms, and then turns to others, Allah, the Exalted, therefore mentioned the command to trust first, and after it mentioned the command to judge with right. How excellent is this order, for most of the subtleties of the Qur'an are deposited in its arrangements and connections.

The second issue: They are unanimous that whoever is a judge is obligated to judge with justice. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾. The implied meaning is: "Indeed, Allah commands you, when you judge between people, to judge with justice." He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ [al-Nahl: 90]. He said: ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾ [al-An'am: 152]. He said: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾ [Sad: 26]. From Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "This nation will remain in good as long as, when it speaks, it is truthful, when it judges, it is just, and when it asks for mercy, it is shown mercy." From al-Hasan, who said: Allah took three things from the judges: that they not follow desire, that they fear Him and not fear people, and that they not sell His signs for a small price. Then he recited: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth﴾ [Sad: 26] up to His saying: ﴿and do not follow desire﴾ [Sad: 26], and he recited: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light, by which the prophets judged﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44] up to His saying: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. Among what indicates the obligation of justice are the verses that reprove injustice. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Gather those who wronged, and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22]. He, peace be upon him, said: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are the wrongdoers, and where are the helpers of the wrongdoers?' They will all be gathered, even whoever sharpened a pen for them or provided an inkwell for them, and they will be gathered and thrown into the Fire." He also said: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], and He said: ﴿So those are their houses, ruined because of what they did wrongfully﴾ [al-Naml: 52].

If it is said: The purpose of injustice is worldly benefit.

Allah answers this objection with His saying: ﴿We did not inhabit them after them except a little, and We were the inheritors﴾ [al-Qasas: 58].

* * *

The third issue: Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The judge should treat the two litigants equally in five things: in entering upon him, in sitting before him, in turning his attention to both of them, in listening to both of them, and in passing judgment upon both of them. He said: What is required of him is equality between them in outward actions, not in the heart. If his heart inclines toward one of them and he loves that his proof should prevail over the other, there is no blame upon him, because he cannot guard against that. He said: He should not prompt either of them with his argument, nor a witness with his testimony, because that harms one of the two litigants. He should not prompt the claimant with the claim or the oath, nor prompt the defendant with denial or admission, nor prompt the witnesses to testify or not to testify. He should not host one of the two litigants without the other, because that breaks the heart of the other. Nor should he accept the hospitality of one of them, nor the hospitality of both while they are still disputing.

"It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) would not host an adversary unless his opponent was with him." The complete discussion of this is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh), and the essence of the matter is that the judge's aim in his ruling should be to deliver the right to its rightful owner, and that this should not be mixed with any other purpose. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And when you judge between people, that you judge with justice﴾.
* * *
The fourth issue: His saying ﴿And when you judge between people, that you judge with justice﴾ is, as it were, an explicit statement that not all people may undertake judgment; rather, it belongs to some of them. Then the verse remains general as to by what means one becomes a judge. When the other proofs showed that the Muslim community necessarily needs a supreme Imam, and that he is the one who appoints the judges and governors in the lands, those proofs became like an explanation of the generality in this verse.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever an excellent instructor of you﴾. That is, "what an excellent thing He instructs you with," or "what an excellent one is He who instructs you." The object of praise is omitted, meaning: "what an excellent thing is that with which He instructs you," namely the commandment to render trusts to their owners and to judge with justice.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾. That is, act in accordance with Allah's command and admonition, for He is most knowing of what is heard and what is seen, and He will recompense you for what proceeds from you. There is another subtle point here: when He commanded, in these verses, judging by way of justice and rendering the trust, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾. That is, if you judge with justice, He hears every heard thing, including that judgment; and if you render the trust, He sees every seen thing, including that. There is no doubt that this is the greatest of the causes of promise for the obedient and the greatest of the causes of warning for the disobedient, and to this the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded in his saying: "Worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you." There is another subtle point: the more the servant's need is greater, the more Allah's care is perfect; and rulers and judges are those to whose rulings Allah has entrusted the interests of His servants, so concern for their judgment and their decisions is greater. He, glory be to Him, is exalted above heedlessness, forgetfulness, and variation in seeing what is seen and hearing what is heard. But even if we supposed that such variation were possible, the most fitting occasion for guarding against heedlessness and forgetfulness would be the time of rulers' and judges' rulings. Since this position is singled out for extra care, He rightly said at the close of this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾. How excellent are these concluding phrases, matching these opening ones.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 59 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most suitable in result.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the shepherds and rulers to act justly towards their subjects, He commanded the subjects to obey the rulers, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah﴾. For this reason ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is incumbent upon the imam to rule by what Allah has revealed and to render the trust, and when he does that, it is incumbent upon the subjects to listen and obey." And in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The Muʿtazilah said: obedience is conformity with the will (irada), while our companions (the Ashʿariyyah) said: obedience is conformity with the command, not conformity with the will. Our proof is that there is no dispute that conformity with the command is obedience; the dispute is whether the commanded act must be willed or not. When we demonstrate that the commanded act may not be willed, it becomes established that obedience is not an expression of conformity with the will. We say that Allah may command what He does not will, because the knowledge of Allah and His report have related that faith will never come from Abu Lahab at all, and this knowledge and this report cannot be removed or reversed into ignorance, while the existence of faith is contrary to and incompatible with this knowledge and this report, and the combination of two opposites is impossible, so the emergence of faith from Abu Lahab is impossible. Allah, exalted is He, knows all these states, so He knows that it is impossible, and one who knows that a thing is impossible does not will it. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, does not will faith from Abu Lahab, though He has commanded him to believe. It is thus established that a command may exist without will, and when this is established, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that obedience to Allah is an expression of conformity with His command, not with His will. As for the Muʿtazilah, they argued that obedience is a term for conformity with the will by the words of the poet:

"Many a one whose chest I have made seethe with rage, who wished for my death, has not obeyed."

He linked obedience to wishing, which is of the same kind as will.

The answer: a rational person knows that the decisive proof we have mentioned should not be opposed by such a feeble argument.

* * *

The second issue: Know that this verse is a noble verse comprising most of the knowledge of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), because the jurists claimed that the roots of the Sharia are four: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma') and analogy (qiyas). This verse comprises the establishment of these four roots in this order. As for the Book and the Sunnah, they are indicated by His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾.

If it is said: Is not obeying the Messenger the same as obeying Allah? What is the meaning of this conjunction?

We say: al-Qadi said: the benefit of this is to explain the two indications. The Book indicates the command of Allah, and from it we inevitably know the command of the Messenger; the Sunnah indicates the command of the Messenger, and from it we inevitably know the command of Allah. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that His saying ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ indicates the obligation of following the Book and the Sunnah.

Page 116

* * *

The third issue: Know that His saying ﴿and those of authority among you﴾ indicates, according to us, that the consensus of the community is a proof (hujjah). The evidence for this is that Allah, exalted is He, commanded obedience to those of authority in this verse with an absolute decisiveness, and whoever Allah commands us to obey with absolute decisiveness must be free from error, for if he were not free from error, then, by supposing that he commits an error, Allah would have commanded that he be followed, and that would be a command to perform that error; and the error, by being an error, is forbidden, so this leads to the combination of command and prohibition regarding a single act in a single respect, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that Allah commanded obedience to those of authority with decisiveness, and it is established that everyone whom Allah commands us to obey with decisiveness must be free from error. So it is established with certainty that those of authority mentioned in this verse must be infallible. Then we say: that infallible one is either the whole community or some of the community. It is not permissible that it be some of the community, because we have shown that Allah, exalted is He, decisively made obedience to those of authority obligatory in this verse, and the decisive obligation of obeying them is conditional upon our knowing them, being able to reach them and benefit from them. We know by necessity that in our time we are unable to know the infallible imam, unable to reach them, and unable to derive religion and knowledge from them. Since this is so, we know that the infallible one whom Allah commanded the believers to obey is not some part of the community nor a group of its groups. Since this is refuted, it is necessary that the infallible one who is meant by His saying ﴿those of authority﴾ be the people of binding and loosing (ahl al-hall wa'l-aqd) of the community, and this necessitates the certainty that the consensus of the community is a proof.

If it is said: The exegetes have mentioned other meanings for "those of authority" besides what you have mentioned. One of them: that what is meant by those of authority is the rightly guided caliphs.

The second: what is meant is the commanders of the expeditions (sara'a). Said Saʿid ibn Jubayr: this verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi, when the Prophet ﷺ sent him as commander over an expedition. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning Khalid ibn al-Walid, whom the Prophet ﷺ sent as commander over an expedition in which ʿAmmar ibn Yasir was present, and a disagreement arose between them over something, so this verse was revealed and commanded obedience to those of authority.

The third: what is meant are the scholars who give fatwas on the legal rulings and teach people their religion. This is the narration of al-Tha'labi from Ibn ʿAbbas and the saying of al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: it is reported from the Rafidah that what is meant by it are the infallible imams. And since the sayings of the community regarding the interpretation of this verse are confined to these meanings, and the view you have supported lies outside them, that is by the consensus of the community void.

The second question: We say that understanding "those of authority" as the commanders and sultans is preferable to what you have mentioned. The following points indicate this:

The first: the commands of the commanders and sultans are binding upon creation, so they are in reality those of authority, whereas the people of consensus have no binding command over creation, so it is preferable to take the word to mean commanders and sultans.

The second: the beginning and end of the verse suit what we have mentioned. As for the beginning of the verse, He, exalted is He, commanded the rulers to render trusts and to observe justice; and as for the end of the verse, He commanded referring to the Book and the Sunnah in what is unclear, and this is only fitting for commanders, not for the people of consensus.

The third: the Prophet ﷺ greatly emphasized encouragement to obey the commanders, saying: "Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys my commander has disobeyed me." This is what can be mentioned of the question against the argument we have given.

The answer: there is no dispute that a group of the Companions and the Successors understood His saying ﴿and those of authority among you﴾ to mean the scholars. When we say that what is meant by it is all the scholars from among the people of binding and loosing, this is not a view outside the views of the community, but rather the choosing of one of their views and affirming it with a decisive proof. Thus the first question is dispelled. As for their second question, it is rebutted, because the meanings they mentioned are weak, while what we have mentioned is a decisive demonstration, so our view is preferable. Moreover, we counter those meanings with other meanings stronger than them:

The first of them: the community is agreed that the commanders and sultans are to be obeyed only in what is known by evidence to be true and correct, and that evidence is nothing but the Book and the Sunnah. Then this is not a separate category apart from obedience to the Book and the Sunnah, nor apart from obedience to Allah and His Messenger, but is included within it, just as the obligation to obey a wife toward a husband, a child toward parents, and a student toward a teacher is included in obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger. But if we take it to mean consensus, this category would not be included under them, because consensus may indicate a ruling for which there is no indication in the Book and the Sunnah, so it is possible to make this category separate from the first two, and this is preferable.

The second: taking the verse to mean obedience to commanders necessitates introducing a condition into the verse, because obedience to commanders is obligatory only when they are with the truth. But if we take it to mean consensus, no condition enters the verse, so this is preferable.

The third: His later saying ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ suggests a prior consensus whose ruling contradicts the ruling of this dispute.

The fourth: obedience to Allah and to His Messenger is obligatory with certainty, and according to us obedience to the people of consensus is obligatory with certainty, whereas obedience to commanders and sultans is not obligatory with certainty; rather, in most cases it is forbidden, since they command only injustice, and in a few cases it is obligatory according to weak conjecture. So taking the verse to mean consensus is preferable, because it places the Messenger and those of authority under one word, His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of authority﴾. So taking "those of authority," which is joined with the Messenger, to mean the infallible is preferable to taking it to mean the wicked, corrupt ruler.

The fifth: the actions of commanders and sultans depend on the fatwas of the scholars, and the scholars are in reality the commanders of the commanders. So taking the word "those of authority" to mean them is preferable. As for taking the verse to mean the infallible imams according to what the Rafidah say, it is far-fetched, for several reasons:

The first of them: what we have mentioned, that their obedience is conditional upon knowing them and being able to reach them. If He obligated us to obey them before knowing them, this would be imposing what cannot be borne; and if He obligated us to obey them once we come to know them and their doctrines, this obligation becomes conditional. But the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those of authority among you﴾ requires absoluteness. Moreover, the verse itself removes this possibility, because He commanded obedience to the Messenger and obedience to those of authority in a single expression, His saying: ﴿and obey the Messenger and those of authority among you﴾. A single expression cannot be both absolute and conditional at once, so since this expression is absolute with regard to the Messenger, it must be absolute with regard to those of authority.

The second: He commanded obedience to those of authority, and "those of authority" is plural, whereas according to them there is at any time only one imam, and taking a plural to mean a singular goes against the apparent meaning.

The third: He said: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. Had the intended meaning of "those of authority" been the infallible imam, it would have been necessary to say: "And if you disagree over anything, refer it to the imam." Thus it is established that the correct interpretation of the verse is what we have mentioned.

* * *

The fourth issue: Know that His saying ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ indicates, according to us, that analogy (qiyas) is a proof. The evidence for this is that His saying ﴿And if you disagree over anything﴾ either means: if you disagree over a matter whose ruling is explicitly stated in the Book, the Sunnah or the consensus; or it means: if you disagree over a matter whose ruling is not explicitly stated in any of these three. The first is invalid, because on that supposition obedience to it was already obligatory, so that
