Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 59 (part 2 of 3):

[Lies] included under His saying: ﴿Obey Allah, and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾. In that case, His saying ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ would be a repetition of what has already passed, and that is impermissible. When this possibility is invalid, the second one is determined, namely that what is meant is: ﴿If you dispute about anything whose ruling is not mentioned in the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus (ijma')﴾. Since that is the case, what is meant by His saying ﴿refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ is not seeking its ruling from the texts of the Book and the Sunnah. It is therefore necessary that what is meant is referring its ruling back to the rulings stated explicitly in cases similar to it, and that is analogy (qiyas). Thus it is established that the verse indicates the command to use analogy.

If it is said: Why could it not be that what is meant by His saying ﴿refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ is: entrust its knowledge to Allah, keep silent about it, and do not engage with it? And also, why could it not be that what is meant is: refer what is not explicitly stated to what is explicitly stated, in that it is not judged except by an explicit text? And also, why could it not be that what is meant is: refer these rulings to the original state of non-liability (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah)?

We reply: As for the first, it is rejected, because this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, divided events into two categories: some whose ruling is explicitly stated, and others for which this is not the case. Then He commanded obedience and submission in the first category, and commanded referral to Allah and to the Messenger in the second category. It is not permissible that this referral means silence, because the event may not admit of that. Rather, it is necessary to end the dispute and contention concerning it by negation or affirmation. Since that is the case, it is impossible to interpret referral to Allah as silence about that event. With this answer, the invalidity of the third question becomes evident.

As for the second question, its answer is that the original state of non-liability is known through the judgment of reason. Therefore, referring the event to it is not a referral to Allah in any way whatsoever. But when we refer the ruling of the event to the rulings explicitly stated concerning it, this is a referral of the event to the rulings of Allah, exalted is He. So interpreting the wording in this way is more appropriate.

* * *

The fifth issue: This verse indicates that the Book and the Sunnah take precedence over analogy absolutely. It is therefore not permissible to abandon acting upon them on account of analogy, nor is it permissible at all to restrict them on account of analogy, whether the analogy is clear (jali) or hidden (khafi), and whether or not that text was previously restricted. The proof of this is that we have explained that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ is a command to obey the Book and the Sunnah, and this command is unrestricted. Thus it is established that following the Book and the Sunnah is obligatory, whether there arises an analogy that opposes them, or one that restricts them, or none at all. Several other considerations confirm this:

The first: The particle "inna" (if), according to the view of many people, expresses a condition. On this view, His saying ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ is explicit that it is not permissible to turn to analogy except when the sources are absent.

The second: He, exalted is He, delayed mention of analogy until after mention of the three sources. This indicates that acting upon it is deferred behind the three sources.

The third: The Prophet (ﷺ) observed this order in the story of Mu'adh, when he deferred independent reasoning (ijtihad) behind the Book, and made its permissibility conditional on not finding the Book and the Sunnah, by his saying: "But if you do not find [it]..."

The fourth: He, exalted is He, commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:34]. Then Iblis did not reject this text entirely; rather he excepted himself from that general command by means of an analogy, which is his saying: ﴿You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾ [Sad 38:76]. Then all rational people agreed that he placed analogy before the text, and for that reason he became accursed. This indicates that restricting a text by analogy is giving precedence to analogy over the text, and that this is impermissible.

The fifth: The Qur'an is certain in its text, because it is established by mass transmission (tawatur), whereas analogy is not like that. Rather, it is speculative (madhnun) in every respect, and what is certain takes precedence over what is speculative.

[p. 119]

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, they are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:45]. If we find the general sense of the Book applicable to the event, and then we do not judge by it but judge by analogy, it follows that we have entered under this generality.

The seventh: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:1]. If the general sense of the Qur'an is present, and then we put forward a restricting analogy, it follows that we have put [ourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger.

The eighth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those who associated will say, "If Allah had willed..."﴾ [al-An'am 6:148], up to His saying: ﴿You follow only assumption﴾ [al-An'am 6:148]. He made following assumption one of the attributes of the disbelievers and one of the strong grounds for censuring them. This requires that acting upon analogy is not permissible at all. This text has been set aside because of what we have explained, that it indicates the permissibility of acting upon analogy; but it indicates that only when texts are absent. Therefore, when texts are present, it must remain on the original basis.

The ninth: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When a hadith is narrated from me, present it to the Book of Allah. If it agrees with it, accept it, and otherwise leave it." There is no doubt that a hadith is stronger than analogy. If a hadith that the Book does not agree with is rejected, then analogy is more deserving of rejection.

The tenth: The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, "falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it; it is a revelation from One who is Wise and Praiseworthy" [Fussilat 41:42]. Analogy confuses the reason of a weak human being, and everyone who has sound reason knows that the first (the Qur'an) is stronger and more deserving through following it.

* * *

The sixth issue: This verse indicates that whatever lies outside these four sources, namely the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, and analogy, is rejected and invalid. This is because He, exalted is He, divided events into two categories:

One of them: those whose rulings are explicitly stated, and in which He commanded obedience. This is His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾.

The second: those whose rulings are not explicitly stated, and in which He commanded independent reasoning. This is His saying: ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾. Since there is no addition to these two categories, and Allah, exalted is He, has commanded in each of them a specific obligation, this indicates that the one who is obligated may not hold on to anything other than these four sources. Once this is established, we say: As for the doctrine of juristic preference (istihsan), which Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) holds, and the doctrine of considerations of public interest (istislah), which Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) holds: if what is meant by them is one of these sources, then this is a change of terminology with no benefit in it. If they are other than these four, then holding them is definitively invalid, because this verse indicates their invalidity, as we have mentioned.

* * *

The seventh issue: Many jurists claimed that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation (lil-wujub). The theologians objected to this, saying: [The verse says] "Obey Allah," and this does not indicate obligation unless it is established that the command is for obligation. This requires that the proof depend upon what it proves, and that is invalid. The jurists may answer this in two ways:

The first: The commands that occur in specific cases indicate recommendation (nadb). So if His saying "Obey" meant that performing the commanded acts is recommended, then this verse would have no benefit left, because mere recommendation was already known from those commands. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it as conveying obligation, so that it is said: the commands indicated that performing those commanded acts is preferable to omitting them, and this verse indicated the prohibition of omitting them. In that case the verse retains a benefit.

The second: He, exalted is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and this is a warning. Just as the possibility that it is specific to His saying ﴿refer it back to Allah﴾ exists, so too the possibility that it returns to both clauses, namely His saying ﴿Obey Allah﴾ and His saying ﴿refer it back to Allah﴾, exists. There is no doubt that caution lies in this. If we judge that this warning returns to the whole, then His saying ﴿Obey Allah﴾ becomes binding as an obligation. It is thus established that this verse indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, and there is no doubt that this is a principle recognized in the Law.

* * *

The eighth issue: Know that what is transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ) is either a statement or an action. As for a statement, obeying it is obligatory, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾. As for an action, it is obligatory for the community to follow him in it, except what the evidence has excepted. This is because we have explained that His saying ﴿Obey﴾ indicates that the commands of Allah are obligatory. Then He, exalted is He, said in another verse describing Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿Follow him﴾ [al-An'am 6:153]. This is a command, so it must be for obligation. Thus it is established that following him is obligatory. Following (al-muta level) is an expression for performing the same act as another, because that other person performed it. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿Obey Allah﴾ requires following the Messenger in all his actions, and His saying ﴿and obey the Messenger﴾ requires following him in all his statements. There is no doubt that these two are principles recognized in the Law.

* * *

The ninth issue: Know that although the apparent meaning of a command, in its original linguistic imposition, does not indicate repetition or immediacy, nonetheless in the usage of the Law it does indicate them. This is indicated by several considerations:

The first: His saying ﴿Obey Allah﴾ can validly be qualified by an exception at any time whatsoever. The ruling of an exception is to exclude what would have been included without it. Therefore His saying ﴿Obey Allah﴾ must encompass all times, and that requires repetition, and repetition requires immediacy.

The second: If this did not indicate that, the verse would become ambiguous, because the specific time and the specific manner are not mentioned. But if we take it in its general sense, the verse becomes clarifying. Interpreting the speech of Allah in the way that makes it clarifying is more appropriate than interpreting it in the way by which it becomes ambiguous and unknown. At most, restriction (takhsis) may enter into it, and restriction is better than ambiguity.

The third: His saying ﴿Obey Allah﴾ attributes the word "obedience" to the word "Allah". This requires that the obligation of obedience upon us is due to our being His servants and to His being God. Thus it is established from this consideration that the basis for the obligation of obedience is servitude and lordship, and that requires the continuance of the obligation of obedience upon all responsible persons until the Day of Resurrection. This is a principle recognized in the Law.

* * *

The tenth issue: He said ﴿Obey Allah﴾, mentioning Him alone, then He said ﴿and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾. This is a lesson from Allah, glorified is He, in this etiquette: that they should not combine in mention His name, glorified is He, with the name of another. But when the matter concerns created beings, this is permissible, as evidenced by His saying ﴿and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾. This is a lesson in this etiquette. For this reason it is narrated that a man was mentioned in the presence of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and said: "Whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger has been guided, and whoever disobeys them has gone astray." Then the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "What a wretched orator you are! Why did you not say: whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger?" or words to this effect. The detailed explanation is that combining the two mentions in one utterance gives the impression of a kind of association and similarity, and He, glorified is He, is exalted above that.

* * *

The eleventh issue: We have already shown that His saying, ﴿And those in authority among you﴾, indicates that consensus (ijma') is a proof. We say: just as it indicates this principle, it also indicates many matters that branch from the doctrine of consensus. We will mention some of them.

The first branch: Our position is that consensus is not concluded except by the statement of the scholars who are able to derive the rulings of God from the texts of the Book and the Sunnah. These are the ones called Ahl al-Hall wal-'Aqd (the people who loosen and bind, i.e., those qualified to decide) in the books of usul al-fiqh (the foundations of jurisprudence). We say: the verse indicates this, because He, exalted is He, made obedience to those in authority obligatory, and those who hold command and prohibition in the Law are none other than this category of scholars.

Page 121

For the speaker who lacks knowledge of how rulings are derived from the texts has no standing in his command and prohibition. Likewise the exegete and the traditionist who lack the capacity to derive rulings from the Qur'an and the Hadith. This indicates what we have mentioned. Since the verse shows that the consensus of those in authority is a proof, we know that the verse indicates that consensus is concluded by the mere statement of this group of scholars. As for the verse's indication that the common person (al-'ammi) is not included in it, this is evident, because it is clear that they are not among those in authority.

The second branch: They differed over whether a consensus that arises after a disagreement (al-ijma' al-hasil 'aqib al-khilaf) is a proof. The more correct view is that it is a proof, and the evidence for it is this verse. That is because we have shown that His saying, ﴿Obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾, requires the obligation to obey the whole body of Ahl al-Hall wal-'Aqd of the community. This includes what arose after a disagreement and what did not. So it is necessary that all of it be a proof.

The third branch: They differed over whether the passing away of the people of an era (inqirad ahl al-'asr) is a condition. The more correct view is that it is not a condition, and the evidence for it is this verse. That is because it indicates the obligation to obey those who reached consensus, and this includes the case where the era has passed and the case where it has not passed.

The fourth branch: The verse indicates that what counts is the consensus of the believers, because He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of the verse, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then said, ﴿and those in authority among you﴾. This indicates that what counts is the consensus of the believers. As for the other sects whose faith is doubtful, they are not counted.

* * *

The twelfth issue: We mentioned that His saying, ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾, indicates the validity of acting upon analogy (qiyas). We say: just as this verse indicates this principle, it also indicates many matters that branch from the doctrine of analogy. We will mention some of them.

The first branch: We have mentioned that His saying, ﴿refer it to Allah﴾, means: refer it to an incident whose ruling Allah has explained. It must be that what is meant is: refer it to an incident resembling it. For if what was meant by referring it were referring it to an incident that differs from it in form and attribute, then referring it to some of the instances would not be preferable to referring it to the rest, and in that case referral would be impossible. So we know that what is meant must be: refer it to an incident that resembles it in form and attribute. Then this meaning we have stated is reinforced by report and transmitted narration. As for the report, when they asked him, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, about kissing the fasting person, he said, peace be upon him: "What do you think if you rinsed your mouth?" meaning rinsing the mouth as a preliminary to eating, just as kissing is a preliminary to intercourse. So just as that rinsing does not break the fast, likewise kissing. And when the woman of Khath'am asked him about the Hajj, he, peace be upon him, said: "What do you think if your father had a debt and you paid it, would it be accepted?" She said: "Yes." He, peace be upon him, said: "The debt of God has more right to be settled." As for the narration, what is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Know the similar cases and the parallels, and measure matters by your judgment." So the whole of what we have mentioned, from the indication of this verse, the indication of the report, and the indication of the narration, shows that His saying, ﴿refer it﴾, is a command to refer a thing to its like. Once this is established, God has made similarity in form and attribute a proof that the ruling in a case not covered by the text is similar to the ruling in the case covered by the text. This is what al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, calls qiyas al-ashbah (analogy by resemblance), and what most jurists call qiyas al-tard (analogy by concomitance). This verse indicates its validity, because once it has been established by evidence that the meaning of His saying, ﴿refer it﴾, is: refer it to its like, we know that the principle relied upon in the domain of analogy is pure resemblance. This is a lengthy investigation, and our purpose is to show how issues are derived from verses; as for a full exhaustive treatment, it is mentioned in the other books.

Page 122

The second branch: The verse indicates that a condition for reasoning by analogy in a matter is that there be no text on it from the Book and the Sunnah, because His saying, ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it﴾, suggests this condition.

The third branch: The verse indicates that if no text from the Book, the Sunnah, or consensus is found in an incident, it is permissible to employ analogy in it in any way. This refutes the view of those who say that analogy may not be used in expiations (kaffarat), prescribed punishments (hudud), and other matters, because His saying, ﴿if you dispute over anything﴾, is general over every incident for which there is no text.

The fourth branch: The verse indicates that whoever establishes a ruling in a case by analogy must analogize it to a case whose ruling has been established by a text, and may not analogize it to a case whose ruling was established by analogy, because His saying, ﴿refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾, apparently suggests that it must be referred to the ruling established by the text of God and the text of His Messenger.

The fifth branch: The verse indicates that if analogy based on a root whose ruling is established by the Qur'an and analogy based on a root whose ruling is established by the Sunnah conflict, then analogy based on the Qur'an takes precedence over analogy based on the report, because He, exalted is He, placed the Book before the Sunnah in His saying, ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, and in His saying, ﴿refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾, and likewise in the report of Mu'adh.

The sixth branch: The verse indicates that if two analogies conflict, one of which is supported by an indication (iima') in the Book of Allah and the other by an indication from a report of the reports of the Messenger of Allah, the first takes precedence over the second, that is, as we mentioned in the fifth branch. These are the principles of usul that we have derived from this verse in less than two hours, and perhaps a person who applies his thinking with thoroughness can derive most of the issues of usul al-fiqh from this verse.

The thirteenth issue: His saying, ﴿those in authority (ulil-amr)﴾, means dhawu al-amr (possessors of authority). Ulu is a plural, and its singular is dhu, irregularly, like al-nisa' (the women), al-ibil (the camels), and al-khayl (the horses); all of these are collective nouns with no singular in the word.

The fourteenth issue: His saying, ﴿if you dispute﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "You differed, and each party said: 'The word is mine.'" The derivation of al-munazaʿa (disputing) is from al-naz' (pulling), which is tugging. Al-munazaʿa is an expression for each of the two adversaries pulling toward a proof that validates his statement, or trying to pull his statement and tear it away from what would corrupt it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and in this there are two issues:

The first issue: This warning may be understood to refer to His saying, ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, and to His saying, ﴿refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The apparent sense of His saying, ﴿if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, implies that whoever does not obey Allah and the Messenger is not a believer. This would imply that the sinner is excluded from faith, but it is to be understood as a threat.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wil)﴾, meaning: that which I have commanded you in this verse is better for you and has a better consequence for you, because ta'wil is an expression for what a thing ultimately leads to, its return and its end.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 60–61:

**Allah the Exalted said:** ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to take their disputes to the false deity (ṭāghūt), though they were commanded to reject it? And Satan wants to lead them far astray.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, made it obligatory in the first verse upon all those who are legally responsible to obey Allah and obey the Messenger, He mentioned in this verse that the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, do not obey the Messenger and are not content with his judgment, and that they only desire the judgment of others. The verse contains several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-zaʿm* (الزَّعْمُ) and *al-zaʿam* (الزَّعَمُ) are two forms, and they are used for the most part only for a statement whose truth is not established. Al-Layth said: The people of Arabic say "zaʿama fulān" (so-and-so claimed) when they doubt about it and do not know whether he spoke truthfully or falsely. Likewise is the explanation of His saying: ﴿This is for Allah, by their claim﴾ [al-Anʿām: 136], i.e., by their false saying. Al-Asmaʿi said: *al-zaʿūm* refers to sheep about which they do not know whether they have fat or not. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-zaʿm* is used for what is true, and he recited for Umayyah ibn al-Salt:

*"And I testify to you that your Lord will surely fulfill for you what He has claimed."*

Having known this, we say: what is meant in this verse is falsehood, because the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

**The second issue:** They mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation:

*The first:* Many of the exegetes said: "A man from the hypocrites disputed with a man from the Jews. The Jew said: 'Between me and you is Abu al-Qasim (the Prophet).' The hypocrite said: 'Between me and you is Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf.' The reason for this was that the Messenger (ﷺ) would judge with truth and did not turn toward bribery, whereas Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf was very eager for bribery. The Jew was in the right and the hypocrite was in the wrong. For this reason the Jew wanted to take the matter to the Messenger, and the hypocrite wanted Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. Then the Jew insisted on his position, so they went to him (ﷺ), and the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) judged in favor of the Jew against the hypocrite. The hypocrite said: 'I am not satisfied. Come, let us go to Abu Bakr.' Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) judged in favor of the Jew, but the hypocrite was not satisfied. The hypocrite said: 'Between me and you is Umar.' So they went to Umar, and the Jew informed him that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and Abu Bakr had judged against the hypocrite, but he did not accept their judgment. Umar said to the hypocrite: 'Is it so?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Wait, I have a need. I will enter and attend to it and come out to you both.' He entered, took his sword, then came out to them and struck the hypocrite with it until he died, and the Jew fled. The hypocrite's people came and complained about Umar to the Prophet (ﷺ). He asked Umar about the matter, and Umar said: 'He rejected your judgment, O Messenger of Allah.' Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came immediately and said: 'He is al-Faruq, who distinguished between truth and falsehood.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umar: '"You are al-Faruq."'" According to this view, the ṭāghūt is Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf.

*Page 124*

*The second narration* concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: Some Jews embraced Islam and some of them were hypocrites. In the Jahiliyyah, when a man of Qurayzah killed a man of al-Nadir, he was killed in retaliation for him, and a blood-money of one hundred wasq of dates was taken from him. But when a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayzah, he was not killed in retaliation; rather, his blood-money of sixty wasq of dates was paid. The Banu al-Nadir were more honorable, and they were allies of the Aws, while Qurayzah were allies of the Khazraj. When the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) migrated to Madinah, a man of al-Nadir killed a man of Qurayzah, and they disputed over it. The Banu al-Nadir said: 'There is no retaliation against us; we owe only sixty wasq of dates, according to what we agreed upon before.' The Khazraj said: 'This is the judgment of the Jahiliyyah. We and you today are brothers, our religion is one, and there is no superiority between us.' The Banu al-Nadir refused this. The hypocrites said: 'Go to Abu Burda al-Kahin al-Aslami.' The Muslims said: 'Rather, go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' The hypocrites refused and went to the soothsayer to judge between them. Then Allah revealed this verse. The Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) invited the soothsayer to Islam, and he embraced Islam. This is the saying of al-Suddi. According to this view, the ṭāghūt is the soothsayer.

*The third narration:* Al-Hasan said: A man from the Muslims had a right against a man from the hypocrites. The hypocrite invited him to an idol to which the people of the Jahiliyyah used to resort for judgment, where a man stood who interpreted the falsehoods of the idol. Therefore, what is meant by the ṭāghūt is that man.

*The fourth narration:* They used to resort for judgment to idols. Their method was that they would cast arrows (*qidāḥ*) in the presence of the idol, and whatever came out of the arrows, they acted upon. According to this view, the ṭāghūt is the idol.

Know that the exegetes agreed that this verse was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites. Then Abu Muslim said: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that he was a hypocrite from the People of the Book, such as that he was a Jew who outwardly professed Islam in the manner of hypocrisy, because His saying, the Exalted: ﴿they claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾ is only fitting for such a hypocrite.

* * *

**The third issue:** The purpose of the speech is that some people wanted to take their dispute to some of the people of tyranny and did not want to take it to Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Qadi said: Resorting to this ṭāghūt must be considered as disbelief, and not being content with the judgment of Muhammad (peace be upon him) is disbelief. This is indicated by several points:

*The first:* He, the Exalted, said: ﴿they desire to take their disputes to the ṭāghūt, though they were commanded to reject it.﴾ So He made resorting to the ṭāghūt a form of believing in it, and there is no doubt that believing in the ṭāghūt is disbelief in Allah, just as rejecting the ṭāghūt is belief in Allah.

*The second:* His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you a judge concerning what is disputed among them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 65], up to His saying: ﴿and submit completely﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 65]. This is an explicit text declaring disbelief for whoever is not content with the judgment of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him).

*The third:* His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment strike them﴾ [al-Nūr: 63]. This indicates that opposing him is a great disobedience. These verses contain evidence that whoever rejects any of the commands of Allah or the commands of the Messenger (peace be upon him) has left Islam, whether he rejects it out of doubt or out of rebellion. This necessitates the correctness of what the Companions held regarding the apostasy of those who withheld zakat, their killing, and the enslavement of their offspring.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Satan wants to lead them far astray﴾ indicates that the disbelief of the disbeliever is neither created by Allah nor willed by Him. Its explanation is from several aspects:

*The first:* If Allah had created disbelief in the disbeliever and willed it from him, what influence would Satan have in it? And if he has no influence in it, why does He blame him for it?

*The second:* He, the Exalted, blamed Satan for wanting this misguidance. If Allah were willing it, He would be more deserving of blame, since whoever censures something and then does it is more deserving of blame. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Most hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 3].

*The third:* His saying, the Exalted, at the beginning of the verse is explicit in expressing amazement that they resorted to the ṭāghūt although they had been commanded to reject it. If that resorting were by the creation of Allah, the amazement would not remain, for it would be said: "They only did it because You created that act in them and willed it from them." Rather, amazement at this amazement is more fitting, for whoever does that to them and then begins to marvel that they did it, his amazement at this would be more fitting.

Know that the conclusion of this argument returns to relying on the method of praise or blame. You have known from us that we do not refute this method except by counter-argument based on knowledge, motive, and will. And Allah knows best.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you﴾. In this there are two issues:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 62–63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth? Then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended only good and reconciliation."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: know that there are two views regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it:

The first: His saying, ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, is a statement that came in between, and what precedes this verse is connected with what follows it in this way: "And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger,' you see the hypocrites turning away from you with [complete] aversion. Then they come to you swearing by Allah, 'We intended only good and reconciliation.'" That is, at first they turn away from you with the utmost aversion, and then after that they come to you and swear by Allah, falsely, that they intended by that turning away nothing but good and reconciliation. On this reading the composition is connected, and that verse came in between like an extraneous statement. This is called i'tiraD (interjection), like the saying of the poet:

Page 126

Indeed, eighty years, and you have reached them, have made my hearing need an interpreter.

So his saying "and you have reached them" is an extraneous statement that came in between, but the condition for such an extraneous statement is that it have some relation in some respect to that purpose, as in this line, for his saying "you have reached them" is a supplication for the addressee and a gentle manner of speech with him. The verse is also like that, because its beginning and end are about describing the vices and disgraces of the hypocrites and the varieties of their cunning and deceit. The verse informs that He, exalted, related about them at the beginning of the verse that they seek judgment from the taghut, although they were commanded to reject it, and they turn away from the Messenger, although they were commanded to obey him. Then He mentioned after this what indicates the severity of their conditions because of these evil deeds, in this world and the Hereafter, and said: ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, that is, how will be the state of that hardship and the state of that calamity. This is the explanation of this view, and it is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, and the choice of al-Wahidi among the later scholars.

The second view: it is a statement connected with what precedes it, and its explanation is that when He related about them in the preceding verse that they seek judgment from the taghut and flee from the Messenger, peace be upon him, with the utmost flight, this indicated the intensity of their aversion to being present with the Messenger and being near him. When He mentioned that, He said: ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, meaning: if their aversion to being present with the Messenger is thus in times of safety, how will their condition be in the severity of grief and regret when they commit a crime for which they fear you, then come to you, whether they wish or not, and swear by Allah, falsely, that we intended by that crime nothing but good and benefit. The purpose of this statement is to show that the aversion in their hearts toward the Messenger has no limit, whether they are absent or present, and whether they are far or near. Then He, exalted, emphasized this meaning by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾, and the meaning is that whoever wants to exaggerate about something says: "This is something none knows but Allah," meaning that because of its abundance and intensity no one can know it except Allah, exalted. Then when the Messenger, peace be upon him, recognized the intensity of their hatred and the extremity of their enmity and aversion, He informed him how he should deal with them, saying: ﴿So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾ This statement, according to what we have established, is well-ordered and coherent, with no need for any omission or implication, and whoever examines the books of tafsir will know how the earlier and later scholars were confused about it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: they mentioned, regarding His saying ﴿a disaster strikes them﴾, several views:

The first: that what is meant is the killing of Umar, their companion who acknowledged that he would not accept the judgment of the Messenger, peace be upon him. So they came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and demanded Umar's blood, and they swore that they did not intend, by going to someone other than the Messenger, anything but benefit. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

The second: Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: what is meant by this disaster is what Allah, exalted, commanded the Messenger, peace be upon him, regarding not taking them along on the campaigns, and that he should single them out for further humiliation and expulsion from his presence. This is His saying, exalted: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is disease and the agitators in Medina do not desist, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except briefly. Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with [severe] slaughter.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60–61] and His saying: ﴿So say, "You will never go out with me, ever."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83]. In sum, such verses bring upon them great humiliation, so these were counted among their calamities, and it befalls them only because of their hypocrisy. By His saying ﴿then they come to you﴾ He meant: at the time of the disaster they swear and make excuses that "we intended by what came from us of courting the disbelievers nothing but righteousness." But they were lying in that, for they concealed the opposite of what they displayed, and they did not intend by that the good, which is righteousness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 62–63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth? Then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended only good and reconciliation."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: know that there are two views regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it:

The first: His saying, ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, is a statement that came in between, and what precedes this verse is connected with what follows it in this way: "And when it is said to them, 'Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger,' you see the hypocrites turning away from you with [complete] aversion. Then they come to you swearing by Allah, 'We intended only good and reconciliation.'" That is, at first they turn away from you with the utmost aversion, and then after that they come to you and swear by Allah, falsely, that they intended by that turning away nothing but good and reconciliation. On this reading the composition is connected, and that verse came in between like an extraneous statement. This is called i'tiraD (interjection), like the saying of the poet:

Page 126

Indeed, eighty years, and you have reached them, have made my hearing need an interpreter.

So his saying "and you have reached them" is an extraneous statement that came in between, but the condition for such an extraneous statement is that it have some relation in some respect to that purpose, as in this line, for his saying "you have reached them" is a supplication for the addressee and a gentle manner of speech with him. The verse is also like that, because its beginning and end are about describing the vices and disgraces of the hypocrites and the varieties of their cunning and deceit. The verse informs that He, exalted, related about them at the beginning of the verse that they seek judgment from the taghut, although they were commanded to reject it, and they turn away from the Messenger, although they were commanded to obey him. Then He mentioned after this what indicates the severity of their conditions because of these evil deeds, in this world and the Hereafter, and said: ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, that is, how will be the state of that hardship and the state of that calamity. This is the explanation of this view, and it is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, and the choice of al-Wahidi among the later scholars.

The second view: it is a statement connected with what precedes it, and its explanation is that when He related about them in the preceding verse that they seek judgment from the taghut and flee from the Messenger, peace be upon him, with the utmost flight, this indicated the intensity of their aversion to being present with the Messenger and being near him. When He mentioned that, He said: ﴿So how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, meaning: if their aversion to being present with the Messenger is thus in times of safety, how will their condition be in the severity of grief and regret when they commit a crime for which they fear you, then come to you, whether they wish or not, and swear by Allah, falsely, that we intended by that crime nothing but good and benefit. The purpose of this statement is to show that the aversion in their hearts toward the Messenger has no limit, whether they are absent or present, and whether they are far or near. Then He, exalted, emphasized this meaning by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾, and the meaning is that whoever wants to exaggerate about something says: "This is something none knows but Allah," meaning that because of its abundance and intensity no one can know it except Allah, exalted. Then when the Messenger, peace be upon him, recognized the intensity of their hatred and the extremity of their enmity and aversion, He informed him how he should deal with them, saying: ﴿So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾ This statement, according to what we have established, is well-ordered and coherent, with no need for any omission or implication, and whoever examines the books of tafsir will know how the earlier and later scholars were confused about it. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 4, verse 64:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah﴾.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded obedience to the Messenger in His saying, ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾, and then related that some of them went to judgment before the *taghut* (false judges or idols; sing. *taghut*) and did not go to judgment before the Messenger, and made clear the ugliness of their way and the corruption of their method, He again encouraged obedience to the Messenger in this verse, saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah.﴾ The verse raises several issues:

**First issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The word *min* ("from") here is an additional particle (*ṣila zā'ida*), and the sense is: "And We did not send a messenger." It is also possible that the sense is: "And We did not send from this kind anyone except that such-and-such," and on this reading the emphasis is more complete.

**Second issue:** Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: The meaning of the verse is: "I did not send any messenger except that I intended that he be obeyed and believed, and I did not send him to be disobeyed." He said: This proves the falsity of the doctrine of the *Mujbira* (the determinists, who hold that man is compelled), because they say that Allah sent messengers in order to be disobeyed; and it is known that the one who disobeys remains in disbelief. Allah has stated their lie in this verse. Even if the Qur'an contained nothing else that proves the falsity of their view except this verse, it would suffice. And on their view it would be necessary that He sent the messengers so that they would be obeyed and so that they would be disobeyed, all together. This shows that their disobedience to the messengers is not willed by Allah, and that He willed only that they be obeyed.

Know that this argument is extremely weak, and its weakness is shown in several ways:

The first: His saying "except to be obeyed" is satisfied, in realizing its meaning, if a single obeyer obeys at a single time. It is not a condition for the realization of its meaning that all people obey at all times. On this reading we say in accordance with its implication: every messenger whom Allah sent was obeyed by some people at some times. Unless it is said that singling out a thing by mention indicates the negation of the judgment for what is other than it, but al-Jubba'i does not hold this. Thus this objection falls on all the readings.

The second: Why could it not be that what is meant is that every disbeliever will necessarily acknowledge it at his death, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in it before his death﴾ [al-Nisa': 159]? Or it may be taken to mean that all will believe in it on the Day of Resurrection. And it is known that a description in the affirmative sense is fulfilled, for its referent to be realized, by its occurrence in some cases and in some states.

[p. 129]

The third: The knowledge of non-obedience together with the existence of obedience are opposites, and opposites cannot coexist; and that knowledge is impossible not to be. Thus obedience is impossible to exist. Allah knows all knowable things, so He knew that obedience is impossible to exist. And one who knows that a thing is impossible to exist does not will it. By this decisive proof it is established that it is impossible for Allah to will from the disbeliever that he be obedient. Therefore it is necessary to interpret this expression so that what is meant by the speech is not will but command.

The sense is: "And We did not send any messenger except that people be commanded to obey him." On this reading the objection falls away.

* * *

**Third issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: The verse indicates that nothing of good and evil, disbelief and faith, obedience and disobedience exists except by the will of Allah, exalted is He. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah﴾. It is not possible that the "permission" here means command and obligation, because there is no meaning to his being a messenger except that Allah commanded obedience to him. So if "permission" meant this, the sense of the verse would become: "And We did not permit obedience to whom We sent except by Our permission," and this is an ugly repetition. Therefore the "permission" must be understood as divine success (*tawfiq*) and assistance (*i'ana*). On this reading the sense of the verse becomes: "And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Our success and Our assistance." This is an explicit statement that He, glorified is He, did not will obedience to the Messenger from all, but does not will it except from the one whom Allah granted success and assisted in it, and they are the believers. As for those deprived of success and assistance, Allah, exalted is He, did not will that from them. Thus it is established that this verse is among the strongest proofs for our doctrine.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** The verse indicates that there is no messenger except that he comes with a law (*shari'a*), so that he may be obeyed and followed in that law. For if he called only to the law of one who came before him, he would not in reality be the one obeyed; rather the one obeyed would be the earlier messenger who is the originator of that law. Allah, exalted is He, has judged that every messenger is obeyed.

* * *

**Fifth issue:** The verse indicates that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from sins and transgressions, because it indicates the obligation to obey them absolutely. If they committed an act of disobedience, it would be obligatory upon us to follow them in that disobedience, so that act of disobedience would become obligatory for us; and its being disobedience makes it forbidden for us. Thus the obligation and prohibition would attach to one and the same thing, and that is impossible.

If it is said: Did you not, in your objection to al-Jubba'i's statement, mention that His saying "except to be obeyed" does not give generality? How then do you rely on it in this issue, when this argument is not complete except on the view that it gives generality?

We say: The apparent wording suggests generality, but we abandoned generality in that issue because of the decisive rational proof which we mentioned, that it is impossible for Him, exalted is He, to will faith from the disbeliever. Because of that decisive counter-proof we turned the apparent meaning away from generality. In this issue there is no decisive rational proof that necessitates impugning the infallibility of the prophets. Thus the difference is clear.

* *

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had come to you, [O Muhammad], and asked forgiveness of Allah and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾.

[p. 130]

On this verse there are several issues:

**First issue:** Regarding the occasion of revelation, there are two views:

The first: What is meant is the hypocrites mentioned earlier, meaning: if, when they wronged themselves by going to judgment before the *taghut* and fleeing from judgment before the Messenger, they had come to the Messenger, shown regret for what they had done, repented of it, asked forgiveness for it, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, by asking Allah to forgive them upon their repentance, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful.

The second: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "A group of hypocrites agreed upon a plot against the Messenger ﷺ, then they entered upon him for that purpose. Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and informed him of it. He ﷺ said: 'Some people entered wishing for a matter they will not attain. Let them stand and ask forgiveness of Allah until I ask forgiveness for them.' But they did not stand. He said: 'Will you not stand?' They did not do so. He ﷺ said: 'Stand, O so-and-so; stand, O so-and-so,' until he counted twelve men among them. They stood and said: 'We had resolved upon what you said, and we repent to Allah for our wronging ourselves; so ask forgiveness for us.' He said: 'Now go out. I was at the beginning of the matter closer to asking forgiveness, and Allah was closer to answering. Go out from me.'"

**Second issue:** One may say: If they had asked forgiveness of Allah and repented in a correct manner, would their repentance not have been accepted? So what is the benefit of joining the Messenger's asking forgiveness to their asking forgiveness?

We answer: The answer to this is in several ways:

The first: That going to judgment before the *taghut* was a contravention of the judgment of Allah, and was also an offence against the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and an introduction of grief into his heart. Whoever's sin is of this kind, it is obligatory upon him to apologize to the one he has wronged for that sin. For this reason it was obligatory upon them to ask the Messenger to ask forgiveness for them.

The second: Since the people did not accept the judgment of the Messenger, that rebellion appeared from them. When they repent, it is obligatory upon them to do what removes that rebellion from them, and that is nothing but going to the Messenger ﷺ and asking him to seek forgiveness.

The third: Perhaps when they came with repentance, they came with it in a flawed manner; so when the Messenger's asking forgiveness is added to it, it becomes deserving of acceptance. And Allah knows best.

**Third issue:** He said: ﴿and the Messenger asked forgiveness for them﴾ and did not say "and you asked forgiveness for them," out of honour for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and because when they come to him they come to one whom Allah has singled out with His message, honoured with His revelation, and made an envoy between Him and His creation; and whoever is so, Allah does not reject his intercession. So the benefit in turning from the second-person address to the third-person address is what we have mentioned.

**Fourth issue:** The verse indicates with certainty that Allah, exalted is He, accepts the repentance of the penitent, because when He mentioned their asking forgiveness, He said after it: ﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾. This answer applies to that statement only if what is meant by His saying "Accepting of repentance and Merciful" is that He accepts their repentance and shows mercy to their humble supplication, and does not reject their asking forgiveness.

﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what is disputed among them and then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided and submit with full acceptance﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 65:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge in what is in dispute between them, then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided, and submit in full submission﴾.

There are several issues here.

The first issue: concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse there are two opinions.

The first, which is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid and al-Shaʿbī, is that this verse was revealed concerning the story of the Jew and the hypocrite. Thus this verse is connected to what precedes it, and this opinion is the one I prefer.

The second is that it is a fresh statement, revealed concerning another story, which is what has been narrated from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr: "A man from the Anṣār disputed with al-Zubayr concerning water with which he irrigated the palm trees. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to al-Zubayr: 'Irrigate your land, then release the water to the land of your neighbour.' The Anṣārī said: 'Because he is the son of your paternal aunt!' So the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed color, then he said to al-Zubayr: 'Irrigate, then hold back the water until it reaches the walls.'"

Know that the ruling in this matter is that whoever's land is closer to the mouth of the valley has the first right to the water, and his right is to complete the irrigation. The Messenger (ﷺ) had permitted al-Zubayr to irrigate by way of leniency. When his opponent failed in courtesy and did not recognize the right of what the Messenger (ﷺ) had commanded out of leniency toward him, the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, commanded him to take his right in full, and to bring his opponent to the bitterness of the truth.

The second issue: the "lā" in His words ﴿fa-lā wa-rabbika﴾ has two opinions.

The first: its meaning is "fa-wa-rabbika" (by your Lord), like His words ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92]. The "lā" is superfluous, for the emphasis of the meaning of the oath, just as it is added in (li-ʾallā yaʿlama) for the emphasis of the obligation of knowledge. And "lā yuʾminūna" (they do not believe) is the answer to the oath.

The second: that it is meaningful. On this reading al-Wāḥidī mentioned two possibilities:

The first: that it negates a matter that preceded, and the sense is: "The matter is not as they claim, that they have believed while they oppose your judgment." Then he began the oath with His words: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge﴾.

The second: that it is for emphasizing the negation that comes afterward, because when it is mentioned at the beginning and at the end of the speech, it is more emphatic and more beautiful.

The third issue: one says "shajara yashjuru shujūran wa-shajaran" when it differs and becomes mixed, and "shājarahu" when he disputes with him, and that is because the speech of some of them interpenetrates with that of others during dispute. From this comes the word "shijār" for the wooden pieces of a howdah, because some of them interlock with others. Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī said: In my view it is derived from the intertwining of trees, for the branches of trees interlace with one another. As for "ḥaraj," it means constriction. al-Wāḥidī said: "ḥaraj" is said of a dense tree that is hardly reachable, and its plural is "ḥarāj." As for "taslīm," it is a form of "tafʿīl," from one says: "salima fulān," meaning he was preserved and no calamity befell him, and "salima hādhā al-shayʾ li-fulān," meaning it became pure for him without any contender. When you make it heavier with the doubled letter and say "sallama lahu," its meaning is that he handed it over to him and made it pure for him. This is the basic sense in the language, and all the usages of "taslīm" return to this basic sense. So their saying "sallama ʿalayhi" means he prayed for him to be safe; "sallama ilayhi al-wadīʿa" means he handed the deposit to him without dispute; "sallama ilayhi" means he was content with his judgment; "sallama ilā fulān fī kadhā" means he left disputing with him about it; "sallama ilā Allāh amrahu" means he entrusted the judgment of his own self to Him, in the sense that he saw for himself no effect or share in his affair, and knew that the true Effector and Creator is Allah alone, with no partner.

* * *

The fourth issue: know that the words of the Exalted ﴿fa-lā wa-rabbika lā yuʾminūna﴾ are an oath by Allah, the Exalted, that they will not become described by the attribute of faith except upon the fulfillment of conditions:

The first of them is His words: ﴿until they make you judge in what is in dispute between them﴾, and this indicates that whoever does not accept the judgment of the Messenger is not a believer.

Know that whoever holds to this verse to demonstrate that there is no way to know Allah, the Exalted, except through the guidance of the infallible Prophet, says:

(Page 132)

Because His words: ﴿they will not believe until they make you judge in what is in dispute between them﴾ explicitly state that faith is not attained for them except by seeking the judgment of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, in everything over which they differ. We see the people of knowledge differing concerning the attributes of Allah, the Exalted: some are negators (muʿaṭṭil), some are anthropomorphists (mushabbih), some are Qadariyya, and some are Jabariyya. Therefore it follows from the ruling of this verse that faith is not attained except by his judgment, his guidance and his direction. They confirmed this by saying that the intellects of most of creation are deficient and not sufficient to grasp these realities, while the intellect of the infallible Prophet is complete and radiant. When the radiance of his light connects with the intellects of the community, their intellects grow strong and are transformed from deficiency to perfection and from weakness to strength, and then they are able to know these divine secrets. What confirms this is that those who were in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) were certain, convinced, and perfect in faith and knowledge, while those who were far from him became confused or differed. These doctrines only came into being after the time of the Companions and the Successors. Thus it is established that the matter is as we have stated. As for holding to this verse, I have seen it in the books of Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Shahrastānī. It is said to him: this reliance on independent reasoning that you mention has only been extracted by your own intellect; if the intellects of most people are deficient, perhaps you mentioned this argument because of the deficiency of your own intellect. And if this possibility stands, it becomes necessary to doubt the soundness of your doctrine and the soundness of this proof you have relied upon. Moreover, knowledge of prophethood depends on knowledge of God; so if knowledge of God depended on knowledge of prophethood, it would lead to circularity, which is impossible.

The second condition: His words: ﴿then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided﴾. Al-Zajjāj said: their breasts should not be constricted by your rulings.

Know that one who is content with the judgment of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, may be content with it outwardly but not in the heart. Therefore this verse makes clear that contentment with it must be present in the heart. Know that the inclination of the heart and its aversion is something beyond human capacity, so the verse does not mean that; rather it means that certainty and conviction must arise in the heart that what the Messenger judges is the truth and the sincere reality.

The third condition: His words: ﴿and submit in full submission﴾. Know that whoever recognizes in his heart that this judgment is truth and reality may rebel against accepting it out of obstinacy, or hesitate in that acceptance. So the Exalted explained that just as faith requires the presence of that certainty in the heart, it also requires submission along with it outwardly. Thus His words ﴿then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided﴾ mean submission inwardly, and His words ﴿and submit in full submission﴾ mean submission outwardly. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fifth issue: the verse indicates that the prophets, peace be upon them, are infallible regarding error in legal opinions and in rulings, because the Exalted made submission to their judgment obligatory and emphasized that obligation, and explained that submission must be present both outwardly and in the heart. That negates the occurrence of error from them. Accordingly, this indicates that His words ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawba: 43], and his legal opinion concerning the captives of Badr, and His words ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1], and His words ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [ʿAbasa: 1], all of these are to be understood in the ways we have summarized in this book.

The sixth issue: some jurists held to His words ﴿then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided﴾ as evidence that the apparent form of a command indicates obligation. This is weak, because "qaḍāʾ" means binding obligation, and there is no dispute that it indicates obligation.

* * *

The seventh issue: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it is not permitted to specify a text by analogy (qiyās), because it indicates that it is obligatory to follow his word and ruling absolutely, and that it is not permitted to deviate from it to something else. Such emphasis as is mentioned in this verse is rarely found in any of the obligations, and this requires giving priority to the general meaning of the Qur'an and the report over the ruling of analogy. His words ﴿then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have decided﴾ point to this, because whenever an analogy occurs to a person that leads to the contrary of the indication of the text, there arises discomfort in the soul. So the Exalted explained that his faith is not perfected unless he does not turn toward that discomfort, and submits to the text with complete submission. This is a strong and good argument for one who is fair.

* * *

The eighth issue: the Mu'tazilah said: If the acts of obedience and disobedience were by the decree of Allah, the Exalted, it would lead to contradiction. That is because if the Messenger decrees for a person that he must not do a certain act, it becomes obligatory upon all the responsible persons to be content with that, since it is the decree of the Messenger, and contentment with the decree of the Messenger is obligatory by the indication of this verse. Then if that man did that act contrary to the Messenger's legal ruling, then if acts of disobedience were by the decree of Allah, that act would be by the decree of Allah, and contentment with the decree of Allah is obligatory; so it would follow that contentment with that act is obligatory upon the responsible persons, since it is the decree of Allah. Thus it would be necessary that they be obliged to be content with both the act and its abandonment together, and that is impossible.

The answer: the intended meaning of the decree of the Messenger is the legislated ruling, and the intended meaning of the decree of Allah is the creative determination and bringing into existence. These are two distinct concepts, so combining them does not lead to contradiction.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verses 66–68:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We had decreed for them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," few of them would have done it. But if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

Know that this verse is connected to what came before it concerning the hypocrites, and to the encouragement for them to be sincere and to abandon hypocrisy. The meaning is: if We had imposed strict obligations on people, such as commanding them to kill and to leave their homelands, that would have been hard for them, and only the fewest would have done it. At that point their disbelief and obstinacy would have become evident. Since We did not do that, out of mercy toward Our servants, but rather limited their obligations to easy matters, let them accept these with sincerity and abandon rebellion and obstinacy, so that they may attain the good of both abodes. There are several issues in this verse:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿أنُ اقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم أوُ اخْرُجُوا﴾ (*an uqtulū*, *aw uskhrujū*) with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* of *an* and on the *wāw* of *aw*. The reason is the transfer of the *ḍamma* of *uqtulū* and of *ukhrujū* onto them. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read both with *kasra* because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn*). Abū ʿAmr read the *nūn* with *kasra* and the *wāw* with *ḍamma*. Al-Zajjaj said: "I do not know of any special feature that distinguishes Abū ʿAmr's choice between these two letters, except that it is a transmitted reading (*riwāya*)." Others said: As for the *kasra* on the *nūn*, it is because *kasra* is the original vowel for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. As for the *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, it is because the *ḍamma* on the *wāw* is better, since it resembles the *wāw* of the pronoun. The majority agreed on the *ḍamma* on the *wāw* of the pronoun, as in ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] and ﴿ولا تَنْسَوُا الفَضْلَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237].

**The second issue:** The pronoun in His statement ﴿ما فَعَلُوهُ﴾ ("they did it") refers to both killing and leaving together, because "the act" is one genus even though its kinds differ. The readers differed concerning His statement ﴿إلّا قَلِيلٌ﴾ ("except a few"). Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿قَلِيلًا﴾ with a *fatḥa* (accusative), and it is thus in the codices of the people of Syria and in the codex of Anas ibn Malik. The rest read it in the nominative. As for the one who read it in the accusative, he analogized negation to affirmation. Your saying *mā jāʾanī aḥadun* ("no one came to me") is a complete sentence, just as your saying *jāʾanī al-qawmu* ("the people came to me") is a complete sentence. Since the exception (*al-mustathnā*) is accusative in affirmation, it is likewise with negation, and the common factor is that the exception is a supplementary element (*faḍla*) that comes after the completion of the sentence. As for the one who read it in the nominative, the reason is that he made it a substitute (*badal*) for the *wāw* in *faʿalūhu*. Likewise every exception after a negative, as in your saying *mā atānī aḥadun illā Zaydun*, with *Zaydun* in the nominative as a substitute for *aḥad*. Thus the case of what follows *illā* is taken to match what precedes it. The same applies to the accusative and genitive, as in your saying *mā raʾaytu aḥadan illā Zaydan* and *mā marartu bi-aḥadin illā Zaydin*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The nominative is more analogical, for the meaning of *mā atā aḥadun illā Zaydun* and *mā atānī illā Zaydun* is one person. Just as they agreed on the nominative in their saying *mā atānī illā Zaydun*, it is necessary that their saying *mā atānī aḥadun illā Zaydun* have the same status.

**The third issue:** The pronoun in His statement ﴿ولَوْ أنّا كَتَبْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("And if We had decreed for them") has two views:

The first, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, is that it refers to the hypocrites. This is because He, may He be exalted, had decreed for the Children of Israel that they kill themselves, and decreed for the emigrants that they leave their homes. So He, may He be exalted, said: If We had decreed killing and leaving the homeland upon these hypocrites, only a few would have done it, out of showing off and seeking reputation. At that point the matter would have become hard for them and their disbelief would have been exposed. Since We did not do that, but imposed on them easy matters, let them abandon hypocrisy and accept faith with sincerity. This view is the choice of Abu Bakr al-Asamm and Abu Bakr al-Qaffal.

The second is that what is meant is: if God had decreed on people what He mentioned, only a few of them would have done it. On this interpretation, both the believer and the hypocrite are included in this statement. As for the pronoun in His statement ﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم فَعَلُوا ما يُوعَظُونَ بِهِ﴾ ("But if they had done what they were admonished with"), it is specific to the hypocrites. It is not far-fetched that the beginning of the verse is general and its end specific. On this interpretation, the "few" must mean the believers. It is related that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas debated with a Jew. The Jew said: "Moses commanded us to kill ourselves, and we accepted that. Muhammad commands you to fight, and you dislike it." He said: "You! If Muhammad had commanded me to kill myself, I would have done it." So this verse was revealed.

It is also related that Ibn Mas'ud said the same, so this verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, among my community are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the firm mountains." And it is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "By Allah, if our Lord had commanded us to kill ourselves, we would have done it. Praise be to Allah, who did not command us with that."

**The fourth issue:** Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i said: Since this verse indicates that He, may He be exalted, did not impose on them what is severe and heavy for them, then it is more fitting that He would not impose on them what they cannot bear. It is said to him: This is binding upon you, because the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He, may He be exalted, did not impose on them these arduous matters only because, had He imposed them, they would not have done them, and had they not done them, they would have fallen into punishment. Then He, may He be exalted, knew of Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab that they would not believe, and that they would gain from the obligation nothing but eternal punishment. Yet despite that, He imposed obligations on them. So whatever you give as an answer to this is our answer to what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

Know that what is meant by His statement ﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم فَعَلُوا ما يُوعَظُونَ بِهِ﴾ is: if they had done what they were charged with and commanded to do. This obligation and command is called admonition (*waʿẓ*) because God's obligations are coupled with promise and threat, with encouragement and warning, with reward and punishment. Whatever is like this is called admonition. Then He, may He be exalted, explained that if they had committed themselves to these obligations, various kinds of benefits would have accrued to them.

The first kind: His statement ﴿لَكانَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ ("it would have been better for them"). It may mean that they would have attained the good of this world and the Hereafter. It may also mean emphasis and preference, namely that this is more beneficial and more excellent for them than anything else, because our saying *khayr* ("good") is used in both senses.

The second kind: His statement ﴿وأشَدَّ تَثْبِيتًا﴾ ("and stronger in firmness"), on which there are several views:

The first: what is meant is that this is closer to their steadfastness in it and their persistence, because obedience calls for its like, and what is done of it at one time calls for persistence in it.

The second: that it is more firm and more lasting, because it is truth, and truth is firm and enduring, while falsehood is transient.

The third: that a person first seeks to attain the good, and once he has attained it, he seeks that this attained state remain firm. So His statement ﴿لَكانَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ points to the first state, and His statement ﴿وأشَدَّ تَثْبِيتًا﴾ points to the second state.

The third kind: His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained that this sincerity in faith is better than what they desire of hypocrisy and more firm and lasting, He explained that just as it is good in itself, it also brings about great goods, namely a great reward and a great recompense. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *idhan* ("then") is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What will come of this good and firmness?" So it was answered: "It is that We will give them from Us a great reward," like His statement ﴿ويُؤْتِ مِن لَدُنْهُ أجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾ [an-Nisa': 40].

I say: He, may He be exalted, has gathered in this verse many indicators, each of which shows the greatness of this reward.

The first: He mentioned Himself with the form of majesty, which is His statement *ātaynāhu* ("We would have given him") and His statement ﴿مِن لَدُنّا﴾ ("from Us"). When the wise giver mentions himself with a word that indicates greatness at the time of promising a gift, that indicates the greatness of that gift.

The second: His statement ﴿مِن لَدُنّا﴾ ("from Us"). This specification indicates emphasis, as in His statement ﴿وعَلَّمْناهُ مِن لَدُنّا عِلْمًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

The third: God, may He be exalted, described this reward as great, and the thing that the Greatest of the great describes as great must be at the peak of magnificence. And how could it not be great, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived"?

The fourth kind: His statement ﴿ولَهَدَيْناهم صِراطًا مُسْتَقِيمًا﴾ ("and We would have guided them to a straight path"), on which there are two views:

One of them: the straight path is the true religion. A parallel is His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿وإنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿صِراطِ اللَّهِ﴾ [ash-Shura: 52–53].

The second: that it is the path that is the road from the plain of resurrection, because He, may He be exalted, mentioned it after mentioning the reward and the recompense. The true religion precedes the reward and recompense, while the path which is the road from the plain of resurrection to Paradise is needed only after entitlement to the reward. So it is more fitting to interpret the word *ṣirāṭ* in this context in this sense.
