The third: that a person first seeks to attain the good, and once he has attained it, he seeks that this attained state remain firm. So His statement ﴿لَكانَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ points to the first state, and His statement ﴿وأشَدَّ تَثْبِيتًا﴾ points to the second state.

The third kind: His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained that this sincerity in faith is better than what they desire of hypocrisy and more firm and lasting, He explained that just as it is good in itself, it also brings about great goods, namely a great reward and a great recompense. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *idhan* ("then") is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What will come of this good and firmness?" So it was answered: "It is that We will give them from Us a great reward," like His statement ﴿ويُؤْتِ مِن لَدُنْهُ أجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾ [an-Nisa': 40].

I say: He, may He be exalted, has gathered in this verse many indicators, each of which shows the greatness of this reward.

The first: He mentioned Himself with the form of majesty, which is His statement *ātaynāhu* ("We would have given him") and His statement ﴿مِن لَدُنّا﴾ ("from Us"). When the wise giver mentions himself with a word that indicates greatness at the time of promising a gift, that indicates the greatness of that gift.

The second: His statement ﴿مِن لَدُنّا﴾ ("from Us"). This specification indicates emphasis, as in His statement ﴿وعَلَّمْناهُ مِن لَدُنّا عِلْمًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

The third: God, may He be exalted, described this reward as great, and the thing that the Greatest of the great describes as great must be at the peak of magnificence. And how could it not be great, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived"?

The fourth kind: His statement ﴿ولَهَدَيْناهم صِراطًا مُسْتَقِيمًا﴾ ("and We would have guided them to a straight path"), on which there are two views:

One of them: the straight path is the true religion. A parallel is His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿وإنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿صِراطِ اللَّهِ﴾ [ash-Shura: 52–53].

The second: that it is the path that is the road from the plain of resurrection, because He, may He be exalted, mentioned it after mentioning the reward and the recompense. The true religion precedes the reward and recompense, while the path which is the road from the plain of resurrection to Paradise is needed only after entitlement to the reward. So it is more fitting to interpret the word *ṣirāṭ* in this context in this sense.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verses 66–68:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We had decreed for them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," few of them would have done it. But if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

Know that this verse is connected to what came before it concerning the hypocrites, and to the encouragement for them to be sincere and to abandon hypocrisy. The meaning is: if We had imposed strict obligations on people, such as commanding them to kill and to leave their homelands, that would have been hard for them, and only the fewest would have done it. At that point their disbelief and obstinacy would have become evident. Since We did not do that, out of mercy toward Our servants, but rather limited their obligations to easy matters, let them accept these with sincerity and abandon rebellion and obstinacy, so that they may attain the good of both abodes. There are several issues in this verse:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿أنُ اقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم أوُ اخْرُجُوا﴾ (*an uqtulū*, *aw uskhrujū*) with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* of *an* and on the *wāw* of *aw*. The reason is the transfer of the *ḍamma* of *uqtulū* and of *ukhrujū* onto them. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read both with *kasra* because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn*). Abū ʿAmr read the *nūn* with *kasra* and the *wāw* with *ḍamma*. Al-Zajjaj said: "I do not know of any special feature that distinguishes Abū ʿAmr's choice between these two letters, except that it is a transmitted reading (*riwāya*)." Others said: As for the *kasra* on the *nūn*, it is because *kasra* is the original vowel for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. As for the *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, it is because the *ḍamma* on the *wāw* is better, since it resembles the *wāw* of the pronoun. The majority agreed on the *ḍamma* on the *wāw* of the pronoun, as in ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] and ﴿ولا تَنْسَوُا الفَضْلَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237].

**The second issue:** The pronoun in His statement ﴿ما فَعَلُوهُ﴾ ("they did it") refers to both killing and leaving together, because "the act" is one genus even though its kinds differ. The readers differed concerning His statement ﴿إلّا قَلِيلٌ﴾ ("except a few"). Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿قَلِيلًا﴾ with a *fatḥa* (accusative), and it is thus in the codices of the people of Syria and in the codex of Anas ibn Malik. The rest read it in the nominative. As for the one who read it in the accusative, he analogized negation to affirmation. Your saying *mā jāʾanī aḥadun* ("no one came to me") is a complete sentence, just as your saying *jāʾanī al-qawmu* ("the people came to me") is a complete sentence. Since the exception (*al-mustathnā*) is accusative in affirmation, it is likewise with negation, and the common factor is that the exception is a supplementary element (*faḍla*) that comes after the completion of the sentence. As for the one who read it in the nominative, the reason is that he made it a substitute (*badal*) for the *wāw* in *faʿalūhu*. Likewise every exception after a negative, as in your saying *mā atānī aḥadun illā Zaydun*, with *Zaydun* in the nominative as a substitute for *aḥad*. Thus the case of what follows *illā* is taken to match what precedes it. The same applies to the accusative and genitive, as in your saying *mā raʾaytu aḥadan illā Zaydan* and *mā marartu bi-aḥadin illā Zaydin*. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The nominative is more analogical, for the meaning of *mā atā aḥadun illā Zaydun* and *mā atānī illā Zaydun* is one person. Just as they agreed on the nominative in their saying *mā atānī illā Zaydun*, it is necessary that their saying *mā atānī aḥadun illā Zaydun* have the same status.

**The third issue:** The pronoun in His statement ﴿ولَوْ أنّا كَتَبْنا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("And if We had decreed for them") has two views:

The first, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, is that it refers to the hypocrites. This is because He, may He be exalted, had decreed for the Children of Israel that they kill themselves, and decreed for the emigrants that they leave their homes. So He, may He be exalted, said: If We had decreed killing and leaving the homeland upon these hypocrites, only a few would have done it, out of showing off and seeking reputation. At that point the matter would have become hard for them and their disbelief would have been exposed. Since We did not do that, but imposed on them easy matters, let them abandon hypocrisy and accept faith with sincerity. This view is the choice of Abu Bakr al-Asamm and Abu Bakr al-Qaffal.

The second is that what is meant is: if God had decreed on people what He mentioned, only a few of them would have done it. On this interpretation, both the believer and the hypocrite are included in this statement. As for the pronoun in His statement ﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم فَعَلُوا ما يُوعَظُونَ بِهِ﴾ ("But if they had done what they were admonished with"), it is specific to the hypocrites. It is not far-fetched that the beginning of the verse is general and its end specific. On this interpretation, the "few" must mean the believers. It is related that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas debated with a Jew. The Jew said: "Moses commanded us to kill ourselves, and we accepted that. Muhammad commands you to fight, and you dislike it." He said: "You! If Muhammad had commanded me to kill myself, I would have done it." So this verse was revealed.

It is also related that Ibn Mas'ud said the same, so this verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, among my community are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the firm mountains." And it is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "By Allah, if our Lord had commanded us to kill ourselves, we would have done it. Praise be to Allah, who did not command us with that."

**The fourth issue:** Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i said: Since this verse indicates that He, may He be exalted, did not impose on them what is severe and heavy for them, then it is more fitting that He would not impose on them what they cannot bear. It is said to him: This is binding upon you, because the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He, may He be exalted, did not impose on them these arduous matters only because, had He imposed them, they would not have done them, and had they not done them, they would have fallen into punishment. Then He, may He be exalted, knew of Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab that they would not believe, and that they would gain from the obligation nothing but eternal punishment. Yet despite that, He imposed obligations on them. So whatever you give as an answer to this is our answer to what you have mentioned.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾

Know that what is meant by His statement ﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم فَعَلُوا ما يُوعَظُونَ بِهِ﴾ is: if they had done what they were charged with and commanded to do. This obligation and command is called admonition (*waʿẓ*) because God's obligations are coupled with promise and threat, with encouragement and warning, with reward and punishment. Whatever is like this is called admonition. Then He, may He be exalted, explained that if they had committed themselves to these obligations, various kinds of benefits would have accrued to them.

The first kind: His statement ﴿لَكانَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ ("it would have been better for them"). It may mean that they would have attained the good of this world and the Hereafter. It may also mean emphasis and preference, namely that this is more beneficial and more excellent for them than anything else, because our saying *khayr* ("good") is used in both senses.

The second kind: His statement ﴿وأشَدَّ تَثْبِيتًا﴾ ("and stronger in firmness"), on which there are several views:

The first: what is meant is that this is closer to their steadfastness in it and their persistence, because obedience calls for its like, and what is done of it at one time calls for persistence in it.

The second: that it is more firm and more lasting, because it is truth, and truth is firm and enduring, while falsehood is transient.

The third: that a person first seeks to attain the good, and once he has attained it, he seeks that this attained state remain firm. So His statement ﴿لَكانَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾ points to the first state, and His statement ﴿وأشَدَّ تَثْبِيتًا﴾ points to the second state.

The third kind: His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained that this sincerity in faith is better than what they desire of hypocrisy and more firm and lasting, He explained that just as it is good in itself, it also brings about great goods, namely a great reward and a great recompense. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *idhan* ("then") is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What will come of this good and firmness?" So it was answered: "It is that We will give them from Us a great reward," like His statement ﴿ويُؤْتِ مِن لَدُنْهُ أجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾ [an-Nisa': 40].

I say: He, may He be exalted, has gathered in this verse many indicators, each of which shows the greatness of this reward.

The first: He mentioned Himself with the form of majesty, which is His statement *ātaynāhu* ("We would have given him") and His statement ﴿مِن لَدُنّا﴾ ("from Us"). When the wise giver mentions himself with a word that indicates greatness at the time of promising a gift, that indicates the greatness of that gift.

The second: His statement ﴿مِن لَدُنّا﴾ ("from Us"). This specification indicates emphasis, as in His statement ﴿وعَلَّمْناهُ مِن لَدُنّا عِلْمًا﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

The third: God, may He be exalted, described this reward as great, and the thing that the Greatest of the great describes as great must be at the peak of magnificence. And how could it not be great, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived"?

The fourth kind: His statement ﴿ولَهَدَيْناهم صِراطًا مُسْتَقِيمًا﴾ ("and We would have guided them to a straight path"), on which there are two views:

One of them: the straight path is the true religion. A parallel is His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿وإنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ﴿صِراطِ اللَّهِ﴾ [ash-Shura: 52–53].

The second: that it is the path that is the road from the plain of resurrection, because He, may He be exalted, mentioned it after mentioning the reward and the recompense. The true religion precedes the reward and recompense, while the path which is the road from the plain of resurrection to Paradise is needed only after entitlement to the reward. So it is more fitting to interpret the word *ṣirāṭ* in this context in this sense.

The statement of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ ﴿That is the bounty from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.﴾

Know that when Allah commanded obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger, by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, then He condemned the way of those who sought judgement from the false deity (taghut) and turned away from the Messenger. Then He repeated the command to obey the Messenger a second time, saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by permission of Allah.﴾ Then He encouraged that obedience by His saying: ﴿It would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾ In this verse He emphasised once more the command to obey Allah and obey the Messenger, saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets and the truthful ones﴾, to the end of the verse. Here there are several issues.

**The first issue: the occasions of revelation.** The scholars mentioned several reports concerning the occasion of revelation:

The first: A group of exegetes narrated that Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), had a very strong love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and little patience in being apart from him. One day he came to him, his face changed, his body emaciated, and sorrow was evident in his face. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him about his condition. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have no pain, except that when I do not see you I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remembered the Hereafter, and I feared that I would not see you there. For if I enter Paradise, you will be in the ranks of the prophets and I in the rank of the common servants, so I will not see you. And if I do not enter Paradise, then I will never see you." Then this verse was revealed.

The second: Al-Suddi said: "Some of the Ansar said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you dwell in Paradise at its highest level, and we long for you; how shall we act?' Then the verse was revealed."

The third: Muqatil said: "It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Messenger of Allah, when we leave you for our families we long for you, and nothing benefits us until we return to you. Then I remember your rank in Paradise; how shall we see you if we enter Paradise?' So Allah revealed this verse. When the Prophet (ﷺ) died, the Ansar came to his son, who was in a garden of his, and informed him of the death of the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: 'O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him until I meet him.' So he became blind on the spot. He loved the Prophet very intensely, so Allah made him with him in Paradise."

The fourth: Al-Hasan said: "The believers said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: 'We have from you only this world. When the Hereafter comes, you will be raised above us in the next life.' So the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved and they grieved, and then this verse was revealed."

The scholars who investigated said: We do not deny the authenticity of these reports, but the occasion of revelation of the verse must be something greater than that, namely the urging towards obedience and encouragement to it. For you know that the particularity of a cause does not undermine the generality of the wording. Therefore this verse is general in respect of all the responsible persons, namely that everyone who obeys Allah and obeys the Messenger has indeed attained the high ranks and noble stations with Allah, the Exalted.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾ requires being content with a single act of obedience, because a word that indicates an attribute suffices for acting upon it in the affirmative sense by the occurrence of that named thing once.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: It is necessary to interpret this other than its apparent meaning, and to take obedience as performing the commanded acts and abstaining from all forbidden acts. For if we took it to mean a single act of obedience, then sinners and disbelievers would be included, since they may perform a single act of obedience. In my view there is another aspect, namely that it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of Islamic legal theory) that a ruling mentioned after an attribute indicates that the ruling is caused by that attribute. Once this is established, we say: His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾ means: whoever obeys Allah in His being the God. Obedience to Allah in His being God is knowing Him and affirming His majesty, might, greatness and self-sufficiency. So this verse became an alert to two great matters concerning the states of the Return:

The first: The source of all felicities on the Day of Resurrection is the illumination of the soul with the lights of the knowledge of Allah. Whoever has more of these lights in his heart, whose purity is stronger, and whose remoteness from being clouded by love of the physical world is more complete, is closer to felicity and more likely to attain salvation.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse the promise to the people of obedience of a great reward, abundant reward and guidance to the straight path. Then He mentioned in this verse their promise of being with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous. What is concluded with in this way must necessarily be more noble and higher than what came before. It is well known that the meaning of their being with them is not that they will be in exactly those same ranks, for that is impossible. Therefore its meaning must be that the deficient souls, if they have completed their connections with the perfect souls in this world through intense love, then when they depart this world and reach the world of the Hereafter, those spiritual connections remain there. Then those pure souls become like polished mirrors facing one another, so that the light is reflected from some of them onto others, and through these reflections their lights become extremely strong. Likewise with those souls: since they have been polished by the cleansing of striving from the dust of love of anything other than Allah, and that is what is meant by obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger, then when the bodily veils are lifted, the lights of the majesty of Allah shine upon them, and then those lights are reflected from some of them onto others, and the deficient souls become complete through those spiritual connections. This possibility came to mind, and Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

**The third issue:** The meaning of being with those who obey Allah and obey the Messenger, together with the prophets and the truthful ones, is not that all of them are at one rank, because that would require equality in rank between the superior and the inferior, and that is not permissible. Rather, the meaning is that they are in Paradise in such a way that each of them is able to see the others, even if the place is distant, because when the veil is removed some of them see others. And when they wish to visit and meet, they are able to do so. This is what is meant by this companionship.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned the prophets, then He mentioned three attributes: the truthful ones (al-siddiqin), the martyrs and the righteous. They agreed that the prophets are distinct from the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous. As for these three attributes, they differed concerning them. Some said: all these attributes belong to one described person, and they are overlapping attributes, for there is nothing impossible in one individual being truthful, a martyr and righteous. Others said: rather, each attribute means a category of people. This view is closer to the truth, because the conjoined item must be different from the item it is conjoined to. Just as the prophets are other than those mentioned after them, so too the truthful ones must be other than those mentioned after them, and likewise for the rest of the attributes. Let us examine these three attributes:

The first attribute: al-siddiq. It is a name for one whose habit is truthfulness. When a verb-quality becomes dominant in someone's habit, when he is described by that act, it is said of him in the form fi''il, as one says: sikkir (a habitual drunkard), shirrib (a heavy drinker), khimmir (a habitual drinker of wine). Truthfulness is a noble, excellent quality among the attributes of believers, and it is sufficient as an excellence of truthfulness that faith is nothing but affirmation (tasdiq), and it is sufficient as a blame for falsehood that disbelief is nothing but denial (takdhib).

Having known this, we say: The exegetes have several views on al-siddiq:

The first: Whoever affirms the whole religion without any doubt entering his mind is a siddiq. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful ones﴾ [al-Hadid: 19].

The second: Some people said: the truthful ones are the most excellent companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him.

The third: The siddiq is a name for the one who was first to affirm the Messenger, peace be upon him, and thus became a model for all other people. If this is the case, then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is the most deserving of creation of this attribute. As for the proof that he was first to affirm the Messenger, peace be upon him: it is well known from the Messenger, peace be upon him, that he said: "I did not present Islam to anyone except that he showed some hesitation, except Abu Bakr, for he did not hesitate." This hadith shows that when the Prophet (ﷺ) presented Islam to Abu Bakr, Abu Bakr accepted it and did not hesitate. So if we assume that his Islam was delayed after the Islam of others, it would follow that the Prophet (ﷺ) was negligent in delaying the presentation of Islam to him. This would not be a defect in Abu Bakr only, but a defect in the Messenger (ﷺ), and that is disbelief. Since the attribution of this negligence to the Messenger is invalid, we know that he (ﷺ) was not negligent in presenting Islam to him. And since the attribution of this negligence to the Messenger is invalid, we know that he (ﷺ) was not negligent in presenting Islam to him. The hadith shows that Abu Bakr did not hesitate at all. From the combination of the two matters it follows that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was the first of people to embrace Islam. As for proving that he was a model for other people in this: even if it were said that the Islam of Ali was earlier than that of Abu Bakr, no sensible person doubts that Ali did not become a model at that time, because Ali was then a small child, and he was also under the upbringing of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and was very close to him by kinship, whereas Abu Bakr was not so close to him by kinship. The faith of one in such a position would be a cause for the desire of all other people to embrace Islam. This is because they agreed that when he (may Allah be pleased with him) believed, a short time after that he brought Uthman ibn Affan, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Uthman ibn Maz'un, may Allah be pleased with them all, until they embraced Islam. So his Islam was the cause of these great companions following him. Thus it is established from the combination of what we have mentioned that he, may Allah be pleased with him, was the first of people to embrace Islam, and it is established that his Islam became the cause of the most excellent companions following him in that Islam. So it is established that the most deserving of the Ummah of this attribute is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Having known this, we say: what we have mentioned indicates that he was the most excellent of creation after the Messenger (ﷺ), and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: Since his Islam was earlier than that of others, his reward must be greater, because of the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection."

[Page 139]

Second: he, after he embraced Islam, strove in the cause of Allah, and his striving led to Islam being attained by the most eminent Companions, such as Uthman, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Uthman ibn Maz'un, and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all. Ali fought on the Day of Uhud and the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) in killing the disbelievers. But the striving of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, led to Islam being attained by those who were the foremost Companions, while the striving of Ali led to the killing of disbelievers. There is no doubt that the former is superior. Furthermore, Abu Bakr strove at the beginning of Islam, when the Prophet ﷺ was in the utmost weakness, whereas Ali fought only on the Day of Uhud and the Day of the Confederates, when Islam was already strong in those days. It is known that striving in a time of weakness is superior to striving in a time of strength. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward﴾ (Al-Hadid: 10). Thus He made clear that supporting Islam when it was weak is greater in reward than supporting it when it was strong. It is established from the totality of what we have mentioned that the person most worthy of this description is the Siddiq (the one who affirms the truth with complete sincerity). Therefore the Muslims unanimously agreed to grant him this title, except for one whose opinion is not taken into account, for he denies it. The interpretation of the Siddiq according to what we have mentioned indicates that there is no rank after prophethood in excellence and knowledge except this attribute, namely that a person be a Siddiq. And just as the proof indicates this, so the wording of the Qur'an indicates it too, for wherever it mentions the Siddiq and the Prophet together, it places no intermediary between them. It says, describing Isma'il: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ (Maryam: 54), and describing Idris: ﴿Indeed, he was a Siddiq, a prophet﴾ (Maryam: 56). And in this verse it says: ﴿from among the prophets and the Siddiqun﴾, meaning that if you rise from the state of siddiqiyyah you reach prophethood, and if you descend from prophethood you reach siddiqiyyah, with no intermediary between them. In another verse He says: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and affirmed it﴾ (Az-Zumar: 33), and He placed no intermediary between them. Just as these proofs indicate the absence of an intermediary, Allah has granted success to this Ummah, described as "the best Ummah," to the point that they made Abu Bakr the Imam after the Messenger, peace be upon him, by way of consensus. When he died, may Allah's good pleasure be upon him, they buried him beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This happened only because Allah, the Exalted, removed the intermediary between the Prophets and the Siddiqun in this verse, and so necessarily the intermediary between them was removed in the aspects we have enumerated.

The second attribute: martyrdom (ash-shahadah). The discussion of martyrs has already occurred in several places in this book, but there is no harm in repeating some of it. We say: it is not permissible for martyrdom to be interpreted as a person being killed by a disbeliever. The following points demonstrate this:

First: this verse indicates that the rank of martyrdom is a great rank in the religion, and being killed by a disbeliever carries no added honor, for such killing may occur to sinners and to those who have no standing with Allah.

Second: believers may say, "O Allah, grant us martyrdom." If martyrdom were the disbeliever's killing of them, they would have been asking Allah for that killing, which is impermissible, because requesting that the disbeliever commit that killing is disbelief. How then could one ask from Allah what is disbelief?

Third: it is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The one who dies of a stomach ailment is a martyr, and the one who drowns is a martyr." So we know that martyrdom is not an expression for being killed. Rather, we say: the shahid (martyr, witness) is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of the active participle, one who bears witness to the correctness of the religion of Allah, the Exalted, sometimes by argument and clear demonstration, and at other times by the sword and the spear. Thus the witnesses are those who uphold justice, and they are the ones Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ (Al 'Imran: 18). And the one killed in the way of Allah is called a shahid because he gave his soul in support of the religion of Allah, and his testimony that it is the truth and that all else is falsehood. And if he is among the witnesses of Allah in this sense, he is among the witnesses of Allah in the Hereafter, as He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation so that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 143).

The third attribute: the righteous (as-salihun). The salih is one who is righteous in his belief and in his action, for ignorance is corruption in belief, and disobedience is corruption in action. When you understand the interpretation of the Siddiq, the shahid, and the salih, the differences among these attributes become clear to you. Every person whose belief is correct and whose action is obedience and free of disobedience is a salih. Then, the salih may be such that he bears witness to the religion of Allah, that it is the truth and that all else is falsehood, and this witnessing is sometimes by argument and proof, and at other times by the sword. And the salih may not be described as one who stands in this witnessing. Thus it is established that everyone who is a shahid is a salih, but not everyone who is a salih is a shahid. The shahid is the most noble type of the salih. Furthermore, the shahid may be a Siddiq or may not be. The meaning of the Siddiq is one who was earlier in faith than others, and whose faith became an example for others. Thus it is established that everyone who is a Siddiq is a shahid, but not everyone who is a shahid is a Siddiq. It follows that the most excellent of creation are the Prophets, peace be upon them, then the Siddiqun, then those who have no rank except the pure rank of martyrdom, then those who have nothing except the pure rank of righteousness. The summary is that the greatest of the angels take the true religion from Allah, the Prophets take it from the angels, as He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ (An-Nahl: 2). The Siddiqun take it from the Prophets. The martyrs take it from the Siddiqun, because we have shown that the Siddiq is the one who takes from the Prophets in the first instance and becomes an example for those after him. The righteous take it from the martyrs. This is the explanation of these ranks. And when you understand this, it becomes clear to you that no one enters Paradise except that he is included in some of these qualities and attributes.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾ (wa hasuna ula'ika rafiqa). On this there are several issues:

First issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (az-Zamakhshari) said: there is in it a sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How excellent are those as companions!"

Second issue: In the lexicon, ar-rifq (companionship, kindness) means gentleness of disposition and subtlety of conduct, and its possessor is rafiq. This is its meaning linguistically. Then a companion is called rafiq because each of them derives benefit (irtifaq) from the other.

Third issue: al-Wahidi said: the reason the word rafiq is singular, though it is an attribute of a plural, is that the Arabs treat rafiq, rasul (messenger), and barid (courier) as applying to both the singular and the plural. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So go, both of you, and say: Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara': 16). And it is not permissible to say: "Excellent are those as a man (rajulan)." In general, this usage is permitted only with a word that functions as an attribute. But if it is a clearly stated noun, such as rajul (man) or imra'ah (woman), it is not permitted. Az-Zajjaj permitted this even with a noun and claimed that this is the view of Sibawayh. It was also said that the meaning of His saying ﴿and excellent are those as companions﴾ is: each one of them is excellent as a companion, just as He said: ﴿Then He brings you out as a child﴾ (Ghafir: 67).

Fourth issue: rafiqan is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it was also said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: each one of them is excellent as a companion.

Fifth issue: Know that He, the Exalted, made clear concerning those who obey Allah and His Messenger that they will be with the Prophets, the Siddiqun, the martyrs, and the righteous. Then He did not dwell on that, but mentioned that they will be companions to them. We have already mentioned that the rafiq is the one from whom one benefits in both residence and travel. So He made clear that these obedient ones will derive benefit from them, and they derive benefit from them only when they receive from them kindness and good. We have mentioned many times how this deriving of benefit works. As for the apparent sense, a person may be with someone without being his companion, but when he is of great compassion and great concern for his affairs, he becomes a companion to him. So He, the Exalted, made clear that the Prophets, the Siddiqun, the martyrs, and the righteous will be to him like companions, owing to the intensity of their love for him and their joy in seeing him.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾. On this there are several issues:

First issue: There is no doubt that His saying "that" (dhalika) refers to everything previously mentioned of the description of the reward. So when He judged all of that to be a bounty from Allah, this indicates that the reward is not obligatory upon Allah. Among the rational proofs for this are several points:

First: the capacity for obedience, if it is suitable only for obedience, then the Creator of that capacity is the One who bestowed obedience, so His act does not oblige Him to anything. And if it is suitable for disobedience as well, then the side of obedience does not outweigh the side of disobedience except by the creation of a motive toward obedience, and the combination of capacity and motive becomes what necessitates the act. So the Creator of this combination is the One who bestowed obedience, and His act does not oblige Him to anything.

Second: Allah's favors upon the servant cannot be counted, and they necessitate obedience and gratitude. And if obedience occurs in return for past favors, it is impossible for it to necessitate reward in the future.

Third: obligation entails deserving blame upon omission, and this deserving conflicts with divinity, so it is impossible for it to apply to the Divine, the Exalted. Thus it is established that just as the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the entire reward is a bounty from Allah, the Exalted, so the decisive rational proofs also indicate this.

The Mu'tazilah said: although the reward is obligatory, it is not impermissible to apply the name "bounty" to it. This is because the servant deserved that reward only because Allah imposed obligations upon him, and imposing obligations is a bounty. Also, He is the One who gave him intellect and capacity, and removed the excuses and obstacles so that the responsible person could perform obedience. So this is like one who gives a garment to another so that he may benefit from it. If the recipient sells it and benefits from its price, that price may be described as a bounty from the giver. Likewise here.

Second issue: His saying ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾ has two possibilities:

One: the sense is "That is the bounty from Allah" (i.e., that is the bounty itself), and the meaning is that this reward, by reason of its complete rank, is itself the bounty from Allah, and that everything else is nothing.

Second: the sense is "That bounty is from Allah," meaning that this bounty mentioned, and this reward mentioned, is from Allah and not from anyone else. There is no doubt that the first possibility is more eloquent.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾. This has a great position in emphasizing what was previously mentioned of the encouragement to obey Allah, because by it He alerts that He knows the manner of obedience, the manner of the recompense, and the bestowal of favor, and this is something that encourages the responsible person toward perfection in obedience and toward guarding against shortcoming in it.

The statement of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ ﴿That is the bounty from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower.﴾

Know that when Allah commanded obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger, by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, then He condemned the way of those who sought judgement from the false deity (taghut) and turned away from the Messenger. Then He repeated the command to obey the Messenger a second time, saying: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by permission of Allah.﴾ Then He encouraged that obedience by His saying: ﴿It would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward.﴾ ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path.﴾ In this verse He emphasised once more the command to obey Allah and obey the Messenger, saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets and the truthful ones﴾, to the end of the verse. Here there are several issues.

**The first issue: the occasions of revelation.** The scholars mentioned several reports concerning the occasion of revelation:

The first: A group of exegetes narrated that Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), had a very strong love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and little patience in being apart from him. One day he came to him, his face changed, his body emaciated, and sorrow was evident in his face. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him about his condition. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have no pain, except that when I do not see you I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remembered the Hereafter, and I feared that I would not see you there. For if I enter Paradise, you will be in the ranks of the prophets and I in the rank of the common servants, so I will not see you. And if I do not enter Paradise, then I will never see you." Then this verse was revealed.

The second: Al-Suddi said: "Some of the Ansar said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you dwell in Paradise at its highest level, and we long for you; how shall we act?' Then the verse was revealed."

The third: Muqatil said: "It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Messenger of Allah, when we leave you for our families we long for you, and nothing benefits us until we return to you. Then I remember your rank in Paradise; how shall we see you if we enter Paradise?' So Allah revealed this verse. When the Prophet (ﷺ) died, the Ansar came to his son, who was in a garden of his, and informed him of the death of the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: 'O Allah, make me blind so that I see nothing after him until I meet him.' So he became blind on the spot. He loved the Prophet very intensely, so Allah made him with him in Paradise."

The fourth: Al-Hasan said: "The believers said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: 'We have from you only this world. When the Hereafter comes, you will be raised above us in the next life.' So the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved and they grieved, and then this verse was revealed."

The scholars who investigated said: We do not deny the authenticity of these reports, but the occasion of revelation of the verse must be something greater than that, namely the urging towards obedience and encouragement to it. For you know that the particularity of a cause does not undermine the generality of the wording. Therefore this verse is general in respect of all the responsible persons, namely that everyone who obeys Allah and obeys the Messenger has indeed attained the high ranks and noble stations with Allah, the Exalted.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾ requires being content with a single act of obedience, because a word that indicates an attribute suffices for acting upon it in the affirmative sense by the occurrence of that named thing once.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: It is necessary to interpret this other than its apparent meaning, and to take obedience as performing the commanded acts and abstaining from all forbidden acts. For if we took it to mean a single act of obedience, then sinners and disbelievers would be included, since they may perform a single act of obedience. In my view there is another aspect, namely that it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of Islamic legal theory) that a ruling mentioned after an attribute indicates that the ruling is caused by that attribute. Once this is established, we say: His saying ﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾ means: whoever obeys Allah in His being the God. Obedience to Allah in His being God is knowing Him and affirming His majesty, might, greatness and self-sufficiency. So this verse became an alert to two great matters concerning the states of the Return:

The first: The source of all felicities on the Day of Resurrection is the illumination of the soul with the lights of the knowledge of Allah. Whoever has more of these lights in his heart, whose purity is stronger, and whose remoteness from being clouded by love of the physical world is more complete, is closer to felicity and more likely to attain salvation.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse the promise to the people of obedience of a great reward, abundant reward and guidance to the straight path. Then He mentioned in this verse their promise of being with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous. What is concluded with in this way must necessarily be more noble and higher than what came before. It is well known that the meaning of their being with them is not that they will be in exactly those same ranks, for that is impossible. Therefore its meaning must be that the deficient souls, if they have completed their connections with the perfect souls in this world through intense love, then when they depart this world and reach the world of the Hereafter, those spiritual connections remain there. Then those pure souls become like polished mirrors facing one another, so that the light is reflected from some of them onto others, and through these reflections their lights become extremely strong. Likewise with those souls: since they have been polished by the cleansing of striving from the dust of love of anything other than Allah, and that is what is meant by obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger, then when the bodily veils are lifted, the lights of the majesty of Allah shine upon them, and then those lights are reflected from some of them onto others, and the deficient souls become complete through those spiritual connections. This possibility came to mind, and Allah knows best the secrets of His speech.

**The third issue:** The meaning of being with those who obey Allah and obey the Messenger, together with the prophets and the truthful ones, is not that all of them are at one rank, because that would require equality in rank between the superior and the inferior, and that is not permissible. Rather, the meaning is that they are in Paradise in such a way that each of them is able to see the others, even if the place is distant, because when the veil is removed some of them see others. And when they wish to visit and meet, they are able to do so. This is what is meant by this companionship.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned the prophets, then He mentioned three attributes: the truthful ones (al-siddiqin), the martyrs and the righteous. They agreed that the prophets are distinct from the truthful ones, the martyrs and the righteous. As for these three attributes, they differed concerning them. Some said: all these attributes belong to one described person, and they are overlapping attributes, for there is nothing impossible in one individual being truthful, a martyr and righteous. Others said: rather, each attribute means a category of people. This view is closer to the truth, because the conjoined item must be different from the item it is conjoined to. Just as the prophets are other than those mentioned after them, so too the truthful ones must be other than those mentioned after them, and likewise for the rest of the attributes. Let us examine these three attributes:

The first attribute: al-siddiq. It is a name for one whose habit is truthfulness. When a verb-quality becomes dominant in someone's habit, when he is described by that act, it is said of him in the form fi''il, as one says: sikkir (a habitual drunkard), shirrib (a heavy drinker), khimmir (a habitual drinker of wine). Truthfulness is a noble, excellent quality among the attributes of believers, and it is sufficient as an excellence of truthfulness that faith is nothing but affirmation (tasdiq), and it is sufficient as a blame for falsehood that disbelief is nothing but denial (takdhib).

Having known this, we say: The exegetes have several views on al-siddiq:

The first: Whoever affirms the whole religion without any doubt entering his mind is a siddiq. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And those who have believed in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful ones﴾ [al-Hadid: 19].

The second: Some people said: the truthful ones are the most excellent companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him.

The third: The siddiq is a name for the one who was first to affirm the Messenger, peace be upon him, and thus became a model for all other people. If this is the case, then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is the most deserving of creation of this attribute. As for the proof that he was first to affirm the Messenger, peace be upon him: it is well known from the Messenger, peace be upon him, that he said: "I did not present Islam to anyone except that he showed some hesitation, except Abu Bakr, for he did not hesitate." This hadith shows that when the Prophet (ﷺ) presented Islam to Abu Bakr, Abu Bakr accepted it and did not hesitate. So if we assume that his Islam was delayed after the Islam of others, it would follow that the Prophet (ﷺ) was negligent in delaying the presentation of Islam to him. This would not be a defect in Abu Bakr only, but a defect in the Messenger (ﷺ), and that is disbelief. Since the attribution of this negligence to the Messenger is invalid, we know that he (ﷺ) was not negligent in presenting Islam to him. And since the attribution of this negligence to the Messenger is invalid, we know that he (ﷺ) was not negligent in presenting Islam to him. The hadith shows that Abu Bakr did not hesitate at all. From the combination of the two matters it follows that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was the first of people to embrace Islam. As for proving that he was a model for other people in this: even if it were said that the Islam of Ali was earlier than that of Abu Bakr, no sensible person doubts that Ali did not become a model at that time, because Ali was then a small child, and he was also under the upbringing of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and was very close to him by kinship, whereas Abu Bakr was not so close to him by kinship. The faith of one in such a position would be a cause for the desire of all other people to embrace Islam. This is because they agreed that when he (may Allah be pleased with him) believed, a short time after that he brought Uthman ibn Affan, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Uthman ibn Maz'un, may Allah be pleased with them all, until they embraced Islam. So his Islam was the cause of these great companions following him. Thus it is established from the combination of what we have mentioned that he, may Allah be pleased with him, was the first of people to embrace Islam, and it is established that his Islam became the cause of the most excellent companions following him in that Islam. So it is established that the most deserving of the Ummah of this attribute is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Having known this, we say: what we have mentioned indicates that he was the most excellent of creation after the Messenger (ﷺ), and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: Since his Islam was earlier than that of others, his reward must be greater, because of the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection."

[Page 139]

Second: he, after he embraced Islam, strove in the cause of Allah, and his striving led to Islam being attained by the most eminent Companions, such as Uthman, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Uthman ibn Maz'un, and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them all. Ali fought on the Day of Uhud and the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) in killing the disbelievers. But the striving of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, led to Islam being attained by those who were the foremost Companions, while the striving of Ali led to the killing of disbelievers. There is no doubt that the former is superior. Furthermore, Abu Bakr strove at the beginning of Islam, when the Prophet ﷺ was in the utmost weakness, whereas Ali fought only on the Day of Uhud and the Day of the Confederates, when Islam was already strong in those days. It is known that striving in a time of weakness is superior to striving in a time of strength. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward﴾ (Al-Hadid: 10). Thus He made clear that supporting Islam when it was weak is greater in reward than supporting it when it was strong. It is established from the totality of what we have mentioned that the person most worthy of this description is the Siddiq (the one who affirms the truth with complete sincerity). Therefore the Muslims unanimously agreed to grant him this title, except for one whose opinion is not taken into account, for he denies it. The interpretation of the Siddiq according to what we have mentioned indicates that there is no rank after prophethood in excellence and knowledge except this attribute, namely that a person be a Siddiq. And just as the proof indicates this, so the wording of the Qur'an indicates it too, for wherever it mentions the Siddiq and the Prophet together, it places no intermediary between them. It says, describing Isma'il: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ (Maryam: 54), and describing Idris: ﴿Indeed, he was a Siddiq, a prophet﴾ (Maryam: 56). Fourth issue: rafiqan is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it was also said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: each one of them is excellent as a companion.

Then He did not dwell on that, but mentioned that they will be companions to them. We have already mentioned that the rafiq is the one from whom one benefits in both residence and travel. So He made clear that these obedient ones will derive benefit from them, and they derive benefit from them only when they receive from them kindness and good. We have mentioned many times how this deriving of benefit works. As for the apparent sense, a person may be with someone without being his companion, but when he is of great compassion and great concern for his affairs, he becomes a companion to him. So He, the Exalted, made clear that the Prophets, the Siddiqun, the martyrs, and the righteous will be to him like companions, owing to the intensity of their love for him and their joy in seeing him.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾. On this there are several issues:

First issue: There is no doubt that His saying "that" (dhalika) refers to everything previously mentioned of the description of the reward. So when He judged all of that to be a bounty from Allah, this indicates that the reward is not obligatory upon Allah. Among the rational proofs for this are several points:

First: the capacity for obedience, if it is suitable only for obedience, then the Creator of that capacity is the One who bestowed obedience, so His act does not oblige Him to anything. And if it is suitable for disobedience as well, then the side of obedience does not outweigh the side of disobedience except by the creation of a motive toward obedience, and the combination of capacity and motive becomes what necessitates the act. So the Creator of this combination is the One who bestowed obedience, and His act does not oblige Him to anything.

Second: Allah's favors upon the servant cannot be counted, and they necessitate obedience and gratitude. And if obedience occurs in return for past favors, it is impossible for it to necessitate reward in the future.

Third: obligation entails deserving blame upon omission, and this deserving conflicts with divinity, so it is impossible for it to apply to the Divine, the Exalted. Thus it is established that just as the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the entire reward is a bounty from Allah, the Exalted, so the decisive rational proofs also indicate this.

The Mu'tazilah said: although the reward is obligatory, it is not impermissible to apply the name "bounty" to it. This is because the servant deserved that reward only because Allah imposed obligations upon him, and imposing obligations is a bounty. Also, He is the One who gave him intellect and capacity, and removed the excuses and obstacles so that the responsible person could perform obedience. So this is like one who gives a garment to another so that he may benefit from it. If the recipient sells it and benefits from its price, that price may be described as a bounty from the giver. Likewise here.

Second issue: His saying ﴿That is the bounty from Allah﴾ has two possibilities:

One: the sense is "That is the bounty from Allah" (i.e., that is the bounty itself), and the meaning is that this reward, by reason of its complete rank, is itself the bounty from Allah, and that everything else is nothing.

Second: the sense is "That bounty is from Allah," meaning that this bounty mentioned, and this reward mentioned, is from Allah and not from anyone else. There is no doubt that the first possibility is more eloquent.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾. This has a great position in emphasizing what was previously mentioned of the encouragement to obey Allah, because by it He alerts that He knows the manner of obedience, the manner of the recompense, and the bestowal of favor, and this is something that encourages the responsible person toward perfection in obedience and toward guarding against shortcoming in it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 71:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution and then go forth in small groups or go forth all together.﴾

Know that after encouraging obedience to Allah and obedience to His Messenger, He (exalted is He) returned to mention the jihad that was mentioned earlier, because it is the most arduous of acts of obedience, and because it is among the greatest matters by which the strengthening of the religion is achieved. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾. And in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-hadhar (caution) and al-hidhr (caution) have one meaning, like al-athar and al-ithr, and al-mathal and al-mithl. It is said: akhadha hadhrahu (he took his caution) when he became alert and guarded himself against that which causes fear, as if he made caution his instrument by which he protects himself and safeguards his soul. The meaning is: be cautious and guard yourselves against the enemy, and do not let him gain access to you. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhshari) mentioned. Al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: in it there are two opinions:

One of them: what is meant by al-hidhr here is weaponry, and the meaning is: take your weapons. Weapons are called hidhr, i.e., take your weapons and be on guard.

The second: that ﴿take your precaution﴾ means be cautious of your enemy, because this command to be cautious includes the command to take up weapons, since taking up weapons is the caution against the enemy. So the interpretation also returns to the first. According to the first opinion, the command explicitly states taking up weapons, and according to the second, taking up weapons is implied by the sense of the speech.

The second issue: One might say: that from which Allah commanded caution, if it is something that must occur, caution will not benefit; and if it is something that does not occur, there is no need for caution. In either case, the command to be cautious is pointless. It is also reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "What is decreed will come to pass, and worry is superfluous." It is also said: caution does not avail against destiny. We say: if this statement were sound, the validity of the legal obligations would be nullified, for it could be said: if a person is among the people of happiness in Allah's decree and destiny, there is no need for faith; and if he is among the people of misery, faith and obedience will not benefit him. This leads to the complete abolition of obligation. The truth in the answer is that since everything is by destiny, the command to be cautious is also included in destiny, so the saying of one who says, "What benefit is there in caution?" is a self-contradictory statement, for since this caution is itself decreed, what benefit is there in this question that impugns caution?

Page 142

The third issue: His saying, (then go forth). It is said: nafara al-qawm yanfiruna nafran wa nafiran when they rose up to fight an enemy and went out to war. And the imam urged (istanfara) the people to jihad against the enemy, so they went forth (nafaru yanfiruna) when he urged them to go forth and called them to it. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And when you are called to go forth, then go forth." And nafir is a name for the people who go forth; from it is said: "So-and-so is neither in the caravan nor in the company that goes forth." The grammarians said: the root of this letter is from nufur and nifar, which is fear. It is said: nafara ilayhi when he fled to it for refuge, and nafara minhu when he fled from it and disliked it. The meaning of the verse is: go forth to fight your enemy.

The fourth issue: All the lexicographers said: al-thubat are scattered groups, whose singular is thubah, and its origin is from thabaytu al-shay', i.e., I gathered the thing. It is also said: thabaytu 'ala al-rajul when you praised him, and its interpretation is that he gathered his good qualities. So His saying, ﴿go forth in small groups or go forth all together﴾, its meaning is: go forth against the enemy either in small groups, scattered, one company after another, or all together, i.e., gathered as one constellation. This meaning is what the poet intended in his saying:

They flew to it in bands and singly.

Similar to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you fear, then on foot or riding﴾, i.e., in whichever of the two states you are, pray.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verses 72–73:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind. So if a disaster strikes you, he says, "Allah has certainly blessed me, for I was not present with them as a witness."﴾ ﴿And if bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say, as if there had never been any affection between you and him, "Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement!"﴾

In this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that His saying, "And indeed among you" (wa-inna minkum), must refer to the believers whom Allah addressed with His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾. The commentators differed on two views.

The first view: what is meant are the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), who used to discourage people from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If it is asked: His saying, "And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind," its sense being, "O you who have believed, indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind." If this one who lags behind is a hypocrite, how did He make the hypocrite a part of the believers in His saying "among you"?

The answer has several aspects:

First: He, exalted is He, counted the hypocrite among the believers in terms of kind (jins), lineage (nasab), and mixing (ikhtilat).

Second: He counted them among the believers according to outward appearance, because outwardly they were resembling the people of faith.

Third: It is as if it were said, "O you who have believed, in your claim and your assertion," like His saying: ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6].

The second view: these ones who lag behind were the weak among the believers. This is the choice of a group of the commentators, who said: "At-tabti'ah (causing to lag) means al-ibta' (lagging) as well. The purpose of this intensification (in the form) is the repetition of the act from him." The lexicographers related that the Arabs say, "Ma abta'a bika ya fulan 'anna" (What has delayed you from us, O so-and-so?). Their use of the preposition bi- indicates that the verb in itself is intransitive. Based on this, the meaning of the verse is that among them are those who lag behind from this purpose and are sluggish in this struggle (jihad). So when the Muslims are victorious, they wish to be with them in order to take the spoils, and if a disaster strikes them, it gladdens them that they were absent. He said: "These are the ones whom Allah intended by His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, what is wrong with you, that when you are told to go forth in the cause of Allah, you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]."

He said: "What indicates that what is meant by His saying 'la-yubatti'anna' is their own lagging, not the discouragement of others, is what He, exalted is He, related of their saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had been with them﴾ at the time of the spoils. If what was meant were the discouragement of others, this statement would have no meaning."

Al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) criticized this view and said: "He, exalted is He, related about these laggards that they say at the time of the affliction of the believers: ﴿Allah has certainly blessed me, for I was not present with them as a witness﴾. So he counts his sitting out of fighting as a blessing from Allah, exalted is He. Such a statement is only fitting for the hypocrites, not the believers. Also, it is not fitting for the believers to be told: ﴿as if there had never been any affection between you and him﴾, meaning the Messenger, [the word] 'affection'. So it is established that it cannot be applied to the believers, and it can only be applied to the hypocrites."

Then he said: "If it is taken to mean lagging and sluggishness, it is valid regarding the hypocrites, because they used to hold back from jihad and be sluggish, and not hasten to it. And if it is taken to mean discouraging others, it is also valid regarding them, for they used to discourage many of the believers through the various kinds of deception they presented to them. So both attributes exist in the hypocrites."

Most of the commentators took it to mean discouraging others. It is as if they distinguished between ab'ata and batta'a, making the first intransitive and the second transitive, just as it is said of aḥabba and ḥabba: the first is intransitive and the second is transitive.

**The second issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: "Man" (who) in His saying ﴿la-man la-yubatti'anna﴾ is connected by the oath (lil-qasam), as if this, if it were your speech, you would say: "Indeed among you is one who swore by Allah that he will certainly lag behind."

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So if a disaster strikes you﴾, meaning from killing, defeat, and hardship of life. "I was not present with them as a witness" means: "I was not present, so that what befell them of trial and hardship would befall me." ﴿And if bounty from Allah comes to you﴾, meaning victory and spoils, ﴿he will surely say: "as if there had never been any affection between you and him, Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement!"﴾ In this there are issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Hafs (from ʿAsim) recited ﴿kaʾan lam takun﴾ with a taʾ (ت) dotted from above, meaning "the affection" (al-mawaddah). The rest read it with a yaʾ (ي) because the verb is placed before (its subject). Al-Wahidi said: "Both recitations (qira'at) have come in the revelation. He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ [Yunus: 57], and in another verse He said: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. So the feminine is the origin, and the masculine is good when the feminine is not real (haqiqi), especially when it is placed as a separation between the verb and the subject."

**The second issue:** al-Hasan read ﴿la-yaqulunna﴾ with a ḍammah on the lam, returning the pronoun to the sense of "man" (who), because His saying ﴿la-man la-yubatti'anna﴾ has the meaning of a group. However, this reading is weak, because "man," although it has the meaning of a group, is singular in form, and the singular aspect has been preferred in His saying: ﴿He said: "Allah has certainly blessed me"﴾ and in His saying: ﴿"Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement!"﴾.

**The third issue:** One may say: if the revelation had been like this: "And if bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say: 'Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement!'", the arrangement would have been correct and good. So how did His saying ﴿as if there had never been any affection between you and him﴾ come in between?

The answer: It is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ) that came in between, and it is of the utmost excellence. Its explanation: He, exalted is He, related about this hypocrite that when a calamity befalls the Muslims, he shows intense joy because he was absent from them. And if they achieve spoils and dominance, he shows intense grief because the spoils have escaped him. Such treatment is not undertaken by a person except toward a foreign enemy, because whoever loves a person rejoices at his joy and grieves at his grief. But when this matter is reversed, that is a display of enmity.

Having understood this introduction, we say: He, exalted is He, related about this hypocrite his joy at the time of the Muslims' misfortune. Then He wanted to relate his grief at the dominance of the Muslims, because the spoils had escaped him. So before mentioning this statement in full, He placed in between His saying: ﴿as if there had never been any affection between you and him﴾. The intended meaning is wonder, as if He, exalted is He, were saying: "Look at what this hypocrite says, as if there is no affection or association at all between you, O believers, and him." This is what is meant by the statement. And although it is a statement placed in between by way of interjection, it is of the utmost excellence.
