Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 74:

﴿Then let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory, We will give him a great reward.﴾

Know that when Allah condemned those who lag behind in jihad, He returned to encouraging it, saying: ﴿Then let them fight in the way of Allah.﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) have two views concerning His words: ﴿who sell the worldly life﴾.

The first: the word (yashrūna) means (yabī'ūna), "they sell."

Ibn Mufarrigh said:

"I sold Burd. Would that after Burd I had become a hāmah (a bird-like spirit)."

He said: Burd was his servant boy, and (shareitu) means (bi'tu), "I sold him," and he wished for death after selling him. So the meaning of the verse is: "Let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter." It is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111] up to His saying: ﴿So rejoice in your transaction which you have made﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111].

The second view: the meaning of His words (yashrūna) is (yashtarūna), "they buy." They said: the ones addressed by this address are the hypocrites who stayed behind from Uhud. The sense of the statement is: "Let those fight who choose the worldly life over the Hereafter." On this interpretation, there must be an omission, whose estimate is: "They believed, then they fought," because it is impossible for the commands of Islamic law to occur before Islam is attained.

In my view there are other possibilities for the verse:

The first: when a person wished to spend this worldly life in the way of Allah, his soul was reluctant to part with it, so he bought it from himself with the happiness of the Hereafter, so that he could be able to give it up in the way of Allah with a contented soul.

The second: Allah commanded fighting together with an explanation of the corruption that causes a person to abandon fighting. For whoever abandons fighting does so only out of desire for the worldly life, and that results in the loss of the happiness of the Hereafter. It is as if it were said to him: "Occupy yourself with fighting, and leave off preferring the perishable over the enduring."

The third: it is as if it were said: "Those who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter only prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter when it is accompanied by happiness, bliss and honor. If that is the case, then let them fight, for by fighting they attain bliss and honor in this world, because by fighting they overcome the enemies and gain wealth." These are aspects that came to mind, and Allah knows best what He intends.

Page 145

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory, We will give him a great reward.﴾ The meaning is: whoever fights in the way of Allah, whether he becomes one slain by the disbelievers or one who overcomes the disbelievers, We will give him a great reward, which is pure and lasting benefit accompanied by honor. It is known that there is no intermediate state between these two conditions. So when the reward is attained under both estimates, no deed is more noble than jihad. This indicates that the fighter must prepare himself for the fact that one of two outcomes is inevitable: either the enemy kills him, or he overcomes the enemy and subdues him. When he resolves on this, he does not flee from the adversary and does not shrink from battle. But if he enters (the battle) without this resolve, how quickly he falls into flight. This is the meaning of the division mentioned by Allah in His words: ﴿is killed or achieves victory﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah and [for] the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children, who say, "Our Lord, take us out of this city whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper."﴾

Know that what is meant by it is His, exalted is He, rebuke of them for abandoning fighting, and this becomes an emphasis on what preceded of the command to jihad. In it are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight﴾, indicates that jihad is obligatory, and its meaning is that there is no excuse for you in abandoning fighting, and the state of the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children from among the Muslims has reached such a degree of weakness. This is a strong exhortation to fighting, and an explanation of the reason for which fighting became obligatory, which is what fighting contains of rescuing these believers from the hands of the disbelievers, because this gathering together with jihad runs in the manner of ransoming a captive.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah﴾, is a rebuke against them for abandoning fighting, and a clarification that they have absolutely no excuse for abandoning it. And if the act of the servant were by the creation of Allah, this statement would be void, because among the greatest excuses is that Allah did not create it, did not will it, and did not decree it. Its answer is mentioned.

The third issue: They agreed that His saying, ﴿and [for] the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children﴾, is connected to what precedes it, and in it there are two views:

One of them: that it is a conjunction with "the way" (sabil), and the meaning is: "What is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah and for the oppressed?"

The second: that it is conjoined with the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, i.e., "in the way of Allah and in the way of the oppressed."

The fourth issue: What is meant by "the oppressed among the men, the women, and the children" is a group of Muslims who remained in Makkah and were unable to emigrate to Madinah, and they used to suffer severe harm from the disbelievers of Makkah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "I and my mother were among the oppressed, among the women and the children."

The fifth issue: al-Wildan (the children) is the plural of al-walad, and its counterpart among what came in the pattern fi'l and fi'lan, such as hizb and hizban, and wirk and wirkan, similarly walad and waldan. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is permissible that by "the men and the women" is meant the free men and the free women, and by "the children" are meant the male slaves and female slaves, because the male slave and the female slave are called al-walid and al-walidah, and their plural is al-wildan and al-wala'id, except that he made here "the children" a plural for the males and females, giving precedence to the males over the females, as one says "fathers" and "brothers." And Allah knows best.
* * *
The sixth issue: Allah mentioned the children only as an exaggeration in describing their oppression, in that the harm reached even the children who are not legally responsible, as a humiliation to their fathers and mothers and a cause of hatred toward them because of their situation; and because the oppressed used to include their children in their supplications, seeking the descent of Allah's mercy through the supplication of their young who had not committed sin, just as the Sunnah has come regarding bringing them out for rain-seeking prayer. Then Allah, exalted is He, related about these oppressed that they used to say: ﴿Our Lord, take us out of this city whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: They agreed that what is meant by "this city whose people are oppressors" is Makkah. That its people are described as oppressors may be because they were polytheists, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13], and it may be because they used to harm the Muslims and inflict upon them all kinds of hardships.

The second issue: One may say: al-qaryah (the city) is feminine, and His saying ﴿whose people are oppressors (al-zalim ahluha)﴾ is an adjective of "the city," and for that reason it is in the genitive case; so it should have been said: al-zalimah ahluha. The answer: the grammarians call this kind of adjective the "attributive adjective in the manner of the active participle" (al-sifah al-mushabbahah bi-ism al-fa'il), and the principle in this section is that when you put the alif and lam on the last word, you make it agree with the first in its masculinity and femininity, as in your saying: "I passed by a woman, good of husband, noble of father" (hasanat al-zawj, karimat al-ab), and "I passed by a man, handsome of slave-girl" (jamil al-jariyah). And when you do not put the alif and lam on the last word, you make it agree with the second in its masculinity and femininity, as in your saying: "I passed by a woman, noble of father" (karim abuha). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿[take us out] of this city whose people are oppressors (al-zalim ahluha)﴾. Had you put the alif and lam on "ahl," you would say: "of this oppressive city (al-zalimah) the people (al-ahl)." It was permissible for al-zalim to be an adjective of "the city" because it is an attribute of "the people," and the people are related to the city; and this degree is sufficient for the correctness of the description, as in your saying: "I passed by a man standing, his father" (qa'im abuhu), where standing belongs to the father, yet you have made it an attribute of the man. This degree was sufficient for the correctness of the description because the purpose of an attribute is specification and distinction, and this purpose is achieved by such an attribute. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Regarding His saying, ﴿and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper﴾, there are two views:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: They mean, "Appoint over us a man from the believers who will be a guardian for us, attend to our interests, and preserve for us our religion and our law." So Allah answered their supplication, for when the Prophet, peace be upon him, conquered Makkah, he appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd as their governor. Thus the protector (wali) was the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the helper (nasir) was 'Attab ibn Usayd, and 'Attab used to give the weak their due against the strong and the humble against the mighty.

The second: What is meant is: "and appoint for us from Yourself a guardianship and a support," and the summary is: "Be You for us a protector and a helper."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut (false deity, tyrant). So fight against the friends of Satan. Indeed, the plotting of Satan is ever weak.﴾

Page 147

Know that when God, exalted is He, explained the obligation of jihad, He explained that the outward form of jihad is not what counts; rather, what counts is the intention and the motive. The believers fight for the purpose of supporting the religion of God and raising His word, while the disbelievers fight in the cause of the Taghut. This verse indicates that everyone whose aim in his action is the pleasure of other than God is in the cause of the Taghut, because when God mentioned this division, namely that fighting is either in the cause of God or in the cause of the Taghut, it became necessary that whatever is other than God be Taghut. Then God commanded those who fight in the cause of God to fight the friends of Satan, and He explained that the plotting of Satan is weak, because God supports His friends and Satan supports his friends, and there is no doubt that Satan's support for his friends is weaker than God's support for His friends. Do you not see that the people of goodness and religion keep their good remembrance throughout the ages, even if in their lifetime they were in the utmost poverty and humiliation, whereas as for kings and tyrants, when they die their traces are effaced, and neither their trace nor their oppression remains in the world? And the kayd (plotting) is the effort to corrupt a state of affairs by way of deceit against it; it is said: kadahu yakiduhu when he strives to inflict harm upon him by way of stratagem. The benefit of inserting (kana) in His saying ﴿kana ḍaʿīfan﴾ (was weak) is for emphasis on the weakness of His plotting; that is, that since it has been (kāna), it has been described with weakness and humiliation.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, verse 77:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakat"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a faction of them fear people as they fear God, or with even greater fear. They say, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us until a near term." Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears God, and you will not be wronged even by a thread."﴾

And in it are several issues:

**The first issue:** Is this verse describing the believers or the hypocrites? There are two views.

The first view is that the verse was revealed concerning the believers. Al-Kalbi said: "It was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, al-Miqdad, Qudamah ibn Maẓʿun, and Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. They were with the Prophet (ﷺ) before they migrated to Medina, and they suffered severe harm from the polytheists. They would complain of this to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and say, 'Permit us to fight them.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would say to them, 'Restrain your hands, for I have not been commanded to fight them, and occupy yourselves with establishing your religion through prayer and zakat.' When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) migrated to Medina and they were commanded to fight them at the battle of Badr, some of them disliked it, so God revealed this verse." Those who hold this view argue that those whom the Messenger needed to tell to refrain from fighting are those who desire to fight, and those who desire to fight are the believers; therefore this shows that the verse was revealed concerning the believers. The answer to this may be that the hypocrites used to display that they were believers and that they wished to fight the disbelievers and wage war against them. When God commanded them to fight the disbelievers, the hypocrites recoiled from it, and what was apparent from them was the opposite of what they had been saying.

The second view is that the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites. Those who hold this view argue that the verse contains matters which show that it is specific to the hypocrites:

First: God said of them, ﴿they fear people as they fear God, or with even greater fear﴾. It is known that this description is fitting only for a hypocrite, because it is not permissible for a believer to fear people more than he fears God, may He be exalted.

Second: God related of them that they said, ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾, and objecting to God is nothing but a characteristic of disbelievers and hypocrites.

Third: God said to the Messenger, ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears God"﴾, and this statement is addressed to one whose desire for this world is greater than his desire for the Hereafter, and that is a characteristic of hypocrites.

Those who hold the first view answered all these points with one word: the love of life and aversion to being killed are among the requirements of human nature. Therefore the fear mentioned in this verse is to be understood in this sense. Their statement, ﴿Why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾, is to be understood as a wish for lightening the obligation, not as a denial of God's obligating it. And God's statement, ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little"﴾, was mentioned not because the people were denying this, but in order that God make them hear this statement, which eases for the heart the matter of this life. Then the aversion to fighting and the love of life would depart from their hearts, and they would proceed to jihad with a strong heart. This is what is contained in the explanation of these two views, and God knows best. However, the preferable view is to understand the verse as concerning the hypocrites, because after this verse God mentioned His saying: ﴿If good befalls them, they say, "This is from God"; and if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you (O Prophet)"﴾, and there is no doubt that this is the speech of hypocrites. So if this verse is connected to the verse we are explaining, and the connected verse concerns the hypocrites, then the verse connected to it must also concern them.

* * *

**The second issue:** The verse indicates that the prescription of prayer and zakat came before the prescription of jihad, and this is the order consistent with reason, because prayer is an expression of glorifying God's command, and zakat is an expression of compassion toward God's creatures. Without doubt, both precede jihad.

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿as the fear of God﴾ (*kakhashyati Allah*) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in which the object is the genitive (muḍaf ilā al-mafʿūl), meaning the fear is directed toward God.

**The fourth issue:** The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿or with even greater fear﴾ suggests doubt, and that is impossible for the Knower of the unseen. There are several interpretations of it:

First: The purpose is to leave the matter ambiguous for the addressee, meaning that they are in one of the two states: equality or greater intensity. This is because, of any two fears, one relative to the other is either less, equal, or greater. God indicated in this verse that their fear of people is not less than their fear of God, so it remains either equal or greater. This does not imply that He is in doubt about it; rather it requires leaving the ambiguity between these two categories for the addressee.

Second: The word ﴿or﴾ (*aw*) is used in the sense of ﴿and﴾ (*wa*), and the meaning is: they fear them as the fear of God and greater fear. There is no contradiction between these two categories, because whoever has greater fear also has, along with it, a fear equal to his fear of God plus additional fear.

Third: This is similar to His saying, ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], meaning that whoever sees them would say this statement. So it is the same here, and God knows best.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿And they said, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?"﴾

Know that these speakers, if they were believers, said this not as an objection to God, but out of fear of death and love of life. And if they were hypocrites, it is known that they denied that the Lord, may He be exalted, had prescribed fighting upon them, so they said that in the sense that He had prescribed fighting upon them according to the claim of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and his assertion. Then they said, ﴿If only You had delayed us until a near term﴾, and this is like the reason for their aversion to the obligation of fighting, meaning: "Why did You not leave us until we die at our appointed times?" Then God answered their doubt by saying: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears God"﴾. We have said that the Hereafter is better for several reasons:

First: The blessings of this world are few, and the blessings of the Hereafter are many.

Second: The blessings of this world are cut off, and the blessings of the Hereafter are everlasting.

Third: The blessings of this world are mixed with worries, griefs, and hardships, while the blessings of the Hereafter are pure, free of turbidity.

Fourth: The blessings of this world are uncertain, for the most luxurious of people does not know what his end will be on the following day, while the blessings of the Hereafter are certain.

All these aspects necessitate the superiority of the Hereafter over this world. However, this preference is attained only by believing, God-fearing people, and for this reason God mentioned this condition, His saying: ﴿for one who fears God﴾. This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever."

* * *

Then God said: ﴿and you will not be wronged even by a thread﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read (*yuẓlamūn*) with the *yāʾ*, referring it back to those mentioned in His saying, ﴿Have you not seen those who were told﴾. The others read it with the *tāʾ*, as direct address. The *tāʾ* reading is supported by His saying, ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little"﴾, since the word (*qul*, "say") implies address.

**The second issue:** The Muʿtazilah (a rationalist school which held that God's justice and the human ability to choose require specific rulings) said: The verse indicates that they deserve reward for their obedience; otherwise, the negation of injustice would not be realized. It also indicates that injustice is possible for God, even though we are certain that He does not do it; otherwise, praising Him for it would not be valid.

**The third issue:** His saying, "and they will not be wronged even a thread," means they will not be deprived of any of the reward for their deeds, the amount of a *fatīl* (the thread in the cleft of a date stone), which is what one twists with one's hand and then discards as something insignificant. This matter has already been discussed.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers built up high.﴾ The purpose of this statement is to rebuke those whom He has reported as saying, when fighting is enjoined upon them, that they fear people as they fear God, or with even greater fear, and say: ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾ Then the Exalted said: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you.﴾ Thus He made clear that there is no escape for them from death, and that jihad is a death that results in the happiness of the Hereafter. Since death is unavoidable, it is better that it occur in a way that results in everlasting happiness than in a way that does not. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Say: "Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing, and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 16]. In the speech of the Arabs, *al-burūj* means castles and fortresses, and its root meaning is "to appear," as in "the woman displayed herself (*tabarrajat*)" when she showed her adornments. *Al-mushayyadah* means "lofty" or "elevated." It has also been read as *mashīdah*. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: it is derived from *shāda*, meaning he raised it, or he plastered it with *al-shayd*, which is gypsum (*al-jiṣṣ*). Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read it with a kasra on the *yā'*, as a description of the towers by the act of their builder, figuratively, as they say *qaṣīdah shā'irah* ("a poem that is poetic"), whereas the poet is in fact its composer.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If good comes to them, they say, "This is from God," and if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say: "All is from God." So what is the matter with these people that they hardly understand any statement?﴾

Know that when the Exalted reported that the hypocrites were reluctant to fight, fearful of death, and not desirous of the happiness of the Hereafter, He reported in this verse another trait of theirs, one that is ugly and even uglier than the first. There is also another aspect to the arrangement: these people who fear death and are reluctant in jihad have the habit that when they fight and strive, if they attain ease and booty, they say, "This is from God," but if some hardship afflicts them, they say, "This is due to the ill omen of being in the company of Muhammad (ﷺ)." This indicates the utmost of their foolishness, ignorance, and severe obstinacy. There are several issues concerning the verse.

The first issue: they mentioned several views regarding *al-ḥasanah* (good) and *al-sayyi'ah* (evil).

The first view: the exegetes said that when the Messenger (ﷺ) arrived, Medina was full of blessings. When the obstinacy of the Jews and the hypocrisy of the hypocrites became apparent, God withheld some of His provision, as is His custom with all nations. The Exalted said: ﴿We sent no prophet to a town without afflicting its people with adversity and hardship﴾ [al-A'raf: 94]. At this point, the Jews and the hypocrites said: "We have never seen anyone more ill-omened than this man. Since he came, our fruits have decreased and our prices have risen." So the words ﴿If good comes to them﴾ mean fertility, cheapness of prices, and continuous rains, and they say, "This is from God." ﴿And if evil befalls them﴾ means drought and high prices, and they say, "This is due to the ill omen of Muhammad." This is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours by right." And if evil afflicted them, they ascribed it to the ill omen of Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. And concerning the people of Salih: ﴿They said, "We see an ill omen in you and in those with you"﴾ [al-Naml: 47].

The second view: by *al-ḥasanah* is meant victory over the enemies and booty, and by *al-sayyi'ah* is meant killing and defeat. Al-Qadi said: the first view is the one to be relied upon, because attributing fertility and cheapness, and abundance and scarcity of blessings, to God is permissible; but attributing victory and defeat to God is not permissible, for when *al-sayyi'ah* means defeat and killing, it is not permissible to attribute it to God. I say: the statement is as he said according to his own school, but according to our school, everything falls under the decree and the predestination of God.

The second issue: know that *al-sayyi'ah* applies to calamity and disobedience, and *al-ḥasanah* applies to blessing and obedience. The Exalted said: ﴿We tested them with good things and bad things, so that they might return﴾ [al-A'raf: 168], and He said: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hud: 114].

Having known this, we say: His saying ﴿If good comes to them﴾ conveys generality over all good things, and likewise His saying ﴿If evil befalls them﴾ conveys generality over all evil things. Then He said after that: ﴿Say: "All is from God."﴾ This is an explicit statement that all good and all evil come from God. Since it has been established, by what we have mentioned, that acts of obedience and acts of disobedience are both included under the name *ḥasanah* and *sayyi'ah*, the verse indicates that all acts of obedience and disobedience are from God, and this is what was to be proven.

If it is said: the intended meaning of *ḥasanah* and *sayyi'ah* here is not obedience and disobedience, and this is indicated by several points:

First: all agree that this verse was revealed concerning fertility and drought, and so it is specific to them.

Second: a *ḥasanah* that means goodness and obedience is not said to "befall" (*aṣābat*) someone; one says "I attained it" (*aṣabtuhā*). In the speech of the Arabs, one does not say "a good thing befell so-and-so" meaning "he did good," or "an evil thing befell him" meaning "he committed disobedience." Accordingly, if what you mention were intended, it would say "If you attain a good thing."

Third: the word *ḥasanah* is used homonymously for obedience and for benefit, and here all the exegetes agreed that benefit is intended, so it is impossible for obedience to be intended, since it is not permissible to use a homonymous word in both of its meanings at once.

The answer to the first: you concede that the specificity of the cause does not undermine the generality of the wording.

The answer to the second: it is correct to say, "There befell me a success from God and a help from God," and "There befell him a forsaking from God," and by this he means by success and help that act of obedience, and by forsaking that act of disobedience.

The answer to the third: everything that is beneficial is a *ḥasanah*. If it is beneficial in the Hereafter, it is obedience, and if it is beneficial in this world, it is present happiness. So the name *ḥasanah* with respect to these two kinds is a term with a shared meaning (*mutawāṭi' al-ishtirāk*), and the objection is removed. Thus it is established that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates what we have mentioned. Among the things that show that nothing else is intended is what is established in the primary intellects: every existent is either necessary in its essence or contingent in its essence. The necessary in its essence is one, and it is God, glorified and exalted. The contingent in its essence is everything other than Him. If the contingent in its essence were independent of an agent, the argument from the contingency and origination of the world to the existence of the Creator would collapse, and it would then follow that the Creator does not exist. If the contingent in its essence is in need of an agent, then since everything other than God is contingent, everything other than God is dependent upon God. This ruling does not differ whether that contingent is an angel, an inanimate object, an action of an animal, or an attribute of a plant. The ruling about the dependence of the contingent in its essence upon the necessary in its essence applies equally to all of them, because of what we have shown: that it is contingent. This proof is clearer and more manifest than the disc of the sun in establishing that the truth is what He, the Exalted, stated, namely His saying: ﴿Say: "All is from God."﴾

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So what is the matter with these people that they hardly understand any statement?﴾ Concerning this there are several issues.

The first issue: since the proof showing that everything other than God depends upon God, in the manner we have summarized, is extremely evident and clear, the Exalted said: ﴿So what is the matter with these people that they hardly understand any statement?﴾ This is in the manner of expressing wonder at their failure to grasp the soundness of this statement despite its clarity. The Mu'tazilah said: rather, this verse indicates the soundness of our position, because if the attainment of understanding and knowledge were by God's creating it, this wonder would have no meaning at all, since the cause of the non-attainment of this knowledge is that He did not create it or bring it into existence, and that would nullify this wonder. Thus the occurrence of this wonder indicates that understanding is brought about only by the servant's own bringing it into existence, not by God's bringing it into existence.

Know that this argument is nothing but an appeal to the method of praise and blame, and we have already mentioned that it is countered by knowledge.

The second issue: the Mu'tazilah said: the exegetes agreed that the meaning of His saying ﴿they hardly understand any statement﴾ is that they do not understand this verse mentioned in this passage. This requires describing the Qur'an as a *ḥadīth* (statement), and *ḥadīth* is a *fa'īl* in the sense of a *maf'ūl*, so it follows that the Qur'an is created (*muḥdath*).

The answer: what you mean by the Qur'an is nothing but these expressions, and we do not dispute that they are created.

The third issue: *al-fiqh* means understanding. It is said: so-and-so was given *fiqh*. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Ibn 'Abbas: "Make him understand (*faqqihhu*) in the interpretation," meaning: make him comprehend it.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger, and sufficient is God as a witness.﴾

Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: It is established that the word sayyi'ah (evil) sometimes applies to affliction and trial, and sometimes applies to sin and disobedience. Then He, exalted is He, attributed the evil to Himself in the first verse, by His saying: ﴿Say: all is from God﴾, and attributed it in this verse to the servant, by His saying: ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾. So it is necessary to reconcile these two verses and remove the contradiction between them. Since sayyi'ah in the sense of calamity and hardship is attributed to God, it must be that sayyi'ah in the sense of disobedience is attributed to the servant, so that the contradiction between these two adjacent verses may vanish. He said: The opponents have compelled themselves to alter the verse, and they read: (fa-min ta'sika) [from your failing], and so they altered the Qur'an and followed the same path as the Rafidah in claiming alteration in the Qur'an.

If it is said: Why did God, exalted is He, distinguish between the good and the evil in this verse, attributing the good, which is obedience, to Himself but not the evil, although both are the act of the servant according to you?

We say: Because the good, although it is the act of the servant, he reached it only through God's facilitation and kindnesses, so attribution to Him was valid. As for the evil, which is the act of the servant, it is not attributed to God Most High in any respect: not because He did it, nor because He willed it, nor because He commanded it, nor because He desired it. Therefore the attribution of this evil to God Most High is entirely cut off from all aspects. This is the end of the man's speech on this point.

We say: This verse indicates that faith came about by God's creation, and the people (the Mu'tazilah) do not say this, so they become refuted by the verse.

We said that the verse indicates this because faith is a good (hasanah), and every good is from God.

We said that faith is a good because good (hasanah) is the pleasant state free of all aspects of ugliness, and there is no doubt that faith is like this. So it is necessary that it be a good, because they agreed that His saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to God﴾ [Fussilat: 33] refers to the statement of testimony (shahadah), and it was said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, God orders justice and good conduct﴾ [al-Nahl: 90], it was said: it is "there is no god but God." Thus it is established that faith is a good. We said that every good is from God because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you﴾ conveys generality over all goods, and then He judged all of them to be from God. So from these two premises, namely that faith is a good and that every good is from God, it necessarily follows with certainty that faith is from God.

If it is said: Why could it not be that what is meant by faith being from God is that God empowered him to it and guided him to knowledge of its goodness, and to knowledge of the ugliness of its opposite, which is disbelief?

We say: All the legal obligations are common in relation to faith and disbelief according to you. Then the servant, by his own choice, brought faith into existence, and there is no place for God's power and His assistance in faith itself. So faith would be cut off from God in every respect, and this would contradict His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God﴾. Thus it is established by the indication of this verse that faith is from God, and the opponents do not say this, so they have become refuted on this question.

Then, if we want to show that disbelief is also from God, we say: In this there are aspects:

The first: that everyone who says faith is from God says disbelief is from God, so the claim that one of them is from God and not the other opposes the consensus of the Community.

The second: if the servant were able to bring about disbelief, then the power suitable for producing disbelief is either suitable for producing faith or not. If it is suitable for producing faith, then the argument returns to the claim that the servant's faith is from him. If it is not suitable for producing faith, then the one capable of something would be incapable of its opposite, and that is impossible according to them. Also, on this assumption power would necessitate its object, and that would preclude his being able over it. Thus it is established that since faith was not from him, disbelief must not be from him either.

The third: since the servant did not originate faith, it is even more fitting that he does not originate disbelief. That is because the one who independently brings a thing into existence is the one able to attain his aim, and we see no sensible person in the world who does not want what is in his heart to be faith, knowledge, and truth, and no one of the intelligent wants what is in his heart to be ignorance, error, and wrong belief. So if the servant originates his own acts and he intends only to attain the true, corresponding knowledge, it must be that only the truth arises in his heart. If faith, which is his intended goal, his sought aim and his desire, is not certainly brought about by him, then it is even more so that ignorance, which he did not desire, did not intend to attain, and which he was utterly averse to and fled from, is not brought into existence by him and his creation. The upshot is that the doubt that faith occurs by the servant's power is stronger than the doubt that disbelief occurs by his power. Since God, exalted is He, explained regarding faith that it is from God, He omitted mention of disbelief for the reason we have mentioned. This is the sum of the discussion in explaining the indication of this verse for the doctrine of our Imam.

* * *

As for what al-Jubba'i argued for his doctrine from His saying: ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.
The answer to it is in two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, said, relating the words of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 80]. He attributed the illness to himself and the cure to God. This does not undermine God being the creator of both illness and cure; rather, he separated them out of observance of courtesy. So too here. For one says: "O Governor of the heavens and the earth," and does not say: "O Governor of the lice, the children and the beetles." So too here.

The second: Most of the exegetes said, in explaining Abraham's words: ﴿This is my lord﴾, that he said this as a question in the mode of denial, as if he said: "Is this my lord?" So too here. As if it were said: The faith that occurred in accordance with His intention, we have already shown it did not occur from him but from God. So this disbelief was neither intended by him, nor desired by him, nor at all pleased with by him. Would it enter the intellect to say that it occurred by him? We have shown that good in this verse includes faith, and evil includes disbelief. As for the reading of whoever reads (fa-min ta'sika), we say: if it is established that one of the Companions or the Successors read it so, there is no objection to it. If it is not established, then the meaning is that whoever took the verse as having come in the mode of denial-question explained the denial-question with this statement, because when he attributed the evil to them in the context of a denial-question, the meaning was that it is not attributed to them. So this speaker mentioned his words (fa-min ta'sika), not out of belief that it is from the Qur'an, but because it serves as an explanation of our statement that it is a denial-question.

Among what clearly indicates that the meaning of these verses is the ascription of all matters to God Most High is His saying after this verse: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾, meaning: you have only the messengership and the conveying, and you have done that and not fallen short. ﴿And sufficient is God﴾

[Page 154]

(as a) witness over your earnestness and your not falling short in discharging the message and conveying the revelation. As for the attainment of guidance, it is not up to you but up to God. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. This is the sum of what came to mind regarding this verse, and God knows best the secrets of His speech.

Then, He, exalted is He, emphasized what we have said.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah. And whoever turns away—We have not sent you as a watcher over them.﴾

The meaning is that whoever obeys the Messenger, because he is a messenger conveying to creation the rulings of Allah, then in reality he has obeyed none but Allah. This, in reality, does not happen except by the grace (tawfiq) of Allah. And as for whoever turns away, "We have not sent you as a watcher over them": whoever Allah has blinded to right guidance and led astray from the path, no one among creation is able to guide him.

Know that whoever Allah has illuminated in his heart with the light of guidance is certain that the matter is as we have mentioned. For you see one proof presented to two persons in one gathering; then one of them increases in faith upon faith when he hears it, and the other increases in disbelief upon disbelief when he hears it. If the one who loves that speech wished to remove from his heart the love of that speech and the belief in its soundness, he would not be able to do so; and if the one who hates it wished to remove from his heart the hatred of that speech and the belief in its corruption, he would not be able. Then, after some days, the lover may have turned into a hater and the hater into a lover. So whoever reflects upon the decisive proof we have mentioned—that it is necessary to ascribe all possible things to the Necessary Existent—then considers within himself the induction we have mentioned, and yet does not become certain that everything is by the decree and destiny of Allah, let him make his own experience one of the strongest proofs that guidance is not attained except by the creation of Allah. For with knowledge of such a proof, and with knowledge of such an induction, when this belief did not arise in his heart, he knows that this is only because Allah has turned him away from it and prevented him from it.

There remain some issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ is among the strongest proofs that he is infallible (ma'sum) in all commands and prohibitions and in everything he conveys from Allah. For if he erred in any of these, his obedience would not be obedience to Allah. Also, it is necessary that he be infallible in all his actions, because He, exalted, commanded following him in His saying: "So follow him" [al-An'am: 153]. Following (muttaba'ah) is the performance of the same act as another, for the sake of that act being the act of that other. So whoever performs the same act is obeying Allah in His saying "So follow him" [al-An'am: 153]. Thus it is established that submission to him in all his statements and in all his actions, except what the proof has specified, is obedience to Allah and submission to the ruling of Allah.

The second issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said in Kitab al-Risalah, in the chapter on the obligation of obedience to the Messenger: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ indicates that every obligation which Allah imposed upon His servants, in the chapters of ablution, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage, and the other chapters in the Qur'an, and that obligation was not explained in the Qur'an, then there is no way for us to fulfil those obligations except through the explanation of the Messenger. And if the matter is so, it necessarily follows that the obedience of the Messenger is the very obedience of Allah. This is the meaning of al-Shafi'i's words.

[Page 155]

The third issue: His saying, ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ indicates that there is no obedience at all except to Allah. This is because obedience to the Messenger, as a messenger, in that wherein he is a messenger, is nothing but obedience to Allah. Thus the verse indicates that there is no obedience to anyone except Allah. Muqatil said concerning this verse: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "Whoever loves me has loved Allah, and whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah." The hypocrites said: "This man has come close to shirk, for he forbids us from worshipping other than Allah, and he wants us to take him as a lord, as the Christians took Jesus." So Allah revealed this verse.

Know that we have explained the manner in which the verse indicates that there is no absolute obedience to the Messenger, and that obedience is only to Allah.

As for His saying, ﴿And whoever turns away—We have not sent you as a watcher over them﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: that what is meant by turning away is turning away in the heart, i.e., O Muhammad, judge by outward appearances, and do not concern yourself with inner states.

The second: that what is meant by it is turning away outwardly.

Then here, concerning His saying, ﴿We have not sent you as a watcher over them﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: its meaning is that you should not grieve over that turning away, nor be saddened by it; for We did not send you to keep people from sins. The reason for this is that peace and blessings be upon him used to be greatly grieved by their disbelief and aversion. So Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this statement to console him, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning that grief.

The second: its meaning is that We did not send you to occupy yourself with restraining them from that turning away. This is like His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256], which was afterwards abrogated (naskh) by the verse of jihad.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 81:

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say, "Obedience." But when they leave your presence, a group of them plot by night other than what you say. And Allah records what they plot by night. So turn away from them and rely upon Allah. And sufficient is Allah as Trustee.﴾

That is, they say when you command them to do something, "Obedience" (ṭāʿah) in the nominative (marfūʿ), meaning: our affair and our matter is obedience. It is also permissible to read it in the accusative (naṣb), meaning: "We obey you with obedience." This is like when the obedient, submissive man says: "Samʿan wa-ṭāʿah" and "Samʿun wa-ṭāʿatun." Sibawayh said: "We heard some of the trustworthy Arabs being asked, 'How did you wake up?' and he would say, 'Praise of Allah and commendation of Him,' as if he had said: 'My matter and my affair is the praise of Allah.'"

Know that the accusative (naṣb) indicates the mere act, whereas the nominative (rafʿ) indicates the permanence and stability of obedience. ﴿When they leave your presence﴾, that is, when they go out from your presence, ﴿a group of them plot by night other than what you say.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: Every matter that they think about much and examine much regarding its benefits and harms is called "mubayyat" (a matter devised by night). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they devise by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 108]. Regarding its derivation there are two views:

The first: it is derived from baytūtah (spending the night), because the best time for thinking is for a person to sit in his house at night, where thoughts are freer and distractions fewer. Since it is generally the case that a person is at home at night, and generally he carefully pursues his thoughts at night, it is therefore called a thoroughly pursued thought "mubayyat."

The second: it is derived from the verse of poetry (bayt al-shiʿr). al-Akhfash said: When the Arabs wished to compose poetry, they exerted great effort in reflecting on it, so they called the thing reflected upon and thoroughly pursued "mubayyat," likening it to a line of poetry in that it is arranged and carefully ordered.

Page 156

The second issue: Allah, exalted is He, singled out a group from among the hypocrites for "tabyīt" (plotting by night). Regarding this specification there are two views:

One of them: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned those whom He knew would remain in their disbelief and hypocrisy, whereas those whom He knew would turn back from that, He did not mention.

The second: this group had kept their nights awake plotting, while others heard and remained silent and did not plot, so they were therefore not mentioned.

The third issue: Abu ʿAmr and Hamzah read ﴿bayyata ṭāʾifatun﴾ with the assimilation of the tāʾ into the ṭāʾ (idghām), while the rest read it with clear pronunciation (idhhār). As for the one who assimilates, there are two explanations:

The first: al-Farraʾ said: They made it sukūn (quiescent) because of the abundance of vowels, and when the tāʾ became quiescent it was assimilated into the ṭāʾ.

The second: the ṭāʾ, the dāl and the tāʾ are from one articulation place (ḥayyiz), so the closeness between them makes them behave like identical letters in assimilation. What further makes this assimilation good is that the ṭāʾ exceeds the tāʾ in emphasis (iṭbāq), so it is good to assimilate the letter of lesser sound into the letter of greater sound. As for the one who does not assimilate, his reason is that they are two letters from two articulation points in two separate words, so each of them must be kept in its own state.

The fourth issue: He said ﴿bayyata﴾ with the masculine form and did not say ﴿bayyatat﴾ with the feminine, because the feminine of ṭāʾifah is not real (ḥaqīqī), and because it carries the meaning of firqah (group) and fawj (troop). The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿bayyata ṭāʾifatun﴾ means they fabricated and embellished the opposite of what they said and what they were commanded, or the opposite of what they said and what they pledged of obedience, because they concealed rejection rather than acceptance, and disobedience rather than obedience.

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah records what they plot by night.﴾ al-Zajjaj mentioned two views concerning it:
One of them: its meaning is that He sends down to you in His Book.

The second: He records that in the pages of their deeds so that they may be recompensed for it.

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, and the meaning is: do not expose their concealment, do not disgrace them, and do not mention them by name. Allah commanded the concealment of the affair of the hypocrites until the affair of Islam becomes firm. Then He said: ﴿And rely upon Allah﴾ concerning their affair, for Allah will suffice you against their evil and will take vengeance upon them. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾ for whoever relies upon Him. The exegetes said: the command to turn away from the hypocrites was at the beginning of Islam, then that was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. This statement is open to scrutiny, because the command to pardon is absolute and therefore indicates only a single instance, so the later revelation of the command to fight does not abrogate it.

**Page 157**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾

Know that when the Exalted related the various kinds of the hypocrites' deceit and plotting, and all of this was because they did not believe that he (ﷺ) was truthful in claiming prophethood, but rather believed that he was a fabricator and a liar, Allah the Exalted therefore commanded them to look and reflect upon the proofs indicating the soundness of his prophethood. He said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾ Thus the Exalted argued with the Qur'an for the soundness of his prophethood. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *tadbir* and *tadabbur* (reflection, considering the outcomes) mean looking into the consequences of matters and their final ends. From this is the saying of the poet:
"Why do they contemplate the last parts of affairs whose first parts have already passed?"
And in eloquent speech it is said: "If I had faced from my affair what I have considered at its back," meaning: if I had known at the beginning of my affair what I came to know of its outcome.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the Exalted argued with the Qur'an for the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), for if the verse is not taken to mean this, it would have no connection at all with what precedes it. The scholars said: the Qur'an's indication of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) is in three respects:
First: its eloquence.
Second: its containing information about the unseen.
Third: its freedom from discrepancy, and this is what is mentioned in this verse.

Then those who hold this view have given three interpretations of the meaning of its freedom from discrepancy:

The first: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: its meaning is that these hypocrites used to conspire in secret toward various kinds of deceit and plotting, and Allah the Exalted would inform the Messenger (peace be upon him) of those states moment by moment, and would tell him about them in detail, and they would find in all of that nothing but truth. So it was said to them: if that had not come about through the information of Allah the Exalted, then the truth would not have been consistently maintained in it, and variations and inconsistencies would have appeared in the words of Muhammad. Since that did not appear, we know that it was nothing but by the informing of Allah the Exalted.

The second, which is the view of most of the theologians (*mutakallimun*, scholars of *kalam*, rational theology): the meaning is that the Qur'an is a great book, comprising many kinds of sciences. Had it been from other than Allah, there would have occurred in it various contradictory statements, because a great and lengthy book cannot be free of that. Since no such thing is found in it, we know that it is not from other than Allah.

If it is objected: Is not His saying ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22-23] like a contradiction of His saying ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]? And are the verses of compulsion (*jabr*) like a contradiction of the verses of divine decree (*qadar*)? And His saying ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92] like a contradiction of His saying ﴿So on that day no man or jinn will be questioned about his sin﴾ [al-Rahman: 39]?

We say: we have explained in this commentary that there is no conflict or contradiction whatsoever between any of them.

The third view regarding our statement "the Qur'an is free from discrepancy": what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned, namely that its meaning is discrepancy in the level of eloquence, so that there is nothing in its whole that would be counted as weak speech, but rather eloquence remains in it from beginning to end in one uniform manner. It is well known that a person, even if he is at the utmost of rhetoric and the highest of eloquence, when he writes a lengthy book containing great meanings, variation must appear in his speech, so that some of it is strong and firm and some of it is feeble and low. Since the Qur'an is not like that, we know that it is indeed a miracle from Allah the Exalted. The Qadi (al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar) gave an example for this, saying: one of us cannot write long scrolls in such a way that no defect or deficiency occurs in any of those letters. Even so, if we saw long scrolls preserved from this kind of defect and deficiency, that would be counted as a miracle; so likewise here.

* * *

**The third issue:** The verse indicates that the Qur'an has a known meaning, contrary to what is said by those who hold that no one knows its meaning except the Prophet and the infallible Imam. For if that were so, the hypocrites would not have been able to know it through reflection, and it would not be permissible for Allah the Exalted to command them to it, to make the Qur'an a proof for the soundness of His prophethood, or to make their inability to produce its like a proof against them, just as it is not permissible to argue against the disbelievers among the Zanj (Black Africans) with such a thing.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates the obligation of rational reflection (*nazar*) and inference (*istidlal*), and the invalidity of blind imitation (*taqlid*). For the Exalted commanded the hypocrites to infer by this proof the soundness of His prophethood. If inference is necessary for the soundness of his prophethood, then it is all the more appropriate that inference be required for knowing the essence and attributes of Allah.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Abu Ali al-Jubba'i said: the verse indicates that the actions of servants are not created by Allah the Exalted, because His saying ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ requires that the act of the servant is not free of discrepancy, and discrepancy and variation are one and the same thing. So if the act of the servant is not free of discrepancy and variation, and the act of Allah does not contain variation, due to His saying ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], then this requires that the act of the servant is not an act of Allah.

The answer: His saying ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency﴾ [al-Mulk: 3] means the negation of inconsistency in that it occurs in accordance with His will, unlike what belongs to others, since the act of others does not occur in accordance with His will absolutely.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 83 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it about. But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them, those who [can] draw conclusions from it among them would have known it. And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few.﴾

Know that He, the Exalted, in this verse relates about the hypocrites another kind of corrupt action: when news of some matter comes to them, whether that matter concerns security or concerns fear, they spread it and disseminate it. This causes harm in several respects:

The first: such rumors (irjafat) are never free of much falsehood.

The second: if the news concerns security, they add many embellishments to it, and when those embellishments are not found, this produces doubt among the weak regarding the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace be upon him, because the hypocrites would attribute those rumors to the Messenger. If the news concerns fear, the matter becomes confused for the weak among the Muslims, and they fall into bewilderment and agitation over it. Thus those rumors were a cause of trial in this respect.

The third aspect: rumor is a cause for strong motivation to intensive investigation and thorough probing, and that leads to the exposure of secrets, and this does not accord with the interest of the city (Madinah).

The fourth: there was intense enmity between the Muslims and the disbelievers, and each of the two groups was preparing instruments of war and seeking opportunity against the other. So whatever was a matter of security for one of the two groups was a matter of fear for the second group. If news of security for the Muslims arose, and of the army and instruments of war being available to them, the hypocrites would spread it, and the news would reach the disbelievers in the shortest time, and they would begin fortifying themselves against the Muslims and guarding against being overpowered by them. And if news of fear for the Muslims arose, they would exaggerate it, add to it, and cast terror into the hearts of the weak and the humble. From this it becomes clear that such rumor was a source of trials and calamities in every respect. Since the matter is so, Allah censured that spreading and that publicizing, and forbade them from it.

Know that his saying "adha'ahu" and "adha'a bihi" are two dialects (lughatan).

* * *

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿But if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them, those who [can] draw conclusions from it among them would have known it.﴾

In this there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning ﴿ulil-amr﴾ (those of authority) there are two opinions:

One: they are the people of knowledge and judgment among them.

The second: they are the commanders of the military expeditions (sara ya). Those who held this view preferred it over the first, saying: "Those of authority (ulil-amr) are those who have command over people, and the scholars are not like that; rather, the commanders are the ones described as having command over the people."

It is answered: when scholars are knowledgeable of Allah's commands and prohibitions, and it is obligatory for others to accept their words, it is not far-fetched that they be called ulil-amr in this respect. What indicates this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, that they may beware﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. He made beware obligatory through their warning and obligated those warned to accept their words, so it is permissible for this reason to apply the name ulil-amr to them.

The second issue: istinbat (inference) in the language means extraction; it is said: "the jurist istanbata" when he extracts the hidden understanding (fiqh) by his effort (ijtihad) and insight. Its origin is from al-nabt, which is the water that emerges from a well when it is first dug; and the Nabateans were so named because of their extracting water from the earth.

The third issue: concerning His saying ﴿those who draw conclusions from it among them﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: they are those very hypocrites who spread rumors, and the sense is: "If these hypocrites who spread rumors had referred security and fear to the Messenger and to those of authority, and sought knowledge of the situation from them, those who draw conclusions from it among them, namely these hypocrites who spread rumors, would have known it, that is, from the side of the Messenger and from the side of those of authority."

The second opinion: they are a group among those of authority. The sense is: "If the hypocrites had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority, its knowledge would have been obtained by those among those of authority who draw conclusions from these events. This is because those of authority are of two kinds: some are inferrers (mustanbitun), and some are not so. So His saying ﴿among them﴾ means: those among the groups of those of authority who infer the hidden matters."

If it is said: if those whom Allah commanded to refer these reports to the Messenger and to those of authority are the hypocrites, how then did He make those of authority "among them" in His saying ﴿and to those of authority among them﴾?

We say: He made those of authority "among them" according to the outward appearance, because the hypocrites display themselves as believers. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾ and His saying: ﴿They would not have done it, except a few of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The fourth issue: this verse indicates that qiyas (analogical reasoning) is a proof (hujjah) in the Sharia. That is because His saying ﴿those who draw conclusions from it among them﴾ is a description of ulil-amr, and Allah has obligated those who receive a matter of security or fear to return to them for knowledge of it. Either they return to them concerning knowledge of these events while the text (nass) on them is present, or they do not return to them when the text is present. The first is invalid, because on this assumption there would be no istinbat, since one who transmits a text concerning an event is not said to have inferred the ruling. Thus it is established that Allah commanded the mukallaf to refer an event to one who infers the ruling concerning it. And were istinbat not a proof, He would not have commanded the mukallaf with this. So it is established that istinbat is a proof, and qiyas is either istinbat or included within it, so it must be a proof. Having established this, we say: the verse indicates several matters:

One: that among the rulings of novel events there is that which is known not by explicit text but by istinbat.

Second: that istinbat is a proof.

Third: that the layman is obligated to follow the scholars in the rulings of novel events.

Fourth: that the Prophet ﷺ was charged with inferring rulings, because He, the Exalted, commanded referral to the Messenger and to those of authority.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿would have known it, those who draw conclusions from it among them﴾ and He did not restrict ulil-amr to this to the exclusion of the Messenger, and this requires that the Messenger and all those of authority are charged with istinbat.

It may be objected: we do not grant that the meaning of ﴿those who draw conclusions from it among them﴾ is ulil-amr; rather the meaning is the hypocrites who spread rumors, according to what you have narrated in this interpretation of the verse. Suppose we grant that the meaning of "those who draw conclusions from it among them" is ulil-amr, yet this verse was revealed concerning events related to wars and jihad. Grant that referring to istinbat is permissible in them; why do you say that it necessarily follows that it is permissible in legal events? For if one of the two matters is analogized to the other, that would be establishing the legal qiyas by legal qiyas, and that is impermissible. Suppose we grant that istinbat in legal rulings falls under the verse. Why do you say that it follows that qiyas must be a proof? Its explanation: it is possible that the meaning of istinbat is the extraction of rulings from hidden texts or from the compositions of texts, or the meaning of extracting rulings from the original state of continuity (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah), or from what is established by the judgment of reason, as most say: that the original state regarding benefits is permissibility and regarding harms is prohibition. Suppose we grant that legal qiyas falls within the verse, but on condition that that qiyas yields knowledge ('ilm), by the proof of His saying: ﴿would have known it, those who draw conclusions from it among them﴾. For He, the Exalted, informed in this verse that knowledge arises from this istinbat, and there is no dispute about such qiyas. The dispute is only about whether qiyas that yields opinion (zann) is a proof in the Sharia or not. The answer:

As for the first objection: it is refuted, because if the meaning of "those who draw conclusions from it" were the hypocrites, it would have been more proper to say: "and if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them, they would have known it," because the conjunction of an explicit noun upon a pronoun, namely His saying ﴿and if they had referred it﴾, is ugly and objectionable.

As for the second objection: it is refuted for two reasons:

The first: His saying ﴿And if there comes to them a matter of security or fear﴾ is general, encompassing everything related to wars and to all other legal events, because security and fear are present in everything related to the domain of obligation. Thus it is established that there is nothing in the verse requiring that it be restricted to matters of war.

The second: suppose the matter is as you mentioned; yet the rulings of wars are known by legal qiyas, and since its permissibility is established, it must be permissible to rely on legal qiyas in all other events, for there is no one who distinguishes. Do you not see that whoever says: qiyas is a proof in the domain of sale but not in the domain of marriage is not heeded? So it is here too.

As for the third objection, namely the interpretation of istinbat as hidden texts or compositions of texts: its answer is that all of that does not leave being textual, and holding fast to a text is not called istinbat. As for his saying: why is it not permissible to interpret it as holding to the original continuity? We say: this is not istinbat; rather it is maintaining what was as it was, and such a thing is not called istinbat at all.

As for the fourth objection, namely his saying that this istinbat is permissible only when knowledge is attained, and legal qiyas does not yield knowledge:

We say: the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: that legal qiyas, according to us, yields knowledge. That is because, after establishing that qiyas is a proof, we are certain that whenever it is predominantly held in opinion that Allah's ruling in the original case is grounded in such-and-such a cause, and then it is predominantly held in opinion that this meaning is present in the derivative case, then there arises an opinion that Allah's ruling in the derivative case is equal to His ruling in the original case. At this opinion we are certain that he is charged to act according to this opinion. The upshot is that the opinion occurs in the path to the ruling, while the ruling itself is certain. This is like when Allah says: whenever it is predominantly held in your opinion that such-and-such, know that in that particular event My ruling is such-and-such. So when the opinion arises, we are certain of the establishment of that ruling.

The second: that knowledge is sometimes used and what is meant by it is opinion. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "If you know something like the sun, then testify." He made knowledge a condition for the permissibility of testimony, and we agree that testimony is permissible on the basis of opinion. Thus it is established that opinion is sometimes called knowledge. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: the apparent sense of this exception suggests that that few did not occur by the grace of Allah nor by His mercy, and it is known that this is impossible. Therefore the exegetes differed and mentioned several views. Some said: this exception refers back to His saying ﴿they spread it about﴾. Others said: it refers back to His saying ﴿those who draw conclusions from it﴾. And others said: it refers back to His saying ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾.

Know that the views cannot exceed these three, because the verse includes information about these three rulings, and it is valid to direct the exception to each of them. Thus it is established that each of these statements is possible.

As for the first view: the sense is: "And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it about, except a few." So He, the Exalted, excluded some of the hypocrites from spreading, just as He excluded them in His saying: ﴿A group of them plotted by night other than what you say﴾.

The second opinion: the exception refers back to His saying: ﴿would have known it from those among them who draw conclusions from it﴾, meaning: "would have known it from those among them who draw conclusions from it, except a few." Al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad said: "The first opinion is preferable, because what is known through istinbat (deduction, drawing out a conclusion), a few know it while most are ignorant of it, and turning the exception to what they mentioned would imply the opposite of that." Al-Zajjaj said: "This is an error, because the intended meaning of this exception is not something extracted by subtle examination and obscure reflection; rather, it is the istinbat of news (drawing out reports). If that is the case, most people know it. Only the one who is utterly dull and ignorant is one who does not know it." It may be said: al-Zajjaj's statement is only valid if we take istinbat to mean merely recognizing reports and rumors. But if we take it to mean istinbat of all rulings, as we have established by proof, then the truth is as al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad stated.

The third opinion: it is connected to His saying: ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾. It is known that turning the exception to what precedes it and is connected to it is preferable to turning it to something distant from it.

Know that this opinion does not hold unless we interpret "bounty" (fadl) and "mercy" (rahmah) as referring to something specific, and there are two aspects to this:

The first, which is the view of a group of exegetes, is that what is meant by Allah's bounty and His mercy in this verse is the sending down of the Qur'an and the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: "And if not for the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the sending down of the Qur'an, you would have followed Satan and disbelieved in Allah, except a few among you." For that few, had Muhammad (ﷺ) not been sent and the Qur'an not been sent down, would not have followed Satan nor disbelieved in Allah. They are like Qss ibn Sa'idah, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, who were believers in Allah before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second aspect is what Abu Muslim mentioned, namely that what is meant by Allah's bounty and His mercy in this verse is His victory and His assistance, which the hypocrites referred to by their saying: ﴿so that I would achieve a great achievement﴾ [al-Nisa': 73]. Thus He, exalted is He, made clear that were it not for the occurrence of victory and triumph in succession, you would have followed Satan and abandoned the religion, except a few among you. These are people of penetrating insight, strong intentions, and firm resolve, from among the excellent believers, who know that it is not a condition of a thing's being true that worldly dominance be attained. Thus the continuous occurrence of conquest and victory does not indicate that it is true, and the continuous occurrence of defeat and humiliation does not indicate that it is false. Rather, the matter of its being true or false rests upon the proof. This is the most correct of the aspects and the closest to verification.

* * *

The second issue: the verse indicates that those who followed Satan were denied by Allah His bounty and His mercy, since otherwise they would not have been followed. This indicates the invalidity of the view of the Mu'tazilah that it is obligatory upon Allah to take care of what is most beneficial in religion. Al-Ka'bi answered this by saying that Allah's bounty and His mercy are general with respect to everyone, but the believers benefited from them while the disbelievers did not benefit from them. So it is correct, by way of metaphor, to say that the disbeliever did not receive from Allah any bounty or mercy in religion.

The reply: taking the word in a metaphorical sense contradicts the original usage.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 84:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah. You are not held responsible except for yourself, and urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve. And Allah is greater in might and greater in punishment.﴾

Know that when Exalted Allah had commanded jihad and encouraged it with the utmost encouragement in the preceding verses, and had mentioned concerning the hypocrites their lack of desire for jihad, and indeed mentioned of them their intense effort to discourage the Muslims from jihad, He returned in this verse to the command to fight, saying: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah.﴾ There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: To what does the fa' (so) in His saying ﴿So fight﴾ relate? There are several views:

The first: It is a response (jawab) to His saying: ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed﴾ [al-Nisa: 74] in terms of meaning, because it indicates the meaning: if you desire success, then fight.

The second: That it is connected to His saying: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ So: ﴿fight in the way of Allah.﴾

The third: That it is connected to the meaning of what was mentioned of the accounts of the hypocrites, and the meaning is that among the characteristics of these hypocrites is such-and-such, so do not give them any consideration and do not heed their actions, but fight.

The second issue: The verse indicates that Allah commanded him to engage in jihad even alone, before calling people to go out to Badr al-Sughra, when Abu Sufyan had arranged to meet the Messenger ﷺ there. Some people disliked going out, so this verse was revealed, and he went out with no one with him except seventy men, and he did not turn to anyone. Had they not followed him, he would have gone out alone.

The third issue: The verse indicates that he ﷺ was the most courageous of creation and the most knowledgeable of them concerning the manner of fighting, because Allah would not have commanded him with this except that he was described with these qualities. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, emulated him when he attempted to go out alone to fight those who withheld zakat. Whoever knows that the whole affair is in the hand of Allah, and that no matter occurs except by the decree of Allah, finds this easy.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿You are not held responsible except for yourself﴾ and concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read as (lā tukallaf) with a jazm on the basis of prohibition, and (lā nukallif) with a nun and a kasra on the lam, meaning: We do not burden anyone except you yourself alone.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the accusative of His saying ﴿nafsaka﴾ is as the object of what has not been named with its subject (maf'ul ma lam yusamma fa'iluh).

The third issue: The verse indicates that if no one else assists him in fighting, it is not permissible for him to abstain from jihad at all. The meaning is: you will be held accountable only for your own action, not the action of others; so when you have performed your action, you are not burdened with the obligation of others.

Know that jihad with respect to someone other than the Messenger, upon him be peace, is among the collective obligations (fard al-kifayat). So if it is not predominantly thought that it will be beneficial, it is not obligatory.
