Unlike the Messenger, upon him be the blessings and peace, for he is certain of help and victory, based on His saying: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], and based on His saying here: ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve,﴾ and "perhaps" from Allah is certainty. Therefore jihad became obligatory upon him even if he were alone.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And urge the believers.﴾ The meaning is that what is obligatory upon the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, is only jihad and urging the people to jihad. If he fulfils these two matters, he has discharged the obligation, and he bears no responsibility for others abandoning jihad.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve.﴾ Concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: 'Asa (perhaps) is one of the particles of approximation, and it contains expectation and hope, and that is impossible with respect to Allah, exalted is He.

The answer to this: 'asa means raising hope (al-ita'), and in raising hope there is no indication of doubt or certainty. Some said: the raising of hope by a generous one is an obligation.

The second issue: al-Kaff means prevention, and al-ba's originally means what is disliked. It is said: "There is no ba's (harm) for you in this matter," meaning no disliked thing. It is also said: "Bi'sa al-shay' hadha" when something is described as bad. His saying: ﴿with a severe punishment (bi-'adhabin ba'is)﴾ [al-A'raf: 165] means disliked. Punishment is sometimes called ba's because it is disliked. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who will protect us from the might of Allah?﴾ [Ghafir: 29]; ﴿When they perceived Our might﴾ [al-Anbiya: 12]; ﴿When they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 84]. The exegetes said: "Perhaps Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve," and He did restrain their might: it became apparent to Abu Sufyan, and he said, "This is a year of drought, and they had no provision except sawiq (roasted barley flour)," so he abandoned going to fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is greater in might and greater in punishment.﴾ It is said: "nakkaltu fulanan" when you punish someone with a punishment that deters others from committing the like of it, from the saying of the people: "nakala al-rajul 'an al-shay'" when a man became fearful of something and refrained from it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We made it a deterrent (nakal) for what was before it and what came after it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66], and He said concerning theft: ﴿as a deterrent (nakal) from Allah for what they earned﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. It is also said: "nakala fulan 'an al-yamin" when he feared it and did not undertake it.

Having known this, we say: the verse indicates that the punishment and deterrence of Allah is greater than the punishment of others and their deterrence. The most sound of the aspects explaining this difference is that the punishment of other than Allah is not perpetual, while the punishment of Allah is everlasting in the Hereafter; the punishment of other than Allah may be escaped from by Allah's granting deliverance, while no one can escape the punishment of Allah; and also, the punishment of other than Allah occurs only in one respect, while the punishment of Allah may reach all the parts, limbs, the spirit and the body.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 85:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will bear a portion of it. And Allah is ever Maqit (Sustainer; Powerful; Keeper of account) over all things.﴾

Concerning this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that there are several views on how this verse relates to what precedes it.

The first: Allah the Exalted commanded the Messenger, peace be upon him, to urge the community to *jihad* (struggle in the way of Allah, often rendered as holy war), and jihad is among the good deeds and noble acts of worship. So the Prophet's urging of the community to jihad was an urging to them toward a good deed and a good act of obedience. Thus Allah explains in this verse that whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in it. The purpose is to show that when he, peace be upon him, urged them to jihad, he earned a great reward for that urging.

The second: When Allah commanded him to urge them to jihad, He mentioned that if they did not accept his command, no blame would fall upon him for their disobedience and defiance. Then in this verse He explains that when they obeyed and accepted the obligation, a great good returned to him from their obedience. It is as if Allah said to the Messenger, peace be upon him: Urge them to jihad. If they do not accept your word, their disobedience will not be a reproach against you; and if they obey you, you will receive the greatest reward from their obedience. This was an encouragement from Allah to His Messenger to strive in urging the community to jihad. The reason that a great reward returned to him, peace be upon him, when they obeyed, while no portion of the burden returned to him from their disobedience, is that he, peace be upon him, exerted effort in encouraging them to obedience and never encouraged them at all to disobedience. Therefore a reward returns to him from their obedience, and no burden returns to him from their disobedience.

The third: It may be said that since he, peace be upon him, used to encourage them to fight and strongly urged them to it, some hypocrites would intercede with the Prophet ﷺ that he permit some of them to remain behind from the expedition. So Allah forbade such intercession and explained that intercession is only good when it is a means to establishing the obedience of Allah. But when it is a means to disobedience of Him, it is forbidden and reprehensible.

The fourth: It may be that some believers were eager for jihad but did not have the equipment for it, so another believer interceded on his behalf with a third believer, so that he might be helped to take part in jihad. This intercession was then an effort to establish obedience, so Allah encouraged such intercession. In all these views, the verse is well connected to what precedes it.

**The second issue:** *Shafa'a* (intercession) is derived from *shaf'* (pair), which means that a person makes himself a pair with the one in need, so that he joins him in asking for it.

Having understood this, we say: There are several views on the intercession mentioned in the verse:

The first: What is meant by it is the Prophet ﷺ urging them to jihad. This is because when he, peace be upon him, commanded them to go out to fight, he made himself an intercessor for them in obtaining the aims connected with jihad. Also, urging someone to something is an expression of commanding them to it, not in the manner of threat but in the manner of gentleness and kindness, and this runs in the path of intercession.

The second: What is meant by it is what we mentioned, that some hypocrites interceded for another hypocrite, asking the Messenger, peace be upon him, to permit him to stay behind from jihad. Or what is meant is that some believers interceded for another believer with a third believer, so that he would obtain what he needed of the implements of jihad.

The third: al-Wahidi reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, the meaning that the good intercession here is that a person's faith in Allah intercedes by fighting the disbelievers, and the evil intercession is that his disbelief intercedes by loving the disbelievers and abandoning harming them.

The fourth: Muqatil said: Intercession to Allah is only by supplication. He cited what Abu al-Darda' narrated, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever supplicates for his Muslim brother in his absence, it is answered for him, and the angel says: 'And for you is the like of that.'" This is the share. As for the evil intercession, it is what was narrated: "The Jews, when they came to the Messenger ﷺ, would say: *As-sam* upon you. *As-sam* means death. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, heard this and said: 'Upon you be the *sam* and the curse! Do you say this to the Messenger?' He ﷺ said: 'I have known what they said, and I said: And upon you.'" And this verse was revealed.

The fifth: al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd said: What is meant is the intercession that takes place among people, one for another. Whatever may be permitted in the religion to be interceded for is a good intercession, and whatever may not be permitted to be interceded for is an evil intercession. Then al-Hasan said: Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a reward in it even if he is not himself interceded with, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever intercedes﴾, and He did not say: "Whoever is interceded with." This is supported by the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "Intercede, and you will be rewarded."

I say: This intercession must have a connection with jihad, otherwise the verse would be cut off from what precedes it. That connection is present in the first two views. As for the last three views, if the intention is to restrict the verse to them, that is invalid; otherwise this verse would be unrelated to what precedes it. If the intention is that these three enter the wording together with the first two, this is permissible, because the specificity of the occasion of revelation does not prevent the generality of the wording.

**The third issue:** The lexicographers said: *Kifl* means portion or share, and from it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28], meaning two shares. It is derived from their saying: *kafaltu al-ba'ir* and *iktafaltuhu*, when you put a cloth over the hump of a camel and ride upon it. It is said *kafaltu al-ba'ir* and *iktafaltuhu* because the rider does not use the whole back, but only a portion of the back. Ibn al-Muzaffar said: One does not say "this is the *kifl* of so-and-so" unless you have provided another with its like, and likewise regarding *nasib* (share). If you mention it singly, do not say "for him is a *kifl*" or "a *nasib*."

If it is asked: Why did He say in the good intercession ﴿will have a *nasib* from it﴾, and in the evil intercession ﴿will bear a *kifl* from it﴾? Is there any benefit in the difference between these two expressions?

We reply: *Kifl* is the name for the share upon which people depend. It is said *kifl* of the camel because you protect the camel's back with that cloth from harm, and the rider protects his body with that cloth from the camel's back striking him so that he is harmed by it. And a guarantor is called *kafil*. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I and the one who supports an orphan are like these two." Thus it is established that *kifl* is the share upon which a person depends in obtaining his interests and warding off harm from himself. Having established this, we say: ﴿Whoever intercedes for an evil cause will bear a *kifl* from it﴾, meaning there will come to him from it a share, which will be a store for him in his livelihood and his return; and the intended meaning is the opposite of that: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment.﴾ The purpose is to alert that intercession which leads to the loss of a right and the strengthening of falsehood is greatly punished by Allah the Exalted.

\* \* \*

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is ever Maqit over all things.﴾ Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding *al-muqit* there are two views:

The first: *Al-muqit* is the one capable of (having power over) a thing. They cited the verse of al-Zubayr ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib:

*"And a man of rancor, I held my soul back from him, and I was over his evil, able to requite (muqit)."*

Another said:

*"Would that I knew, and I would know, when they bring it forth unfolded and I am called: is the bounty mine or against me, when I am called to account, that I am over the reckoning (muqit)?"*

al-Nadr ibn Shumayl recited:

*"Be steadfast, do not despair, and be one of vigilance, for I am over what displeases them (muqit)."*

The second: *Muqit* is derived from *qut* (sustenance). It is said: *qattu al-rajul* when you guard a man's soul by providing him with what sustains him. The name of that thing is *qut*, which is that which has no surplus beyond the measure of need. So the *muqit* is the guardian who gives a thing according to the measure of need. Then al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whichever of the two meanings it is, the interpretation is correct, namely that He, the Exalted, is able to deliver the share and the *kifl* of the recompense to the intercessor just as He delivers it to the one interceded for: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil; and no part of the recompense of the one interceded for is diminished by reason of what reaches the intercessor. And on the second meaning, He, the Exalted, is the Guardian of things, a witness over them; nothing of our states is hidden from Him. He knows that the intercessor intercedes for a right or for a falsehood, and He is Guardian over him, so He recompenses each according to what He knows of him.

**The second issue:** He said ﴿And Allah is ever Maqit over all things﴾ to alert that His being capable over things that are capable of being done is an attribute that has been established for Him from eternity, and is not a newly originated attribute. So the word ﴿ever (*kana*)﴾ is unrestricted, without being limited by saying that it was from such a time or such a state; this indicates that it has existed from eternity to eternity.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 86 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted said: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with a better one than it, or return it. Indeed, Allah is ever Reckoner of all things.﴾

There are two views regarding the connection (nazm) of this verse:

The first: When He commanded the believers to fight (jihad), He also commanded them that if the enemies inclined to peace, they should likewise be content with it. So His saying, ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with a better one than it, or return it﴾ is like His saying, ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61].

The second: In jihad, a man would meet another man in the land of war or near it, and he would greet him with salam, but he might not pay attention to his salam and would kill him, and it may become apparent that he was a Muslim. So Allah forbade the believers from this and commanded them that whoever greets them and honors them with some form of honor, they should respond with the like of that honor or more. For if he is a disbeliever, it does no harm to the Muslim to respond to that disbeliever's honor with some form of honor. But if he is a Muslim and they kill him, there is in that the greatest harm and corruption. There are several issues regarding the verse:

The first issue: Tahiyyah is a form (taf'ilah) from ḥayyaytu, and originally it was taḥyiyah, like tawṣiyah and tasmiyah. The Arabs prefer the taf'ilah form over the tafʿīl form in quadriliteral roots, such as His saying, ﴿and the burning of Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94]. Thus it is established that the origin of tahiyyah is taḥyiyah, then they assimilated the yā' into the yā'.

The second issue: Know that the custom of the Arabs before Islam was that when some of them met others, they would say: "Ḥayyāka Allāh" (may Allah give you life), derived from ḥayāh (life), as if he were praying for him to have life. So tahiyyah for them was an expression for one saying to another, "Ḥayyāka Allāh." When Islam came, this was replaced by salam (peace), and they made tahiyyah a name for salam. Allah said: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be, "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]. From this is the saying of the one praying: "At-taḥiyyātu lillāh" (all greetings are for Allah), meaning that peace from calamities belongs to Allah. The poetry speaks of this. ʿAntarah said:

"I greeted a campsite whose traces had long been effaced."

Another said:

"Indeed we greet you, O Salmā, so greet us."

Know that the saying of one to another, "As-salāmu ʿalayka" (peace be upon you), is more complete and perfect than saying "Ḥayyāka Allāh," and its explanation is from several aspects:

First: The living person, if he is sound, is certainly alive, but it is not the case that if he is alive he is sound. His life may be accompanied by calamities and afflictions. Thus it is established that saying "As-salāmu ʿalayka" is more complete and perfect than saying "Ḥayyāka Allāh."

Second: Salam is one of the names of Allah the Exalted. Beginning with the mention of Allah, or with one of His attributes indicating that He wills to preserve safety for His servants, is more complete than saying "Ḥayyāka Allāh."

Third: The saying of a person to another, "As-salāmu ʿalayka," contains good news of safety, whereas saying "Ḥayyāka Allāh" does not convey that. So this is more complete. Among what indicates the excellence of salam are the Qur'an, the traditions, and reason. As for the Qur'an, it is from several aspects:

First: Know that Allah the Exalted sent salam upon the believer in twelve places:

The first of them: He, the Exalted, as if sent salam upon you in eternity. Do you not see that He said in describing His own essence: "Al-Malik, al-Quddūs, as-Salām" (the King, the Holy, the Source of Peace) [al-Hashr: 23].

The second: He sent salam upon Noah and made for you a share of that salam, when He said: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you"﴾ [Hud: 48]. What is meant by this is the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The third: He sent salam upon you through the tongue of Jibril, when He said: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord with every matter. Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾ [al-Qadr: 4-5]. The commentators said: He (peace be upon him) feared for his nation that they would become like the nations of Musa and ʿIsa (peace be upon them both), so Allah said: "Do not be concerned about that. Even if I take you out of this world, I have made Jibril your successor; he will descend to your nation every Night of Decree and convey to them salam from Me."

The fourth: He sent salam upon you through the tongue of Musa (peace be upon him), when he said: ﴿And peace upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. So when you are one who follows guidance, the salam of Musa reaches you.

The fifth: He sent salam upon you through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ), when he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ [al-Naml: 59]. Everyone whom Allah guides to faith has been chosen by Him, as He said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾ [Fatir: 32].

The sixth: He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to give salam by way of direct address, when He said: ﴿And when those who believe in Our verses come to you, say, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-An'am: 54].

The seventh: He commanded the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) to give salam to you, saying: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with a better one than it, or return it﴾.

The eighth: He sent salam upon you through the tongue of the Angel of Death, when He said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Nahl: 32]. It is said that the Angel of Death says into the ear of the Muslim: "Peace greets you," and says: "Answer me, for I long for you, and the Gardens and the wide-eyed maidens (ḥūr ʿīn) long for you." When the believer hears the good news, he says to the Angel of Death: "For the bearer of good news from me is a gift, and there is no gift more precious than my soul, so take my soul as a gift for you."

The ninth: Salam comes from the pure and purified spirits. Allah said: ﴿As for if he was of the companions of the right, then, "Peace be to you from the companions of the right"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90-91].

The tenth: Allah sent salam upon you through the tongue of Ridwan, the keeper of Paradise, when He said: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] up to His saying: ﴿And its keepers will say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have become good"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

The eleventh: When they enter Paradise, the angels visit them and greet them. Allah said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24].

The twelfth: Salam comes from Allah without intermediary, and this is His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be, "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44], and His saying: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. At that point, the salam of all things vanishes, because the created cannot remain under the manifestation of the light of the Creator.

The second aspect: Among the Qur'anic proofs indicating the excellence of salam is that the times most in need of safety and honor are three: the time of beginning, the time of death, and the time of resurrection. When Allah honored Yahya (peace be upon him), He honored him only by promising him salam in these three times, when He said: ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 15]. ʿIsa (peace be upon him) also mentioned this, saying: ﴿And peace upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 33].

The third aspect: When Allah the Exalted mentioned the honor of Muhammad (peace be upon him), He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with [full] greeting﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. It is related in the exegesis that the Jews, when they entered, would say: "As-sām ʿalayka" (death be upon you). The Messenger (peace be upon him) grieved over this matter, so Allah sent Jibril (peace be upon him) and said: "If the Jews say, 'As-sām ʿalayka,' I say from the pavilions of majesty: 'As-salām ʿalayka'" (peace be upon you). And He revealed His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and greet him with [full] greeting﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

As for the reports indicating the excellence of salam: it is narrated that ʿAbdullah ibn Salam said: "When I heard of the arrival of the Messenger (peace be upon him), I entered among the crowds, and the first thing I heard from him was: 'O people, spread the salam, feed the food, maintain the ties of kinship, and pray at night while people are asleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace.'"

As for what indicates the excellence of salam from the standpoint of reason, there are several aspects:

First: They said: The greeting of the Christians is placing the hand over the mouth; the greeting of the Jews among themselves is a gesture with the fingers; the greeting of the Magians is bowing; the greeting of the Arabs among themselves is to say "Ḥayyāka Allāh"; and for kings it is to say "Anʿim ṣabāḥan" (may you have a pleasant morning); and the greeting of the Muslims among themselves is to say: "As-salāmu ʿalayka wa raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuh." There is no doubt that this greeting is the most noble and honored of greetings.

Second: Salam implies safety from calamities and afflictions. There is no doubt that striving to attain protection from harm is more important than striving to attain benefit.

Third: A promise of benefit a person may or may not be able to fulfill, but a promise to avoid harm, he is certainly able to fulfill it, and salam indicates this. Thus it is established that salam is the best type of greeting.

* * *

The third issue: Some people have said: Whoever enters a house, it becomes obligatory upon him to greet those present, and they argued for this with several points:

First: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. And the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Spread the salam," and the command indicates obligation.

Second: Whoever enters upon a person is like one seeking something from him. Then the one entered upon does not know whether he seeks it for good or for evil. So when he says, "As-salāmu ʿalayka," he has given him good news of safety and assured him against fear. And removing harm from a Muslim is obligatory. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The Muslim is one from whose hand and tongue the Muslims are safe." So it is necessary that salam be obligatory.

Third: Salam is one of the symbols (sha'a'ir) of the people of Islam, and displaying the symbols of Islam is obligatory. However, the well-known view is that salam is sunnah, and this is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakhaʿi.

As for responding to salam, they have agreed (ijmāʿ) that it is obligatory, and several points indicate this:

First: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with a better one than it, or return it﴾.

Second: Abandoning the response is humiliation, humiliation is harm, and harm is forbidden.

* * *

The fourth issue: The ultimate form of salam is to say: "As-salāmu ʿalaykum wa raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuh," based on the evidence that this amount is what is reported in the tashahhud (the testimony in prayer).

Know that He, the Exalted, said: ﴿greet with a better one than it, or return it﴾. The scholars said: The better form is that when a Muslim says, "As-salāmu ʿalayka," mercy is added to his reply; if he mentions salam and mercy at the beginning, blessing is added to his reply; and if he mentions all three at the beginning, he repeats them in the reply.

It is reported that a man said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "As-salāmu ʿalayka, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "Wa ʿalayka as-salām wa raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuh." Another said: "As-salāmu ʿalayka wa raḥmatu Allāh," and he said: "Wa ʿalayka as-salām wa raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuh." A third came and said: "As-salāmu ʿalayka wa raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuh," and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Wa ʿalayka as-salām wa raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuh." The man said: "You have short-changed me, for where is the saying of Allah: ﴿greet with a better one than it﴾?" He (ﷺ) said: "You did not leave any excess for me, so I returned to you what you mentioned."

[p. 167]

[Page 170]

**Fifth issue:** The one initiating says, "As-salamu alaykum," and the one responding says, "Wa alaykumu as-salam." This is the good order. What occurred to me regarding this is that when he says "As-salamu alaykum," the initiation falls upon the mention of Allah, and when the responder says "Wa alaykumu as-salam," the conclusion falls upon the mention of Allah. This corresponds to His saying: ﴿He is the First and the Last﴾ [al-Hadid: 3]. Also, since the initiation and the conclusion are with the mention of Allah, it is hoped that what lies between them becomes accepted by its blessing, as in His saying: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hud: 114]. So if the one initiating differs and says, "Wa alaykumu as-salam," he has opposed the Sunnah. Therefore, it is better for the responder to say, "Wa alaykumu as-salam," because since the first has left the opening with the mention of Allah, this one should not leave the closing with the mention of Allah.

**Sixth issue:** If he wishes, he may say, "Salamun alaykum," and if he wishes, he may say, "As-salamu alaykum." Allah said regarding Noah: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us"﴾ [Hud: 48]. And He said about the Friend (Abraham): ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord"﴾ [Maryam: 47]. And He said in the story of Lot: ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 25]. And He said about Yahya: ﴿And peace was upon him﴾ [Maryam: 15]. And He said about Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants"﴾ [an-Naml: 59]. And He said about the angels: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you"﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 23–24]. And He said about the Lord of Might: ﴿Peace, a word from a Merciful Lord﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. And He said: ﴿Say, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-An'am: 54]. As for with the definite article (al-salam), it is His saying about Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace is upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. And He said about Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born and the day I die﴾ [Maryam: 33]. It is established that all of these are permissible. As for the conclusion of the prayer, the definite article (alif-lam) is necessary by consensus. The scholars differed regarding the other occasions: is indefiniteness (tankir) better, or definiteness (ta'rif)? It was said that indefiniteness is better, and this is indicated by several points:

First: The word "salam" in indefinite form occurs frequently in the Qur'an, so it is better.

Second: Everything that came from Allah, the angels, and the believers came in the indefinite form, as we have enumerated in the verses. As for the definite form, it only occurred in a person's greeting of himself. Musa (ﷺ) said: ﴿And peace is upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47], and Isa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And peace is upon me﴾.

Third, which is the rational meaning: the word "salam" with the definite article indicates the essence of the reality, while the indefinite indicates the essence of the reality together with the attribute of perfection. So this is preferable.

* * *

**Seventh issue:** He (ﷺ) said: "The Sunnah is that the rider greets the one walking, the one on horseback greets the one on a donkey, the young greets the elder, the few greet the many, and the standing greets the seated."

I say: As for the first (the rider greeting the walker), it is for two reasons:
One: The rider has more dignity, so his greeting brings the removal of fear.
Two: Pride is more fitting for him, so he is commanded to initiate the greeting, breaking that pride. As for the standing greeting the seated, it is because he is the one who has come to them, so this arriving person must begin by opening with good for the one he has reached.

**Eighth issue:** The Sunnah regarding greeting is to say it aloud, because it is stronger in bringing joy into the heart.

**Ninth issue:** The Sunnah regarding greeting is to spread it widely and generally, because singling out (some people) causes estrangement.

**Tenth issue:** Shaking hands during greeting is the custom of the Messenger (ﷺ). He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "When two Muslims shake hands, their sins fall away just as leaves fall from a tree."

**Eleventh issue:** Abu Yusuf said: Whoever says to another, "Convey my greetings to so-and-so," it becomes obligatory for him to do so.

**Twelfth issue:** If a single man approaches you, say, "Salamun alaykum," and intend the man and the two angels, for when you greet these two, they return the greeting to you. And whoever the angel greets is safe from the punishment of Allah.

**Thirteenth issue:** If you enter an empty house, then greet. There are several points regarding this:
First: You greet from Allah upon yourself.
Second: You greet whoever is in it from the believing jinn.
Third: You seek safety by the blessing of the greeting from whoever is in the house of the devils and harmful creatures.

**Fourteenth issue:** The Sunnah is that the one initiating the greeting be in a state of purity, and likewise the one responding. It is narrated that a man greeted the Messenger (ﷺ) while he was relieving himself, so he got up, performed tayammum, and then returned the greeting.

**Fifteenth issue:** The Sunnah, when two people meet, is that they both hasten to greet, to show humility.

* * *

**Sixteenth issue:** Let us mention the occasions on which one does not greet, and they are eight:

First: It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A Jew should not be greeted first." Abu Hanifa said: One should not initiate greeting in a letter or in anything else. From Abu Yusuf: Do not greet them and do not shake their hands, and when you enter, say, "Peace be upon those who follow guidance." He permitted initiating the greeting to them when there is a need for it. As for when they greet us, most scholars say it should be answered with, "Wa alayk." The origin of this is that they used to say when entering upon the Messenger (ﷺ): "As-sam alayka" (death upon you), and the Prophet (ﷺ) would say, "Wa alaykum," and the Sunnah followed this practice. Then there is a branch here: if we say to them, "Wa alaykumu as-salam," is it permissible to mention mercy (rahmah) in it? Al-Hasan said it is permissible to say to the disbeliever, "Wa alaykumu as-salam," but one should not say, "wa rahmatullah," because that is an invocation for forgiveness.
It is related from al-Sha'bi that he said to a Christian, "Wa alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullah." He was asked about this, and he said: "Does he not live by the mercy of Allah?"

Second: If he enters on Friday while the imam is delivering the sermon, it is not appropriate to greet, because people are occupied with gathering. If he greets and some return it, there is no harm, but if they limit themselves to a gesture, that is better.

Third: If he enters the bathhouse and sees people wearing their waist-wraps, he greets them; if they are not wearing them, he does not greet them.

Fourth: It is preferable to omit greeting the one reciting the Qur'an, because if he is occupied with answering, it cuts off his recitation. The same applies to one occupied with narrating hadith or discussing knowledge.

Fifth: One does not greet the one occupied with the adhan and the iqamah, for the reason we mentioned.

Sixth: Abu Yusuf said: One does not greet the backgammon player, nor the singer, nor the one who releases pigeons. In the same category is everyone occupied with some kind of sin.

Seventh: One does not greet the one who is occupied with relieving himself. A man passed by the Messenger (ﷺ) while he was relieving himself, and greeted him. The Messenger (ﷺ) went to a wall, performed tayammum, and then returned the reply, and said: "Had I not feared that you would say, 'I greeted him and he did not return the reply,' I would not have answered you. When you see me in this state, do not greet me, for if you greet me, I will not return it to you."

Eighth: When a man enters his house, he greets his wife. If a non-related woman is present there, he does not greet them both.

* * *

**Seventeenth issue:** Regarding the rules of the reply, and they are eight:

First: Returning the greeting is obligatory, because of Allah's saying: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with something better than it or return it﴾ [an-Nisa: 86]. And because abandoning the reply is humiliation, harm, and forbidden. From Ibn Abbas: No man passes by a group of Muslims, greets them, and they do not return his greeting, except that the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) is removed from them, and the angels return it to him.

Second: Returning the greeting is a communal obligation (fard kifayah): if some of them perform it, it is dropped from the rest. But it is best for all of them to return the greeting, to show honor and to emphasize it.

Third: It is obligatory immediately (ala al-fawr). If he delays until the time has passed, then if he answers after the time has passed, that is considered an initiation of greeting and not a reply.

Fourth: If a greeting is received in a letter, then replying to it in writing is also obligatory, because of Allah's saying: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with something better than it or return it﴾.

Fifth: If he says, "As-salamu alaykum," then what is obligatory is that he says, "Wa alaykumu as-salam."

Sixth: It is narrated from Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "He should not return it loudly," meaning not with a great raising of the voice.

Seventh: If a non-related woman greets him, and he fears accusation or temptation in returning the greeting to her, then returning it is not obligatory; rather, it is better that he not do so.

Eighth: Where we have said he should not greet, if he greets anyway, it is not obligatory for her to return it, because he has done a forbidden act, so its existence is like its non-existence.

* * *

**Eighteenth issue:** Know that the word "tahiyyah" (greeting), as we have explained, has become a metaphor for honor, so all kinds of honoring fall under the term "tahiyyah."

Having known this, we say: Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever gives a gift to someone other than a mahram relative has the right to take it back as long as he has not been compensated for it. But if he has been compensated for it, there is no taking back. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: He has the right to take it back with regard to a child, but he does not have the right to take it back with regard to a stranger. Abu Bakr al-Razi used this verse as evidence for the correctness of Abu Hanifa's view, for His saying: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with something better than it or return it﴾ includes greeting, and it includes giving gifts. Its implication is the obligation to return it when it is not met with something better. If the obligation is not established, then at least it is permissible. Al-Shafi'i said: This command is to be understood as recommendation (nadb), with evidence that if he is compensated with something less than it, the possibility of returning it falls away by consensus, even though the apparent meaning of the verse requires that he bring something better. Then al-Shafi'i argued for his position with what Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It is not lawful for a man to give a gift and then take it back, except a father regarding what he gives his child." This is an explicit text that the gift of a stranger it is forbidden to take back, and the gift of a child it is permissible to take back.

* * *

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Reckoner﴾. And regarding this there are issues:

**First issue:** Regarding "Hasib" (Reckoner) there are two views:
The first: It means "one who calls to account for deeds," like "akil" (eater), "sharib" (drinker), and "jalis" (companion), meaning "mu'akil" (one who eats with), "mu'arrib" (one who drinks with), and "mujalis" (one who sits with).
The second: It means "sufficient," as in their saying, "hasbi kadha" (my sufficiency is such-and-such), meaning "kafi" (sufficient for me). From this is His saying: ﴿Allah is sufficient for me﴾ [at-Tawbah: 129].

**Second issue:** The purpose of this is a warning (wa'id). We have explained that one of them would greet a Muslim man, and then that Muslim would not inquire into his condition; rather, he might kill him out of greed for his spoils. So Allah forbade that and said: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with something better than it or return it﴾, and beware of exposing him to killing.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Reckoner﴾, meaning: He will call you to account for your deeds, and He is sufficient in bringing the reward of your deeds to you. So be cautious of violating the obligations. This indicates the great concern with preserving lives and preventing their being wasted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 87:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah! There is no god but Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾.

On this verse there are several issues.

The First Issue: Regarding the manner of its arrangement (al-nazm), there are two views.

The first: We have explained that the purpose of His saying ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it﴾ is that a Muslim man should not become one who is killed. Then He, exalted is He, reinforced this with a warning in His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever over all things an Reckoner﴾. Then He intensified the emphasis of that warning with this verse. In this verse He clarified that monotheism (tawhid) and justice ('adl) are mutually entailing. So His saying ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is an allusion to monotheism, and His saying ﴿He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an allusion to justice. This is like His saying ﴿Allah testifies that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, [He is] maintaining justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], and like His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], which is an allusion to monotheism. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], which is an allusion to justice. Likewise, in this verse He clarified that it is necessary, by His judgment and wisdom, that He gather the first and the last in the place of the Resurrection, and then He will grant justice to the oppressed against the oppressors. There is no doubt that this is a severe threat.

The second: It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: Whoever greets you and salutes you, then accept his greeting, honor him, and deal with him according to the outward appearance, for the inner states are known only to Allah, there is no god but Him. The inner states of creatures are only revealed to creatures on the Day of Resurrection.

The Second Issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is either a predicate of the subject, or a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), and the predicate is ﴿He will surely gather you﴾. The lam is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), and the implied meaning is: "By Allah, He will surely gather you."

The Third Issue: One might say: Why did He not say "He will gather you on the Day of Resurrection" (fi yawm al-qiyamah)?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: The meaning is "He will gather you at death or in the graves until the Day of Resurrection."

The second: The implied meaning is: "He will join you to that Day and gather between you and it, by gathering you in it."

[Page 173]

The Fourth Issue: Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible to say that the Resurrection (al-qiyamah) was named "qiyamah" because people rise (yaqumun) from their graves. It is also permissible to say that it was named by this name because people stand (yaqumun) for the reckoning. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-qiyam is al-qiyamah, like al-tilab and al-tilabah.

* * *

The Fifth Issue: Know that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, established that the Resurrection will certainly occur, and made the proof for this merely the report of Allah, exalted is He, about it. This is correct, because among the foundational matters (al-masa'il al-usuliyyah) are two kinds: some, where knowledge of the validity of prophethood depends on knowledge of their validity, and some where it does not.

The first is like our knowledge that the world requires a Creator who knows all that is known and is capable of all that is possible. For if we do not know this, we cannot know the truthfulness of the Prophets. So every matter of this kind cannot be established by the Qur'an or by the reports of the Prophets, peace be upon them, otherwise circular reasoning (al-dawr) would occur.

As for the second kind, which is the body of matters where knowledge of the validity of prophethood does not depend on knowledge of their validity, all of these can be established by the speech and report of Allah. It is known that the occurrence of the Resurrection is of this kind. Therefore, it is indeed possible to establish it by the Qur'an and by the speech of Allah. Thus it is established that reasoning about the occurrence of the Resurrection from Allah's report about it is valid reasoning.

* * *

The Sixth Issue: His saying ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ is an interrogative in the form of denial, and its purpose is to show that it is necessary that He be truthful, and that lying and failing to fulfill His word are impossible for Him.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they built this on their principle, which is that He, exalted is He, knows that lying is ugly, and knows that He is independent of it, and whoever is so, it is impossible for him to lie. We say that He knows the ugliness of lying and knows that He is independent of it, because lying is ugly by virtue of being lying, and Allah, exalted is He, has no need of anything at all, and it is established that He knows all that is known, so it is necessary to be certain that He knows these two matters. As for the claim that whoever is so, it is impossible for him to lie, this is evident, because lying is a direction of aversion, not a direction of invitation. So when it is free of an opposing need, it remains purely harmful, and therefore the issuing of lying from Him is impossible.

As for our companions (the Ash'arites), their proof is that if He were a liar, His lying would be eternal. If His lying were eternal, the cessation of His lying would be impossible, because non-existence is impossible for the eternal. And if the cessation of His lying were impossible eternally, His being truthful would be impossible, because the existence of one of two opposites prevents the existence of the other opposite. So if He were a liar, it would be impossible for Him to be truthful. But this is not impossible, because we know by necessity that whoever knows something is not prevented from making a judgment about it that conforms to what is judged, and knowledge of this validity is necessary. So when the possibility of truthfulness exists, the impossibility of lying is necessarily present. Thus it is established that we must be certain that He, exalted is He, is truthful.

* * *

The Seventh Issue: The Mu'tazilah used this verse to prove that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is created (muhdath). They said: Because He described it as "hadith" in this verse, and in His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best hadith﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], and "hadith" means what is newly occurring (al-hadith) or what is brought into being (al-muhdath).

Our answer to them is: You judge only the createdness of speech that consists of letters and sound, and we do not dispute its createdness. What we claim to be eternal is something other than these letters and sounds. The verse does not indicate at all the createdness of that thing, by agreement between us and you. As for us, this is evident. As for you, you deny the existence of a speech other than these letters and sounds, so how can you claim that this verse indicates its createdness? And Allah knows best.

**The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, Verse 88**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with you that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites, when Allah has overturned them for what they have earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾

Know that this is another type of the states of the hypocrites, which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned. Here there are several issues.

**The First Issue:** They mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse.

The first: It was revealed concerning a people who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his family as Muslims, and stayed in Medina for as long as Allah willed. Then they said, "O Messenger of Allah, we wish to go out to the desert, so permit us to do so." He permitted them. When they went out, they kept travelling stage after stage until they joined the polytheists. The believers then spoke about them. Some of them said, "If they were Muslims like us, they would have stayed with us and been patient as we were patient." Others said, "They are Muslims, and it is not for us to attribute disbelief to them until their affair becomes clear." So Allah, exalted is He, made their hypocrisy clear in this verse.

The second: The verse was revealed concerning a people who professed Islam in Mecca, and used to help the polytheists against the Muslims. The Muslims disagreed about them and quarrelled, so the verse was revealed. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: The verse was revealed concerning those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the Day of Uhud and said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." The Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) disagreed about them. Among them, one group said, "They have disbelieved," and others said, "They have not disbelieved." So this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Zayd ibn Thabit. Some, however, criticised this view and said, "The context of the verse contradicts it, and they were from the people of Mecca," referring to His saying: ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the cause of Allah.﴾

The fourth: The verse was revealed concerning a people who went astray, took the wealth of the Muslims, and set off with it to Yamamah. The Muslims disagreed about them, so the verse was revealed. This is the statement of 'Ikrimah.

The fifth: They are the 'Uraniyyun, who raided and killed Yasar, the freed slave of the Messenger (ﷺ).

The sixth: Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning the people of the slander (al-ifk).

**The Second Issue:** Regarding the meaning of the verse, there are two aspects.

The first: The word ﴿two groups﴾ (fi'atayn) is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) construction, like your saying: "What is wrong with you standing?", meaning, "What is wrong with you in the state of standing?" This is the view of Sibawayh (a grammarian, d. c. 180 AH).

The second: It is in the accusative as the predicate of kāna (the verb "to be"), and the implied meaning is: "What has happened to you, that you have become two groups concerning the hypocrites?" This is an interrogative in the sense of denunciation, meaning: Why do you differ about their disbelief when the evidences of their disbelief and hypocrisy are manifest and clear? It is not for you to differ concerning it; rather, you must be certain of their disbelief.

**The Third Issue:** Al-Hasan said: He named them hypocrites even though they displayed disbelief, because they were described by the attribute they had been upon previously. The meaning of His saying ﴿two groups﴾ is what we have explained: a group among them used to incline towards them, defend them, and befriend them, while another group among them distanced themselves from them and opposed them. So they were forbidden from this and commanded to be upon one way in distancing, disassociating and declaring them disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said, informing about their disbelief: ﴿And Allah has overturned them for what they have earned.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues.

**The First Issue:** *Al-raks* means returning a thing from its end to its beginning. Thus *al-raks*, *al-naks*, *al-marku's* and *al-manku's* are one and the same. From this root comes the word *rikss* for dung, because it has been returned to a base state, namely the state of impurity, and it is also called *raji'* (returned) for this same meaning. It has two forms: *rakasahum* and *arkasahum*, and [they] *irtakasu*, meaning they apostatised. Umayyah said:

*"So they are overturned in the scalding fire of Hell, for they were sinners, and they spoke falsehood and lies."*

**The Second Issue:** The meaning of the verse is that He returned them to the rulings of the disbelievers, of humiliation, abasement, captivity and killing, for what they earned, that is, for what they displayed of apostasy after they had been upon hypocrisy. This is because as long as the hypocrite holds outwardly to the two testimonies, we have no way to kill him. But when he displays disbelief, then Allah, exalted is He, applies to him the rulings of the disbelievers.

**The Third Issue:** Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿Allah has overturned them﴾ (arkasahum). We have already mentioned that *arkasa* and *rakasa* are two forms.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a theological school that stresses divine justice and human free will) said: The intended meaning of His saying ﴿whom Allah has sent astray﴾ is not that He Himself created misguidance in them, for the well-known reasons; and because He, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿Allah has overturned them for what they have earned.﴾ So He made clear that He only returned and expelled them because of their earning and their actions, and this negates the view that their misguidance occurred by the creation of Allah. On this basis, they interpreted His saying ﴿whom Allah has sent astray﴾ in several ways:

The first: It means that Allah, exalted is He, judged them to be misguided and disbelieving, just as one says, "So-and-so declares so-and-so a disbeliever and misguided," meaning that he judged him so and reported about him.

The second: The meaning is: Do you wish to guide to Paradise those whom Allah has sent astray from the path of Paradise? This is because He, exalted is He, will send the disbelievers astray on the Day of Resurrection from being guided to the path of Paradise.

The third: That this misguidance is to be explained as withholding the *lutf* (divine favour or grace that inclines the servant towards obedience).

We have mentioned in many places in this book the weakness of these interpretations. Then we say: Suppose they were correct. Yet when He informed about their disbelief and misguidance, and that they would not enter Paradise, then the problem arises, because the transformation of Allah's knowledge into ignorance is impossible, and what leads to an impossibility is itself impossible. Among the things that indicate that the intended meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, sent them astray from the religion is His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ For the believers in this world were only seeking faith from the hypocrites and striving to bring them into it.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, you will never find for him a way.﴾ So its meaning must be that when He, exalted is He, sent them astray from faith, it became impossible for any created being to find a way to bring them into faith. And this is clear.

**The First Issue:** When He, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ [An-Nisa: 88], and this was an interrogative in the sense of denunciation, He confirmed this improbability by saying: They have reached such a degree in disbelief that they wish that you, O Muslims, would become disbelievers. **The second issue:** His saying, ﴿So that you would be equal﴾ [فَتَكُونُونَ سَواءً] is in the nominative (raf') by coordination (nasaq) with ﴿you disbelieve﴾ [تَكْفُرُونَ]. The meaning is: they wish that you would be [the same]. The fa' is coordinating (ʿatifah), and it is not permissible to make this the response (jawab) to the wish. Had he intended this with the interpretation "when they disbelieve, they become equal," it would have been in the accusative (nasb). A similar example is His saying, ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. If it were said, "fa-yudhinu" [so that they would compromise] as a response (jawab), that would be permissible grammatically. Similar is His saying, ﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your weapons and your belongings, so they could swoop down on you﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]. The meaning of His saying, ﴿so that you would be equal﴾, is equal in disbelief. The intended meaning is that you and they would be equal, but He suffices with mentioning the addressees instead of mentioning others, because the meaning is clear given that they were already mentioned. Know that when He, exalted is He, explained to the believers their disbelief and their extreme excess in that disbelief,

after that He explained to the believers the manner of associating with them, so He said: ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾. In this there are issues:

**The first issue:** The verse indicates that it is not permissible to befriend polytheists, hypocrites, and those notorious for heresy and atheism. This is reinforced by the general statement of His, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. The reason for this is that the most precious and greatest thing for all creation is religion, because it is the matter by which one draws near to Allah, exalted is He, and by which one seeks the means to attain happiness in the Hereafter. When this is so, the enmity arising because of it is the greatest kind of enmity. And when this is so, seeking love and allegiance is forbidden in the situation in which the greatest causes of enmity exist. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate﴾. Abu Bakr al-Razi (al-Jassas) said: The implied meaning is "until they embrace Islam and emigrate," because emigration in the way of Allah does not occur except after Islam. Thus the verse indicates the obligation of emigration after Islam, and that even if they embrace Islam, there is no allegiance between us and them except after emigration. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿You have nothing of their allegiance until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72].

Know that this obligation was binding only during the time when emigration was mandatory. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am free of every Muslim who lives among the polytheists, and I am free of every Muslim who is with a polytheist." So emigration was obligatory until Mecca was conquered, and then the obligation of emigration was abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancellation of a ruling by a later revealed text). It is narrated from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Mecca: "There is no emigration after the Conquest, but there is jihad and intention." It is related from al-Hasan that the ruling of the verse remains valid for everyone who remains in the Abode of War while considering the obligation of emigration to the Abode of Islam to be still in force.

**The third issue:** Know that emigration sometimes occurs by moving from the abode of disbelief to the abode of faith, and at other times occurs by moving away from the deeds of the disbelievers to the deeds of the Muslims. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The emigrant is one who abandons what Allah has forbidden." The scholars who investigate (al-muhaqqiqun) said: Emigration in the way of Allah is an expression for emigrating from abandoning His commands and committing His prohibitions. Since all these matters are relevant, Allah, exalted is He, mentioned a general term that encompasses all of them, so He said: ﴿until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾. He, exalted is He, did not say "until they emigrate from disbelief," but said: ﴿until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾, which includes emigrating from the abode of disbelief and emigrating from the symbols of disbelief. Then He, exalted is He, did not limit Himself to mentioning emigration, but qualified it by its being in the way of Allah, because emigration from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam, or from the symbols of disbelief to the symbols of Islam, may occur for some worldly purpose. What is considered is that such emigration occurs for the sake of the command of Allah, exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 90:**

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them a protector or a helper.﴾ The meaning is: if they turn away from the emigration (hijra) and remain in their places outside Medina, then seize them whenever you are able to overpower them, and kill them wherever you find them, within the sacred territory and outside it. And do not take from among them, in this situation, a protector who would take charge of any of your affairs, nor a helper who would support you against your enemies.

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the killing of these disbelievers, He made an exception to it in two places.

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant.﴾

In this are several issues:

The first issue: concerning His words ﴿yasilun﴾ (join/reach), there are two views.

The first: they arrive at them and become connected to them. The meaning is that whoever enters into the covenant of those who were already within your covenant, these also are within your covenant. Al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It may also enter into the verse that a people intend to come to the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) but that aim becomes impossible for them, so they seek refuge with a people who have a covenant with the Muslims until they find a way to him.

The second view: that His words ﴿yasilun﴾ mean "they are related by lineage." This is weak, because most of the people of Makkah were connected to the Messenger (ﷺ) through lineage, and yet he (ﷺ) had permitted the blood of the disbelievers among them.

The second issue: they differed over who the people were with whom the Muslims had a covenant. Some said they were the Aslam, for there was a covenant between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When he (ﷺ) went out toward Makkah, he made a truce with Hilal ibn Uwaymir al-Aslami, on the condition that he would not disobey him or assist against him, and that whoever joined Hilal and sought refuge with him would have the same protection as Hilal. Ibn Abbas said they were the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat, and Muqatil said they were Khuza'a and Khuzayma ibn Abd Manat.

Know that this contains a great glad tiding for the people of faith, because when He lifted the sword from those who sought refuge with those who had sought refuge with the Muslims, then lifting the punishment in the Hereafter from those who sought refuge in the love of Allah and the love of His Messenger is more fitting. And Allah knows best.

The second place of exception: His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or those who come to you, their hearts constrained from fighting you or fighting their own people. And had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they keep away from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

[Page 178]

The first issue: His words ﴿Or those who come to you﴾ may be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the relative clause of ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who), and the sense would be: except those who join the covenanted ones, or those whose hearts are constrained so that they do not fight you. It may also be a conjunction on the attribute of ﴿qawm﴾ (a people), and the sense would be: except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant, or who join a people whose hearts are constrained so that they do not fight you. The first is preferable, for two reasons:

One: His words ﴿So if they keep away from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.﴾ He mentioned this after His words ﴿then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾, and this indicates that the cause that makes it obligatory to refrain from harming them is their abstention from fighting. This accords only with the first possibility. As for the second possibility, the cause that makes it obligatory to refrain from harming them is their joining with those who abstained from fighting.

Two: making abstention from fighting the direct cause for refraining from harming them is better than making joining those who abstained from fighting the direct cause, because on the first reading, abstention from fighting is a direct cause for refraining from harm, whereas on the second reading it becomes a remote cause.

The second issue: His words ﴿their hearts constrained﴾ mean their hearts are too narrow to fight, so they do not want to fight you because you are Muslims, and they do not want to fight them because they are their kin. They differed about the grammatical position of His words ﴿their hearts constrained﴾ and mentioned several views:

The first: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) with ﴿qad﴾ implied, because ﴿qad﴾ brings the past closer to the present. Do you not see that they say: "qad qamat al-salah" (the prayer has been established), and it is said: "Fulan came to me, his mind has gone," meaning Fulan came to me, having lost his mind. The sense of the verse is: or they came to you in a state in which their hearts were constrained.

The second: it is a predicate after a predicate, as if He had said: "or they came to you," and then informed after that: ﴿their hearts constrained﴾. On this reading, His words ﴿their hearts constrained﴾ are an apposition (badal) to ﴿they came to you﴾.

The third: the sense may be: they came to you as a people whose hearts were constrained, or they came to you as men whose hearts were constrained. On this reading, His words ﴿their hearts constrained﴾ are in the accusative because they are an attribute of an accusative noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, except that the modified noun in the accusative of circumstance was omitted and its attribute was put in its place. And His words ﴿that they fight you or fight their own people﴾ mean their hearts were constrained from fighting you and from fighting their own people, so they are neither against you nor with you.

* * *

The third issue: they differed over whether those whom Allah excepted are from among the disbelievers or from among the believers. The majority said: they are from among the disbelievers. The meaning is that He made it obligatory to kill the disbeliever except when he is a covenanted person or one who has abstained from fighting, for then it is not permitted to kill them. On this reading, the claim of abrogation (naskh) is necessary, because the disbeliever who has abstained from fighting may still be killed.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: when He made emigration obligatory upon everyone who became Muslim, He excepted the one who has an excuse, saying: ﴿except those who join﴾. These are a group of believers who set out to the Messenger for emigration and support, but on their way there were disbelievers, so they could find no path to him for fear of those disbelievers. So they went to a people between whom and the Muslims there was a covenant, and they stayed with them until they could be delivered. Then He excepted, after that, those who came to the Messenger and do not fight the Messenger or his companions, because they fear Allah, exalted is He, regarding him; nor do they fight the disbelievers either, because they are his kin, or because he left his children and wives among them, so he fears that if he fought them they would kill his children and companions. These two groups of Muslims are not lawful to fight, even though emigration and fighting the disbelievers have not been found from them.

The fourth issue: His words, exalted is He: ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you﴾. Tasliṭ (giving power) in the language is derived from salāṭa, which is sharpness, and what is meant is that Allah, exalted is He, bestowed favor upon the Muslims by restraining the might of the covenanted ones. The sense is: the constraint of their hearts from fighting you is only because Allah cast terror into their hearts, and had He strengthened their hearts to fight the Muslims, they would have overpowered them. Our companions said: this indicates that it is not ugly for Allah, exalted is He, to give power to a disbeliever over a believer and to strengthen him against him.

[Page 179]

As for the Mu'tazilites, they answered this in two ways:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: we have already shown that the people whom Allah, exalted is He, excepted are believers, not disbelievers. The second: al-Kalbi said: He, exalted is He, informed that if He willed He would have done it. This only indicates that He is able to do wrong, which is our doctrine too. The fifth issue: the lam in His words ﴿then they would have fought you﴾ is the answer to ﴿law﴾ (if), by repetition or as a substitution, on the interpretation: "And had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and had Allah willed, they would have fought you."
