The third narration: It is related that Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, who was a maternal brother of Abu Jahl, embraced Islam and emigrated to Medina out of fear of his people, and that was before the Messenger's (ﷺ) migration. So his mother swore that she would neither eat nor drink nor sit under a roof until he returned. So Abu Jahl went out, and with him al-Harith ibn Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah, and they came to him and prolonged the conversation. Abu Jahl said: "Does not Muhammad command you to be dutiful to your mother? Turn back, be good to your mother, and you remain upon your religion." So he returned. When they neared Mecca, they bound his hands and feet, and Abu Jahl flogged him a hundred lashes, and al-Harith flogged him another hundred. He said to al-Harith: "This is my brother, so who are you, O Harith? By Allah, if I find you alone I will kill you." It is also related that al-Harith said to Ayyash when he returned: "If your former religion was guidance, then you have abandoned it, and if it was misguidance, then you have now entered into it." This grieved Ayyash, and he swore to kill him. When he entered upon his mother, his mother swore that the bond would not be removed from him until he returned to his former religion, so he did so. Then he later emigrated and al-Harith also embraced Islam and emigrated. Ayyash met him alone and did not perceive his Islam, so he killed him. When he was informed that he had been a Muslim, he regretted his deed and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "I killed him and did not perceive his Islam." So this verse was revealed.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and it is not [for a believer]﴾ (wa-ma kana) has two aspects:

The first: that is, "and it is not in what He brought from his Lord and entrusted to him."

The second: "It was not for him at any time," and the purpose of it is to show that the prohibition of killing was established from the first time of legal obligation.

The third issue: His saying ﴿except by mistake﴾ (illa khata'an) has two views:

The first: that it is an exception of the connected kind (istithna' muttasil). Those who hold this view have mentioned several aspects:

The first: that this exception came in the sense of meaning, because His saying ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ means that a person is held accountable for killing except when the killing is a killing by mistake, in which case he is not held accountable for it.

The second: that the exception is also correct according to the apparent wording, and the meaning is that it is not permissible for a believer to kill a believer at all, except in the case of mistake. This is when he sees on him the emblem of the disbelievers, or finds him in their army and thinks him a polytheist. In this case it is permissible to kill him, and there is no doubt that this is a mistake, for he thought him to be a disbeliever while he was not a disbeliever.

The third: that there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, and the intended meaning is: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake." A similar example is His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35], whose interpretation is: "It is not for Allah to take a son," because nothing is forbidden to Him; rather He negates from Himself what is not fitting for Him. Likewise He said: ﴿It was not for you to grow its trees﴾ [al-Naml: 60], meaning: "You would not be able to grow them," because He did not forbid them from growing trees, but He negated that they had the capacity to cause them to grow, for He alone is capable of causing trees to grow.

The fourth: that the difficulty in taking this exception as connected lies in the statement that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, and this would require permitting the killing of a believer in some circumstances, which is impossible. However, this difficulty arises only if we accept that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, and that is disputed among the jurists of legal theory (usul). The correct view is that it does not imply this, because the exception only removes the ruling from the excepted item, not the predicate from it. When the effect of the exception is only to remove the ruling, the excepted item remains neither judged by negation nor by affirmation, and then the difficulty is dispelled. Among what indicates that an exception from a negation is not an affirmation is His saying, peace be upon him: "There is no prayer except with purification, and no marriage except with a guardian." And it is said: "There is no kingship except by men, and no men except by wealth." The exception in all these examples does not make the excepted ruling an affirmation. And Allah knows best.

The fifth: Abu Hashim, one of the leaders of the Mu'tazilah, said: The construction of the verse is: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer and remain a believer, except that he kills him by mistake, in which case he remains a believer." He said: The meaning is that the killing of a believer by a believer removes him from being a believer, except when it is by mistake, for then it does not remove him from being a believer. Know that this speech is based on the premise that the sinner (fasiq) is not a believer, and that is a false principle. And Allah knows best.

The second view: that this exception is disconnected (munqati') with the meaning of "but" (lakin), and its counterpart in the Qur'an is abundant. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]; and He said: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor faults﴾ [al-Najm: 32]; and He said: ﴿They hear therein no vain speech nor sin, except the saying: "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25–26]. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Concerning the accusative case of His saying ﴿khata'an﴾ (by mistake), there are several aspects:

The first: that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the meaning is: "It is not fitting that he kill him for any cause, except for the cause of it being a mistake."

The second: that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and the meaning is: "He does not kill him at all except in the state of its being a mistake."

The third: that it is an adjective of the verbal noun (sifah lil-masdar), and the meaning is: "except a killing by mistake."

* * *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation paid to his family, unless they forgo it as charity.﴾

In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Killing is of three kinds: intentional ('amd), mistaken (khata'), and quasi-intentional (shibh 'amd).

As for intentional killing: it is that one intends to kill him with a means which is known to lead to death, whether that means is wounding or not. This is one statement of al-Shafi'i.

As for mistaken killing, it is of two kinds:

One of them: that he intends to shoot a polytheist or a bird, but hits a Muslim.

The second: that he thinks him a polytheist, for example because he bears the emblem of the disbelievers. The first is a mistake in the act, and the second is a mistake in the intention.

* * *

The second issue: Abu Hanifah said: Killing by a heavy object is not pure intentional killing; rather it is mistaken and quasi-intentional, so it falls under this verse, and in it diyah and expiation are obligatory, and retaliation (qisas) is not obligatory. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is pure intentional killing, in which retaliation is obligatory. As for the proof that it is killing, the Qur'an and the report indicate it. As for the Qur'an, He, exalted is He, related of Musa, peace be upon him, that he struck the Egyptian (al-qibti) and thereby finished him off. Then that striking is called killing, as evidenced by His relating that the Egyptian said on the second day: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ [al-Qasas: 19], while what proceeded from Musa peace be upon him yesterday was nothing but a striking. So it is established that the Egyptian called it killing. Also, Musa, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, called it killing when he said: ﴿My Lord, I have killed a soul from them, so I fear they will kill me﴾ [al-Qasas: 33]. The exegetes agreed that what is meant by it is the killing of that Egyptian by that striking. Also, Allah, exalted is He, called it killing when He said: ﴿And you killed a soul, and We delivered you from distress and tried you with a trial﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]. So it is established that the striking was killing, by the statement of the Egyptian, by the statement of Musa, and by the statement of Allah, exalted is He. As for the report, it is his saying (ﷺ): "Verily, the victim of mistaken intentional killing is the victim of the whip and the staff; in it is a hundred camels." So he called it killing. Thus by these two proofs it is established that killing occurred. As for its being intentional, the one who doubts it falls into sophistry (safsaṭah), for whoever strikes a man's head with a millstone, or crucifies him, or drowns him, or chokes him, then says: "I did not intend to kill him," that is either a liar or a madman, or it is transgression, and no Muslim disputes it. Thus it is established that it is intentional transgressive killing, so retaliation is obligatory by the text and by reason.

Page 183

As for the text: it is all the verses indicating the obligation of retaliation, such as His saying: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you in the case of the slain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]; ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]; ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾ [al-Isra': 33]; ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]; ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same way he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194].

As for reason: the purpose of prescribing retaliation is the preservation of souls and lives from being wasted. He said: ﴿And for you in retaliation is life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179]. And since the purpose of prescribing retaliation is the preservation of souls and lives from being wasted, and the wasting is by the heavy object just as it is by the sharp one, the need for a deterrent prescription in one of the two cases is like the need for it in the other, and there is no difference between the two cases in the wasting itself; the difference lies only in the instrument of wasting. And the necessary knowledge is established that this is not a valid distinction. When discourse in the jurisprudential matters reaches this limit, it has attained the utmost degree of verification for one who has abandoned imitation (taqlid).

They argued with His (ﷺ) saying: "Verily, the victim of mistaken intentional killing is the victim of the whip and the staff; in it is a hundred camels," and it is general, whether the whip and the staff are small or large.

The answer: His saying "the victim of mistake" indicates that the meaning of mistake must be present in it. We have shown that whoever chokes a person or strikes his head with a millstone, then says: "I did not intend to kill him," every sane person by the immediacy of his intellect knows that he is lying in this claim. Therefore this kind must be understood as striking with a small staff, so that the meaning of mistake remains in it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Issue Three:** Abu Hanifa said: Premeditated killing does not require expiation (kaffarah), while al-Shafi'i said it does. Abu Hanifa argued from this verse, saying that His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾ is a condition for the obligation of expiation, and when a condition is absent, the conditioned thing does not occur. It is said to him: Indeed He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free, believing women, may marry from what your right hands possess of believing maidservants﴾ [an-Nisa: 25]. So His saying ﴿whoever cannot afford﴾ [an-Nisa: 25] was not, by your view, a condition for the permissibility of marrying a slave woman, and likewise here. Then we say: What proves that expiation is obligatory for premeditated killing is the report (khabar) and analogy (qiyas).

As for the report, it is what Wathila ibn al-Asqa' narrated, saying: "We came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning a companion of ours who had made the Fire obligatory for himself through killing, and he said: 'Free a slave on his behalf, and Allah will free with each limb of his a limb of his from the Fire.'"

As for analogy, the purpose of freeing a slave is that Allah frees him from the Fire, and the need for this aim is greater in premeditated killing. Therefore the need for making expiation obligatory there is greater, and Allah knows best.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, also mentioned another argument from analogy by resemblance (qiyas al-shabah), saying: When expiation was made obligatory for killing game while in the state of ihram, we equated the one who kills intentionally with the one who kills by mistake, except regarding sin. So likewise regarding killing a believer. There is another confirmation of this argument, namely that it is said: Allah, exalted is He, stated the ruling there concerning the intentional killer, and we made it obligatory upon the one who erred. Here He stated it concerning the one who erred, so it is more fitting that it be made obligatory upon the intentional killer, since the intentional killer's need for an emancipation that frees him from the Fire is even greater. That is more appropriate.

* * *

**Issue Four:** Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: A slave is not acceptable (for expiation) unless he has prayed and fasted. Al-Shafi'i, Malik, al-Awza'i and Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with them all, said: A child is acceptable if one of his parents is a Muslim.

The proof of Ibn Abbas is this verse, for He, exalted is He, made the freeing of a believing slave obligatory, and a believer is one who is described by faith. Faith is either assent (tasdiq), or action ('amal), or both together. In all these possibilities, all of it is missing from a child, so he is not a believer, and therefore he is not acceptable.

The proof of the jurists is that His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾ includes a child, so likewise His saying ﴿then freeing a believing slave﴾ should include a child.

* * *

**Issue Five:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The blood-money (diyya) for premeditated killing and for quasi-intentional killing (shibh al-'amd) is aggravated and in three categories: thirty hiqqah (she-camels in their fourth year), thirty jadha'ah (she-camels in their fifth year), and forty khalifah (pregnant she-camels) with their offspring in their wombs.

As for pure mistaken killing, it is lightened: twenty bint makhad (female camels in their second year), twenty bint labun (female camels in their third year), twenty ibn labun (male camels in their third year), twenty hiqqah, and twenty jadha'ah. As for Abu Hanifa, he also says this for all of them except one thing, for he made ibn makhad obligatory in place of bint labun.

The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that He, exalted is He, made blood-money obligatory in the Qur'an without explaining its manner. So in determining its manner we turned to the Sunnah and analogy, and we did not find in the Sunnah anything that indicates it.

As for analogy, there is no room for considerations of appropriateness (munasabat) and rational causes (ta'lilat) in determining the causes and determining the numbers. So nothing remains here except analogy by resemblance. We see that blood-money was made obligatory on a cause stronger than the cause that makes zakat obligatory. Then we saw that the Law did not make bint makhad a part of zakat, so it must also not be a part of blood-money.

The proof of Abu Hanifa is that the original state of freedom from liability (bara'ah) was established, and the default for what is established is that it continues. So the original freedom from liability remains. One does not depart from this proof except for a stronger proof. We say: The first (the lesser amount) is agreed upon, so we acknowledge its obligation; as for what exceeds it, it must remain in the original negation.

The answer: The liability (dhimmah) is occupied by the obligation of blood-money, and the default for what is established is that it continues. We have seen that there is consensus that the obligation is discharged by paying the greater amount that has been mentioned for it, so it must be that this discharge does not occur by paying the lesser amount within it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Issue Six:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If camels are not available, then what is obligatory is either one thousand dinars or twelve thousand dirhams. Abu Hanifa said: Rather, what is obligatory is ten thousand dirhams.

The proof of al-Shafi'i is what 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb narrated from his father from his grandfather, who said: "The value of blood-money in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eight hundred dinars or eight thousand dirhams. When 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, became caliph, he stood up delivering a sermon and said: Indeed the camels have risen in price. Then 'Umar set it upon the people of gold at one thousand dinars, and upon the people of silver at twelve thousand." The point of the argument is that 'Umar mentioned this in the gathering of the Companions and no one objected to it, so it was a consensus (ijma').

The proof of Abu Hanifa is that taking the lesser amount is more appropriate, and its answer has already been given.

* * *

**Issue Seven:** Abu Bakr al-Asamm and the majority of the Khawarij said: Blood-money is obligatory upon the killer. They said: This is indicated by several points.

First: His saying ﴿then freeing a believing slave﴾ is without doubt an obligation of this freeing, and an obligation must have a person upon whom that act is obligatory. The one mentioned before this verse is the killer, namely His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾. This sequence necessitates the certainty that this freeing was made obligatory by Allah upon him and not upon anyone else.

Second: This offense came from him, and what is reasoned is that liability is not required except from the one who destroyed (the property or life). At most, in this matter, this act came from him by way of mistake. But the mistaken act persists in the values of destroyed property and the compensation for injuries (arsh), even though those guarantees are required only from the one who destroyed. So likewise here.

Third: He, exalted is He, made two things obligatory in this verse: freeing a believing slave and paying full blood-money. Then consensus was established that freeing is obligatory upon the perpetrator. So likewise the blood-money must be obligatory upon the killer, since the wording is the same in both places.

Fourth: The 'aqilah (the paternal kin who bear blood-money) have not committed any offense or anything resembling an offense, so it is necessary that nothing be imposed upon them, according to the Qur'an and the report. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and He said: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾ [al-An'am: 29], and He said: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. As for the report, what has been narrated is that Abu Ramtha entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) with his son, and he, peace be upon him, said: "Who is this?" He said: "My son." He said: "He does not commit an offense against you, and you do not commit an offense against him." It is known that the purpose of this is not to report about the offense itself. Rather, the purpose is to clarify that the effect of your offense does not extend to your child, and vice versa. All of this indicates that imposing blood-money upon the offender is more appropriate than imposing it upon others.

Fifth: The texts indicate that a person's property is protected and that no one has any right to take it from him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade﴾ [an-Nisa: 29]. He, peace be upon him, also said: "Every person has a right to his earnings." And He said: "The sanctity of a Muslim's property is like the sanctity of his blood." And He said: "The property of a Muslim is not lawful except with his good pleasure." We have set aside acting upon these general statements in matters for which we know from the explicit text of the Qur'an that they make taking permissible, as we said regarding zakat, and as we said regarding taking guarantees. As for imposing blood-money upon the 'aqilah, the reliance in it is upon a single report (khabar al-wahid), and specifying the general wording of the Qur'an by a single report is not permissible, because the Qur'an is certain and a single report is probable, and giving precedence to the probable is not permissible. Also, this is a single report which came in a matter that affects everyone, so it is rejected. Also, it is a single report which came in opposition to all the fundamental principles of the Law, so it must be rejected.

As for the jurists, they relied upon the report, the narration of the Companions, and the verse. As for the report: what al-Mughira narrated, that a woman struck the belly of another woman and she miscarried a dead fetus, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that the 'aqilah of the one who struck must pay a ghurrah (a slave or servant as compensation). Then Hamal ibn Malik stood up and said: "How shall we pay for one who neither drank nor ate, nor cried out nor showed signs of life? Such a claim should be disregarded." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is the rhymed prose of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era)." As for the narration of the Companions: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled against 'Ali that he should pay the blood-money on behalf of the client (mawla) of Safiyya bint 'Abd al-Muttalib when the client committed an offense, and 'Ali was the son of Safiyya's brother. And he ruled for al-Zubayr with her inheritance. This indicates that blood-money is only obligatory upon the 'aqilah. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Issue Eight:** The position of most jurists is that the blood-money of a woman is half the blood-money of a man. Abu Bakr al-Asamm and Ibn 'Atiyya said: Her blood-money is the same as the blood-money of a man.

The proof of the jurists is that 'Ali, 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud ruled accordingly, and because a woman's share in inheritance and her testimony is half that of a man, so likewise in blood-money.

The proof of al-Asamm is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then freeing a believing slave and a blood-money (diyah) paid to his family﴾. And they agreed that the ruling of this verse includes both men and women, so the ruling in it must be established equally. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Issue Nine:** They agreed that the blood-money for mistaken killing is paid in installments over three years: one-third in the first year, two-thirds in the two years, and the whole within three years. This was widely transmitted from 'Umar, and none of the predecessors (salaf) disagreed with him in it, so it was a consensus.

**Issue Ten:** There is no difference regarding this blood-money between paying from it the debts, executing from it the bequest, and dividing the remainder among the heirs according to Allah's prescribed shares. It was narrated that a woman came seeking her share of her husband's blood-money. 'Umar said: "I know of nothing for you. The blood-money is only for the 'asabah (male agnatic relatives) who bear it on his behalf." Then some of the Companions testified that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him to give the wife an inheritance from her husband's blood-money, so 'Umar ruled accordingly.

Now that we have mentioned these issues, let us return to the interpretation of the verse. We say: His saying ﴿then freeing a believing slave﴾ means: then upon him is the freeing of a slave. "Tahrir" (freeing) is an expression for making him free, and "hurr" (free) means pure. Since man in his original creation was created to be an owner of things, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29], his being owned becomes an attribute that clouds and disturbs the requirement of humanity. Therefore the removal of ownership was named "tahrir," meaning the purification of that person from what clouds his humanity. The word "raqabah" (neck) is an expression for a person (nasamah), just as "ra's" (head) may also be used as an expression for a person, as in their saying: "So-and-so owns such-and-such heads of slaves." By "a believing neck" is meant every slave who is under the rule of Islam according to the jurists. According to Ibn Abbas, only a slave who has prayed and fasted is acceptable, and we have already mentioned this issue.

As for His saying ﴿and a blood-money paid to his family﴾, al-Wahidi said: "Diyah" comes from "wadyah," like "shiyah" from "washy." The original form is "wadiyah," and the waw was dropped. It is said: "Wada fulan fulanan," meaning he paid his blood-money to his guardian. Then the Law specialized this word for what is paid as compensation for a life, and not for what is paid as compensation for destroyed property, nor for what is paid as compensation for limbs and organs.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unless they forgo it as charity.﴾ Its original form is yatasaddaqū, and the ta' was assimilated into the ṣād, making yaṣṣaddaqū. The meaning of tasaddaq is giving. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And give us charity; indeed God rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88]. The meaning is: unless they give up the blood-money as charity, forgoing it and waiving the blood-money. The author of al-Kashshaf said: The construction of the verse is: the blood-money becomes due upon him and it is to be handed over until they forgo it as charity. On this reading, ﴿an yaṣṣaddaqū﴾ is in the accusative place as an adverb of time, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to his family, meaning "unless they are charitable."
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then [the freeing of] a believing slave﴾.

Know that in the first verse He, exalted is He, mentioned that whoever kills a believer by mistake, upon him is the freeing of a slave and the handing over of the blood-money. In this verse He mentioned that whoever kills a believer by mistake from a people hostile to us, upon him is the freeing of a slave, and He was silent about mentioning the blood-money. Then He mentioned after that that if the one killed was from a people between you and them is a covenant, the blood-money becomes due. The silence about imposing the blood-money in this verse, given its mention in what precedes this verse and in what follows it, indicates that the blood-money is not obligatory in this case.

Having established this, we say: the word "min" (from) in His saying ﴿from a people hostile to you﴾ either means that this slain person is one of the inhabitants of the abode of war, or it means that he is related to them by lineage. The second is invalid, since there is consensus that a Muslim living in the abode of Islam, and all of his relatives, are disbelievers; if he were killed by mistake, blood-money would be due for his killing. Since this division is invalid, the first is determined. So the meaning is: if the one killed by mistake is from the inhabitants of the abode of war and he is a believer, then what is obligatory because of his killing by mistake is the freeing of a slave; as for the blood-money, it is not obligatory.

Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: Just as this verse indicates this meaning, analogy strengthens it. As for the fact that blood-money is not due: if we made blood-money due for the killing of a Muslim residing in the abode of war, then whoever wanted to raid the abode of war would need to investigate every person to know whether he is a Muslim or not, and that is difficult and burdensome, and it would lead to people refraining from raiding. Therefore it is better to drop the blood-money from his killer, because it was he who forfeited his own blood by his choice to reside in the abode of war. As for expiation (kaffārah), it is the right of God, exalted is He, because when that person was killed, a human being who was constant in worshipping God, exalted is He, perished, and a slave cannot be constant in worshipping God; so when he frees him, he has put him in the place of that slain person in constancy in acts of worship. Thus it is clear that analogy requires the dropping of the blood-money and requires the continuation of expiation. And God knows best.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant, then blood-money handed over to his family and the freeing of a believing slave﴾. And in it are issues:

The first issue: ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾, in it there are two opinions:

The first: that what is meant by it is the Muslim, because He, exalted is He, first mentioned the condition of the Muslim who kills by mistake, then mentioned the condition of the Muslim killed by mistake when he is among the people of war, then mentioned the condition of the Muslim killed by mistake when he is among the people of treaty and the protected people (ahl al-dhimmah). There is no doubt that this is a fine sequence, so it is permissible to interpret the wording this way. What confirms the soundness of this view is that His saying ﴿But if he was﴾ must refer back to something previously mentioned, and what was previously mentioned is the believer killed by mistake. So the wording must be taken to refer to him.

The second opinion: that what is meant by it is the dhimmi, and the sense is: if the one killed is from a people between you and them is a covenant. The meaning of the killed being "from them" is that he is upon their religion and creed. The proponents of this view criticized the first opinion on several grounds:

First: a Muslim killed by mistake, whether he is from the people of war or from the people of protection, is included under His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then the freeing of a believing slave and blood-money handed over to his family﴾. So if the intended meaning of this verse were the believer, this would be coordinating a thing with itself, which is impermissible. By contrast, if the believer killed by mistake is from the inhabitants of the abode of war, He mentioned him again only to explain that blood-money is not due for his killing. But in this verse He has imposed blood-money and expiation; so if the intended meaning were the believer, this would be a repetition without benefit, and that is not permissible.

Second: if what was meant were what you have mentioned, the blood-money would not be handed over to his family, because his family are disbelievers who do not inherit from him.

Third: His saying ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾ requires that they be from that people in the attribute that was explicitly stated, namely the existence of a covenant between them. The fact that he is "from them" is ambiguous; one does not know in which respects he is from them. If we take it to mean that he is from them in that attribute, the ambiguity disappears, and that is preferable. And if the verse indicates that he is from them in being a covenanted person, he must be a dhimmi or a covenanted person like them.

These objections may be answered:

As for the first: its answer is that He, exalted is He, mentioned the ruling for the believer killed by mistake, then mentioned one of its two divisions, namely the believer killed by mistake who is among the inhabitants of the abode of war, and explained that blood-money is not due for his killing. He then mentioned the second division, namely the believer killed by mistake who is among the inhabitants of the places of the protected people, and explained that blood-money and expiation are due for his killing. The purpose of this is to show the difference between this division and what precedes it.

As for the second: its answer is that his family are the Muslims to whom his blood-money is directed.

As for the third: its answer is that the word "min" became explained in the preceding verse by the word "fi" (in), meaning "in a people hostile to you." So here too the meaning must be that and nothing else.

Know that the benefit of this discussion appears in a legal question: the position of Abu Hanifa is that the blood-money of a dhimmi is like the blood-money of a Muslim. Al-Shafi'i, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: the blood-money of a Jew or a Christian is a third of the blood-money of a Magian, and the blood-money of a Magian is two-thirds of a tenth of the blood-money of a Muslim. Abu Hanifa argued for his view with this verse: ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾, meaning by it the dhimmi; then He said: ﴿then blood-money handed over to his family﴾, so God, exalted is He, made the full blood-money obligatory for them. We say: we have shown that the verse was revealed concerning the believers, not concerning the protected people, so the argument falls. Moreover, even granting that it was revealed concerning the protected people, it would not support their aim, because He, exalted is He, made in this verse a "blood-money handed over," and this requires the imposition of something among the things called blood-money. Why then do you say that the blood-money He imposed on the dhimmi is the blood-money He imposed on the Muslim? Why could it not be that the blood-money of the Muslim is a fixed amount and the blood-money of the dhimmi is another amount? For blood-money has no meaning except the property paid in exchange for a life. If you claim that the amount of blood-money in the case of the Muslim and in the case of the dhimmi is the same, that is disputed, and the dispute arose only over this point; so this argument falls. And God knows best.

The second issue: One may ask: why did He put the freeing of a slave before the blood-money in the first verse, while here the order is reversed? For if the order had a meaning, the objection would fall on one of the two verses. This is like His saying: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating and say, "Hittah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and in another verse: ﴿Say "Hittah" and enter the gate﴾ [al-A'raf: 161]. And God knows best.

The third issue: Regarding those between us and them is a covenant, there are two opinions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: they are the protected people from among the People of the Book.

The second: al-Hasan said: they are the covenanted among the disbelievers.
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting for two consecutive months, as a repentance from God﴾. That is: upon him is that instead of the slave, if he is poor. Masruq said that it is a substitute for the whole of the expiation and the blood-money. Consecutiveness is obligatory, so that if he breaks the fast for a day, he must begin again, unless the breaking is due to menstruation or postpartum bleeding. His saying ﴿as a repentance from God﴾ is in the accusative with the sense of the fasting mentioned before, as if it were said: act upon what God has made obligatory upon you for the sake of repentance from God, that is, so that God may accept your repentance. It is like the saying: "I did such-and-such out of fear of harm."

If it is said: killing by mistake is not a sin, so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿as a repentance from God﴾? We say that there are several answers to this:

The first: that it contains two kinds of shortcoming, for it is apparent that if he had exercised full caution, that act would not have occurred from him. Do you not see that whoever kills a Muslim thinking he is a hostile non-Muslim combatant, if he had exercised full caution and investigation, it is apparent that he would not have fallen into it? And whoever shoots at a game animal, misses, and hits a person, if he had been cautious, he would shoot only at a place where he is certain there is no person, and then he would not fall into that incident. So His saying ﴿as a repentance from God﴾ is a reminder that he was negligent in leaving off caution.

The second answer: His saying ﴿as a repentance from God﴾ refers to the fact that He, exalted is He, permitted him to carry out fasting in place of manumission when unable to do it; for when God, exalted is He, accepts the repentance of a sinner, He has lightened the burden on him. Since lightening is one of the necessary consequences of repentance, the word "repentance" was used to mean lightening, by naming the necessary consequence with the name of what necessitates it.

The third answer: when a believer experiences such a mistake, he regrets it and wishes that it had not happened, so God, exalted is He, called that regret and that wish "repentance."
* * *
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is ever Knowing and Wise﴾. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, knows that he did not intend and did not deliberately do it, and is Wise in that He does not hold him to account for that mistaken act, for wisdom requires that a person be held to account only for what he chooses and deliberately does.

Know that the People of the Sunnah, since they believe that the acts of God, exalted is He, are not caused by the pursuit of benefits, said: the meaning of His being Wise is that He knows the outcomes of affairs. The Mu'tazilah said: this verse refutes this view, because He coordinated the Wise with the Knowing; so if the Wise were the Knowing, this would be coordinating a thing with itself, which is impossible.

The answer: wherever the word "Wise" occurs in the Qur'an coordinated with "Knowing," what is meant by "Wise" is that He makes His acts firm and sound. So firmness and knowledge both refer to the manner of the act. And God knows best.

The Exalted said: ﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the ruling on unintentional killing, He mentioned after it the explanation of the ruling on intentional killing. It has rulings, such as the obligation of retaliation (qisas) and blood-money (diyya). He, may He be exalted, mentioned those in Surat al-Baqara, where He says: ﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. Therefore, here He restricted Himself to explaining what it contains of sin and threat. There are issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: The Wa'idiyya (those who hold to the certainty of punishment) argued from this verse on two matters:

One of them: on the certainty of the threat against sinners (fussaq).

The second: on their abiding in the Fire. The basis of the argument is that the word "man" (whoever), in the context of a condition, conveys generality (istighraq). We have fully examined their argument in Surat al-Baqara in the commentary on His words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqara: 81], and we went to great lengths in answering it. Al-Wahidi claimed that the scholars took many routes in answering this verse. He said: "I do not accept any of them, because those they mentioned are either specification (takhsis), or counter-argument (mu'arada), or implied supplement (idmar), and the wording does not indicate any of that." He said: "What he relied upon are two points:

The first: the consensus of the exegetes that the verse was revealed concerning an unbeliever who killed a believer, and then he mentioned that story.

The second: that His words ﴿so his recompense is Hell﴾ mean the future, i.e., he will be recompensed with Hell, and this is a threat. He said: 'Breaking a threat is generosity.' In our view, Allah may break the threat against believers. This is the essence of his speech, which he claimed was better than what others have said."

I say: As for the first point, it is weak, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause (sabab). So when it is established that the word indicating generality is present, its revelation concerning unbelievers does not harm that generality, and this statement collapses entirely. Then we say: just as the generality of the wording requires that it applies to every killer described by the stated attribute, so too here there is another point that prevents restricting this verse to the unbeliever. Its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: He, may He be exalted, commanded the believers to strive against the unbelievers, then taught them what they need when they are occupied with jihad. He began with His words: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by error﴾ [al-Nisa': 92], and in this verse He mentioned three expiations: the expiation for killing a Muslim in the abode of Islam, the expiation for killing a Muslim while he dwells among the people of war, and the expiation for killing a Muslim while he dwells among the people of dhimma and covenant. Then He mentioned after it the ruling on intentional killing, coupled with the threat. Since the explanation of the ruling on unintentional killing is an explanation of a ruling specific to Muslims, the explanation of the ruling on intentional killing, which is like the opposite of unintentional killing, must also be specific to believers. If it is not specific to them, then at least they are included in it.

The second: He, may He be exalted, said after this verse: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of Allah, verify, and do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ [al-Nisa': 94]. The exegetes agreed that these verses were revealed concerning a group of Muslims who met a people, who then embraced Islam, but they killed them and claimed they had embraced Islam out of fear. On this basis, this verse came to forbid believers from killing those who manifest faith. This too requires that His words ﴿and whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ were revealed to forbid believers from killing believers, so that there is coherence. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that what precedes this verse and what follows it prevents it from being specific to unbelievers.

The third: It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that linking a ruling to an appropriate attribute indicates that this attribute is the effective cause ('illa) of that ruling. By this method we know that His words ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 38] and His words ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog each one of them﴾ [al-Nur: 2]: the cause requiring amputation is theft, and the cause requiring flogging is fornication. Likewise here, the cause requiring this threat must be this intentional killing, because this attribute is appropriate to that ruling, so it follows that the ruling is caused by it. Since this is the case, it follows that wherever this meaning is found, this ruling arises, and by this aspect no basis remains for the claim that the verse is specific to the unbeliever.

The fourth: The ground for deserving this threat is either disbelief or this specific killing. If the ground of this threat is disbelief, then disbelief was present before this killing, and in that case this killing has no effect at all on this threat. On this assumption, this verse would be like saying: "Whoever intentionally kills a soul, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah is angry with him." Since intentional killing would have no effect on this threat, it would be treated like the soul itself and like all other matters that have no effect on this threat. It is known that this is false. If, however, the ground of this threat is that it is intentional killing, then it must be said: wherever killing occurs, this threat occurs, and in that case this objection falls away. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that this aspect which al-Wahidi approved is worthless.

As for the second of the two aspects he chose, it is utterly corrupt, because the threat is a type of report (khabar). If one permits breaking it with respect to Allah, one permits lying about Allah, and this is a great error, bordering on being disbelief, for the wise have unanimously agreed that He is exalted above lying. Moreover, if one permits lying about Allah in the threat on account of his statement that breaking a threat is generosity, then why not permit breaking in the stories and reports for the sake of some benefit? It is known that opening this door leads to attacking the Qur'an and the entire Shari'a. Thus it is established that each of these two aspects is worthless.

Al-Qaffal, in his tafsir, related another aspect, which is the answer, and said: The verse indicates that the recompense for intentional killing is what has been mentioned, but it does not say whether He will bring this recompense to him or not. A man may say to his slave: "Your recompense is that I will do such-and-such to you," but then not do it. This answer is also weak, because it has been established by this verse that the recompense for intentional killing is what has been mentioned, and it has been established by other verses that He brings recompense to those deserving it. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]. He said: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]. He said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7-8]. Indeed, He, may He be exalted, mentioned in this verse what indicates that He will bring this recompense to them, namely His words: ﴿and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾

صفحة ١٩١
For the statement that this is his recompense has been made by His words: ﴿his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾ So if His words ﴿and prepare for him a great punishment﴾ were a report about the deserving of punishment, it would be repetition. If we take it to be a report that He will do it, repetition does not arise, and so that is preferable.

Know that we say: this verse is specified in two cases:

One of them: when the intentional killing is not transgression, as in retaliation (qisas), for this threat does not apply to it at all.

The second: intentional killing which is transgression, when he repents from it, for the threat does not apply to it. Since it is established that specification enters this verse in these two cases, we specify this generality in the case where pardon has occurred, based on His words: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. Also, this verse is one of the generalities of threat, while the generalities of promise are more numerous than the generalities of threat. What he mentioned in favour of the generalities of threat we have already answered, and we showed that the generalities of promise are preponderant. All of this we have mentioned in Surat al-Baqara in the commentary on His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqara: 81].

* * *

The second issue: It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: the repentance of one who commits intentional transgressive killing is not accepted. The majority of scholars said: it is accepted, and the following arguments point to this:

The first argument: disbelief is greater than this killing, so if repentance from disbelief is accepted, then repentance from this killing is more deserving of acceptance.

The second argument: His words at the end of Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, and do not commit adultery—and whoever does that will meet a penalty. The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein humiliated, except one who repents and believes and does righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 68-70]. If the repentance of one who commits intentional killing along with the other grave sins mentioned in this verse is accepted, then the repentance of one who commits intentional killing alone being accepted is more fitting.

The third argument: His words ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ are a promise of pardon for everything other than disbelief, so pardon after repentance is more fitting. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 94–96 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of Allah, then investigate carefully﴾.

Know that the purpose of this verse is to emphasise the prohibition of killing believers, and to command those who fight in jihad to exercise caution in this matter, lest they shed unlawful blood on the basis of a weak interpretation. This emphasis indicates that the preceding verse is addressed to the believers. There are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited here, and likewise in al-Hujurat, "fatabayyanu" (with the verb from tabayyana) ... no; they recited "fa-tathabbatu" (with the verb from thabata, thubatan), while the rest recited it with the nun, from al-bayan (clarification). The two meanings are close. Whoever preferred tathabbut said: it is the opposite of rushing forward, and what is meant in the verse is deliberation and abandoning haste. Whoever preferred tabayyun said: what is meant by tathabbut is clarification, so clarification is more eloquent and more complete.

The second issue: The word ḍarb (striking) means travelling in the land for trade or for jihad, and its origin is striking with the hand. It is a metaphor (kinayah) for hastening in travel, for when one strikes a person, the movement of his hand at that strike is swift, so striking was made a metaphor for hastening in travel.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "when you go forth in the way of Allah" is: when you make raids and travel to jihad.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾.

He intended submission and surrender to the Muslims, and from it is His saying: ﴿and they will offer peace to Allah that Day﴾ [al-Nahl: 87], that is, they submitted to the command. As for whoever recited "al-salam" with an alif, it has two meanings:

One of them: the intended meaning is the greeting which is the salutation of the Muslims, that is: do not say to one who greets you with this salutation, "He only said it out of fear," so that you attack him with the sword in order to take his property; rather, hold back and accept from him what he has shown.

The second: the meaning is: do not say to one who has withdrawn from you and has not fought you, "You are not a believer." The root of this is from safety (salamah), because one who withdraws seeks safety.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was recited "mu'manan" with a fatha on the mim, from amanahu, meaning: "We will not grant you safety."

The third issue: Concerning the cause of the revelation of this verse there are reports:

The first report: "Mirdas ibn Nahik was a man from the people of Fadak. He embraced Islam, and none of his people embraced it besides him. The detachment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went to his people, and their commander was Ghalib ibn Fadalah. The people fled, but Mirdas remained, trusting in his Islam. When he saw the horsemen, he drove his sheep to a ridge of the mountain. When they caught up with him and shouted takbir, he too shouted takbir and descended, and said: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon you.' Usamah ibn Zayd killed him and drove off his sheep. They informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was greatly distressed and said: 'You killed him in order to seize what he had.' Then he recited the verse to Usamah. Usamah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, ask forgiveness for me.' He said: 'How [will you do] when he has recited, "There is no god but Allah"!' Usamah said: 'He kept repeating it until I wished that I had not embraced Islam until that day. Then he asked forgiveness for me and said: "Free a slave."'"

The second report: "The killer was Muhallam ibn Jathamah. 'Amir ibn al-Adbat met him and greeted him with the greeting of Islam, but there had been an old enmity between Muhallam and him in the Jahiliyyah, so he struck him with an arrow and killed him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was angered and said: 'May Allah not forgive you.' Seven days had not passed when he died. They buried him, but the earth expelled him three times. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Indeed the earth would accept one who is worse than him, but Allah wished to show you the magnitude of the sin in His sight.' Then he commanded that stones be thrown upon him."

The third report: "Miqdad ibn al-Aswad experienced an event similar to that of Usamah. He said: 'I said, O Messenger of Allah, what do you think if I meet a man of the disbelievers and he fights me and strikes one of my hands with the sword, then takes refuge in a tree and says: "I have submitted to Allah, the Exalted"; shall I kill him, O Messenger of Allah, after that?' The Messenger of Allah said: 'Do not kill him.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he cut off my hand!' He, upon him be prayer and peace, said: '[Do not kill him], for if you kill him, he will be in your position after you have killed him, and you will be in his position before he uttered his word which he uttered.'"

And from Abu 'Ubaydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you thrusts the spear at a man, and his point reaches the hollow of his throat, and he says, 'There is no god but Allah,' let him lift the spear from him."

Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no contradiction between these reports; perhaps the verse was revealed upon the occurrence of all of them together, and each party thought that it was revealed concerning its own incident. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: They differed over whether the repentance of a zindiq (heretic) is accepted. The jurists accepted it and argued for this with several points:

The first: this verse, for He, exalted is He, did not distinguish in this verse between the zindiq and others, but rather made this obligatory for all.

The second argument: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], which is general over all kinds of disbelievers.

The third argument: there is no doubt that the zindiq is commanded to repent, and repentance is accepted absolutely, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25]. This is general over all sins and all kinds of creatures.

The fifth issue: The Islam of a child is valid according to Abu Hanifah, while al-Shafi'i said it is not valid.

Abu Hanifah said: this verse indicates the validity of a child's Islam, because His saying: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ is general concerning the child and the adult.

Al-Shafi'i said: if his Islam were valid, it would be obligatory, for if it were not obligatory, that would be permission for disbelief, which is impermissible. But it is not obligatory upon him, because of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: "The pen is lifted from three: from the child until he reaches maturity," the hadith [continues]. And Allah knows best.

The sixth issue: Most jurists said: if a Jew or a Christian says, "I am a believer," or says, "I am a Muslim," he is not judged to be Muslim by this alone, because his belief is that what he is upon is Islam and is faith. If he says, "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," then according to some people he is not judged to be Muslim, because among them are those who say that he is the Messenger of Allah to the Arabs only, not to all; and among them are those who say that Muhammad, who is the true Messenger, is yet to come after what has come, and will come after that. Rather, he must acknowledge that the religion he was upon was false, and that the religion现存 among the Muslims is the truth. And Allah knows best.

* *
* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You seek the goods of this worldly life, but with Allah are abundant gains﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: all the goods of the world are ʿaraḍ, with a fatha on the ra'. It is said: the world is a present ʿaraḍ from which the pious and the wicked alike take. ʿArḍ with a sukun on the ra' is what is other than dirhams and dinars. The goods of the world were called ʿaraḍ because it is transient, perishing, not lasting. From this the theologians call whatever is contrary to substance among created things an ʿaraḍ, because of the brevity of its duration. So His saying: ﴿with Allah are abundant gains﴾ means: abundant reward. By calling it ʿaraḍ, He, exalted is He, drew attention to its being swift to perish and near to ending; and by His saying: ﴿with Allah are abundant gains﴾, to the fact that Allah's reward is described as lasting and enduring, as He said: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 46].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus you were before﴾. This requires a comparison of these addressees with those who offered peace. The verse does not explain in what respect this comparison occurred, so the exegetes gave several views concerning it:

The first: the meaning is that when you first entered Islam, you uttered the word of testimony, and I preserved your blood and your property without inquiry, on the basis of knowledge that your heart agrees with what is on your tongue. So it is incumbent upon you to treat those who enter Islam as you were treated, and to take the outward statement at face value, and not to say that their readiness to utter this word was out of fear of the sword. This is what most exegetes chose, and it has a difficulty: for they may say, "Our faith was not like the faith of these people, for we believed by free will and choice, whereas these people displayed faith under the shadows of swords; how then can one be compared with the other?"

The second view: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that you used to conceal your faith from your people, just as this one who summoned you concealed his faith from his people; then Allah bestowed His favour upon you by strengthening you until you made your religion manifest. So you should treat them with the same treatment. This too has a difficulty, for concealing faith was not general among them.

The third: Muqatil said: the meaning is "thus you were before the Hijrah, when you were among the disbelievers, secure from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah by the word, 'There is no god but Allah'; so accept from them the like of that." This is subject to the first difficulty. The closer view, in my opinion, is to say: whoever moves from one religion to another, at first a slight inclination arises from a weak cause, then that inclination continues to strengthen and grow until it is complete and firm and the transition takes place. It is as if it were said to them: "You, at the beginning, only a slight inclination arose in you from weak causes toward Islam; then Allah bestowed Islam upon you by strengthening that inclination and affirming aversion from disbelief. Likewise these people: just as a slight inclination toward Islam arose in them through this fear, accept from them this faith, for Allah, exalted is He, will confirm the sweetness of faith in their hearts and strengthen that desire in their breasts." This is my view on the matter.

*"Then Allah bestowed His favour upon you"*: This has two possibilities:

The first: that this is connected with His saying: ﴿Thus you were before﴾, meaning: your faith was like their faith in that only the verbal utterance was recognised from it without what was in the heart; or in that it was at the beginning of the matter attained through a weak cause, then Allah bestowed His favour upon you, in that He strengthened the light of faith in your hearts and helped you to act upon it and love it.

The second: that this is detached from this place and connected to what precedes it. This is because when the people killed the one who had said, "There is no god but Allah," Allah, exalted is He, forbade them this deed and explained to them that it was among the grave matters. After that He said: "Then Allah bestowed His favour upon you," meaning: He favoured you by accepting your repentance from that reprehensible act.

* Then He repeated the command to clarify, saying: "then investigate carefully" (fa-tabayyanu). Repeating the command to clarify indicates emphasis in warning against that act.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾. What is meant by it is a threat and a restraint against displaying [wrongdoing], as opposed to concealing it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not equal are those believers who sit [at home] other than the disabled and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and lives over those who sit [at home] by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best [reward], but Allah has preferred the mujahidin over those who sit [at home] with a great reward, [as] degrees from Him and forgiveness and mercy. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that concerning the manner of the arrangement (nazm) there are several views:

The first: what we have mentioned, that when He encouraged jihad, He followed that with an explanation of the rulings of jihad. The first category of the rulings of jihad is the warning to Muslims against killing Muslims, and the explanation of the situation regarding their killing: how it is in the case of killing by mistake, how in the case of deliberate killing, and how in the case of killing through a mistaken interpretation. When He had mentioned that ruling, He followed it with another ruling, namely the explanation of the superiority of the mujahid over others, and this is this verse.

**[Page 7]**

The second aspect: When Allah the Exalted rebuked them for what had come from them, namely killing the one who uttered the words of testimony, it may have occurred to their hearts that it was better to avoid jihad, lest they fall into a similar prohibited act because of it. Therefore Allah the Exalted immediately mentioned this verse, explaining the superiority of the mujahid over others, to remove this doubt.

The third aspect: When Allah the Exalted rebuked them for what had come from them, namely killing the one who uttered the testimony, He mentioned immediately after it the virtue of jihad, as if it were said: whoever engages in jihad has attained this great rank with Allah the Exalted, so its doer should guard against that lapse, lest it diminish his great station in the religion because of this lapse. And Allah knows best. In the verse there are several issues:

**[Issue] First:** It has been read as "ghayru ulī al-ḍarar" with all three vowels on *ghayr*. With *raf'* (nominative), it is an adjective (ṣifah) of "al-qā'idūn" (those who sit back), and the meaning is: "The ones who sit back, other than those with a harm, are not equal to the mujahidun." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿or the male attendants who have no need of women﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. We have mentioned the permissibility that *ghayr* may be an adjective of a definite noun, in His saying: ﴿not of those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7]. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible for *ghayr* to be nominative by way of exception, and the meaning is: "The ones who sit back and the mujahidun are not equal, except those with a harm; for they are equal to the mujahidun," i.e., those whom harm has kept back from jihad. The discussion of the nominative of the exception after a negation has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿They did not do it, except a few of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 66].

As for the reading with *naṣb* (accusative), there are two possibilities:

The first: It is an exception from "al-qā'idīn" (those who sit back), and the meaning is: "The ones who sit back are not equal, except those with a harm." This is the preference of al-Akhfash.

The second: It is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning is: "The ones who sit back in a state of health are not equal to the mujahidun," as you say: "Zayd came to me not sick," i.e., "Zayd came to me healthy." This is the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Farra', and like His saying: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you, not violating the hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1].

As for the reading with *jarr* (genitive), it is on the assumption that *ghayr* is made an adjective of "al-mu'minin" (the believers). This is the explanation of the modes of these readings.

Then here is another discussion: Al-Akhfash said: The reading with *naṣb* as an exception is preferable, because its purpose is to exclude a group who were unable to go out. It is narrated in the tafsir (exegesis) that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the virtue of the mujahidun over those who sit back, a group of those with a harm came and said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Our condition is as you see, and we desire jihad; is there any way for us?" So this was revealed: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾, and Allah excluded them from the whole category of those who sit back. Others said: The reading with *raf'* is preferable, because the original status of the word *ghayr* is that it is an adjective, and even if it is an adjective, the intended purpose and desired aim of the exception is achieved by it; for in both cases it removed those with a harm from that inferior rank. And if this intended purpose is achieved under both assumptions, and the original status of the word *ghayr* is that it is an adjective, then the reading with *raf'* is preferable.

**[Issue] Second:** *al-ḍarar* (harm) means deficiency, whether it is by blindness, lameness, or sickness, or it is due to lack of readiness (provision).

**[Issue] Third:** The summary of the verse: The believers who sit back in good health and the mujahidun in the way of Allah are not equal. They differed over whether His saying ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ indicates that the believers who sit back with harm are equal to the mujahidun or not. Some said: It does not indicate this, because if we take the word *ghayr* as an adjective and say that specification by an adjective does not indicate negation of the ruling for what is other than it, then this is not necessary. And if we take it as an exception and say that an exception from a negation is not an affirmation, then this also is not necessary. But if we take it as an exception and say that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, then it necessitates the view of equality.

Know that this equality for those with harm, according to those who hold it, is conditional upon another condition, which Allah the Exalted mentioned in Surat al-Tawbah, namely His saying: ﴿There is no blame on the weak nor on the sick﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], up to His saying: ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

Know that the view of this equality is not far-fetched, and it is indicated by both transmission and reason. As for transmission: the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said upon returning from some of his expeditions: "Behind you in Medina are people; you did not travel any journey nor cross any valley except that they were with you. Those are people whom excuse has held back." And the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "When the servant falls ill, Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: Write for My servant what he used to do in health, until he recovers."

Some exegetes, in explaining His saying: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5], ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward never to be cut off﴾ [al-Tin: 6], mentioned that whoever becomes decrepit, Allah the Exalted writes for him the reward of what he used to do before his decrepitude, without any reduction of it at all.

And they mentioned, in explaining his saying (ﷺ), peace be upon him: "The intention of the believer is better than his deed," that what the believer intends of persistence in faith and righteous deeds, if it remained forever, would be better for him than the deed which he accomplished during his lifetime.

As for reason: The purpose of all acts of obedience and worship is the illumination of the heart with the light of knowledge of Allah the Exalted. If the mujahid and the one who sits back are equal in this, then they are equal in reward; and if the one who sits back attains a greater share of this absorption, he is greater in reward.

**[Issue] Fourth:** One may say: He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. He mentioned the lives before the properties. But in the verse we are dealing with, namely His saying: ﴿and the mujahidun in the way of Allah with their properties and their lives﴾, He mentioned the property before the lives. What is the reason for this?

Its answer: The soul is nobler than property. The buyer mentioned the soul first, to alert that the desire for it is stronger; and the seller delayed mentioning it, to alert that the difficulty concerning it is greater, so he does not agree to surrender it except at the last of the stages.

Know that when He the Exalted clarified that the mujahidun and those who sit back are not equal, and that inequality may admit excess and may admit deficiency, He therefore revealed it, saying: ﴿Allah has preferred the mujahidun with their properties and their lives over those who sit back by a degree﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]. Regarding the accusative of His saying "daraja(tan)" (a degree), there are several possibilities:

The first: The preposition is elided, and the assumed reading is: "by a degree." When the preposition was elided, the verb reached it and governed it.

The second: His saying "daraja(tan)" means "a virtue," and the assumed reading is: "Allah preferred the mujahidun with a virtue," as one says: "Zayd honored ʿAmr with honor (ikrām)." The benefit lies in the indefiniteness and the magnification.

The third: "Daraja(tan)" is accusative as a specification (tamyīz).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Nisa': 95], i.e., to each of those who sit back and the mujahidun, Allah has promised the best. The jurists said: In this there is evidence that the obligation of jihad is a collective obligation (farḍ al-kifāyah), not an individual obligation upon every person; for He the Exalted promised the best to those who sit back just as He promised it to the mujahidun, and if jihad were obligatory individually, the one who sits back would not be deserving of Allah's promise of the best to him.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has preferred the mujahidun over those who sit back with a great reward﴾ ﴿degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 95–96]. In this there are issues:

**[Issue] First:** Regarding the accusative of His saying "ajran" (a reward), there are two possibilities:

The first: It is governed by His saying "faḍḍala" (preferred), because it has the meaning of their saying: "He rewarded them with a reward (ājarahum ajran)." Then His saying: ﴿degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying "ajran."

The second: It is accusative as a specification, and "darajāt" (degrees) is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān), and "maghfiratan wa raḥmatan" (forgiveness and mercy) are coordinated with "darajāt."

**[Issue] Second:** One may say: He the Exalted first mentioned "a degree" (daraja), and here "degrees" (darajāt). The answer to this is in several aspects:

The first: What is meant by "daraja" is not one degree in number, but in kind; and one in kind includes many of the same type. That is the great reward, and the lofty degrees in Paradise, which are forgiveness and mercy.

The second: The mujahid is superior to the one who sits back who is among those with harm by one degree, and to the one who sits back who is among the healthy by several degrees. This answer only holds if we say that His saying ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ does not necessitate that the mujahidun and those with harm who sit back become equal.

[Page 9]

The third: Allah preferred the mujahidun in this world by one degree, which is the spoil of war, and in the Hereafter by many degrees in Paradise, through grace, mercy, and forgiveness.

The fourth: He said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿And Allah has preferred the mujahidun over those who sit back with a great reward﴾, and it is not possible that the intended "mujahid" here is only the one who strives with property and life, otherwise there would be repetition. Therefore the intended meaning must be: whoever is a mujahid in an absolute sense in all matters, meaning in outward action, which is jihad with the self, property, and heart, and this is the most noble type of striving. As he (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad." The outcome of this jihad is turning the heart away from attention to other than Allah toward absorption in obedience to Allah. And since this station is higher than what precedes it, therefore He made the virtue of the first a "degree," and the virtue of this second "degrees."

**[Issue] Third:** The Shi'ah said: This verse indicates that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him, is superior to Abū Bakr. That is because ʿAlī was more engaged in jihad, so the amount in which there is disparity, Abū Bakr was among those who sat back in it, and ʿAlī was among those who stood. If that is so, then ʿAlī must be superior to him, by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah has preferred the mujahidun over those who sit back with a great reward﴾.

It is said to them: Indeed, ʿAlī's, peace be upon him, direct killing of the disbelievers was more than the Messenger's direct killing of them. Then by the ruling of this verse, ʿAlī would be superior to Muhammad (ﷺ), and no sensible person says this.

If you say: The Messenger's striving against the disbelievers was greater than ʿAlī's striving with them, because the Messenger (ﷺ) struggled against the disbelievers by establishing proofs and clear evidence and removing doubts and misguidance, and this jihad is more perfect than that jihad; then we say: Accept from us the like of this concerning Abū Bakr. For when Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) first embraced Islam, he strove to bring all people to Islam, until ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Ṭalḥah, al-Zubayr, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn embraced Islam at his hand. He used to exaggerate in encouraging people to faith and in defending Muhammad (ﷺ) with his self and his wealth. ʿAlī at that time was a child, no one would accept his word, and he was not able to defend Muhammad (ﷺ), peace be upon him. So the jihad of Abū Bakr was superior to the jihad of ʿAlī in two respects:

One of them: The jihad of Abū Bakr was at the beginning of the matter, when Islam was in extreme weakness, whereas the jihad of ʿAlī appeared in Medina in the expeditions, when Islam was strong at that time.

The second: The jihad of Abū Bakr was by calling to the religion, and most of the excellent among the Ten (al-ʿAsharah) embraced Islam at his hand; and this kind of jihad is the profession (ḥirfah) of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Whereas the jihad of ʿAlī was by killing, and there is no doubt that the first is superior.

**The fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that the bliss of Paradise is attained only through works, because the difference in deeds necessitated a difference in reward and merit. This shows that the cause (*'illah*) of reward is the deed. Also, if deeds did not necessitate reward, the reward would be a gift (*hibah*) and not a wage (*ajr*). But God called it a wage (*ajr*), so this view is invalid. It is said to them: Why is it not permissible to say that the deed is the cause of the reward, but not in itself; rather, the Lawgiver (*al-Shari'*) makes that deed necessitate it?

**The fifth issue:** The Shafi'iyyah said: The verse indicates that occupying oneself with voluntary acts (*nawafil*) is better than occupying oneself with marriage (*nikah*). This is because we have explained that jihad is a collective obligation (*fard 'ala al-kifayah*) by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And to each God has promised the best [reward]﴾. Had jihad been an individual obligation (*fard 'ayn*), the one who stays back from jihad would not have been promised the best [reward] by God.

Having established this, we say: When a group undertakes jihad, the obligation is lifted from the rest. So if they [i.e., the others] proceed to it, it is undoubtedly a voluntary act. Then His saying: ﴿And God has preferred those who strive over those who sit back by a great reward﴾ encompasses all who strive,

Page 10

whether their jihad is obligatory or recommended (*mandub*). The one occupied with marriage is among those who sit back from jihad. Thus it is established that occupying oneself with recommended jihad is better than occupying oneself with marriage. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 94–96 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the way of Allah, then investigate carefully﴾.

Know that the purpose of this verse is to emphasise the prohibition of killing believers, and to command those who fight in jihad to exercise caution in this matter, lest they shed unlawful blood on the basis of a weak interpretation. This emphasis indicates that the preceding verse is addressed to the believers. There are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited here, and likewise in al-Hujurat, "fatabayyanu" (with the verb from tabayyana) ... no; they recited "fa-tathabbatu" (with the verb from thabata, thubatan), while the rest recited it with the nun, from al-bayan (clarification). The two meanings are close. Whoever preferred tathabbut said: it is the opposite of rushing forward, and what is meant in the verse is deliberation and abandoning haste. Whoever preferred tabayyun said: what is meant by tathabbut is clarification, so clarification is more eloquent and more complete.

The second issue: The word ḍarb (striking) means travelling in the land for trade or for jihad, and its origin is striking with the hand.
