Moreover, entitlement to a share of the spoils is connected with taking possession of them, since they do not become spoils except after being taken into possession. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of spoils (ghanimtum min shayʾ)﴾ (Al-Anfāl: 41). And God knows best.

* * *

Then the Almighty said: ﴿And God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He forgives what he did of sitting back until he set out, and has mercy on him by completing the reward of striving.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 101 (part 1 of 2):

God Most High says: ﴿And when you journey in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may inflict harm upon you. Indeed, the disbelievers are ever an open enemy to you.﴾

Know that among the matters a fighter (mujahid) needs is knowing how to perform the prayer in a time of fear and while occupied with fighting the enemy. For this reason God Most High mentions it in this verse. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: It is said "qasara fulanun salatahu" (so-and-so shortened his prayer), "aqsaraha" and "qassaraha," all of which are permissible. Ibn 'Abbas recited "taqsuru" from "aqsara," and al-Zuhri recited it from "qasara." This is evidence for the three dialects.

The second issue: Know that the word qasr (shortening) implies lightening, because it is not explicit as to whether what is meant is shortening in the number of rak'ahs or in the manner of performing them. Therefore, two views arose regarding the verse:

The first, which is the view of the majority, is that what is meant is shortening in the number of rak'ahs. Then those who hold this view also differed on two views:

The first: that what is meant is the prayer of the traveller, namely that every prayer that is four rak'ahs in the settled state becomes two rak'ahs when travelling. Accordingly, shortening applies only to the Dhuhr, 'Asr and 'Isha' prayers; as for Maghrib and Subh, shortening does not apply to them.

The second: that what is meant by this verse is not the travel prayer but the prayer of fear. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and a group. "Ibn 'Abbas said: God prescribed the prayer of residence as four rak'ahs, the prayer of travel as two rak'ahs, and the prayer of fear as one rak'ah, through the tongue of your Prophet Muhammad" (ﷺ). These two views are branches of the position that the meaning of qasr is reducing the number of rak'ahs.

The second view: that what is meant by qasr is introducing lightening into the manner of performing the rak'ahs, namely that one suffices with gesture and signal in place of bowing and prostration, that walking during the prayer is permitted, and that the prayer is valid when the garment is stained with blood. This is the prayer performed in the heat of close combat. This view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Tawus. Those who hold this view argue for its soundness by saying that the fear of harm from the enemy does not cease when one performs two rak'ahs with their full description; rather, that fear is intensified during the heat of close combat. This is weak, because it can be said: when the traveller's prayer has few rak'ahs, he can perform it in a way that his opponent does not know he is praying; but when the rak'ahs are many, the duration is long and he cannot perform them in a moment of the enemy's heedlessness.

Know that the basis of the possibility is what we mentioned: that qasr implies lightening, and lightening is achieved by removing some rak'ahs just as it is achieved by making gesture and signal stand in place of bowing and prostration.

Know that taking the word qasr as dropping some rak'ahs is preferable, and several points indicate this:

The first: what was narrated from Ya'la ibn Umayyah, who said: "I said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him): How do we shorten the prayer when we are secure, and God Most High has said: ﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear﴾? He said: I wondered at what you wonder at, so I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'It is a charity which God has given you, so accept His charity.'" This indicates that the qasr mentioned in the verse is shortening in the number of rak'ahs, and that this was understood by them from the meaning of the verse.

The second: qasr is an expression for performing a part of something and limiting oneself to it. As for performing something else instead, that is not called qasr or iqtisar. It is known that making gesture stand in place of bowing and prostration, permitting walking in the prayer, and permitting the prayer with a garment stained with blood, are none of them qasr; rather all of them are the establishment of new rulings and the substitution of one thing for another. So interpreting qasr as we have mentioned is preferable.

The third: the "min" in His saying "min al-salah" (of the prayer) is partitive, and that requires the permissibility of limiting oneself to part of the prayer. Thus it has been established by these points that interpreting qasr as dropping some rak'ahs is preferable to interpreting it as what they mentioned of gesture and signal.

The fourth: the word qasr was specific in their usage to reducing the number of rak'ahs. For this reason, "when the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed Dhuhr with two rak'ahs, Dhu al-Yadayn said: Has the prayer been shortened, or have you forgotten?"

The fifth: that qasr in the sense of altering the prayer is mentioned in the verse after this verse, so it must be that what is meant by this verse is explaining qasr in the sense of dropping rak'ahs, lest repetition result. And God knows best.

* * *

The third issue: al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: qasr is a concession (rukhsah); if the mukallaf wishes he may complete the prayer, and if he wishes he may suffice with the shortened form. Abu Hanifa said: qasr is obligatory; if the traveller prays four rak'ahs without sitting after the two, his prayer is invalid; and if he sits between them for the duration of the tashahhud, his prayer is complete. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, argued for his view with several points:

The first: the apparent sense of God's saying: ﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾ indicates non-obligation, for one does not say "there is no blame upon you" regarding the performance of an obligatory prayer. Rather this expression is used only to lift a burden concerning that thing; as for making it obligatory specifically, this expression is not used for it. As for Abu Bakr al-Razi, he answered this by saying that what is meant by qasr in this verse is not reducing the rak'ahs but lightening the actions. We have shown by proof that it is not permissible to interpret the verse as he said, so this excuse falls. The author of al-Kashshaf mentioned another point in this regard, saying: since they were accustomed to completing the prayer, it might occur to them that there was a deficiency upon them in shortening, so He removed the blame from them so that their hearts would be content with shortening. It is said to him: this possibility would occur to them only if the Lawgiver had said to them: "I have permitted you this shortening"; but if He had said: "I have made this shortening obligatory upon you, and forbidden you to complete, and made it invalidate your prayer," this possibility would not occur to any intelligent person at all, so this speech would not be fitting for Him.

The second argument: what was narrated that 'Aisha (may God be pleased with her) said: "I performed 'umrah with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from Medina to Mecca. When I arrived at Mecca I said: O Messenger of God, may my father and mother be sacrificed for you, I shortened and I completed, I fasted and I broke my fast. He said: You have done well, O 'Aisha! And he did not blame me for it." 'Uthman used to complete and also shorten, and no denunciation from the Companions of him was made known.

The third argument: all the concessions of travel were legislated by way of permission, not by way of definite obligation; so likewise here. They argued with the hadiths, among them what 'Umar narrated in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is a charity which God has given you, so accept His charity." The apparent meaning of the command is obligation. And from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), when he went out as a traveller, prayed two rak'ahs."

The answer: these hadiths indicate that qasr is legislated and permitted, but the discussion concerns whether anything other than it is permitted. Since the wording of the Qur'an indicates the permissibility of other than it, the view that this is so is preferable. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: some said: the travel prayer is two rak'ahs, complete rather than shortened. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, the travel prayer was confirmed and the prayer of residence was increased.

Know that the wording of the verse refutes this, for we have shown that what is meant by qasr in the verse is lightening the rak'ahs. Had the matter been as they mentioned, this would not be qasr in the travel prayer; rather that would be an addition to the prayer of residence. And God knows best.

* * *

The fifth issue: Dawud and the people of the Zahir claimed that a short journey and a long journey are equal in the permissibility of the concession, while the majority of jurists claimed that travel which has not been limited to a specific measure does not carry the concession. The people of the Zahir argued from the verse, saying: God's saying: ﴿And when you journey in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾ is a compound sentence of a condition, and the consequent of the condition is journeying in the land, and the result is the permissibility of qasr. When the condition is fulfilled, the result must follow from it, whether the travel which is the condition is long or short. At most it might be said: this requires the concession to be obtained when a person moves from one neighbourhood to another, and from one house to another. But we say:

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: if moving from one neighbourhood to another is not called journeying in the land, then the difficulty is removed; and if it is called that, we say: the Muslims agreed that it is not considered, so this is a specification that entered this text by the indication of consensus, and the general after specification is a proof, so it is necessary that the text remain applicable to travel, whether short or long.

The second: God's saying ﴿And when you journey in the land﴾ indicates that He made journeying in the land a condition for the obtaining of this concession. If journeying in the land were the name for mere movement, that would be obtained constantly, because a person throughout his life does not cease from moving from the house to the mosque, and from the mosque to the market. And if it were constantly obtained, it would be impossible to make it a condition for the establishment of this ruling. Since God made journeying in the land a condition for the establishment of this ruling, we know that it is distinct from mere movement, and that is what is called travel (safar). It is known that the name of travel applies to the near and to the far, so we know the verse indicates the obtaining of the concession in mere travel.

As for the jurists, they said: the early generation agreed that the least travel is determined. They said: what indicates this is that reports on the matter have come down:

The first report: what was narrated from 'Umar that he said: one shortens on a full day. Al-Zuhri and al-Awza'i said likewise.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: if it exceeds a day and a night, one shortens.

The third: Anas ibn Malik said: the criterion is five farsakh.

The fourth: al-Hasan said: a journey of two nights.

The fifth: al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: from Kufa to al-Mada'in, which is a journey of three days; and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. Al-Hasan ibn Ziyad narrated from Abu Hanifa that if one travels to a place which is a journey of two days and more than the third day, the qasr is permitted; and Ibn Sama'ah narrated the same from Abu Yusuf and Muhammad.

The sixth: Malik and al-Shafi'i said: four barid, each barid being four farsakh, each farsakh being three miles by the miles of Hashim, the grandfather of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who measured the miles of the desert; each mile is twelve thousand feet, which is four thousand paces, since every three feet is one pace. The jurists said: the people's disagreement on these statements indicates the existence of a consensus that the ruling is not tied to mere travel.

The people of the Zahir said: the jurists' turbulence over these statements indicates that they did not find in the matter a strong proof for determining the duration; for if a clearly indicative proof had existed in the matter, this turbulence would not have arisen. As for the silence of the rest of the Companions about the ruling of this matter, perhaps it was because they believed that this verse indicates the ruling is tied to mere travel, so this ruling was established for mere travel by the ruling of this verse; and when a ruling is mentioned in the text of the Qur'an, there is no need for them to exert ijtihad and deduction. For this reason they remained silent about this matter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 101 (part 2 of 2):

Know that the companions of Abu Hanifa relied, in determining the period at three days, on his saying (peace be upon him): "The traveler wipes [over his leather socks] for three days." This implies that if the wiping does not take place for three days, the person is no longer a traveler, and if he is not a traveler, the concessions prescribed for travel do not apply. As for the companions of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him), they relied on what Mujahid and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: O people of Makkah, do not shorten the prayer for less than four burud (postal distances), from Makkah to 'Usfan." The people of the literal reading (Ahl al-Zahir) said: The discussion of this has several aspects:

The first: It is an attempt to restrict the general meaning of the Qur'an by a solitary report (khabar al-wahid, a report transmitted by one narrator or a few), and this is, according to us, impermissible, for two reasons:

The first: The Qur'an and the solitary report are both shared in the indication of the ruling by the wording of each of them, but the Qur'an's text is definitively transmitted (maqtu' al-matn), while the report's text is only probably transmitted (maznun al-matn). So the Qur'an is stronger in its indication than the report, and preferring the weaker over the stronger is not permitted.

The second: It is reported in a report that he (peace be upon him) said: "When a hadith is related from me, present it to the Book of Allah the Exalted. If it agrees with it, accept it, and if it contradicts it, reject it." This report indicates that every report that comes in contradiction to the Book of Allah the Exalted is rejected. Since this report comes in contradiction to the general meaning of the Book, it must be rejected.

The second aspect, in refuting these reports: they are solitary reports that came concerning an event in which the need to know its ruling is widespread, so they must be rejected. We say that the need for it is widespread because most of the Companions were, for most of the time, traveling or on campaign. Since the concessions of travel are restricted to a specified journey, the need to know the measure of a journey that entitles one to these concessions is a general need for the responsible persons. Had the matter been so, they would have known it and transmitted it through mass transmission (tawatur), especially since it contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Since the matter is not so, we know that these are weak reports that are to be rejected. And if this is the case,
[p. 18]
how is it permissible to abandon the apparent meaning of the Qur'an because of them?

The third: The evidences of the Shafi'is and the evidences of the Hanafis have become mutually opposed and contradictory, and when they conflict, they cancel each other out, so it becomes necessary to return to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. This is the complete discussion on this point.

What I hold on this matter is to say: The words "idha" (when) and "in" (if) only indicate that the condition is followed by the consequence. As for the condition being followed by that consequence at all times, this is not necessary, as evidenced by the fact that if a man says to his wife, "If you enter the house," or "When you enter the house, you are divorced," then if she enters once, the divorce takes effect, but if she enters a second time, it does not take effect. This shows that the words "idha" and "in" do not indicate generality at all. Once this is established, the argument of the literalists from the verse falls away, for the verse indicates only that striking the earth (travel) brings about these concessions once. According to us, the matter is so when the journey is long. As for a short journey, it would fall under the verse only if we said that the word "idha" implies generality, and since it has been established that the matter is not so, the argument falls away. Once this is established, it becomes clear that the evidences by which the jurists held to a specified measure are not in contradiction to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and so they are accepted and sound. And Allah knows best.

* * *

The sixth issue: Dawud and the people of the literal reading claimed that the permissibility of shortening (qasr) is restricted to the state of fear. They argued that Allah the Exalted made this ruling conditional upon fear, in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾. Something conditional on a thing is absent when that condition is absent, so the permissibility of shortening should not be established in a state of security. They said: It is not permissible to lift this condition by a solitary report, for that would imply abrogating the Qur'an by a solitary report, which is impermissible. This statement has been difficult for some people, who mentioned strained interpretations of the verse in order to escape from this argument.

But in my view there is no obscurity in this, because we have explained, in the commentary on His saying the Exalted: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], that the words "in" (if) and "idha" (when) indicate that when the condition is fulfilled, the conditioned matter is realized, but they do not indicate that when the condition is absent, the conditioned matter is necessarily absent. We supported the soundness of this statement with many verses. Once this is established, we say: His saying, "if you fear," implies that when fear occurs, the concession is granted, but it does not imply that when there is no fear, the concession is not granted. Given this, the verse is silent about the state of security, neither by negation nor by affirmation. Establishing the concession in a state of security by a solitary report is establishing a ruling on which the Qur'an was silent, by a solitary report, and that is not impermissible. What is impermissible is establishing a ruling by a solitary report contrary to what the Qur'an indicates, and we do not hold that.

If it is said: On this basis, since this ruling is established both in a state of security and in a state of fear, what is the benefit of restricting it to the state of fear?

We say: The verse was revealed concerning most of the journeys of the Prophet (ﷺ), and most of them were not free of fear of the enemy. So Allah mentioned this condition because it is the most common in occurrence. Some people have answered this by saying that the shortening mentioned in the verse means being content with gesturing and signaling in place of bowing and prostration. This is the prayer in a state of extreme fear, and there is no doubt that this prayer is restricted to a state of fear, for at a time of security it is not permissible to perform this prayer, and it is neither prohibited nor valid. And Allah knows best.

Then it is said to the people of the literal reading: The apparent meaning of this verse implies that shortening is not permissible except when there is fear arising from the tempting of the disbelievers. As for if fear arises from another cause, shortening would not be permissible. If they accept this, they are safe from criticism, though it is far-fetched. If they do not accept it, the contradiction is pressed upon them, for He the Exalted said:
[p. 19]
﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾, and this implies that the condition is this specific fear. They may reply: Either it is said that the Companions and the Community reached a consensus (ijma') that any fear is sufficient, or no consensus was reached. If a consensus was reached, then we say: We have departed from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an on the basis of a consensus, which is a definitive proof, and so it was not permissible to oppose it by a speculative proof. If no consensus was reached, then the objection falls away, for we commit ourselves to the view that shortening is not permissible except with this specific fear. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾, there are two opinions regarding the interpretation of this "tempting" (fitnah):

The first: that you fear they may tempt you away from completing the bowing and prostration throughout it.

The second: if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you through their enmity. The summary is that every trial, calamity, and hardship is a fitnah.

* * *

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers have ever been to you a clear enemy﴾. The meaning is: the enmity that exists between you and the disbelievers is ancient, and now you have openly shown your opposition to them in religion, and their enmity has increased. Because of the intensity of enmity, they have proceeded to fight you and to seek your destruction if they are able. If your prayer is long, they may find the opportunity to kill you. Therefore, I have granted you the concession of shortening the prayer. He said "'aduwwan" (an enemy) and did not say "a'da'an" (enemies) because "'aduww" is used for both the singular and the plural. He the Exalted said: ﴿For they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 77].

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 102–103 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their arms. Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group come who have not prayed and let them pray with you, and let them take their precaution and their arms. Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your arms and your belongings, so they could incline upon you in a single inclination. And there is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain-related discomfort or if you are ill; and take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. And when you are secure, establish prayer. Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse the state of shortening the prayer in terms of its quantity in number, He explained in this verse its state in terms of its manner. And in it are issues:

Page 20

The first issue: Abu Yusuf and al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said: the prayer of fear was specific to the Messenger ﷺ and is not permissible for anyone else. Al-Muzani said: it was established and then abrogated (nuskhat). Abu Yusuf argued for his position with two aspects:

The first: that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them﴾, apparently requires that the establishment of this prayer is conditioned upon the Prophet ﷺ being among them, because the word "idha" (when) indicates a condition.

The second: that altering the form of the prayer is contrary to the general evidence, but we permitted that in the case of the Messenger ﷺ so that the people would obtain the merit of praying behind him. As for the case of other than the Messenger, peace be upon him, this meaning is not attained, because the merit of praying behind the second imam is like that of praying behind the first, so there is no need there to alter the form of the prayer. As for the rest of the jurists, they said: since this ruling was established in the case of the Prophet ﷺ by the ruling of this verse, it must be established in the case of others, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and follow him﴾ [al-A'raf: 158]. Do you not see that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103] did not necessitate that the Messenger ﷺ be specific to it, to the exclusion of the rest of the community after him? As for holding to the word "idha," the answer is: its implication is affirmation upon the existence of the condition, but non-existence upon the non-existence of the condition is not granted. As for holding to attaining the merit of praying behind the Prophet ﷺ, it is not permissible that it be a cause for permitting the alteration of the prayer, because it is not permissible that seeking merit necessitates abandoning an obligation. Thus this argument is refuted, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: The description of the prayer of fear is that the imam divides the people into two groups and leads them in one rak'ah. Then, when they have finished the rak'ah, what do they do? In this there are sayings:

The first: that this group completes the salam from the single rak'ah and goes to face the enemy, and the other group comes, and the imam prays with them one more rak'ah and gives the salam. This is the view of those who hold that the prayer of fear for the imam is two rak'ahs and for the people is one rak'ah. This is related from Ibn Abbas, Jabir ibn Abd Allah, and Mujahid.

The second: that the imam prays with that group two rak'ahs and gives the salam, then that group goes to face the enemy, and the other group comes, and the imam prays with them again two rak'ahs. This is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: that the imam prays with the first group one complete rak'ah, then the imam remains standing in the second rak'ah until this group prays one more rak'ah, and they recite the tashahhud and give the salam and go to face the enemy. Then the second group comes and they pray with the imam standing in the second rak'ah one rak'ah, then the imam sits in the tashahhud until the second group completes the second rak'ah, then the imam gives the salam with them. This is the saying of Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, and the position of al-Shafi'i.

The fourth: that the imam prays with the first group one rak'ah, and they return to face the enemy, and the second group comes and he prays with them the rest of the prayer, and they depart to face the enemy. Then the first group returns and they complete the rest of their prayer with recitation, and they depart to face the enemy. Then the second group returns and they complete the rest of their prayer with recitation. The distinction is that the first group caught the beginning of the prayer and are in the position of those behind the imam, whereas the second group did not catch the beginning of the prayer, and the one who is late (masbuq) in what he makes up is like the one praying alone. This is the saying of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and the position of Abu Hanifah.

Know that the varying narrations have come concerning this prayer, so perhaps he ﷺ prayed it with them at different times according to what was beneficial. The disagreement among the jurists arose only regarding which of these divisions is the most excellent and most in conformity with the apparent meaning of the verse. As for al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him), he said: the verse contradicts the narrations upon which Abu Hanifah relied, and he explained this from two aspects:

The first: that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed﴾. This indicates that the first group had prayed by the time the second came, whereas according to Abu Hanifah the matter is not so, because according to him the second group comes while the first is still in the prayer and has not finished it.

The second: that His saying: "then let them pray with you" apparently indicates that the entire prayer of the second group is with the imam, because the absolute statement "I prayed with the imam" indicates that you caught the entire prayer with him, whereas according to the view of Abu Hanifah the matter is not so.

As for the companions of Abu Hanifah, they said: the verse conforms to our position, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you﴾. This indicates that the first group had not finished the prayer, but they pray one rak'ah, then they are behind the second group for guarding. Al-Wahidi answered this, saying: this only applies if we make the prostration and being behind you apply to one group, and that is not the case; rather it applies to two groups: the prostration is for the first, and being behind you, meaning guarding, is for the second group. And Allah knows best.

Let us return to the explanation of the verse, so we say: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them﴾, meaning: and when you, O Prophet, are among the believers in their military campaigns and their fear: ﴿and establish prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you﴾. The meaning: make them into two groups, let a group of them stand with you, then lead them in prayer, and let them take their arms. The pronoun is either for those praying or for others. If it is for those praying, they said: they take from the weapons what does not occupy them from the prayer, such as the sword and the dagger, because that is closer to caution and more preventive of the enemy's advance upon them. If it is for others than those praying, there is no discussion about it. It is possible that this is a command to both groups to carry weapons, because that is closer to caution.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then when they have prostrated, let them be﴾.

That is: the non-praying group: ﴿behind you﴾ guarding you. We have mentioned that performing the first rak'ah with the imam in the prayer of fear is like it is in the prayer of security; the difference occurs only in performing the second rak'ah in it, and we have mentioned the positions of the people concerning it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed, let them pray with you﴾. We have shown that this verse indicates the soundness of al-Shafi'i's position.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and let them take their precaution and their arms﴾. The meaning: He, exalted is He, made precaution, which is vigilance and alertness, an instrument the warrior employs, and therefore it was joined with the weapons in taking, and both were made objects of taking. Al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: in it is a concession for the one in fear during prayer, that he may devote part of his thought to other than the prayer.

If it is said: why did He mention in the first verse only "their arms," and in this verse mention "their precaution and their arms"?

We say: because at the beginning of the prayer the enemy rarely becomes aware that the Muslims are in prayer, rather they assume them to be standing for the purpose of fighting. As for the second rak'ah, the disbelievers have become aware that they are in prayer, so here they seize the opportunity to attack them. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, specified this place with added warning, and said: ﴿and let them take their precaution and their arms﴾.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your arms and your belongings, so they could incline upon you in a single inclination﴾. That is: by fighting. From Ibn Abbas and Jabir: "The Prophet ﷺ prayed the Dhuhr with his companions, and the polytheists saw that, and they said after that: how wretched is what we did, in that we did not advance upon them, and they resolved upon that at the next prayer, so Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ of their secrets through this verse."

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain-related discomfort or if you are ill﴾

Page 22

The meaning is that if carrying the weapon becomes impossible, either because rain's moisture reaches it and it becomes blackened and its sharpness is spoiled, or because some weapons are lined and become heavy on their wearer when wet with water, or because the man is ill and carrying the weapon is burdensome for him, then in these cases he may set down the carrying of the weapon.

* * *

Then He said: "and take your precaution." The meaning: since He permitted them to put down the weapons during rain and during illness, He commanded them once more to be alert, watchful, and to exert great effort in caution, lest the enemy become bold against them, scheming to incline upon them and seizing the opportunity of the Muslims' laying down their arms. In this there are issues:

The first issue: His saying at the beginning of the verse: ﴿and let them take their arms﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, so it requires that taking up arms be obligatory. Then this was reinforced by another proof, namely that He said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain-related discomfort or if you are ill﴾, so He restricted the lifting of blame for laying down the weapon to these two situations, and this necessitates that beyond these two situations, sin and blame are incurred by laying down the weapon.

Some said: it is a confirmed sunnah, but the more correct is what we have explained. Then the condition is that one should not carry a najis weapon if he is able to avoid it, and should not carry a spear except at the edge of the row, and in general in such a way that no one is harmed by it.

**The second issue:** Abu 'Ali al-Jurjani, the author of *al-Nazm* (the book *Nazm al-Qur'an*), said: His saying, the Exalted, (And take your precaution) indicates that it was permissible for the Prophet ﷺ to perform the prayer of fear in a manner in which he was cautious and not heedless of the enemy's scheming. What the Qur'an revealed in this passage is the manner of caution, because the enemy on that day at Dhat al-Riqa' was facing the qiblah, while the Muslims were facing away from the qiblah. Whenever they faced the qiblah, they would have their backs to their enemy. Therefore, they were commanded to form two groups: one group facing the enemy, and another group with the Prophet, peace be upon him, facing the qiblah. As for when the Prophet ﷺ was at 'Usfan and at Batn Nakhl, he did not divide his companions into two groups. This was because the enemy was facing away from the qiblah, while the Muslims were facing towards it. So they could see the enemy while they were in prayer, and they had no need for caution except during prostration. Therefore, when the first row prostrated, the second row remained guarding them. When they finished prostrating and stood up, they moved back, and the second row came forward and prostrated. While standing, the first row guarded the second row. Thus, it has been established by what we have mentioned that His saying, the Exalted, (Take your precaution) indicates the permissibility of these modes. What indicates that the meaning of this verse is what we have mentioned is that if we did not interpret it in this way, it would become pure repetition without any benefit, and the actions of the Messenger at 'Usfan and at Batn Nakhl would contradict the text of the Qur'an, which is impermissible. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: Allah, the Exalted, commanded caution, and this indicates that the servant is able to act and to refrain, and to do all the forms of caution. This indicates that the actions of servants are not created by Allah, the Exalted. The answer to this is what preceded regarding the counter-argument of knowledge and motive. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates the obligation of caution against the enemy, and therefore it indicates the obligation of caution against all presumed harms. By this method, taking up treatment with medicine, treatment by hand, and avoiding plague, and avoiding sitting beneath a leaning wall, are all obligatory. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾. In this there is a question: How does the command to take caution correspond to His saying: "Indeed, Allah..."

[Page 23]

﴿Has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾? Its answer: When He, the Exalted, commanded caution against the enemy, this might give the impression of the enemy's strength and power. So Allah, the Exalted, removed this impression by informing that He will humiliate them, forsake them, and will not give them victory at all, so that He strengthens the hearts of the Muslims, and they know that the command to take caution is not because of the strength and prestige they have, but rather in order for fear to arise in the hearts of the believers. Then they will be humbly turning to Allah, the Exalted, asking Him to aid them with victory and success. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you encounter a force, stand firm and remember Allah often that you may be successful﴾ [al-Anfal: 45].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: When you have completed the prayer of fear, then persist in remembering Allah in all circumstances, for what you are in of fear and caution with the enemy is worthy of persistence in remembering Allah and humbly turning to Him.

The second: The intended meaning of "remembrance" is the prayer. That is: Pray standing while you are occupied with fighting and engagement, sitting while you are occupied with shooting, and on your sides when many wounds are upon you and you fall to the ground. Then, when you are at ease when the war lays down its burdens, establish the prayer, and make up what you prayed in the state of fighting.

This is apparent according to the school of al-Shafi'i, who held that prayer is obligatory on a warrior in the state of fighting if its time arrives, and when they are at ease, they must make it up. However, there is a difficulty with this opinion, which is that the meaning of the verse would become: "When you have completed the prayer, then pray," and this is far-fetched, because interpreting the word "remembrance" as prayer is a figurative usage (majaz), so one does not resort to it except by necessity.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And when you have completed the prayer, then remember﴾. Know that this verse is preceded by two rulings:

The first of them: the explanation of shortening (qasr), which is the prayer of travel.

The second: the prayer of fear. Then His saying: "And when you are at ease" (fa-idha itma'nantum) may carry the opposite of the two matters. It may be that the intended meaning of "being at ease" is that the person no longer remains a traveler, but becomes a resident. According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "When you become residents, then establish the prayer in full without any shortening at all." And it may be that the intended meaning of "being at ease" is that the person no longer remains agitated in heart, but becomes calm of heart and calm of soul because fear has departed. According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "When fear has departed from you, then establish the prayer in the state you know, and do not change any of its conditions or forms."

Then, when Allah, glorified and exalted, had elaborated at length on the types of prayer, mentioning the prayer of travel and then mentioning the prayer of fear after it, He concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times﴾. That is: an obligation with set times. By "decree" (kitab) here is meant "written," as if it were said: "a prescribed and timed obligation." Then the ha' was dropped from "mawquut" just as the verbal noun is placed in the position of the passive participle, and the verbal noun is masculine. The meaning of "mawquut" is that it was prescribed upon them at specified times. It is said: waqqatahu and waqatahu (lightened form). And it was recited: ﴿And when the messengers are appointed a time﴾ [al-Mursalat: 11] with the lightened form.

* * *

Know that Allah, the Exalted, clarified in this verse that the obligation of prayer is determined by specific times, except that Allah, the Exalted, summarized the mention of the times here and explained them in other verses, and they are five:

First: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Maintain with care the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. His saying "the prayers" (al-salawat) indicates the obligation of three prayers, and His saying "and the middle prayer" prevents it from being one of those three, otherwise there would be repetition. So it must be beyond the three, and it cannot be that the obligatory prayers are four, otherwise there would be no middle among them. So it is necessary to make them five so that a middle is obtained. Just as this verse indicates the obligation of five prayers, it also indicates the non-obligation of the witr (odd prayer), for otherwise the obligatory prayers would be six, and then there would be no middle. So this verse indicates that the obligatory prayers are five, although it does not indicate the explanation of their times.

Second: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night and the recitation of dawn﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. The obligatory prayers from the decline to the darkness are Dhuhr and 'Asr, the obligatory ones from the darkness to dawn are Maghrib and 'Isha', and the obligatory one at dawn is the Subh prayer. This verse gives the impression that Dhuhr and 'Asr have one time, and Maghrib and 'Isha' have one time.

Third: His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So exalt Allah when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17]. What is meant by it are the two prayers occurring at the two ends of the day, which are Maghrib and Subh. Then He said: ﴿And to Him is the praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you reach noon﴾ [al-Rum: 18]. His saying "in the late afternoon" (ashiyyan) means the prayer occurring in the depth of the night, which is the 'Isha' prayer. And His saying "when you reach noon" means the prayer occurring in the depth of the day, which is the Dhuhr prayer. Just as in His saying "when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning" He mentioned the night prayer before the day prayer, so likewise in His saying "in the late afternoon and when you reach noon" He mentioned the night prayer before the day prayer. Thus, four prayers are mentioned in this verse. As for the 'Asr prayer, Allah, the Exalted, singled it out by mention in His saying: "By the afternoon" [al-'Asr: 1], honoring it by singling it out for mention.

Fourth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the approaching portions of the night﴾ [Hud: 114]. His saying "the two ends of the day" indicates the obligation of the Subh prayer and the obligation of the 'Asr prayer, because they are like those occurring at the two ends, even though the Subh prayer occurs before the first end begins, and the 'Asr prayer occurs before the second end begins.

His saying "and in the approaching portions of the night" indicates the obligation of Maghrib and 'Isha'. Some of them used this verse as evidence for the obligation of the witr, saying: "Because zulaf is a plural, and its least number is three, so three prayers must be obligatory at night, in acting upon His saying: 'and in the approaching portions of the night.'"

Fifth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And exalt the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night exalt Him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. His saying "before the rising of the sun and before its setting" is an allusion to the Subh and 'Asr prayers, and it is like His saying: "And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the approaching portions of the night." His saying "and during the hours of the night" is an allusion to Maghrib and 'Isha', and it is like His saying: "and in the approaching portions of the night." Just as they argued with His saying "and in the approaching portions of the night," they likewise argued against it with His saying "and during the hours of the night," because His saying "hours of the night" (anaa' al-layl) is a plural whose least number is three. This is the collection of verses indicating the five times for the five prayers.

Know that the determination of the prayers by these five times is of the utmost beauty and perfection when considered rationally. Its explanation is that everything in the states of this world has five stages:

The first of them: the stage of coming into existence and entering into being, as a human is born and remains in growth and development for a known period. This period is called the age of growth and development.

The second stage: the period of standing, which is that the thing remains in the attribute of its perfection without increase or decrease. This period is called the age of youth.

The third stage: the period of maturity, which is that a hidden deficiency appears in the human. This period is called the age of maturity.

The fourth stage: the period of old age, which is that apparent and clear deficiencies appear in the human until he dies and perishes. This period is called the age of old age.

The fifth stage: that its traces remain for a period after its death, then ultimately those traces are erased, nullified, and vanish, and nothing of it remains in this world, no news and no trace. These five stages apply to all events of this world, whether it is a human or other animals or plants. And the sun, by its rising and setting, undergoes these five states, because it...

[Page 25]

When the sun rises from its place of rising, its condition resembles the condition of a newborn when it is born. Then its height continues to increase, its light grows stronger, and its heat intensifies, until it reaches the middle of the sky, where it stands still for a while. Then it descends, and hidden deficiencies appear in it until the time of ʿAṣr. Then from the time of ʿAṣr, manifest deficiencies appear in it, so its light weakens and its heat diminishes, and its decline and weakness increase until sunset. Then, when it sets, some traces of it remain on the horizon of the west, which is the twilight (al-shafaq). Then those traces vanish, and the sun becomes as though it had never existed in the world. So when these five states have occurred for it, and they are wondrous matters that none can bring about except Allah the Exalted, Allah the Exalted, without doubt, made prayer obligatory at each of these five states. So at the approach of the sun to rising, He made obligatory the Fajr prayer, in gratitude for the great blessing that results from the departure of that darkness and the arrival of light, and because of the departure of sleep, which is like death, and the arrival of wakefulness, which is like life. And when the sun reached the furthest point of elevation, and then the sign of decline appeared in it, He made obligatory the Ẓuhr prayer, in glorification of the Creator, who is able to turn the conditions of the heavenly and earthly bodies from one opposite to another, so He made the sun, after the furthest point of its height and exaltation, lowered from that loftiness, entering the age of middle years (al-kuhūla), which is the hidden deficiency. Then, when the period of middle years ended and it entered the beginning of the time of old age, He, the Exalted, made the ʿAṣr prayer obligatory.

And how excellent is what al-Shāfiʿī (raḥimahu Allāh) said: the beginning of ʿAṣr is when the shadow of each thing becomes twice its length. That is because from this time the manifest deficiencies appear. Do you not see that from the beginning of the time of Ẓuhr until the time of ʿAṣr, according to al-Shāfiʿī's view (raḥimahu Allāh), the shadow has only increased by the length of the object? Then, in a subtle moment, its shadow becomes twice its length. This indicates that from the time when an object's shadow becomes equal to it, the sun begins its manifest deficiencies. Then, when the sun sets, this state resembles what happens when a person dies. So without doubt, Allah the Exalted made the Maghrib prayer obligatory at this state. Then, when the twilight has set, it is as though the traces of the sun have been erased, and no news or trace of it remains in the world. So without doubt, Allah the Exalted made the ʿIshāʾ prayer obligatory. Thus it is established that the obligation of the five prayers at these five times accords with rational principles and wise foundations, and Allah knows best the secrets of His acts.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 102–103 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their arms. Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group come who have not prayed and let them pray with you, and let them take their precaution and their arms. Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your arms and your belongings, so they could incline upon you in a single inclination. And there is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain-related discomfort or if you are ill; and take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. And when you are secure, establish prayer. Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse the state of shortening the prayer in terms of its quantity in number, He explained in this verse its state in terms of its manner. And in it are issues:

Page 20

The first issue: Abu Yusuf and al-Hasan ibn Ziyad said: the prayer of fear was specific to the Messenger ﷺ and is not permissible for anyone else. Al-Muzani said: it was established and then abrogated (nuskhat). Abu Yusuf argued for his position with two aspects:

The first: that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them﴾, apparently requires that the establishment of this prayer is conditioned upon the Prophet ﷺ being among them, because the word "idha" (when) indicates a condition.

The second: that altering the form of the prayer is contrary to the general evidence, but we permitted that in the case of the Messenger ﷺ so that the people would obtain the merit of praying behind him. As for the case of other than the Messenger, peace be upon him, this meaning is not attained, because the merit of praying behind the second imam is like that of praying behind the first, so there is no need there to alter the form of the prayer. As for the rest of the jurists, they said: since this ruling was established in the case of the Prophet ﷺ by the ruling of this verse, it must be established in the case of others, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and follow him﴾ [al-A'raf: 158]. Do you not see that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103] did not necessitate that the Messenger ﷺ be specific to it, to the exclusion of the rest of the community after him? As for holding to the word "idha," the answer is: its implication is affirmation upon the existence of the condition, but non-existence upon the non-existence of the condition is not granted. As for holding to attaining the merit of praying behind the Prophet ﷺ, it is not permissible that it be a cause for permitting the alteration of the prayer, because it is not permissible that seeking merit necessitates abandoning an obligation. Thus this argument is refuted, and Allah knows best.

* * *

The second issue: The description of the prayer of fear is that the imam divides the people into two groups and leads them in one rak'ah. Then, when they have finished the rak'ah, what do they do? In this there are sayings:

The first: that this group completes the salam from the single rak'ah and goes to face the enemy, and the other group comes, and the imam prays with them one more rak'ah and gives the salam. This is the view of those who hold that the prayer of fear for the imam is two rak'ahs and for the people is one rak'ah. This is related from Ibn Abbas, Jabir ibn Abd Allah, and Mujahid.

The second: that the imam prays with that group two rak'ahs and gives the salam, then that group goes to face the enemy, and the other group comes, and the imam prays with them again two rak'ahs. This is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: that the imam prays with the first group one complete rak'ah, then the imam remains standing in the second rak'ah until this group prays one more rak'ah, and they recite the tashahhud and give the salam and go to face the enemy. Then the second group comes and they pray with the imam standing in the second rak'ah one rak'ah, then the imam sits in the tashahhud until the second group completes the second rak'ah, then the imam gives the salam with them. This is the saying of Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, and the position of al-Shafi'i.

The fourth: that the imam prays with the first group one rak'ah, and they return to face the enemy, and the second group comes and he prays with them the rest of the prayer, and they depart to face the enemy. Then the first group returns and they complete the rest of their prayer with recitation, and they depart to face the enemy. Then the second group returns and they complete the rest of their prayer with recitation. The distinction is that the first group caught the beginning of the prayer and are in the position of those behind the imam, whereas the second group did not catch the beginning of the prayer, and the one who is late (masbuq) in what he makes up is like the one praying alone. This is the saying of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and the position of Abu Hanifah.

Know that the varying narrations have come concerning this prayer, so perhaps he ﷺ prayed it with them at different times according to what was beneficial. The disagreement among the jurists arose only regarding which of these divisions is the most excellent and most in conformity with the apparent meaning of the verse. As for al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him), he said: the verse contradicts the narrations upon which Abu Hanifah relied, and he explained this from two aspects:

The first: that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed﴾. This indicates that the first group had prayed by the time the second came, whereas according to Abu Hanifah the matter is not so, because according to him the second group comes while the first is still in the prayer and has not finished it.

The second: that His saying: "then let them pray with you" apparently indicates that the entire prayer of the second group is with the imam, because the absolute statement "I prayed with the imam" indicates that you caught the entire prayer with him, whereas according to the view of Abu Hanifah the matter is not so.

As for the companions of Abu Hanifah, they said: the verse conforms to our position, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you﴾. This indicates that the first group had not finished the prayer, but they pray one rak'ah, then they are behind the second group for guarding. Al-Wahidi answered this, saying: this only applies if we make the prostration and being behind you apply to one group, and that is not the case; rather it applies to two groups: the prostration is for the first, and being behind you, meaning guarding, is for the second group. And Allah knows best.

Let us return to the explanation of the verse, so we say: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them﴾, meaning: and when you, O Prophet, are among the believers in their military campaigns and their fear: ﴿and establish prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you﴾. The meaning: make them into two groups, let a group of them stand with you, then lead them in prayer, and let them take their arms. The pronoun is either for those praying or for others. If it is for those praying, they said: they take from the weapons what does not occupy them from the prayer, such as the sword and the dagger, because that is closer to caution and more preventive of the enemy's advance upon them. If it is for others than those praying, there is no discussion about it. It is possible that this is a command to both groups to carry weapons, because that is closer to caution.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then when they have prostrated, let them be﴾.

That is: the non-praying group: ﴿behind you﴾ guarding you. We have mentioned that performing the first rak'ah with the imam in the prayer of fear is like it is in the prayer of security; the difference occurs only in performing the second rak'ah in it, and we have mentioned the positions of the people concerning it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed, let them pray with you﴾. We have shown that this verse indicates the soundness of al-Shafi'i's position.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and let them take their precaution and their arms﴾. The meaning: He, exalted is He, made precaution, which is vigilance and alertness, an instrument the warrior employs, and therefore it was joined with the weapons in taking, and both were made objects of taking. Al-Wahidi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: in it is a concession for the one in fear during prayer, that he may devote part of his thought to other than the prayer.

If it is said: why did He mention in the first verse only "their arms," and in this verse mention "their precaution and their arms"?

We say: because at the beginning of the prayer the enemy rarely becomes aware that the Muslims are in prayer, rather they assume them to be standing for the purpose of fighting. As for the second rak'ah, the disbelievers have become aware that they are in prayer, so here they seize the opportunity to attack them. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, specified this place with added warning, and said: ﴿and let them take their precaution and their arms﴾.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your arms and your belongings, so they could incline upon you in a single inclination﴾. That is: by fighting. From Ibn Abbas and Jabir: "The Prophet ﷺ prayed the Dhuhr with his companions, and the polytheists saw that, and they said after that: how wretched is what we did, in that we did not advance upon them, and they resolved upon that at the next prayer, so Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ of their secrets through this verse."

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain-related discomfort or if you are ill﴾

Page 22

The meaning is that if carrying the weapon becomes impossible, either because rain's moisture reaches it and it becomes blackened and its sharpness is spoiled, or because some weapons are lined and become heavy on their wearer when wet with water, or because the man is ill and carrying the weapon is burdensome for him, then in these cases he may set down the carrying of the weapon.

* * *

Then He said: "and take your precaution." The meaning: since He permitted them to put down the weapons during rain and during illness, He commanded them once more to be alert, watchful, and to exert great effort in caution, lest the enemy become bold against them, scheming to incline upon them and seizing the opportunity of the Muslims' laying down their arms. In this there are issues:

The first issue: His saying at the beginning of the verse: ﴿and let them take their arms﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, so it requires that taking up arms be obligatory. Then this was reinforced by another proof, namely that He said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your arms because of rain-related discomfort or if you are ill﴾, so He restricted the lifting of blame for laying down the weapon to these two situations, and this necessitates that beyond these two situations, sin and blame are incurred by laying down the weapon.

Some said: it is a confirmed sunnah, but the more correct is what we have explained. Then the condition is that one should not carry a najis weapon if he is able to avoid it, and should not carry a spear except at the edge of the row, and in general in such a way that no one is harmed by it.

**The second issue:** Abu 'Ali al-Jurjani, the author of *al-Nazm* (the book *Nazm al-Qur'an*), said: His saying, the Exalted, (And take your precaution) indicates that it was permissible for the Prophet ﷺ to perform the prayer of fear in a manner in which he was cautious and not heedless of the enemy's scheming. What the Qur'an revealed in this passage is the manner of caution, because the enemy on that day at Dhat al-Riqa' was facing the qiblah, while the Muslims were facing away from the qiblah. Whenever they faced the qiblah, they would have their backs to their enemy. Therefore, they were commanded to form two groups: one group facing the enemy, and another group with the Prophet, peace be upon him, facing the qiblah. As for when the Prophet ﷺ was at 'Usfan and at Batn Nakhl, he did not divide his companions into two groups. This was because the enemy was facing away from the qiblah, while the Muslims were facing towards it. So they could see the enemy while they were in prayer, and they had no need for caution except during prostration. Therefore, when the first row prostrated, the second row remained guarding them. When they finished prostrating and stood up, they moved back, and the second row came forward and prostrated. While standing, the first row guarded the second row. Thus, it has been established by what we have mentioned that His saying, the Exalted, (Take your precaution) indicates the permissibility of these modes. What indicates that the meaning of this verse is what we have mentioned is that if we did not interpret it in this way, it would become pure repetition without any benefit, and the actions of the Messenger at 'Usfan and at Batn Nakhl would contradict the text of the Qur'an, which is impermissible. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: Allah, the Exalted, commanded caution, and this indicates that the servant is able to act and to refrain, and to do all the forms of caution. This indicates that the actions of servants are not created by Allah, the Exalted. The answer to this is what preceded regarding the counter-argument of knowledge and motive. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates the obligation of caution against the enemy, and therefore it indicates the obligation of caution against all presumed harms. By this method, taking up treatment with medicine, treatment by hand, and avoiding plague, and avoiding sitting beneath a leaning wall, are all obligatory. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾. In this there is a question: How does the command to take caution correspond to His saying: "Indeed, Allah..."

[Page 23]

﴿Has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾? Its answer: When He, the Exalted, commanded caution against the enemy, this might give the impression of the enemy's strength and power. So Allah, the Exalted, removed this impression by informing that He will humiliate them, forsake them, and will not give them victory at all, so that He strengthens the hearts of the Muslims, and they know that the command to take caution is not because of the strength and prestige they have, but rather in order for fear to arise in the hearts of the believers. Then they will be humbly turning to Allah, the Exalted, asking Him to aid them with victory and success. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you encounter a force, stand firm and remember Allah often that you may be successful﴾ [al-Anfal: 45].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: When you have completed the prayer of fear, then persist in remembering Allah in all circumstances, for what you are in of fear and caution with the enemy is worthy of persistence in remembering Allah and humbly turning to Him.

The second: The intended meaning of "remembrance" is the prayer. That is: Pray standing while you are occupied with fighting and engagement, sitting while you are occupied with shooting, and on your sides when many wounds are upon you and you fall to the ground. Then, when you are at ease when the war lays down its burdens, establish the prayer, and make up what you prayed in the state of fighting.

This is apparent according to the school of al-Shafi'i, who held that prayer is obligatory on a warrior in the state of fighting if its time arrives, and when they are at ease, they must make it up. However, there is a difficulty with this opinion, which is that the meaning of the verse would become: "When you have completed the prayer, then pray," and this is far-fetched, because interpreting the word "remembrance" as prayer is a figurative usage (majaz), so one does not resort to it except by necessity.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And when you have completed the prayer, then remember﴾. Know that this verse is preceded by two rulings:

The first of them: the explanation of shortening (qasr), which is the prayer of travel.

The second: the prayer of fear. Then His saying: "And when you are at ease" (fa-idha itma'nantum) may carry the opposite of the two matters. It may be that the intended meaning of "being at ease" is that the person no longer remains a traveler, but becomes a resident. According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "When you become residents, then establish the prayer in full without any shortening at all." And it may be that the intended meaning of "being at ease" is that the person no longer remains agitated in heart, but becomes calm of heart and calm of soul because fear has departed. According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "When fear has departed from you, then establish the prayer in the state you know, and do not change any of its conditions or forms."

Then, when Allah, glorified and exalted, had elaborated at length on the types of prayer, mentioning the prayer of travel and then mentioning the prayer of fear after it, He concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times﴾. That is: an obligation with set times. By "decree" (kitab) here is meant "written," as if it were said: "a prescribed and timed obligation." Then the ha' was dropped from "mawquut" just as the verbal noun is placed in the position of the passive participle, and the verbal noun is masculine. The meaning of "mawquut" is that it was prescribed upon them at specified times. It is said: waqqatahu and waqatahu (lightened form). And it was recited: ﴿And when the messengers are appointed a time﴾ [al-Mursalat: 11] with the lightened form.

* * *

Know that Allah, the Exalted, clarified in this verse that the obligation of prayer is determined by specific times, except that Allah, the Exalted, summarized the mention of the times here and explained them in other verses, and they are five:

First: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Maintain with care the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. His saying "the prayers" (al-salawat) indicates the obligation of three prayers, and His saying "and the middle prayer" prevents it from being one of those three, otherwise there would be repetition. So it must be beyond the three, and it cannot be that the obligatory prayers are four, otherwise there would be no middle among them. So it is necessary to make them five so that a middle is obtained. Just as this verse indicates the obligation of five prayers, it also indicates the non-obligation of the witr (odd prayer), for otherwise the obligatory prayers would be six, and then there would be no middle. So this verse indicates that the obligatory prayers are five, although it does not indicate the explanation of their times.

Second: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night and the recitation of dawn﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. The obligatory prayers from the decline to the darkness are Dhuhr and 'Asr, the obligatory ones from the darkness to dawn are Maghrib and 'Isha', and the obligatory one at dawn is the Subh prayer. This verse gives the impression that Dhuhr and 'Asr have one time, and Maghrib and 'Isha' have one time.

Third: His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So exalt Allah when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17]. What is meant by it are the two prayers occurring at the two ends of the day, which are Maghrib and Subh. Then He said: ﴿And to Him is the praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you reach noon﴾ [al-Rum: 18]. His saying "in the late afternoon" (ashiyyan) means the prayer occurring in the depth of the night, which is the 'Isha' prayer. And His saying "when you reach noon" means the prayer occurring in the depth of the day, which is the Dhuhr prayer. Just as in His saying "when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning" He mentioned the night prayer before the day prayer, so likewise in His saying "in the late afternoon and when you reach noon" He mentioned the night prayer before the day prayer. Thus, four prayers are mentioned in this verse. As for the 'Asr prayer, Allah, the Exalted, singled it out by mention in His saying: "By the afternoon" [al-'Asr: 1], honoring it by singling it out for mention.

Fourth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the approaching portions of the night﴾ [Hud: 114]. His saying "the two ends of the day" indicates the obligation of the Subh prayer and the obligation of the 'Asr prayer, because they are like those occurring at the two ends, even though the Subh prayer occurs before the first end begins, and the 'Asr prayer occurs before the second end begins.

His saying "and in the approaching portions of the night" indicates the obligation of Maghrib and 'Isha'. Some of them used this verse as evidence for the obligation of the witr, saying: "Because zulaf is a plural, and its least number is three, so three prayers must be obligatory at night, in acting upon His saying: 'and in the approaching portions of the night.'"

Fifth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And exalt the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night exalt Him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. His saying "before the rising of the sun and before its setting" is an allusion to the Subh and 'Asr prayers, and it is like His saying: "And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the approaching portions of the night." His saying "and during the hours of the night" is an allusion to Maghrib and 'Isha', and it is like His saying: "and in the approaching portions of the night." Just as they argued with His saying "and in the approaching portions of the night," they likewise argued against it with His saying "and during the hours of the night," because His saying "hours of the night" (anaa' al-layl) is a plural whose least number is three. This is the collection of verses indicating the five times for the five prayers.

Know that the determination of the prayers by these five times is of the utmost beauty and perfection when considered rationally. Its explanation is that everything in the states of this world has five stages:

The first of them: the stage of coming into existence and entering into being, as a human is born and remains in growth and development for a known period. This period is called the age of growth and development.

The second stage: the period of standing, which is that the thing remains in the attribute of its perfection without increase or decrease. This period is called the age of youth.

The third stage: the period of maturity, which is that a hidden deficiency appears in the human. This period is called the age of maturity.

The fourth stage: the period of old age, which is that apparent and clear deficiencies appear in the human until he dies and perishes. This period is called the age of old age.

The fifth stage: that its traces remain for a period after its death, then ultimately those traces are erased, nullified, and vanish, and nothing of it remains in this world, no news and no trace. These five stages apply to all events of this world, whether it is a human or other animals or plants. And the sun, by its rising and setting, undergoes these five states, because it...

[Page 25]

When the sun rises from its place of rising, its condition resembles the condition of a newborn when it is born. Then its height continues to increase, its light grows stronger, and its heat intensifies, until it reaches the middle of the sky, where it stands still for a while. Then it descends, and hidden deficiencies appear in it until the time of ʿAṣr. Then from the time of ʿAṣr, manifest deficiencies appear in it, so its light weakens and its heat diminishes, and its decline and weakness increase until sunset. Then, when it sets, some traces of it remain on the horizon of the west, which is the twilight (al-shafaq). Then those traces vanish, and the sun becomes as though it had never existed in the world. So when these five states have occurred for it, and they are wondrous matters that none can bring about except Allah the Exalted, Allah the Exalted, without doubt, made prayer obligatory at each of these five states. So at the approach of the sun to rising, He made obligatory the Fajr prayer, in gratitude for the great blessing that results from the departure of that darkness and the arrival of light, and because of the departure of sleep, which is like death, and the arrival of wakefulness, which is like life. And when the sun reached the furthest point of elevation, and then the sign of decline appeared in it, He made obligatory the Ẓuhr prayer, in glorification of the Creator, who is able to turn the conditions of the heavenly and earthly bodies from one opposite to another, so He made the sun, after the furthest point of its height and exaltation, lowered from that loftiness, entering the age of middle years (al-kuhūla), which is the hidden deficiency. Then, when the period of middle years ended and it entered the beginning of the time of old age, He, the Exalted, made the ʿAṣr prayer obligatory.

And how excellent is what al-Shāfiʿī (raḥimahu Allāh) said: the beginning of ʿAṣr is when the shadow of each thing becomes twice its length. That is because from this time the manifest deficiencies appear. Do you not see that from the beginning of the time of Ẓuhr until the time of ʿAṣr, according to al-Shāfiʿī's view (raḥimahu Allāh), the shadow has only increased by the length of the object? Then, in a subtle moment, its shadow becomes twice its length. This indicates that from the time when an object's shadow becomes equal to it, the sun begins its manifest deficiencies. Then, when the sun sets, this state resembles what happens when a person dies. So without doubt, Allah the Exalted made the Maghrib prayer obligatory at this state. Then, when the twilight has set, it is as though the traces of the sun have been erased, and no news or trace of it remains in the world. So without doubt, Allah the Exalted made the ʿIshāʾ prayer obligatory. Thus it is established that the obligation of the five prayers at these five times accords with rational principles and wise foundations, and Allah knows best the secrets of His acts.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 104:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not falter in pursuing the people. If you are suffering pain, then indeed they suffer pain just as you suffer pain, and you hope from Allah for what they do not hope. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

Know that when Exalted is He mentioned some of the rulings that the fighter (mujahid) needs to know, He returned once more to urging jihad, and said: ﴿And do not falter﴾, meaning: do not weaken and do not be slack, ﴿in pursuing the people﴾, meaning: in seeking out the disbelievers with fighting. Then He presented the proof against them concerning this, saying: ﴿If you are suffering pain, then indeed they suffer pain just as you suffer pain.﴾ The meaning is: the occurrence of pain is a common element between you and them. Since the fear of pain did not prevent them from fighting you, how could it prevent you from fighting them? Then He elaborated on the proof and explained that the believers are more deserving of perseverance in fighting than the polytheists, because the believers affirm reward and punishment, resurrection and gathering, whereas the polytheists do not affirm these. So if they, despite their denial of resurrection and gathering, exert themselves in fighting, then you, O believers, who affirm that in this jihad there is a great reward for you and that in abandoning it there is a great punishment upon you, are more deserving of being diligent in this jihad. This is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you hope from Allah for what they do not hope﴾. It is also possible that what is meant by this hope is what Allah promised them in His saying: ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [At-Tawbah: 33], and in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for those of the believers who follow you﴾ [Al-Anfal: 64].

There is also a third aspect, which is that you worship the God who is All-Knowing, All-Powerful, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, so it is valid for you to hope for His reward. As for the polytheists, they worship idols, which are inanimate objects, so it is not valid for them to hope for reward from those idols or to fear punishment from them.

Al-A'raj recited: (an takūnū ta'lamūn) with a fatḥah on the hamzah, meaning: "do not falter because you are suffering pain," and His saying ﴿then indeed they suffer pain just as you suffer pain﴾ is a reason (ta'līl) given.

* * *
