The second: If it occurred by God's creation, the servant would not deserve any recompense for it at all, and that is false, because the verse indicates that the servant deserves recompense for his deed. Know that the discussion of this kind of argument is repeated in this book.

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿ولا يَجِدْ لَهُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ ولِيًّا ولا نَصِيرًا﴾ .
قالَتِ المُعْتَزِلَةُ: دَلَّتِ الآيَةُ عَلى نَفْيِ الشَّفاعَةِ، والجَوابُ مِن وجْهَيْنِ:

(And he will not find for himself, besides God, any protector or helper.)
Then God, exalted is He, said: "And he will not find for himself, besides God, any protector or helper." The Mu'tazilites said: The verse indicates the negation of intercession. The answer is in two respects:

الأوَّلُ: أنّا قُلْنا إنَّ هَذِهِ الآيَةَ في حَقِّ الكُفّارِ.

The first: We have said that this verse concerns the unbelievers.

والثّانِي: أنَّ شَفاعَةَ الأنْبِياءِ والمَلائِكَةِ في حَقِّ العُصاةِ إنَّما تَكُونُ بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، وإذا كانَ كَذَلِكَ فَلا ولِيَّ لِأحَدٍ ولا نَصِيرَ لِأحَدٍ إلّا اللَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى.

The second: The intercession of the prophets and angels on behalf of the disobedient occurs only by God's permission, exalted is He. Since this is so, there is no protector for anyone and no helper for anyone except God, glorified and exalted is He.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer—those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged even by the size of a naqir.﴾

Masruq said: When the verse "Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it" ﴿4:123﴾ was revealed, the People of the Book said to the Muslims: "We and you are equal." So this verse was revealed down to His words: ﴿And who is better in religion?﴾ There are several issues in it:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim, recited "yudkhalūna al-jannata" (they are made to enter Paradise) with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a fatḥah on the khāʾ, in the passive voice (mā lam yusammi fāʿiluh), and likewise in Surat Maryam and in Ḥā Mīm al-Mu’min. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the khāʾ in all these surahs, taking the entering as attributed to them (the active). Both are acceptable, but the first is better, because it is more majestic, and it points to a rewarder who caused them to enter Paradise, and it accords with ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾.

As for the second reading, it corresponds to His words: ﴿Enter Paradise, you and your spouses﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 70], and to His words: ﴿Enter it in peace﴾ [al-Hijr: 46]. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: They said: The distinction between the first and second "man" is that the first is partitive (li-l-tabʿīḍ), and the meaning is: whoever does some of the righteous deeds, since no one can do all of the righteous deeds. Rather, the meaning is that if he does some of them while being a believer, he deserves the reward.

Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs that the perpetrator of a major sin does not remain eternally in the Fire, but is transferred to Paradise. This is because we have shown that the perpetrator of a major sin is a believer. Given this, we say: if the perpetrator of a major sin has prayed, fasted, performed Hajj, and paid zakat, then by the ruling of this verse he must enter Paradise, and by the ruling of the verses indicating the threat against wrongdoers he must enter the Fire. As for entering Paradise and then being transferred to the Fire, that is invalid by consensus; or entering the Fire and then being transferred to Paradise—that is the truth from which there is no escape. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: The naqir is a small pit on the back of the date-pit from which the palm tree sprouts; the meaning is that they will not be diminished even by the measure of the place where the date-pit sprouts.

If it is said: How did Allah specify the righteous as those who will not be wronged, when others are likewise, as He said: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], and He said: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 108]?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: that the pronoun in His words ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ refers to the doers of evil and the doers of righteous deeds together.

The second: that whatever does not fall short of the reward is, by not increasing the punishment, more fitting. This is the ruling among created beings, so Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this ruling in accordance with what is customary among people.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, made the attainment of salvation and success in Paradise conditional upon a person being a believer, He explained faith and clarified its excellence in two respects:

The first: that it is the religion which includes the manifestation of perfect servitude, humility, and submission to Allah, may He be exalted.

The second: that it is the religion upon which Abraham, peace be upon him, was, and each of these two aspects is an independent reason for encouraging the religion of Islam.

As for the first aspect: know that the religion of Islam is built upon two matters: belief (i'tiqad) and action ('amal). As for belief, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿submits himself﴾; this is because Islam is submission and humility. The face is the most excellent of a person's organs, so when a person knows his Lord with his heart and affirms His lordship and his own servanthood, he has submitted his face to Allah. As for action, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿while being a doer of good﴾, and it includes doing good deeds and abandoning evil deeds. So reflect upon this concise expression and how it contains all the aims and purposes. Also, His saying: ﴿submits himself to Allah﴾ conveys restriction (hasr), meaning: he submitted himself to Allah and did not submit to anyone other than Allah. This is an alert that the perfection of faith is not attained except when all affairs are entrusted to the Creator and one shows disavowal of power and strength. Also, in it there is an alert to the corruption of the method of one who seeks help from other than Allah. The polytheists used to seek help from idols and say: "These are our intercessors with Allah." The Dahriyya and the naturalists seek help from the spheres, the stars, the natures, and others. The Jews used to say, to ward off the punishment of the Hereafter from themselves: "We are the descendants of the prophets." The Christians used to say: "the third of three." So all the sects have sought help from other than Allah.

As for the Mu'tazila, in reality their faces have not submitted to Allah, because they hold that the obedience which necessitates their reward is from themselves, and the disobedience which necessitates their punishment is from themselves; so in reality they hope only in themselves and fear only themselves. As for the People of the Sunnah, who entrusted the management, the bringing into being, the origination, and the creation to the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, and who believed that there is no originator and no effector except Allah, they are the ones who submitted their faces to Allah, relied entirely upon the grace of Allah, and their gaze was cut off from everything other than Allah.

Page 46
As for the second aspect in demonstrating the virtue of Islam: it is that Muhammad, peace be upon him, called people only to the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him. It is well known among all people that Abraham, peace be upon him, did not call except to Allah, may He be exalted, as he said: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you associate﴾ [al-An'am: 78]. He did not call to the worship of a sphere, nor to the obedience of a star, nor to prostration to an idol, nor to seeking help from a nature; rather his religion was the call to Allah and turning away from everything other than Allah. The call of Muhammad, peace be upon him, was close to the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, in circumcision, and in the acts related to the Ka'bah: such as praying toward it, circumambulating it, the sa'y, the stoning, the standing (at 'Arafat), the shaving of the head, and the ten words mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. Since it is established that the law of Muhammad, peace be upon him, was close to the law of Abraham, and the law of Abraham is accepted by all, this is because the Arabs take no pride in anything as they take pride in being connected to Abraham; as for the Jews and Christians, there is no doubt that they also take pride in him. If this is established, it necessarily follows that the law of Muhammad is accepted by all.
* * *
As for His saying: ﴿hanifan﴾, there are two discussions:
The first: it is permissible that it be a circumstantial state (hal) of the one followed, and that it be a state of the follower, as when you say: "I saw a rider," for it is permissible that the rider be a state of the one seen and of the seer.

The second discussion: the hanif is the one who inclines, and its meaning is that he inclines away from all religions, because whatever is other than it is false; and the truth is that he inclines away from every outward and inward thing. The realization of the matter is this: falsehood, though it is far from the falsehood opposed to it, may be close to the falsehood similar to it; but as for truth, it is one, so it inclines away from everything other than it, like the center which is at the utmost distance from all parts of the circle.

If it is said: the apparent meaning of this verse requires that the law of Muhammad, peace be upon him, be identical with the law of Abraham, and on this basis Muhammad, peace be upon him, would not be the bearer of an independent law, and you do not say this.

We reply: it is permissible that the religion of Abraham is included within the religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him, while this religion includes beautiful additions and noble benefits.

* * *
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾, and in it there are issues:
The first issue: concerning the connection of this verse with what precedes it, and in it there are two views:

The first: when Abraham, peace be upon him, reached such height of rank in religion that Allah took him as an intimate friend, he was worthy that his character and his way be followed.

The second: when He mentioned the religion of Abraham and described him as hanif, then He said after it: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾, this indicates that He, glorified is He, only took him as a friend because he was knowledgeable of that law and performing those obligations. Confirming this is His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them, He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. This indicates that He, glorified is He, only made him an imam for creation because he fulfilled those words.

Having established this, we say: since the verse indicates that Abraham, peace be upon him, attained this lofty station, namely being an intimate friend of Allah, the Exalted, by reason of his acting upon that law, this is an alert that whoever acts upon this law must attain the greatest of stations in religion, and this conveys a great encouragement toward this religion.

If it is said: what is the position of His saying: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾?
We reply: this sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyya) with no place in terms of i'rab, and its parallel is what came in poetry, such as the saying:

"and calamities are many"

A parenthetical clause by its nature serves to emphasize that statement, and the matter here is so, as we have explained.

The second issue: they mentioned several views concerning the derivation of khalil:

The first: the khalil of a person is the one who enters into the interior of his affairs and secrets, and whose love has entered into the inner parts of his heart; and there is no doubt that this is the utmost degree of love.

It has been said: when Allah made Abraham, peace be upon him, see the higher and lower kingdom, and he called the people time after time to the oneness of Allah, and prevented them from worshipping the star, the moon, and the sun, and prevented them from worshipping idols; then he surrendered himself to the fires, his son to sacrifice, and his wealth to guests, Allah made him an imam for creation and a messenger to them, and gave him the good news that kingship and prophethood would be in his offspring. For these distinctions He named him khalil, because Allah's love for His servant is an expression of His will to bring goodness and benefits to him.

The second view on the derivation of the name Khalil: that he is the one who agrees with you in your characteristics. I say: it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Take on the character of Allah." It seems that when Abraham, peace be upon him, reached in this domain a degree that no one among those before him had reached, Allah therefore specially honored him with this distinction.

The third view: the author of al-Kashshaf said: the khalil is the one who walks along with you on your path, from al-khall, which is the path in the sand; and this view is close to the second view, or it may be understood as his great obedience to Allah and his not rebelling, outwardly or inwardly, against the judgment of Allah, as Allah informed about him by His saying: ﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit, he said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131].

The fourth view: the khalil is the one who fills your gap as you fill his gap; and this view is weak, because when Abraham, peace be upon him, was a khalil with Allah, it was impossible to say that he fills the gap; and from here we know that khalil cannot be explained in that way.

As for the commentators, they mentioned several views on the occasion of revelation of this title:

The first: when the sand that his servants brought became fine flour, his wife said: "This is from your Egyptian khalil," and Abraham said: "Rather, it is from my khalil, Allah."

The second: Shahr ibn Hawshab said: an angel descended in the form of a man and mentioned the name of Allah with a sweet, moving voice. Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "Mention it once more." He said: "I will not mention it for nothing." He said: "All my wealth is yours." So the angel mentioned it with a voice more moving than the first. He said: "Mention it a third time and you may have my children." The angel said: "Rejoice, for I am an angel who has no need of your wealth or your child; the purpose was only to test you." When he offered wealth and children for hearing the mention of Allah, Allah therefore took him as khalil.

The third: Tawus narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when Gabriel and the angels entered upon Abraham in the form of handsome young men, and the Khalil thought they were his guests, he slaughtered a fat calf for them and brought it near them, and said: "Eat, on condition that you mention the name of Allah at its beginning and praise Him at its end." Gabriel said: "You are the khalil of Allah," and this description was revealed. I say: in this there is, in my view, another aspect: when the essence of the soul is luminous, radiant, lofty, and little attached to bodily pleasures and corporeal states, and then to such a noble, sacred essence are added deeds which increase its polish from bodily impurities, and thoughts which increase its illumination with sacred knowledge

Page 48
and divine manifestations, such a person becomes deeply immersed in the world of holiness and purity, detached from the ties of body and sense. Then this person continues to increase in these noble states until he becomes such that he sees none but Allah, hears none but Allah, moves only by Allah, rests only by Allah, and walks only by Allah. It is as if the light of the majesty of Allah has spread through all his bodily powers, permeated them, penetrated their substances, and reached into their essences. Such a person is truly described as a khalil, because the love of Allah has permeated all his powers. To this points the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in his supplication: "O Allah, place light in my heart, light in my hearing, light in my sight, and light in my nerves."

The third issue: some Christians said: since the name khalil may be applied to a specific person as an honor and distinction, why may the name "son" not be applied to Jesus, peace be upon him, as an honor and distinction?

Its answer: the difference is that being a khalil is an expression of excessive love, and that does not imply kinship; whereas "son" implies kinship, and God is exalted above the sharing of nature with contingent beings and resemblance to created things.

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾. And in this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the connection of this verse with what precedes it, and in this there are several aspects:

The first: the meaning is that God did not take Abraham as a khalil (intimate friend) because of any need he had of him in some matter, as is the friendship of human beings. And how could that be conceived when to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? Since this is so, how could it be conceived that He would be in need of a feeble human being? Rather, He took him as a khalil purely by grace, benevolence and generosity; and because he was sincere in servitude, God singled him out for this honour. The point is that his being a khalil might suggest kinship of kind, so He, glorified is He, removed the notion of similarity and resemblance by this statement.

The second: God, Exalted is He, mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to this place many kinds of command, prohibition, promise and threat. So here He makes clear that He is the God of the originated things and the Originator of existent beings and possible beings, and whoever is like this is a king to be obeyed. Therefore it is obligatory upon every intelligent person to submit to His obligations and to yield to His command and prohibition.

The third: since God, Exalted is He, mentioned the promise and the threat, and these cannot be fulfilled except when two things are present:

One of them: complete power, related to all existent and possible beings.

The second: complete knowledge, related to all particulars and universals, so that the obedient and the disobedient, the good-doer and the evildoer, are not confused for Him. So He indicated the perfection of His power by His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and the perfection of His knowledge by His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾.

The fourth: since He, glorified is He, described Abraham as His khalil, He made clear that, together with this intimate friendship, he is a servant of Him; this is because to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. This runs parallel to His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93], and to His saying: ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels who are near [to Him]﴾ [an-Nisa': 172]. That is: the angels, with their perfection in the attribute of power and strength and in the attribute of knowledge and wisdom, when they did not disdain the servitude of Allah, how could the Messiah, with the weakness of his humanity, disdain the servitude of Allah?! Likewise here: that is, if everyone in the heavens and the earth is His dominion through His subjugation and the executing of His divinity, how could it be conceived that God's taking Abraham, peace be upon him, as a khalil would take him out of the servitude of God?! All these aspects are good and harmonious.

The second issue: He said: ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ and did not say "who" (man), because He took the sense of kind, and what is rational, when mentioned and meant as a kind, is mentioned with "ma" (what).

Page 49
The third issue: His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾ has two aspects:
One of them: what is meant by it is encompassing in knowledge.

The second: what is meant by it is encompassing in power, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and others you were not able to attain, which Allah has already encompassed﴾ [al-Fath: 21]. Those who hold this view say: One may not object that since His saying ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ indicates the perfection of power, then if we took His saying ﴿and Allah is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾ to mean the perfection of power, repetition would follow. This is because we say: His saying ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in its apparent meaning, indicates only that He, exalted is He, is powerful and owner of all that is in the heavens and the earth, and does not indicate that He is powerful over what would be outside them and other than them. So when He said ﴿and Allah is ever, of all things, encompassing﴾, it indicates that He is powerful over an infinity of possible objects outside these heavens and earth; and further, the chain of decree and destiny in all existent and possible beings ends only with His bringing into existence, His creating and His originating. This is the exposition of this view. However, the first view is better, because we have explained that divinity and the fulfilment of promise and threat occur and are perfected only through the combination of power and knowledge; so it is necessary to mention both together. He mentioned power before knowledge because it is established in the science of the foundations (usul al-din, theology) that knowledge of God is knowledge of His being powerful, and then after knowing that He is powerful, His being knowing is known, since the act, by its origination, indicates power, and by the firmness and perfection in it indicates knowledge. And there is no doubt that the former is prior to the latter.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 4, Verse 127**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry, and concerning the weak among the children, and that you should stand up for orphans with justice. Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it."﴾

Know that Allah's custom in arranging this Noble Book is set in the best of ways. He mentions some rulings, then right after them He mentions many verses of promise, encouragement and warning, and mixes with them verses that indicate the majesty of Allah, the greatness of His power and the magnitude of His divinity. Then He returns once more to explaining the rulings. This is the best kind of arrangement and the closest to affecting hearts, because the imposition of difficult deeds is not received with acceptance unless it is coupled with promise and threat, and promise and threat do not affect the heart unless there is certainty of the utmost perfection of the one from whom the promise and threat proceed. So it becomes clear that this arrangement is the best of arrangements suited to calling to the true religion.

Having understood this, we say: He, glorified is He, mentioned at the beginning of this surah many kinds of laws and obligations. Then He followed them with a description of the states of the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and went into it at length. Then He concluded those verses that indicate the greatness of Allah's majesty and the perfection of His grandeur. Then after that He returned to explaining the rulings, saying: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

[p. 50]

**First issue:** Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *al-istiftā'* (seeking a fatwa, i.e., a legal opinion) is requesting a fatwa. It is said: "I asked the man about the matter (*istaftaytu*) and he gave me a fatwa (*afatani ifta'an*), and *futyā* and *fatwā*." These are two nouns placed in the position of *al-ifta'* (giving a fatwa). It is also said: "I interpreted (*aftaytu*) for so-and-so a dream he saw," if I interpreted it. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Joseph, O man of truth, give us an interpretation concerning seven fat cows﴾ [Yusuf: 46]. The meaning of *al-ifta'* is the manifestation of what is unclear, and its root is from *al-fata*, which is the young man who has grown strong and matured. So the meaning is: it is as if he gains strength through his explanation of what was unclear, and becomes strong and vigorous.

**Second issue:** Scholars mentioned two opinions regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse:

The first: The Arabs did not give women or children any share of inheritance, as we mentioned at the beginning of this surah. So this verse was revealed concerning giving them inheritance.

The second: The verse was revealed concerning paying the dowry to them. An orphan girl would be under a man's guardianship; if she was beautiful and had wealth, he would marry her and consume her wealth; and if she was plain, he would prevent her from marrying others until she died, so that he could inherit from her. Then Allah revealed this verse.

**Third issue:** Know that *al-istiftā'* does not occur about the essence of women, but about a condition of theirs and an attribute of theirs. That condition is not mentioned in the verse, so it was general, not indicating the matter about which the asking occurred.

As for His saying, ﴿and what is recited to you﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: It is in the nominative case by being the subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence), and the implied meaning is: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited in the Book also gives you a ruling concerning them." That which is recited in the Book is His saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾ [al-Nisa': 3].

The summary of the speech is this: they had asked about many conditions of women. Whatever of these had a ruling that was not clarified, He mentioned that Allah gives them a ruling about it. And whatever of them had a ruling clarified in the preceding verses, He mentioned that those recited verses give them a ruling about it. He made the indication of the Book regarding this ruling a giving of a fatwa from the Book. Do you not see that it is said in the well-known figurative usage: "The Book of Allah has clarified this ruling for us"? And just as this is permissible, it is also permissible to say: "The Book of Allah gave a fatwa with such-and-such."

The second opinion: His saying ﴿and what is recited to you﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿in the Book﴾ is its predicate (*khabar*), and this is a parenthetical clause (*jumlah mu'taridah*). The intended meaning of "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). The purpose of this is to magnify the status of this verse that is recited to them, and that justice and fairness regarding the rights of orphans is among the great matters with Allah, the Exalted, which must be observed and safeguarded, and whoever neglects them is a wrongdoer who disregards what Allah has magnified. Its parallel in the magnification of the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4].

The third opinion: It is in the genitive case by being an oath, as if it were said: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and I swear by what is recited to you in the Book." An oath is also for the purpose of magnification.

The fourth opinion: It is conjoined (*'atf*) to the genitive noun in His saying "concerning them" (*fihinna*), and the meaning is: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them and concerning what is recited to you in the Book regarding the orphan women." Al-Zajjaj said: This view is very far-fetched, considering both the wording and the meaning. As for the wording, it requires conjoining an explicit noun to a pronoun, and that is not permissible, as we explained in His saying: ﴿...by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ [al-Nisa': 1]. As for the meaning, this view requires that He, the Exalted, gave a fatwa on those matters and also gives a fatwa about what is recited from the Book, and it is known that this is not what is intended. What is intended is that He, the Exalted, gives a fatwa about the matters they asked about.

Two questions remain here:

**First question:** With what is His saying ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ connected?

[p. 51]

We say: In the first opinion, it is a complement (*silah*, the clause completing) of "is recited" (*yutla*), i.e., "is recited to you concerning their meaning." As for the other opinions, it is an apposition (*badal*) to "concerning them" (*fihinna*).

**Second question:** What is the annexation (*idafah*) in ﴿the orphan women﴾?

Answer: The Kufans said: its meaning is "concerning the women who are orphans," so the attribute has been annexed to the noun, as you say: "the day of Friday" and "the truth of certainty." The Basrans said: annexing an attribute to a noun is not permissible, so one does not say "I passed by the rising (*ṭāli'ah*) of the sun." This is because the attribute and the described thing are one thing, and annexing a thing to itself is impossible. This reasoning is weak, because the described thing may remain without the attribute, and that shows that the described thing is other than the attribute. Then the Basrans built upon this view and said: the women in the verse are other than the orphans, and the intended "women" are the mothers of the orphans, to whom their orphan children were annexed. This is supported by the fact that the verse was revealed about the story of Umm Kuhhah, who had orphans.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means what was made obligatory for them of inheritance. This is according to the one who says the verse was revealed about the inheritance of orphans and young children. According to the rest, the intended meaning of His saying ﴿what is prescribed for them﴾ is the dowry (*sadaq*).

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and whom you desire to marry﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: This may carry the meaning of desire or of aversion. If you take it as desire, the meaning is: "and you desire to marry them." If you take it as aversion, the meaning is: "and you turn away from marrying them because of their plainness." The companions of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, used this verse as evidence that it is permissible for someone other than the father or the paternal grandfather to marry off a young girl. There is no proof for them in it, because it is possible that the intended meaning is: "and you desire to marry them once they reach maturity." The evidence for the correctness of our position is that Qudamah ibn Maz'un married the daughter of his brother 'Uthman ibn Maz'un to 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. Then al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah proposed to her and encouraged her mother regarding the wealth. They came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Qudamah said: "I am her paternal uncle and the executor of her father's will." The Prophet ﷺ said: "She is young, and she is not to be married except with her permission," and he separated her from Ibn 'Umar. Moreover, the verse contains no more than mention of the guardians' desire to marry the orphan girl, and that does not indicate permissibility.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and the weak among the children﴾. It is in the genitive case, conjoined to "the orphan women." In the pre-Islamic period they did not give inheritance to children or to women, but only to the men who had reached the capacity to bear great affairs, to the exclusion of children and women.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and that you should stand up for orphans with justice﴾. It is in the genitive case, conjoined to "the weak." The sense of the verse is: "What is recited to you in the Book gives you a ruling concerning the orphan women, and concerning the weak, and concerning your standing up for orphans with justice." ﴿Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾: He will reward you for it, and nothing of it is lost with Allah.

[Page 52]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment or aversion from her husband, there is no blame upon them if they make a settlement between themselves; and settlement is better. And souls are made to be prone to stinginess. And if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾

Know that this is among the matters about which Allah the Exalted informed that He gives them a ruling concerning women, which had not been mentioned earlier in this surah. It contains several issues.

**First issue:** Some have said that this verse resembles His saying: ﴿And if anyone of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 6), and His saying: ﴿And if two groups among the believers fight, then make settlement between them﴾ (Al-Hujurat: 9). Here, the word ﴿imra'ah﴾ (a woman) is in the nominative case because of a verb implied by the verb that explains it, ﴿fear﴾ (khafat). The same applies to all the verses we have recited. And Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** Some have said: "khafat" means "knew." Others said it means "thought." Both of these are abandoning the apparent meaning without need. Rather, what is meant is fear itself. However, fear only arises when the signs indicating the occurrence of the fear appear. Those signs here are that a man says to his wife: "You are ugly," or "You are old, and I want to marry a young, beautiful woman." The word *ba'l* means husband. Originally, *ba'l* means master, and then the husband was called by it because he is like a master to the wife. Its plural is *bu'ulah*. This was discussed earlier in Surah al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 228). *Nushuz* can come from either spouse, and it is the aversion of each of them to the other. Its derivation is from *nashaz*, which means what is raised above the ground. The *nushuz* of a man towards a woman is that he turns away from her, frowns at her face, abandons intercourse with her, and treats her badly in companionship.

**Third issue:** The commentators mentioned several reasons for the revelation of the verse:

First: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning Ibn Abi al-Sa'ib. He had a wife and children by her, and she was old. He intended to divorce her, so she said: "Do not divorce me, and leave me to attend to the affairs of my children, and divide the nights for me each month as few nights." The husband said: "If it is so, then that is better for me."

Second: It was revealed concerning the story of Sawdah bint Zam'ah. The Prophet, may peace and blessings be upon him, intended to divorce her, so she requested that he keep her and give her turn to 'A'ishah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, permitted that, and did not divorce her.

Third: It is narrated from 'A'ishah that she said: "It was revealed concerning a woman who is with a man, and the man wants to exchange her for another. She says: 'Keep me and marry someone else, and you are free from the obligation of maintenance and equal division.'"

**Fourth issue:** His saying ﴿nushuzan aw i'radan﴾ (ill-treatment or aversion). By *nushuz* is meant showing harshness in speech, or action, or both. By *i'rad* is meant silence regarding good and evil, lack of kindness, and harm. This is because such aversion strongly indicates estrangement and dislike.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they make a settlement between themselves﴾, and in this there are issues:

**First issue:** The Qur'anic reciters Ibn 'Amir... (Ascribed reading detail follows.) 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿yuslihā﴾ with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *lam*, with the *alif* removed, from *al-islah* (reconciliation). The rest recited *yaṣṣālaḥā* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *sad*, with an *alif* between the *sad* and the *lam*, and with the *sad* shaddah, from *al-taṣāluh* (mutual reconciliation). *Yaṣṣālaḥā* originally is *yataṣālaḥā*. The *ta'* was made silent and merged into the *sad*. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿when they will all be overtaken therein (*idda'arakū*)﴾ (Al-A'raf: 38). Its original form is *tadārakū*. The *ta'* was made silent and replaced by the *dal* because of the closeness of their articulation points, and merged into the *dal*. Then a hamzah was added for beginning with it, so it became *iddārakū*.

[Page 53]

Having known this, we say: whoever recited ﴿yuslihā﴾, the reason is that *islah* is used for reconciliation during dispute and quarrel. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever fears injustice or sin from a testator and makes reconciliation between them﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 182), and He said: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾ (An-Nisa': 114). Whoever recited *yaṣṣālaḥā*, which is the preferred reading of most scholars, said: the meaning of *an yaṣṣālaḥā* is that they agree with each other, and this fits this context better. In the reading of 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is: ﴿there is no blame upon them that they reconciled (ṣālaḥā)﴾. In this reading, *ṣulḥan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun. The original would have been to say *taṣālaḥā*, but it came like His saying: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ (Nuh: 17), and His saying: ﴿and devote yourself to Him with devotion﴾ (Al-Muzzammil: 8), and the saying of the poet:

*"And after your gift of a hundred camels in succession."*

**Second issue:** Settlement only occurs regarding something that is a right for the wife. A woman's rights against her husband are: the dower, or maintenance, or equal division. These three are what a woman is able to demand from her husband, whether he wills or not. As for intercourse, it is not like that, because the husband cannot be compelled to have intercourse.

Having known this, we say: this settlement refers to when the woman gives up all or part of her dower to the husband, or waives his obligation of maintenance, or waives equal division, and her purpose in this is that her husband not divorce her. If the reconciliation is made on that basis, it is permissible.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and settlement is better﴾, and in this there are issues:

**First issue:** *Al-sulh* (settlement) is a singular noun to which the definite article has been added. Does a singular noun with the definite article indicate generality or not? What we have supported in the principles of jurisprudence is that it does not indicate generality, and we mentioned many proofs for it.

If we say that it does indicate generality, then here there is a discussion: when there is a known prior referent, is it better to interpret it as general or as referring to the prior known item? The more correct view is that interpreting it as referring to the prior known item is better. This is because we only interpret it as encompassing all cases out of necessity; if we did not say that, it would become ambiguous and lose its meaning. When there is a known prior referent, this difficulty is removed, so it is obligatory to interpret it that way.

Having known this premise, we say: some people interpreted His saying ﴿and settlement is better﴾ as encompassing all cases, and some interpreted it as referring to the prior known item, meaning: settlement between the spouses is better than separation. The first group relied on it for the issue that settlement by denial is permissible, as is the view of Abu Hanifah. As for us, we have made clear that interpreting this expression as referring to the prior known item is better, so their argument is refuted. And Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: this clause is a parenthetical insertion, and so is His saying ﴿and souls are made to be prone to stinginess﴾. However, it is a parenthetical insertion that emphasizes the intended meaning, so the purpose is achieved.

**Third issue:** He first mentioned His saying ﴿so there is no blame upon them if they make settlement﴾. His saying ﴿there is no blame﴾ may suggest that it is a concession, and the aim in it is the removal of sin. So Allah the Exalted explained that just as there is no blame or sin in this settlement, it also contains great good and abundant benefit, for if they reconcile on something, that is better than that they separate or persist in ill-treatment and aversion. As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿and souls are made to be prone to stinginess﴾:

Know that *shuhh* is stinginess, and what is meant is that stinginess is treated as something close to the souls and inherent to them, meaning that souls are naturally inclined to stinginess. Then it may be that what is meant is that the woman is stingy in giving up her share and her right. It may also be that what is meant is that the husband is stingy in spending his life with her despite the ugliness of her face, the advanced age of her body, and the absence of pleasure in her company.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you do good and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, and in this there are several possibilities:

**First:** It is addressed to the husbands, meaning: if you do good by remaining with your wives even if you dislike them, and you are certain of ill-treatment and aversion, and what leads to harm and dispute, then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do of kindness and piety, Acquainted, and He will reward you for it.

**Second:** It is addressed to the husband and the wife, meaning: if each of you does good to the other and avoids wrongdoing.

**Third:** It is addressed to others than them, meaning: if you do good in reconciling between them, and you guard against leaning towards one of them.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* related that 'Imran ibn Hittan al-Khariji was one of the ugliest of the children of Adam, and his wife was one of the most beautiful of them. One day she looked at him and then said: "Praise be to Allah." He said: "What is wrong with you?" She said: "I praised Allah that I and you are among the people of Paradise, because you were given a wife like me and you gave thanks, and I was given a husband like you and I was patient, and Allah has promised Paradise to His servants who are grateful and His servants who are patient."

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: This indicates that the obligation to do what is beyond one's capacity (taklif ma la yutaq) is neither occurring nor permissible to occur. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 132–134:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We had instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and [now] you, to fear Allah. But if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others. And ever is Allah, over that, Competent.﴾ ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing.﴾

Page 56

There are two views on the connection of this verse with what precedes it:

The first: When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He enriches each of them from His bounty, and that He is All-Encompassing, He pointed to something that is like an explanation of His being All-Encompassing, saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning: whoever is like this must necessarily be vast in power, knowledge, generosity, grace and mercy.

The second: When He, exalted is He, commanded justice and kindness toward orphans and the needy, He made clear that He did not command these things out of need for the deeds of His servants, for how could it be conceived that the Owner of the heavens and the earth is in need of human action, given the weakness and deficiency that man has? Rather, He commanded them out of regard for what is best for them in their worldly life and their Hereafter.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and [now] you, to fear Allah﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: The meaning of the verse is that the command to fear Allah is a general law for all nations, which has not been subject to abrogation (naskh) or alteration, but is rather the injunction of Allah for the first and the last.

The second issue: His saying ﴿min qablikum﴾ (from before you) has two views:

The first: It is connected to "wassaynā" (We instructed), meaning: And We had instructed those before you who were given the Scripture.

The second: It is connected to "ūtū" (were given), meaning: Those who were given the Scripture before you, We instructed them with that. His saying "wa-iyyākum" (and [now] you) is in conjunction with ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾. Al-Kitāb (the Scripture) is a generic noun encompassing the heavenly books, and what is meant is the Jews and the Christians.

The third issue: His saying ﴿an-ittaqū Allāh﴾ (to fear Allah) is like your saying: "I ordered you to good." Al-Kisā'ī said: It is said, "I instructed you to do such-and-such" and "to do such-and-such" [both forms], and it is said, "Did I not order you to go to Zayd," and "to go to Zayd" [both forms]. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿I have been commanded to be the first to submit﴾ [al-An'am: 14], and He said: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city﴾ [an-Naml: 91].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾. His saying ﴿wa-in takfurū﴾ (but if you deny) is a conjunction with His saying ﴿fear Allah﴾, and the meaning is: We commanded them and commanded you to piety, and We said to them and to you: if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: He, exalted is He, is their Creator and Owner, and the Bestower upon them of all kinds of blessings, so it is the right of every rational being to be submissive to His commands and prohibitions, hoping for His reward and fearing His punishment.

The second: Even if you deny, to Allah belongs whatever is in His heavens and whatever is in His earth of all kinds of creatures, among them those who worship Him and fear Him; and He is, with that, free of need of their creation and of their worship, and deserving of being praised for the abundance of His blessings. Even if none of them praises Him, He is praiseworthy in His essence, whether they praise Him or do not.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

If it is said: What is the benefit of repeating His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾?

We say: He, exalted is He, mentioned these words in this verse three times, to establish three matters:

The first of them: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His bounty﴾, and what is meant by it is His being bountiful and generous. So He mentioned after it His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and the purpose is to establish that He is vast in generosity and munificence.

The second: He said: ﴿But if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and what is meant by it is that He, exalted is He, is exempt from the obedience of the obedient and from the sins of the sinners, so His majesty does not increase through acts of obedience nor decrease through sins and misdeeds. So after it He mentioned His saying ﴿for indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

Page 57

The purpose of it is to establish that He is free of need of all in Himself.

The third: He said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others. And ever is Allah, over that, Competent.﴾ What is meant by it is that He, exalted is He, is capable of annihilation and creation: if you disobey Him, He is capable of destroying you entirely and annihilating you, and of bringing into being another people who will occupy themselves with His worship and glorification. So the purpose here is to establish that He, glorified and exalted is He, is capable of all things that are capable of being done. When a single proof indicates many things signified, it is good to mention that proof so that it may be used to demonstrate one of those things; then one mentions it a second time so that it may be used to demonstrate the second, and then a third time so that it may be used to demonstrate the third.

This repetition is better and more fitting than relying on mentioning the proof only once, because when the proof is mentioned again, what necessitates knowledge of the thing signified comes to mind, so the knowledge attained of that signified thing becomes stronger and clearer. Thus it becomes clear that this repetition is of the utmost beauty and perfection.

Also, when you repeat it three times, and on each occasion you derive from it the affirmation of another attribute of the majesty of Allah, the mind is alerted, because the creation of the heavens and the earth indicates noble secrets and sublime objectives. At that point a person strives to reflect upon them and to derive from their states and attributes the attributes of the Creator, glorified and exalted is He. And since the overall purpose of this Noble Book is to turn minds and understandings away from preoccupation with other than Allah toward total immersion in the knowledge of Allah, and this repetition serves to achieve and reinforce this aim, it is therefore of the utmost beauty and perfection.

His saying ﴿and ever is Allah, over that, Competent﴾ means: He, exalted is He, has always been and will always be described as capable of all things that are capable of being done. For if His power over things were newly originated, the origination of that power would require another power, and an infinite regress would follow.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The meaning is: those who desire by their striving only the spoils are mistaken; for with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. Why then would one suffice with seeking the reward of this world, when it is as nothing compared to the reward of the Hereafter? If he were rational, he would seek the reward of the Hereafter, so that he would obtain it, and the reward of this world would come to him as a consequence?

If it is said: How did the "fa" (then) enter the response of the conditional, when with Him, exalted is He, is the reward of this world and the Hereafter, whether this desire occurs or not?

We say: The sense of the statement is: with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter for him, if Allah, exalted is He, wills it; and on this assumption the consequent is linked to the condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing﴾, meaning: He hears their speech, that they seek from jihad nothing but the spoils, and He sees that they do not strive in jihad nor exert themselves in it except when expecting to win the spoils. This is like a rebuke from Him, exalted is He, to them concerning these deeds.

So the purpose here is to establish that He, glorified and exalted is He, is capable of all things that are capable of being done. When a single proof indicates many things signified, it is good to mention that proof so that it may be used to demonstrate one of those things; then one mentions it a second time so that it may be used to demonstrate the second, and then a third time so that it may be used to demonstrate the third.

This repetition is better and more fitting than relying on mentioning the proof only once, because when the proof is mentioned again, what necessitates knowledge of the thing signified comes to mind, so the knowledge attained of that signified thing becomes stronger and clearer. Thus it becomes clear that this repetition is of the utmost beauty and perfection.

Also, when you repeat it three times, and on each occasion you derive from it the affirmation of another attribute of the majesty of Allah, the mind is alerted, because the creation of the heavens and the earth indicates noble secrets and sublime objectives. At that point a person strives to reflect upon them and to derive from their states and attributes the attributes of the Creator, glorified and exalted is He. And since the overall purpose of this Noble Book is to turn minds and understandings away from preoccupation with other than Allah toward total immersion in the knowledge of Allah, and this repetition serves to achieve and reinforce this aim, it is therefore of the utmost beauty and perfection.

His saying ﴿and ever is Allah, over that, Competent﴾ means: He, exalted is He, has always been and will always be described as capable of all things that are capable of being done. For if His power over things were newly originated, the origination of that power would require another power, and an infinite regress would follow.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The meaning is: those who desire by their striving only the spoils are mistaken; for with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. Why then would one suffice with seeking the reward of this world, when it is as nothing compared to the reward of the Hereafter? If he were rational, he would seek the reward of the Hereafter, so that he would obtain it, and the reward of this world would come to him as a consequence?

If it is said: How did the "fa" (then) enter the response of the conditional, when with Him, exalted is He, is the reward of this world and the Hereafter, whether this desire occurs or not?

We say: The sense of the statement is: with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter for him, if Allah, exalted is He, wills it; and on this assumption the consequent is linked to the condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing﴾, meaning: He hears their speech, that they seek from jihad nothing but the spoils, and He sees that they do not strive in jihad nor exert themselves in it except when expecting to win the spoils. This is like a rebuke from Him, exalted is He, to them concerning these deeds.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We had instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and [now] you, to fear Allah. But if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others. And ever is Allah, over that, Competent.﴾ ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing.﴾

Page 56

There are two views on the connection of this verse with what precedes it:

The first: When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He enriches each of them from His bounty, and that He is All-Encompassing, He pointed to something that is like an explanation of His being All-Encompassing, saying: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning: whoever is like this must necessarily be vast in power, knowledge, generosity, grace and mercy.

The second: When He, exalted is He, commanded justice and kindness toward orphans and the needy, He made clear that He did not command these things out of need for the deeds of His servants, for how could it be conceived that the Owner of the heavens and the earth is in need of human action, given the weakness and deficiency that man has? Rather, He commanded them out of regard for what is best for them in their worldly life and their Hereafter.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and [now] you, to fear Allah﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: The meaning of the verse is that the command to fear Allah is a general law for all nations, which has not been subject to abrogation (naskh) or alteration, but is rather the injunction of Allah for the first and the last.

The second issue: His saying ﴿min qablikum﴾ (from before you) has two views:

The first: It is connected to "wassaynā" (We instructed), meaning: And We had instructed those before you who were given the Scripture.

The second: It is connected to "ūtū" (were given), meaning: Those who were given the Scripture before you, We instructed them with that. His saying "wa-iyyākum" (and [now] you) is in conjunction with ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾. Al-Kitāb (the Scripture) is a generic noun encompassing the heavenly books, and what is meant is the Jews and the Christians.

The third issue: His saying ﴿an-ittaqū Allāh﴾ (to fear Allah) is like your saying: "I ordered you to good." Al-Kisā'ī said: It is said, "I instructed you to do such-and-such" and "to do such-and-such" [both forms], and it is said, "Did I not order you to go to Zayd," and "to go to Zayd" [both forms]. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿I have been commanded to be the first to submit﴾ [al-An'am: 14], and He said: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city﴾ [an-Naml: 91].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And ever is Allah Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾. His saying ﴿wa-in takfurū﴾ (but if you deny) is a conjunction with His saying ﴿fear Allah﴾, and the meaning is: We commanded them and commanded you to piety, and We said to them and to you: if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: He, exalted is He, is their Creator and Owner, and the Bestower upon them of all kinds of blessings, so it is the right of every rational being to be submissive to His commands and prohibitions, hoping for His reward and fearing His punishment.

The second: Even if you deny, to Allah belongs whatever is in His heavens and whatever is in His earth of all kinds of creatures, among them those who worship Him and fear Him; and He is, with that, free of need of their creation and of their worship, and deserving of being praised for the abundance of His blessings. Even if none of them praises Him, He is praiseworthy in His essence, whether they praise Him or do not.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾

If it is said: What is the benefit of repeating His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾?

The first of them: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His bounty﴾, and what is meant by it is His being bountiful and generous. So He mentioned after it His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and the purpose is to establish that He is vast in generosity and munificence.

The second: He said: ﴿But if you deny, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and what is meant by it is that He, exalted is He, is exempt from the obedience of the obedient and from the sins of the sinners, so His majesty does not increase through acts of obedience nor decrease through sins and misdeeds. So after it He mentioned His saying ﴿for indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.
