[p. 58]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more capable of looking after both of them. So do not follow [your] desires, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The first issue concerns the connection of the verse with what precedes it, and there are several aspects.

The first: When the mention of women, *nushuz* (marital discord), and reconciliation between them and their husbands had preceded, [Allah] followed it with the command to stand up in fulfilling the rights of Allah exalted and to bear witness, in order to uphold the rights of Allah. In sum, it is as if it were said: If you occupy yourself with obtaining your desires, you are for yourself and not for Allah; and if you occupy yourself with obtaining what Allah has commanded, you are for Allah and not for yourself. Undoubtedly this station is higher and more noble. So this verse is an emphasis on what preceded of the obligations.

The second: When Allah exalted prohibited people from falling short in seeking the reward of this world, and commanded them to be seekers of the reward of the Hereafter, He mentioned this verse after it, and explained that the perfection of a person's happiness lies in his speech being for Allah, his action being for Allah, his movement being for Allah, and his stillness being for Allah, until he becomes one of those who are at the last of the levels of humanity and the first of the levels of the angels. But when he reverses this matter, he is like an animal whose ultimate concern is finding fodder, or a beast of prey whose ultimate concern is harming an animal.

The third: In this surah the command to the people to act justly had preceded, as He said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with orphans﴾ [an-Nisa': 3], and He commanded them to call witnesses when handing over the wealth of orphans to them. Then after that He commanded them to expend themselves and their wealth in the way of Allah. In this surah He also related the story of Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq and the gathering of his people to defend him with falsehood and to bear false witness against the Jew. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded in these verses to reconcile with the wife. It is known that this is a command from Allah to His servants to be standing firm in justice, bearing witness for Allah against everyone, even against themselves. So this verse served as an affirmation of everything mentioned in this surah of the kinds of obligations.

The second issue: *qawwam* is an intensive form of *qa'im*, and *al-qist* means justice. So this is a command from Him, exalted is He, to all the responsible persons to be exceedingly diligent in choosing justice and avoiding injustice and bias. His saying ﴿witnesses for Allah﴾ means: you establish your testimonies for the sake of Allah, as you have been commanded to establish them, even if the testimony is against yourselves, your fathers, or your relatives. The testimony of a person against himself has two interpretations:

The first: that he acknowledges himself, because acknowledgment is like testimony in that it makes the right binding.

The second: that what is meant is that even if the testimony is harmful to yourselves and your relatives, namely that one testifies against someone from whom harm is feared, such as a tyrannical ruler or other than him.

The third issue: concerning the accusative case of *shuhada'* (witnesses), there are three possibilities:

The first: it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of *qawwamin*.

The second: that it is the predicate, on the basis that *kunu* (be) has two predicates.

The third: that it is a qualifier of *qawwamin*.

The fourth issue: He placed the command to stand in justice before the command to bear witness, for several reasons:

The first: most people's habit is that they command others to do what is right, but when the matter comes to themselves they abandon it, to the extent that the worst ugliness, when it proceeds from them, is considered a matter of leniency and the finest of goodness, whereas when it proceeds from others it is considered a matter of dispute. So Allah, glorified is He, alerted in this verse to the evil of this way. That is because He, exalted is He, first commanded them to stand in justice, then secondly commanded them to bear witness against others, as an alert that the good way is for a person's striving against himself to be greater than his striving against others.

The second: standing in justice is an expression for averting the harm of punishment from others, that is, from the one upon whom the right lies, and averting harm from oneself takes precedence over averting harm from others.

[p. 59]
The third: standing in justice is an act, while testimony is a statement, and the act is stronger than the statement.

If it is said: Indeed He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. Here He placed the testimony before standing in justice, whereas here He placed standing in justice first. So what is the difference?

We say: the testimony of Allah exalted is an expression of His being the Creator of created things, and His standing in justice is an expression of the guardianship of those who stand in justice with equity over those created things. Thus there it is necessary that testimony precede standing in justice. As for servants, standing in justice is an expression of his being observant of justice and distant from injustice, and it is known that as long as a person is not so, his testimony against others is not accepted. So it has been established that what is obligatory in His saying ﴿Allah bears witness﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18] is that that testimony precede standing in justice. And what is obligatory here is that the testimony be after standing in justice. Whoever reflects will know that these secrets are among those that cannot be reached except through divine support. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more capable of looking after both of them﴾. That is: if the one testified against is rich or poor, do not withhold the testimony, either out of seeking the pleasure of the rich or showing mercy to the poor. So Allah is more capable of [managing] their affairs and their interests. The proper wording of the speech would have been: "Allah is more capable of it," because His saying ﴿if one is rich or poor﴾ means: if either of these two is [the case]. But He constructed the pronoun in agreement with the meaning rather than the wording, meaning: Allah is more capable of the poor and the rich. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿Allah is more capable of them﴾, which refers back to His saying ﴿or parents and relatives﴾. 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read: ﴿if one is rich or poor﴾, with *kana* being the complete (intransitive) verb.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not follow [your] desires, lest you not be just﴾. The meaning: abandon following desire until you become described by the attribute of justice. The realization of the statement is that justice is an expression for abandoning the following of desire, and whoever abandons one of two opposites has thereby attained the other. So the structure of the verse is: "do not follow desire for the sake of being just," that is: abandon following desire for the sake of being just.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾. In the verse there are two readings. The majority read ﴿wa-in talwu﴾ with two waws, and Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read *talu*. As for the reading *talwu*, it has two possibilities:

One of them: that it means repelling and turning away, from the saying "lawahu haqqahu" when he delayed and repelled him (his right).

The second: that it means distortion and alteration, from the saying "law al-shay'" when he twisted it, and from this one says "iltawa hadha al-amr" when it became entangled and difficult, as a comparison to a twisted thing. As for *talu*, it has two possibilities:

The first: that *wilayah* of a thing is attending to it and occupying oneself with it, and the meaning is: that you attend to it and complete it, or you turn away from it. Then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted, so He will reward the one who does good and attends with his goodness, and the one who does evil and turns away with his evil. The summary: if you turn away from establishing it, or you refuse to establish it.

The second: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible to say *talu*, its origin being *talwu*, then the waw was changed to a hamzah, then the hamzah was deleted and its vowel was placed on the preceding unvowelled consonant, so it became ﴿wa-in talu﴾. This is the weaker of the two possibilities. As for His saying ﴿then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, it is a threat and warning to the wrongdoers, and a promise of goodness to the obedient.

[Page 60]

The Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers and the Last Day has certainly strayed far astray.﴾

And in this there are several issues:

The First Issue: Regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are two views.

The first: it is connected to His saying: ﴿Be persistent in upholding justice﴾, because a person cannot be persistent in upholding justice unless he is firmly rooted in faith in the things mentioned in this verse.

The second: when the Exalted explained the many rulings in this surah, He followed them with the command to believe.

The Second Issue: Know that the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, indicates a command to attain what is already attained (tahsil al-hasil), and there is no doubt that this is impossible. For this reason the exegetes gave several interpretations, which are confined to two positions:

The first: the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, is the Muslims. Then, in explaining the verse on the basis of this position, there are several interpretations:

The first: the meaning is, "O you who have believed, persist in faith and remain steadfast upon it." Its sum returns to this meaning: "O you who have believed in the past and the present, believe in the future." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So know that there is no god except Allah﴾ [Muhammad: 19], although he (ﷺ) already knew that.

Second: "O you who have believed by way of imitation, believe by way of reasoning."

Third: "O you who have believed on the basis of good proofs, believe on the basis of detailed evidences."

Fourth: "O you who have believed through detailed evidences in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, believe that the true essence of the greatness of Allah does not reach your intellects, and likewise the states of the angels, the secrets of the books and the attributes of the messengers do not reach our intellects in detail."

Fifth: it was narrated that a group of the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you and your Book, and in Moses and the Torah and 'Uzair, and we disbelieve in whatever else there is of books and messengers." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Rather, believe in Allah and His messengers, and in Muhammad and his Book, the Qur'an, and in every book that came before it." They said: "We will not do that." Then this verse was revealed, and they all believed.

The second view: the addressees of His saying, "believe," are not the Muslims. In explaining the verse on the basis of this view, there are several interpretations:

First: the address is to the Jews and the Christians, and the implied meaning is: "O you who have believed in Moses and the Torah, and Jesus and the Gospel, believe in Muhammad and the Qur'an."

Second: the address is to the hypocrites, and the implied meaning is: "O you who have believed with the tongue, believe with the heart." This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41].

Third: it is an address to those who believed at the beginning of the day and disbelieved at its end. The implied meaning is: "O you who believed at the beginning of the day, believe also at its end."

Fourth: it is an address to the polytheists. Its implied meaning is: "O you who have believed in al-Lat and al-'Uzza, believe in Allah."

Most of the scholars preferred the first view, because the word "believer," when used without qualification, refers only to Muslims.

The Third Issue: Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr recited, "wa-l-kitābi lladhī nuzzila 'alā rasūlihi wa-l-kitābi lladhī unzila," in the passive voice (ʿalā mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu), while the rest recited nazzala and anzala in the active voice with a fatha. Whoever read it in the passive voice, his evidence is His saying: ﴿so that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44], and in another verse He said: ﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 114]. Whoever read it with a fatha, his evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], and His saying: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder﴾ [al-Nahl: 44]. Some scholars said: both are good, except that the damma is more majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow your water﴾ [Hud: 44].

* * *

[Page 61]

The Fourth Issue: Know that in this verse He commanded belief in four things:

First: Allah.

Second: His Messenger.

Third: the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger.

Fourth: the Book which He sent down before.

And He mentioned five matters in disbelief:

The first of them: disbelief in Allah.

The second: disbelief in His angels.

The third: disbelief in His books.

The fourth: disbelief in His messengers.

The fifth: disbelief in the Last Day.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿has certainly strayed far astray﴾. And in the verse there are questions:

The First Question: Why did He mention the Messenger before the Book in the ranks of faith, but reverse the order in the ranks of disbelief?

The Answer: Because in the stage of descent, from the knowledge of the Creator to the creation, the Book precedes the Messenger; and in the stage of ascent, from the creation to the Creator, the Messenger precedes the Book.

The Second Question: Why did He mention three things in the ranks of faith, namely belief in Allah, in the Messenger, and in the books, but mention five things in the ranks of disbelief, namely disbelief in Allah, in the angels, in the books, in the messengers, and in the Last Day?

The Answer: Whenever belief in Allah, in the messengers and in the books is achieved, belief in the angels and the Last Day is inevitably achieved as well. For a person may claim that he believes in Allah, in the messengers and in the books, and then deny the angels and deny the Last Day, claiming that he interprets the verses concerning the angels and the Last Day figuratively (ta'wil). Since this possibility exists, He explicitly stated that whoever denies the angels and denies the Resurrection is a disbeliever in Allah.

The Third Question: How was it said to the People of the Books, ﴿and the Book which He sent down before﴾, when they were not disbelievers in the Torah and the Gospel, but rather believers in them?

The answer to this has two aspects:

First: they believed only in these two, and they did not believe in every book that was sent down. So they were commanded to believe in all the books that were sent down.

Second: their belief in some of the books and not others is not valid, because the path of faith is the miracle (mu'jizah). If the miracle is present in all of them, then abandoning belief in some of them is a challenge to the miracle, and if the miracle is challenged, it becomes impossible to affirm any of them. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and they desire to take a path between that. Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾ [al-Nisa': 150–151].

The Fourth Question: Why did He say, "He sent down upon His Messenger and He sent down before"?

The Answer: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Because the Qur'an was sent down in installments, distributed over twenty years, unlike the books before it. I say: the discussion on this has already preceded in the explanation of His saying: ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel, before﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 3–4].

The Fifth Question: His saying, ﴿and the Book which He sent down before﴾, is a singular noun. Which of the books is intended by it?

The Answer: It is a generic noun (ism jins), so it is suitable for generality.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 137–138:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief — Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way.﴾ ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Regarding this there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded faith and encouraged it, He explained the corruption of the way of one who disbelieves after faith, so He mentioned this verse.

Know that concerning it there are many opinions:

The first: that what is meant is those from whom disbelief recurs after faith many times and repeatedly. This indicates that faith has no weight in their hearts, for if faith had weight and standing in their hearts, they would not abandon it for the slightest cause. And whoever has no weight of faith in his heart, it is apparent that he does not believe in Allah with a sound, valid faith. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾. It does not mean that if they came with sound faith it would not be valid; rather, what is meant is denial and astonishment in the manner we have mentioned. Likewise, we see the sinner who repents and then returns, then repents and returns: it is hardly hoped that he will remain steadfast, and the likely outcome is that he dies in sin. So it is the same here.

The second: Some said: the Jews believed in the Torah and in Moses, then disbelieved by (rejecting) Uzair, then believed in David, then disbelieved by (rejecting) Jesus, then increased in disbelief at the coming of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace.

The third: Others said: what is meant is the hypocrites. Their first faith is their outward profession of Islam, and their disbelief after that is their hypocrisy, the inner state being contrary to the outer. Their second faith is that whenever they met a group of Muslims they said, "We are believers." Their second disbelief is that when they entered upon their devils they said, "We are with you; we are only mocking." Their increase in disbelief is their striving and effort in devising kinds of deceit and scheming against the Muslims. The outward profession of faith may also be called faith, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The intention is not to specify this number; rather, what is meant is their wavering, as He said: ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those﴾ [an-Nisa: 143]. He said: What indicates this is His saying after this verse: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾

The fourth: Some people said: what is meant is a group of the People of the Book who intended to create doubt among the Muslims, so they would show faith at times and disbelief at other times, as Allah, exalted is He, reported about them that they said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, perhaps they will return﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]. And His saying ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ means that they reached in this the limit of mockery and ridicule of Islam.

The second issue: The verse indicates that disbelief may occur after faith, and this refutes the view of those who hold the doctrine of al-Muwafah (the condition of dying upon Islam), which is that a condition for the validity of Islam is that one dies upon Islam. They answer this by saying: we take faith here to mean the outward display of faith.

The third issue: The verse indicates that disbelief admits of increase and decrease, so faith too must be like that, since they are two opposites that are mutually exclusive; when one admits of gradation, the other does likewise. They mentioned several explanations of this increase:

[Page 63]
The first: that they died in their disbelief.
The second: that they increased in disbelief because of sins they committed while in disbelief. On this view, since committing sins during disbelief is an increase in disbelief, likewise performing acts of obedience during faith must be an increase in faith.

The third: that the increase in disbelief occurred only through their saying: ﴿We are only mocking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14]; and this indicates that mockery of the religion is the greatest degree of disbelief and its strongest level.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾, and regarding this there are two questions:

The first: The ruling mentioned in this verse is either conditioned on what precedes repentance or on what follows it. The first is invalid, because disbelief before repentance is not mentioned absolutely, and then these conditions mentioned in this verse would be lost. The second is also invalid, because disbelief after repentance is forgiven, even if it occurs a thousand times. So on both assumptions the question stands.

The answer to it has several aspects:

The first: We do not take His saying "Indeed those who" in the sense of generality; rather we take it to refer to a known, previously identified group, meaning specific people whom Allah, exalted is He, knew would die in disbelief and never repent of it. So His saying ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾ is a report of their dying in disbelief, and on this reading the question disappears.

The second: The statement came in accordance with the common and usual case, namely that everyone who frequently shifts from Islam to disbelief has no weight or greatness of Islam in his heart, and the apparent state of such a person is that he dies in disbelief, as we have established.

The third: The ruling mentioned in the verse is conditioned on not repenting from disbelief. As for the questioner's statement that on this assumption the mentioned attributes are lost, we say: singling them out by mention indicates that their disbelief is more heinous, their betrayal greater, and their punishment on the Day of Resurrection more severe. This is like His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], where He singled them out for mention for the sake of honour; and likewise His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

The second question: In His saying ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾, the lam (لِيَغْفِرَ) is for emphasis, so the phrase ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ اللَّهُ لِيَغْفِرَ لَهُمْ﴾ expresses the negation of emphasis, and this is not fitting for this context; what is fitting is the emphasis of negation. So what is the reason for it?

The answer: When the negation of emphasis is mentioned in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum), what is meant by it is intensifying the emphasis of the negation.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿nor will He guide them to a way﴾. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: this indicates that He, glorified and exalted, did not guide the disbeliever to faith, contrary to the Mu'tazilah. They answered that it is to be understood as a prevention of additional grace (lutf), or that He will not guide them in the Hereafter to Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that whoever takes the preceding verse as referring to the hypocrites says: He, exalted is He, made clear that He will not forgive them their disbelief nor guide them to Paradise; then He said: just as He does not bring them to the abode of reward, He brings them, in addition, to the greatest kinds of punishment, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾ His saying "give good tidings" is sarcasm directed at them, and the Arabs say: "Your greeting is the blow, and your reproach is the sword."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 137–138:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief — Allah will not forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way.﴾ ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Regarding this there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded faith and encouraged it, He explained the corruption of the way of one who disbelieves after faith, so He mentioned this verse.

Know that concerning it there are many opinions:

The first: that what is meant is those from whom disbelief recurs after faith many times and repeatedly. This indicates that faith has no weight in their hearts, for if faith had weight and standing in their hearts, they would not abandon it for the slightest cause. And whoever has no weight of faith in his heart, it is apparent that he does not believe in Allah with a sound, valid faith. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾. It does not mean that if they came with sound faith it would not be valid; rather, what is meant is denial and astonishment in the manner we have mentioned. Likewise, we see the sinner who repents and then returns, then repents and returns: it is hardly hoped that he will remain steadfast, and the likely outcome is that he dies in sin. So it is the same here.

The second: Some said: the Jews believed in the Torah and in Moses, then disbelieved by (rejecting) Uzair, then believed in David, then disbelieved by (rejecting) Jesus, then increased in disbelief at the coming of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace.

The third: Others said: what is meant is the hypocrites. Their first faith is their outward profession of Islam, and their disbelief after that is their hypocrisy, the inner state being contrary to the outer. Their second faith is that whenever they met a group of Muslims they said, "We are believers." Their second disbelief is that when they entered upon their devils they said, "We are with you; we are only mocking." Their increase in disbelief is their striving and effort in devising kinds of deceit and scheming against the Muslims. He said: What indicates this is His saying after this verse: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾

The fourth: Some people said: what is meant is a group of the People of the Book who intended to create doubt among the Muslims, so they would show faith at times and disbelief at other times, as Allah, exalted is He, reported about them that they said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, perhaps they will return﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]. And His saying ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ means that they reached in this the limit of mockery and ridicule of Islam.

The second issue: The verse indicates that disbelief may occur after faith, and this refutes the view of those who hold the doctrine of al-Muwafah (the condition of dying upon Islam), which is that a condition for the validity of Islam is that one dies upon Islam. They answer this by saying: we take faith here to mean the outward display of faith.

The third issue: The verse indicates that disbelief admits of increase and decrease, so faith too must be like that, since they are two opposites that are mutually exclusive; when one admits of gradation, the other does likewise. They mentioned several explanations of this increase:

[Page 63]
The first: that they died in their disbelief.
The second: that they increased in disbelief because of sins they committed while in disbelief. On this view, since committing sins during disbelief is an increase in disbelief, likewise performing acts of obedience during faith must be an increase in faith.

The third: that the increase in disbelief occurred only through their saying: ﴿We are only mocking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14]; and this indicates that mockery of the religion is the greatest degree of disbelief and its strongest level.

Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: this indicates that He, glorified and exalted, did not guide the disbeliever to faith, contrary to the Mu'tazilah. * * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that whoever takes the preceding verse as referring to the hypocrites says: He, exalted is He, made clear that He will not forgive them their disbelief nor guide them to Paradise; then He said: just as He does not bring them to the abode of reward, He brings them, in addition, to the greatest kinds of punishment, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment.﴾ His saying "give good tidings" is sarcasm directed at them, and the Arabs say: "Your greeting is the blow, and your reproach is the sword."

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿الَّذِينَ يَتَّخِذُونَ الكافِرِينَ أوْلِياءَ مِن دُونِ المُؤْمِنِينَ أيَبْتَغُونَ عِنْدَهُمُ العِزَّةَ فَإنَّ العِزَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا﴾ .

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honor with them? Indeed, honor belongs entirely to Allah.﴾

الَّذِينَ (alladhina): It is in the accusative case as a term of censure (dhamm), meaning "I intend those who...", or in the nominative case, meaning "they are those who...". The exegetes agree that the intended meaning of "those who take" (alladhina yattakhidhuna) is the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), and the intended meaning of "the disbelievers" (al-kafirin) is the Jews. The hypocrites used to befriend them, and some of them would say to others: "The affair of Muhammad will not be completed," so the Jews would say that honor and protection belong to them.

* * *
ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿أيَبْتَغُونَ عِنْدَهُمُ العِزَّةَ﴾ Al-Wahidi said: The original meaning of ʿizzah (honor, might) in the language is intensity and severity. From it, the hard, firm earth is called ʿazzaz. It is said: "The illness has intensified (istaʿazza) upon the patient," when his illness becomes severe and he nearly dies. ʿAzza al-hamm means it became intense. From it comes "ʿazza ʿalayya an yakuna kadha," meaning "it was difficult for me that it should be so." ʿAzza al-shay' means when a thing becomes scarce to the point that it is hardly found, because its demand has intensified. Fulan ista'azza bi-fulan means when his back becomes strong by means of him. A ewe that is ʿazuz is one whose milking is intense and difficult. ʿIzzah means strength, transferred from intensity, because the two meanings are close. And al-ʿAziz is the strong, the invincible, as opposed to the humiliated (al-dhalil).

Having understood this, we say: The hypocrites were seeking honor and strength through their association with the Jews. Then He, exalted is He, refuted this opinion of theirs by His saying: ﴿Indeed, honor belongs entirely to Allah.﴾

If it is said: This seems to contradict His saying: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers.﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]

We say: Complete power belongs to Allah, and everyone other than Him became capable by His empowering, and became honored by His bestowing honor. So the honor that came to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and to the believers, was obtained only from Allah, exalted is He. Thus the matter, upon careful examination, is that honor belongs entirely to Allah.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than that.﴾

The exegetes said: The polytheists used to engage in discussion about the Qur'an in their gatherings, mocking it, so God the Exalted revealed: ﴿And when you see those who engage in [vain talk] concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than that﴾ [al-An'am: 68]. This verse was revealed in Mecca. Then the rabbis of the Jews in Medina used to do the same as the polytheists did, and those who sat with them and agreed with them in that speech were the hypocrites. So God the Exalted, addressing the hypocrites, said: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in*

صفحة ٦٥
*the Book that when you hear the verses of God being rejected and mocked﴾. The meaning is: when you hear disbelief in the verses of God and mockery of them. But the act of hearing has been attached to the verses, and what is intended is the hearing of the mockery. Al-Kisa'i said: This is like saying, "I heard Abdullah being blamed."

I have another view on this, which is that the meaning is: when you hear the verses of God while they are being rejected and mocked. On this interpretation there is no need for what al-Kisa'i said: "do not sit with them until they engage in a conversation other than disbelief and mockery."

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾.

The meaning is: O hypocrites, you are like those rabbis in disbelief. The people of knowledge said: This indicates that whoever is content with disbelief is a disbeliever, and whoever is content with an evil he sees and mixes with its people, even if he does not directly participate, is in sin in the same position as the one who directly participates, as evidenced by the fact that God mentioned the word "like" here. This applies when the sitter is content with that sitting. As for when he is displeased with their speech and sat only out of taqiyyah (dissimulation) and fear, the matter is not so. Based on this subtle point we said that the hypocrites who used to sit with the Jews, and who used to slander the Qur'an and the Messenger, were disbelievers like those Jews. And the Muslims who were in Medina, when they were in Mecca and sat with the disbelievers who slandered the Qur'an, they remained upon faith. The difference is that the hypocrites sat with the Jews by choice, while the Muslims sat with the disbelievers out of necessity.

Then God the Exalted confirmed that the hypocrites are like the disbelievers in disbelief, saying: ﴿Indeed, God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them﴾.

He means: just as they gathered together in mocking the verses of God in this world, so they will gather together in the punishment of Hell on the Day of Resurrection. And he intended "jami'un" (gatherer) with tanwin, since He had already gathered them, but the tanwin was omitted for lightness of pronunciation, while it is intended in reality.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 141:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who wait [to see] what happens to you. If there is a victory for you from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" And if the disbelievers have a share [of victory], they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿those who wait [to see] what happens to you﴾ may be a substitute (badal) for ﴿those who take﴾, or an attribute (sifah) of the hypocrites, or in the accusative (nasb) for censure (dhamm). His saying ﴿wait [to see]﴾ means: they await whatever occurs of good or evil. ﴿If there is a victory for you﴾, i.e., dominance over the Jews, they say to the believers, "Were we not with you?", meaning: "Then give us a share of the spoils." ﴿And if the disbelievers have a share﴾, meaning the Jews have a share, i.e., a triumph over the Muslims, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you?" It is said: "He gained mastery (istahwadha) over so-and-so," meaning he overcame him. There are two interpretations of this verse:

The first: that it means, "Did we not overcome you and have the ability to kill and capture you, and then did we not do any of that, and protect you from the Muslims by discouraging them from you and making them imagine what weakened their hearts, and by being lax in supporting them against you? So give us a share of what you have obtained."

The second: that the meaning is that those disbelievers and Jews had resolved to enter Islam, but then the hypocrites warned them against that, exaggerated in turning them away from it, and made them hope that the affair of Muhammad would weaken and your affair would grow strong. When the disbelievers achieved an attack on the Muslims, the hypocrites said, "Did we not overcome you in your opinion about entering Islam, and prevent you from it, and tell you that his affair would weaken and your affair would grow strong? So when you witnessed the truth of our words, give us a share of what you have found." The summary is that the hypocrites bestow favour upon the disbelievers, saying, "We are the ones who guided you to these benefits, so give us a share of what you have found."

If it is asked: why did he call the Muslims' success a "victory" (fath) and the disbelievers' success a "share" (nasib)?

We say: to magnify the status of the believers and to belittle the portion of the disbelievers, because the success of the believers is a great matter, for which the gates of heaven are opened until the angels descend with victory upon the friends of Allah. As for the success of the disbelievers, it is nothing but a base portion that passes away, and nothing remains of it except blame in this world and punishment in the end.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾, i.e., between the believers and the hypocrites. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, did not lay down the sword against the hypocrites in this world, but deferred their punishment until the Day of Resurrection.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾. Regarding this there are two statements:

The first, which is the statement of Ali (peace be upon him) and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): that it refers to the Resurrection, as evidenced by it being conjoined to His saying: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

The second: that it refers to this world, but it is restricted to proof (hujjah). The meaning is that the proof of the Muslims prevails over the proof of everyone, and no one may overcome them with argument and evidence.

The third: that it is general over all, except what the evidence specifies. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) had several rulings based on this: among them, that if a disbeliever seizes the property of a Muslim and secures it in the territory of war, he does not come to own it, by the indication of this verse; among them, that a disbeliever may not buy a Muslim slave, by the indication of this verse; and among them, that a Muslim is not killed for a dhimmi, by the indication of this verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them﴾. The explanation of deception (khida') has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿they deceive Allah and those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9]. Al-Zajjaj said in explaining this verse: ﴿they deceive Allah﴾, i.e., they deceive the Messenger of Allah, meaning they show him faith and conceal disbelief, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. His saying ﴿but He is deceiving them﴾ means: He will requite them with punishment for their deception. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: He, exalted is He, will deceive them in the Hereafter. That is, He gives them light as He gives the believers; then when they reach the bridge (sirat), their light is extinguished and they remain in darkness. The evidence is His saying: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses, not seeing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17].

[p. 67]

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily﴾. That is, when they stand up to prayer with the Muslims, they stand up

[p. 67 continues]
lazily (kusala), meaning sluggish and slow, and this is the linguistic meaning of laziness (kasal). The cause of this laziness is that they find it burdensome in the present and do not hope for any reward from it, nor do they fear any punishment for abandoning it. So the motive for abandoning it was strong from these standpoints, while the only motive for doing it was fear of people. When the motive for an action is of this kind, the action is performed with laziness and listlessness. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Kusala" has been read with a damma and with a fatha on the kaf, as the plural of kaslan, like sukara as the plural of sakran.

* *
* * *
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They show off to the people and do not remember God except a little﴾. The meaning is that they do not stand up to prayer except for the sake of showing off and seeking reputation, not for the sake of religion.

If it is said: what is the meaning of murā'āh (showing off), which is a form of mufā'alah from ru'yah (seeing)?

We say: the one who shows off makes them see his deed, and they see it as deserving approval. As for His saying ﴿and do not remember God except a little﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: the intended meaning of "remembering God" is prayer, and the meaning is that they pray only a little, because whenever none of the outsiders are with them they do not pray; and when they are with people, at the onset of the time of prayer they exert themselves until they become hidden from people's eyes.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembering God" is that during their prayer they remember God only a little, namely that which is manifest, such as the takbirs; but what is hidden, such as the recitation and the tasbihs, they do not remember.

The third: the intended meaning is that they do not remember God at all times, whether or not that time is a time of prayer, except rarely and seldom. The author of al-Kashshaf said: Thus we see many of those who outwardly profess Islam; if you were to keep company with him for days and nights, you would not hear from him a single tahlil or tasbih, but the talk of this world occupies his days and times, and he never ceases from it.

The fourth: Qatadah said: It was said "except a little" only because God, may He be exalted, did not accept it, and whatever God rejects, its abundance is little, and whatever God accepts, its little is abundant.

* * *
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those; and whoever God leads astray, you will not find for him a way﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: "wavering" (mudhabdhabin) is either a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of His saying "they show off," or of His saying "and do not remember God except a little." It may also be in the accusative as a term of blame.

The second issue: mudhabdhabin means: bewildered. The real meaning of "mudhabdhab" is one who is repelled from both sides, that is, is pushed back and driven away, so that he does not settle on one side. However, the dhabdhabah includes a repetition that is not in the dhabb (repelling). So the meaning is: whenever he inclines toward one side, he is repelled from it.

Know that the reason for this is that an action depends on its motive. If the motive for the action is the aims related to the conditions of this world, wavering and instability increase, because the benefits and causes of this world are changeable and quickly transformed. When the action follows the motive, and the motive follows the aim, and the aim is quick to change and alter, then change necessarily occurs in

[p. 68]
inclination and desire, and perhaps motives and deterrents conflict, so the person remains in bewilderment and hesitation. As for the one whose aim in his action is to produce lasting goods and to acquire spiritual felicities, and who knows that these objectives are lasting matters, free of change and transformation, this person is necessarily steadfast and firm. For this reason God, may He be exalted, described the people of faith with steadfastness, saying: ﴿God makes firm those who believe﴾ [Ibrahim: 27], and He said: ﴿Surely in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28], and He said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾ [al-Fajr: 26].

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas read "mudhabdhibin" with a kasra on the second dhal, and the meaning is: they cause their hearts or their religion or their opinion to waver, in the sense of "yatadhabdhabun" (they waver), just as "salsal" and "tasalsal" have the same meaning. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is "mutadhabdhibin." And from Abu Ja'far: "mudabdibin" with the unpointed dal. It seems the meaning is that they are sometimes in one path (dubbah) and sometimes in another, so they do not remain on a single path. lazily (kusala), meaning sluggish and slow, and this is the linguistic meaning of laziness (kasal). The cause of this laziness is that they find it burdensome in the present and do not hope for any reward from it, nor do they fear any punishment for abandoning it. So the motive for abandoning it was strong from these standpoints, while the only motive for doing it was fear of people. When the motive for an action is of this kind, the action is performed with laziness and listlessness. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They show off to the people and do not remember God except a little﴾. The meaning is that they do not stand up to prayer except for the sake of showing off and seeking reputation, not for the sake of religion.

If it is said: what is the meaning of murā'āh (showing off), which is a form of mufā'alah from ru'yah (seeing)?

We say: the one who shows off makes them see his deed, and they see it as deserving approval. As for His saying ﴿and do not remember God except a little﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: the intended meaning of "remembering God" is prayer, and the meaning is that they pray only a little, because whenever none of the outsiders are with them they do not pray; and when they are with people, at the onset of the time of prayer they exert themselves until they become hidden from people's eyes.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembering God" is that during their prayer they remember God only a little, namely that which is manifest, such as the takbirs; but what is hidden, such as the recitation and the tasbihs, they do not remember.

The third: the intended meaning is that they do not remember God at all times, whether or not that time is a time of prayer, except rarely and seldom. The author of al-Kashshaf said: Thus we see many of those who outwardly profess Islam; if you were to keep company with him for days and nights, you would not hear from him a single tahlil or tasbih, but the talk of this world occupies his days and times, and he never ceases from it.

The fourth: Qatadah said: It was said "except a little" only because God, may He be exalted, did not accept it, and whatever God rejects, its abundance is little, and whatever God accepts, its little is abundant.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 144–145:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, censured the hypocrites for wavering, at one time turning toward the disbelievers and at another toward the Muslims, without settling with either group, He forbade the Muslims in this verse from doing the same as them, saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers.﴾ The reason for it is that the Ansar in Medina had foster-ties, alliance and affection with the Banu Qurayzah. They said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whom shall we ally ourselves with?" He said: "With the emigrants (muhajirin)." So this verse was revealed.

The second opinion is what al-Qaffal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: that this is a prohibition to the believers from allying themselves with the hypocrites. He says: "I have already made clear to you the characteristics and ways of the hypocrites, so do not take them as allies."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you want to give Allah a clear proof against yourselves?﴾

If we take the first verse to mean that He, exalted is He, forbade the believers from allying themselves with the disbelievers, then the meaning of this verse is: "Do you want to give Allah a clear proof against you for being hypocrites?" The intended meaning is: "Do you want to give the people of the religion of Allah, namely the Messenger and his community, a clear proof?" If we take the first verse to refer to the hypocrites, the meaning is: "Do you want to give Allah a proof against you in your punishment, because of your alliance with the hypocrites?"

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Layth said: "The darak (level) is the farthest depth of a thing, such as the sea or the like. Accordingly, what is meant by the lowest level is the farthest depth of Hell. The origin of this word is from idrak in the sense of reaching (lahuq), from which come idrak al-ta'am (the food ripening) and idrak al-ghulam (the boy reaching maturity). So the darak is the stratum that one reaches." Its apparent meaning is that Hell has layers, and the apparent meaning is that the most severe of them is the lowest. Al-Dahhak said: "The darajat (degrees) are when some are above others, and the darak (levels) are when some are lower than others."

The second issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, on the authority of Asim, read ﴿fi al-darki﴾ with a sukun on the ra' (الدَّرْكِ), while the rest read it with a fatha on the ra' (الدَّرَكِ). Al-Zajjaj said: "They are two dialects, like al-sham' and al-shama' (candle). However, the preferred reading is with the fatha on the ra', because it is more commonly used." Abu Hatim said: "The plural of al-darak is adrak, like jamal and ajmal (camel, camels), and faras and afras (horse, horses). The plural of al-dark is adruk, like fals and afuls (fils, fils) and kalb and akhluk," (correction: the plural cited is ukluk as the source gives) — rendered as: like kalb and akleb (dog, dogs).

The third issue: Ibn al-Anbari said: "He, exalted is He, said of the hypocrites that they are in the lowest level, and He said of the family of Pharaoh: ﴿Cause the family of Pharaoh to enter the severest punishment.﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. Which of them is in greater punishment, the hypocrites or the family of Pharaoh?" He answered: "It is possible that the severest punishment is only in the lowest level, and both groups are gathered in it."

The fourth issue: Since the hypocrite is in greater punishment than the disbeliever, because he shares his disbelief and there is added to it another kind of disbelief, namely mockery of Islam and its people, and because, while they outwardly profess Islam, they are able to learn the secrets of the Muslims and then inform the disbelievers of them, the trial from these hypocrites was multiplied. For these reasons Allah made their punishment greater than the punishment of the disbelievers.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will not find for them a helper.﴾ This is a threat to them. Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this as evidence for the affirmation of intercession (shafa'a) on behalf of the sinful (fasiq) among the people of prayer. They said: "He, exalted is He, singled out the hypocrites with this threat. If this applied to those other than the hypocrites, it would not be a deterrent from hypocrisy as such." This is not an argument from the implication of the text (dalil al-khitab), rather the way of argument in it is that He mentioned it in the context of warning against hypocrisy; so if it applied to someone even without hypocrisy, it would no longer be a deterrent from it as such.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Except those who repent, amend, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those are with the believers, and Allah will give the believers a great reward.﴾

Know that this verse contains severe threats against the hypocrites, because He, exalted is He, stipulated four matters for the removal of punishment from them:

The first of them: repentance (tawbah).

The second: amending the deed (islah al-'amal). Repentance is abandoning the ugly, and amending the deed is an expression for undertaking the good.

The third: holding fast to Allah (i'tisam bi-Allah). This means that his purpose in repentance and in amending his deed is seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, and not seeking the benefit of the moment. For if his aim were the acquisition of benefits and the repelling of harms, he would quickly change from repentance and from amending his deed. But when his aim is the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, and the happiness of the Hereafter, and holding fast to the religion of Allah, he remains upon this path and does not deviate from it.

The fourth: sincerity (ikhlas). The reason for it is that He, exalted is He, commanded them:

Firstly: to abandon the ugly.

Secondly: to do the good.

Thirdly: that their purpose in that abandoning and doing be seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He.

Fourthly: that this purpose, which is seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, be pure, and that no other purpose be mixed with it.

When these four conditions are fulfilled, then at that point He said: ﴿Those are with the believers﴾, and He did not say "those are believers." Then He placed the reward of the believers in the context of honour, because the hypocrites were joined to them, so He said: ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward.﴾ These indications point to the fact that the state of the hypocrite is severe in the sight of Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing.﴾

In it are several issues:

First issue: Does He punish you for the sake of vengeance, or for seeking benefit, or for repelling harm? All of that is impossible with respect to Him, because He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient, free from needs, and exalted above bringing benefits or repelling harms. Rather, the intended purpose of it is to move the responsible persons (mukallafin) to do the good and to avoid the ugly. So when you do the good and leave the ugly, how would it befit His generosity to punish you?

Second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: This verse supports our view, because it indicates that He, glorified is He, did not create any creature for the purpose of punishment and retribution, for His saying ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful and believe?﴾ is explicit that He did not create anyone for the purpose of punishing. Also, the verse indicates that the doer of gratitude and faith is the servant, and that is not an act of Allah, exalted is He; otherwise the meaning would become: "Why would Allah punish you when He creates gratitude and faith in you?" And it is known that this is not coherent. The answer to these statements has already been given.

Third issue: Our companions (aṣḥabuna) said: This verse indicates that He does not punish the perpetrator of a major sin (ṣāḥib al-kabirah), because we assume the discussion concerns one who is grateful and believes and then proceeds to drink wine or commit fornication. Such a person must not be punished, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful and believe?﴾ If they say: "We do not concede that the perpetrator of a major sin is a believer," we reply: We have mentioned the many arguments in this book that he is a believer.

Fourth issue: Regarding the precedence of gratitude over faith, there are two views:

The first: that it is in the order of inversion, i.e., "if you believe and are grateful," because faith precedes all other acts of obedience.

The second: if we say that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not require sequential order, then the question disappears.

The third: that when a person reflects upon himself, he sees the great blessing present in his creation and arrangement, so he gives a general thanks, then when he completes his reflection on knowing the Bestower, he believes in Him, and then gives a detailed thanks. Thus that general gratitude precedes faith, and for this reason He mentioned it first.

The second: if we say that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not require sequential order, then the question disappears.

The third: that when a person reflects upon himself, he sees the great blessing present in his creation and arrangement, so he gives a general thanks, then when he completes his reflection on knowing the Bestower, he believes in Him, and then gives a detailed thanks. Thus that general gratitude precedes faith, and for this reason He mentioned it first.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing.﴾ Because when He commanded them to be grateful, He named the reward for gratitude "gratitude" by way of metaphor (isti'arah). So what is meant by His being "Appreciative" (shakir) is that He rewards for gratitude, and what is meant by His being "Knowing" ('alim) is that He knows all particulars, so error never occurs in Him at all, and therefore He surely conveys the reward to the grateful and the punishment to the one who turns away.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 148:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged. And Allah is ever Hearing and Knowing.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first issue:** Regarding the manner of its composition (al-nazm), there are two views.

The first: When He, exalted is He, exposed the hypocrites, disclosed their shame, and uncovering concealment was not fitting for the Merciful and Generous, He mentioned something that serves as an excuse for this. He said: ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged.﴾ That is, He, exalted is He, does not love the display of disgraceful and shameful matters, except regarding one whose harm is great and whose deceit and scheming are abundant. At that point, it is permissible to expose his disgraceful acts. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Mention the wicked person for what is in him, so that people may be wary of him." These hypocrites had abundant deceit, scheming, and wronging toward the Muslims, and their harm was great. Therefore, for this reason, Allah mentioned their disgraceful acts and revealed their secrets.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned in the preceding verse that these hypocrites, if they repent and become sincere, become among the believers. It is possible that some of them would repent and be sincere in their repentance, yet still not be spared, after that, from reproach and blame from some Muslims because of what had proceeded from them in the past of hypocrisy. So in this verse He made clear, exalted is He, that He does not love this practice, and He does not approve of the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has wronged himself and persisted in his hypocrisy, for He does not dislike that.

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, does not will for His servants the commission of abominable acts, nor does He create them. This is because the love of Allah, exalted is He, is an expression for His willing. So when He said: ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech﴾, we know that He does not will that. Furthermore, if He were the creator of the actions of the servants, He would be willing them, and if He were willing them, He would have loved the bringing about of the public utterance of evil speech, and that contradicts the verse.

The answer: Love, according to us, is an expression for granting reward for an act. On this understanding it is valid to say that He willed it but did not love it, and Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** The people of knowledge said: He, exalted is He, does not love the public utterance of evil speech, nor does He love anything other than public utterance either. Rather, He, exalted is He, mentioned this attribute only because its actual circumstance necessitated it, as in His saying: ﴿When you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully﴾ [al-Nisa': 94], and investigation is obligatory in the case of accusation and in the case of establishing (a judgment). Likewise here.

**The fourth issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿except by one who has been wronged﴾, there are two views, because the exception is either disjunct (munqati') or connected (muttasil).

The first view: It is a connected exception. On this assumption, there are two opinions:

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said this is from the omission of the modified noun, with the sense: "except the public utterance of one who has been wronged." Then the modified noun was omitted and the modifier (the noun in the genitive) was placed in its position.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: The verbal noun (maṣdar) here is placed in the position of the agent, and the meaning is: "Allah does not love the one who publicly utters evil speech, except one who has been wronged."

The second view: This exception is disjunct, and the meaning is: "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, but the one who has been wronged has the right to make his grievance public."

**The fifth issue:** What does the one who has been wronged do? There are several opinions:

The first: Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah does not love raising the voice with that which offends others, except the one who has been wronged, for he has the right to raise his voice in supplication against the one who wronged him.

The second: Mujahid said: (It is permitted) except that he informs of the wrong done to him by the one who wronged him.

The third: It is not permissible to reveal hidden and concealed conditions, because that becomes a cause for people to fall into backbiting and for that person to fall into suspicion. But the one who has been wronged, it is permissible to reveal his wronging, by mentioning that he was robbed or usurped. This is the view of al-Asamm.

The fourth: al-Hasan said: (It is permitted) except that he takes revenge against his wrongdoer. It was said: The verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), for a man insulted him and he remained silent several times, then he responded to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood up, and Abu Bakr said: "He insulted me while you were sitting, but when I responded to him, you got up." He said: "An angel was answering on your behalf, and when you responded to him, that angel left and the Devil came, so I did not sit when the Devil came." Then this verse was revealed.

**The sixth issue:** A group of the major reciters, namely al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, read ﴿مَن ظَلَمَ﴾ (man zalama, with a fatha on the ẓā'). There are two views on this:

The first: His saying ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech﴾ is a complete statement, and His saying ﴿except by one who has been wronged﴾ is a statement disconnected from what precedes it, and the sense is: "But whoever has wronged, leave him and let him be." Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: It means "but whoever has wronged himself, then he publicly utters evil speech, being unjust and transgressing."

The second: The exception is connected, and the sense is: "except whoever has wronged (zalama)," for it is permissible to publicly utter evil speech along with him.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is ever Hearing and Knowing﴾, which is a warning against transgression in the public utterance that has been permitted. The meaning is: Let him fear Allah, and let him say only the truth, and not slander a concealed person with evil, for he then becomes disobedient to Allah by that. He, exalted is He, is Hearing of what he says and Knowing of what he conceals.

"The Exalted said: ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent.﴾

Know that the foundations of good deeds, despite their multitude, are confined to two matters: truthfulness with the Truth (Allah), and good conduct with creation. What relates to creation is confined to two categories: bringing benefit to them and warding off harm from them. So His saying ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it﴾ is a reference to bringing benefit to them, and His saying ﴿or pardon﴾ is a reference to warding off harm from them. Thus all kinds of good and acts of righteousness are included in these two phrases.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾. In this there are several interpretations:

The first: He, the Exalted, pardons on both sides while He has power to take vengeance, so you should follow the practice of Allah, the Exalted. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: Indeed Allah is Pardoning to whoever pardons, and Competent to bestow reward upon him.

The third: al-Kalbi said: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, is more capable of pardoning your sins than you are of pardoning your companion's."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verses 150–151:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and intend to make distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and intend to adopt between that a way.﴾ ﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, spoke about the way of the hypocrites, He returned to speak about the doctrines of the Jews and the Christians and their contradictions, and at the end of this surah He mentioned various kinds of this sort:

The first type: from their falsehoods is their belief in some of the prophets and not others. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾, for the Jews believed in Musa (Moses) and the Torah and disbelieved in ʿIsa (Jesus) and the Injil (Gospel), and the Christians believed in ʿIsa and the Injil and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. ﴿And intend to make distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾, meaning they intend to make distinction between belief in Allah and His messengers. ﴿And intend to adopt between that a way﴾, meaning between belief in all and disbelief in all, a way, i.e., an intermediary, which is belief in some and not others.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

First issue: concerning the predicate of "inna" (indeed) there are two opinions:

One of them: it is omitted, as if it were said, "they have gathered the shameful deeds."

The second: it is His saying ﴿Those are the disbelievers﴾. The first is better for two reasons:

One of them: it is more eloquent, because when the answer is omitted, the imagination goes every way of defect, and when it is mentioned it remains restricted to what is mentioned.

The second: it is the end of the verse (ra's al-ayah), and the best is that the predicate not be separated from the subject.

Second issue: they were disbelievers in truth for two reasons:

The first: the evidence that indicates the prophethood of some is nothing but the miracle (mu'jiz), and when it is evidence of prophethood, it necessarily follows that wherever it occurs, prophethood occurs. If we allow in some cases the occurrence of a miracle without truthfulness, then it becomes impossible to use it as proof of truthfulness, and then disbelief in all the prophets follows. Thus it is established that whoever does not accept the prophethood of any one of them is necessarily a disbeliever in all of them.

If it is said: Grant that disbelief in all the prophets is necessary for them, but it does not follow that when some implications are directed at a person, that person must be one who holds them. So imposing disbelief is one thing, and committing to disbelief is another, and since the people did not commit to that, how can they be judged as disbelievers?

We say: When the implication is hidden, such that it needs thought and reflection, the matter is as you have said. But when it is clear and evident, there is no difference between implication and commitment.

The second: that acceptance of some prophets, if it is for the sake of submission to the obedience and judgment of Allah the Exalted, it obliges acceptance of all, and if it is for seeking leadership, then that is in reality disbelief in all the prophets.

Third issue: concerning His saying (ḥaqqan, "in truth") there are two aspects:

The first: it is in the accusative as in your saying: "Zayd is your brother, truly" (ḥaqqan), the implied meaning being: I have informed you of this meaning with a true information.

The second: the implied meaning is: "Those are the disbelievers in disbelief that is true." Al-Wahidi criticized this and said: disbelief cannot be true in any respect.

The answer: the intended meaning of this "truth" is the complete one, and the meaning is: those are the disbelievers in complete disbelief, established, true with certainty.
