Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the threat, He followed it with the promise, saying: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them, those – He will give them their rewards. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ And there are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Why did He say ﴿do not make distinction between any of them﴾, when distinction (tafriq) requires two or more? The answer is that "aḥad" (any one) is a word that applies equally to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. Two things indicate this:

The first: the validity of the exception (istithna').

The second: the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿You are not like any one of the women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32].

Having understood this, the sense of the verse is: "and do not make distinction between two of them or between a group."

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) have used this verse to establish pardon (al-'afw) and the non-nullification of deeds (ʿadam al-iḥbāṭ). They said: Allah, exalted is He, promised those who believe in Allah and His messengers that He will give them their rewards. What is understood from this is that He will give them their rewards for that belief; otherwise this verse would not be fit to be an encouragement to belief. This necessitates certainty of the non-nullification (of deeds), and certainty of pardon and of bringing them out of the Fire after they have been admitted into it.

The third issue: 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read (yu'tīhim) with the ya' (third person), the pronoun referring to the name of Allah, while the rest read it with the nun (first person plural). The latter is preferable for two reasons:

One of them: it is more majestic (afkham).

The second: it is consistent with His saying (wa-a'tadna), [which is in the first person plural].

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿soon He will give them their rewards﴾ means that giving them is certain to occur, though it may be delayed. The purpose of (sawfa) is to emphasize and confirm the promise, not to indicate that it is delayed.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The meaning is that He promised them the reward, then informed them afterward that He would overlook their misdeeds, pardon them, and forgive them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 153–154:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. But they had asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God openly," so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf after the clear proofs had come to them, yet We pardoned that, and We gave Moses clear authority.﴾ ﴿And We raised the mount above them for their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant.﴾

Know that this is the second kind of the ignorance of the Jews. They said: "If you are a messenger from God, then bring us a Book from heaven all at once, just as Moses brought the tablets." It was also said: they asked that a Book be sent down from heaven to so-and-so and a Book to so-and-so, saying that you are the Messenger of God. It was also said: a Book that we may witness as it is sent down. They proposed this only as a means of obstinacy, because the miracles of the Messenger had already preceded and occurred, so demanding more was a form of obstinacy.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿They had asked Moses for something greater than that.﴾ He attributed the asking to them, although it was their forefathers who did it in the days of Moses, peace be upon him, and they were the seventy chiefs, because they were upon their way, pleased with their request, and alike to them in obstinacy.
Know that the purpose of the verse is to explain the obstinacy with which they were created. It is as if it was said: when a Book was sent down to Moses from heaven, they were not content with that measure, but asked him for vision by way of direct observation. This indicates that the request of these people for a Book to be sent down to them from heaven was not for the sake of seeking guidance, but purely out of stubbornness.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿They had asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God openly," so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing.﴾ This story we have explained in Surah al-Baqarah, and the Mu'tazilah's use of this verse to negate the vision we have answered there.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Then they took the calf after the clear proofs had come to them.﴾ The meaning is to show the completeness of their ignorance and their persistence in disbelief, for after the Torah had been sent down to them, they did not suffice with asking for vision openly, but added to it the worship of the calf, and this indicates the utmost distance of them from seeking the truth and the religion. The meant by "the clear proofs" in His saying: ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾ are several matters:
First: that He, exalted is He, made what He showed them of the thunderbolt to be clear proofs, for the thunderbolt, although it is one thing, indicated the power of God exalted, His knowledge, His eternity, that He is unlike bodies and accidents, and the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him, in his claim to prophethood.

Second: that the meant by the clear proofs is the sending down of the thunderbolt and their being brought back to life after He had caused them to die.

Third: that they only worshipped the calf after they had witnessed the miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, which he displayed in the time of Pharaoh: the staff, the white hand, the splitting of the sea, and other overpowering miracles. The purpose of this speech is that these people, O Muhammad, ask you to send down to them a Book from heaven. Know, O Muhammad, that they ask it of you only out of obstinacy and contentiousness, for God sent down this Book to Moses and sent down to him all the other overpowering miracles. Then they asked for vision by way of obstinacy and turned to the worship of the calf, and all of this indicates that they are created with contentiousness, obstinacy, and distance from the path of truth.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So We pardoned that﴾, meaning: We did not uproot the worshippers of the calf. ﴿And We gave Moses clear authority﴾, meaning: although the people of Moses had gone to extremes in displaying contentiousness and obstinacy with him, yet We helped him and strengthened him, so his affair became great and his opponent weakened. In this there is good news for the Messenger ﷺ by way of alerting, and an allusion that these disbelievers, although they oppose him, in the end he will prevail over them and subdue them. Then He, exalted is He, related from them the rest of their ignorance and their persistence in their falsehoods:
The first of them: that He, exalted is He, raised the mount above them for their covenant, and in this there are several aspects:

The first: that they gave a covenant that they would not turn back from the religion, then they turned back from it and intended to revert, so God raised the mount above them so that they would fear and not break the covenant.

The second: that they refused to accept the law of the Torah, so God raised the mountain above them until they accepted, and the meaning becomes: We raised above them the mount in order that they might give the covenant of accepting the religion.

The third: that they gave the covenant on the basis that if they intended to turn back from the religion, God would punish them with whatever kind of punishment He wished; so when they intended to abandon the religion, God overshadowed them with the mount, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above them for their covenant﴾.

Second: His saying: ﴿And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating"﴾, and its explanation has passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

Third: His saying: ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: ﴿Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, in which there are two views:

The first: Do not transgress by hunting fish on it. Al-Wahidi said: it is said "ʿadā ʿalayhi" with the utmost hostility, enmity, and aggression, meaning he wronged him and exceeded the limit, and from it is His saying: ﴿lest they revile God in enmity﴾ [al-An'am: 108].

The second: Do not transgress on the Sabbath, from "ʿadw" in the sense of attendance (al-hadar), and the meaning is the prohibition of work and earning on Saturday, as if He said to them: remain still from work on this day and sit in your dwellings, for I am the Provider.

The second issue: Nafi' recited "lā taʿaddūn" with a quiescent ʿayn and a shaddah on the dal, and he intended "lā taʿtadū" (do not transgress). His proof is His saying: ﴿And you knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65], so in this very story there came "iftaʿalū" (ifta'alū), then he assimilated the tā' into the dāl because they are close in articulation, and because the dāl is stronger than the tā' in voicing. Many of the grammarians deny the joining of two quiescent letters when the second of them is assimilated and the first is not a letter of softness, such as dābbah and shābbah; and it was said to them, and they say: the lengthening (madd) becomes a substitute for the vowel. Warsh related from Nafi': "lā taʿaddūn" with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shaddah on the dāl, and that is because when he assimilated the tā' into the dāl he moved its vowel to the ʿayn. The rest (read) "taʿdū" with a ḍammah on the dāl and a quiescent ʿayn, in its literal form.

The third issue: al-Qaffal said: the firm covenant (mithaq ghalith) is the covenant strongly confirmed to the utmost degree of confirmation, and this is clear in what they claim from the Torah.

Then He said: ﴿So We pardoned that﴾, meaning: We did not uproot the worshippers of the calf. ﴿And We gave Moses clear authority﴾, meaning: although the people of Moses had gone to extremes in displaying contentiousness and obstinacy with him, yet We helped him and strengthened him, so his affair became great and his opponent weakened. In this there is good news for the Messenger ﷺ by way of alerting, and an allusion that these disbelievers, although they oppose him, in the end he will prevail over them and subdue them. Then He, exalted is He, related from them the rest of their ignorance and their persistence in their falsehoods:
The first of them: that He, exalted is He, raised the mount above them for their covenant, and in this there are several aspects:

The first: that they gave a covenant that they would not turn back from the religion, then they turned back from it and intended to revert, so God raised the mount above them so that they would fear and not break the covenant.

The second: that they refused to accept the law of the Torah, so God raised the mountain above them until they accepted, and the meaning becomes: We raised above them the mount in order that they might give the covenant of accepting the religion.

The third: that they gave the covenant on the basis that if they intended to turn back from the religion, God would punish them with whatever kind of punishment He wished; so when they intended to abandon the religion, God overshadowed them with the mount, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above them for their covenant﴾.

Second: His saying: ﴿And We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating"﴾, and its explanation has passed in Surah al-Baqarah.

Third: His saying: ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a firm covenant﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: ﴿Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾, in which there are two views:

The first: Do not transgress by hunting fish on it. Al-Wahidi said: it is said "ʿadā ʿalayhi" with the utmost hostility, enmity, and aggression, meaning he wronged him and exceeded the limit, and from it is His saying: ﴿lest they revile God in enmity﴾ [al-An'am: 108].

The second: Do not transgress on the Sabbath, from "ʿadw" in the sense of attendance (al-hadar), and the meaning is the prohibition of work and earning on Saturday, as if He said to them: remain still from work on this day and sit in your dwellings, for I am the Provider.

The second issue: Nafi' recited "lā taʿaddūn" with a quiescent ʿayn and a shaddah on the dal, and he intended "lā taʿtadū" (do not transgress). His proof is His saying: ﴿And you knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65], so in this very story there came "iftaʿalū" (ifta'alū), then he assimilated the tā' into the dāl because they are close in articulation, and because the dāl is stronger than the tā' in voicing. Many of the grammarians deny the joining of two quiescent letters when the second of them is assimilated and the first is not a letter of softness, such as dābbah and shābbah; and it was said to them, and they say: the lengthening (madd) becomes a substitute for the vowel. Warsh related from Nafi': "lā taʿaddūn" with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shaddah on the dāl, and that is because when he assimilated the tā' into the dāl he moved its vowel to the ʿayn. The rest (read) "taʿdū" with a ḍammah on the dāl and a quiescent ʿayn, in its literal form.

The third issue: al-Qaffal said: the firm covenant (mithaq ghalith) is the covenant strongly confirmed to the utmost degree of confirmation, and this is clear in what they claim from the Torah.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of God, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are wrapped (ghulf)"﴾.

Regarding this, there are several issues.

**First issue:** Concerning what the "bi" (with/because of) in His words ﴿So for their breaking﴾ governs, there are two opinions.

The first is that it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "So for their breaking of their covenant, and so on, We cursed them and incurred Our wrath upon them." Omission is more emphatic, because when something is omitted the mind goes in every direction. The evidence for the omitted element is that the things mentioned are attributes of blame, which points to the curse.

The second is that what the "bi" governs is His words: ﴿for injustice from those who became Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ (Surah al-Nisa, 160). This is the view of al-Zajjaj, who claimed that His words ﴿for injustice from those who became Jews﴾ are a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿So for their breaking﴾.

Know that the first opinion is preferable, and two points support it:

One: The distance between His words ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾ and His words ﴿for injustice﴾ spans two verses, so making one a substitute for the other is very far-fetched.

Two: The offences mentioned are very grave. Their disbelief in God, their killing of the prophets, and their denial of obligation by saying "Our hearts are wrapped" are among the greatest sins. Mentioning great sins is only fitting when followed by a great punishment, whereas forbidding some foods is a light punishment, so it is not fitting to attach it to these grave offences.

**Second issue:** The scholars agree that the "ma" in His words ﴿So for their breaking﴾ is an extra, redundant particle, and the sense is: "So for their breaking of their covenant." We have examined this matter thoroughly in the commentary on His words ﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran, 159).

**Third issue:** God attached the particle "bi" to several matters:

The first is the breaking of the covenant.

The second is their disbelief in the signs of God. What is meant is their disbelief in the miracles. We have already explained that whoever denies the miracle of one messenger has denied the miracles of all the messengers. For this reason God judged them to be disbelievers in the signs of God.

The third is their killing of the prophets without right, and we have explained its interpretation in Surah al-Baqarah.

The fourth is their saying ﴿Our hearts are wrapped﴾. Al-Qaffal mentioned two possibilities regarding this:

One: that "ghulf" is the plural of "ghilaf" (covering), and the original form is "ghulufun" with the lam vowelled, which was lightened by sukun, just as it is said "kutb" and "rusl" with the ta and sin made quiescent. The meaning according to this is that they said, "Our hearts are wrapped," that is, they are receptacles for knowledge, so we have no need of any knowledge other than what we have. Thus they denied the prophets by this statement.

The second: that "ghulf" is the plural of "aghlaf," which means one covered with a wrapping, that is, with a covering. The meaning according to this is that they said, "Our hearts are in coverings, so they do not understand what you say." A parallel to this is what God related in His words: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier"﴾ (Surah Fussilat, 5).

* *
* * *

Then God said: ﴿Rather, God has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾.

If we take the preceding verse according to the first interpretation, the meaning of this verse is that God refuted their claim that their hearts are receptacles for knowledge, and explained that He sealed them and set a seal upon them, so the effect of the call and the clarification does not reach them. This fits our school (madhhab). If we take the preceding verse according to the second interpretation, the meaning of this verse is that God refuted their claim that their hearts are in coverings and wrappings. This fits the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. However, the first interpretation is preferable, and it is the one that matches His words: ﴿Rather, God has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾, that is, they do not believe except in Moses and the Torah. This is a report from them according to their own claim and assertion. Otherwise, we have explained that whoever disbelieves in one messenger and one miracle cannot possibly believe in any of the messengers at all.

Fifth: His words ﴿and their disbelief, and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾.

Know that when they attributed fornication to Mary, because they denied God's power to create a child without a father, and whoever denies God's power to do that is a disbeliever, since it necessarily follows that every child born is preceded by a parent without any first, and that entails the belief in the eternity of the world and of time, and a disparagement of the existence of the Creator who chooses. Without doubt, these people:

First: denied God's power to create a child without a father.

Second: attributed fornication to Mary.

So what is meant by His words ﴿and their disbelief﴾ is their denial of God's power, and by His words ﴿and their saying against Mary a tremendous slander﴾ is their attribution of fornication to her. Since the two are distinct, the conjunction is appropriate. This accusation became a "tremendous slander" because at the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, there appeared miracles and marvels that showed her innocence of every defect, such as His words ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates﴾ (Surah Maryam, 25), and such as the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, while he was an infant separated from his mother. All of these are decisive proofs of Mary's innocence, peace be upon her, from every suspicion. Therefore God described the Jews' accusation against her as a tremendous slander. Likewise, He described the hypocrites' accusation against 'A'isha as a tremendous slander, when He said: ﴿Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 16). This indicates that the Rafidah, who slander 'A'isha, stand in the same position as the Jews who slander Mary, peace be upon her.

Sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah"﴾.

This indicates a great disbelief on their part, because they said, "We did that," and this indicates that they were eager to kill him and striving to do so. There is no doubt that this degree alone is great disbelief.

If it is said: The Jews were disbelievers in 'Isa, his enemies, intending to kill him. They called him "the sorcerer, son of a sorceress" and "the doer, son of the doer [of evil]." So how could they say, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah"?

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: They said it in mockery, like the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 27], and like the saying of the disbelievers of Quraysh to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6].

The second: It is possible that Allah placed a good mention in place of their ugly mention in relating their words, elevating 'Isa (peace be upon him) above what they used to say about him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, related from the Jews that they claimed they had killed 'Isa (peace be upon him), Allah refuted them in this claim and said: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.﴾ There are two questions regarding the verse:

The first question: The verb ﴿shubbiha﴾ (it was made to appear) is attributed to what? If you attribute it to the Messiah, then he is the one being made to resemble, not the one resembled. If you attribute it to the one killed, then the one killed has not been previously mentioned.

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: It is attributed to the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur), and it is like your saying: "It was imagined to him" (khuyyila ilayhi). As if it was said: "But resemblance occurred to them."

The second: It is attributed to the pronoun of the one killed, because His saying, ﴿They did not kill him﴾, indicates that the killing fell upon another, so that other became mentioned by this means, and so it was good to attribute ﴿shubbiha﴾ to him.

The second question: If it is permissible to say that Allah, exalted is He, casts the likeness of one person upon another person, this opens the door to sophistry (safsata). For when we see Zayd, perhaps he is not Zayd, but the likeness of Zayd was cast upon him. At that point marriage, divorce, and ownership would no longer be trustworthy. Also, it leads to casting doubt on tawatur (mass transmission of reports), because the report of tawatur only yields knowledge on the condition that its chain ends, in the final analysis, at what is perceived by the senses. If we permit the occurrence of such a confusion in sensory matters, then criticism of tawatur is directed, and that necessitates casting doubt on all the sharia. The respondent cannot answer this by saying that this is specific to the time of the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them), because we say: Even if what you mentioned is correct, that is known only through proof and demonstration. Whoever does not know that proof and that demonstration must not be certain of anything in sensory matters, and must not rely on any of the mass-transmitted reports. Furthermore, in our time, if miracles have ceased, the path of karamat (saintly wonders) remains open, and then the aforementioned possibility returns in all eras. In sum, opening this door necessitates casting doubt on tawatur, and casting doubt on it necessitates casting doubt on the prophethood of all the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them). This is a branch that entails casting doubt on the foundations, so it is rejected.

The answer: The positions of the scholars differed on this matter and they mentioned several views:

The first: Many of the theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: When the Jews intended to kill him, Allah, exalted is He, raised him to the heavens. The leaders of the Jews feared that strife would arise among their common folk, so they took a man, killed him, crucified him, and deceived the people into thinking that he was the Messiah. The people did not know the Messiah except by name, because he had little contact with people. By this means the question is resolved. It cannot be said that the Christians transmit from their predecessors that they witnessed him killed, because we say: The tawatur of the Christians ends at a small number of people, and it is not unlikely that they agreed upon a lie.

The second way: He, exalted is He, cast his likeness upon another person, and then there are several views on this:

The first: When the Jews knew that he was present in such-and-such house with his companions, Yahudha, the head of the Jews, ordered a man from among his companions called Tayṭayus to enter upon 'Isa (peace be upon him) and bring him out to kill him. When he entered upon him, Allah brought 'Isa (peace be upon him) out through the roof of the house and cast the likeness of 'Isa upon that man, so they thought he was him and crucified and killed him.

The second: They appointed a man to guard 'Isa, and 'Isa (peace be upon him) went up into the mountain and was raised to the heavens. Allah cast his likeness upon that guard, so they killed him while he was saying, "I am not 'Isa."

The third: When the Jews were determined to seize him, there were ten of his companions with 'Isa. He said to them: "Who will buy Paradise by having my likeness cast upon him?" One of them said, "I will." So Allah cast the likeness of 'Isa upon him, and he was brought out and killed, and Allah raised 'Isa (peace be upon him).

The fourth: There was a man who claimed that he was one of the companions of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and he was a hypocrite. He went to the Jews and guided them to him. When he entered with the Jews to seize him, Allah, exalted is He, cast his likeness upon him, so he was killed and crucified. These views are conflicting and contradictory, and Allah knows best the realities of matters.

* *
* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾. In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Know that in His saying, ﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning him﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: They are the Christians, because they all agree that the Jews killed him, except that the major Christian sects are three: the Nestorians (al-Nusturiyya), the Melkites (al-Malkaniyya), and the Jacobites (al-Ya'qubiyya).

As for the Nestorians, they claimed that the Messiah was crucified with respect to his humanity (nasut), not with respect to his divinity (lahut). Most of the philosophers hold a view close to this, and they said: Because it has been established that the human being is not a reference to this physical frame; rather, he is either a noble body that flows through this body, or a spiritual substance that is essentially immaterial and governs this body. So the killing fell upon this frame, but the soul, which in reality is 'Isa (peace be upon him), was not touched by the killing. It cannot be said: "Every human being is like that, so what is the point of this specification?" Because we say: His soul was holy, supernal, heavenly, intensely radiant with divine lights, and greatly close to the spirits of the angels. When the soul is like that, its suffering from killing and the destruction of the body does not become great. Then, after separating from the darkness of the body, it escapes into the expanse of the heavens and the lights of the world of majesty, and its joy and happiness there become great. It is known that these states are not attained by all people; rather, from the beginning of the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) until the Day of Resurrection, they are attained only by a few individuals. This is the purpose of specifying 'Isa (peace be upon him) with this condition.

As for the Melkites, they said: The killing and crucifixion reached the divinity (lahut) through perception and awareness, not through direct contact. The Jacobites said: The killing and crucifixion fell upon the Messiah, who is a substance produced from two substances. This is the explanation of the views of the Christians on this subject, and it is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning him are in doubt about it﴾.

The second opinion: The intended meaning of "those who differed" is the Jews, and in this there are two views:

The first: When they killed the person who was made to resemble him, the likeness had been cast upon his face, and the likeness of 'Isa's body had not been cast upon him. So when they killed him and looked at his body, they said: "The face is the face of 'Isa, but the body is the body of another."

The second: Al-Suddi said: The Jews imprisoned 'Isa together with ten of the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) in a house. A man from the Jews entered upon them to bring him out and kill him, so Allah cast the likeness of 'Isa upon him, and 'Isa was raised to the heavens. They took that man and killed him, thinking he was 'Isa (peace be upon him). Then they said: "If this is 'Isa, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is 'Isa?" That is their disagreement about him.

The second issue: Those who reject qiyas (analogical reasoning) (nufat al-qiyas) used this verse as evidence and said: Acting on qiyas is following assumption (zann), and following assumption is blameworthy in the Book of Allah, by evidence that it is mentioned only in the context of blame. Do you not see that He, exalted is He, described the Jews and the Christians here in the context of blame with this, saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾? He also said in Surat al-An'am, in censure of the disbelievers: ﴿They follow nothing but assumption, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116], and He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, assumption does not avail against the truth at all﴾ [Yunus: 36]. All of this indicates that following assumption is blameworthy.

The answer: We do not concede that acting on qiyas is following assumption, because when a decisive proof has indicated the acting upon qiyas, the ruling derived from qiyas is known, not merely assumed. This discussion has depth and there is a debate in it.

* *
* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾ ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾.

Know that this expression may bear two meanings:

One of them: the certainty of the non-killing. The other: the certainty of the non-doing. On the first interpretation the meaning is: He, exalted is He, informed that they were doubtful as to whether they had killed him or not. Then He informed Muhammad that certainty has been reached that they did not kill him. On the second interpretation the meaning is: They were doubtful as to whether they had killed him himself. Then He emphasized that by saying that they killed that person, but not with certainty that he was 'Isa (peace be upon him); rather, when they killed him they were doubtful whether he was 'Isa or not. The first possibility is preferable, because He, exalted is He, said after it, ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾, and this statement is valid only if certainty and conviction of the non-killing preceded it.

As for His saying, ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read ﴿bal rafa'ahu Allahu ilayhi﴾ with the assimilation (idgham) of the lam into the ra' (in the word bal), while the rest read without assimilation. The argument of the two is the closeness of the articulation point of the lam to that of the ra', and the ra' is stronger than the lam by virtue of the trill (takrir) in it. For this reason it is not permitted to assimilate the ra' into the lam, because the less (in strength) is assimilated into the more (in strength). The argument of the others is that the ra' and the lam are two letters from two words, so leaving assimilation is preferable.

The second issue: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) argued from His saying, ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾, in proving a direction (jiha).

The answer: The intended meaning is raising to a place in which the judgment of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He, does not apply, as in His saying: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 100]. The migration at that time was to Medina. And Ibrahim said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99].

The third issue: The raising of 'Isa (peace be upon him) to the heavens is established by this verse. A parallel to this verse is His saying in Al 'Imran: ﴿Indeed, I will cause you to die and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55]. Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned, following what He had explained of the many kinds of trial and affliction that reached 'Isa, that He raised him to Himself, this indicates that his being raised to Him is greater in terms of reward than Paradise and all the bodily pleasures in it. This verse opens for you the door to knowing the spiritual felicities.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And God is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾

By "might" (ʿizzah) is meant perfection of power, and by "wisdom" (ḥikmah) perfection of knowledge. Thereby He draws attention to the fact that the raising of ʿIsa from this world to the heavens, although it seems beyond the reach of humans, is not beyond reach with respect to My power and My wisdom. This is similar to His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1], for the Night Journey (al-isra'), although it is beyond the reach of Muhammad's power, is easy with respect to the power of the True One, glorified be He.

* * *

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾

Know that when Almighty God mentioned the disgraceful acts of the Jews and the ugliness of their deeds, and explained that they intended to kill ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and clarified that they did not achieve that aim, while ʿIsa attained the greatest of ranks and the most exalted of stations, He explained that these Jews, who were extremely hostile towards him, would not leave this world except after believing in him. So He said: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death.﴾

Know that the word (in) here carries the meaning of the negative (ma), as in His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71]. So the sense becomes: "There is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him." Yet we see that most Jews die without believing in ʿIsa (peace be upon him).

The answer comes in two ways:

The first: It is narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab who said: al-Hajjaj said: "I have never recited it except that something troubles me within myself about it," meaning this verse, "for I strike the neck of a Jew and do not hear that from him." So I said: "When death comes to the Jew, the angels strike his face and his back, and say: 'O enemy of God, ʿIsa came to you as a prophet and you denied him.' He then says: 'I believe that he is the servant of God.' And you say to the Christian: 'ʿIsa came to you as a prophet and you claimed that he is God and the son of God.' He says: 'I believe that he is the servant of God.' So the People of the Book believe in him, but at a time when that belief does not benefit them." Al-Hajjaj sat upright and said: "From whom did you transmit this?" I said: "Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Hanafiyyah narrated it to me." He began tapping the ground with a stick and then said: "You have taken it from a clear spring." It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he interpreted it in this way. ʿIkrimah said to him: "What if he falls from the roof of a house, or burns, or is eaten by a beast?" He said: "He speaks it in the air, and his soul does not leave until he believes in him." This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: (illa la-yu'minunna bihi qabla mawtihi) with a ḍammah on the nūn, meaning: "And there is none of them but they will surely believe in him before their death," because "ahad" (anyone) applies to the whole group. The author of al-Kashshaf said: The benefit of God's informing us of their belief in ʿIsa before their death is that, since they know that belief in him is inevitable, believing in him at a time when that belief will benefit them is better than believing in him at a time when it will not benefit them.

The second answer, concerning the root of the question: His saying "before his death" means before the death of ʿIsa, and the intention is that the People of the Book who are alive at the time of his descent will necessarily believe in him. Some theologians said: His descent from heaven to the world is not prevented, but he will descend only when the obligations are lifted, or in such a way that he is not recognised. For if he descended while the obligations remained, in a manner by which it is recognised that he is ʿIsa (peace be upon him), then he would either be a prophet, and there is no prophet after Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), or not a prophet, and that is impermissible for prophets. But this difficulty seems weak to me, because the line of prophets ended with the mission of Muhammad ﷺ; at his mission that period came to an end, so it is not far-fetched that after his descent he becomes a follower of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him).

* * *

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.﴾ It has been said: he will bear witness against the Jews that they denied him and reviled him, and against the Christians that they associated partners with him. Likewise every prophet is a witness over his nation.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And God is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾

By "might" (ʿizzah) is meant perfection of power, and by "wisdom" (ḥikmah) perfection of knowledge. Thereby He draws attention to the fact that the raising of ʿIsa from this world to the heavens, although it seems beyond the reach of humans, is not beyond reach with respect to My power and My wisdom. This is similar to His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1], for the Night Journey (al-isra'), although it is beyond the reach of Muhammad's power, is easy with respect to the power of the True One, glorified be He.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them, and because of their hindering many from the way of Allah, and their taking of usury though they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the disgraceful deeds of the Jews and the ugly acts of the disbelievers, He mentioned after it His severity toward them in this world and in the Hereafter. As for His severity toward them in this world, it is that He, exalted is He, forbade them good things that had been lawful for them before that, as He said in another place: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs or their entrails carry, or what is mixed with bone. That is how We requited them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful.﴾ [al-An'am: 146]. Then He, exalted is He, explained what is like the effective cause (al-'illah al-mujibah) of these severities.

واعلم أنه تعالى لما وصف طريقة الكفار والجهال من اليهود، وصف طريقة المؤمنين منهم، فقال: ﴿لكن الراسخون في العلم منهم والمؤمنون يؤمنون بما أُنزل إليك وما أُنزل من قبلك والمقيمين الصلاة والمؤتون الزكاة والمؤمنون بالله واليوم الآخر أولئك سنؤتيهم أجرًا عظيمًا﴾.

صفحة ٨٤

وفي الآية مسائل:

المسألة الأولى: اعلم أن المراد من ذلك عبد الله بن سلام وأصحابه، الراسخون في العلم الثابتون فيه. وهم في الحقيقة المستدلون، بأن المقلد يكون بحيث إذا شُكِّك يَشُكّ، وأما المستدل فإنه لا يتشكك البتة. فالراسخون هم المستدلون. والمؤمنون، يعني المؤمنين منهم، أو المؤمنين من المهاجرين والأنصار. وارتفع الراسخون على الابتداء (mubtada’, subject)، و(يؤمنون) خبره (khabar, predicate). وأما قوله: ﴿والمقيمين الصلاة والمؤتون الزكاة﴾ ففيه أقوال:

الأول: رُوي عن عثمان وعائشة أنهما قالا: إن في المصحف لحنًا، وستقيمه العرب بألسنتها.

واعلم أن هذا بعيد، لأن هذا المصحف منقول بالنقل المتواتر عن رسول الله ﷺ، فكيف يمكن ثبوت اللحن فيه؟

الثاني: وهو قول البصريين: إنه نُصب على المدح (madh, praise) لبيان فضل الصلاة. قالوا: إذا قلت: مررتُ بزيدٍ الكريمِ، فلك أن تجرّ الكريمَ لكونه صفةً لزيد، ولك أن تنصبه على تقدير (أعني)، وإن شئت رفعتَ على تقدير (هو الكريم). وعلى هذا يُقال: جاءني قومُكَ المُطعِمين في المَحَل والمُغيثون في الشدائد، والتقدير: جاءني قومك، أعني المُطعِمين في المحل، وهم المُغيثون في الشدائد. فكذا ههنا، تقدير الآية: أعني المقيمين الصلاة، وهم المؤتون الزكاة. طعن الكسائي في هذا القول وقال: النصب على المدح إنما يكون بعد تمام الكلام، وههنا لم يتم الكلام، لأن قوله: ﴿لكن الراسخون في العلم﴾ منتظرٌ للخبر، والخبر هو قوله: ﴿أولئك سنؤتيهم أجرًا عظيمًا﴾.

والجواب: لا نسلّم أن الكلام لا يتم إلا عند قوله: (أولئك)، لأنا بيّنا أن الخبر هو قوله: (يؤمنون). وأيضًا، لِمَ لا يجوز الاعتراض بالمدح بين الاسم والخبر؟ وما الدليل على امتناعه؟ فهذا القول هو المعتمد في هذه الآية.

والقول الثالث: وهو اختيار الكسائي، وهو أن (المقيمين) مخفوض بالعطف على (ما) في قوله: ﴿بما أُنزل إليك وما أُنزل من قبلك﴾، والمعنى: والمؤمنون يؤمنون بما أُنزل إليك وما أُنزل من قبلك، وبالمقيمين الصلاة. ثم عطف على قوله: (والمؤمنون) قوله: ﴿والمؤتون الزكاة﴾. والمراد بالمقيمين الصلاة الأنبياء، وذلك لأنه لم يخلُ شرعُ أحدٍ منهم من الصلاة. قال تعالى في سورة الأنبياء، عليهم الصلاة والسلام، بعد أن ذكر أعدادًا منهم: ﴿وأوحينا إليهم فعل الخيرات وإقام الصلاة﴾ [الأنبياء: ٧٣]. وقيل: المراد بالمقيمين الصلاة الملائكة، الذين وصفهم الله بأنهم الصافّون، وهم المسبّحون، وأنهم يسبّحون الليل والنهار لا يفترون. فقوله: ﴿يؤمنون بما أُنزل إليك وما أُنزل من قبلك﴾ يعني: يؤمنون بالكتب، وقوله: ﴿والمقيمين الصلاة﴾ يؤمنون بالرسل.

الرابع: جاء في مصحف عبد الله بن مسعود: "والمقيمون الصلاة" بالواو، وهي قراءة مالك بن دينار والجحدري وعيسى الثقفي.

المسألة الثانية: اعلم أن العلماء على ثلاثة أقسام:

الأول: العلماء بأحكام الله تعالى فقط.

والثاني: العلماء بذات الله وصفات الله فقط.

والثالث: العلماء بأحكام الله وبذات الله. أما الفريق الأول فهم العالمون بأحكام الله وتكاليفه وشرائعه.

وأما الثاني: فهم العالمون بذات الله وبصفاته الواجبة والجائزة والممتنعة.

وأما الثالث: فهم الموصوفون بالعاملين، وهم أكابر العلماء. وإلى هذه الأقسام الثلاثة أشار النبي ﷺ بقوله: "جالِس العلماءَ، وخالِط الحكماءَ، ورافِق الكُبَراءَ".

وإذا عرفتَ هذا فنقول: إنه تعالى وصفهم

صفحة ٨٥

بكونهم راسخين في العلم، ثم شرح ذلك فبيّن أولًا: كونهم عالمين بأحكام الله تعالى، وعاملين بتلك الأحكام. فأما علمهم بأحكام الله فهو المراد من قوله: ﴿والمؤمنون يؤمنون بما أُنزل إليك وما أُنزل من قبلك﴾، وأما عملهم بتلك الأحكام فهو المراد بقوله: ﴿والمقيمين الصلاة والمؤتون الزكاة﴾. وخصّهما بالذكر لكونهما أشرف الطاعات، لأن الصلاة أشرف الطاعات البدنية، والزكاة أشرف الطاعات المالية. ولما شرح كونهم عالمين بأحكام الله وعاملين بها، شرح بعد ذلك كونهم عالمين بالله، وأشرف المعارف العلمُ بالمبدأ والمعاد. فالعلم بالمبدأ هو المراد بقوله: ﴿والمؤمنون بالله﴾، والعلم بالمعاد هو المراد من قوله: ﴿واليوم الآخر﴾. ولما شرح هذه الأقسام ظهر كونُ هؤلاء المذكورين عالمين بأحكام الله تعالى وعاملين بها، وظهر كونُهم عالمين بالله وبأحوال المعاد. وإذا حصلت هذه العلوم والمعارف ظهر كونهم راسخين في العلم، لأن الإنسان لا يمكنه أن يتجاوز هذا المقام في الكمال وعلوّ الدرجة. ثم أخبر عنهم بقوله: ﴿أولئك سنؤتيهم أجرًا عظيمًا﴾.

**[p. 86]**

Allah Most High says: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.﴾ ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses directly.﴾ ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah Most High related that the Jews asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to send down to them a book from the heaven, and then mentioned after that they did not ask for this in order to be guided but out of obstinacy and stubbornness, and related many kinds of their disgraceful and ugly conduct, and the discourse extended to this point, He now began to answer that doubt, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ The meaning is: We agree on the prophethood of Noah, Abraham, Ishmael and all those mentioned in this verse, and that Allah revealed to them. There is no way to know that they were prophets and messengers of Allah except through the manifestation of miracles upon them, and each one of them had a different kind of miracle specifically. Allah did not send down to each of these mentioned a complete book like what He sent down to Moses. Since the non-descent of a book upon these all at once did not invalidate their prophethood, rather the manifestation of one kind of miracle upon them was sufficient to establish their prophethood, we know that this doubt is void, and that the Jews' insistence on demanding this miracle is false. The clarification of this matter is that the establishment of the signified depends on the establishment of the evidence. Then, when the evidence has been obtained and is complete, demanding another evidence is a request for more and a display of obstinacy and stubbornness. Allah, glorified and exalted, does what He wills and decides what He intends, so no one has the right to object to Him by asking why He gave this messenger this miracle and that other messenger a different miracle. This answer mentioned here is the answer mentioned in His saying: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra' 90] up to His saying: ﴿Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra' 93], meaning: you only claimed to be a messenger, and a messenger necessarily has a miracle that indicates his truthfulness, and that has been achieved. As for bringing everything that is demanded from you, that is not a condition of messengerhood. This is a well-founded answer to the doubt the Jews raised, and it is the principal purpose of this verse.

**The second issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: *al-Iyha'* (revelation) is informing in a hidden manner. Allah Most High says: ﴿So he signaled to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 11], meaning he gestured to them. And He said: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples: "Believe in Me"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 111], and He said: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ [al-Nahl 68], and ﴿We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ [al-Qasas 7]. The intended meaning of revelation in these three verses is *al-ilham* (inspiration).

**The third issue:** They said: Allah Most High only began with mentioning Noah because he was the first prophet upon whose tongue Allah legislated the rulings, the lawful and the unlawful. Then He said: ﴿and the prophets after him﴾. Then He singled out some of the prophets for mention because they are superior to others, like His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah 98].

Know that the prophets mentioned in this verse, apart from Moses (peace be upon him), are twelve, and Moses was not mentioned with them. That is because the Jews said: "If you are a prophet, O Muhammad, bring us a book from the heaven all at once, as Moses (peace be upon him) brought the Torah all at once." So Allah Most High answered this doubt by stating that these twelve prophets were all prophets and messengers, although not one of them brought a book like the Torah all at once. Then He concluded the mention of the prophets with His saying: ﴿And to David We gave the Psalms﴾, meaning: you have acknowledged that the Psalms are from Allah. Yet it was not sent down to David all at once on tablets, as the Torah was sent down to Moses (peace be upon him) all at once on the tablets. This shows that the descent of a book not in the manner in which the Torah descended does not impair the book being from Allah. This is a strong and fine argument.

**The fourth issue:** The people of linguistics said: *al-Zabur* is the book, and every book is a *zabur*. It is on the pattern *fa'ul* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like *al-rasul* (messenger), *al-rakub* (what is ridden) and *al-halub* (what is milked). Its root is from *zabartu*, meaning "I wrote." We have already mentioned what is related to it at His saying: ﴿with clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ [Al 'Imran 184].

**The fifth issue:** Hamzah recited *zuburan* (زَبُورًا) with a *dammah* on the *zay* throughout the Qur'an, and the rest recited it with a *fathah*. Hamzah's argument is that *al-zabur* is originally a verbal noun (*masdar*), then it was used in the sense of the object, as in their saying *darb al-amir* ("the Amir's striking") and *nasj fulan* ("so-and-so's weaving"), so it became a noun, then it was pluralized as *zubur*, like *shuhud* and *shuhud* (witnesses). When a verbal noun is used in place of the object, its plural may be formed, just as *kitab* is pluralized as *kutub*. Accordingly, *al-zabur* is the book, and *al-zubur* with a *dammah* on the *zay* means the books. As for the recitation of the rest, it is preferable because it is more widely known, and its recitation is more common.

* * *

Then Allah Most High said: ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you.﴾

**[p. 87]**

Know that the words *rusulan* (رُسُلًا, "messengers") is in the accusative case by an implied verb that is explained by His saying: ﴿We have related to you﴾. The meaning is that He Most High only mentioned the states of some of the prophets in the Qur'an, while most of them are not mentioned in detail.

* * *

**[p. 86]**

Allah Most High says: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah Most High related that the Jews asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to send down to them a book from the heaven, and then mentioned after that they did not ask for this in order to be guided but out of obstinacy and stubbornness, and related many kinds of their disgraceful and ugly conduct, and the discourse extended to this point, He now began to answer that doubt, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ The meaning is: We agree on the prophethood of Noah, Abraham, Ishmael and all those mentioned in this verse, and that Allah revealed to them. There is no way to know that they were prophets and messengers of Allah except through the manifestation of miracles upon them, and each one of them had a different kind of miracle specifically. Allah did not send down to each of these mentioned a complete book like what He sent down to Moses. Since the non-descent of a book upon these all at once did not invalidate their prophethood, rather the manifestation of one kind of miracle upon them was sufficient to establish their prophethood, we know that this doubt is void, and that the Jews' insistence on demanding this miracle is false. The clarification of this matter is that the establishment of the signified depends on the establishment of the evidence. Then, when the evidence has been obtained and is complete, demanding another evidence is a request for more and a display of obstinacy and stubbornness. Accordingly, *al-zabur* is the book, and *al-zubur* with a *dammah* on the *zay* means the books. As for the recitation of the rest, it is preferable because it is more widely known, and its recitation is more common.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 166:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And Allah suffices as a witness.﴾

There are two issues in this verse.

The first issue: Know that the word "lakin" (but) is not used to begin a sentence, because it signals istidrak (a correction or qualification of what came before). Regarding what this correction addresses, there are two opinions.

The first: all of these verses are a reply to His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾ [An-Nisa' 153]. This statement implies that this Qur'an is not a book sent down to them from heaven. So it is as if it were said: even though they testify that the Qur'an was not sent down to him from heaven, yet Allah bears witness that it was sent down to him from heaven.

The second: when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾, the people said: "We do not bear witness to you concerning that." So ﴿But Allah bears witness﴾ was revealed.

The second issue: the witness of Allah is known through the fact that He sent down to him this Qur'an, which reached such a height of eloquence in wording and nobility in meaning that the first and the last (of mankind) were unable to produce its equal. This was therefore a miracle (mu'jiz), and the manifestation of a miracle is a testimony that the one claiming (prophethood) is truthful. Since His witness was known only through the sending down of the Qur'an, He therefore said: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾, meaning: He bears witness for you to prophethood through this Qur'an which He has sent down to you.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾, and concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: when He said: ﴿bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾, He explained the nature of that sending down, namely that He sent it down with perfect knowledge and far-reaching wisdom. Thus His saying ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ functions like the speech of one who says: "I wrote with the pen" and "I cut with the knife." What is meant by His saying ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ is the description of the Qur'an as possessing utmost excellence and ultimate perfection. This is similar to what is said of a man renowned for perfection of virtue and knowledge, when he composes a book and thoroughly perfects its writing: "He composed this only with the perfection of his knowledge and virtue," meaning that he took the totality of his sciences as an instrument and means to composing this book. This indicates that the composition is described as having utmost goodness and ultimate beauty. So it is here as well, and Allah knows best.

Page 89

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: the verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, has knowledge ('ilm), because it establishes the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. Had His knowledge been identical with His essence, it would necessitate attributing a thing to itself, which is impossible.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and the angels bear witness﴾. The angels' witness to him is known through this: the manifestation of a miracle at his hand indicates that Allah, exalted is He, has witnessed to his prophethood. And when Allah has witnessed to that, the angels have inevitably also witnessed to it, because it is established in the Qur'an that they do not precede Him in speech. The meaning is as if it were said: "O Muhammad, if these Jews deny you, do not care about them, for Allah, exalted is He, the Lord of the worlds, confirms you in this, and the angels of the seven heavens confirm you in this. Whoever is confirmed by the Lord of the worlds and by the angels of the Throne, the Chair and all seven heavens, does not heed the denial of the basest of people, who are these Jews."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾. The meaning is: "And Allah suffices as a witness," and the discussion of such a construction has already preceded.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 167–169:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and commit wrong – Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path,﴾ ﴿except the path of Hell, wherein they will abide forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾

Know that this is one of the attributes of the Jews who were mentioned earlier. The meaning is that they disbelieved in Muhammad and in the Qur'an, and they barred others from the way of Allah, by casting doubts into their hearts, such as their saying: "If he were a messenger, he would have brought his Book all at once from the heaven, just as the Torah was revealed to Moses," and their saying: "Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the Torah that the law of Moses will not be changed or abrogated until the Day of Resurrection," and their saying: "Prophets only come from the offspring of Aaron and David." And His saying: ﴿They have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ This is because the most astray of people is one who is in error while believing himself to be right, then he uses that error to acquire wealth and status, and then he exerts his utmost effort to cast others into the same error. Such a person has undoubtedly reached the furthest extreme of error and the greatest of ends. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said concerning them: ﴿They have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ When He, exalted is He, described the manner of their going astray, He mentioned after it their threat, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and commit wrong﴾ – [wrong toward] Muhammad by concealing the mention of his mission, and wronging their common folk by casting doubts into their hearts – ﴿Allah will never forgive them.﴾

And know that if we take His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ as referring to the previously known [group], there is no need to supply a condition in this threat, because we understand the threat in the verse as applying to peoples whom Allah knew would die in disbelief. If we take it as general (al-istighraq, encompassing all disbelievers), we supply within it the condition of not repenting. Then He said: ﴿nor will He guide them to a path,﴾ ﴿except the path of Hell.﴾

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿wherein they will abide forever.﴾ The meaning is that He, exalted is He, will not guide them on the Day of Resurrection to Paradise, but rather will guide them to the path of Hell. ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ Khalidin (abiding) is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl), and its governing element (al-‘amil) is the sense of "li-yahdiyahum" (to guide them), because it is in the position of "We will punish them, abiding [therein]." And abadan (forever) is in the accusative as an adverb of time. ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ The meaning is that nothing is impossible for Him, so delivering pain to them, one thing after another without end, is easy for Him, even though it is impossible for others.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 170:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had answered the doubt of the Jews in many ways and had explained the corruption of their way, He mentioned a general address that encompasses them and encompasses others, concerning the call to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord.﴾ And this "truth" has two aspects:

The first: that he came with the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is miraculous, so it necessarily follows that he came with the truth from his Lord.

The second: that he came with the call to worship Allah and to turn away from other than Him, and reason indicates that this is the truth, so it necessarily follows that he came with the truth from his Lord.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So believe; it is better for you.﴾ That is: believe, and that belief will be better for you than what you are in, that is, more praiseworthy in its outcome than disbelief. ﴿But if you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need from your belief, because He is the Owner of the heavens and the earth and their Creator, and whoever is like this is not in need of anything.﴾ It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth,﴾ and whoever is like this is capable of sending down severe punishment upon you if you disbelieve. It is also possible that the meaning is: that if you disbelieve, then to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and He has servants who worship Him and submit to His command and judgment.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise.﴾ That is: Knowing, nothing of the deeds of His servants, the believers and the disbelievers, is hidden from Him; and Wise, He does not waste the work of any worker among them, nor does He equate the believer with the disbeliever, or the evildoer with the doer of good. This is like His saying: ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 4, verse 171–173:

Page 91

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a spirit from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, "Three"; desist – it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels who are near [to Him]. And whoever disdains from His worship and is arrogant – He will gather them to Himself all together.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and will increase them from His bounty. But as for those who disdained and were arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment. And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any ally or any helper.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had answered the doubts of the Jews, He then spoke in this verse with the Christians. The implied sense is: "O People of the Scripture, [i.e., the Christians], do not commit excess in your religion," that is, do not go to extremes in exalting the Messiah. This is because He, exalted is He, related that the Jews exaggerate in disparaging the Messiah, while these Christians exaggerate in exalting him, and both extremes of their approach are blameworthy. Therefore He said to the Christians: ﴿do not commit excess in your religion﴾. His saying: ﴿and do not say about Allah except the truth﴾ means: do not describe Allah as indwelling or uniting with the body or soul of a human being, and declare Him free of these states. Having prohibited them from the path of excess, He guided them to the path of truth, which is that the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, is a messenger of Allah and His servant.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and His word which He directed to Mary﴾.
Know that we explained "the word" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], and the meaning is that he came into being by the word of Allah and His command, without intermediary and without a drop of semen, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. As for His saying: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: It is the custom of people that when they describe something with the utmost purity and cleanliness, they say that it is a spirit. Since Jesus was not formed from the semen of a father but was formed from the breath of Jibril – peace be upon him – he was therefore described as a spirit. The word "from Him" (minhu) expresses honour and distinction, just as one says: "This is a blessing from Allah," meaning that this blessing is complete and noble.

The second: He was a means of life for creation in their religions, and whoever is like that is described as a spirit. He, exalted is He, said in describing the Qur'an: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [ash-Shura: 52].

The third: "A spirit from Him" means a mercy from Him. It was said in explaining His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He supported them with a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22], meaning with a mercy from Him. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I am only a mercy sent as a gift." So since Jesus was a mercy from Allah upon creation, in that he guided them to their interests in their religion and their worldly affairs, he was therefore named a spirit from Him.

The fourth: The spirit (ruh) in the speech of the Arabs means breath, for ruh and rih (wind) are close in meaning. Thus "the spirit" is an expression for the breath of Jibril, and His saying "from Him" means that this breathing from Jibril was by the command and permission of Allah, and so it is "from Him." This is like His saying: ﴿So We breathed into it from Our spirit﴾.

The fifth: His saying "a spirit" (ruhun) introduces indefiniteness into the word "spirit," and that indicates glorification. So the meaning becomes: "and a spirit among the noble, holy, and exalted spirits." His saying "from Him" is an attribution of that spirit to Himself for the sake of honour and exaltation.

Page 92

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, meaning: Jesus is among the messengers of Allah, so believe in him just as you believe in all the other messengers, and do not make him a god.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not say, "Three"; desist – it is better for you﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The meaning is: "Do not say that Allah, exalted is He, is one in essence and three in hypostases (aqanim)."

Know that the doctrine of the Christians is extremely obscure, and what can be gathered from it is that they affirm an essence described by three attributes. However, although they call them attributes, in reality they are essences, as evidenced by their permitting that it indwell in Jesus and in Mary in its very self, and otherwise they would not permit it to indwell another and then separate from that other a second time. So although they call them attributes, in reality they affirm multiple essences subsisting in themselves, and that is pure disbelief. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say, "Three"; desist.﴾ As for if we take "three" to mean that they affirm three attributes, this cannot be denied. And how could we not say that, when we say: He is Allah, there is no god but Him, the King, the Holy, the Peace, the Knowing, the Living, the Powerful, the Willing, and we understand from each of these words something other than what we understand from the other word? And there is no meaning to a plurality of attributes except that. So if the affirmation of a plurality of attributes were disbelief, it would necessarily follow that the whole Qur'an is rejected, and that reason is rejected, since we know by necessity that what is understood from His being knowing is other than what is understood from His being powerful or living.

The second issue: His saying "three" (thalathatun) is the predicate of an omitted subject. Then they differed in determining that subject in several ways:

The first: What we have mentioned, that is: "Do not say the hypostases are three."

The second: Al-Zajjaj said: "Do not say our gods are three," because the Qur'an indicates that the Christians say that Allah, the Messiah, and Mary are three gods, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116].

The third: Al-Farra' said: "Do not say they are three," like His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. This is because placing Jesus and Mary alongside Allah, exalted is He, in this expression gives the impression that the two of them are gods. In sum, we do not see any doctrine in the world more feeble and further from reason than the doctrine of the Christians.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Desist; it is better for you﴾. We have already mentioned the grammatical reason for its accusative form at His saying: ﴿So believe; it is better for you﴾ [an-Nisa': 170].

Then He emphasized monotheism by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾. Then He declared Himself free of having a son by His saying: ﴿Exalted is He above having a son﴾. The proofs of Allah's being free of having a son we have mentioned in detail in Surat Al 'Imran and in Surat Maryam. Al-Hasan recited: ﴿in yakuna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza of "an" and a raf' (damma) on the nun of "yakuna," meaning: "Exalted is He; there is not for Him a son." On this reading the statement consists of two clauses.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.
Know that in every place where He, exalted is He, declared Himself free of having a son, He mentioned His being King and Owner of whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. He said about Maryam: ﴿There is none in the heavens and earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. The meaning is: whoever owns all the heavens and the earth and everything in them owns Jesus and Mary, because they were in the heavens and on the earth, and they were not greater than others in essence and attributes. And if He owns what is greater than them, then He owns them all the more; and if they are owned by Him, how can it be conceived, along with this, that they could be His son or wife?

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.﴾ The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, is sufficient in governing created beings and in preserving what has come into existence, so there is no need, along with Him, to affirm another god. This is an allusion to what the theologians mention: that since He, exalted is He, knows all knowable things and is powerful over all possible things, He is sufficient for divinity; and if we supposed another god along with Him, that god would be idle and without benefit, and that is a deficiency, and a deficient being cannot be God.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 4, verse 176:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the *kalalah* (one who dies leaving neither ascendants nor descendants): if a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, she shall have half of what he left; and he inherits from her if she has no child. But if there are two (sisters), they shall have two-thirds of what he left; and if there are siblings, men and women, then for the male is the equivalent of the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray. And Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that He, the Exalted, spoke at the beginning of the surah about the rules of wealth, and concluded its end with the same subject, so that the last part would resemble the first. The middle of the surah includes debate with the deviant sects that oppose the religion. The people of knowledge said: Allah the Exalted revealed two verses concerning the *kalalah*. One of them was in winter, and it is the one at the beginning of this surah; the other was in summer, and it is this verse. For this reason this verse is called the "verse of summer." We have already mentioned that *kalalah* is a term that applies both to the heir and to the deceased. If it applies to the heir, it refers to anyone other than the parent or the child. If it applies to the deceased, it refers to one who dies and is not inherited from by either parent or by any child.

Then He said: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, she shall have half of what he left﴾. The word *imru'un* (a man) is in the nominative by means of an implied pronoun explained by the apparent noun that follows. The position of ﴿leaving no child﴾ is nominative as a qualifier, meaning: if a man dies who has no child.

Know that the apparent meaning of this verse contains three restrictions:

The first: the apparent meaning of the verse implies that the sister takes half when there is no child. But when there is a child, she does not take half. The matter is not like that. Rather, the condition for the sister to take half is that the deceased has no son's child. If he has a daughter, the sister still takes half.

The second: the apparent meaning of the verse implies that if the deceased has no child, the sister takes half. This is not so. Rather, the condition is that the deceased has neither child nor parent, because a sister does not inherit in the presence of a parent, by consensus.

The third: the words ﴿and he has a sister﴾ mean a sister from both father and mother, or from the father alone, because the sister from the mother and the brother from the mother have had their ruling clearly stated by Allah at the beginning of the surah, by consensus.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿and he inherits from her if she has no child﴾. This means that the brother takes the entire inheritance of the sister when the sister has no child. However, this brother must be from both father and mother, or from the father alone. As for the brother from the mother, he does not take the whole inheritance.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But if there are two (sisters), they shall have two-thirds of what he left; and if there are siblings, men and women, then for the male is the equivalent of the share of two females﴾. This verse indicates that the sister mentioned is not only the sister from the mother. It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said in his sermon: "Indeed, the verses that Allah revealed in Surat an-Nisa' concerning the obligatory shares are: The first of them concerns the child and the parent. The second concerns the husband, the wife, and the siblings from the mother. The verse with which Surat an-Nisa' ends was revealed concerning the siblings and sisters from both father and mother. The verse with which Surat al-Anfal ends was revealed concerning the relatives (*uli al-arham*)."

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾. Concerning this there are several views:

The first: the Basran grammarians said: the noun governed here is omitted, and its implied meaning is: Allah makes clear to you the aversion to going astray. He omitted the governed noun, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82).

The second: the Kufan grammarians said: the negative particle is omitted, and the meaning is: Allah makes clear to you so that you do not go astray. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ (Fatir 41), meaning: lest they cease.

The third: al-Jurjani, the author of *al-Nazm*, said: Allah makes clear to you the error, so that you may know that it is error and avoid it.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾. So His clarification is true and His explanation is truthful.

Know that this surah contains a wonderful subtlety. Its beginning includes a demonstration of the perfection of Allah's power, for He said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul﴾ (an-Nisa' 1). This indicates the vastness of power. Its end includes a demonstration of the perfection of knowledge, which is His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾. These two attributes are the ones by which lordship, divinity, majesty, and might are established. By them it is obligatory upon the servant to be obedient to the commands and prohibitions and submissive to all obligations.

The author said: I finished the tafsir of this surah on Tuesday, the twelfth of Jumada al-Akhirah, in the year five hundred and ninety-five.
